summary:
The patient was admitted for low-intensity residential mental health treatment of neuro-developmental and autism spectrum and intellectual disability disorders associated with aggressive and disruptive behaviors and persistent depressive disorder and co-morbid features of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).  The patient had received mental health treatment with various levels of care including extensive treatment in the past that included therapy and medication with family support and involvement.  Despite the best efforts of community providers with supports within the educational system with an individual educational program and specialized education services, the patient worsened with a decline in functioning and social isolation and aggressive behaviors. 

The patient presented with anxiety, depression, hopelessness, and affective instability with limited insight and fair judgment associated with anxiety symptoms that were prominent; the patient exhibited coping and personality traits that reflected poor control of impulses with high risk for repeated violations of boundary issues and problems with maintaining emotional control in the context of the developmental disorder (autism spectrum disorder) and the addiction to the internet.

There were no acute general medical conditions or substance use disorders in this case. The patient was prescribed mood stabilizing and antidepressant medication to address anxiety, depression, and her aggressive outbursts:  Luvox and Trileptal, as well as N-acetylcysteine (NAC) and vitamin supplements.

The health plan's determination is overturned.

The patient required the admission and the continued structure and monitoring of a residential setting through date of discharge.  The residential level services and transitional living were medically necessary in order to effectively address the patient's risk of self-harm and problematic behaviors, continue to learn adequate coping skills to achieve better control of impulses and boundaries with peers and family, and prevent treatment failure, while the treatment team and family worked toward a clinically appropriate disposition with continued mental health services to address the co-occurring mood and developmental disorders and ADHD, including the aggressive and disruptive behaviors associated with autism spectrum disorder and persistent depressive disorder.  The patient had a history of failing to benefit from prior treatment episodes and demonstrated residual symptoms and behaviors that had persisted despite multiple treatment episodes; the patient lacked the insight and control of impulses to remain engaged in treatment in a less restrictive setting during the time frame under review.  These factors support the assertion that the patient could not have been effectively treated at a lower level of care through discharge, at which time the patient was working on the remaining psychological issues with improved insight, impulse control, and coping skills, per the health plan's case notes and submitted documentation.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Detoxification 

Treatment: Inpatient detoxification Admission

The insurer denied the Inpatient Admission. The denial was reversed.
This is a male patient who was admitted to this inpatient substance detoxification treatment in early 2019 for alcohol/substance detoxification treatment. He had withdrawal symptoms including tremors, sweats, nausea, elevated blood pressure of 143/89, irritable mood, anxiety, teary eyes, sleeping problems, and agitation. He had a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment of Alcohol (CIWA) score of 11 and a Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) score of 10. He was consuming alcohol and substances heavily. He had 11 past inpatient substance detoxification treatments and a past inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment. He had depression, as well as hypertension. He was unemployed. He was started on a Librium protocol with a taper for detoxification from alcohol during this admission. He also took Venlafaxine, in addition to Benadryl at that time. He was scheduled for discharge and opted for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment at a later date.
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. In this case, this patient had been drinking alcohol daily and using cocaine and had reports of withdrawal symptoms. According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), he did require this 24-hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated in outpatient detoxification settings. This was evidenced by his continued use of substances despite past multiple inpatient detoxification treatments. It was reported that he had 11 prior detoxification treatments, as well as a prior inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment. He required detoxification medication, including Librium, which he took during this admission for alcohol detoxification treatment. He was at risk for worsened withdrawal symptoms if not in this 24-hour setting, including severe and life-threatening withdrawal symptoms. The risk of life-threatening and complicated withdrawal such as delirium tremens can occur three to four days after alcohol use; therefore, he required this inpatient substance detoxification treatment with the recommendation for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment. Additionally, he required inpatient detoxification treatment prior to inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment. He also lacked coping skills and the ability to identify relapse triggers. He had comorbid psychiatric issues including depression, as well as comorbid medical issues including hypertension. He was at risk for worsened withdrawal and required 24-hour inpatient hospital detoxification.

summary: The patient presented for inpatient detoxification and substance-related treatment to address severe substance use disorder with opioid (Heroin), Cocaine and cannabis class substances of abuse. The patient has a longstanding history of severe substance use disorder beginning at age 12 years, with cannabis and subsequent use of cocaine at age 17 and heroin at age 29. He reported a past history of severe withdrawal symptoms when attempting to curtail his use. At the time of presentation for treatment he was using up to 15 bags of Heroin with intravenous (IV) administration on a daily basis and was using $20-$50 worth of Cocaine three to six times per week with IV administration. His self-referral was prompted by his desire to stop using substances with IV use, and health concerns. He has no prior history of substance use disorder treatment. The patient was admitted to detoxification treatment with comprehensive detoxification protocol with a Methadone taper, and medications as needed (prn) for comfort, including medications to address pain and aches, anxiety, insomnia and diarrhea/abdominal cramps. The patient initially had moderately severe symptoms of withdrawal that persisted throughout all of his inpatient stay but had diminished in intensity by the time of discharge. The patient reported chills, joint pain, body aches, and abdominal cramps and was restless with diaphoresis scoring 16 on the Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS). The health plan's determination of medical necessity is overturned. The patient in this case presented with continuous daily use of Heroin, cannabis and the frequent use of Cocaine in the context of chronic health issues that were drug related. His risk for withdrawal complications in the context of persistent symptoms of withdrawal and intense craving did warrant the continued inpatient level services and monitoring with withdrawal management. The inpatient treatment of this patient's substance use disorders with detoxification and withdrawal management did require the continued structure of an inpatient level setting and 24-hour monitoring, in view of the patient's clinical presentation and course of treatment. Withdrawal symptoms were appropriately managed with tapering dosages of Methadone requiring monitoring and supportive measures, including nicotine replacement therapy and comfort medications, as noted in the clinical summary.

The patient had received a comprehensive medical evaluation prior to admission. She engaged in therapeutic interventions within the treatment milieu including group, individual and educational sessions. The treatment team and case manager were working to develop a safe and clinically appropriate discharge plan and disposition in concert with her family.

By the last day of her brief inpatient stay, the patient was noted to be adherent to medication and participating in the therapeutic interventions. She was calmer with normal speech that was clear and thoughts that were linear and logical, as before. She denied suicidal ideation or any urges to self-harm. Discharge planning had occurred and the patient was discharged with clinically appropriate aftercare and continued medications, as well as the safety plan developed in concert with her daughter with whom she lived and follow up appointments for continued mental health services.

Diagnosis: Anorexia nervosa
  
Treatment: Residential treatment for an eating disorder

The insurer denied the Residential treatment for an eating disorder. The denial was reversed.

This is a female patient who was admitted for inpatient residential treatment for eating disorder symptoms because she had weight loss with a weight of 101.3 lbs. Her ideal body weight (IBW) was 127, so she was 80% of her IBW.  She also had restricting eating behavior, decreased caloric intake, excessive exercising, and medical issues; including bradycardia, hypotension, presyncope, amenorrhea, low body weight, severe mitral regurgitation, poor response to past outpatient treatment, and she had a major recent and rapid weight disruption.  She had a heart rate of 37 initially. She had a diagnosis of anorexia nervosa.  She also had co-morbidities of anxiety and depression, and past alcohol and benzodiazepine use. She took Zyprexa and Trazodone.  She left against medical advice (AMA) and did not attend the recommended Partial Hospital Program (PHP) due to financial concerns, missing her family, and a desire to get back to work. She was discharged.

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient residential treatment for eating disorder as not medically necessary; stating that she did not require 24-hour treatment and could have been treated in a less restrictive level of care.

The chart notes provided enough specific evidence to support the patient required 24-hour residential treatment.  The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Eating Disorders indicates the least restrictive level of care for safe and effective treatment is appropriate.  It also reports that patients with weights of less than 85% of ideal body weight, severe co-morbid psychiatric symptoms, poor to fair motivation, preoccupation with intrusive, repetitive thoughts about eating for 4-6 hours per day, or necessity for supervision of all meals to avoid restricting behaviors, are candidates for residential treatment. The APA guidelines indicate patients that need supervision at all meals are in need of 24-hour residential treatment.  Anorexia nervosa is a chronic and difficult disorder to treat, so she required more than outpatient treatment during this time to treat her symptoms, as eating disorder symptoms worsened in terms of weight loss, and medical consequences. 

As a result, inpatient residential treatment for eating disorder was medically necessary. The health care plan did not act reasonably, with sound medical judgment or in the best interest of the patient.  

The carrier's denial of coverage for residential treatment for an eating disorder is reversed.  The medical necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Mood and anxiety symptoms; depressed mood
 
Treatment: Pre-service request for transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy

The insurer denied coverage for pre-service request for transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy. The denial is reversed. 

This patient is a female who had mood and anxiety symptoms including mood swings, depressed mood, chronic suicidal ideation, depersonalization, posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms, and obsessive compulsive symptoms including ruminating and obsessing. She had diagnoses of Major Depressive Disorder-Severe without psychotic symptoms, Borderline Personality Disorder, PTSD, Obsessive Compulsive Disorder, and Severe Cannabis Use Disorder.  She had past medication trials including Paxil, Duloxetine, Trazodone, Depakote, and Lyrica.  She had been in individual outpatient mental health treatment twice per week and also had group therapy.  She had Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and Mentalization based therapy as well.  The request was for transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy (TMS) to help with obsessive compulsive symptoms. The insurer denied coverage for the pre-service request for transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy.

This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for pre-service request for transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy (TMS) beginning on a specified date as the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved TMS for the treatment of Obsessive Compulsive Disorder in 2018.  Also, according to Clinical Psychiatric News October 2019 page 14, Deep Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Lifts OCD Symptoms by Bruce Jancin, it states that high frequency deep transcranial magnetic stimulation directed at the anterior cingulate cortex and medial prefrontal cortex proved to be safe and effective nonpharmacological treatment for symptoms of obsessive compulsive disorder in an international random, sham controlled, double blind clinical trial that earned the device clearance from the Food and Drug Administration.  This was based on a 2018 multi-center study of 100 patients randomized to treat with the transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy (TMS) device and the results reported that 38% of the patients treated with the TMS device had greater than 30% reduction in obsessive compulsive symptoms as measured with the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (YBOCS) compared to 11% in controls.  

This patient is a complex patient with multiple diagnoses including Major Depressive Disorder-Severe without psychotic symptoms, Borderline Personality Disorder, PTSD, Obsessive Compulsive Disorder, and Severe Cannabis Use Disorder.  The FDA approved Neurostar Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Therapy for the treatment of depression in October 2008 and indicated for the treatment of Major Depressive Disorder in patients who failed or who did not have satisfactory improvement from one past antidepressant medication at or above minimal effective dose and duration in the current episode. Also, the FDA approved Brainsway H1 coil (deep TMS) in 2013 for Major Depressive Disorder in which one failed at least 2 antidepressant medications during the current treatment episode.  It also was FDA approved for obsessive compulsive disorder in 2018.   

As a result, reverse the previous decision and approve the pre-service request for transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy (TMS) beginning on a specified date.  The health care plan did not act reasonably, or with sound medical judgment, or in the best interests of the patient.

The carrier's denial of coverage for the pre-service request for transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy beginning on a specified date is reversed. The medical necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance abuse
 
Treatment: Inpatient Substance Treatment 

The insurer denied the Inpatient Substance Treatment.  The denial was reversed.   

This is a male patient with a history of alcohol and heroin/cocaine use for almost 2 decades. He reports having been in substance detoxification treatment programs in the past. He has a past history of hospitalization for a stab wound and liver disease. He presented to a facility for detoxification and rehabilitation for alcohol, opioid, and cocaine use. While in treatment he received Clonidine and Depakote. The patient left against medical advice (AMA) prior to the completion of his treatment.

He required treatment to monitor and prevent severe, complicated, and life threatening withdrawal as he was considered at risk for that 3-4 days after cessation of use and he could not stop use or get treatment for alcohol and substances without being in a sober, structured, supervised therapeutic inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatment as it was not likely that he could safely be managed in an outpatient setting. He lacked the coping skills and relapse prevention skills also to maintain abstinence outside of this 24 hour inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatment. 

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders report that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. It also reports that patients using large amounts of alcohol or benzodiazepines are at a higher risk of having delirium tremens (DT's) 3-4 days after cessation of use. It also states that patients with co-morbid medical conditions complicating that management of withdrawal are candidates for inpatient hospital treatment.

As a result, the determination is to reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for inpatient hospital treatment. It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably and with sound medical judgment or in the best interests of the patient.  

The carrier's denial of coverage for the inpatient rehabilitation services is reversed. The medical necessity is substantiated.

1)	American Psychiatric Association Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders

summary:

The proposed health service of inpatient residential treatment was medically necessary for this patient.

The admission and continued inpatient residential level of services, structure, and monitoring provided in this case are warranted in view of the severity of the alcohol use disorder and associated symptoms of co-morbid depression and anxiety, as well as the psychosocial stressors and functional impairments in this case scenario.  The patient could not have been safely or effectively managed with lower level services during the time interval under review, especially in view of the safety concerns and severity of psychopathology in this patient.  The inpatient residential level services that included intensive rehabilitation treatment and treatment for the mental disorders with medication and therapy (CBT & ERP) were clinically appropriate and consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice.  The services were provided with evidence-based treatment that are known to benefit patients with severe alcohol use disorder and co-occurring mood and anxiety disorders, as well as providing services to address treatment issues in a patient with severe psychosocial stressors and high risk for relapse or suicidal behavior.  Thus, the patient's severity of alcohol use disorder and associated symptoms of depressive disorder and anxiety disorder and other symptoms related to persistent craving and/or PAWS did warrant and necessitate the admission and the continued inpatient residential level services, as proposed, with the plan for step down to lower level services once the patient had stabilized with work on a relapse prevention plan and improved coping skills and the ability to achieve abstinence with sober supports in working toward discharge with the support of his family. 

Moreover, the patient presented with high risk for relapse in view of an inadequate recovery environment, a relative lack of coping skills, and readiness to change that was being addressed with motivational techniques.  Indeed, the additional time spent with motivational techniques and developing a solid step down were essential to a successful therapeutic outcome in this case, including family focused sessions to improve or enhance sober supports.  Again, the psychosocial stressors in this case were substantial in the context of acute symptoms of depression and anxiety and family conflicts that were significant triggers to use alcohol and cannabis.  These clinical features and treatment dimensions did support the necessity for the inpatient residential level services and the continued structure and monitoring and intensity of services provided at the inpatient residential level of care, as requested, through step down to lower level of care treatment..

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient mental health treatment. The denial was upheld.

This patient is a male who was admitted to inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital due to depression and anxiety. He reported overwhelmed anxiety and depression with suicidal ideation though denied plan or intent. He had used cocaine a few weeks prior to admission. He was smoking cannabis. He had past suicide attempts by Tylenol and opiates overdose. He had a past but not current history of alcohol, opiate, and benzodiazepine use. He had past inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatment. He had past legal issues for drugs sale. He had diagnoses of Major Depressive Disorder, PTSD, cocaine abuse, cannabis use, and anxiety disorder. He took Remeron, Risperidone, and Paxil and was discharged with referral to outpatient mental health treatment.

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital as not medically necessary treatment. They stated that he did not have active suicidal or homicidal intent or plan, had no psychosis, and was not considered an imminent danger to self or others.

This reviewer agrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital as the chart notes did not provide enough specific evidence to support that he could only be treated safely and effectively in a 24 hour acute psychiatric hospital then or that he could not be treated in a less restrictive level of care then. 

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Suicidal Behaviors reports that patients with suicidal intent or plan are in need of inpatient treatment, but this patient had reports of suicidal ideation without intent or plan. He had reports of depression and anxiety and substance use including recent cocaine use which he reports may have contributed to worsened symptoms but there was no specific evidence reported to support that he was considered an imminent danger to self or others or that he had inability to adequately care for his basic needs. He had medication changes which resulted in improvement as he had Remeron added to Paxil and Risperidone. It was reported that he was not fully compliant with his psychrotrophic medications. There were no reports of suicidal intent or plan throughout his hospital stay.

Inpatient mental health treatment at this hospital was not medically necessary. It appeared that the health care plan acted reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interests of the patient then.

summary:
Diagnosis: Alcohol and substance Use

Treatment: inpatient substance detoxification service

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient detoxification service. The denial was reversed.

This patient is a male, who was admitted to this inpatient substance detoxification treatment for alcohol and heroin detoxification treatment.  He had withdrawal symptoms including stomach cramps, flushing and chills, dilated pupils, high blood pressure and heart rate of 160,100, and 101, bone and joint discomfort, nasal stuffiness, and moist eyes. He reportedly was drinking 2 pints of vodka per day with a 40 year history and inhaling 8-10 bags of heroin per day. He reportedly had a history of suicidal ideation and mood symptoms.  He had pending legal issues.  He reportedly had past substance detoxification treatment.  He reportedly had 2 detoxification medications including; Methadone and Valium.  He was referred to inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment and discharged.

The insurer denied coverage for continued inpatient substance detoxification treatment, as not medically necessary treatment. They stated that he had no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium, and that after a specified date he had Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) and Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment of Alcohol (CIWA) scores of 1. 

This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for continued inpatient substance detoxification treatment. He was discharged. The chart notes did provide enough specific evidence to support that he needed this level of care. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders report that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. In this case, the patient had use of multiple substances including heroin and alcohol and was at risk for death from overdose.  

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) he did require 24 hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive setting as he continued to use substances despite multiple past inpatient substance detoxification treatments, needed two detoxification medications including Methadone and Valium to modify withdrawal from alcohol and heroin, had long term multiple substances of use including using heroin and alcohol , continued to use despite legal consequences, and he needed 24 hour treatment then as he was at risk for worsened withdrawal symptoms if not in this 24 hour setting then, and he likely would have relapsed again as evidenced by relapsing after past treatments.  He also had comorbid psychiatric issues including depression and suicidal ideation.  He was at risk for severe, life threatening, and complicated withdrawal including delirium tremens which could occur four days after stopping use. He had a 5 day Methadone and Valium taper which reportedly was completed and was then referred to inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment. It also was necessary to get detoxification treatment prior to inpatient substance residential treatment and he could not successfully be detoxified in an outpatient setting.  

As a result, the determination is to reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for continued inpatient substance detoxification. It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably, with sound medical judgment or in the best interests of the patient.

The carrier's denial of coverage for the inpatient detoxification service is reversed. The medical necessity is substantiated.

The patient's history of substance abuse (frequency and quantity), and the severe psychosocial stressors and functional impairments reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder and the need for a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management.  The patient was at high risk for treatment failure if the detoxification and withdrawal management were to be attempted at a lower level of care, and he needed the support and motivational enhancement therapy to facilitate his step down for residential rehabilitation treatment.  The insurer denied coverage for inpatient substance detoxification. The denial was reversed.

This patient is a male who was admitted to this inpatient substance detoxification treatment due to alcohol and substance detoxification treatment. He had withdrawal symptoms including tremors, sweats, agitation, anxiety, irritable mood, nausea, and had a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) of 8 and Clinical Opioid Withdrawal Score (COWS) as high as 8 during his treatment stay. He was drinking alcohol, using heroin, crack, and methamphetamine. He reportedly had past inpatient substance detoxification treatment more than a decade ago and had past inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment. He was put on a 5 day Ativan protocol and was discharged to a substance inpatient rehabilitation treatment for further treatment.

The insurer denied coverage for continued inpatient substance detoxification treatment as not medically necessary. They stated that he had no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium. They stated that he did not require 24 hour inpatient substance detoxification treatment as of then, and they recommended a less restrictive level of care then.

This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for continued inpatient substance detoxification treatment. He was discharged to an inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment for further treatment. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. In this case this patient had been using multiple serious substances of use including heroin, crack, and methamphetamine and drinking alcohol.

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) he did require continued 24 hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated in outpatient detoxification settings as he continued to use alcohol and multiple substances despite reports that he had a past inpatient substance detoxification treatment and inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment. He also required and needed detoxification medication to modify withdrawal and prevent severe, complicated, or life threatening withdrawal. The risk of life complicated withdrawal such as delirium tremens can occur 4 days after alcohol use so he required the entire time.

Based on the above, the medical necessity for the Inpatient substance detoxification is substantiated. The insurer's denial is reversed.

summary:
This case involves an adult admitted for acute inpatient psychiatric treatment. The patient was brought to the emergency department for urgent psychiatric care after becoming increasingly anxious in the context of anorexia nervosa with restricted intake. The patient had a history of mood disorder best characterized as severe major depressive disorder and co-morbid eating disorder with anorexia nervosa, restricting type. The patient presented with a decline in functioning and inability to care for self with somatic symptoms including pallor, dizziness and dehydration. Patient had been hospitalized recently with discharge and non-compliance with  outpatient treatment that included medication management and therapy, as patient failed to follow-up with aftercare with worsening symptoms of the psychiatric disorders including panic attacks and poor nutritional intake.
The mental status examination revealed depressed mood with anhedonia and low self-worth. Patient reported morbid thoughts and inability to function. There was no evidence for mania. Sleep, appetite, energy levels and volition were disturbed. Affect was blunted and anxious with pressured speech and poor eye contact. Patient displayed thought blocking with slowed mentation and had suicidal ideation without a plan.
The patient was admitted to acute inpatient level services with close observation, structured milieu therapy, and pharmacotherapy with Effexor, Klonopin and as needed (prn) medications for insomnia supplemented with vitamins and nutritional supports. Meals and intake were monitored with ensure supplements. Patient tended to isolate and was noted to be anergic and withdrawn. Patient began to engage in therapy with improved mood and affect, and more expressive emotion. Intake improved to 75 to 100% of  meals. The patient's eating disorder and co-morbid psychiatric conditions and severity of symptoms warranted the admission for inpatient level services, as proposed. The patient had failed to respond to treatment at a lower level of care despite receiving intensive treatment and services in the context of a recrudescence of symptoms and deterioration in functioning. Moreover, safety concerns, the need for the structure of an inpatient setting, and the intensity of services provided by the acute inpatient program including assistance with meals and basic activities of daily living with active treatment could not have been and could not be effectively provided at a lower level of care. The patient had failed to respond or sustain a response to clinically appropriate, intensive treatment in the community with medication management and therapy; thus, the treatment plan with respect to acute inpatient level care was necessary to address the disordered eating with restricted intake and to manage the anxiety and mood disturbance. The health plan's determination of medical necessity is overturned in whole.
The requested services are medically necessary in this case and is consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published practice guidelines, and the scientific literature, referenced below.

summary:
Diagnosis: Schizophrenia, unspecified type
Treatment: Continued Acute Inpatient Mental Health Treatment for Adults 

The Continued Acute Inpatient Mental Health Treatment for Adults is medically necessary for this patient, in part. 

Specifically, the Continued Acute Inpatient Mental Health Treatment is medically necessary for an additional 16 days. Any dates of service beyond that point would require additional review and is not considered medically necessary at this time.

The patient's continued hospital stay for treatment of an exacerbation of a psychotic disorder (schizophrenia) does require the continued inpatient level services, structure, and monitoring. The patient's severity of symptoms, and inability to effectively participate in treatment at a lower level of care, persistent functional impairment, and treatment issues related to persistent symptoms of acute psychosis were clinical factors and treatment dimensions that necessitated continued acute inpatient hospital care, structure, and monitoring, as proposed. The medication treatment and safety monitoring, the support of functioning and the continued application of multimodal treatments, as well as assurance of medication adherence, were factors that did warrant the continued inpatient level treatment in view of the persistent symptoms of bizarre thought content and paranoid thinking; the patient could not have been effectively managed at a lower level of care. 

The patient's admission and continued treatment is reasonable and in the best interest of the patient. Any dates of service beyond that date require additional review. 

The patient had severe symptoms of psychosis complicated by a decline in functioning and safety issues together with a high risk for medication non-adherence due to persistent symptoms of psychosis. He had deteriorated to the point that he was a safety risk with disorganized and perceptual disturbance/paranoid thinking, and, poor insight and impaired judgment that persisted throughout his stay. Additionally, outpatient treatment had failed to prevent a relapse. Again, the patient could not have been safely or effectively managed at a lower level of care or in a less restrictive environment. The continued stay was necessary to develop a safe and clinically appropriate discharge plan and disposition that would effectively support his continued treatment.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance abuse
 
Treatment: Inpatient substance residential treatment, medication, monitoring

The insurer denied continued inpatient substance residential treatment. The denial was reversed.

This is a male who was admitted to inpatient substance residential treatment after a 5 day hospital stay for altered mental status, acute hypokalemia, acute renal failure, and acute vomiting. He reportedly was using 5-10 bars of Xanax per day, drinking more than 6 drinks 1-3 times per week, smoking 2 grams of cannabis per day, and using MDMA 
0.3 grams 1-2 times per month. He was in treatment in a dual diagnosis partial hospital program 2 weeks prior to this admission. He had a past psychiatric hospitalization and had diagnoses of Major Depressive Disorder and Anxiety Disorder as well as Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). His longest abstinence was 1 year. 

The APA Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders indicates inpatient treatment is primarily for individuals whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. According to the LOCADTR, this patient met criteria for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment as he continued to use multiple substances despite past recent substance rehabilitation treatments. He was unable to stop substance use without being in a sober and supervised therapeutic inpatient setting. Without this structured and supervised treatment he likely would have relapsed quickly.  

The National Institute on Drug Abuse: Principles of Addiction Treatment: A Research Based Guide reports the best treatment outcomes occur with longer durations of treatment. This patient required 24-hour residential treatment as he was at high risk to continue use without this treatment setting, and 2 weeks in this setting was not enough time for him to develop the necessary skills for abstinence. 

Based on the above, the medical necessity for Residential Substance Use Treatment is substantiated. The insurer's denial is reversed.

This is a young male patient who presented to the emergency department with hallucinations.  It was reported that he was sent from the shelter after being seen talking to himself.  He has a past medical history of Schizophrenia.  He has had a previous incarceration.  His reported symptoms include auditory hallucinations, responding to internal stimuli, religious preoccupation, talking to himself, laughing inappropriately, and pacing in hallways aimlessly.  It was noted that the patient was non-compliant with his medication administration, which resulted in changing his drug treatment to intramuscular injection.  The patient was discharged when stabilized. 


The APA Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Schizophrenia reports that patients with hallucinations, delusional thinking, disorganized thinking or behavior, suicidal or homicidal plan or intent, agitation, or aggressive behavior, or inability to adequately care for basic needs are candidates for hospitalization.

In this case this patient still had psychotic symptoms during the denial period, including responding to internal stimuli, talking to self, religious preoccupation, laughing inappropriately out loud, and with his history of noncompliance and lack of support, he was at risk for worsened symptoms if discharged prematurely while still having psychotic symptoms.  He had command auditory hallucinations on admission and past incarceration, so he was at risk if not in this 24-hour hospital setting.  He had multiple medication changes and eventually took IM Invega sustenna due to his past noncompliance with medications. 

Based on the above, the medical necessity for the continued inpatient psychiatric is substantiated.  The insurer's denial is reversed.

summary: The patient is an adult  with schizoaffective disorder, depressed type and co-occurring substance use disorder (cocaine, cannabis and alcohol). Patient was admitted to acute inpatient level services with severe symptoms of depression, suicidal ideation, psychosis with delusions and morbid preoccupations, command auditory hallucinations telling patient to harm self or others, and motor agitation. The patient's admission had been precipitated by worsening depression with suicidal ideation and psychosis in the context of severe substance use disorder and non-compliance with his mental health treatment. Patient was using up to three pints of vodka in a day together with 10-15 blunts of marijuana mixed with cocaine;  also tobacco dependent at ¼ pack per day. Patient had stopped  medication, risperidone, at an unknown dose. The patient endorsed symptoms of depression with the command auditory hallucinations, reports of visual hallucinations (seeing shadowy figures) and paranoid thinking that patient was being followed and that thoughts were being controlled; Patient was erratic in behavior and superficially cooperative at the time of presentation in the context of drug and alcohol use with the large quantities of cannabis and alcohol. The patient had been non-adherent with medications and non-compliant with outpatient treatment in the context of active substance abuse with alcohol, cocaine and cannabis, as well as use of tobacco. The patient is homeless living on the street and in shelters, unemployed, and has limited or no social supports. The patient was admitted to acute inpatient level care on after medical screening in the emergency department. The patient's treatment plan included safety-monitoring, access to group and milieu therapies, and resumption of medications with an initial dose of risperidone at one milligrams (mg) twice daily, titrated as clinically appropriate. He received vitamin replacement therapy and as needed (prn) medications to address withdrawal from alcohol or nicotine. The patient was initially depressed, paranoid, and socially withdrawn. However after several days, was increasingly cooperative with staff and became medication adherent;  tended to isolate with social withdrawal and minimal participation in the therapeutic activities during the first week of his inpatient stay. The patient's delusions/morbid preoccupations and hallucinations persisted, and patient remained dysphoric with motor agitation and labile affect addressed with safety monitoring and prn medications while risperidone was titrated to three mg twice daily together with Cogentin. a discharge plan was completed including plans for after care and return to the community with housing/shelter. At the time of discharge the patient was better focused, calmer, and displaying better judgment with improved mood and brighter affect. Inpatient Mental Health Treatment is medically necessary for this patient. The admission and the continued inpatient stay for the dates of service  could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care. The patient's symptoms of psychosis and mood disorder together with continued risk of impulsive behavior and suicidal risk prompted the necessity for the admission and the continued acute inpatient level structure and monitoring provided through discharge. The case is complicated by active substance use disorders; and non-compliance with treatment and medication adherence problems in the context of severe psychosocial stressors. . Medically necessary treatment included safety monitoring and maintaining abstinence from substances of abuse while titrating medications and initiating a long-acting injectable antipsychotic medication that was critical to the patient's treatment in the context of past non-compliance with medication treatment with oral medications. This male was admitted to inpatient substance detoxification treatment for substance detoxification treatment.  He had multiple withdrawal symptoms and had a Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) score of 10.  He was using tens of bags of intravenous (IV) heroin daily with a four year history of use, multiple bags of IV cocaine with a four year history of use, and was using nonprescription Methadone 1-3 times over the past month.  He had four past inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatments. He had a disease of the liver, as well as depression and anxiety.  He had a five day Methadone protocol and was discharged with a recommendation for inpatient substance rehabilitation.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment.  In this case, this patient had use of multiple substances and was at risk for overdose and severe withdrawal symptoms.  According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), he required 24-hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive setting. This was evidenced by his continued use of multiple serious substances in large amounts despite multiple past inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatments. He lacked coping skills to maintain abstinence and had difficulty identifying triggers for use.  He required and received detoxification medication to modify withdrawal from heroin.  If he were prematurely discharged from this detoxification, he likely would have relapsed and also been at risk for worsened withdrawal symptoms. 

The carrier's denial of coverage for the continued inpatient substance abuse services is reversed.  The medical necessity is substantiated.

Treatment: Inpatient admission

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient admission. The denial was reversed.

He reportedly was drinking 2 bottles of wine per day, using 10 tabs of benzodiazepine, had past heroin use, cocaine and cannabis use. He last used the morning of admission. He had a positive toxicology for cannabis. He had multiple past inpatient detoxification treatments including a recent one 1 month prior to admission. He had past jail time and had past Methadone treatment. H had a reported history of homelessness. He had a medical history significant for hepatitis, hypertension, pancreatitis, and hip pins. He had anxiety and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). He was put on a Lorazepam detoxification. He was discharged.

The insurer denied coverage for continued inpatient detoxification treatment in this hospital.

This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for continued inpatient detoxification treatment in this hospital. The chart notes provided enough specific evidence to support that he required 24 hour hospital treatment for detoxification. The APA Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. 

In this case this patient had been drinking large amounts of alcohol daily and had multiple substances of use as well including benzodiazepine use, a history of heroin use, cocaine and cannabis use. He was at high risk for overdose and also for severe, complicated, and life threatening withdrawal symptoms. He had a reported history of multiple medical issues including hepatitis, hypertension, pancreatitis, and hip pins. He reportedly had an elevated CIWA and had active alcohol withdrawal symptoms. 

According to the LOCADTR he did require 24 hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated in outpatient detoxification settings as he continued to use large amounts of alcohol and substances daily despite medical issues, legal issues, and past inpatient substance detoxification treatments. Also, he required and needed detoxification medication to modify withdrawal and needed 24 hour treatment then as he was at risk for worsened withdrawal symptoms if not in this 24 hour setting then including severe and life threatening withdrawal symptoms. It was reported that he had detoxification medication (Lorazepam) to modify withdrawal and prevent more severe, complicated, or life threatening withdrawal symptoms. It was unlikely that he would remain abstinent while still having withdrawal symptoms so he required the time in this treatment
setting to stop withdrawals and decrease the chance that he would relapse again when not in this 24 hour setting and also to prevent possible life threatening withdrawal symptoms.

As a result, the determination is to reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for continued inpatient substance detoxification. It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably or in the best interests of the patient.

Diagnosis:  Substance abuse/addiction
Treatment:  Substance Abuse:Inpatient

The patient with a history of opiate and cocaine use disorder was admitted to an inpatient detox unit.  Urine was positive for opiates, cocaine, and methadone.  Vital signs were all in normal range.  Patient endorsed using heroin and cocaine daily; 7-8 bags/day and $80/day, respectively.  Patient last used, about 1/2 daily amount.  Patient did not endorse using methadone as a drug of abuse and staff did not document any discussion of why urine was positive for methadone.  To the triaging nurse, the patient complained of nausea, sweats, abdominal pain, teary eyes, joint pain and rhinorrhea.  Later to the physician the patient complained additionally of trouble sleeping, anxiety, yawning, tremors, irritability, and headache.  On physical exam the patient was tremulous, anxious and had moist eyes, flushed face and dilated pupils.  The initial Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) score was 14.  The facility completed an admission Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR).  In it staff indicated the patient lacked support for early recovery.  The template instructions indicate that if this box is checked it should result in medically supervised withdrawal, and if the patient does have supports, it should result in outpatient referral.  Staff also indicated the patient is at risk for moderate withdrawal.  The patient reported a history of 9 previous detox stays and one previous rehab stay.  Patient denied any psychiatric history, including no previous diagnosis, treatment, suicidality or hallucinations.  The patient has sickle cell trait/anemia but no other chronic conditions and is not on any home medications.
Patient reported living stably with a family member and being satisfied with her current housing.  Patient was admitted to the detox unit and placed on a five day methadone taper.  The patient was educated on medication assisted treatment (MAT) by the Credentialed Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Counselor (CASAC) but declined to learn more.  There are no repeated COWS assessments.  Patient had agreed to a plan for rehab but then changed her mind and elected to go home.  Patient was given a Narcan kit at discharge.  The health plan's determination of medical necessity is upheld in whole.  The patient's presentation is consistent with clinically mild opiate withdrawal.  Nothing on  presentation stands out as uniquely related to a crash from cocaine, but some of the general complaints could be related to that as well.  Opiate and cocaine withdrawal are not medically dangerous on their own and are usually appropriate for outpatient management.  Inpatient detox for opiates or cocaine is recommended only in special circumstances such as having epilepsy, an unstable heart condition, an unstable psychiatric condition, etc.  The patient had no unstable medical conditions, no psychiatric history, and was stably housed with family and was receiving public assistance.  There is no documentation in this chart that substantiates the patient has a lack of supports.  This reviewer completed a LOCADTR using the information documented in the medical record, and it resulted in a recommendation for outpatient detox with medication assistance.  This result is also consistent with medical opinion that inpatient detox was not medically necessary.

The patient is a female with diagnoses of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) and Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD). Case notes document that the patient has suffered from AUD for an extended period of time, about 20 years. She has required 2 or 3 detoxifications and a 30 day rehabilitation program. She has been treated by an outpatient provider with trazodone and Wellbutrin. Prior to the admission under review, the patient was drinking unknown but excessive amounts of alcohol for at least a weekend prior to admission, resulting in her missing a week of work. Additionally, she experienced insomnia and loss of appetite. She attributes her drinking to the stress of ongoing arguments between her husband and her son, the husband's stepson. She fell and hit her head when she was drunk. After she was medically stabilized and became sober, she was admitted to IMHT. On admission, she was documented to complain of low mood, anorexia, insomnia, emotional distress at the ongoing arguments at home. She denied suicidal or homicidal ideation, hallucinations or delusions. After becoming sober, she expressed an interest in an evaluation by a psychiatrist. She did not suffer any brain injury from her fall. She was treated at the IMHT level with Wellbutrin, trazodone, lorazepam, vitamins, and assessed according to the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) protocol. She appeared calm and cooperative and cognitively intact and was discharged to outpatient followup.

The health plan's determination is upheld. The IMHT was not medically necessary for this patient. Her AUD and possible MDD could have been treated safely and effectively in an Intensive Outpatient Substance Abuse Treatment (IOSAT) program. She was not at risk of harm to self or others. She showed no signs of DT's. She had no psychosis. She had no head injury of significance. Her cognition was intact. The IOSAT program could manage both her alcohol use disorder and her depressive symptoms, as well as setting up a family therapy program for one of the triggering or more likely continuing factors in the patient's chronic disorder, the arguments at home.

The patient received motivational techniques and ongoing counseling including case management to work toward a safe and clinically appropriate discharge plan and disposition back to his community MMTP. He did continue with detoxification treatment and was maintained on fall and seizure precautions. The patient was discharged with recommendations for clinically appropriate aftercare with plans for continued use of methadone, as well as recommendations for continued mental health treatment and involvement in 12-step recovery meetings with Alcoholic and Narcotics Anonymous (AA and NA). He was discharged in satisfactory condition.
The subject under review is the medical necessity of the inpatient admission and continued stay for detoxification treatment.

The health plan's determination is overturned.

The continued inpatient services and detoxification treatment and withdrawal management for severe substance use disorder and other services noted in the clinical summary could not have been safely and effectively provided at a lower level of care, as noted in the answer to question 1 above. This patient's substance use disorders and clinical features and treatment dimensions did warrant the admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level setting and 24-hour monitoring in view of the severity of the substance use disorders with multiple substances of abuse, and the continued use of Xanax and cannabis in the context of methadone maintenance treatment. Withdrawal symptoms were managed with tapering dosages of phenobarbital and continued use of methadone requiring monitoring and as needed (prn) medications, as well as the availability of comfort medications and nicotine replacement therapy to prevent the onset of encephalopathy. Seizure and fall precautions were provided. Counseling and educational sessions with motivational techniques together with case management services were appropriately provided to motivate the patient's transition back to rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment in the community. Thus, the patient did require a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management during the time frame under review with associated substance use disorder treatments, as it was reasonable that the patient would have been unable to abstain from the substances of abuse if detoxification and treatment were to be attempted at a lower level of care.

Diagnosis:  Schizophrenia
Treatment:  Mental Health Inpatient

The case involves an adult admitted to acute inpatient psychiatric services for an exacerbation of a chronic psychotic disorder best characterized as schizophrenia, unspecified type.  The patient had shown increasing symptoms of psychosis following discontinuation of his medication, olanzapine and Depakote.  Patient deteriorated over a three week time frame with onset of aggressive behavior with threats toward family and destruction of home property.  Patient had a history of increasing levels of aggression over a five year period and had been diagnosed with schizophrenia at age 18 when there was a change in his behavior.  His presentation with emergency medical services included bizarre and erratic behavior, disorganized and delusional thoughts with paranoid thinking together with motor agitation, and increasing responses to internal stimuli.  Patient was brought to the emergency department, and was subsequently admitted after medical clearance that included physical examination, laboratory assessment and drug screen.  The assessment included no abnormal or remarkable laboratory findings including a negative drug screen consistent with history.  Mental Status Examination on admission:  The patient was psychotic and cognitively impaired with thought blocking, laconic speech, and response to internal stimuli.  Patient was uncooperative and guarded with poor eye contact.  Patient displayed motor agitation with irritable mood. Insight was limited and judgment impaired.  Patient demonstrated poor attention and concentration due to the internal stimuli and disorganized thought patterns with tangential thought production that was illogical and incoherent with frequent bouts of talking to self or responding to internal stimuli.  The patient's treatment plan included safety monitoring and medication targeting mood disturbance and psychosis, as well as the opportunity for therapy and psycho-education provided in the therapeutic milieu.  The patient was uncooperative initially, but gradually became more cooperative with treatment.  The Health plan's determination of medical necessity is overturned in whole.  The patient had severe symptoms with an acute exacerbation of schizophrenia associated with disorganized thought patterns and responses to internal stimuli that were associated with erratic and problematic behavior.  The case was complicated by medication changes with subsequent onset of aggressive behavior and decline in functioning.  The patient had deteriorated to the point that he was a safety risk, and, outpatient treatment had failed to prevent a relapse precipitated by medication changes.  During the time interval under review, the patient remained at risk for aggressive behavior and required continued inpatient structure and monitoring while receiving active treatment.  The patient could not have been safely or effectively managed during the time interval under review at a lower level of care or in a less restrictive treatment setting.  The patient's severity of symptoms and risk for continued aggressive behavior and safety issues related to persistent symptoms of psychosis together with the co-morbid autism spectrum disorder with intellectual deficiency, were clinical factors and treatment dimensions that warranted the continued acute inpatient hospital care, structure, and monitoring as proposed through discharge.  The medication adjustments and safety monitoring together with attention to the compliance issues in this case were medically necessary in this case scenario; the intensity of services and safety issues related to erratic/aggressive behavior and affective instability could not have been effectively addressed or managed at a lower level of care during the time interval under review.

This is a patient who was admitted following medical screening in the emergency department, to acute inpatient level services for monitoring and detoxification and withdrawal management of moderately severe alcohol and stimulant (crack-cocaine) and sedative-hypnotic-anxiolytic (benzodiazepine) use disorders. The patient was using an anxiolytic (Xanax) on an intermittent and frequent basis. The patient was using large amounts of alcohol with up to one pint of liquor per day plus beer, and crack cocaine. The patient had experienced severe alcohol/anxiolytic withdrawal in the past and had moderately severe withdrawal at the time of admission with sweats, tremors, nausea, headache, and auditory hallucinations, as well as anxiety, irritability and restlessness. She had experienced severe withdrawal symptoms in the past requiring detoxification including detoxification treatment in the past year with relapse. She also reported frequent blackouts, but no history of alcohol or drug withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens.
The patient has a co-occurring psychiatric disorder that included unspecified depressive disorder treated with Wellbutrin and trazodone. She denied psychiatric hospitalization, or suicidal or self-harming behaviors.
General medical issues included hypertension, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), asthma, osteoporosis and genital herpes treated with amlodipine, pravastatin, famotidine, Zovirax and Singulair with albuterol inhaler. 
The patient was admitted to acute inpatient level of care and placed on a detoxification regimen with a Librium together with vitamin replacement therapy and medical monitoring. Following her third day of treatment, the patient began to participate actively in counseling and educational sessions, as her withdrawal symptoms diminished and she was feeling better. Her mental status examination included persistent symptoms of depression with associated symptoms of anxiety, fatigue and insomnia. She had no severe symptoms such as mania, psychosis, perceptual disturbance or severe cognitive impairment. She was treated with Wellbutrin and trazodone, as noted and as needed (PRN) medications to address pain, anxiety, agitation insomnia. Vitamins were continued, as well as the comfort medications and monitoring, and assistance with daily activities.
The patient was initially ambivalent about treatment and required motivational techniques and ongoing counseling including case management to work toward a safe and clinically appropriate discharge plan and disposition. She did continue with detoxification treatment was maintained on fall and seizure precautions. The health plan's determination is overturned. The adult inpatient treatment of this patient's substance use disorders did warrant the admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level setting and 24-hour monitoring in view of the severity of the substance use disorders with multiple substances of abuse, and the associated psychosocial stressors and impairment of functioning. Withdraw symptoms were managed with tapering dosages of benzodiazepine requiring monitoring and as needed medications, as well as the availability of comfort medications and vitamin replacement therapy to prevent the onset of encephalopathy. Seizure and fall precautions were provided. Counseling and educational sessions with motivational techniques together with case management services were appropriately provided to motivate the patient's transition to rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment. General medical and co-occurring psychiatric disorders were treatment with continued use of the patient's medications. Thus, the patient did require a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management during the time frame under review with associated substance use disorder treatments, as it was reasonable that the patient would have been unable to abstain from the substances of abuse if detoxification and treatment were to be attempted at a lower level of care.
Medical necessity for the admission and the continued inpatient services, is met in this case, and is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice, published practice guidelines, and American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, referenced below. This answer is also consistent with NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) LOCADTR 3.0 Criteria and Guidelines.

summary:
This is a patient referred by his community providers to a residential mental health treatment facility with admission in order to address severe symptoms of major depressive disorder and co-occurring substance use disorder with cannabis and alcohol. The admission to residential care was prompted by worsening symptoms of depression together with school avoidance/refusal and behavioral problems in the context of severe cannabis use disorder and trauma related symptoms. The patient is also diagnosed with severe major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder including panic attacks and social anxiety, and cannabis use disorder.
The patient has had ongoing issues with persistent symptoms of depression and anxiety that had been treated since 2014 precipitated by an inappropriate sexual encounter when he was coerced into having sex with a male peer. He continued to engage in sexual contact that was viewed as problematic by the patient and his family due to religious and other cultural norms. Moreover, the patient developed trauma related symptoms and began coping with cannabis and alcohol use with avoidance of social contacts and school refusal. Despite ongoing treatment efforts, the patient had worsening symptoms of depression and anxiety with self-destructive and self-defeating behaviors that included social withdrawal, decline in academic functioning and escalating use of cannabis. The patient had also experienced family stress related to his substance use and increasing symptoms of depression resulting in a profound sense of hopelessness and low self-worth and other complications of the co-morbid psychiatric conditions despite receiving therapy and medication to address the mood and anxiety disturbances.
The patient was referred for and admitted to the residential program that offered comprehensive services including programming to include intensive family therapy and other therapeutic interventions to address the patient's co-occurring disorders.
Initial evaluation upon referral for residential care had revealed a mental status examination that was free of severe psychiatric symptoms such as psychosis, mood cycling or mania, formal thought disorder, severe cognitive impairment or homicidal ideation. The patient was described as having limited insight, impaired judgment and poor impulse control. Mood was dysphoric, and affect was anxious with generalized symptoms of anxiety and social anxiety with apprehension, tension, sleep disturbance, irritability, and excessive worry as well as trauma-related symptoms that included flashbacks, avoidance, numbing behavior, and nightmares. He was guarded and apathetic, indifferent, and demoralized with past and passive suicidal thoughts and deficient coping skills. He also exhibited attention and concentration problems and poor eye contact with slow speech and thought blocking.
The patient underwent comprehensive psychiatric evaluation with ongoing safety monitoring and treatment planning that included therapeutic interventions to improve coping skills including cognitive behavioral techniques (dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) to address distress tolerance, mindfulness, emotional regulation and interpersonal relationships and functioning. The treatment plan included the goals of improved coping; breaking the cycle of self-destructive behaviors with regard to the substance use; and, the development of healthy relationships. Individual, group and family therapies were provided, and he had access to recovery groups including peer-supported and therapist led recovery groups. He had safety monitoring and structure to support abstinence from substances of abuse. He was maintained on his medication with adjustments as clinically appropriate and Focalin was added to a regimen of Abilify, Prozac and Lamictal.
The health plan's determination is overturned.

The patient's admission and continued residential level treatment is reasonable and in the best interest of the patient; he had and continues to display clinical features and symptoms that necessitated/necessitate the admission and the continued residential level services as he struggles to engage in treatment and has affective instability that does require residential level structure and monitoring with active treatment. He has a history of treatment failure with lower level services and had recently displayed significant problematic behaviors with maladaptive coping, emotional regulation problems, distress problems, interpersonal functioning problems and day-to-day functioning problems that included academic failure due to school refusal in the context of severe mood, anxiety and substance use disorders complicated by attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and trauma related symptoms. He continues to represent a safety risk and relapse risk, and could not have been effectively managed in a less restrictive treatment environment.
Moreover, the monitoring, structure and intensity of residential services were medically necessary in keeping with prevailing standards of medical practice, American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria the application of NY State OASAS LOCADTR 3.0 Criteria and Guidelines.

summary:
Central Nervous System/Neuromuscular Disorder - Other

Mental Health: Inpatient

The patient is a male who was stated to be "shouting and screaming" in the context of a diagnosis of Tourette syndrome. He received inpatient level of care for five days. The patient was reported to be "not doing well-not sleeping, impulsive, easily agitated." The record indicates that for the prior 8 months, the patient had been nonadherent to psychiatric medications including risperidone 1 mg by mouth daily at bedtime and citalopram 20 mg every morning. The patient stated that he came to the hospital to get back on medication and to get into "an apartment program." 

The initial mental status exam indicated that there was no suicidal or homicidal ideation, intent, or plan. The patient was not documented to have any unstable medical problems or any issues related to withdrawal from substances. A physical exam showed that his teeth were intact and his mouth was without lesions. This is despite there being a statement that the patient needed to be urgently seen by a dentist for fitting of a mouth guard related to Tourette syndrome. The patient was described as receiving individual, group, and milieu therapy. He was described as participating in groups and taking medications.

The health plan denied the inpatient stay as not medically necessary. 

The health plan's determination is upheld. Essentials for a continued hospitalization include the diagnosis of a psychiatric disorder as defined by both the criteria of the American Psychiatric Association's Diagnostic and Statistical Manual (DSM)-55. Among many others, these guidelines include as requirements:
1) The psychiatric disorder must be of such severity as to cause significant impairment of daily functioning in at least two important areas of the person's life such as work performance, social interactions, or family relationships.
2) The treatment proposed must be relevant to the problems diagnosed and adjudged likely to benefit the patient.
3) Other available less restrictive treatment resources must have been considered and determined to be not available or not appropriate to the patient's needs or have been attempted and proven unsuccessful. Examples of less restrictive treatment resources would include, but are not limited to, residential treatment, day treatment, or intensive outpatient care.

The clinical documentation that has been provided does not establish medical necessity for inpatient hospitalization. The patient was described as shouting and screaming and having tics related to his Tourette's syndrome. Clinical documentation does not establish that this posed a threat to his health or safety. The patient could have been safely and effectively treated at a lower level of care.

summary:
Diagnosis: Anxiety Disorder; Bipolar Disorder

Treatment: Inpatient psychiatric hospital admission

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient psychiatric hospital admission. The denial reversed.

This patient is a man admitted for inpatient psychiatric treatment.  He was initially diagnosed with Anxiety Disorder.  He was discharged with the diagnosis of Bipolar Disorder. The insurer has denied coverage for the entire inpatient hospitalization.

The medical record indicated the patient had a four month history of paranoia and excessive fears about being killed by falling air conditioners.  He was noted to have bizarre and tangential thinking and periods of incoherence.  He reported auditory hallucinations.  He had been unable to stay at his home due to overwhelming paranoia and fear.  He reported severe anxiety, insomnia, and ongoing hallucinations.  He was being treated as an outpatient with Seroquel and IM aripiprazole.  There was a history of barbiturate and alcohol abuse.  There was a history of multiple Emergency Room and hospitalization admissions over the previous four months.  Following admission he was treated with an increased dosage of quetiapine and lamotrigine.  He showed improvement such that he was able to be discharged.

Based upon the information available the patient medically required acute inpatient psychiatric treatment. The patient had acute psychotic symptoms consisting of incoherent and tangential thinking, paranoid delusions and auditory hallucinations.  He had not responded to outpatient treatment, including oral and IM antipsychotic medications.  He could not safely conduct himself at home.  As such there were no safe or effective alternatives to treatment outside of acute psychiatric hospitalization. 

This finding is consistent with the general standards of psychiatric care as well as the American Psychiatric Association (APA) Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Bipolar Disorder.  The health plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient in their determination to deny coverage for inpatient psychiatric care as of a specified date.  

The carrier's denial of coverage for the inpatient psychiatric hospital admission is reversed.  The medical necessity is substantiated.

Treatment: Inpatient substance rehabilitation

This patient is a male was admitted to inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment after a detoxification. He reportedly was found unresponsive after drinking 1 liter if vodka and taking Xanax and went to the Emergency Department (ED).  He then had reports of withdrawal symptoms including sweats, tremors, increased heart rate, and agitation and was given Librium in the ED.  He then took Ativan for detoxification after that prior to inpatient rehabilitation.  He reportedly could not maintain abstinence despite multiple past treatments.  He lacked a sober support and lived alone and was isolative. He reportedly was taking Propranolol for increased heart rate and anxiety.  He reportedly was working on better identification of relapse triggers, improving insight and coping skills as well as impulse control and decision making.  

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment. His reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for rehabilitation treatment as the chart notes provided enough specific evidence to support that he required this 24 hour residential treatment.  The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that inpatient treatment is indicated primarily for individuals whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting.  In this case this patient was considered in need of 24 hour substance rehabilitation treatment as he was using multiple substances including large amounts of alcohol and Xanax which put him at high risk for overdose, and he reportedly was found unconscious and unresponsive on a specified date due to this which put him at serious risk of danger to self. He could not stop use on his own.

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) he met criteria for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment as he continued to use large amounts of alcohol daily with the benzodiazepine Xanax despite negative consequences including legal arrests, driving under the influence, and being found unconscious and unresponsive.  He was considered a high risk patient with lack of supports who lived alone.  He reportedly lacked coping skills to maintain abstinence, needed to better identify relapse triggers, needed motivation for change, needed sober supports, better decision making and impulse control, he needed to develop relapse prevention skills. The National Institute on Drug Abuse: Principles of Addiction Treatment: A Research Based Guide- report that the best treatment outcomes occur with longer durations of treatment.  It also states that recovery from drug addiction is a long term process and that treatment techniques to increase motivation for treatment are necessary to prevent dropout rates.  In this case this patient required this 24 hour rehabilitation treatment as he was at high risk to continue use alcohol and Xanax without this 24 hour therapeutic substance rehabilitation treatment setting and needed to develop the necessary skills for abstinence.  

The carrier's denial of coverage for the substance use rehabilitation is reversed.  The medical necessity is substantiated.
