It was reported that he had a history of a past suicide attempt.  He had a positive toxicology for opiates and amphetamines.  He had diagnoses of Bipolar Disorder and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD).  He had a recent psychiatric hospitalization and was discharged after a 27-day stay.  He reported fleeting hallucinations, and he had impaired social skills.  He remained depressed in mood with feelings of hopelessness and helplessness and had medication changes.  He had Fluoxetine tapered and then discontinued, and he was started on Trintellix.  This medication was increased.  He also took Nortriptyline, Trazodone, Alprazolam, and Lithium.  He was discharged.

The insurer denied coverage for continued inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital as not medically necessary treatment.  This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for continued inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital.  The charts notes provided enough specific evidence to support that he required 24-hour hospitalization until discharge, as he was considered a high risk patient.  The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Suicidal Behaviors report that patients with past suicide attempts are at high risk of suicide and that past suicide attempts are the strongest risk factor for suicide.  It also reports that patients with comorbid substance use and bipolar disorder and patients with hopelessness are at increased risk for suicide.  The patient had all of these reported.

He continued to report dysphoric and depressed mood and feelings of hopelessness and helplessness, and Trintellix was increased.  He continued to report dysphoric and depressed mood and feelings of hopelessness and helplessness afterwards. He was motivated to engage in substance use disorder and rehabilitation treatment and re-achieve sobriety. Mental status examination showed euthymic mood, anxious affect with irritability and withdrawn demeanor. He reported insomnia, low energy, fatigue and poor concentration. He reported intense cravings and post-acute withdrawal symptoms (PAWS). Insight, judgment and impulse controls were limited, impaired and poor.
The patient's treatment included intensive services, monitoring, and residential level structure. The patient participated in recreational/activity therapies designed to support sober living and life skills together with group, individual and educational sessions. He readily engaged in substance use disorder treatment. Again, he had mild withdrawal or post-acute withdrawal symptoms during his stay that included anxiety, irritability, abdominal cramps and nausea. He was prescribed Wellbutrin to address mood and anxiety and trazodone and vistaril to address anxiety and insomnia, as well as vitamin replacement therapy.

The patient was discharged from the inpatient psychiatric hospital setting as soon as a less-restrictive treatment setting was appropriate.  

The patient represented an elevated risk of dangerous behaviors including self-injury, and suicide, and there was no less-restrictive treatment environment appropriate.  Therefore the treatment was medically necessary.  While the patient was not endorsing active suicidality or homicidality, the patient remained depressed.  The patient had multiple static risk factors for potentially dangerous behaviors, including substance abuse, prior suicidality, and diagnosis with a severe mental illness.  Therefore the patient represented a chronic risk of potentially dangerous behaviors.  The fact that patient remained depressed and with ongoing medication changes were acute risk factor for dangerous behaviors.  Furthermore, the fact that there was no less-restrictive environment of care appropriate suggests that ongoing inpatient psychiatric hospitalization was medically necessary and should be covered by the patient's health plan.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
 
Treatment: Continued Residential Substance Abuse Treatment with Inpatient Behavioral Stay

The insurer denied the Continued Residential Substance Abuse Treatment with Inpatient Behavioral Stay. The denial was reversed.

This is a male patient with a history of multiple substance treatments that included inpatient treatment. He presented to a residential rehabilitation facility for substance rehabilitation treatment. His presenting symptoms included poor eating and sleeping, decreased energy, depressive, and anxiety. It was reported that his daily drug use included crack/cocaine, ecstasy, cannabis, and alcohol. While in treatment he attended multiple daily group therapy sessions and attended weekly individual therapy treatment. The patient was discharged from treatment due to noncompliance with the program rules and drug use. 

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that inpatient treatment is indicated primarily for individuals whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. In this case this patient was considered in need of 24 hour substance rehabilitation treatment as he continued to use substances despite multiple negative consequences to use including incarceration, loss of multiple employments, changing residences, and relational strains. 

According to the LOCADTR he met criteria for inpatient substance residential rehabilitation treatment as he continued to use multiple substances despite multiple past inpatient substance treatments including recent inpatient substance treatments. Also, despite negative consequences of substance use including incarceration, loss of multiple employments, changing residences, and relational strains, he could not stop using multiple substances without the 24 hour therapeutic supervised and structured programming of this therapeutic residential treatment setting. It was reported that he continued to have cravings, urges to use substances, intrusive thoughts, impulses to stop treatment, fears of relapsing, and he needed more time in this sober and therapeutic setting to learn better coping and relapse prevention skills, improve insight into use, better deal with triggers and improve identifying them. He needed to better identify emotions and how it contributed to substance use. 

The National Institute on Drug Abuse: Principles of Addiction Treatment: A Research Based Guide- reports that research indicates that most addicted individuals needs at least 3 months in treatment to significantly reduce or stop their drug use and that the best treatment outcomes occur with longer durations of treatment. It also states that recovery from drug addiction is a long term process and that treatment techniques to increase motivation for treatment are necessary to prevent dropout rates. He reportedly had cravings and urges and eventually used crack/cocaine during his stay, and he had multiple past and recent inpatient rehabilitation treatments, and he still was unable to stop multiple substances of use. Without this structured and supervised therapeutic residential treatment, he likely would have relapsed sooner and been at risk for another overdose so he needed a significant amount of time in this treatment setting to give him the best chance of abstinence. 
It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably or in the best interests of the patient.

Based on the above, the medical necessity for continued Residential Substance Abuse Treatment with Inpatient Behavioral Stay is substantiated.  The insurer's denial is reversed.

summary:
Diagnosis: Schizophrenia and bipolar disorder 
Treatment: Continued inpatient admission
The insurer denied continued inpatient admission.
The denial is upheld.
The proposed continued inpatient admission was not medically necessary.
This was one of the multiple psychiatric admissions for this male with diagnoses of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder who was brought to the hospital by ambulance due to allegedly aggressive behavior in the context of medication noncompliance.  
The patient was unemployed. 
The patient's outpatient social worker noted that he appeared disorganized and internally preoccupied, talking to himself in a senseless way. She saw him the following day and described him as uncooperative and unable to have a conversation. The patient's grandmother, with whom he lived, reported that he had been aggressive to her, but no details are provided.
During the evaluation in the emergency department, the patient stated that there was nothing wrong with him. He reported that he did not know why he was brought to the hospital. He was guarded and uncooperative. As per his mother and sister in law, the patient had been noncompliant with his monthly intramuscular (IM) and oral medications. He was accompanied to the hospital by his ACT program doctor. The grandmother stated he had been irritable since he stopped taking his medications and that she did not feel safe with him if he did not take his medications.
Upon admission the patient was described as being irritable, anxious, and uncooperative, with loud, pressured speech. He had no insight and denied any mental problems stating that he did not need medications. He had racing thoughts, poor judgment, poor impulse control, flat affect, and unkempt appearance. He nevertheless sat quietly in the emergency room. He felt nervous and was given Ativan orally. He denied suicidal or homicidal ideation and denied hallucinations.
The patient was maintained on risperidone, Depakote, Cogentin, IM Risperdal Consta, and various somatic medications. 
Progress notes report that the patient was calm, cooperative and compliant with medications. He denied auditory or visual hallucinations and denied suicidal and homicidal ideation. He continued to have some thought blocking and thought disorganization. He had received 25 milligrams (mg) of Risperdal Consta. He was isolative and preferred to stay in his bed. 
The patient was calm and reported feeling OK. He denied any perceptual disturbances. He took all his medications with no side effects. He showed improvement exhibited by increased ability to share and engage in a discussion group. He was able to discuss the reasons for taking his medication and identify positive coping skills. Overall, he was described as calm, pleasant, and less disorganized than previously. 
The patient continued to improve in all parameters and was discharged to the care of the ACT program.
The only rationale provided in the appeal letter for continued acute inpatient care is that the patient remained socially isolated and psychologically disorganized. These symptoms are chronic and consistent with the patient's diagnosis. Notes during the period in question show steady improvement. There were no behavioral outbursts at any time. There was no suicidal or homicidal ideation. The patient was compliant with his medications.
There is no documented history of danger to self or others. The patient accepted long acting depot medications, in addition to his daily antipsychotic medications, while in the hospital. The patient had intensive outpatient follow up by an ACT psychiatrist and social worker. The chronic, relatively minor thought disordered problems described could have been addressed safely and equally effectively by the ACT program in a less intensive community treatment setting. Nothing in the documentation provided suggests that the patient required 24-hour daily confinement.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance and alcohol use disorder
 
Treatment: Inpatient detoxification admission 

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient detoxification admission. The denial is reversed. 

This patient is a male and was admitted to this inpatient substance detoxification treatment for alcohol, Xanax, and heroin detoxification. He had withdrawal symptoms including tremors, joint pain, irritable mood, and anxiety. He reportedly had been drinking 1/2 pint of vodka per day with 6 beers for with over three decades, using 4 mg of Xanax per day for more than a decade, and inhaling 3 bags of heroin per day for over a decade. He had past reported multiple inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatments. He also reportedly had a diagnosis of bipolar depression in addition to his alcohol, Xanax, and heroin use disorders. He also had past psychiatric hospitalizations for past reported suicide attempts. He was put on a Librium protocol for detoxification and was discharged with a referral to substance residential rehabilitation treatment scheduled.

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient substance detoxification treatment. This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient substance detoxification treatment as the as the chart notes did provide enough specific evidence to support that he needed this level of care. The APA Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. In this case this patient had use of multiple substances including large amounts of alcohol, Xanax, and heroin and was at risk for death from overdose as result of this use. 
According to the LOCADTR he did require 24 hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive setting as he continued to use multiple serious substances of use despite multiple past inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatments, and he needed two detoxification medications including Librium and Clonidine to modify withdrawal from alcohol, Xanax, and heroin. Also, he had reports of long term multiple substances of use and was at risk for worsened withdrawal symptoms if not in this 24 hour setting then including severe, complicated, and life threatening withdrawal such as delirium tremens due to the large amount of alcohol and Xanax use. Also, he likely would have relapsed again as evidenced by relapsing after past treatments.
As a result, the recommendation is to reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for inpatient substance detoxification. It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably or in the best interests of the patient.

Based on the above, the medical necessity for the inpatient detoxification admission is substantiated.  The insurer's denial is reversed.

2) LOCADTR

The treatment plan included the goals of improved coping; breaking the cycle of self-destructive behaviors; and, the development of healthy relationships. Individual, group and activity therapies and family focused sessions are provided, as clinically appropriate. During the dates in question the patient actively participated in the treatment plan and was engaged in therapeutic interventions in the context of a residential program with structure, intensive treatment, and social supports. The treatment course and case records/notes and updates reflect engagement with the treatment plan, but continued bouts of anxiety and anger and continued daydreaming. Therapeutic interventions were continued with appropriate monitoring including the use of bupropion and Vyvanse and melatonin to address symptoms of depression, the ADHD and sleep disturbance. The health plan's determination of medical necessity is upheld. The treatments to address maladaptive coping, distress problems, interpersonal functioning problems and day-to-day functioning problems were amenable to treatment at a lower level of care. Alcohol abuse/Addiction
Substance abuse: inpatient

The patient is an adult who presented to the emergency department with a request for detoxification services. The patient was using alcohol on a continuous daily basis with two to four pints of liquor together with intermittent use of cocaine with approximately $200 worth, as well as cannabis (marijuana and K2/Spice) and heroin with 10-20 bags on a frequent basis. Patient presented with a blood alcohol level of zero and mild symptoms of withdrawal with a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) scale score of 3 and Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) scale score of 2 reflecting minimal or light withdrawal symptoms. Patient has a history of schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type with last treatment for this disorder five years prior to presentation. Patient had received multiple past substance use disorder treatments including at least two detoxification treatment episodes and four substance-related rehabilitation treatments with one residential and three outpatient treatment episodes. 

The patient has a history of past psychiatric hospitalization for the mood and psychotic disorder, as well as a history of overdose. Patient was receiving no current treatment for a psychiatric disorder. The patient provided no history of withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens or severe alcohol or drug withdrawal symptoms, and did report blackouts. Patient was tobacco dependent. Patient was medically screened and admitted for inpatient level detoxification with plans for a four day detoxification treatment episode with Librium and methadone tapers, vitamin replacement therapy and comfort medications, as well as resumption/continuation of  usual psychotropic medication, low dose risperidone. Laboratory assessment and electrocardiogram (EKG) were unremarkable and drug screen was positive for cocaine and opioids consistent with history. Mental Status Examination: The patient was cooperative with good eye contact.  Speech was clear and thought production was linear and logical. There were no severe symptoms on mental status examination such as cognitive impairment, severe mood disturbance, psychosis or perceptual disturbance, or suicidal ideation. Patient presented with anxiety/irritability dysphoria and withdrawal symptoms that included nausea and gastrointestinal upset, chills, aches, rhinorrhea, piloerection and sweats. Patient also had limited insight, impaired judgment and poor to fair control of  impulses. Patient reported decreased appetite and sleep disturbance and fatigue with malaise. Patient was compliant with treatment, and progress notes indicate that social with peers and had no apparent distress during stay. Patient tolerated the taper of methadone and Librium and was placed on Campral with discontinuation of the risperidone. Patient was discharged upon completion of the detoxification treatment and was advised to attend 12-step recovery groups and referred to rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment. Health plan's determination is upheld in whole. 

Detoxification treatment could have been safely and effectively provided with lower level services. The patient in this case was using alcohol on a continuous daily basis with intermittent use of cocaine and cannabis and frequent or near daily use of heroin. There were no co-morbid general medical problems or co-occurring psychiatric disorders that would have warranted admission for inpatient level services, and the patient's schizoaffective disorder was stable and was not being actively treated. Moreover, the withdrawal symptoms were not reported to be severe, and were mild or light, and the patient's clinical symptoms were not serious enough to necessitate inpatient level detoxification treatment or monitoring. There were no safety concerns in this case and no history of complicated withdrawal from drugs or alcohol. The patient was considered to be motivated for detoxification treatment, and had access to substance use disorder services in the community.

summary:
Substance Abuse/Addiction - Substance Abuse/Addiction
Substance Abuse Inpatient

The patient is a male who received inpatient substance abuse treatment related to diagnoses of alcohol withdrawal, cocaine use disorder, cannabis use disorder, and sedative, hypnotic, or anxiolytic use disorder. The patient was also stated to have a diagnosis of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Urine drug screen  was positive for opiates, cocaine, benzodiazepines, methamphetamine, and barbiturates. The patient reported using heroin 25 bags per day,  4 milligrams (mg) of Xanax per day, and non-prescribed methadone 20 to 30 mg per day one to two times per week.
Clinical history was significant for multiple past episodes of substance use disorder treatment including detoxification and rehabilitation level of care. Medical history was significant for hepatitis C and negative for seizures, asthma, hypertension, heart disease, and diabetes. He had a history of treatment for ADHD. There was no surgical history. He denied any history of psychiatric hospitalizations. He denied any suicidal or homicidal ideation.
On admission, the patient reported nausea, trouble sleeping, anxiety, yawning, tremors, irritability, diarrhea, headaches, abdominal pain, rhinitis and teary eyes. In separate documentation, the patient also reported in the last 12 months having diarrhea and vomiting as well as insomnia and lightheadedness. The patient was placed on detoxification protocols for both opioids and benzodiazepines. Initial Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) was 16 and Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) was 13.
The subject under review is the medical necessity of the inpatient substance abuse treatment.

The health plan's determination is overturned.

The patient did have serious medical symptoms that needed to be managed in and inpatient setting to be effective. Benzodiazepines were the substance the patient was using with the greatest potential for harm. Opioids were also being used, creating a difficult management situation given potential interactions between opioids and benzodiazepines and their associated withdrawal protocols. The patient clearly met criteria for multiple substance use disorders and did not have any substance use disorders in full remission. Use of 4 mg of Xanax per day put the patient at risk for seizures from withdrawal that could be life-threatening. His withdrawal management from both opioids and benzodiazepines could not have been safely managed at a lower level of care. 24 hour medical supervision was needed. The patient was not adequately performing responsibilities in work, social, and family roles. The patient was poorly connected to a support network. He could not manage triggers. He could not be managed in a lower level of care setting.
Using the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) tool, the appropriate Level of Care is inpatient rehabilitation.
Benzodiazepines have a potentially life-threatening withdrawal syndrome. Additionally, the situation was complicated by opioid withdrawal and the interactions between withdrawal protocols for sedative and opioid use disorders. The patient had a high risk of relapse and poor supports.
Inpatient level of care was medically necessary.

Mental Health: Inpatient

The patient is a woman with diagnoses of schizoaffective disorder (SCZAD) and Cannabis use disorder (CnUD). The patient presented to the emergency department (ED) with complaints of acute agitation, depressed mood, persecutory and paranoid delusions, beliefs in a conspiracy against her, fear of death threats. On evaluation in the ED, she also was noted to be hyperactive with pressured speech. She feared she would "lash out" at people. This fear indicated danger to others. She had clearly decompensated and required acute admission. 

The health plan's determination is overturned in part. Admission and dates of service (DOS) at the IMHT level of care were medically necessary for 10 days. After the 10 days, the patient could have been discharged. 

This patient's illness was severe and chronic. She faced severe psychosocial distress with homelessness and unemployment. She was non-compliant with her outpatient treatment. She was at risk for readmission if discharged before fully stabilized. This patient had to be treated for both her psychotic and mood symptoms. The treatment team for this patent recommended use of long acting intramuscular (IM) neuroleptics to prevent relapse. She had multiple past admissions. Future readmissions would most likely be less frequently required with long acting IM neuroleptics. Case notes document that she was still irritable and talkative, preoccupied, experiencing paranoid delusions, and refusing groups. She was less irritable and began to attend groups but not stabilized. She continued to refuse her long acting injectable of antipsychotic. She had a positive attitude for the first time, saying "It's going to be all right. I have a positive attitude." She had no suicidal or homicidal ideation. She was not delusional. Therefore, she could safely with good medical judgment be discharged after 10 days.

summary:
Diagnosis: Eating disorder and depression 
Issue under review: Intensive outpatient mental health services 

Determination: The Intensive outpatient mental health services were not medically necessary. 

The patient is a teen-aged female. She was admitted to this program for treatment of an eating disorder and depression. The patient previously had intensive outpatient treatment at a different program. Prior to that, she was in an inpatient facility. Precipitating reasons for these admissions are not described. 

The patient's treatment plan at the time of admission to the current program included 31 authorized sessions. At that time, the patient was described as being ambivalent about recovery. She became angry during a family session. Staff reported that she was not completing her meals and needed supplements, which she often did not take. Her parents were concerned about the patient going away to college in the fall. Authorization was given for some additional sessions. The program planned a discharge date. 

At no time was the patient in any acute medical distress. Her weight varied from approximately 122 pounds to 127 pounds, which for her height of 63 inches placed her within several pounds of her ideal body weight. 

The patient reported smoking marijuana three times weekly and did not plan to discontinue it. One note reports a history of substance-abuse and three "overdoses," but no details were provided regarding these episodes or use of other drugs except for mention of possible past use of cocaine, benzodiazepines, and psychedelics. The patient did not want to attend AA/NA (Alcoholics Anonymous/Narcotics Anonymous) meetings or disclose her drug use to her parents. 

She was provided cognitive behavioral therapy, dialectical behavioral therapy, group therapy, family therapy, meal support, and exposure therapy for three hours daily, four days a week. Her medications included fluoxetine 10 mg daily and quetiapine 75 mg at bedtime. 

The documentation reviewed does not reflect any significant medical or psychiatric distress. The patient made conscious choices about weight loss and continued substance use. While these choices may not have been in her ultimate best interest, they did not place her in immediate or significant danger and there was no evidence of any health consequences. They could have been appropriately addressed in a less intensive mental health outpatient setting for the dates of service under review.

Mental Health: Residential

The patient is a female diagnosed with moderately severe and recurrent major depressive disorder, persistent depressive disorder, unspecified anxiety disorder, unspecified eating and feeding disorder, psychological factors affecting physical condition (ulcer with bleeding), obsessive compulsive personality, and elements of unspecified and other posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) including complicated bereavement. The patient presented with worsening symptoms of her anxiety and depression in the context of the eating disorder and grief associated with the recent death of her father.

The patient was referred for residential treatment by her community clinicians due to her decline in functioning and worsening symptoms of the co-morbid psychiatric disorders, as well as over-use of her Ambien and over the counter medications used to numb self. Again, at the time of admission to residential level services, the patient had experienced worsening symptoms precipitated by multiple stressors with functional impairment and somatic symptoms of anxiety and depression.

The patient attended residential services with the structure, intensity of services and monitoring consistent with residential programming with occupation-specific programming including intensive therapy and nutritional supports with a meal plan. Specifically, she received individual, group, activity-based, wellness and other therapeutic interventions. During the course of treatment, she was noted to make slow and steady progress with ongoing sessions together with individual, group and other evidence-based psychosocial therapeutic interventions that included cognitive behavioral techniques and mindfulness/yoga and involvement in transference-based treatment. She remained on her psychotropic regimen of Lamictal and Lexapro with supplemental zaleplon, Abilify and gabapentin to address residual symptoms of depression, insomnia and anxiety.

In summary, progress notes during the timeframes under review from indicate that the patient was gaining independence but struggling with residual symptoms of anxiety and depressive ruminations associated with grief, and, bouts of intense anxiety with regard to her past trauma and the bereavement. In this regard, the patient exhibited high body distress with high levels of anxiety with regard to any consideration of transition to lower level services. She remained medically stable, and she did not pose safety concerns which were monitored. She remained on her medications targeting anxiety, depression, and trauma-related symptoms. Again, there were no general medical complications and she tolerated her medications without adverse effects with adherence. The patient was noted to be ready for discharge with a discharge date pending. Plans were in place for an appropriate step down with supports. She remained in residential care with continued supervision and structure and intensive mental health services in order to continue working on her coping skills and her trauma and grief related problems. The subject under review is the medical necessity for continued residential mental health treatment.

The health plan's determination is overturned, in part.

For a certain portion of the time frame the requested service of residential mental health treatment is medically necessary for this patient.  The documented records reflect the intensity of services, structure and monitoring consistent with residential level treatment and standards of care. Moreover, the services provided are in keeping with prevailing standards of medical practice for the conditions under treatment in this case with evidence-based treatments; and, the requested services/treatment being provided in this case were clinically appropriate, and are backed by credible scientific evidence known to benefit patients with the conditions diagnosed in this case. The duration of services were clinically appropriate and medically necessary and provided with well-established treatments known to benefit patients with the comorbid conditions diagnosed in this case and noted in the clinical summary. The patient could not have been effectively treated with lower level services or in a less restrictive treatment setting prior to a specific date, at which time the patient was capable of a step down to lower level services and treatment. This answer is consistent with the scientific literature and guidelines referenced below.

summary:
Mental Health - Depression
Mental Health Inpatient

The patient is a female admitted for acute inpatient psychiatric care. The patient presented with worsening symptoms of depression, suicidal ideation with plan to hang self or cut or jump in front of a train. She had comorbidity that included eating disorder and trichotillomania with skin picking, and severe psychosocial stressors that include childhood sexual and physical abuse, as well as social isolation and a decline in functioning. She had failed to benefit from multiple medication trials and outpatient therapy and had two recent partial hospital program (PHP) stays with persistent symptoms. Again, her clinical presentation was complicated by an unspecified eating disorder that had included restricted intake, and binge eating with purging and laxative abuse. At the time of presentation, the patient was anxious and dysphoric with hopelessness, worthlessness and prominent suicidal thoughts. She had diminished sleep, appetite, energy, concentration and volition. There were no symptoms of mania, thought disorder, psychosis or severe cognitive impairment. However, the patient did endorse auditory hallucinations and was noted to have poor control of impulses and urges to self-harm with cutting, as she had a history of self-injury with cutting and attempts at asphyxiation with wrapping a cord around her neck.

The patient has a history of a depressive disorder, obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD), eating disorder, and borderline personality disorder that had been treated with outpatient therapy and medications; she had received partial hospital program (PHP) services at least twice more recently. There was history of psychiatric hospitalizations and suicide attempt by overdose. There was trauma history with a sexual and physical abuse as a child with reports of flashbacks and nightmares that had worsened. She also had a history of hair pulling and skin picking, as noted, as well as self-harming behavior with cutting her thighs with a razor.

The patient received a comprehensive, psychiatric evaluation upon admission and was diagnosed with major depressive disorder, recurrent and severe with psychotic features and with borderline personality disorder as the primary diagnoses together with past history of comorbid conditions. The patient's treatment plan included safety monitoring, individual and group therapy, education, and medication as before with adjustments. There was also consideration of another course of electroconvulsive therapy that was subsequently dismissed due to the nature of her personality disorder and patient preference.

The patient was medication adherent and participating more actively in her treatment. She had intermittent suicidal ideation requiring safety monitoring and continued to endorse auditory hallucinations that were consistent with the borderline traits. She had improved mood and functioning with diminished anxiety. The treatment team had determined that the patient would require residential level aftercare, and plans were made for a safe and clinically appropriate discharge and disposition.

The health plan's determination is overturned, in whole.

The patient's severity of symptoms, and inability to participate in treatment at lower levels of care, functional decline, and risk of relapse necessitated the continued acute inpatient care through discharge. The presenting and continuing symptoms of depressive disorder were not amenable to treatment at a lower level of care during the time interval under review, in view of the worsening depression while in outpatient treatment with high risk for suicidal behavior, disordered eating and maladaptive coping in association with borderline personality disorder. The patient's progress notes clearly indicate that the patient displayed continued symptoms that required inpatient level structure and monitoring with medication adjustments and evidence-based therapeutic interventions. Specifically, she remained anxious with persistent symptoms of the borderline personality disorder requiring medication adjustments and intensive psychotherapy and counseling. Moreover, the patient continued to experience severe bouts of anxiety/irritability, and other symptoms that would necessitate inpatient level psychiatric services with continued symptoms of severe and recurrent major depression and borderline features that required ongoing safety monitoring with a safe and clinically appropriate step down to residential level care.

summary:
Diagnosis: Unspecified Disruptive Impulse-Control, Conduct Disorder, Cannabis-Related Disorder, Reactive Attachment Disorder
 
Treatment: Mental health residence

The insurer denied coverage for mental health residence. The denial is upheld. 

This patient is a male who was admitted to this inpatient mental health residential treatment due to behavioral symptoms including disrespectful behavior, verbal abuse at times, property damage, truancy at school, and taking items from the home. He also demonstrated impulsivity, hyperactivity, and it was reported that he had a change in attitude towards his family, school, and sports since several years ago. He had reported diagnoses of Conduct Disorder, Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), and Cannabis Use Disorder. 
	
The insurer denied coverage for inpatient mental health residential treatment as not medically necessary treatment. This reviewer agrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient mental health residential treatment as the chart notes do not provide enough specific evidence to support that he could only be treated in a 24-hour residential treatment or could not be treated in a less restrictive level of care.

The American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry (AACAP) Practice Parameters for the Assessment and Treatment of Children and Adolescents with Conduct Disorder report that the least restrictive level of care for safe and effective treatment is appropriate.  In this case, the chart notes did not have enough specific evidence to support that he could not be treated in a less restrictive setting. Notes on admission did not report imminently dangerous behavior, suicidal or homicidal ideation, psychotic symptoms, inability to function, severe depressive symptoms, manic episodes, or dangerous substance use behavior.

Notes in early-2018 reported that his mood was anxious and within normal limits, and he was working on relationship building. They also reported that he was struggling with communication. Notes one month later reported that he was working on developing insight into how cognition precedes feelings that precede aggressive behavior.  Another month later notes reported that he was using attachment based therapy. He did not have specific reported identifiable and quantifiable treatment goals that could only be achieved in a 24-hour residential treatment setting or that could not be achieved in a less restrictive program setting.  His treatment goals of improving communication, relational issues, insight, behavioral control, and decision making did not require only 24-hour residential treatment.  Also, there was no reported specific documentation stating that he failed a less restrictive level of care, such as a partial hospital program.  Furthermore, there were no reports that he was evaluated by a child/adolescent psychiatrist during his time for diagnosis or treatment recommendations. 

As a result, uphold the previous decision and deny continued residential treatment. The health care plan acted reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interests of the patient.

The carrier's denial of coverage for mental health residence is upheld.  The medical necessity is not substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse

Treatment: Inpatient Substance Abuse Services

The insurer denied the Inpatient Substance Abuse Services.  The denial was reversed. 

This is a male patient who was admitted to inpatient substance detoxification treatment in late 2018 for alcohol and heroin detoxification treatment.  He had withdrawal symptoms including tremors, nausea, irritable mood, anxiety, teary eyes, diarrhea, elevated heart rate of 95, elevated systolic blood pressure of 130, and a CIWA of 10.  He had a positive toxicology for opiates, cocaine, and benzodiazepines and a blood alcohol level of 0.4.  The patient reported that he was homeless and lacked coping skills, and a sober support system.  He had a history of numerous past inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatments with a most recent substance treatment in late 2018.  He reportedly had a 29 year history of alcohol use; drinking 12 beers per day.  He also reported daily crack use as well as benzodiazepines. He was put on a Librium protocol during his inpatient admission but left against medical advice.

The APA Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment.  In this case, this patient had use of multiple serious substances of use including heroin, alcohol, and benzodiazepines.  He was at high risk for death from overdose and severe, complicated, and life threatening withdrawal.  According to the LOCADTR he did require 24 hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive setting as he continued to use substances despite numerous past inpatient detoxification and rehabilitation treatments.  Also, he needed detoxification medication to modify withdrawal including Librium.

The patient lacked the coping skills.  The patient had reported Schizoaffective Disorder also.  It was unlikely that he would remain abstinent while having withdrawal symptoms.  He had reports of withdrawal symptoms including tremors, nausea, irritable mood, anxiety, teary eyes, diarrhea, elevated heart rate of 95, and elevated systolic blood pressure of 130.  His CIWA score was 10 initially so he required the time in this treatment setting.  The patient could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in an outpatient setting as he likely would still would use alcohol, benzodiazepines, and crack if not in a 24 hour setting for detoxification.  The risk of delirium tremens can occur even 4 days after stopping alcohol use and this is considered a life threatening withdrawal so he was still considered at risk. This is a male patient with a history of depression and polysubstance abuse. It was reported the patient had several past substance abuse treatments with relapses. He presented to an alcohol and substance treatment facility with complaints of withdrawal symptoms including sweats, nausea, dry heaves, and agitation. He had a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) score of 9. The patient reported smoking several cannabis joints per day and smoking multiple bags of heroin over the past month. The patient was treated with a Librium taper, Campral to assist in targeting alcohol craving and Remeron for sleep and depression. The patient was discharged to a substance rehabilitation treatment facility when a bed became available. 

The APA Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. This was the case with this patient. This patient had multiple past substance detoxification treatments and still was drinking large amounts of alcohol, using cocaine, heroin, and cannabis and was at risk for overdose. It was not likely that the patient could attend an outpatient substance detoxification treatment due to his continued use despite past inpatient substance treatments. Thus, the patient required inpatient level of care for his substance detoxification treatment. 

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), the patient did require 24-hour treatment as he needed detoxification medications including Librium to modify withdrawal and had a long history of heavy heroin and alcohol use as well as cocaine, other opiates, and cannabis use putting the patient at high risk for overdose and needing 24 hour treatment due to this risk. The patient was noted to continue to use large amounts of serious substances and alcohol so outpatient treatment for detoxification was not considered safe as the patient needed 24-hour monitoring and treatment for detoxification. The patient was also at risk for severe, complicated, and life threatening withdrawal due to the large amount of his daily alcohol use. The patient was considered a high risk for relapse and even required Campral to ease his urges. The patient needed to be discharged from this hospital setting to an inpatient substance/alcohol rehabilitation setting to ensure that the patient did not relapse prior to the rehabilitation treatment. However, inpatient substance/alcohol rehabilitation setting did not have a bed available so the patient required continued inpatient treatment to prevent relapse outside of a 24-hour setting prior to going to this inpatient rehabilitation treatment. It was not likely that the patient would be able to remain abstinent if discharged home after the detoxification if he did not go to the 24 hour therapeutic and supervised rehabilitation treatment from the hospital. The patient also had comorbid depression and anxiety and lacked sober supports for outpatient detoxification to be a safe and effective option. 

The health care plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment and in the best interests of the patient.

This is a male patient who had a history of inpatient substance residential treatment but was unable to stop due to the short length of stay. He presented to a rehabilitation treatment facility for substance rehabilitation due to his continued use of cocaine, opiates and heroin, inhalants, hallucinogens, cannabis, and amphetamines. While in rehabilitation he attended individual and group therapy. His medication regimen included Wellbutrin and Lamictal. 

According to the American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders intensive outpatient programs are programs that provide an intensive, structured treatment experience for individuals with substance use disorders who require more services than those generally available in traditional outpatient settings. Alternatively, these programs are sometimes used as "step-down" programs for individuals leaving hospital or residential settings who are at a high risk of relapsing because of problems with motivation, the presence of frequent cravings or urges to use a substance, poor social supports, immediate environmental cues for relapse and/or availability of substances, and co-occurring medical and/or psychiatric disorders. The aim is to prepare the individual for transition to less intensive outpatient services and increased self-reliance through the practice and mastery of relapse prevention skills and the active use of self-help programs. 

The National Institute on Drug Abuse: Principles of Addiction Treatment: A Research Based Guide- reports that the best treatment outcomes occur with longer durations of treatment. Recovery from drug addiction is a long term process. It also states that treatment techniques to increase motivation for treatment are necessary to prevent dropout rates. His multiple serious substances of use significantly impaired his functioning so he did require at least substance intensive outpatient program treatment at least 3 hours per day 3 days per week so he met LOCADTR criteria for IOP treatment then. He did not have the reported coping skills to stop use without this intensive outpatient program treatment and needed this structure, supervision,  and support to monitor unsafe behaviors, improve coping skills and insight, identify relapse triggers, improve relapse prevention skills, make better choices, increased his support, and to try to maintain abstinence In this case this patient met criteria for at least intensive outpatient program treatment as he was a high risk patient who continued to use multiple serious substances of use despite past inpatient substance residential treatment, past negative consequences to use including 2 overdoses resulting in hospitalizations, past illegal activities including robbing and stealing, and he was homeless at one point. He was generally motivated for treatment and described as cooperative with a full range of affect with nervousness, tension, irritability, sleep disturbance, and aches due to the onset of opioid withdrawal. The records reflect individual therapy, generally on a weekly basis, but psychiatric appointments were by telemedicine rather than in person. There is no evidence that the provider was on site for any of the appointments, and it should be noted that this treatment episode occurred prior to the COVID-19 pandemic. Some of the treatments that were provided include EMDR (eye movement desensitization and reprocessing) and Clozaril. Other treatment modalities included games, puzzles, cards, and spending time with a horse. 

Many of the records consist of simple night shift time logs. Others are self-harm checklists, which were generally negative. Others were narrative descriptions of telephone conversations between staff and the patient's parents, who were at times at odds over the treatment plan.

The patient's health plan denied coverage on the basis of, "The care provided by this facility was not consistent with level of care guidelines as the medical records demonstrate very few groups and individual therapy sessions. In addition, at the time of your daughter's admission, the facility could not be authorized for services due to the service components for medical oversight not being consistent with guidelines for mental health residential setting."

No, the Residential mental health services  was not medically necessary. 

This patient's problems were consistent with her Axis II Cluster B (borderline personality disorder) diagnosis. Although the patient had at times engaged in parasuicidal behaviors, there was no documented evidence of true, imminent danger to self or others. While she also reportedly had an eating disorder, her physical and laboratory states were unremarkable. Finally, as noted by the health plan, the patient's care as documented in the records reviewed was far below generally accepted standards. Nothing in the documentation reviewed indicates that this patient could not have been treated safely and more appropriately in a less intensive community setting with strong, face to face parental involvement.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Inpatient Substance Abuse Rehabilitation
The insurer denied the Inpatient Substance Abuse Rehabilitation.
The determination is upheld.

The patient presented requesting detoxification treatment and completed detoxification treatment with transfer for inpatient rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment to address substance use disorder with stimulants (cocaine); alcohol; and opioids (heroin), as well as use of Klonopin together with alcohol. The patient had no history of withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens or other episodes of severe withdrawal symptoms. He had a history of substance use disorder with multiple prior treatments with relapses no substantial periods of sobriety in the past. He was using cocaine at approximately $50 per day; and, daily use of alcohol with up to two pints of vodka; and, opioids with up to 20 bags of heroin, as well as six Klonopin tablets per day or intermittently. His use of heroin was in spite of being in an outpatient treatment program with medication assisted treatment with Suboxone.
His substance use had escalated over a several year time frame and was associated with significant decline in functioning and other consequences within social, occupational, and primary support domains. The patient had previously engaged in substance use disorder treatment and the last treatment episode had occurred immediately prior to his presentation to an emergency department.
The patient provided a history of a psychiatric disorder and treatment for mood and anxiety disturbance treated with Effexor, Seroquel and Klonopin. There was a history of multiple psychiatric hospitalizations. His diagnoses included major depressive disorder and unspecified anxiety disorder.
There were no acute general medical issues in this case. The patient has chronic conditions including obesity and hepatitis C positivity. He was tobacco dependent. He had been medically screened at the time of his admission for detoxification and substance-related treatments.
Evaluation on admission for inpatient level services revealed a mental status examination that was free of severe psychiatric symptoms. He was generally motivated for rehabilitation treatment. The patient was described as cooperative with fluent speech and anxious or dysphoric mood, and, diminished focus or concentration with limited insight with regard to the substance use disorder. He had no evidence of acute mania, thought disorder, psychosis, perceptual disturbance or severe cognitive impairment. He did not report suicidal or homicidal ideation.
The patient is single and unemployed and homeless. He was estranged from his ex-girlfriend and minor child. He has limited social support and coping skills. There were no prominent legal issues or trauma history in this case.
The patient was admitted to inpatient rehabilitation treatment following detoxification with continued use of Suboxone and replacement of vitamins and nicotine. He was provided comprehensive evaluation and treatment that included focus on coping skills, relapse prevention techniques with identification of triggers, education about the disease model of addiction, and, involvement with groups and individual therapy, as well as 12-step recovery groups and other therapeutic activities. Psychiatric evaluation was provided and he was prescribed/continued with his usual psychotropic medications including medication assisted treatment with Suboxone.
Throughout the brief inpatient stay, the patient was engaged in treatment with intensive services, sober housing, monitoring, and structure provided within the inpatient substance use disorder treatment program. The patient had no severe withdrawal symptoms or post-acute withdrawal symptoms. The patient was participating actively in treatment, and had no complications with respect to biomedical, general medical, emotional or other treatment domains. Mental status examinations/progress notes reflected stable mood with sleep, appetite and energy that were okay. However, he threw a glass of water on another patient on the day of discharge resulting in an administrative discharge with referral for clinically appropriate aftercare and continuation of his prescribed medications.
The health plan documents, appeal documents, and correspondence from the health plan and treatment facility, as well as case records and summary, and the health plan's case notes, and, the health plan's rationale for the denial of certification for coverage of the requested treatment, were reviewed. This case is a New York State mandated review with the application of NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Guidelines/Criteria.
At issue is the medical necessity of Inpatient Substance Use Disorder Rehabilitation Services.
The requested health service/treatment of Inpatient Rehabilitation is not medically necessary for this patient.
The patient presented with substance use disorders with use of heroin, alcohol and cocaine while participating in medication assisted treatment with Suboxone. He received inpatient detoxification treatment transitioning to inpatient level rehabilitation treatment. He readily engaged in treatment with continued use of Suboxone and his medications to address mood and anxiety disorders with tolerability and adherence. During the time interval under review, the patient was noted to be in no apparent distress with improved functioning and active participation in treatment including positive interactions with staff and peers until the day of discharge. The application of NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria (referenced below) did indicate that the patient was clinically appropriate for treatment with lower level care in a less restrictive treatment setting, as the health plan asserts. Thus, medical necessity for the admission and the continued Inpatient stay is not met in this case scenario consistent with American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, the scientific literature and published guidelines, referenced below.

summary:
Mental Health
Mental Health: Inpatient

Diagnosis: Depression
Treatment: Inpatient mental health inpatient
The insurer denied inpatient mental health inpatient stay. The health plan's determination is overturned. 

This case involves a female who was medically screened in the emergency department and admitted for acute inpatient psychiatric treatment. The patient had become increasingly depressed with self-harming behavior (cutting) and suicidal ideation and deterioration in functioning culminating in her presentation. She had a history of bipolar disorder and severe depressive episodes associated with suicidal behavior and psychiatric treatment with therapy and medications. Her presentation was characterized by worsening symptoms of depression and suicidal ideation in the context of multiple psychosocial stressors and substance use disorder with cannabis and alcohol, as well as past use of opioids and history of medication assisted treatment with Suboxone.

The Behavioral Health Inpatient Level of Care is medically necessary for this patient.
The patient required the admission and continued acute inpatient level care and the continued structure of an acute inpatient level setting through discharge in order to provide safety monitoring and to administer treatment for the psychiatric disturbance while conducting an evaluation, and while observing functioning with the resumption/adjustment of clinically appropriate medications including continued medication assisted treatment for opioid use disorder.
The medical necessity for acute inpatient level structure and monitoring is reasonable and in the patient's best interest in view of the patient's severe symptoms of mood disorder and co-occurring substance use disorders; in view of the severe psychosocial stressors; and in view of the need for continued active treatment in the context of deteriorated functioning and persistent symptoms representing a safety concern and needing inpatient level structure and supervision.
Additionally, the inpatient stay during the time interval under review is medically necessary in order to monitor the response to medications, to insure that the patient will have a sustained response to treatment, and to continue to address the acute risk of suicidal behavior in the context of severe symptoms of bipolar mood disorder with depression and the co-occurring substance use disorders that were only in partial remission. The necessity for the admission and the continued inpatient level services reflects sound medical judgment in keeping with prevailing standards of professional practice, and with the published practice guidelines and criteria, referenced below, as well as New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews, as well as NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Guidelines.

summary:
Substance Abuse
Substance Abuse: Inpatient
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Inpatient Substance Abuse Treatment
The insurer denied the Inpatient Substance Abuse Treatment. The health plan's determination is upheld. 

The patient is an adult male who self-referred and requested detoxification from alcohol. The patient was using alcohol on a continuous daily basis with up to one pint of liquor per day together with crack cocaine and cannabis intermittently. He reported a history of poly-substance use beginning in adolescence. The patient provided no history of withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens or severe alcohol withdrawal symptoms; vital signs were normal, and the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) scale score was 10 with mild symptoms including mild tremor or shakes and reports of nausea, irritability and anxiety. The urine drug screen was positive for cocaine. There was no reported use of other illicit drugs or other drugs of abuse. 

The Inpatient Substance Abuse Treatment was not medically necessary for this patient.
The proposed inpatient detoxification treatment and other inpatient medical services noted in the clinical summary could have been safely and effectively provided at a lower level of care. The clinical features and indicated treatment dimensions of this patient's alcohol use disorder, and other substance use disorders, did not require or warrant the structure of an inpatient setting or 24-hour monitoring. The patient displayed no serious disturbance of mental status despite having a history of ongoing substance use disorder with alcohol and ongoing treatment for an unspecified depressive disorder. Moreover, the patient had been evaluated and cleared with regard to safety concerns in the emergency department, and did not show evidence for suicidal or aggressive behavior or risk, or severe cognitive impairment or psychosis, or perceptual disturbance, or general medical concerns that would have warranted an inpatient level admission and treatment.
Thus, admission for detoxification treatment and 24-hour monitoring, and the requested inpatient level services were not medically necessary in this case scenario. The indicated treatment for alcohol use disorder in this case could have been provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment and stabilization in the emergency department.

summary:
Diagnosis: disorganized schizophrenia.
Treatment: Mental Health Inpatient
The insurer denied inpatient mental health treatment. The health plan's determination is overturned in part. 6 additional days with discharge on the 7th day were medically necessary. 

The patient is a woman with diagnoses of disorganized schizophrenia (DSCZ) and diabetes mellitus II (DMII). The patient was brought by Emergency Medical Services (EMS) to the hospital, with the EMS activated by her case worker. The concern was that she was not adequately caring for herself. On mental state examination, the patient was documented to be euthymic, without suicidal or homicidal ideation; she denied auditory hallucination (AH) but most likely she was responding to internal stimuli. She showed poor insight and poor judgment. Her feet were dirty, and she was malodorous. She was not taking any medications for her DSCZ or her metformin.

This patient's DSCZ was chronic and severe. She was not taking care of her serious medical disorder, DMII, or of her activities of daily living (ADL) in general and appeared to be in denial of her DSCZ. She was not taking any psychotropic medication. The question is how much improvement was necessary to safely discharge the patient with good medical judgment. She was still disheveled and unkempt. She was isolative with poor ADLs. The patient was euthymic, denying AH, even though she may have been continuing to experience them. She never stopped talking to "no one." After education about the need to take her medications, she promised to take them including her psychotropic medications. She was documented to say she was getting better and feeling better. This was an indication of some improvement, but her anti-psychotic medication was not considered adequate. She was transitioned to Haldol. She was taking her medication as directed. While she would most likely experience continued symptoms of DSCZ in any context, the fact that she showed improvement overall and some awareness of the need to take both her medical and psychiatric medications, her care could continue in a less restrictive environment.
On the 7th day, the patient could be discharged with good medical judgment, in accord with current standards of best care, and in accord with the medical literature.

 The insurer denied the inpatient rehabilitation. The denial is upheld in whole.

The patient is a male who was transitioned from detoxification treatment to inpatient substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment to continue to address substance use of stimulants (crack cocaine); cannabis (marijuana); tobacco, and alcohol. The patient had no past history of withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens or severe withdrawal symptoms. He had a history of substance use disorder with onset in adolescence with alcohol, escalating to daily continuous use with subsequent use of crack cocaine at age 25 years. He was using one to two pints of liquor plus beer together with $100 worth of crack cocaine with daily use. He was also using marijuana intermittently. His substance use had resulted in psychosocial problems including homelessness and unemployment. He self-referred to substance use disorder treatment with medical clearance and detoxification treatment prior to beginning inpatient rehabilitation treatment.

The patient exhibited limited insight and impaired judgment with questionable control of impulses. There were no severe symptoms on mental status examination; the patient had no symptoms of severe depression, mania, psychosis, perception, cognition, or thought disorder. He reported sleep disturbance, but no other somatic symptoms.

The rehabilitation treatment included focus on coping skills, relapse prevention techniques with identification of triggers, education about the disease model of addiction, and involvement with 12-step recovery groups. The patient engaged in treatment and intensive services, sober housing, monitoring, and structure provided within the inpatient treatment program. The patient participated actively with treatment, and showed no significant symptoms or signs of withdrawal, and had no complications of rehabilitation treatment. He received vitamin and nicotine replacement therapy and comfort medications including trazodone and Vistaril to address anxiety and insomnia. The patient participated in therapy. He was actively participating in treatment with treatment plans to address coping skills and to develop sober supports. He had no complications during his brief inpatient stay and transferred to a sister rehabilitation program with plans for continued substance use disorder treatment. The subject under review is the medical necessity for the inpatient rehabilitation. 

The health plan's determination is upheld in whole.

The requested health service/treatment of inpatient rehabilitation is not medically necessary for this patient. The inpatient rehabilitation was amenable to treatment at a lower level of care. The patient was motivated and able to effectively engage in rehabilitation services, and the patient did not need the continued structure or monitoring of an inpatient setting or the intensity of therapy and services in order to effectively participate in rehabilitation substance abuse treatment. There were no biomedical or psychiatric complications, or severe psychiatric symptoms in this case that would have required continued residential level behavioral health and substance-related services. Moreover, the patient was motivated to participate in rehabilitation treatment. Thus, the requested benefit of inpatient rehabilitation was not medically necessary for this patient.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder, Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)

Treatment: Residential Mental Health Treatment for Children and Adolescents

The insurer denied the Residential Mental Health Treatment for Children and Adolescents. 

The denial was overturned.

This is a male patient who was admitted to this inpatient mental health residential treatment due to continued mood and behavioral symptoms putting him and others at risk of harm.  He was in a wilderness program and required this more intensive treatment in the residential treatment.  He had severe depressive symptoms including depressed mood, suicidal thoughts, self-harm behaviors, anxiety attacks, aggression, property destruction, poor emotional regulation, poor coping skills, low self-esteem, feelings of helplessness and worthlessness, obsessive compulsive symptoms, poor impulse control, poor attention, and social anxiety.  He had reportedly been using alcohol and cannabis.  He had a history of stealing, vandalizing, past suicide attempts by overdose and cutting, and had 2 past reported psychiatric hospitalizations.  He had diagnoses of Major Depressive Disorder, Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), Social Anxiety Disorder, Obsessive Compulsive Disorder, and Body Dysmorphic Disorder.  He had reportedly taken medication including antidepressant medications, mood stabilizers, ADHD medications, anti-anxiety medications, and had individual, group, and family therapy.  He was discharged to a more intensive and higher level of care.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Suicidal Behaviors report that patients with past suicide attempts are at high risk for suicide and this patient had multiple past suicide attempts by serious methods including overdose and cutting and during the denial period still was making attempts to self-harm or suicide so he was at high risk for suicide.  It was reported according to notes he self-harmed, had property destruction, threatened his safety, ingested hand sanitizer to harm self, and he still had emotional dysregulation and poor coping skills.  It was reported that he locked himself in his room to inhale toxic vapors from substances that he stole from art class, tried to inebriate himself with hand sanitizer and rubbing alcohol, hid the containers, had a suicide notes, used his fingernails and objects to self-harm, was physically aggressive, emotionally dysregulating, tried to take a razor to self-harm, and he required physical restraints. He had an active treatment plan as he had reportedly taken medication including antidepressant medications, mood stabilizers, ADHD medications, anti-anxiety medications, individual, group, and family therapy.  This was a complex and high risk patient who required at least the intensive structured, supervised therapeutic mental health residential treatment in this setting.  He even tried suicide and self-harm attempts in this setting so he required an even higher level and intensity of treatment to better assure his safety and to try to improve emotional regulation and coping skills which is why he was discharged to a more intensive and higher level of care.  He was a high risk patient with severe depression and anxiety, poor impulse control, co-morbid alcohol and substance use, poor coping skills and emotional regulation who required at least 24 hour residential treatment. 

It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably, with sound clinical judgment, or in the best interests of the patient then.  

The carrier's denial of coverage for Residential Mental Health Treatment for Children and Adolescents is overturned.  The medical necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis:  Major Depressive Disorder (MDD).
Treatment:  Inpatient Mental Health.

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient hospital admission.  The denial is partially overturned.

This patient is a male, who was admitted for inpatient mental health treatment due to his active, depressive symptoms including suicidal ideation and plan, depressed mood, hopelessness, helplessness, poor activities of daily living (ADL's), as well as alcohol and benzodiazepine use.  The patient had a reported diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD).  The patient reported a history of self-injurious behavior including cutting self and multiple past psychiatric hospitalizations.  The patient was admitted and was treated with Sertraline, Abilify, and Naltrexone.  The patient was discharged.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Major Depressive Disorder reports that the least restrictive level of care for safe and effective treatment is appropriate.  It also states that patients with suicidal intent or plan or behaviors, or who present as an imminent danger to self or others are in need of hospital treatment.  It also states that patients with inability to adequately care for their basic needs or severe psychomotor slowing may need hospitalization.  This was the case for this patient initially, as he reported multiple suicidal plans and intent with severe depression.  The patient still had reports of significant depression from specified dates according to the chart notes provided.  Notes from a specified date reported that the patient had depressed mood, blunted affect, isolative and guarded behavior, poor self-care, internal preoccupation, intrusive thoughts, thought blocking, and psychomotor retardation.  The patient was still at risk to harm self.  Notes reported that the patient was still depressed in mood with flat affect, guilt, was unkempt, and spoke about feeling hopeless as a trigger to drinking.  The patient was still at risk for harm to self and supported the need for continued 24-hour hospital treatment then.  

However, as of a specified date, the patient's chart notes did not report severe depressive symptoms.  Notes reported that the patient was feeling good, had no craving for alcohol anymore, and that he denied anhedonia, depression, suicidal or homicidal ideation, plan, or intent, or hallucinations, and his insight and judgment were improving with fair impulse control.  Notes reported that the patient denied depression, suicidal or homicidal ideation, plan, or intent, or hallucinations, and that he felt ready for discharge because he was not suicidal anymore.  Notes reported that the patient denied depression, suicidal or homicidal ideation, plan, or intent, or hallucinations.  The patient reportedly was discharged. 

Based on the review of the medical record, the chart notes did not report that this patient had severe depressive symptoms, suicidal ideation, plan, or intent, severe psychomotor retardation, and did not have reports of specific identifiable or quantifiable treatment goals or objectives that could only be achieved in a 24-hour hospital setting then or that could not be achieved in a less restrictive setting then. 

The health plan acted reasonably with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient to deny coverage for inpatient hospital stay for specified dates.  However, the health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient to deny coverage for inpatient hospital stay for other dates specified.

The carrier's denial of coverage for the inpatient hospital admission should be partially overturned.

summary:
Diagnosis:  Mental Health/ Depression.
Treatment:  Mental Health Outpatient. 

The insurer denied transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) therapy.  The denial is overturned in whole.

The patient diagnosed with major depressive disorder, severe without psychotic features and co-morbid generalized anxiety disorder.  The patient has a documented history of multiple medication treatments for depression including treatment with more than two disparate classes of medication and at least four or more trials with antidepressant medications Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor (SSRIs,) serotonin norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI), and Wellbutrin, as well as combination treatment with Klonopin and Wellbutrin.

Yes, the requested health service/treatment of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) is medically necessary for this patient.

Repetitive TMS therapy as a primary or adjunctive therapy for treatment of major depression has generally been evaluated in patients who have treatment refractory or pharmaco-resistant depression, as defined by one or more, antidepressant medication treatment failures with or without augmentation, and with or without psychotherapy, especially cognitive behavioral therapy.  Transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy, as applied in major depression, is considered to be a safe treatment by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).  The data as reflected in peer reviewed medical literature supports this assertion.

Specifically, when treatments with antidepressant medication with or without augmentation, electroconvulsive therapy, and/or psychotherapy (especially cognitive behavioral therapy) have failed, then TMS is an appropriate treatment for major depressive disorder.  This assertion is noted in the American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorder, referenced below, and consistent with the scientific literature pertaining to TMS and its application to depressive disorder.

Thus, the proposed treatment of recurrent major depressive disorder using TMS therapy with a clinically appropriate number of sessions of adequate dose including a maintenance taper is medically necessary in this case.  The usual number of TMS treatment may vary depending on the individual treatment plan and need for booster sessions.
