summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse. 
Treatment: Substance Abuse Outpatient. 

The insurer denied the intensive outpatient substance use treatment. The denial is overturned, in whole. 

The patient is a male referred by his outpatient mental health providers for residential mental health treatment to address behavioral disturbances in the context of mood and attention disorders and co-occurring substance use disorder associated with impaired functioning and problematic behaviors. The patient was diagnosed with longstanding severe and recurrent major depressive disorder; attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD); and, severe co-occurring substance use disorders with severe cocaine, hallucinogen, tobacco and cannabis use disorders including the use of crack cocaine and over-the-counter medications-Benadryl and dextromethorphan (DXM). He was also using other substances of abuse intermittently including alcohol, amphetamines, benzodiazepines, opioids (heroin) and inhalants. His drugs of choice were used in a combination resulting in states of intoxication and overdoses and erratic behavior. 

The patient has a history of lengthy outpatient and more restrictive mental health and substance use disorder treatments without sustained benefit, as well as acute inpatient level psychiatric treatment for suicidal and self-harming behaviors as well as emergency treatment for at least two potentially lethal overdoses. There has been a suicidal behavior and inappropriate behaviors with associated impulse control problems and frequent bouts of intoxication associated with erratic behavior. 

Initial evaluation upon admission Intensive Outpatient Program [IOP] services revealed a mental status examination that was free of severe psychiatric symptoms such as psychosis, thought disorder, severe cognitive impairment or active suicidal ideation. The patient was cooperative with a guarded and paranoid stance in the context of oppositional behaviors and disregard for rules/authority. Mood was dysphoric and affect was anxious together with the history of emotional dysregulation and problematic behaviors that included academic failure due to behavioral issues, and behaviors that were self-destructive or reflective of severe mood disturbance and self-treatment with substances of abuse. The patient's anxiety included social anxiety associated with problematic interpersonal functioning. He was described as depressed with anxious demeanor and passive suicidal thoughts that were persistent. Insight was limited and judgment impaired with poor control of impulses. Moreover, his executive functioning was deficient including organizing, sequencing, problem solving and decision-making. 

Eventually the patient was able to fully engage in treatment and was noted to gradually gain insight and showed improved control of impulses. He remained dysphoric with anxiety that included social anxiety, apprehension, nervousness, tension, sleep disruptions, irritability and excessive worry. Family-focused sessions were beginning to gain traction and served to facilitate steady improvement that was modest. The patient was treatment plan compliant and had started to work earnestly with regard to behavioral interventions and other evidence-base therapies while participating in milieu and activity therapies designed to build self-confidence and life skills. The patient was noted to increasingly be more at ease with peers and staff, and better engaged with group and individual sessions including the incorporation of better coping skills. He had frequent family focused sessions to address issues within the family constellation and to prepare for a step down to lower level care. He consistently denied suicidal ideation or urges to self-harm during the last weeks of the treatment episode. He achieved mood regulation and became better motivated to participate in treatment including involvement in peer support groups and other therapeutic interventions to support abstinence from the multiple substances of abuse. 

After great deliberations, the patient was subsequently referred for clinically appropriate aftercare. The correspondence and case summary indicates that he had steadily participated in mental health services with better functioning and improved mood during the last three weeks of his inpatient residential stay-IOP treatment with boarding. He was noted to be at risk for regression upon return home prompting the recommendations for continued intensive mental health and substance use disorder treatment. Again, the treatment team recommendations for clinically appropriate aftercare were to have continued involvement with intensive and structured therapy, as well as psychiatric aftercare and other interventions to support abstinence and a recovery from severe substance use disorders. He was discharged with immediate step down for the extended care and lower level mental health and substance use disorder services and treatment. 

The subject under review is the medical necessity for the intensive outpatient substance use treatment. 

The requested health service/treatment of intensive outpatient substance use treatment is medically necessary for this patient. 

The patient's admission and continued IOP level treatment through discharge is reasonable and in the best interest of the patient; he continued to display clinical features and symptoms that necessitated the admission and the continued IOP level services as he struggled to engage in treatment and had intermittent bouts of affective instability that did warrant the IOP level structure and monitoring with active treatment. He had a history of treatment failure with lower level services and had recently displayed significant and problematic behaviors with maladaptive coping, emotional regulation problems, distress problems, interpersonal functioning problems and day-to-day functioning problems that included academic failure in the context of severe mood and substance use disorders complicated by ADHD. He continued to represent a safety risk and relapse risk and could not have been effectively managed in a less restrictive treatment environment through discharge. Moreover, the monitoring, structure and intensity of services were medically necessary in keeping with prevailing standards of medical practice and the application of NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Guidelines, referenced below.

summary:
Diagnosis:  Substance Abuse.
Treatment:  Inpatient Substance Abuse stay. 
The insurer denied the inpatient stay.  The health plan's determination is overturned. 

The patient is an adult male who presented for detoxification and substance-related services.  The patient has a history of severe substance use disorders with alcohol, opioid (heroin), stimulants (cocaine), and cannabis (marijuana) class substances of abuse.  He has a history of multiple detoxification treatment episodes with relapses.  He was using a 12-pack of 24 ounce beer on a continuous daily basis together with up to six bags of heroin with intravenous (IV) administration, as well as intermittent use of non-prescribed methadone and tobacco (½ pack per day) and one joint of marijuana and $20 worth of cocaine one to two times per week.

The patient's treatment could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario.  The patient in this case was using large quantities of alcohol and heroin on a daily continuous basis together with intermittent use of methadone, cocaine and cannabis that did warrant the admission and the continued inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring. Detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments pertinent to the detoxification treatment episode could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment that was provided at the time of admission.  Moreover, the patient's social environment was not conducive to an effective detoxification, and the patient had struggled with withdrawal symptoms, which were being effectively addressed with Librium and methadone protocols and supportive measures.  The patient had associated clinical features that included lack of sober supports and limited insight, impaired judgment and poor control of impulses. Diagnosis: Depressive symptoms and multiple substance use  

Treatment: Inpatient mental health treatment

The insurer denied coverage for continued inpatient mental health treatment. The denial was reversed.

This patient is a female who was admitted to this inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital due to worsened depressive symptoms and multiple substance use. She had worsened depressed and irritable mood, agitation, anhedonia, low appetite, paranoid delusions, anger, and noncompliance, was loud, fearful, and had poor insight and judgment. She was using multiple substances. She had a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder. She was prescribed the medications: Wellbutrin and Abilify. She was discharged to an inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment.

The insurer denied coverage for continued inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital as not medically necessary treatments. This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital as not medically necessary as the chart notes did provide enough specific evidence to support that she still required 24 hour hospital treatment. The APA Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Major Depressive Disorders reports that treatment settings for patients with major depressive disorder include a continuum of possible levels of care and in general, patients should be treated in the least restrictive setting that is most likely to prove safe and effective. It states that the psychiatrist should choose an appropriate site of treatment after evaluating the patient's clinical condition, including symptom severity, co-occurring conditions, level of functioning, and available support system. The estimated degree of risk to self and to others is another significant determinant of treatment setting. The decisions about treatment setting should also include consideration of the patient's ability to adequately care for him- or herself, provide reliable feedback to the psychiatrist, and cooperate with treatment of the major depressive disorder.

In this case this patient was unable to care for herself adequately if not in 24 hour treatment, as she had depressive symptoms and dangerous behavior. She had noncompliance and a history of using multiple serious substances. She still was agitated and loud during the denial period and could not be safely discharged to outpatient treatment as she needed to be discharged from this 24 hour hospital setting to a 24 hour inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment. She was a high risk for relapse without the 24 hour supervision and structure of a therapeutic inpatient substance rehabilitation setting. The notes on a specified date reported that she was screaming at a visitor, was loud, and agitated. The notes on another date reported that she was loud, verbally abusive, threatening to punch staff in the face, irritable, and argumentative. She was intrusive and then discharged to the inpatient substance rehabilitation setting. She was considered unable to care for herself without these 24 hour supports and still had agitation, threatening behavior, and mood symptoms until discharge putting herself and others at risk of danger. 

As a result, the determination to reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for continued inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital. It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably or in the best interests of the patient.  .

Based on the above, the medical necessity for inpatient hospital admission is substantiated.  The insurer's denial is reversed.

This patient is a female who was admitted to inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital due to self mutilatory behavior by cutting herself with a knife, depressed mood, crying, agitation, and she reported stressors.  She reportedly had a history of opiate use and was on Methadone maintenance in addition to taking Haldol, Venlafaxine, Klonopin, and Lorazepam.  She reportedly was homeless.  She had past reported suicide attempts, self-injurious behavior, and past psychiatric hospitalizations.  She also was in the Personalized Recovery Orientation Service (PROS) program.  The patient was discharged.

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital as not medically necessary treatment.  This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital for a specified range but agree with the decision to deny coverage for other days specified as the chart notes supported that she was considered a danger to self by cutting self with her past history of suicide attempts, current depressed mood and crying and stressors, and her past history of opiate use.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Suicidal Behaviors reports that patients with past suicide attempts are at high risk for suicide and that past suicide attempts are the single most reliable predictor of suicide.  It also states that patients with major depressive episodes and a history of substance use are at increased risk for suicide.  This patient had worsened depressive symptoms and stressors and cut herself with a knife, so she was a danger to self.  Even though she reported that this was not a suicide attempt, it is appropriate and standard care to assess a patient with past suicide attempts and current self-injurious behavior and depressive symptoms with a history of substance use who is homeless and has current stressors for a few days even when they deny suicidality, as they are still considered at risk for suicide.  

The APA Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Suicidal Behaviors report also that patients may require more time in the hospital to better assess suicide because they sometimes do not tell the truth regarding their suicidal thoughts in order to leave the hospital and that observation in the hospital is appropriate to better ensure their safety.  This patient was considered a high risk patient and benefitted from remaining in the hospital and being observed and assessed for safety for a few days until a specified range.  However, as of a date indicated there were no reports of further suicidal ideation, plan, or intent, or self-injurious behavior, severe depressive symptoms, withdrawal symptoms, severe agitation, aggression, psychotic symptoms, or acute medical instability. 
 
As a result, modify the insurer's decision and approve continued inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital from a specified range but deny continued inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital for a specified couple of days.  It appeared that the insurer acted reasonably and in the best interests of the patient from a specified range but not for a specified couple of days.

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient psychiatric treatment. The denial was reversed.

This patient is a male admitted for acute inpatient psychiatric treatment.  He was diagnosed with Bipolar Disorder, Current Episode Depressed, Severe, without psychotic features. The medical record indicates the patient indicate that he was hospitalized after attempting suicide by cutting his wrists with a box cutter.  He reported being severely depressed.  He reported hopelessness in the context of family and financial stressors as well as homelessness.  He reported several months of cycling between mania and depression.  There was information that he went to train tracks but he denied this was a result of suicidality.  He had a history of multiple hospitalizations over the previous months, and he had been discharged from a prior hospitalization. On admission his medications were reported as Depakote and Abilify.  Upon admission he denied suicidal or homicidal ideation or intent.  He was guarded.  Following admission he was Abilify and Depakote.  Notes over the next several days document the patient reported ongoing depression, helplessness and hopelessness.  He was noted to be isolating, withdrawn, with deteriorated functioning.

On a specified date he was prescribed Zyprexa.  As of another date it was documented that the patient was going to most groups and unit activities, was friendly but asocial, had organized thinking, and euthymic mood.  He was compliant with medication treatment and he denied suicidal ideation.  He continued to be improved with some variation in his mood over the next week.  He began to be screened by housing programs. He began to show increased irritability with verbal outbursts, intrusiveness, behavioral agitation, and sexual disinhibition; he was treated with Zyprexa, Risperdal (with plan to use long acting injectable medication), Depakote, trazodone, and Prozac. He continued to report a mixture of depressive and manic symptoms, and the patient's brother expressed concern regarding his suicide potential.  Over the course of the next two weeks he continued to have symptoms of depression and was continually assessed as being unable to be safely discharged without a comprehensive treatment plan which was not able to be affected.  He continued to display depressive symptoms and a flat affect.  Application was made for transfer to a long-term hospital setting.   

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment. Based upon the information available the patient medically required ongoing acute inpatient psychiatric care until a long term care transfer could be accomplished; as such the insurer's denial of coverage for inpatient psychiatric treatment is reversed. He had ongoing symptoms of Bipolar Disorder and was assess as being at high suicidal risk if outside a hospital setting. His treatment team made appropriate efforts to reduce his symptoms such that a discharge could be affected, and once they determined that this was not likely to happen they effected an involuntary commitment and pursued long-term hospitalization.  Until such time as the patient is able to be transferred to a long-term care hospitalization he requires ongoing acute treatment.  It would have been unsafe to discharge the patient to a lower level of care in the interim.

This finding is consistent with the general standards of psychiatric care, the APA Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Bipolar Disorder, and InterQual Behavioral Health Criteria 2018 Adult and Geriatric Psychiatry, Hospitalization, Psychiatric, Adult, Mental Health Criteria.  

Based on the above, the medical necessity for the inpatient mental health treatment is substantiated.  The insurer's denial is reversed.

The patient is a male who was admitted following medical screening to acute inpatient level services for monitoring and detoxification and withdrawal management of opioid use disorder with use of two to three grams of heroin daily with intravenous (IV) administration. The patient had experienced severe opioid withdrawal in the past and had mild to moderately severe withdrawal at the time of admission with body aches, bone pain, nausea, abdominal cramps and diarrhea, as well as anxiety, irritability and restlessness with Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) scale score of 11. He also had extensive substance use disorder treatment in the past including at least two detoxification and inpatient rehabilitation treatment episodes, and he had participated in medication assisted treatment with methadone and Suboxone together with outpatient treatment.

The patient was admitted to acute inpatient level care and placed on a detoxification regimen with a methadone taper together with nicotine replacement therapy, and medical monitoring. Following his third day of treatment, the patient began to participate actively in counseling and educational sessions, as his withdrawal symptoms diminished, and he was feeling better. His mental status examination included persistent symptoms of anxiety and irritability with associated symptoms of insomnia. He had no severe symptoms such as mania, psychosis, perceptual disturbance or severe cognitive impairment. He was treated with clonidine, Vistaril and gabapentin and as needed (prn) medications to address pain, nausea, diarrhea, anxiety, agitation and insomnia. Comfort medications and monitoring were continued. 
The patient was initially ambivalent about treatment and required motivational techniques and ongoing counseling including case management to work toward a safe and clinically appropriate discharge plan and disposition. Again, he was provided education and counseling during the remaining inpatient stay. The patient was discharged with recommendations for clinically appropriate aftercare, as well as recommendations for involvement in 12-step recovery meetings with Alcoholic and Narcotics Anonymous (AA and NA). He declined transfer for inpatient rehabilitation treatment and was discharged with referral for intensive outpatient program (IOP) level rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment.

The health plan's determination is overturned.

The proposed inpatient services and detoxification treatment and withdrawal management for severe use disorder and other services noted in the clinical summary could not have been safely and effectively provided at a lower level of care, as noted in the answer to question 1 above. The adult inpatient treatment of this patient's substance use disorder did warrant the admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level setting and 24-hour monitoring in view of the severity of the substance use disorder and the associated psychosocial stressors and impairment of functioning. Withdrawal symptoms were managed with tapering dosages of methadone requiring monitoring and prn medications, as well as the availability of comfort medications and nicotine replacement therapy. Counseling and educational sessions with motivational techniques together with case management services were appropriately provided to motivate the patient's transition to rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment. Thus, the patient did require a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management during the time frame under review with associated substance use disorder treatments, as it was reasonable that the patient would have been unable to abstain from the substances of abuse if detoxification and treatment were to be attempted at a lower level of care.

Diagnosis: Substance Use

Treatment: Residential substance use treatment admission

The insurer denied coverage for residential substance use treatment admission. The denial reversed.

This patient is a male who was admitted to this inpatient substance residential treatment for inpatient substance detoxification with a Librium protocol. He had a
2-decades history of substance use.  He was using Xanax and Klonopin, as well as Fentanyl and Roxicodone.  He had an overdose two months prior to this admission. He had withdrawal symptoms including nausea, vomiting, sweating, stomach cramping, anxiety, irritable mood, and runny nose with a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment of Alcohol (CIWA) score of 9.  He had a Librium protocol and was admitted for substance rehabilitation.  He had a history of 10+ past inpatient substance treatments and had diagnoses of Sedative Use Disorder and Opiate Use Disorder.  He also had a reported diagnosis of Unspecified Anxiety Disorder.  He took Tegretol, Clonidine, and Buprenorphine which was discontinued.  It was reported that sober living was recommended upon discharge, but he was discharged back to his apartment. 

The insurer denied coverage for continued inpatient substance residential treatment as not medically necessary treatment. This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for continued inpatient substance residential treatment as the chart notes provided enough specific evidence to support that he required this 24-hour inpatient substance residential rehabilitation treatment.  The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that inpatient treatment is indicated primarily for individuals whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting.  

In this case, this patient was considered in need of 24-hour substance rehabilitation treatment as he was using multiple serious substances including Xanax and Klonopin, as well as Fentanyl and Roxicodone.  He was at risk for another overdose and was also considered at risk for severe and life-threatening complicated withdrawal due to the use of multiple serious substances including opiates and benzodiazepines.  Additionally, he had an overdose two months prior to admission.  According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), he met criteria for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment as he continued to use multiple substances despite multiple past inpatient substance treatments including 10+ inpatient substance treatments.  
He was unable to stop substance use without being in a sober and supervised therapeutic inpatient substance residential setting.  Also, the National Institute on Drug Abuse: Principles of Addiction Treatment: A Research Based Guide- reports that research indicates that most addicted individuals need at least three months in treatment to significantly reduce or stop their drug use and that the best treatment outcomes occur with longer durations of treatment.  

As a result, reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for continued inpatient substance residential treatment.  The health care plan did not act reasonably or with sound medical judgment or in the best interests of the patient.

The carrier's denial of coverage for the residential substance use treatment admission is reversed.  The medical necessity is substantiated.

This patient is a male who was admitted to this inpatient hospital after presenting with chest pain, facial injury, back pain, headache, anxiety, loss of consciousness, and a reported asthma attack after being physically attacked by a group.  He reported that he was punched and that a weapon was used.  He also was treated with a Librium protocol for alcohol detoxification.  He had withdrawal symptoms including nausea, tremors, insomnia, anxiety, fatigue, irritable mood, increased heart rate of 99, and agitation.  He was drinking 1 pint to 1/5 per day of liquor and reported the last drink on the morning of admission.  He had a history of blackouts.  He had multiple past inpatient detoxification treatments and 5 past inpatient rehabilitation treatments.  He had past legal issues.  He lacked sober supports.  He became agitated and was physically and verbally aggressive.  He was administratively discharged.

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient substance detoxification treatment stating that it was not medically necessary.

This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient substance detoxification treatment as the chart notes provided did support that he required 24-hour hospital detoxification treatment.  The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment.  In this case, this patient had been drinking large amounts of alcohol daily and had current withdrawal symptoms including nausea, tremors, insomnia, anxiety, fatigue, irritable mood, increased heart rate of 99, and agitation.  

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), he did require 24-hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated in outpatient detoxification settings.  This was evidenced by his continued use of large amounts of alcohol despite multiple past inpatient detoxification treatments and past inpatient rehabilitation treatments.  He continued to drink large amounts of alcohol daily.  He also required detoxification including Librium to modify withdrawal and prevent more severe, complicated, or life-threatening withdrawal.  It was unlikely that he would remain abstinent while still having withdrawal symptoms; therefore, he required the time in this treatment setting.  The risk of complicated withdrawal such as delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use.  As such, he required inpatient alcohol detoxification treatment.  Additionally, he had a reported history of Bipolar Disorder and Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) after the 911 attacks.

As a result, reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for inpatient substance detoxification.  The health care plan did not act reasonably, or with sound medical judgment, or in the best interests of the patient.

The patient was noted to be disoriented, confused, agitated, and unable to care for self. summary:
Diagnosis: Substance use; withdrawal symptoms

Treatment: Substance use medically supervised inpatient rehabilitation

The insurer denied coverage for substance use medically supervised inpatient rehabilitation. The denial reversed.

This patient is a male who was admitted to this inpatient hospital treatment for inpatient withdrawal management. He had withdrawal symptoms including nausea, tremors, sweats, elevated heart rate of 105, anxiety, teary eyes, irritable mood, and sleeping problems. He was drinking large amounts of alcohol daily including 2 pints of liquor and 25 beers per day, and was smoking crack and cannabis per day. He had multiple past detoxifications in recent years. He took Sertraline. He was given Librium for withdrawal management for a specified range and was then discharged.

The insurer denied coverage for this inpatient substance use medically supervised hospital treatment for inpatient withdrawal management as not medically necessary treatment then. This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient substance use medically supervised hospital treatment for inpatient withdrawal management as the chart notes provided enough specific evidence to support that he required 24-hour hospital treatment for detoxification. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. In this case, this patient had been drinking very large amounts of alcohol daily and had active withdrawal symptoms. He was at risk for more severe, complicated, and life- threatening withdrawal symptoms and required 24-hour inpatient substance hospital treatment for detoxification.

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), he did require 24-hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated in outpatient detoxification settings. This was evidenced by the fact that he continued to use very large amounts of alcohol and was smoking crack and cannabis daily with multiple prior inpatient detoxification treatments. Also, he required and needed detoxification medication including Libriumto modify withdrawal. He needed 24-hour treatment as he was at risk for worsened withdrawal symptoms if not in this 24-hour setting, including severe and life-threatening withdrawal symptoms. It was unlikely that he would remain abstinent while having withdrawal symptoms; therefore, he required the time in this treatment setting to stop withdrawals and decrease the chance that he would relapse again when not in this 24-hour setting.

The risk of complicated withdrawal such as delirium tremens can occur 4 days after alcohol use; therefore, he required the entire time in the inpatient setting. He also did not have the coping skills to maintain abstinence and to be treated in a less restrictive setting other than this inpatient detoxification hospital treatment, as he could not stop substance use outside of a 24-hour hospital setting. As a result, reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for inpatient substance hospital treatment for medically supervised inpatient withdrawal management. The health care plan did not act reasonably, or with sound medical judgment, or in the best interests of the patient.   

Based on the above, the medical necessity for the substance use medically supervised inpatient rehabilitation is substantiated.  The insurer's denial is reversed.

Also, the MCG Inpatient Residential Behavioral Health Level of Care-Child and Adolescent medical necessity guidelines report that if the patient has moderately or severe psychiatric or behavioral symptoms requiring 24-hour daily treatment or serious dysfunction in daily living then the patient meets criteria for residential treatment. It also states that for discharge there needs to be sufficient support at a lower level of care, absence of suicidal or homicidal thoughts or thoughts of harm to self or others. 

Despite the inpatient care received from a specified date forward, clinical guidelines support that this patient's persistent pattern of abusive behavior and mood instability indicates that this patient's inpatient 24-hour care from a specified date forward and continuous inpatient stay are medically necessary for this patient to make further, clinical progress to prevent harm to the patient and to others.

The health place did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.

The carrier denial of coverage for the Residential Mental Health Treatment is reversed.  The medical necessity is substantiated.

She was admitted to inpatient residential mental health treatment after being hospitalized for psychotic and mood symptoms. It was reported she had auditory, visual, tactile hallucinations, paranoia, perceptual disturbance, depressed and angry mood, posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms, anxiety, and feelings of shame, self-loathing, loneliness, and hopelessness. 

The medical records provided did not provide specific evidence to support that she could only be safely and effectively treated in this inpatient residential mental health treatment then or that she could not safely and effectively treated in a less restrictive setting.  The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Schizophrenia report that the least restrictive level of care for safe and effective treatment is appropriate.  It also states that patients with hallucinations, delusional thinking, disorganized thinking or behavior, suicidal or homicidal plan or intent, agitation, or aggressive behavior are candidates for inpatient treatment.  In this case the patient had improvement in her clinical condition from admission as she denied psychotic symptoms, had less reported depressive symptoms, and she denied suicidal ideation, and there were no reports of out of control behavior.  

The notes on a specified date reported that she denied psychotic symptoms, still had depressed mood but had less depression and was feeling better, had brighter affect, was more energized and forward looking, had no hallucinations or delusions, was goal directed in thought process, and she was not taking antipsychotic medication anymore.   She reportedly was taking Wellbutrin.  Notes reported that psychosis appeared to have resolved with no antipsychotic medications.  It was reported that after an increase in Wellbutrin dosage, she had significant mood benefits.  It also was reported that her current presentation was close to her baseline.  There were no reports of suicidal or homicidal ideation, self-injurious, threatening, or aggressive behavior.  The notes reported that she was moved to a step down residential treatment.  The notes on notes from reported that she was at baseline with some variability of mood.  She reportedly denied psychotic symptoms despite not taking antipsychotic medications.  She responded to the medication changes and treatment and was no longer reporting psychotic symptoms, had less reported depressive symptoms, and denied suicidal or homicidal ideation.  

The chart notes as of the day of admission did not provide enough specific evidence to support that she was still having severe psychiatric symptoms requiring 24 hour mental health residential treatment then.  As of then, the chart notes did not report specific identifiable and quantifiable treatment objectives or goals that could only be achieved in a 24 hour mental health residential treatment or that she could not be treated in a less restrictive level of care.  

It appeared that the health care plan acted reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interests of the patient.  

The carrier's denial of coverage for the continued residential treatment mental health services is upheld.  The medical necessity is not substantiated.

He was given intravenous (IV) Ativan and was put on a Librium protocol for detoxification from alcohol. He was treated and discharged after 3 days of inpatient stay.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that patients who fail to achieve abstinence, relapse frequently, fail to cooperate with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, have current abuse of other substances with very heavy use or tolerance that places them at high risk for complicated withdrawal, are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. In this case, this patient had active alcohol withdrawal symptoms and elevated blood pressures. 

The patient's comorbid medical condition of hypertension put him at risk medically as he continued to have elevated blood pressures in the setting of alcohol withdrawal, and required stabilization. According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), the patient was at high-risk for complicated and life-threatening withdrawal symptoms and therefore required 24-hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated in a less restrictive detoxification setting.

The patient presented with active withdrawal symptoms that required two detoxification medications to stabilize his withdrawal symptoms. He was at risk for worsened withdrawal symptoms. The patient's risk of life complicated withdrawal such as delirium tremens can occur 4 days after alcohol use. The patient used large amounts of alcohol and required the entire time of inpatient stay in this hospital detoxification setting.

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.

Based on the above, the medical necessity for inpatient admission is substantiated.  The insurer's denial should be overturned.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance abuse/Mental health. 
Treatment: Partial hospital program (PHP) level substance use disorder treatment and mental health treatment. 

The insurer denied the partial hospital program (PHP) level substance use disorder treatment and mental health treatment. The denial is overturned. 

This case involves an adult female admitted to partial hospital program (PHP) level substance use disorder treatment of severe alcohol use disorder and a co-occurring mood disorder. The admission for partial hospital program (PHP) level substance use disorder rehabilitation services occurred in the context of a history of failed treatment episodes in the past with residential treatment, and the admission represented her fifth attempt at substance use disorder treatment. Her presentation for substance use disorder treatment was prompted by deterioration in family and social functioning. She was using alcohol on a daily continuous use in large quantity including box wine and vodka. She had a history of frequent blackouts and drinking to the point of passing out with a binge pattern of use and had experienced delirium tremens (DTs) in the past. The patient denied use of other substances of abuse. 

The patient had been treated in the past for co-occurring major depressive disorder and unspecified anxiety disorder with panic attacks and social and generalized symptoms of anxiety, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and she had a past diagnosis of borderline personality with trauma history (post-traumatic stress disorder). Her psychotropic medication regimen included Prozac, Buspar, and trazodone with as needed (PRN) use of hydroxyzine and past treatments with Concerta and Adderall. 

During her brief stay, the patient began working to develop a plan for step down to intensive outpatient program (IOP) level treatment including work with her family to assure better sober supports. There was consideration of restarting a stimulant to address her problems with attention and concentration. She was discharged from PHP level services with step down to intensive outpatient program (IOP) level care for continued rehabilitation services and the development of a safe and clinically appropriate discharge plan. The discharge plan called for continued intensive treatment of the co-occurring disorders to include involvement in peer-supported recovery groups with the obtainment of a sponsor. 

Yes, the requested health service of Partial Hospital Program Treatment was medically necessary for this patient. 

The Partial Hospital Program Treatment was medically necessary for this patient in order to effectively address the continuing clinical needs for rehabilitation treatment of severe alcohol use disorder with evidence-based psychosocial treatments, and to work toward relapse prevention; in order to address the patient's lack of awareness of the seriousness of her illnesses with psycho-education and recovery groups; and in order to address issues within the social environment including development of an appropriate disposition with sober supports; and, in order to work on coping skills that will be necessary in building a sober support system and continued recovery efforts with community providers and engagement with 12-step recovery groups and a sponsor. 

The patient was noted to have ongoing cravings and persistent post-acute withdrawal symptoms that rendered her at high risk for relapse. A psychotropic medication regimen was used for treatment of the co-occurring psychiatric disorders combined with cognitive behavioral therapy and trauma-related interventions. The patient's continued struggle with mood disturbance and severe psychosocial stressors warranted the admission and continued PHP level structure and monitoring to assure abstinence while working on the development of relapse prevention plan and coping skills that were critical in this case together with necessary gains with insight that facilitated acquisition of better coping skills. 

Thus, the admission and continued PHP level treatment provided the clinically appropriate components of the treatment that were provided with necessary and appropriate structure, intensity of services, and monitoring. The continued PHP treatment through discharge was therefore medically necessary including continued monitoring for abstinence for the duration of the proposed treatment in order to achieve stability and make a safe transition to lower level treatment and transition to IOP level care. None of this therapeutic work could have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in view of the multiple, complicating factors in this case for the time interval under review.

summary:
Diagnosis: Unspecified psychosis.
Treatment: Continued Inpatient Behavior Services.
The insurer denied the Continued Inpatient Behavior Services.
The denial is overturned. 

Yes, the Continued inpatient behavioral health services was medically necessary.

The patient is a male with a history of mental illness.

The patient has a chronic psychotic illness. He was initially brought in to the ER by the police after having acted in a bizarre and erratic manner in the community, including a violent assault on a police officer.  He received a chemical restraint due to his behaviors.  He was evaluated and noted to be paranoid and delusional.  He was medically cleared for hospitalization and was admitted.

The patient received treatment by a multidisciplinary team, including psychiatry, nursing, and therapy staff.  He received individual and group therapy.  He received a psychopharmacology evaluation, and Clozapine was re-titrated to 200mg PO (by mouth) BID (twice daily).  He attacked a peer and a staff member, and Haldol was used for agitation.  The patient was noted to have tested positive for COVID-19 and was kept in isolation at one point.  

It was explicitly noted by the patient's social worker "he remains in need of inpatient psychiatric treatment to address psychotic process that persists."  The patient was noted to have poor insight and limited judgement.  

The patient received Haldol as a prn (as needed) for agitation and was noted to have attacked two peers and a staff member over the prior weekend.  He was noted by the doctor to be "quite malodorous."  

The patient was discharged another facility.

The patient represented an acutely elevated risk of dangerous behaviors, and there was no less-restrictive treatment environment appropriate.  The acute risk factors of psychosis with the chronic risk factors of potentially dangerous behaviors suggest that the patient would have been at an acute risk of aggressive or self-injurious behaviors (including but not limited to suicide) were he to have been discharged from the inpatient hospital setting.  The patient was discharged from the inpatient psychiatric hospital setting as soon as a less-restrictive treatment setting was appropriate. Therefore, the treatment was medically necessary.  While the patient was not endorsing active suicidality or homicidally, the patient remained psychotic.  The patient had multiple static risk factors for potentially dangerous behaviors, including history of violence and diagnosis with a severe mental illness.  Therefore, the patient represented a chronic risk of potentially dangerous behaviors.  The fact that patient remained psychotic was an acute risk factor for dangerous behaviors.  Furthermore, the fact that there was no less-restrictive environment of care appropriate suggests that ongoing inpatient psychiatric hospitalization was medically necessary and should be covered by the patient's health plan.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major depressive disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD), and generalized anxiety disorder 
Treatment: Continued inpatient mental health admission 

The insurer denied the continued inpatient mental health admission. The denial is upheld. 

No, the proposed treatment was not medically necessary. 

The patient is a female with diagnoses of major depressive disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD), and generalized anxiety disorder who was admitted under mental health arrest due to suicidal ideation nine days after discharge from a residential treatment program. She also had a history of self-injury by scratching herself with her fingernails. The patient's clinical presentation throughout her stay was highly suggestive of a severe cluster B personality disorder. Although there was no actual documented history of true suicide attempts, the patient reported virtually continual suicidal ideation, usually with plans such as choking herself with a blanket or by head-banging. She had poor boundaries, engaged in behaviors which were destructive to other patients' treatment plans, and indulged in staff splitting. Her frequent statements regarding suicidality were evasive and ambiguous. 

The treatment team acknowledged the patient's chronic thoughts of self-harm but recognized her ability to keep herself safe by reaching out for support. Discharge was planned for later that week. However, at another meeting, the patient's mother expressed concern about the patient's safety at home and requested a second opinion. The patient wanted to change her location on the unit, feeling that she could not communicate with her treatment team. The treatment team yielded to this apparent splitting behavior, and the decision was made to transfer the patient's care to a different treatment team where she remained on 15 minute checks. 

The patient went home on a pass "so that she can better assess her risk of lethality and readmission." The patient continued to report suicidal ideation and was evaluated for electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). She reported increased suicidal ideation after her first session. The patient asked for ECT to be continued. She stated that her goal was to be discharged by the end of the month, but she had refused ECT stating that she did not think it was working and was experiencing side effects as well as increased suicidal ideation. 

The team pointed out to the patient the contradiction in her commitment and her persistence in continuing her schoolwork with college plans while at the same time being persistent in reporting suicidal ideation.

Another change in unit location was made due to the patient's issues with boundaries and her giving other patients advice that contradicted their treatment plans. Discharge was planned for at the patient's request.  The patient stated she planned to stay with her father upon discharge. She was discharged on that date with an extensive safety plan. 

The patient presented chronic suicidal ideation which was vague and devoid of specific lethal plans or intent. There was no documented history of true suicidal behavior. The patient generally expressed plans which were at most para-suicidal in nature. The patient's clinical presentation at discharge was no different than it was at the time of admission and reflected an inability to benefit from the current level of care. The treatment team's agreeing to the patient's and possibly her mother's requests was not in the best interest of the patient. Nothing in the documentation reviewed indicates that this patient's treatment could not have been carried out equally safely and effectively in a less intensive setting.

summary:
Diagnosis:  Substance and alcohol use disorder 
Treatment:  Inpatient detoxification admission 

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient detoxification admission. The denial is reversed.  

This patient is a male was admitted to this inpatient substance detoxification treatment for alcohol, Xanax, and heroin detoxification.  He had withdrawal symptoms including tremors, joint pain, irritable mood, and anxiety.  He reportedly had been drinking 1/2 pint of vodka per day with 6 beers for with over three decades, using 4 mg of Xanax per day for more than a decade, and inhaling 3 bags of heroin per day for over a decade.  He had past reported multiple inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatments.  He also reportedly had a diagnosis of bipolar depression in addition to his alcohol, Xanax, and heroin use disorders.  He also had past psychiatric hospitalizations for past reported suicide attempts.  He was put on a Librium protocol for detoxification and was discharged with a referral to substance residential rehabilitation treatment scheduled.  

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient substance detoxification treatment.  This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient substance detoxification treatment, as the as the chart notes did provide enough specific evidence to support that he needed this level of care.  The APA Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, who fail to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, who currently abuse of other substances, who have very heavy use or tolerance, putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal, are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment.  In this case this patient had use of multiple substances, including large amounts of alcohol, Xanax, and heroin, and was at risk for death from overdose as result of this use.  

According to the LOCADTR he did require 24 hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive setting, as he continued to use multiple serious substances of use despite multiple past inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatments, and he needed two detoxification medications including Librium and Clonidine to modify withdrawal from alcohol, Xanax, and heroin.  Also, he had reports of long term multiple substances of use and was at risk for worsened withdrawal symptoms if not in this 24-hour setting then, including severe, complicated, and life threatening withdrawal, such as delirium tremens, due to the large amount of alcohol and Xanax use.  Also, he likely would have relapsed again as evidenced by relapsing after past treatments.  

As a result, the recommendation is to reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for inpatient substance detoxification.  It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably or in the best interests of the patient.  

Based on the above, the medical necessity for the inpatient detoxification admission is substantiated.  The insurer's denial is reversed.

He was later found to have a urinary tract infection. While in the emergency department, he reported that he had become increasingly depressed with suicidal ideation with a plan. He reported deterioration in functioning and had stopped his psychotropic medication four months earlier. He has a history of bipolar disorder with severe depressive episodes and psychiatric treatment with therapy and medications, as well as past treatment for co-occurring substance use disorders. 
The mental status examination revealed dysphoric mood with anxiety including apprehension, nervousness, tension, irritability, and excessive worry. Sleep, appetite, energy levels and volition were disturbed.  He was withdrawn with motor agitation and was irritable and demanding and uncooperative with the psychiatric evaluation. There was no psychosis or other signs of cognitive impairment, but he reported perceptual disturbance with command auditory hallucinations. Judgment was markedly impaired, and suicidal risk was judged to be moderately severe.
There are no legal issues or trauma/abuse history reported in this case. 
The patient was admitted with plans for close observation, safety monitoring, structured milieu therapy, and pharmacotherapy with Seroquel, Depakote and Prozac, as well as vitamin and nicotine replacement therapy. He continued to exhibit mood disturbance with dysphoria and labile affect. He had bouts of mood cycling with argumentative and demanding behavior, loud speech, poor concentration, and persistently impaired judgment and limited insight. He denied active suicidal ideation and the auditory hallucinations resolved. He was medication adherent with tolerability. 
The patient's mood improved and he continued to take medications without adverse effect. He denied suicidal ideation, plan or intent. 
The patient was discharged from inpatient level care with step down to the community for clinically appropriate aftercare.

The continued acute inpatient level structure and monitoring is reasonable in view of the patient's severe symptoms of mood disorder and co-occurring substance use disorders; in view of the severe psychosocial stressors in this case with limited social supports; and, in view of the need for continued active treatment in the context of deteriorated functioning.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major depressive disorder
Treatment: continued inpatient mental health services
The insurer denied coverage for continued inpatient mental health services.
The denial is upheld.

This is a male patient who was admitted for inpatient mental health treatment due to worsened depressive symptoms including feeling very depressed in mood, suicidal thoughts multiple times per day without intent or plan, psychomotor retardation, worthlessness, tearfulness, helplessness, command auditory hallucinations, poor activities of daily living (ADLs), and noncompliance. The patient reported daily cannabis use and alcohol use days prior to admission. The patient's urine toxicology was positive for cannabinoids. The patient had a diagnosis of major depressive disorder with psychotic features, and was treated with sertraline and Zyprexa. The patient reportedly improved and was discharged on day 8 of admission.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Major Depressive Disorders report that the least restrictive level of care for safe and effective treatment is appropriate and that patients with suicidal plan or intent or behaviors, severe depressive symptoms, or inability to adequately care for basic needs are candidates for hospitalization. Based on the review of the medical record, as of day 5 of admission, there were no reports of suicidal or homicidal ideation, intent, or plan, inability to adequately care for basic needs, manic episodes, and psychotic symptoms, self-injurious, aggressive, threatening, or agitated behavior to warrant and justify for inpatient level of care.  As of day 5 of admission, the chart notes did not provide enough specific evidence that the patient was an imminent danger to self or others or unable to adequately care for his basic needs. Also, as of then, there were no reports of specific identifiable or quantifiable treatment goals or objectives that could only be achieved in a 24-hour acute psychiatric hospital setting or that could not be achieved in a less restrictive setting. Thus, the continued inpatient mental health services from day 5 of admission forward were not medically necessary for this patient. 

The health plan acted reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient.

The carrier's denial of coverage for the continued inpatient mental health services from day 5 of admission forward should be upheld. The medical necessity is not substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder), major mood disorder
Treatment: Continued partial hospitalization mental health treatment 
The insurer denied the Continued partial hospitalization mental health treatment.
The denial is upheld. 

This female has been attending this partial hospital program (PHP) with diagnoses of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and major depression. The patient reportedly witnessed domestic violence, had violent outbursts toward her mother, and was sexually promiscuous. She has a highly conflicted relationship with her parents. She had multiple psychiatric hospitalizations following suicidal or para-suicidal behaviors and ideation. 

As per an appeal letter the patient has made great progress in the current program. 

No significant behavioral problems were noted. Specific behaviors noted as supporting continued care at this level were that the patient frequently interrupted group sessions and participated in side conversations instead of being attentive and respectful to a speaker. 

The appeal letter states that if the patient were to return home during this time, she would very likely fall back into old behaviors that ultimately could lead to her experiencing intense suicidal ideation. The utilization review specialist argues in the appeal letter that, "It is generally accepted in the behavioral health community that effective treatment of individuals with mental health or substance use disorders is not limited to alleviation of the current symptoms. Rather, effective treatment requires treatment of the chronic underlying conditions as well."

No, the proposed treatment is not medically necessary. 

The UR specialist is correct in her statement that "effective treatment of individuals with mental health or substance use disorders is not limited to alleviation of the current symptoms" and that "effective treatment requires treatment of the chronic underlying conditions as well."

This does not however mean that ongoing effective treatment requires the current level of care or cannot be effective in an ongoing but less restrictive treatment program. Progress notes available for review show no evidence of active major depression, suicidality, or behavioral dyscontrol. The patient's mood was repeatedly described as bright. The minor instances of defiance cited in the lengthy appeal letter do not constitute a reasonable rationale for indefinite continuation of the current level of care. Based on the documentation reviewed, treatment could have continued safely and effectively in a less restrictive setting.

Additionally, the patient was diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) or executive dysfunction that contributed to his difficulties with emotional regulation and anger/irritability.
The patient has longstanding issues with self-esteem, confidence, and relationship problems together with stressors within the primary support, educational and social environment domains; the patient has been in past treatment settings with continued symptoms of depression, anxiety and anger related symptoms together with a history of impulsive aggression and verbal violence toward family members and destruction of property, social withdrawal, and mood instability associated with substance use with daily continuous use of cannabis and intermittent use of other substances of abuse, as noted. The patient was referred to IOP treatment after being administratively discharged from a Wilderness Program (outdoor behavioral health program) in order to address the problematic behaviors and core symptoms of depression, anxiety and relationship/family problems including parent-child relational problems and his lack of motivation and the moderately severe substance use disorder with cannabis.
The patient has a history of outpatient treatments without sustained benefit. There have been violent and aggressive behaviors related to anger and impulse control problems. The patient has conflict with parents that did include lack of motivation and problematic behavioral disruptions that included violent behavior and the abuse of cannabis and other substances.
Initial evaluation upon admission revealed a mental status examination that was free of severe psychiatric symptoms such as psychosis, thought disorder, severe cognitive impairment or active suicidal ideation. Mood was dysphoric and irritable, and, affect was anxious together with a history of problematic behaviors that included impulsive aggression/anger and conflict with parents, and other behaviors that were self-destructive or reflective of severe mood disturbance including social withdrawal and self-treatment with substances of abuse. The patient's anxiety and anger were associated with problematic interpersonal functioning. He was described as depressed with anxious demeanor, but superficially cooperative and calm during the assessment. Insight was limited and judgment impaired with poor control of impulses.
The patient had no acute general medical conditions. The patient is supported in his treatment effort by family. He is a college student and is single.
The patient was referred and admitted and underwent a comprehensive evaluation with treatment planning that included therapeutic interventions to improve coping skills and self-esteem, as well as cognitive behavior therapy to address the mood and anxiety disorder. The treatment plan included the goals of improved coping; breaking the cycle of self-destructive behaviors including anger issues and impulsive aggression; and the development of healthy relationships and functioning.

The patient has a history of treatment failure with lower level services prior to admission to the IOP program and had recently displayed significant oppositional/aggressive behaviors with maladaptive coping, emotional regulation problems, distress problems, interpersonal functioning problems and day-to-day functioning program in the context of severe mood and anxiety disorders complicated by moderately severe substance use disorder. He continued to represent a safety risk, and could not have been effectively managed in a less restrictive treatment environment during the dates of service provided. summary:
Diagnosis: Substance abuse
Treatment: Inpatient substance abuse treatment 
The insurer denied the inpatient substance abuse treatment.
The denial is overturned. 

The patient is a male requesting detoxification treatment and admitted to acute inpatient level care in order to address substance use disorder with opioid (heroin), alcohol, and stimulant (cocaine) class substances, as well as use of cannabis, hallucinogen and sedative-hypnotic-anxiolytic class drugs of abuse. The patient had been using up to 12 bags of heroin with intravenous (IV) administration together drinking three pints of liquor daily. He was using cocaine intermittently with use of crack or freebase cocaine with IV administration of up to one gram. He has no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens. He had a history of prior detoxification and substance use disorder treatments with up to twenty to fifty treatment episodes many of which were back-to-back. His self-referral for treatment was prompted by multiple stressors including housing, primary support, social environment and other psychosocial domains.

The patient was admitted to detoxification treatment with a comprehensive detoxification protocol with tapering dosages of methadone and Librium, and clonidine as needed, and prn medications for comfort, as well as vitamin replacement therapy and use of Depakote for seizure prophylaxis. The program provided for case management with referral to sober housing and access to rehabilitation treatment that included comprehensive evidence-based treatments. During detoxification the patient engaged in counseling sessions focusing on education about the disease model of addiction, and, involvement with counseling and milieu activities including peer support and education sessions to motivate the patient to proceed to rehabilitation treatment. Vital signs remained normal during his brief stay. 

Yes, the proposed treatment, inpatient substance abuse treatment, was medically necessary for this patient.

The requested Inpatient admission and continued treatment could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. The patient in this case was using heroin, together with alcohol on a daily continuous basis with intermittent use of other substances of abuse including cocaine that did warrant inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring for the duration of the protocol; detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments pertinent to the detoxification treatment episode could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment that was provided at the time of admission.  Moreover, the patient had a positive drug screen that included opioids and benzodiazepines, as well as PCP and cocaine. He had moderate and persistent withdrawal symptoms, and, the patient's social environment was not conducive to detoxification in the context of limited insight, impaired judgment and poor control of impulses.

Thus, the adult inpatient detoxification treatment and withdrawal management of this patient's substance use disorder did warrant the admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level detoxification setting with 24-hour monitoring and use of as needed (PRN) medications. The patients history of substance abuse (frequency and quantity) together with the severe psychosocial stressors and functional impairments reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder and the need for a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management, as the patient was at high risk for treatment failure if the continued detoxification and withdrawal management were to be attempted at a lower level of care. Therefore, medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published practice guidelines, the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and the scientific literature, referenced below, and, New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews including the appropriate application of the NY State OASAS LOCADTR Tool that requires the patient in this scenario default to the higher level of care.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse

Treatment: Inpatient detoxification admission 
 
The insurer denied the inpatient detoxification admission. The denial was overturned.

This is a male patient who was admitted to inpatient detoxification treatment. He had withdrawal symptoms that included nausea, diarrhea, sweats, anxiety, tremors, sleeping problems, diffuse discomfort, nasal stuffiness, dilated pupils, irritable mood, and he had a CIWA of 12. He reportedly had many past inpatient detoxification treatments including a recent one 1/2020. He reportedly had a positive toxicology for opiates and methadone. He was using 4-5 bags of IV heroin per day, 70 mg of Methadone, and drinking twelve 24 ounce beers per day, using cannabis, and had reports of intranasal cocaine use. He reportedly was put on an Ativan and Methadone taper and discharged.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. In this case this patient had use of multiple substances including large amounts of alcohol, heroin, Methadone, and cannabis and was at risk for severe, complicated and life threatening withdrawal as well as death from overdose. 

According to the LOCADTR he did require 24 hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive setting as he continued to use substances and alcohol despite multiple past inpatient detoxification treatments including a recent one 2020, and he needed 2 detoxification medications including Ativan and Methadone to modify withdrawal, had long term multiple substances of use including using alcohol, heroin, methadone, and cannabis. He needed 24 hour treatment then as he was at risk for worsened withdrawal symptoms if not in this 24 hour setting then, and he likely would have relapsed again as evidenced by relapsing after multiple past treatments. He reportedly lacked coping skills and ability to identify relapse triggers and was struggling to remain abstinent and continued to relapse despite so many past inpatient detoxification treatments. Also, his environment was not conducive to recovery as evidenced by his continued use.  As a result, the recommendation is to reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for continued inpatient substance detoxification. summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse.

Treatment: Inpatient admission.

The insurer denied the inpatient admission.

The denial was overturned.

This is a male patient who was admitted to the hospital for inpatient substance detoxification treatment. He had reports of withdrawal symptoms that included nausea, tremors, lightheadedness, sleeping problems, irritable mood, and anxiety, and had a CIWA of 11 and COWS of 10. He reportedly was drinking three 6 packs of beer per day, snorting 10-12 bags of crack per day, and using heroin 1 bag inhaled. He reportedly had multiple past inpatient substance detoxification treatments and past inpatient rehabilitation treatment. He reportedly had a significant history of alcohol use. He reportedly was put on a Librium protocol for detoxification treatment and left against medical advice (AMA).
  
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. It also states that patients with past complicated or life threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens are in need of inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal and reports that patients with comorbid medical condition that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification. 

The US Department of Health and Human Services-Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) Center for Substance Abuse Treatment reports that inpatient treatment is necessary if the ability to attend outpatient treatment daily is a problem, one is unable to follow up in outpatient treatment, if medical conditions complicate the treatment of withdrawal, if one has previous withdrawal seizures of delirium tremens, or if one does not have the capacity for informed consent. In this case this patient had been using multiple serious substances of use in large amounts including drinking three 6 packs of beer per day, sorting 10-12 bags of crack per day, and using heroin 1 bag inhaled and he was at high risk for overdose as well as severe, complicated, and life threatening withdrawal symptoms so he required inpatient substance detoxification treatment in this hospital then.

According to the LOCADTR he did require 24 hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated in outpatient detoxification settings as he continued to use alcohol, crack, and heroin despite past multiple inpatient detoxification and rehabilitation treatments. He required and needed detoxification medication including Librium which he required until discharge for detoxification treatment. He was at risk for worsened withdrawal symptoms if not in this 24 hour setting then including severe and life threatening withdrawal symptoms. The risk of life complicated withdrawal such as delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use so he required at least the entire time in this inpatient substance hospital detoxification treatment. He was considered a high risk patient medically for overdose and severe, complicated and life threatening withdrawal. He reportedly left AMA before the detoxification treatment was complete but he did require the detoxification treatment. 

It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably, with sound medical judgment, or in the best interests of the patient.  

Based on the above, the medical necessity for the inpatient admission is substantiated.  The insurer's denial is overturned.

summary:
Diagnosis: Severe Depression, Suicidal Ideation

Treatment: continued inpatient behavioral health hospital services

The insurer denied coverage for continued inpatient behavioral health hospital services.

The denial is modified.

This is a female patient who was admitted for inpatient behavioral health treatment due to severe depressive symptoms including depressed mood, hopelessness and helplessness, suicidal thoughts of wanting to die, and she reportedly overdosed on pills the night prior to admission as she reported that she was tired of living. The patient had multiple medical problems. The patient had been drinking alcohol excessively also. The patient was admitted and was treated with Ativan and Librium protocol. The patient's medication regimen was also adjusted to target and treat her depressive symptoms. The patient was stabilized and was discharged one month later.

The American Psychiatry Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Suicidal Behaviors reports that patients with suicide attempts are at high risk for suicide as past suicide attempts are the single most reliable predictor of suicide. The APA Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Suicidal Behaviors also reports that patients with feelings of hopelessness, major depressive episodes, substance/alcohol use are at higher risk for suicide and she had severe depressive symptoms, hopelessness, and was drinking excessively, and had a suicide attempt the night prior to admission so she was considered a high risk for suicide. It also reports that patients may require more time in the hospital to better assess suicide because they sometimes do not tell the truth regarding their suicidal thoughts in order to leave the hospital and that observation in the hospital is appropriate to better ensure their safety. 

This patient was considered a high risk patient and benefitted from remaining in the hospital and being observed and assessed for safety until day 24 of admission as the chart notes reported continued severe depressive symptoms until then but not as of the days to follow. Notes up to day 24 of admission reported that she had days of depressed and irritable mood, hopelessness and helplessness. She continued to report severe depressive symptoms until then and had medication changes so she required continued hospitalization. However, after day 25 of admission, the chart notes reported that the patient was more motivated, less anxious, had brighter affect, and was compliant with medication. The patient denied suicidal ideation, and was compliant. As of day 25 of admission, the chart notes did not report severe depressive symptoms for the patient, and provided no support that the patient only required 24-hour hospital treatment then. Also, there were no reports of specific identifiable treatment goals or objectives that could only be achieved in this 24-hour hospital treatment or that could not be achieved in a less restrictive setting as of day 24 of admission. Thus, while inpatient behavioral health treatment up to day 24 of admission was medically necessary, the continued inpatient behavioral health treatment thereafter was not medically necessary. 

Based on the above, the medical necessity for inpatient behavioral health hospital services up to day 24 of admission is substantiated and the medical necessity for inpatient behavioral health hospital services thereafter is not substantiated. The insurer's denial should be modified. Approve up to day 24 of admission. Deny the subsequent dates.
