summary:
Diagnosis: Schizoaffective Disorder.
Treatment: Inpatient mental health stay.
The insurer denied the inpatient mental health stay.
The determination is overturned.

The patient was admitted to acute inpatient psychiatric services for an exacerbation of a chronic psychotic disorder best characterized as schizoaffective disorder or undifferentiated type schizophrenia. The patient had shown increasing symptoms of psychosis following discontinuation of her oral medication with the onset of bizarre delusions and erratic behavior, disorganized thoughts with paranoid thinking together with motor agitation, and increasing responses to internal stimuli that included auditory hallucinations. She was brought to the emergency department by emergency services and was subsequently admitted after medical clearance that included a physical examination, laboratory assessment and drug screen. Her assessment included no abnormal or remarkable laboratory findings including a negative drug screen consistent with her history. She was noted to have a sickle cell trait.
The patient has a history of psychiatric treatment, including multiple psychiatric hospitalizations, but no report of suicidal behavior. There are no substance-related disorders in this case and no acute general medical issues. The patient had been involved with the assertive community treatment (ACT) team with use of Abilify and Abilify Maintena.
On Mental Status Examination on admission, the patient was psychotic and cognitively impaired with thought blocking, clear speech, racing and disorganized thoughts and response to internal stimuli. She was guarded and only superficially cooperative with poor eye contact. She displayed motor agitation with irritable and dysphoric mood. Insight was limited and judgment impaired. She denied suicidal ideation or aggressive impulses despite the recent bouts of aggression, and did not show evidence for overt features of mania or severe cognitive impairment (delirium or dementia) despite having poor attention and concentration due to the internal stimuli and mental confusion and distractibility with the disorganized thought patterns with tangential thought production. She reported auditory hallucinations with paranoid themes.
The patient was single and domiciled with her mother, and unemployed/disabled with government subsidies. There were no legal issues.
The patient's treatment plan included safety monitoring and medication targeting mood disturbance and psychosis, as well as the opportunity for therapy and psycho-education provided in the therapeutic milieu. The patient was variably cooperative but guarded and refused some of her medications during the initial week of her inpatient stay. The patient continued to display severe symptoms of psychosis with essentially little change in her mental status examination, and continued response to auditory hallucinations. She had received risperidone with an injection of Invega Sustenna, and there were plans for continued use of Invega Sustenna with tapering of the oral antipsychotic medication with Cogentin supplementation, as well as as needed (PRN) use of Haldol and Ativan for agitation and Benadryl and trazodone for insomnia.
She continued to display guarded behavior but was increasingly calmer and more socially appropriate with participation in groups and milieu activities focusing on social skills, reality testing and illness recovery. Again, the patient gradually became more at ease and was more receptive to participating in educational groups and other group sessions focusing on social skills with ongoing monitoring and development of a relapse prevention plan focusing on medication compliance/adherence. She received a second injection of Invega Sustenna with plans for continued treatment in the community with assertive community treatment (ACT level treatment) and return home. Case management was involved in developing a safe and clinically appropriate discharge plan with the resumption of ACT level treatment and referral to a sickle cell clinic. She was discharged, at which time she was no longer deemed to be a danger to herself or others and had resolved her auditory hallucination and paranoid thinking with improved mood and diminished anxiety and better control of impulses and better ability to comply with treatment.
 The health plan documents and appeal letters were reviewed, as well as case records and correspondence from the health plan and the treatment facility. The health plan level of care guidelines/medical necessity criteria were reviewed, as submitted. The dates under review were denied certification of coverage by the health plan for inpatient level treatment on the basis of medical necessity criteria. This case is a New York State mandated review. The issue under review is the medical necessity of continued inpatient mental health stay.
The patient's continued hospital stay for treatment of an exacerbation of a chronic psychotic disorder (schizophrenia spectrum disorder) associated with non-adherence and non-compliance with outpatient treatment and risk for aggressive behavior did warrant the continued stay through discharge. The patient's severity of symptoms, and the treatment refractory nature of her psychotic disorder, as well as the patient's inability to benefit from treatment at a lower level of care, functional decline, and safety issues related to persistent symptoms of psychosis, were clinical factors and treatment dimensions that warranted the continued acute inpatient hospital care, structure, and monitoring as proposed through discharge.
The medication changes and adjustments and safety monitoring together with attention to the compliance issues in this case were medically necessary in this case scenario; the intensity of services and safety issues related to erratic behavior and affective instability could not have been effectively addressed or managed at a lower level of care during the time interval under review.
The additional treatments were medically necessary in order to continued active treatment that included medication administration, evidence-based psychosocial therapy and other therapeutic interventions to address reality testing and social skills, to develop a safe and clinically appropriate discharge plan and disposition, and, to monitor the response to medication including the work with community providers for a step down to ACT level care and continued use of a long-acting injectable antipsychotic medication that were clinical factors and treatment dimensions that did require the continued inpatient mental health stay as requested. Thus, medical necessity is met. These answers are consistent with the scientific literature and practice guideline, referenced below, as well as prevailing standards of medical practice and NY State instruction for this review.

summary:
Diagnosis: Auditory hallucinations
Treatment: Continued Inpatient admission 
The insurer denied the Continued Inpatient admission.
The denial is overturned. 

The patient is a male, for whom this was the first psychiatric admission. He was brought to the hospital by EMS and police, who were called by his girlfriend. The patient presented auditory hallucinations and erratic behavior for the previous several weeks. At times, he told his girlfriend that there was a demon inside of him or that someone did voodoo on him. The patient denied substance use other than alcohol and cannabis.

At the time of admission, the patient was described as psychotic, disorganized, and barely able to carry on a conversation due to his psychotic state and internal preoccupation. The patient endorsed some paranoia and a recent increase in praying and possible religious preoccupation. He described feeling "weird and different" recently, and waking up feeling like the day would turn out badly. He appeared to have thought blocking and to be responding to internal stimuli. 

A physician's progress note reports that the patient had refused medication, had periods of irritability, and was less logical in his thoughts and speech than the previous day. He was however able to show kindness to another patient. The following morning the patient's speech was illogical, and he was given Haldol 5 mg.

Yes, the Continued Inpatient admission was medically necessary. 

A severe, acute psychotic episode in this young man with no prior history of psychosis or apparent predisposing factors warranted an additional week of observation and stabilization, after initial improvement, in the interest of safety and preventing regression and re-hospitalization. Discharging or stepping down the patient would not have been consistent with generally accepted practice and guidelines in the Psychiatry community. To do so would have placed his health and safety, as well as the health and safety of his family and community at risk.

summary:
Diagnosis: Mood disorder
Treatment: Residential mental health
The insurer denied the residential mental health. 
The denial is upheld. 

No, the Mental Health Residential Treatment Level of Care is not medically necessary. 

The patient is a male. He has diagnoses of major depressive disorder, recurrent, moderate, parent-child conflict, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. He was admitted to this residential facility to address his psychological and substance abuse issues. The patient's home environment is described as chaotic and stressful due to parental arguments and verbal abuse on the part of his father, who reportedly was intimidating, demeaning, verbally abusive and historically physically abusive. 

The patient had engaged in self-cutting, but there was no evidence of active suicidality, nor evidence of any recent such behavior. The patient had made comments indicating passive suicidal ideation. 

The patient's substance abuse history includes daily use of marijuana, various psychedelics, anxiolytics, and pain medications although specific quantities and frequencies are not specified. The patient has a history of verbal aggression toward his mother including yelling, name-calling, swearing, arguing, and taunting. Non-verbal aggression includes posturing, pushing, and slamming doors. 

The patient was described as being depressed with lack of motivation, poor sleep, poor appetite, lethargy, difficulty concentrating, and feelings of worthlessness. He also had ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) symptoms including inattention, difficulty focusing, and distractibility, but refused to take medication for ADHD. He reportedly had been prescribed Lexapro by an outpatient psychiatrist. He had been in treatment for several years with two psychologists, one of whom wrote that he "navigated" the patient to this facility. 

In the facility the patient was treated with individual psychotherapy, milieu therapy, and group therapy. He refused medications, stating he only wanted "organic things" in his body. This facility utilized various movement therapies, equine therapy, art therapy, yoga, mindfulness exercises, and breathing techniques.

For the dates of service under review, the patient showed no evidence of suicidality, behavioral dyscontrol, psychosis, inability to care for his ADLs (activities of daily living), danger to self or others, or any other problem which would require 24-hour daily supervision and treatment. He was cooperative with treatment. There was no evidence of significant acting out behaviors. His behavioral problems which prompted this admission were described as clear reactions to a pathological home situation. For the dates of service under review, nothing in the documentation reviewed indicates that this patient would not have been better served by treatment in a less restrictive community setting with intensive parental involvement.

summary:
Mental Health
Inpatient Mental Health

Diagnosis: Reactive Attachment Disorder
Treatment: Inpatient Mental Health Stay
The insurer denied the Inpatient Mental Health Stay.
The determination is overturned in part.

The patient has co-morbid diagnoses of reactive attachment disorder; autism spectrum disorder; posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD); attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), combined type; and, voyeuristic behavioral disorder associated with affective instability, impulsive aggression, and decline in social, family and other psychosocial functioning domains. The patient was brought to emergency services and admitted to acute inpatient level care for impulsive and aggressive behavior of a sexual nature with sexual assaultive behavior. The patient has a history of longstanding problems with impulse control with comorbid psychiatric conditions including the additional diagnosis of a reactive attachment disorder with subsequent development of enduring mood dysregulation, impulsive aggression and inappropriate sexual behavior, and decline in functioning in all relevant domains. 
The patient presented with limited insight and impaired judgment associated with the affective instability and constricted affect. He exhibited coping and personality traits/coping skills that reflected impaired judgment and poor control of impulses with the presenting features, as noted, and safety concerns. 
The patient has a trauma history and an attachment disorder reflecting early childhood trauma. The patient participated in milieu treatment modalities while his medications were monitored with psychiatric management. He was making progress and had remained engaged in treatments that included group, individual and family-focused sessions.
He was noted to be functioning better with a greater ability to manage his impulses but did not show improved insight; he was reluctant to discuss the reason for his admission, but indicated that he would do so with subsequent treatment in a residential program. 
The issue under review is the medical necessity of Inpatient Mental Health Services.
The services are medically necessary in part.
The patient's clinical history and presenting features did warrant the continued structure and monitoring of an inpatient setting with the intensity, scope, duration, and structure of inpatient level services in order to effectively address the patient's risk of relapse, continue to learn adequate coping skills to engage in an ongoing therapeutic process, and prevent treatment failure, while the treatment team and family worked toward a clinically appropriate disposition with continued mental health services to address the severe and persistent symptoms of the mental disorders diagnosed in this case. The patient has a history of failing to benefit from treatment in the community, and more recent risk for inappropriate sexual behavior and aggressive/violent behavior in the context of severe symptoms related to comorbid reactive attachment disorder (RAD) and ADHD and PTSD. His behavioral disturbances in the context of family and social impairments and severe symptoms associated with impulsive and aggressive behavior complicated the case as well as the potential for high risk behaviors that required continued intensive services. These factors support the assertion that the patient could not have been effectively treated at a lower level of care up until when the patient was fully prepared for a transition and immediate transfer to residential level care.
A reasonable residential program had been identified and the patient was deemed to be ready and fully prepared for discharge to residential care.

summary:
Diagnosis:  Depressive symptoms.
Treatment:  Mental Health Residential Treatment.

The insurer is denied coverage for Mental Health Residential Treatment.  The denial is overturned.

This is a female patient, who was admitted to inpatient mental health residential treatment due to severe mental symptoms and eating disorder symptoms.  She had depressive symptoms including depressed mood, suicidal thoughts, feelings of hopelessness, loss of interest, low self-esteem, isolation, decreased energy, poor concentration, anxious mood, obsessing and ruminating, worrying, somatic complaints, feeling overwhelmed, and panic like symptoms.  She had food restriction during the week, including calorie counting with no more than 900 calories per day, distorted body image, maladaptive eating behaviors, binging on weekends, and her lowest recent weight was 80 lbs on more than one occasion.  She currently reportedly weighed 106.6 lbs. and was 5"4" with a body mass index (BMI) of 18.3. She had reported diagnoses of Major Depressive Disorder-Recurrent, Generalized Anxiety Disorder, and Unspecified Eating Disorder.  She had a reported history of alcohol and cannabis use and experimentation with Xanax. 

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Major Depressive Disorders reports that the psychiatrist should determine the least restrictive setting for treatment that will be most likely not only to address the patient's safety, but also to promote improvement in the patient's condition.  It also states that the determination of an appropriate setting for treatment should include consideration of the patient's symptom severity, co-occurring psychiatric or general medical conditions, available support system, and level of functioning.

In this case this patient still had reports of depressive symptoms, including suicidal thoughts, during the denial period, and she still reportedly was considered at risk without learning more coping skills to better deal with her depressive, anxiety, and eating disorder symptoms. 

Notes reported increased anxiety, depressed mood, tearfulness, disappointment, fears, and she reported that she was not ready to leave this treatment setting yet, as she thought she needed more time.  It was reported that she needed more work on trust, resentment, and communication.  Notes reported that she had urges of high intensity to over exercise, had concerns about her home and being a burden on her family, and she reported feeling exhausted, stressed, and overwhelmed. 

Continued inpatient mental health residential treatment to the present and for another month until and including is medically necessary.  The patient can be reevaluated at that time to assess further treatment needs and also progress with treatment.  It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably or in the best interests of the patient.

The carrier's denial of coverage for continued Mental Health Residential Treatment is overturned.  The medical necessity is substantiated.

3)  American Psychiatric Association Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Suicidal Behaviors.

summary:
Diagnosis:  Major Depressive Disorder.
Treatment:  Inpatient Stay.

The insurer denied the Inpatient Stay.  The determination is upheld.

The patient was admitted to the inpatient level of care due to depression, superficial cut of her right forearm and suicidal ideation.  The patient had been referred by her therapist, due to repetitive thoughts of suicidal ideation with a plan to jump off of a building.  The patient had no previous hospitalizations.  She was not on medications at the time of admission.  The only previous treatment was psychotherapy.  She was diagnosed with major depressive disorder, mood disorder, rule out (r/o) attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).  She was labile and despondent.  She patient had labs and an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) was slightly low.  Consent was pending to switch the patient to Haldol instead of Seroquel, due to this lab value.  At issue is the medical necessity of a continued inpatient stay. 

The continued inpatient stay was not medically necessary.  The documentation did not reflect the patient had active suicidal ideation with plan, homicidal ideation with plan or command hallucinations.  There was no documentation that the patient was physically aggressive, acutely manic or sexually inappropriate.  The patient had a low ANC, but there was no indication of significant medical instabilities that required around the clock medical care.  The patient did not require emergency medications, restraints or seclusions.  The documentation did not reflect that a 24-hour therapeutic environment was medically necessary on an inpatient unit.

By day three of the inpatient stay under review the patient was tolerating Haldol well.  She was showing improvement and was less despondent.  The patient had 1:1 counseling.  Vitals signs were stable.  She was apprehensive and despondent.  Haldol was started at 2 milligrams (mg)mg at night.  There were no command hallucinations.  The patient was able to contract for safety.  The patient denied imminent suicidality or homicidality.  She was disorganized and irritable, with multiple somatic complaints or irritability, apprehension, insomnia and agitation.  She had anxiety.  She responded to Haldol the previous night and the dose was increased to 5 mg.  Zoloft was also increased to 75 mg.  

On day seven of the inpatient stay under review she had anxiety, irritability and depression.  The patient was sleeping better.  She had no psychosis and was able to contract for safety.  On day nine she had improvement and was less irritable.  There was no psychosis.  The patient was still preoccupied, apprehensive and labile.

On day nine of the inpatient stay she had some insomnia, vague somatic symptoms and irritability.  She was somewhat disorganized and apprehensive.  There was no psychosis.  The patient was able to contract for safety and denied suicidality or homicidality.  On day ten she showed improvement.  There were no adverse events.  The patient was able to contract for safety.  She patient was showing improvement with medication.  On day twelve the patient was noted to have galactorrhea.  Prolactin levels were ordered.  On day thirteen the patient showed improvement.  Haldol was discontinued due to concerns of lactation.  Zoloft was increased to 100 mg.  On day fourteen the patient was placed on Trazodone for sleep instead of Haldol.  The patient was able to fully contract for safety and discharge planning had started.  On day fifteen she showed improvement.  She was able to contract for safety.  Disorganization and irritability had subsided.  The patient was discharged to outpatient care the next day.

summary:
Diagnosis: Nausea and vomiting (substance abuse).
Treatment: Inpatient admission.
The insurer denied the inpatient admission.
The denial is upheld. 

This is a woman with a history including alcohol abuse, seizures, and bipolar disorder who presented for evaluation of withdrawal.  ED records note tremors and vomiting.  There was no suicidal ideation (SI) / homicidal ideation (HI) or hallucinations.  Vital signs (VS) were as follows: 98.3, 96, 16, 153/106, and 100%.  Exam at admission was unremarkable.  Labs revealed the following: white blood cell (WBC) 8.63, hemoglobin/hematocrit (H/H) 11.4/35.6,and platelets (Plt) 176. Basic metabolic panel (BMP) was unremarkable.  Alcohol (EtOH) was negative.  Venous blood gas (VBG) was 7.46/42/51/30.  Electrocardiogram (EKG) was with normal sinus rhythm (NSR).  The patient was admitted for alcohol withdrawal.  Plan included Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) protocol.  The following day vital signs were stable (VSS).  The patient was feeling better.  She has mild tremors.  The patient's vomiting resolved and she was tolerating a liquid diet.  The patient was discharged.

No, the inpatient admission was not medically necessary.

This patient was admitted for alcohol withdrawal.  The patient did not have active comorbid conditions.  The patient was hemodynamically stable and afebrile.  She did not have tachycardia or arrhythmia.  At time of admission, there is no documentation of persistent vomiting, delirium, seizures, or gross tremor.  Labs were unremarkable.  The patient remained hemodynamically stable.  Her symptoms were resolving.  She was tolerating by mouth (PO).  The patient was clinically stable and did not have findings of severe alcohol withdrawal that required an acute inpatient level of care.  She had not failed management in a lesser level of care.  The requested inpatient admission was not medically necessary.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Inpatient Substance Abuse Treatment
The insurer denied the Inpatient Substance Abuse Treatment.
The determination is overturned.

The patient is a homeless male and was admitted to inpatient substance use treatment for the treatment of alcohol and cocaine use disorder. During admission, his provider stated that it was the patient's desire to obtain withdrawal management from alcohol as well as get help to stay away from cocaine. A Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR-3) had been used to determine the appropriate service level. According to this tool, he did not require the services because his vital signs were stable with a blood pressure of 144/78 and pulse of 94 beats per minute. There were only very mild withdrawal symptoms noted by his provider. There were no acute medical or mental health conditions and his condition did not require 24-hour-a-day nursing care and monitoring. His need for ongoing relapse prevention treatment of substance use symptoms could have been safely treated in a less restricted level of care such as rehabilitative services in a residential setting as recommended by LOCADTR-3 tool.
He was placed on a five day Librium protocol during his admission. He reported drinking two pints of liquor and 2 six packs of beer on a daily basis. He was also smoking crack cocaine one to two times per week. His blood alcohol level on admission was 0.133 and his toxicology came back positive for cocaine and benzodiazepines. However, he denies any recent use. He admitted to having blackouts and not feeling well at the time of his admission. Based on his presentation, the medical team felt that medical supervision was necessary. He has a history of more than 20 treatment episodes and he was unable to remain stable and drug-free on his own. He lacks a sober support network and he was in need of building better coping skills and identifying triggers/stressors. His goal was to complete detoxification services and step down to inpatient rehabilitation services. He successfully completed detoxification and did step down to rehab services in this facility.
A Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA)-AR score was 12 and no acute detoxification symptoms were noted. His existing signs/symptoms include nausea, trouble sleeping, anxiety, and hot/cold sweats. On admission, his vital signs were 144/78 with pulse of 94. A detox Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) was performed. Per this analysis, he was incapacitated by substance. He had no risk of physical harm or risk of severe withdrawal or complications or comorbidities. He had risk of moderate withdrawal. He had a lack of support for early abstinence, and therefore he was recommended inpatient medically supervised withdrawal treatment. Librium protocol was started for alcohol dependency detoxification and he was also given other comfort medications.
A progress note indicates that he safely completed detoxification and has accepted a referral. He has been observed following rules and regulations of the unit and he is not in need of mental health referral. He was stable upon discharge. He is still in need of coping skills, a recovery action plan and sober support network. At issue is the medical necessity of inpatient substance abuse treatment.
The requested health service/treatment of inpatient substance abuse treatment was medically necessary for this patient. As explained above, the patient's toxicology was positive for cocaine and benzodiazepine along with blood alcohol level of 0.131. He has no safe environment. He was at risk of developing severe withdrawal symptoms. Therefore, he was appropriately admitted to inpatient level of care and he received appropriate treatment with detox medication and monitoring of his withdrawal symptoms.
Per LOCATDR, it was noted that the patient had alcohol use disorder. He met criteria for tolerance and/or withdrawal. It was noted that he requires vital sign monitoring and requires medication management of withdrawal symptoms. He had no significant medical conditions or significant psychiatric disorders reported. No M 80 availability in the community was noted. No interpersonal or personal skills deficits were indicated. No available resources were endorsed during the interview. Therefore, LOCATDR recommendation was residential. However, several discrepancies were identified with the initial LOCATDR: the review of submitted documents revealed that at the time of assessment, the patient has a blood alcohol (BAL) level which is high (0.131) which could mask the patient's withdrawal symptoms. He was clearly having risk of withdrawal at the time of admission since he was able to tolerate higher amounts of alcohol. He had a significant history of alcohol use disorder with multiple previous trials of detoxes and treatments. He was reportedly homeless and had no active treatment, or social support which increase his risk. Additional to his alcohol use, his toxicology was positive with benzodiazepines which is another significant factor which could contribute/worsen his conditions and would complicate his detoxification and treatment. Individuals under the influence are generally poor historians, and therefore may not be able to provide reliable a history regarding past severe withdrawal seizures, such as seizures. Therefore, it was appropriate for this patient to be safely treated at the offered level of care.

summary:
Diagnosis: Schizophrenia
Treatment: Inpatient hospital admission
The insurer denied the inpatient hospital admission.
The denial was upheld. 

This is a female patient with a history of schizophrenia. It was reported that the patient had multiple past hospitalization for psychiatric treatment. The patient presented to the emergency department (ED) by her mother for erratic and disorganized behavior. She was admitted for inpatient mental health treatment due to psychotic symptoms including persecutory delusions, disorganized thinking and behavior, erratic behavior, noncompliance with medication and psychiatric outpatient follow up, poor sleep and appetite. The patient was admitted and was restarted on Haldol and was also given Haldol Decanoate. She attended group therapy and it was noted that the patient was calm and cooperative, mood-congruent and full range of effect. At the time period of discharge, it was documented that the patient refused to go to her husband's home and was not welcomed into her mother's house. Thus, the patient was discharged to a shelter.
    
The American Psychiatric Association  (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Schizophrenia reports that patients with hallucinations, delusional thinking, disorganized behavior, suicidal or homicidal plan or intent, agitation, or aggressive behavior are candidates for inpatient treatment.  In this case there were no reports of further serious psychotic symptoms such as delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized behavior, suicidal or homicidal ideation, intent, or plan, manic symptoms, aggressive, threatening, self-injurious, or agitated behavior, withdrawal symptoms or acute medical instability.  

Documentation reported that the patient was calm and cooperative, had congruent mood, denied hallucinations or delusions, had goal directed thought process, fair judgment and insight, denied suicidal or homicidal ideation, was sleeping well and had better ADL's. The patient was calm and cooperative with normal range mood, and was compliant with medications though withdrawn. The patient was discharged to shelter as it was reported that she refused to go to her husband's home and was not welcomed to return to her mother's house.  

The health plan acted reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient. 

Based on the above, the medical necessity for the continued inpatient hospital admission is not substantiated.  The insurer's denial should be upheld.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance abuse

Treatment: Inpatient detoxification admission

The insurer has denied coverage for inpatient detoxification admission

The denial is overturned. 

This male patient was admitted for inpatient detoxification treatment from alcohol, Xanax, and heroin.  The patient reportedly had past withdrawal seizure, and had current active withdrawal symptoms including body aches, nausea, hot and chills, anxiety, and insomnia. The patient reported having a relapse 1 month ago and was drinking alcohol, and using Xanax and heroin. The patient had inpatient detoxification treatment in the past. The patient was admitted and was treated with phenobarbital and methadone protocol, and remained on the methadone protocol until the day of discharge.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment.  It also states that patients with past complicated or life threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens are in need of inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal and reports that patients with comorbid medical condition that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification.  Also, the United States Department of Health and Human Services-Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) Center for Substance Abuse Treatment reports that inpatient treatment is necessary if the ability to attend outpatient treatment daily is a problem, one is unable to follow up in outpatient treatment, if medical conditions complicate the treatment of withdrawal, if one has previous withdrawal seizures of delirium tremens, or if one does not have the capacity for informed consent. 

In this case, this patient had past reported alcohol withdrawal seizures which required inpatient medical detoxification treatment and was in current withdrawal from three different substances (i.e. alcohol, Xanax, and heroin) and was at risk for severe, complicated, and life threatening withdrawal as well as overdose.  

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), this patient required 24-hour treatment as he could not have been safely and effectively treated for detoxification in a less restrictive setting as he continued to use alcohol, Xanax, and heroin daily, and required and received two detoxification medications (i.e. phenobarbital and methadone) to modify  this patient's active withdrawal symptoms from alcohol, Xanax, and heroin and prevent another withdrawal seizure, such as delirium tremens. The patient was a high risk for relapse and overdose, as this patient has been continuing the use of several serious substances despite past inpatient detoxification treatment. During admission, notes indicated that the patient continued with detoxification protocol for alcohol, benzodiazepines, and heroin. The patient still had withdrawal symptoms, including myalgia and diaphoresis and continued with the methadone and phenobarbital protocol.  It was reported that he needed stabilization with methadone dosage prior to rehabilitation treatment. The patient required and received detoxification treatment until discharge. Thus, inpatient hospital admission was medically necessary for this patient.

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient. 

The carrier's denial of coverage for inpatient substance abuse admission should be reversed. The medical necessity is substantiated.

2)	US Department of Health and Human Services-Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) Center for Substance Abuse Treatment

3)	Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR)

summary:
Diagnosis: Mental Health/Depression 
Treatment: Mental Health Inpatient 
The insurer denied part of the inpatient mental health hospital stay
The denial is upheld in whole

The patient who presented for acute inpatient level care transferred from general medical services to address respiratory problems and urinary retention following a suicide attempt and overdose. 

No, the requested health service/treatment of Inpatient Hospital Stay is not medically necessary for this patient.
The continued acute inpatient mental health stay and treatment from is not medically necessary for this patient. The patient no longer required the structure or the 24-hour monitoring of an acute inpatient level of care in order to administer continued treatment for the psychiatric disturbance and comorbid conditions including continued treatment for the substance use disorders and support of daily activities and general medical conditions.

summary:
Diagnosis:  Schizoaffective disorder.
Treatment:  Inpatient Mental health stay.

The insurer denied the inpatient mental health stay.  The health plan's determination is overturned in part.  36 days of inpatient mental health treatment was medically necessary. 

The patient is a woman with diagnoses of schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, who was admitted to inpatient psychiatry after medical evaluation and stabilization.  She had additional diagnoses of morbid obesity and diabetes mellitus.  Case notes document that on admission, the patient was severely ill, malodorous with swollen legs and sores, showing poor activities of daily living.  She had clearly been unable to maintain proper hygiene.  She had not been able to adhere to her medications (risperidone and Depakote) for several months.  She previously failed several trials of anti-psychotic medication.  She had consistently refused Clozaril.  She showed thought blocking, grandiose delusions, and a labile mood.  She had poor judgment and poor impulse control.  She was initially treated with dual anti-psychotics of paliperidone and Haldol plus Depakote, but then the regimen was simplified to Haldol and Depakote alone.  She received psychoeducation, behavioral management, and group treatment.  A good plan for follow-up with ACT was made.  High stressors included homelessness and inability to function in a job.  She had little support.  She showed severe functional impairment.  

36 days of inpatient mental health treatment was medically necessary.  For this patient with severe chronic illness and medical comorbidities and high functional impairment and multiple psychosocial stresses, there is no simple single datum or finding to support discharge.  Rather, a cluster of symptoms and signs of improvement in what appeared to be a stable baseline is a reasonable standard.  This patient had to be treated for both her psychotic and mood symptoms.  Complex psychopharmacology is required in treatment of schizoaffective disorder. Patients with schizoaffective disorder may require trials with different antipsychotic medications.  

On the proposed day of discharge by the health plan, the patient showed a brief pause in her symptomatology with some logical conversation and good appetite.  However, she did not remember refusing medications, setting herself up for relapse.  For this patient to be safely discharged with good medical judgment, a period of several days of baseline mental status and non-threatening behavior are necessary for several reasons.  A single day of moderate improvement was not enough.  She was at high risk if discharged because her disorder was chronic and severe with high functional impairment, and she lacked evidence of consistent improvement adequate for movement to a lower level of care.  She had been non-adherent to her medications for months.  She was homeless.  She had no significant dependable support.  She had severe medical comorbidities.  The case notes document that the patient waxed and waned in her symptoms as her medications were increased, primarily the paliperidone, along with psychoeducation, and behavioral teaching about the need for adequate hygiene.  She had a labile mood and was agitated.  Her hygiene continued to be poor.  She had become malodorous again with poor self-care and was responding to internal stimuli.  She was sad and depressed, illogical in thinking and continued to have grandiose delusions and required directions to shower.  She had no abnormal psychomotor activity, but her mood was dysphoric.  She had grandiose delusions.  Eventually she was calm in affect, with a stable but mildly dysphoric mood.  She had no delusions or hallucinations, no suicidality or homicidality.  The same mental status exam was noted with case notes documenting what appeared to be a baseline by day 36 of inpatient status.  She was noted to be slowly but progressively stabilizing.  Unfortunately, no approval was achieved for a long-acting injectable anti-psychotic (LAI).

The recent use of cannabis was thought to have precipitated the patient's onset of paranoia and anxiety.  There was a history of "psychogenic seizures" and trauma-related symptoms following a sexual assault. The mental status examination revealed a guarded and uncooperative female with depressed mood and anxious affect.  The patient was tobacco dependent with mild use.  There were no acute general medical conditions.  Urine drug screen was consistent with history and positive for cannabis/tetrahydrocannabinol (THC).

The patient was admitted for close observation, safety monitoring, structured milieu therapy, and pharmacotherapy with adjustments.  The patient remained depressed, anxious and motor agitated with pacing and bouts of psychotic terror requiring as needed (prn) use of Haldol and Ativan.  Prozac was stopped and Seroquel was increased with titrations from 25 milligrams (mg) to 200 mg daily; she was medication adherent with tolerability. 

The patient became increasingly cooperative with treatment and more social with peers with improved mood and reality testing.  She reported feeling better and had no additional bouts of agitation or screaming episodes.  A family conference was held with case management in order to address discharge planning.  By the day of discharge, the patient's symptoms were mostly improved.

At issue is the medical necessity of continued inpatient mental health stay.

The patient required the continued acute inpatient level care and the structure and monitoring of an acute inpatient level setting in order to remain safe and to administer treatment for her psychiatric disturbance and co-occurring substance use disorder.  She warranted the continued inpatient level care while conducting an evaluation of response to medication adjustments (discontinuation of Prozac and titration of Seroquel), and while observing her functioning and maintaining abstinence from cannabis. Treatment: Inpatient hospital admission.

The insurer denied the inpatient hospital admission. 

The denial was overturned.   

This is a male patient who was admitted to inpatient mental health treatment due to depressive symptoms including depressed mood, suicidal ideation and reports that he did not trust himself to be alone, anhedonia, worthlessness, sleeping problems, panic attacks, anxiety disorganized behavior including walking aimlessly outside, and substance use. The patient's history was significant for two past psychiatric hospitalizations. The patient reportedly lived with his mother. During inpatient stay, the patient was treated with multiple medications, including Lexapro. The patient reported having feelings of improvement and was discharged with instruction for community aftercare.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Major Depressive Disorders reports that treatment settings for patients with major depressive disorder include a continuum of possible levels of care and in general, patients should be treated in the least restrictive setting that is most likely to prove safe and effective. It states that the psychiatrist should choose an appropriate site of treatment after evaluating the patient's clinical condition, including symptom severity, co-occurring conditions, level of functioning, and available support system. The estimated degree of risk to self and to others is another significant determinant of treatment setting. Decisions about treatment setting should also include consideration of the patient's ability to adequately care for him- or herself, provide reliable feedback to the psychiatrist, and cooperate with treatment of the major depressive disorder. 

The patient was not psychiatrically stable as he had sudden mental status changes going from good to bad quickly without warning signs which resulted in confusion and upsetting the patient. It was reported that the patient had thought-blocking, had racing thoughts, poor concentration, and minimal interaction, thought blocking, and dysphoric mood, feeling alone, anxious, and talking to himself in the middle of his admission.  The patient was discharged after a day of observation without severe psychiatric symptoms. Based on the review of the medical record, the patient exhibited significant psychiatric symptoms, was not at his baseline, and was at high risk for worsened symptoms during his denied hospitalization stay. 
The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient.

Based on the above, the medical necessity for the continued inpatient hospital stay is substantiated.  The insurer's denial should be overturned.

This patient is a male who was admitted to this inpatient hospital treatment due to severe psychiatric symptoms including command auditory hallucinations to kill himself, suicidal thoughts, disorganized thinking, disruptive behavior, noncompliance with medications, depressed mood, and alcohol withdrawal symptoms including moderate tremors, anxiety, and an irritable mood. He had a past alcohol withdrawal seizure. He was uncooperative, had poor hygiene, and limited insight and judgment. He had a blood alcohol level (BAL) of 399 initially. He was drinking 2 pints of liquor and 12 ounces of beer daily. He had diagnoses of Schizoaffective Disorder, as well as Alcohol Use Disorder. He had multiple past psychiatric hospitalizations and past inpatient detoxification treatments. He was put on a Librium taper and it was reported that he took Librium. He also took Abilify and Trazodone. He was discharged. The insurer denied coverage for continued inpatient behavioral health treatment.

This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for continued inpatient behavioral health treatment in this hospital for specified dates but agrees with the decision to deny inpatient behavioral health treatment in this hospital for other specified dates. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Schizophrenia reports that patients with hallucinations, delusional thinking, disorganized thinking or behavior, suicidal or homicidal plan or intent, agitation, or aggressive behavior, or inability to adequately care for basic needs are candidates for hospitalization. Initially, this patient had reports of command auditory hallucinations to kill himself, suicidal thoughts, disorganized thinking, disruptive behavior, noncompliance with medications, depressed and irritable mood, and limited insight and judgment. He had poor hygiene and was uncooperative. Notes on a specific date reported that he still required and received detoxification medication, Librium 10 mg, twice to modify withdrawal and prevent complicated and life-threatening withdrawal. 

The APA Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. In this case, this patient had been using large amounts of alcohol daily and had withdrawal symptoms. Additionally, he had a prior complicated alcohol withdrawal including a prior withdrawal seizure and was at risk for complicated and life-threatening withdrawal. He had received detoxification medication until a specific date. 

According to the LOCADTR, he did require 24-hour inpatient detoxification treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive setting. This was due to the fact that he continued to use large amounts of alcohol and needed detoxification medication with multiple doses of Librium for detoxification. The risk of life-threatening and complicated withdrawal such as delirium tremens can occur days after alcohol use; therefore, he required this time from a specified range as he was receiving detoxification medication at that time, but not thereafter.

The insurer acted reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interests of the patient from a specified range, but not from another specified date range.

Based on the above, the insurer's denial for the continued stay in a behavioral health hospital is modified.

He denied suicidal ideation or aggressive impulses. He lacked coping skills and demonstrated only fair insight. He had symptoms of anxiety and grief symptoms related to the recent loss of his brother.

The inpatient level substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment included the opportunity to participate in groups, individual counseling, education and 12-step recovery groups with peer support. The patient reported that he was using alcohol and opioid (heroin) class substances of abuse with a past history of poly-substance use.  He reported using up to 48 ounces of beer three to six times per week and approximately two bundles of heroin daily.  He presented without a score on the CIWA (clinical institute withdrawal assessment) scale and COWS (clinical opiate withdrawal scale) score of 1 with complaints of anxiety and insomnia, as well as sweats and gastrointestinal upset.  He has a history of unspecified anxiety and bipolar mood disorders with no current treatment, but a history of psychiatric treatment and hospitalization.  He had received multiple past substance use disorder treatments, including recent detoxification treatment a few days prior.  He later admitted to using Fentanyl the day of his admission despite a negative drug screen that was only positive for methadone consistent with his recent detoxification treatment episode.

The patient provided no history of withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens or severe alcohol or drug withdrawal symptoms.  The patient had no acute general medical problems, but he was diagnosed with hypertension, obesity and asthma with a rescue inhaler.

The patient was medically screened and admitted for inpatient level detoxification with plans for a five day detoxification treatment episode with Methadone, vitamin replacement therapy and comfort medications.  His laboratory assessment was normal or unremarkable, as well as his physical examination that was consistent with history. Vital signs were normal on presentation and throughout his stay.

On Mental Status Examination, the patient was cooperative with good eye contact. Speech was clear and thought production was linear and logical.  There were no severe symptoms on mental status examination such as thought disorder, cognitive impairment, severe mood disturbance, psychosis or perceptual disturbance, or suicidal ideation. 

The patient presented with anxiety and insomnia.  He had fair control of his impulses. 

The patient was admitted for inpatient detoxification with a five day Methadone taper.  Vital signs were consistently normal and the patient was in no apparent distress.  The patient slept and received meals the first hospital day.  His monitoring occurred without incident, and he was to attend group sessions and receive counseling with recommendation for clinically appropriate aftercare.  He also had the opportunity to participate in 12-step meetings.  He received vitamin replacement therapy.  He reported "not feeling well" and was discharged with transfer to another hospital for continuing care.

The proposed inpatient stay and detoxification treatment and other medical services could have been safely and effectively provided at a lower level of care.  The treatment did not require the structure of an inpatient setting or 24-hour monitoring.  The patient displayed no serious disturbance of mental status despite having a history of unspecified anxiety and bipolar disorder and ongoing substance use disorders with alcohol and opioid class substances of abuse.  The patient did not show evidence for suicidal or aggressive behavior or risk, or severe cognitive impairment or psychosis, or perceptual disturbance, or other emotional disturbances that warranted an inpatient level admission and treatment.  There were no severe symptoms of withdrawal or biomedical issues, and the patient had received detoxification treatment and rehabilitation substance use treatment recently. Thus, an inpatient admission was not medically necessary.

summary:
Diagnosis: Alcohol and Substance Abuse
 
Treatment: inpatient detoxification treatment 

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient detoxification treatment. The denial is reversed. 

This patient is a male who was admitted to this inpatient detoxification treatment for substance and alcohol detoxification treatment.  He had withdrawal symptoms including tremors, nausea, vomiting, sweats, chills, agitation, body aches, anxiety, uncontrollable cravings, elevated blood pressure of 142/94, flushed skin, headache, lethargy, restless legs, and rhinorrhea. The patient had a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) score of 13.  He had a past withdrawal seizure from Xanax one year prior to admission.  He was drinking alcohol daily, including two 24-ounce beers/drinks, using up to 6 mg of Klonopin per day, using cocaine and multiple dollars-worth of cannabis daily, and Oxycontin. He had poor coping skills.  He was in outpatient substance treatment and was still using multiple serious substances. He was put on a detoxification protocol with Valium for a specified numbers time frame. He also took Prozac, Tegretol, and Gabapentin.  He was discharged. This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient detoxification treatment as the chart notes did provide enough specific evidence to support that he required this level of care.  

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders report that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment.  It also states that patients with past complicated or life-threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens are in need of inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal. They also report that patients with comorbid medical conditions that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification.  This patient could not safely be treated in an outpatient or PHP detoxification as he had active withdrawal from multiple substances including benzodiazepines and alcohol. In addition, he had a history of a past withdrawal seizure which is considered complicated withdrawal that requires 24-hour detoxification treatment.  He was using large amounts of multiple serious substances and was at risk for overdose or more severe, complicated, or life-threatening withdrawal. 

Also, despite outpatient substance treatment, legal problems and violence related to substance use, he could not maintain abstinence.  He also required and needed detoxification medication (Valium) to modify withdrawal and needed 24-hour inpatient detoxification treatment as he was at risk for worsened withdrawal symptoms if not in this 24-hour setting. It is reported that delirium tremens can occur within 3-4 days after stopping alcohol use.  This patient was having active withdrawal symptoms on admission that continued throughout the admission. He was at risk for complicated and life-threatening withdrawal symptoms for several days after admission.  According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), he did require 24-hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated in outpatient or PHP detoxification settings.

The health care plan did not act reasonably, or with sound medical judgment, or in the best interests of the patient. 

The carrier's denial of coverage for the inpatient hospital services at the inpatient detoxification level of care is reversed.  The medical necessity is substantiated.

There is a medical history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, GERD (gastroesophageal reflux disease), HCV (Hepatitis C virus), and chronic back pain.

The patient was initially admitted to the psychiatric unit for depression, suicidal ideation, and alcohol withdrawal.  She was found to have stroke-like symptoms and was transferred to the medical ward, where she was treated for a UTI and returned to the psychiatric ward.  More medical tests were required and the patient again returned to the medical ICU for fever and delirium.  She returned to the psychiatric unit 13 days later.  

The patient was treated by a multidisciplinary team including psychiatry, nursing, and therapy staff.  She was treated with individual and group therapy.  She received substance abuse treatment.  She received a psychopharmacology evaluation and was treated with Tegretol 200mg BID, Seroquel 100mg daily, Clonazepam 1mg PO TID, and Donepezil 10mg daily.  Tegretol was increased to a total of 1000mg in divided doses.  Seroquel was increased to 400mg PO QHS.  Gabapentin was started and increased to 100mg TID.  Prozac 20mg was added.  Clonazepam was tapered off and Topamax was started and tapered to 150mg PO BID.  Melatonin was added for sleep.  Remeron was added at 15mg PO QHS.  An assisted outpatient treatment order was obtained through Suffolk County.  Community Residence Housing was secured as was outpatient psychiatric treatment and a plan was in place for this prior to discharge.

It is clearly documented that discharging the patient without appropriate community resources and supports "would likely result in a decompensation of [the patient's] mental health, possibly leading again to a life-threatening crisis."

The patient represented an elevated risk of dangerous behaviors including aggressive behaviors, self-injury, and suicide, and there was no less-restrictive treatment environment appropriate.  Therefore the treatment was medically necessary.  While the patient was not endorsing active suicidality or homicidality, the patient remained with multiple static risk factors for potentially dangerous behaviors, including substance abuse, suicide attempts, and diagnosis with a severe mental illness.  Therefore the patient represented a chronic risk of potentially dangerous behaviors.  The fact that patient remained without any outpatient treatment resources and without demonstrated treatment adherence were acute risk factor for dangerous behaviors.  Furthermore, the fact that there was no less-restrictive environment of care appropriate suggests that ongoing inpatient psychiatric hospitalization was medically necessary and should be covered by the patient's health plan.

The patient represented an acutely elevated risk of dangerous behaviors, and there was no less-restrictive treatment environment appropriate.  The acute risk factors of recent delirium and no significant treatment resources in the outpatient setting with the chronic risk factors of potentially dangerous behaviors suggest that the patient would have been at an acute risk of aggressive or self-injurious behaviors (including but not limited to suicide) were she to have been discharged from the inpatient hospital setting.  The patient was discharged from the inpatient psychiatric hospital setting as soon as a less-restrictive treatment setting was appropriate.

The patient presented with a request for detoxification treatment and was medically screened and admitted to inpatient level services for the detoxification of alcohol; the patient had been using up to two pints of rum plus beer daily. The patient was also using up to 3 grams of cocaine per day, up to 6 milligrams (mg) of Xanax three to six times per week, and two blunts of hallucinogens (phencyclidine) (PCP) daily. The patient's  substance use disorders had their onset in young adulthood with the initial use of alcohol and progression of the disease with subsequent use of cocaine, PCP and Xanax. The patient had no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens but reported inadvertent overdoses and blackouts. The referral was prompted by the patient's desire to receive substance abuse treatment in the context of continued use of substances despite participating in multiple past treatment episodes with approximately 38 prior treatments, with the last detoxification occurring earlier in the month. The patient presented with mild symptoms of withdrawal with a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) scale score of 2/67 with sweats, gastrointestinal upset, anxiety and restlessness together with normal vital signs or a mildly elevated blood pressure. Again, the patient had received past detoxification treatments.
There were no acute general medical or psychiatric issues in this case.  Laboratory assessment was unremarkable except for a urine drug screen that was positive and elevated liver functions consistent with the  history including the presence of cocaine, benzodiazepine and PCP.
A mental status examination was free of severe symptoms such as thought disorder, mood disturbance, psychosis, cognitive impairment or perceptual disturbance. The patient was deemed to be motivated to enter detoxification treatment and had minimal symptoms of withdrawal at the time of admission, as noted.
The patient was admitted and placed on a detoxification regimen with a Librium taper, comfort medications, as well as vitamin replacement therapy. The detoxification was uncomplicated about withdrawal management, though the patient required ongoing use of Clonidine for anxiety/agitation and Benadryl for insomnia. The patient received counseling and education from the staff. The clinical course was uncomplicated with continued normal vital signs and the patient was discharged with clinically appropriate aftercare and immediate referral/admission to rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment.

The health plan's determination of medical necessity is upheld, in whole.

The requested benefit of detoxification treatment and withdrawal management and other medical services could have been safely and effectively provided with lower level services. The patient in this case was using alcohol on a continuous daily basis together with other substances of abuse including PCP, cocaine and Xanax. There were no co-morbid general medical problems or co-occurring psychiatric disorders in this case that would have warranted admission for inpatient level services. Moreover, the withdrawal symptoms were not reported to be severe, and the patient's clinical symptoms were not serious enough to necessitate inpatient level detoxification treatment or monitoring. There were no safety concerns in this case and no history of complicated withdrawal from drugs or alcohol despite reports of blackouts and a history of overdoses. The patient was motivated for detoxification treatment and had access to substance use disorder services in the community. Moreover, the patient had recently received detoxification treatment with discharge earlier in the same month of this presentation. The patient is a male diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), Intermittent explosive disorder and parent-child relational problem. The patient also had history attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). The patient has been inpatient consistently. The patient has history of aggression. The patient was not homicidal or psychotic on admission. There were no acute medical concerns. The patient has no issues with sleep or appetite. The patient denied having self-injurious behaviors. The patient is medicated with Adderall 30 milligrams (mg) every (q) day, Seroquel 200mg q day, Sertraline 100mg q day. There was no plan to change medication doses. The patient had been inpatient prior to admission. On admission, the patient had some fleeting suicidal ideation rated as a 1/10. Prior to admission, the patient has some oppositional behaviors, hit the wall when upset and had some scratching behaviors. The patient did not require medical attention. 

Prior to inpatient the patient had assaulted mother with physical aggression about 2 months prior to admission. The patient has also been verbally aggressive. The patient has history of multiple inpatient admissions. He has been in a group home due to aggression with mom. The patient has a history of having an argument with father and police were involved. Father has a restraining order. The patient is noted to be oppositional and his mother does not feel safe with him. The patient punched a wall about 2 weeks prior to admission. Father is noted to be "bipolar" and there is history of the patient witnessing domestic violence between parents. The patient has experimented with drugs in the past, last use 6 months prior to admission. 

Per the appeal letter, the patient was highly reactive, had non-compliance with programming and repeatedly found sharp objects to self-harm. The injuries worsened over time in Residential Treatment Center (RTC) due to deeper self-injury. In one example, the patient got a metal object from a binder and the staff had to sit with him for 3 hours to process until he gave it up. The patient had the object in his mouth and a level 4 hold needed to occur for the patient to hand it over. At the time of the patient's time, the patient reported he swallowed four staples. It is unknown when these two events occurred. 

The subject under review is the medical necessity for the residential treatment care. 

The residential mental health treatment was medically necessary for this patient. Given the information provided for the dates of service under review, which was shortly after admission following a long inpatient admission, the patient was significantly mood labile, oppositional, engaging in frequent self-harm, swallowing metal objects and punching walls. The patient endorsed intermittent suicidal ideation with plans when he was highly emotionally dysregulated. The patient required staff intervention frequently when dysregulated in order to calm down. There is no indication the patient could have been safely managed in a less restrictive environment due to danger to self or others during this time. Therefore, the previous denial should be overturned in full.

This is a female patient with a psychiatric history of Bipolar Disorder and Substance Use Disorder. She was transferred from a medical unit where she had been treated for pneumonia to inpatient psychiatric unit due to depressive and anxiety symptoms, suicidal ideation with plan to end her life, recent violent behavior, hopelessness and helplessness, and anxiety. The patient reportedly was using multiple substances and had a positive toxicology for cocaine, opiates, and benzodiazepines. Her medical treatment included Seroquel, Lexapro, Tegretol, and Buspirine and individual supportive treatment. The patient was then discharged to a substance rehabilitation treatment.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Bipolar Disorders reports that the least restrictive level of care for safe and effective treatment is appropriate and also that patients with severe agitation, aggression, psychotic symptoms, suicidal or homicidal plan or intent or attempts, manic episodes, severe major depressive episodes, or inability to adequately care for basic self-care needs are in need of hospital treatment. In this case, this patient had continued reports of severe depressive symptoms during the denial period and also reportedly was considered a high risk of relapse for cocaine, opiates, and benzodiazepines if not transferred to a 24-hour inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment upon discharge.  The patient was considered a high risk for overdose.  It was reported that the patient was severely depressed with dysphoric mood, feelings of hopelessness and helplessness, and she was isolative with impaired attention. Notes reported that the patient was still hopeless and helpless with anxiety and depressed mood. Notes reported that the patient was depressed and anxious but less. It also reported that she could not manage on her own and was awaiting placement to inpatient substance rehabilitation facility. The patient found placement at which point, the patient was discharged and transferred for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment. 

Based on the review of the medical record a literature, this was a high risk patient who had severe depressive symptoms and suicidal ideation in conjunction with multiple substance use including cocaine, opiates, and benzodiazepines. The patient was at high risk for relapse and overdose if not appropriately transferred to a 24-hour structured and supervised treatment setting upon discharge. According to the APA Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Suicidal Behaviors, patients with hopelessness, bipolar disorder, and substance use are at higher risk for suicide. This was the case for this patient who continued to report depressive symptoms including depressed and hopelessness throughout the inpatient stay. Thus, inpatient hospital treatment was medically necessary for this patient.  

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient.

The carrier's denial of coverage for inpatient mental health treatment should be overturned. The medical necessity is substantiated.

The patient notably lacked coping skills, needed to better identify relapse triggers, and needed to learn relapse prevention skills. Without this structured and supervised therapeutic residential treatment, the patient likely would have relapsed again as evidence by her history of relapses despite inpatient substance treatment and outpatient substance treatments in the past. Inpatient substance use rehabilitation was medically necessary for this patient.

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient.

summary:
Diagnosis:  Major Depressive Disorder and Polysubstance Abuse.
Treatment:  IOP treatment.   
The insurer denied IOP treatment.  The determination is overturned.

The patient is an adolescent female who presented for intensive outpatient program (IOP) level treatment for co-occurring disorders including major depressive disorder and social anxiety disorder in the context of polysubstance use disorder and severe psychosocial stressors.  The patient was abusing her Adderall (snorting) together with intermittent use of alcohol, hallucinogens, benzodiazepines, cocaine and cannabis, all of which were in the mild range except for the cannabis use disorder that was severe with persistent use.  She was having problems at school and at home with worsening symptoms of anxiety and depression and the co-occurring substance use that compounded her mental health conditions.

The patient's presentation for IOP treatment followed partial hospital program (PHP) level treatment with step down to IOP level care.  Again, she was receiving IOP level programming in the context of the severe psychosocial stressors and with encouragement from her parents, with whom she lived.  She had family stress related to her substance use and other stressors within the educational and social environment domains.

She presented with mood disturbance, social phobia and severe substance-related problems that had resulted in functional impairments and inability to maintain abstinence.  She had no prior substance use disorder treatment.  At the time of presentation, the patient was also reporting symptoms of depression and anxiety, for which she was prescribed medication-Prozac.  The patient provided no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens.  She was medically screened and admitted for IOP level treatment with three days per week and three hours per day programming.  

There were no severe symptoms on mental status examination.  The patient was at high risk for suicidal behavior with few protective factors despite denial of suicidal ideation.  She had symptoms of depression including dysphoric mood and irritability with anxious affect and the social phobia.  The patient had limited knowledge of substance use disorder treatment and demonstrated impaired judgment, due to her underlying psychiatric disorders and poor decision-making skills, and directly due to the substance use including poor control of impulses, and cognitive impairment with memory and concentration difficulties, as well as underlying cognitive difficulties noted on previous neuropsychological testing.

The patient was admitted for IOP treatment. Her clinical course progressed slowly without incident.  However, she continued to display affective disturbance and reported intense craving during the initial weeks of treatment.  The patient was engaged in group and family focused sessions.  She received ongoing psychiatric management with titration of the Prozac as clinically appropriate to 40 mg, addressing symptoms of anxiety and depression.  She also was participating actively in group and educational sessions with the goal of developing improved coping skills and maintaining abstinence with periodic drug testing that was negative.

The case record indicates that the patient was working on issues within the family constellation and working to develop relapse prevention skills, as well as involvement in peer-supported recovery groups per her treatment plan.  The treatment plan also called for continued medication management.  Her mental status had improved with good sleep and appetite, improved mood and diminished anxiety with resolution of cravings and other persistent effects of the substance use.  She had gained insight with better judgment and control of impulses.  The treatment team was considering referrals and recommendations for clinically appropriate aftercare and consideration of a sober supports and participation in peer-supported recovery groups with continued support from her parents.

The case records, health plan documents, appeal documents, and correspondence from the health plan were reviewed, as well as records from prior evaluations and treatment.  This review is a New York State review with the application of NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria.

Yes, the requested health service/treatment of intensive outpatient mental health treatment for 3 days a week, and 3 hours a day  is medically necessary for this patient.
The patient presented with a mood and anxiety disturbance and was using multiple substances of abuse on a daily continuous basis with severe psychosocial stressors and functional impairments that did warrant continued IOP level structure, monitoring and services.  The continued treatment for the co-occurring disorders diagnosed in this case could not have been effectively provided at a lower level of care for the time interval under review.  Moreover, the patient's social environment was not conducive to lower level treatment, and the patient had previously struggled with craving in the context of the mood disturbance and associated symptoms of anxiety with limited insight, impaired judgment and poor control of impulses.

Thus, despite the progress noted, the clinical features and treatment dimensions did necessitate the continued structure of an IOP level setting with intensive treatment, structure, supports, and monitoring for abstinence.  The patient's history of substance use (frequency and quantity) together with the severe psychosocial stressors and co-occurring psychiatric disorders do reflect a complicated clinical picture and do support the need for a safe and effective treatment setting, especially with regard to recent worsening of her co-occurring conditions.  The documentation clearly indicates that the patient was at high risk for treatment failure if the continued treatment were to be attempted at a lower level of care.  Therefore, medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published practice guidelines, ASAM Criteria, and the scientific literature, referenced below, and consistent with the appropriate application of NY OASAS LOCADTR 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines, referenced below.

Mental Health
Mental Health: Inpatient

Diagnosis: bipolar disorder
Treatment: Inpatient mental health. The insurer denied the inpatient mental health stay. The health plan's determination is overturned in part. 15 days are medically necessary. 

The patient is a male with diagnoses of bipolar disorder (BPD) with psychotic features versus (vs.) schizoaffective (SCZD) disorder admitted to Behavioral Health Inpatient Treatment (BHIT).

The requested treatment of BHIT for 15 days is medically necessary. Discharge before this would be against this patient's best interests in view of his multiple psychosocial stressors, past history, and comorbid conditions. Poor social attachment is associated with increased suicide risk. This patient has multiple stressors which interact with his genetic predisposition to increase his suicide risk. This patient had a clear genetic predisposition in addition to multiple psychosocial stressors. The only acceptable goal for treatment of bipolar disorder is sustained euthymia, without psychotic features. Considering all his risk factors, it is medically necessary and reasonable to require several days of sustained improvement to avoid discharge premtaurely for this patient. The evidence from case notes supports sustained improvement, leading to the judgment that it would be in the best interest of the patient and in accord with current standards of best care that the patient be discharged on day 15. Discharge prior would have a high probability of relapse and the need for rehospitalization.
