summary:
Substance Abuse/Addictions
Substance Abuse: Inpatient

The patient is a male who presented for detoxification and substance-related services. The patient has an 18 year history of severe substance use disorders with opioid (heroin and methadone), stimulants (cocaine), other substance of abuse (PCP), and cannabis (marijuana) class substances of abuse. He had a history of multiple substance use disorder treatment episodes, but relapsed and was using a up to 10 bags of cocaine and up to 10 bags of heroin with intravenous (IV) administration, two bags of hallucinogens (phencyclidine) and one marijuana blunt, as well as tobacco (½ pack per day). Again, he had multiple prior substance use disorder treatments including a rehabilitation treatment episode with a chronic relapsing course since adolescence.

The health plan's determination is overturned. The inpatient detoxification is clinically appropriate, and medically necessary in this case scenario. The requested medical services could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. The patient in this case was using large quantities of heroin together with cocaine, as well as PCP and marijuana that did warrant the admission and the continued inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring. Detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments pertinent to the detoxification treatment episode could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment that was provided at the time of admission. Moreover, the patient's social environment was not conducive to an effective detoxification, and the patient had struggled with withdrawal symptoms (tremor, sweats, nausea, anxiety, irritability, restlessness and insomnia) which were being effectively addressed with methadone and supportive measures. The patient had associated clinical features that included lack of sober supports and limited insight, impaired judgment and poor control of impulses. Thus, the adult inpatient stay and continued detoxification treatment of this patient's substance use disorders did necessitate the continued structure of an inpatient level setting with withdrawal management and psychosocial supports, and 24-hour monitoring. The patient's history of substance abuse (frequency and quantity) together with the severe psychosocial stressors and functional impairments do reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder and the need for a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management as the patient was at high risk for treatment failure if detoxification and withdrawal management were to be attempted at a lower level of care. Therefore, medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published practice guidelines, American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, scientific literature, and the of NYS LOCADTR 3.0 Criteria.

summary:
Diagnosis: Mental Health/depression
Treatment: Mental health inpatient
The insurer denied the Mental health impatient stay. The denial was overturned.

This case involves a patient admitted for acute inpatient psychiatric treatment. The patient had become increasingly anxious and depressed with suicidal ideation, plan and intent in the context of psychosocial stressors that included primary support and occupational, housing and social environment domains. the patient had reconnected with an ex-boyfriend despite a history of physical and emotional abuse.  the patient had cut off communication with a daughter and had lost job three weeks prior to presentation. Patient was kicked out of the boyfriends housing after an argument and was wandering the streets barefoot, intoxicated and crying. Patient was brought to the emergency department by Emergency Medical Services (EMS) which resulted in evaluation and admission for inpatient level psychiatric treatment.
At the time of  admission, the patient had a blood alcohol level of 308 and  was noted to be severely depressed with persistent suicidal ideation wanting to die from carbon monoxide poisoning. Functioning had deteriorated with social isolation and an increase in drinking with up to one gallon of vodka per day and intermittent use of cocaine. the patient underwent medical screening with the admission for acute inpatient psychiatric evaluation and treatment and safety monitoring. Patient had a history of mood disorder best characterized as recurrent and severe major depressive disorder without psychotic features and severe symptoms of anxiety and panic attacks. The patient was previously involved in outpatient treatment with medication and therapy services, but had not followed up and had been non-adherent with past treatment with Zoloft and Effexor and Abilify.
The patient's mental status examination revealed a depressed mood with hopelessness, helplessness, anhedonia, and morbid thought content that included thoughts of death and suicidal ideation wanting to die from carbon monoxide poisoning.  Sleep, appetite, energy levels, concentration, and volition were disturbed. Insight and judgment were limited due to the severity of depression and associated symptoms of anxiety and alcohol dependence. There was active substance use disorder with alcohol, tobacco and cocaine with a drug screen positive for cocaine. The patient was admitted to acute inpatient level services and maintained on close observation with structured milieu therapy, and pharmacotherapy with antidepressant and anxiolytic medication supplemented with medication to enhance sleep and address anxiety. Patient was placed on a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) protocol with Ativan and received vitamin and nicotine replacement therapy. The psychotropic regimen included Remeron, titrated as clinically appropriate with the availability of as needed (prn) medications for anxiety and insomnia. Group and individual psychotherapy were provided as well as other therapeutic interventions to facilitate better coping and functioning and reality testing. The post-acute withdrawal symptoms from alcohol gradually diminished without complications. The team was working on a discharge plan to include a clinically appropriate step down and safety plan in view of the patient's history of non-adherence and history of quickly decompensating with past treatment episodes. the patient had improved and no longer had a plan or intent of suicide. Patient was more actively participating in therapeutic activities. Medications were tolerated with improved mood and diminished anxiety; and, the patient was adherent with medications and compliant with treatment plan. The daughter participated in a discharge planning meeting on the day of discharge in order to plan for a safe and clinically appropriate disposition. The health plan determination of medical necessity is overturned in whole.
The patient's Continued Psychiatric Acute Inpatient Level of was clinically appropriate, reasonable, and in the best interest of the patient. The patient had severe symptoms of depression,  was a safety risk, and, outpatient treatment had failed to prevent the worsening symptoms of depression with onset of severe symptoms in the context of a potential for a lethal suicide attempt with alcohol and cocaine use, and with deterioration in functioning. The patient remained a safety risk and functionally impaired with high risk for relapse if discharged from acute inpatient level care prior and, the patient needed to reach a stable baseline of functioning with assurance of medication tolerability with a solid disposition and safety plan prior to discharge from inpatient level care.
Thus, it was medically necessary for this patient with severe and recurrent major depressive disorder to remain in the acute inpatient setting.

summary:
Diagnosis: Chronic lower back pain.
Treatment: Psychological testing.
The insurer denied the psychological testing.
The denial is overturned. 

Yes, the Psychological Testing was medically necessary.

The patient is a male with chronic low back pain for whom a spinal cord stimulator was recommended. As part of the pre-surgical screening, a psychological evaluation was ordered prior to the SCS (spinal cord stimulator) placement. 

The usage of pre-psychological screening prior to SCS trial and implant is a Medicare requirement, and is typically required by most insurers. While it may not be "standard of care," it is utilized by the vast majority of pain management physicians prior to SCS trial, primarily in part that is a requirement by most carriers. It is rare to find an insurance plan that does not require this or at least cover this.  

The usage or pre-SCS psychological screening has been shown to be effective in the literature at preventing unnecessary procedures.  In fact, it has been shown that the success rate of implantation of SCS is improved by pre-surgical psychological evaluation, as those with poor prognosis due to pre-existing psychological issues are either excluded, are receive appropriate treatment for those issues prior to consideration of the procedure. Pre-surgical psychological testing is commonly attached to the work up for SCS, in most cases it is considered as part of the work up to determine if the patient is an appropriate candidate for SCS.  Given the above, the requested psychological testing was medically necessary and should be covered.

summary:
Diagnosis: Schizoaffective Disorder 
Treatment:  Inpatient Mental Health Stay 

The insurer denied the inpatient mental health stay. The health plan's determination is overturned. 

This is a patient with schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type and co-occurring substance use with the use of cocaine and cannabis. She was admitted to acute inpatient level services with severe symptoms of psychotic and mood disorder with acute symptoms of psychosis and agitation. The patient's admission had been precipitated by aggressive and threatening behavior at her homeless shelter in the context of severe substance use disorder and non-compliance with her mental health treatment. She had stopped her medication, risperidone at an unknown dose. The patient had required police intervention because she was spitting at the other residents at the shelter and was threatening harm. She was combative and assaultive when the police arrived and required intramuscular (IM) medication upon arrival at the emergency department. 
The patient has a history of multiple prior admissions for psychiatric treatment for schizoaffective disorder. The patient had been non-adherent with medications and non-compliant with outpatient treatment in the context of active substance abuse with cocaine and cannabis. She had a history of violent and aggressive behavior when manic. There were no acute general medical issues in this case; and laboratory assessments were normal or unremarkable with a positive drug screen consistent with history. 
The patient is homeless living in shelters, unemployed, and has limited or no social supports. She had been arrested at the time of her encounter with police with a court date pending. 

On the Mental Status Examination on admission, the patient appeared unkempt and disheveled with guarded stance and uncooperative behavior, and psychotic symptoms that included paranoid thinking with irritable and labile affect. She displayed an irritable mood with anxiety and slowed mentation. She had decreased concentration, sleep, and volition. Her speech was coherent but disorganized. Insight and judgment were limited and impaired with poor control of impulses. 

The patient was admitted to acute inpatient level care after medical screening in the emergency department. The patient's treatment plan included safety-monitoring, access to group and milieu therapies, and resumption of medications with an initial dose of risperidone at one milligram twice daily, titrated as clinically appropriate. The patient was initially paranoid and socially inappropriate with labile affect and continued agitation, she remained dysphoric and irritable with hostility, anger, tension and excitability requiring medication adjustments with the addition of Cogentin and Neurontin, as well as use of Invega Sustenna at an initial dose of 234 mg. She had persistent motor agitation and labile affect addressed with safety monitoring and as needed (prn) medications while her oral risperidone was titrated to three mg twice daily together with Cogentin. The patient made unsteady progress with participation in select groups focusing on illness education, illness recovery, and reality testing. She had bouts of erratic behavior with pacing and motor agitation. She was medication adherent and compliant with her treatment plan. Her agitation eventually resolved and her mood improved with better sleep and improving insight. She received a second dose of Invega Sustenna at 156 mg with plans for outpatient aftercare to address the co-occurring schizoaffective disorder and substance use disorders with plans for another injection of the Invega Sustenna after 30 days and continued use of oral risperidone, Neurontin and Cogentin and with referral for housing and other services to support abstinence from substance of abuse. 

A discharge plan was completed including plans for after care and a return to the community with housing/shelter. At the time of discharge, the patient was better focused, calmer, and displaying better judgment with improved mood and brighter affect. Discharge occurred with clinically appropriate aftercare in collaboration with community providers to include mental health services with a safety plan, as well as recommendations to address the co-occurring substance use disorders. 

The health plan documents including case notes, and appeal documents were reviewed, as well as correspondence from the health plan and the treatment facility. Case records were reviewed with summary and progress notes and other documents. This case is a New York mandated review. 

At issue is the medical necessity of continued inpatient mental health admission and stay.
The requested health service/treatment of Continued inpatient mental health admission and stay is medically necessary for this patient. 

The patient's symptoms of psychosis and mood disorder together with continued risk of impulsive and aggressive behavior prompted the necessity for the admission and the continued acute inpatient level structure and monitoring provided through discharge. The case is complicated by active substance use disorders; and non-compliance with treatment and medication adherence problems in the context of severe psychosocial stressors with homelessness and limited social supports. The residual symptoms of mood disorder and psychosis; risk for aggressive behavior, co-occurring substance use disorders, and treatment issues related to arranging a safe and appropriate discharge plan together with a history of medication non-adherence warranted the continued services at an acute inpatient level of care. Medically necessary treatment included safety monitoring and maintaining abstinence from substances of abuse while titrating medications and initiating a long-acting injectable antipsychotic medication that was critical to the patient's treatment in the context of past non-compliance with medication treatment with oral medications. The inpatient stay thru discharge was therefore clinically appropriate and medical necessary including the inpatient level structure, intensity of services with evidence-based psychosocial interventions, and 24-hour monitoring through the day of discharge when the patient had reached a level of stability that she could return to the community with clinically appropriate follow-up and aftercare. This answer is consistent with the scientific literature, American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria and published practice guideline, referenced below, as well as New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews and the application of NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Guidelines.

The patient presented with no acute general medical issues though patient had chronic conditions that included gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and Seasonal Allergies and was nicotine dependent. The patient has history of multiple past treatment episodes with relapses and co-occurring bipolar mood disorder and unspecified anxiety disorder with recent non-compliance with mental health follow up and non-adherence of psychotropic medication regimen.

The patient was receiving treatment for sedative-hypnotic-anxiolytic (benzodiazepine), cannabis (marijuana), and alcohol use disorders. She was diagnosed with unspecified depressive disorder with associated symptoms of anxiety that served to trigger her substance use. The patient's alcohol and cannabis and sedative-hypnotic-anxiolytic substance-related disorders were severe with daily continuous use of Xanax together with prescribed Klonopin and use of marijuana up to four times per week with intermittent binge drinking of one-third bottle at a time. The patient's substance use started at adolescents with escalating use in the context of high-risk behaviors including impulsive aggression and self-harm. She had been suspended from school multiple times and had been hospitalized to address the problematic behaviors occurring while intoxicated. 

The requested substance user treatment could not have been effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. The patient in this case presented with a co-occurring mood disturbance with associated symptoms of anxiety and use of large quantities of drugs and alcohol with severe psychosocial stressors and functional impairments that did warrant the admission and the continued IOP level structure, monitoring and services. The patient's social environment was not conducive to lower level treatment as peers were using substances of abuse and the patient was not sufficiently motivated to maintain abstinence without the continued IOP structure. And, the patient struggled with craving in the context of the mood disturbance and associated symptoms of anxiety with limited insight, impaired judgment and poor control of impulses.

Thus, the clinical features and treatment dimensions in this case did warrant the continued structure of an IOP level setting with intensive treatment, structure, supports, and safety monitoring. The patient's history of substance use (frequency and quantity) together with the severe psychosocial stressors and co-occurring psychiatric disorder do reflect a complicated clinical picture, and does support and the need for a safe and effective treatment setting, especially in regard to the history of school suspensions and aggressive behaviors and the potential for high risk behaviors while under the influence of alcohol and drugs. She did not engage in unsafe or significantly inappropriate behavior toward herself or others.  Reported inappropriate sexualized behavior was described as being that which she engaged in prior to attending this program.  She did not require intensive staff intervention to keep her or others safe. The patient reportedly had recent homelessness, and had multiple past psychiatric hospitalizations. The patient was admitted and was treated with Risperidone and Trazodone.  The patient was stabilized and discharged to a men's shelter. 

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Schizophrenia reports that patients with hallucinations, delusional thinking, disorganized behavior, suicidal or homicidal plan or intent, agitation, or aggressive behavior are candidates for inpatient treatment.  In this case after several days the patient had no reports of further serious psychotic symptoms such as delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized behavior, suicidal or homicidal ideation, intent, or plan, manic symptoms, aggressive, threatening, self-injurious, or agitated behavior, withdrawal symptoms or acute medical instability.  

Several days into the patient's admission it was reported that the patient denied suicidal or homicidal ideation, had no hallucinations or delusions, no behavioral issues, and that he was compliant and cooperative.  Notes at that time reported that the patient denied hallucinations, delusions, suicidal or homicidal ideation. Continued dated notes through his discharge reported that the patient had no hallucinations or delusions, denied suicidal or homicidal ideation, was cooperative and had goal directed thought process. His mood was good, and that he had no hallucinations or a delusion, denied suicidal or homicidal ideation, and was cooperative. Several days after his admission the patient had no reports of acute or severe mental health or behavioral symptoms that required 24-hour acute hospital treatment, and there were no reports of specific identifiable or quantifiable treatment goals or objectives that could only be achieved in a 24-hour acute psychiatric hospital treatment setting as of then or that could not be achieved in a less restrictive level of care as of then. Thus, continued inpatient mental health stay was not medically necessary for this patient.

The health plan acted reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient.

The carrier's denial of coverage for the inpatient admission continued inpatient mental health stay should be upheld.  The medical necessity is not substantiated.

Patient has a history of bipolar disorder and severe depressive episodes and psychiatric treatment with therapy and medications, as well as multiple psychiatric hospitalizations. The patient has a history of mood disorder best characterized as bipolar I disorder with manic and depressive episodes and multiple psychiatric hospitalizations for severe symptoms of the mood disorder and an unspecified anxiety disorder. Patient was receiving outpatient psychiatric treatment with medications, but had failed to follow up after the last psychiatric hospitalization.
The patient has a history of substance use disorders, as noted with active substance use and consequences of  use that includes legal charges, dropping out of college and unemployment. The mental status examination revealed sad affect and anxiety including apprehension, nervousness, tension, irritability, and excessive worry. Sleep, appetite, energy levels and volition were disturbed. The patient exhibited depressed mood with suicidal ideation, hopelessness and anhedonia. Patient was withdrawn with motor agitation. There was no psychosis or other signs of cognitive impairment or perceptual disturbance. Judgment was markedly impaired, and suicidal risk was judged to be moderately severe with poor control of impulses and limited insight together with  struggles with maintaining abstinence. The patient was admitted to inpatient level care with plans for close observation, safety monitoring, structured milieu therapy, and pharmacotherapy initially with olanzapine, bupropion and clonazepam, as well as vitamin and nicotine replacement therapy. The patient continued to exhibit severe symptoms of depression with dysphoria and sad affect. For the DOS in question , the patient had bouts of mood cycling with irritable dysphoria, distractibility and concentration problems, and disorganized thought production. The medications were titrated as clinically appropriate. The patient was discharged from inpatient level care with step down to the community and referral for clinically appropriate aftercare. summary:
Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder
Treatment: Inpatient mental health stay
The insurer is denied coverage for inpatient mental health stay.
The denial is partially overturned.

This is a female patient who was admitted to this inpatient mental health treatment due to a suicide attempt by overdose. She reported a depressed mood, worthlessness, poor energy, poor sleep, agitation, starting fights, self-injurious behavior including cutting her arm, and she had reports of dissociative episodes and past aggression including killing a cat and aggressive threats with a knife. She had Major Depressive Disorder, Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). Her hospital course of treatment and management included Gabapentin, Hydroxyzine, suicidal precaution, Zoloft, Sertraline, levothyroxine, ibuprofen, individual and group therapy. She was medically stable and discharged.

The insurer denied coverage for continued inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital as not medically necessary treatment. They stated that she had no suicidal or homicidal ideation or plan, self-harm behavior, or psychosis, and had no restraints or seclusion.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Suicidal Behaviors reports that patients with suicide attempts are at high risk for suicide as past suicide attempts are the single most reliable predictor of suicide. It also reports that patients may require more time in the hospital to better assess suicide because they sometimes do not tell the truth regarding their suicidal thoughts in order to leave the hospital. They also note that observation in the hospital is appropriate to better ensure their safety. This patient was considered a high risk patient and benefitted from remaining in the hospital and being observed and assessed for safety, which was 2 days after last reporting suicide ideation with depression. Notes reported that she had suicidal ideation, sad mood, and was frustrated with being in the seclusion room. She reported that she dissociated during her last suicide attempt. Notes reported depressed and angry mood and concern regarding her dissociative episodes which involved suicide attempts and killing an animal in the past. Notes reported that she was overwhelmed, had self-injurious behavior including scratching her arm, and residential treatment was discussed. Notes reported that she had trauma nightmares, and psychological testing was recommended for dissociative episodes. Notes reported that she had suicidal ideation, but did not act out on it because she was on this 24-hour hospital unit, and she reported guilt, shame, depressed mood, and anger. Notes reported that she continued to struggle with low mood and maladaptive coping strategies and there was concern for her safety if not in this setting and if she went home prematurely. Notes reported that she still had suicidal ideation. After observing her 2 more days without reports of suicidal ideation, plan, or intent, or severe depressive symptoms, the chart notes no longer provided enough specific evidence to support that she still required 24-hour hospital treatment after that. Notes reported euthymic mood, no safety concerns, and she denied suicidal or homicidal ideation. Notes reported euthymic mood, and she denied suicidal or homicidal ideation or self-injurious behavior. Notes reported that she was discharged.

As a result, modify the previous decision and approve coverage for continued inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital for specified dates but deny coverage for continued inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital beyond those dates. The insurer acted reasonably, with sound medical judgment, and in the best interests of the patient for part of the stay but not the rest.

Based on the above, the medical necessity for the inpatient mental health stay is partially overturned.

Treatment: Continued Partial Hospitalization Substance Use Treatment 
The insurer denied the Continued Partial Hospitalization Substance Use Treatment. The denial is overturned.
The Continued Partial Hospitalization Substance Use Treatment was medically necessary for this patient in order to effectively address the continuing clinical needs for rehabilitation treatment of severe substance use disorders with evidence-based psychosocial treatments and medication assisted treatment with gabapentin and Wellbutrin, and to work toward relapse prevention; in order to address the patient's lack of awareness of the seriousness of her illnesses with psycho-education and recovery groups; and in order to address issues within the social environment including an appropriate disposition with sober supports, especially in working with the patient's clinical providers in developing a clinically appropriate disposition; and in order to work on coping skills that will be necessary in building a sober support system and continued recovery efforts with community providers and engagement with 12-step recovery groups and a sponsor. The patient was noted to be in the early stage of change with the need for medication assisted treatment, especially in view of ongoing cravings and persistent post-acute withdrawal symptoms. Wellbutrin was used for treatment of the co-occurring mood disorder combined with Trileptal. The patient's continued struggle with mood disturbance and severe psychosocial stressors warranted the continued PHP level structure and monitoring to assure abstinence while working on the development of relapse prevention plan and coping skills that were critical in this case together with necessary gains with insight that facilitated acquisition of better coping skills. 
Thus, the continued PHP level treatment provided the clinically appropriate components of the treatment that were provided with clinically appropriate structure, intensity of services, and monitoring. The continued PHP treatment through discharge was therefore medically necessary including continued monitoring for the duration of the proposed treatment in order to achieve a safe transition to lower level treatment and transition to IOP level care. None of this therapeutic work could have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in view of the multiple, complicating factors in this case for the time interval under review.
This answer is consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice and ASAM criteria and scientific literature and published practice guidelines referenced below, as well as the application of NY STATE OASAS LOCADTR 3.0 Criteria that is applicable to this NY State mandated case review.
In this case scenario, the patient's co-occurring psychiatric disorders, persistent post-acute withdrawal symptoms and intense cravings, and lack of awareness or limitations of insight together with the seriousness of the substance use disorders is illustrated by her continued use despite functional decline and engagement in high-risk behaviors potentially impacting general health (dangerous combinations of drugs and unprotected sex), and despite having access to treatment in the community. 
The presence of high-risk behaviors and trauma related symptoms complicate this case. Additionally, the patient's co-occurring mental health issues that included mood disturbance and trauma symptoms were triggering the patient's use of substances including prominent and persistent symptoms. The patient recovery environment was not sufficient for treatment with lower level services during the time frame under review considering these clinical factors and treatment dimensions, and the patient did not have sober supports to sustain a recovery effort until she had worked with her family and committed to a recovery process.

Treatment: Continued Inpatient admission

Yes, the Continued inpatient admission was medically necessary.

The patient is a female with a history of mental illness who received inpatient psychiatric treatment.

The patient has been diagnosed with schizophrenia.  She has a history of medication non-compliance, prior inpatient hospitalizations.  She lives in an independent living facility and is on SSI (supplemental security income).  She has hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and asthma.  She has a history of aggressive behavior.

The patient was brought into the hospital in the context of worsening psychosis and aggression.  She was making delusional and paranoid statements and was noted to be medication non-compliant.  She was medically cleared for psychiatric hospitalization and was hospitalized.  She was treated by a multidisciplinary team including psychiatry, nursing, and therapy staff.  She received group and individual treatment.  She received a psychopharmacology evaluation and was started on Risperidone, Depakote, and Cogentin.  Invega Sustenna was utilized during the hospitalization.

The patient represented an elevated risk of dangerous behaviors, including aggressive behaviors, self-injury, and suicide, and there was no less-restrictive treatment environment appropriate.  Therefore, the treatment was medically necessary.  While the patient was not endorsing active suicidality or homicidality, the patient remained grossly psychotic.  The patient had multiple static risk factors for potentially dangerous behaviors, including prior aggression, medical comorbidities, and diagnosis with a severe mental illness.  Therefore, the patient represented a chronic risk of potentially dangerous behaviors.  The fact that patient remained psychotic was acute risk factor for dangerous behaviors.  Furthermore, the fact that there was no less-restrictive environment of care appropriate suggests that ongoing inpatient psychiatric hospitalization was medically necessary and should be covered by the patient's health plan.

The insurer denied coverage for continued Substance Use Disorder Services.  The denial is reversed. 

This patient is a male admitted to residential substance use treatment after a reported hospitalization due to a withdrawal seizure.  It was reported that the patient's seizure was related to his withdrawal, and his Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) score was 10.  The patient was also noted to have withdrawal symptoms including headache, body aches, restlessness, tremors, insomnia, and anxiety.  The patient was treated with Librium for detoxification and had completed treatment.  The patient then had substance rehabilitation treatment but then had another withdrawal seizure and required Librium for breakthrough treatment and an Emergency Department (ED) evaluation.  When the patient returned to the facility, he was started on Keppra to prevent seizure.  The patient's substance use history included drinking up to 12 drinks per day with regular use of alcohol since early adulthood and first use as a child, using up to 4 mg of Xanax per day, and smoking heavy amount of cannabis, also.  The patient refused past substance treatment.  The patient had suicidal and homicidal ideation while in rehabilitation treatment, as well as purging behavior, and was not reported at his baseline function and health status. 

The American Psychiatry Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment.  It also reports that patients with past withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens are in need of 24-hour inpatient detoxification.  In this case, this patient met the APA recommendation for 24-hour inpatient/residential detoxification. 
 
According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), the patient required 24-hour treatment, as he needed detoxification medication and received detoxification medication of Librium on a specified date, as he had another reported withdrawal seizure and was at high risk for delirium tremens and life threatening withdrawal.  The patient required multiple detoxification treatments with Librium, initially and then again after his withdrawal seizure that required Emergency Department (ED) evaluation and addition of Keppra to his medication regimen. 

The American Psychiatry Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that inpatient treatment is indicated primarily for individuals whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting.  In this case this patient was considered in need of 24-hour substance rehabilitation treatment.  Also, the National Institute on Drug Abuse: Principles of Addiction Treatment: A Research Based Guide- reports that the best treatment outcomes occur with longer durations of treatment.  It also states that recovery from drug addiction is a long term process and that treatment techniques to increase motivation for treatment are necessary to prevent dropout rates.  In this case, this patient required this 24-hour residential substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatment. 

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient. 

The carrier's denial of coverage for continued Substance Use Disorder Services is reversed.  The medical necessity is substantiated.

The patient reported the he had multiple past inpatient detoxification and rehabilitation treatments. The patient was admitted and was treated on a 5 day Librium protocol and taper. The patient completed the Librium taper and was discharged.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. In this case, this patient had been drinking large amounts of alcohol daily up to 4-5 pints per day and had a long history of alcohol use with experiences of blackouts in the past. On hospital presentation, the patient had active withdrawal symptoms and was at risk for more severe, complicated, or even life threatening withdrawal symptoms.

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), this patient required 24-hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated in a less restrictive setting. The patient's pattern of alcohol use was significant with large amount of daily intake despite having multiple, past inpatient detoxification and rehabilitation treatments. At the time of hospital presentation, the patient had active withdrawal symptoms and was deemed medically necessary to treat with the Librium protocol to modify his withdrawal symptoms.

Notes reported that the patient was started on a Librium protocol. Notes reported that the patient was still taking Librium for detoxification. Notes reported that the patient was still on the Librium protocol and was having a good effect from the detoxification treatment. Notes reported that the patient was still on the Librium treatment for detoxification. The patient was then stable for discharge to rehab.

The patient required this inpatient treatment setting to treat his withdrawal and also to prevent the chance for relapse and life-threatening complications. The patient was appropriately discharged.

He was noted to be in a debilitated state with mental confusion and decline in functioning representing a safety issue. Thus, the patient was subsequently admitted after medical clearance that included physical examination, laboratory assessment, chest x-ray, and electrocardiogram (EKG), and admitted for acute inpatient psychiatric services for treatment of the exacerbation of his chronic psychotic disorder best characterized as unspecified schizophrenia.

The patient has a history of psychiatric treatment for schizophrenia with multiple inpatient hospitalizations, and a history of medication non-adherence.

There were no acute general medical problems in this case. He was obese with gynecomastia.

The patient is homeless and lives in a shelter. He is unemployed. There was no evidence for substance use and no legal issues in this case.
Mental Status Examination on admission: The patient was guarded with poor eye contact and cognitively impaired with thought disorder and perceptual disturbance characterized by auditory hallucinations and preoccupation with internal stimuli. He displayed irritable and dysphoric mood with anxiety, nervousness, apprehension, tension, and excess worry together with ideas of reference to being followed by the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and others. He demonstrated disorganized thought processing with thought blocking and with content that was illogical and incoherent. He had decreased concentration, energy, sleep, and volition, and presented with impaired judgment, poor insight and poor control of impulses with inability to care for self.

The patient's treatment plan included safety monitoring and resumption of antipsychotic medication targeting symptoms of psychosis, as well as supportive measures to encourage oral intake and to facilitate reality testing. He had the opportunity to participate in group therapy and psychoeducation provided within the milieu, as well as activity therapies to support healthy living and social skills. Risperidone and Cogentin were prescribed and titrated as clinically appropriate to 4 milligrams (mg) twice daily (bid) with plans to proceed to the use of a long-acting injectable formulation. 

On the day of discharge, the patient was noted to be more stable with linear thought processing that was more logical, and goal directed. He was euthymic with fair insight and judgment. He denied hallucinations and demonstrated clear speech with better eye contact and communication skills. There were no remaining safety issues, and an aftercare appointment had been arranged with case management. He was discharged to a shelter with medication, as indicated.

The subject under review is the medical necessity for the inpatient stay.

The health plan's determination is overturned, in whole.

The requested health service/treatment of inpatient stay was medically necessary. The patient's continued hospital stay for treatment of an exacerbation of a psychotic disorder (schizophrenia) did require the inpatient level services, structure, and monitoring through discharge. The medication adjustments and safety monitoring together with attention to the need for a safe and clinically appropriate discharge and disposition, the support of functioning and the continued application of multimodal treatments, as well as assurance of medication adherence, were factors that did warrant the continued inpatient level treatment through discharge; the patient could not have been effectively managed at a lower level of care during the time interval under review.

The patient was discharged from the inpatient psychiatric hospital setting as soon as a less-restrictive treatment setting was appropriate.

The patient is a female with a history of mental illness.  She is interested in pursuing TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) treatment for depression a new provider.

The patient has been diagnosed with major depressive disorder, single episode, severe without psychotic features.  She was previously treated with TMS in 2019 with 48 sessions.  She had been taking Sertraline 50 milligrams (MG) since 2019, Wellbutrin, and Vyvanse.  She previously took Prozac, Zoloft, Wellbutrin, Trazodone, Trintellix, Luvox, Lexapro, Seroquel, and Lamictal.

She was evaluated by the new provider and was noted to have a HAMD (Hamilton Depression Rating Scale) score of 42 and a Beck score of 53.  The new provider is a board-certified psychiatrist who recommended this treatment.  She received 36 TMS treatments with the new provider in 2020.  After that, she was noted to have a HAMD of eight and a Beck score of five.  She is noted to be "handling situations better because of the TMS."

The patient has a history of treatment refractory depression.  She has tried and failed many different medications.  The patient had treatment with rTMS previously, but with a different provider.  The patient was not satisfied with the application of treatment from that previous provider so she pursued the FDA-approved treatment for her condition - rTMS, with a new provider. Her symptoms were very severe at the time of her initial evaluation and improved substantially with the treatment. The patient is a female with a history of mental illness who received inpatient psychiatric hospitalization.

The patient has a history of mental illness including diagnosis with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and major depressive disorder.  She has a history of prior suicide attempt and alcohol abuse.  She has a medical history of malnourishment and hypertension.

She was initially evaluated in the emergency room after ingesting alcohol and pills as a suicide attempt.  She was admitted to the medical service and was treated.  She was medically cleared for psychiatric admission.  She was treated by a multidisciplinary team including psychiatry, nursing, and therapy staff.  She received group and individual therapy.  She received a psychopharmacology evaluation and was started on Wellbutrin, Abilify, Minipress, and other as needed (PRN) medications for her symptoms.  

The patient was noted to have poor judgment, limited insight, guarded, suspicious, and selectively compliant with medications.  The patient was also noted to be agitated, irritable, guarded, and her judgment remained poor, as well as isolated and not interacting with peers. 
The patient was discharged to follow up psychiatric care.

The patient represented an acutely elevated risk of dangerous behaviors and there was no less-restrictive treatment environment appropriate.  The acute risk factors of recent suicide attempt with the chronic risk factors of potentially dangerous behaviors suggest that the patient would have been at an acute risk of self-injurious behaviors (including but not limited to suicide) were she to have been discharged from the inpatient hospital setting.  The patient was discharged from the inpatient psychiatric hospital setting as soon as a less-restrictive treatment setting was appropriate. Therefore, the treatment was medically necessary.  While the patient was not endorsing active suicidality or homicidality, the patient remained acutely symptomatic.  The patient had multiple static risk factors for potentially dangerous behaviors including recent suicide attempt, prior suicide attempt, and substance abuse and diagnosis with a severe mental illness.  Therefore the patient represented a chronic risk of potentially dangerous behaviors.  The fact that patient remained with depressive symptoms and limited treatment compliance were acute risk factors for dangerous behaviors.  Furthermore, the fact that there was no less-restrictive environment of care appropriate suggests that ongoing inpatient psychiatric hospitalization was medically necessary and should be covered by the patient's health plan.

The patient is a male. He presented with a request for detoxification services. The patient was using alcohol on a continuous daily basis with approximately one pint of vodka and two six-packs of beer, together with use of two grams of cocaine and up to twelve bags of heroin with inhalation. He was using up to 12 mg of Xanax and marijuana with four blunts per day. He was also participating in a methadone maintenance treatment program (MMTP) with a daily dose of 40 mg. He was diagnosed with poly-substance use with opioid, stimulant, alcohol, cannabis and sedative-hypnotic-anxiolytic class substances.

The patient has a history of unspecified bipolar disorder with depressive episodes and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and no current treatment or psychotropic medications. 

The patient had received multiple past substance use disorder treatments with detoxification but little or no treatment with rehabilitation due to declining aftercare. 

The patient had no acute general medical problem or significant chronic medical issues. He had snorted a pen tip that required removal, and he was known to be HIV and hepatitis C and B positive. The patient provided no history of withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens or severe alcohol withdrawal symptoms. He was tobacco dependent. 

The patient was medically screened and admitted for inpatient level detoxification with plans for a five-day detoxification treatment episode with Librium, vitamin replacement therapy and comfort medications, as well as continued use of methadone at the confirmed dose of 40 mg daily.

On Mental Status Examination, the patient was cooperative, groomed and casually dressed with good eye contact. Speech was clear and thought production was linear and logical. There were no severe symptoms on mental status examination such as thought disorder, cognitive impairment, severe mood disturbance, psychosis or perceptual disturbance, or suicidal ideation. He presented with moderate symptoms of withdrawal including nausea, sweats, yawning, and tremor, and he reported insomnia and low energy, but no other somatic complaints or symptoms reflecting drug or alcohol withdrawal symptoms.
The patient is single, homeless and housed, and unemployed. There was no report of current legal issues, but unspecified trauma history with a diagnosis of PTSD.

The patient was admitted on for inpatient detoxification and withdrawal management. The patient's brief hospital course progressed without incident. The patient slept and received meals. His monitoring occurred without incident, and he had the opportunity to attend group sessions and receive counseling with recommendation for clinically appropriate aftercare. 

The patient was discharged against medical advice and declined to proceed directly to rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment. He was advised to attend 12-step recovery groups and proceed to rehabilitation treatment when ready.

The proposed inpatient stay and detoxification treatment and other medical services noted in the clinical summary could have been safely and effectively provided at a lower level of care. The acute inpatient treatment of this patient's substance use disorder did not require the structure of an inpatient setting or 24-hour monitoring. The patient displayed no serious disturbance of mental status despite having a history of bipolar disorder and PTSD and despite ongoing active substance use disorders. Moreover, the patient did not show evidence for suicidal or aggressive behavior or risk for self-harm, or severe cognitive impairment or psychosis, or perceptual disturbance that would have warranted an inpatient level admission and treatment. There were no severe/objective symptoms of withdrawal or biomedical issues in this case, and the patient had knowledge of substance use disorder treatment protocols- as he was participating in a methadone treatment program for opioid use disorder. The patient had fair insight and control of impulses, and the working knowledge of substance use disorder treatment with a past history of multiple treatment episodes, as noted. Thus, admission for detoxification treatment with 24-hour monitoring, and the requested inpatient level services were not medically necessary in this case scenario.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Use Disorder
Treatment: Inpatient rehabilitation admission
The insurer is denied coverage for inpatient rehabilitation admission
The denial is reversed. 

This patient was a male who was admitted to inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment after completion of inpatient substance detoxification treatment. The patient had a long history of alcohol use and was drinking large amounts of alcohol including 1 pint of vodka and a few 16 ounce beers daily. The patient's urine toxicology was positive for benzodiazepines. The patient's medical issues included atrial fibrillation and hypertension. The patient had multiple past inpatient detoxification and rehabilitation treatments and still relapsed. The patient attended individual and group therapy and was discharged
.
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that inpatient treatment is indicated primarily for individuals whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. In this case, this patient was considered in need of 24-hour substance rehabilitation treatment as he reportedly was using large amounts of alcohol daily including 1 pint of vodka and a few 16 ounces of beer daily. 

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), the patient met the clinical criteria for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment as he continued to use large amounts of alcohol daily and had a positive benzodiazepine toxicology screen despite multiple past inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatments. The patient reportedly lacked coping skills and the ability to identify relapse triggers to stop use. The patient reportedly lacked insight and judgment. The patient was also noted to have a sad mood and anxiety. The patient was unable to stop alcohol use without being in a sober and supervised therapeutic inpatient substance rehabilitation setting then, and he was admitted after completing an inpatient substance detoxification treatment. 

Notes reported that the patient was keeping to himself. Notes reported that the patient was working on improving coping skills and working on sobriety and relapse prevention. Notes reported that the patient was motivated for treatment, working on coping with stressors. Notes reported that the patient was working on stress management, assertiveness and communication. Notes reported that the patient was encouraged to verbalize better. Notes reported that the patient was verbalizing more in individual therapy and was more engaged in group therapy and was receptive to working on coping skills and recovery skills, as well as decision making. Notes reported that the patient was working on coping mechanisms. The patient was discharged.  

Without this structured and supervised therapeutic rehabilitation treatment, the patient was likely to have relapsed quickly as evidenced by this patient's pattern of relapses after multiple past inpatient detoxification and rehabilitation treatments. Based on literature review, inpatient rehabilitation admission was medically necessary for this patient.

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient.

Based on the above, the medical necessity for the inpatient rehabilitation admission is substantiated.  The insurer's denial should be reversed.

The patient is a female with a history of major depressive disorder, recurrent and severe without psychotic features. The patient has a documented history of multiple medication treatments for depression including treatment with more than two disparate classes of medication and at least four or more trials with antidepressant medications (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors [SSRIs], serotonin norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor [SNRI], Trintellix, Viibryd, and Wellbutrin), as well as combination treatment with an SSRI and Wellbutrin. Additionally, the patient has been treated with psychotherapy including cognitive behavioral therapy and dialectical behavioral therapy (cognitive behavioral therapy [CBT] & dialectical behavior therapy [DBT]) as well as counseling and supportive psychotherapy.

Mental status examination reveals depressed mood, sad affect with anxiety, and anhedonia together with hopelessness, helplessness and low self-worth with guilt and depressive ruminations. She has loss of interest and low energy with fatigue and other neuro-vegetative disturbances related to depression including insomnia with only five hours of sleep nightly or less. Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ)-9 score was at 20-27 at the time of evaluation for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) therapy reflecting severe symptoms of depression. She rates her anxiety and depression at an 8 of 10 severity, respectively. She is noted to be motivated for treatment for TMS therapy but has rejected electroconvulsive therapy on the basis of risk versus benefits and the potential for adverse effects that could impact her occupational and day-to-day functioning.

The health plan's determination is oveturned in whole.

Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) Therapy for Major Depressive Disorder is medically necessary for this patient.
Repetitive TMS therapy as a primary or adjunctive therapy for treatment of major depression has generally been evaluated in patients who have treatment refractory or pharmaco-resistant depression, as defined by one or more, antidepressant medication treatment failures with or without augmentation, and with or without psychotherapy, especially cognitive behavioral therapy. Transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy, as applied in major depression, is considered to be a safe treatment by the FDA. The data as reflected in peer reviewed medical literature supports this assertion.
Specifically, when treatments with antidepressant medication with or without augmentation, electroconvulsive therapy, and/or psychotherapy (especially cognitive behavioral therapy) have failed, then TMS is an appropriate treatment for major depressive disorder. This assertion is noted in the American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorder, referenced below, and consistent with the scientific literature pertaining to TMS and its application to depressive disorder.
As noted in the answer to question 1, the requested service, repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), is reasonable, clinically appropriate, medically necessary and consistent with prevailing standards of care based on the scientific literature and practice guidelines, referenced below. The patient in this case has demonstrated that her depressive disorder is treatment refractory with multiple failed trials of antidepressant medications of disparate mechanisms of action with augmentation, as noted in the clinical summary.
The patient has also failed to achieve a remission of symptoms with combined treatment with psychotherapy (CBT, DBT and Supportive Psychotherapy) and medication regimens, as noted in the clinical summary. ECT has been rejected on the basis of risk-benefit analysis. Thus, the proposed treatment of recurrent major depressive disorder using rTMS therapy is medically necessary in this case.

This was the eighth psychiatric inpatient admission for this female with a history of depression, anxiety, ADHD, questionable exposure to trauma, and recent self-injury, who was admitted after having made a suicide attempt by overdose of lamotrigine. The patient also has history of purging and self-cutting. In addition to her multiple inpatient stays, the patient had completed three partial hospitalization programs.

She reported that in the week prior to admission she had been feeling more depressed with more frequent and persistent thoughts of suicide in the context of continued relational problems with family and peers. She reported a sexual assault a week prior to admission, which she described as being minimized or dismissed by family. She was concerned that there was "no case" as per law enforcement. 

After an altercation with her father she took an excessive dose of the lamotrigine and then sent a message to her ex-boyfriend who told her grandmother. At the urging of her ex-boyfriend she agreed to call 911 and went to a different facility for an evaluation. She was released, but the following day she complained of stomach pains and lightheadedness and again called 911 and was taken to yet another hospital for medical evaluation but was discharged without any intervention. She spoke to her outpatient therapist who encouraged her grandmother to bring her to the hospital.

The patient had been seeing a nurse practitioner and a therapist as an outpatient. Past medication trials include aripiprazole, Vyvanse, vortioxetine, clonidine, Adderall, and lamotrigine. 

The patient was treated with individual therapy, group therapy, and pharmacotherapy. Her inpatient medications included aripiprazole,  20 mg daily, clonidine, 0.1 mg at bedtime, Vyvanse, 30 mg daily, vortioxetine, 10 mg daily, and hydroxyzine 25 mg, three times daily as needed for anxiety. 

The patient expressed passive suicidal ideation and thoughts of self-injurious behavior throughout her stay. She was, however, future oriented, expressing her desire to go home or to a partial hospital, while at the same time stating that she would likely not feel safe at home as there were continuing stressors.

This patient has a long history of para suicidal statements and behaviors. The precipitating event, a self-reported overdose several days earlier, did not require medical attention, and was immediately reported to others by the patient. This would not indicate lethal intent or true imminent suicidality. While this patient presented a chronic risk of self-harm, there is no historic evidence of true suicidality, and the patient's statements regarding suicidality were often made in the context of a euthymic mood and future orientation. The documentation reviewed does not support continued need for an acute level of inpatient care. Generally accepted standards for patients with similar pathology include acute inpatient stays limited to brief periods when there is clear and imminent danger of potential harm to self or others. At no time beyond the date of service in question did this patient provide evidence of credible, serious, imminent danger to self or others.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: 2 days/units of Inpatient Substance Abuse Services
The insurer is denied coverage for 2 days/units of Inpatient Substance Abuse Services.
The denial is overturned. 

This is a male patient who was admitted to the hospital for opioid detoxification. The patient reportedly had acute withdrawal symptoms including sweats/chills, tremors, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, muscle cramps, malaise, fatigue, watery eyes, anxiety, and irritable mood. The patient reportedly was using up to 20 bags of intravenous (IV) heroin per day and also using methadone off the street at times. The patient had a positive toxicology for opiates and methadone. The patient reportedly had multiple past inpatient substance detoxification treatments and rehabilitation treatments. The patient reportedly was homeless and unemployed. The patient's had a medical history of liver disease. His Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) score was reported to be 8. The patient was treated with Methadone taper and protocol. The patient reportedly left against medical advice (AMA).

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. This was the case with this patient. This patient had multiple past substance detoxification treatments and rehabilitation treatments including 10 detoxifications, 5 rehabilitations and 1 residential treatment in the past. Despite these multiple treatment history, the patient still relapsed and could not stop use. It was reported that the patient would do anything and go to any extent to obtain heroin. It was not likely that the patient could attend a less restrictive level of care than an inpatient substance detoxification treatment. The patient also was at risk for accidental overdose as well as severe withdrawal as he had acute, active withdrawal symptoms on admission and during the denial period. Notes reported that the patient exhibited continued withdrawal symptoms including chills, red and watery eyes, and bone pain; the patient was treated with Methadone for detoxification. Notes reported that the patient was still taking Methadone for withdrawal but he left against medical advice (AMA).

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), the patient required 24-hour treatment as the patient needed detoxification medications to modify his withdrawal and had a history of heavy intravenous (IV) heroin use putting him at high risk for overdose and severe withdrawal. The patient also had multiple past inpatient treatments and continued to use heroin despite the negative consequences to his use including negative relational issues and medical issues including hepatitis C infection. The patient also lacked sober supports, was homeless, and unemployed. It was also reported that the patient had a high tolerance which put him more at risk for life-threatening overdose and/or withdrawal. Thus, inpatient detoxification was medically necessary for this patient.

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient.

The carrier's denial of coverage for the 2 days/units of Inpatient Substance Abuse Services should be overturned. The medical necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance abuse disorder
Treatment: Inpatient detoxification
The insurer denied the inpatient detoxification.
The denial is overturned. 

The patient is a female requesting detoxification treatment and admitted to acute inpatient level care in order to address substance use disorder with opioid (heroin) class substance, as well as the past use of cannabis and stimulant (crack cocaine) class drugs of abuse. The patient had been using up to 20 bags of heroin with intravenous (IV) administration. She had a history of prior detoxification and substance use disorder treatments with up to four treatment episodes with relapse. She rapidly progressed to using two bundles of heroin daily. She had severe withdrawal symptoms when attempting to cut down and had developed an abscess at an injection site requiring antibiotic treatment. Her self-referral for treatment was prompted by multiple stressors including occupational, primary support, social environment and other psychosocial domains.

The patient has a history of psychiatric disorder with unspecified anxiety and depressive disorders. She denied psychiatric hospitalization or suicidal or self-harming behavior. She had an inadvertent drug overdose requiring emergency medical services.

The patient presented without acute co-morbid general medical issues. Laboratory assessments were unremarkable or normal with a positive drug screen consistent with history. The patient is an everyday smoker and tobacco dependent at one pack per day. She has a history of lower back pain that contributes to her use of opioids.

The patient is single and unemployed with housing, living with her father. She did not report trauma or abuse history, or legal issues. She reported a family history of substance use disorder reflecting genetic predisposition. She reported having family support from parents and siblings but was without sober supports and had stopped attending recovery groups.

Evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination that was free of severe psychiatric symptoms. She was generally motivated for treatment but was only contemplative at best. She was described as polite and cooperative with a full range of affect with apprehension, nervousness, tension, irritability, sleep disturbance, and aches due to the onset of opioid withdrawal. Speech was clear with organized thoughts that were free of delusions. There was no evidence for a thought disorder, mania, psychosis or cognitive impairment or other severe symptoms as noted. The patient denied suicidal or homicidal ideation and did not have perceptual disturbance. Insight was limited with impaired judgment and poor control of impulses. Her onset of withdrawal symptoms included anxiety, restlessness, agitation, tremor, nausea and diarrhea and abdominal cramps, sweats, chills and body/bone aches.

The patient was admitted to detoxification treatment with a comprehensive detoxification protocol with use of Suboxone when appropriate, and clonidine as needed, and as needed (PRN) medications for comfort, as well as nicotine replacement therapy and smoking cessation education. The program provided for case management with referral to sober housing and access to rehabilitation treatment that included comprehensive evidence-based treatments. During detoxification the patient engaged in counseling sessions focusing on education about the disease model of addiction, and, involvement with counseling and milieu activities including peer support and education sessions to motivate the patient to proceed to rehabilitation treatment. Vital signs remained normal during her brief stay. The patient was maintained on a psychotropic medication regimen of Lexapro, Neurontin and Seroquel together with PRN medications for agitation and anxiety (Vistaril and Thorazine). Nutritional supports and fluid replacement were provided and continued use of antibiotic therapy.

The patient initially was hampered by withdrawal symptoms and the desire to leave treatment on the first two days of detoxification. The patient more actively engaged with detoxification treatment and therapeutic activities within the treatment milieu; she was cooperative and feeling better with diminishing withdrawal symptoms. Withdrawal symptoms remained mild, but persisted with aches, pain, anxiety and insomnia requiring prn medications, as noted, and monitoring. Case management was working on a safe and clinically appropriate discharge plan and disposition.  The patient was discharged with immediate transfer to substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment and plans for continued medication assisted treatment with Suboxone and involvement in recovery groups.

Yes, the proposed treatment, inpatient detoxification, was medically necessary for this patient.

The requested inpatient admission and continued treatment could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. The patient in this case was using heroin in large quantities with IV administration that did warrant inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring for the duration of the protocol; detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments pertinent to the detoxification treatment episode could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment that was provided at the time of admission.  Moreover, the patient had significant and persistent withdrawal symptoms, and, the patient's social environment was not conducive to detoxification in the context of limited insight, impaired judgment and poor control of impulses including a recent drug overdose.

Thus, the adult inpatient detoxification treatment and withdrawal management of this patient's substance use disorder did warrant the admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level detoxification setting with 24-hour monitoring and use of PRN medications. The patient's history of substance abuse (frequency and quantity) including a history of drug overdose and presentation with co-occurring anxiety and mood disorders and the severe psychosocial stressors and functional impairments reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder and the need for a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management, as the patient was at high risk for treatment failure if the continued detoxification and withdrawal management were to be attempted at a lower level of care. Therefore, medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published practice guidelines, ASAM Criteria, and the scientific literature, referenced below, and, New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews including the appropriate application of the NY State OASAS LOCADTR Tool that requires the patient in this scenario default to the higher level of care.

The requested benefit of inpatient detoxification was medically necessary and clinically appropriate in this case scenario and is therefore a covered service in this case. The patient's clinical features and treatment dimensions did warrant inpatient level detoxification services thru discharge and did necessitate the monitoring that is provided with inpatient level treatment including the use of comfort medications, together with counseling and educational sessions and peer support, and the continued treatment for the mood and anxiety disorders. Case management services were critical in this case to motivate the patient to proceed to rehabilitation treatment with formal substance use disorder treatment with a safe and clinically appropriate disposition. Moreover, the admission and the continued substance abuse detoxification treatment through discharge could not have been safely or effectively provided with lower level services, as noted above. Thus, the requested benefit is not excluded under the plan, and should be covered in keeping with prevailing standards of care pertaining to substance use disorder services including the application of ASAM Criteria and the New York State OASAS LOCADTR 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines, referenced below.

summary:

Treatment: inpatient substance admission 

The insurer denied the inpatient substance admission. The denial was overturned.

This is a male patient with a history of alcohol abuse, cocaine abuse, heroin abuse, benzodiazepine abuse, schizophrenia, depression, liver disease, and prior detoxification who was admitted to the hospital due to alcohol and substance withdrawal, and the need for detoxification treatment. The patient reportedly had withdrawal symptoms and required two detoxification medications including Librium and Suboxone. The patient also reported suicidal ideation, homicidal threats, and had depression. The patient reportedly was drinking 1 pint of vodka per day and he reportedly took 5-6 Klonopin pills the day prior to coming into the hospital. The patient reportedly was homeless and unemployed. The patient was also treated with Seroquel and Effexor. The patient was cleared for discharge to inpatient substance rehabilitation.
  
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. It also states that patients with past complicated or life threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens are in need of inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal and reports that patients with comorbid medical condition that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification. 

This patient could not safely be treated in a less restrictive detoxification treatment level of care as he was at risk for severe, complicated, and life threatening withdrawal due to his large amount of daily alcohol use. The patient also reportedly took a large amount of benzodiazepine including 5-6 Klonopin prior to hospital admission, and also was taking opiates and had a history of cocaine use. The patient was at risk for overdose, as well. The patient's polysubstance use was also complicated by medical issues such liver disease, and psychiatric instability. The patient reportedly had suicidal ideation, homicidal threats, and had depression, and was noncompliant with psychotropic medication. This put this patient at danger to self and others. The patient was noted to be homeless, unemployed, and lacked sober support. 

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), the patient required 24-hour treatment as he could not have been safely and effectively treated in outpatient detoxification settings or a less restrictive setting. The patient's continuous use of large amounts of alcohol and substances despite medical issues and psychiatric issues including suicidal ideation, depression, and homicidal threats and noncompliance to treatment indicated inpatient level of care for detoxification. The patient's need for two detoxification medications to modify his withdrawal symptoms and to prevent life-threatening withdrawal also indicate the severity of this patient's needs that require inpatient level of care. It was reported that the patient had detoxification medication of Librium and Suboxone as well as prn Ativan until his discharge to the inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment. 

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient.

Based on the above, the medical necessity for continued inpatient substance admission is substantiated.  The insurer's denial should be overturned.
