This patient is a male was admitted to this inpatient substance residential treatment for substance and alcohol rehabilitation treatment. He was using intravenous heroin 2 grams and drinking whiskey. He was taking 5 Zubsolv tablets by snorting and had recent cocaine use consisting of 1 ball. He had legal issues, relapses after prior inpatient substance treatments, and had prior reported withdrawal symptoms. He had depression and anxiety and was also taking Lexapro, Remeron, and melatonin. It was reported that he also took Naltrexone. His longest reported abstinence was several months when he took Vivitrol. He attended groups and was discharged to Footprints to Recovery.

This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for continued inpatient substance residential treatment as the chart notes provided enough specific evidence to support that he required this level of care. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that residential treatment is indicated primarily for individuals who do not meet clinical criteria for hospitalization but whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. Residential facilities provide a safe and substance-free environment in which residents learn individual and group living skills for preventing relapse. In this case, this patient was considered in need of continued 24 hour residential treatment as he needed more time in this 24 hour inpatient therapeutic structured and supervised setting to learn more coping skills, relapse prevention skills, improve insight, better identify triggers, improve motivation, and learn the reasons for past relapses.  He could not stop using substances including heroin, Zubsolv, cocaine, and alcohol despite negative consequences of use and past inpatient substance treatments.

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), he met criteria for inpatient substance residential rehabilitation treatment as he continued to use multiple serious substances and alcohol despite the negative consequences of substance use such as legal issues. He could not stop using multiple substances without the 24 hour therapeutic, supervised and structured programming of this therapeutic residential treatment setting. Notes reported that he needed to work on decreasing depression, anxiety, and cravings, work on distress tolerance and emotional regulation techniques, and needed education on relapse prevention. Notes reported that he was working on recovery skills. Notes reported that he was working on triggers, reasons for past relapses, coping skills, and relapse prevention skills. The National Institute on Drug Abuse: Principles of Addiction Treatment: A Research Based Guide reports that research indicates that that the best treatment outcomes occur with longer durations of treatment and states that recovery from drug addiction is a long term process. As a result, reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for continued inpatient substance residential rehabilitation treatment. The health care plan did not act reasonably, or with sound medical judgment, or in the best interests of the patient. 

Based on the above, the medical necessity for residential substance use treatment is substantiated.  The insurer's denial is overturned.

He had been non-compliant with psychiatric treatment.  He was noted to be belligerent, uncooperative, with loose associations, thought blocking, and disorganized thought process. He received group and individual treatment. Speech was clear with organized thoughts that were free of delusions. There was no evidence for a thought disorder, mania, psychosis or cognitive impairment. His onset of withdrawal symptoms included anxiety, irritability, insomnia, agitation, nausea, sweats, tremor and headaches with a CIWA (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment) scale score of 12.

This patient is a male who was admitted for inpatient detoxification treatment. The patient reportedly had withdrawal symptoms including nausea, vomiting, tremors, urges, sleeping problems, teary eyes, sweats, irritable mood, anxiety, lightheadedness, and had a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment of Alcohol (CIWA) score of 15. The patient reportedly was drinking 1 pint of vodka per day and 6 16 ounce beers, using bags of intranasal heroin per day, and also using crack/cocaine per day. The patient also had a history of alcohol use, history of heroin use, and history of cocaine use. The patient reportedly was using methadone. The patient reported multiple inpatient detoxification treatments and rehabilitation treatments with the most recent one. The patient was noted to be unemployed, and had a positive toxicology for opiates, cocaine, methadone, and benzodiazepines. The patient was admitted and was treated with Librium protocol. The patient was on the Librium protocol and also was treated with methadone protocol; the patient's last methadone protocol was on the day of discharge. The patient was discharged to a substance inpatient rehabilitation treatment.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from treatment at a less restrictive level of care, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. It also states that patients with past complicated or life threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens are in need of inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal and reports that patients with co-morbid medical condition that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification.

The patient had active reported withdrawal symptoms including nausea, vomiting, tremors, urges, sleeping problems, teary eyes, sweats, irritable mood, anxiety, lightheadedness, and had a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment of Alcohol (CIWA) score of 15 at the time of admission. The patient needed 24-hour treatment then as he was at risk for worsened withdrawal symptoms if not in this 24-hour setting, such as delirium tremens. The risk of delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use so this patient was considered at risk for this life-threatening withdrawal complication. The patient was also at risk for overdose as he was using large amounts of alcohol with heroin and crack/cocaine daily.

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient.

Dimension 1: Acute Intoxication and/or Withdrawal Potential -The patient had post-acute withdrawal symptoms after her relapse. It seems that she had become sick due to also being on buprenorphine. Post acute withdrawal symptoms were described as nausea, tiredness, pain. There was no evidence of acute withdrawal symptoms.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. It also states that patients with past complicated or life-threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens are in need of inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal. The patient is a female admitted to acute inpatient psychiatric services for an exacerbation of a chronic psychotic disorder best characterized as schizoaffective disorder, depressed type.  The patient had shown increasing symptoms of psychosis following discontinuation of her oral medication with onset of bizarre delusions and erratic behavior, disorganized thoughts with paranoid thinking together with motor agitation, and increasing responses to internal stimuli that included command auditory hallucinations.  She was brought to the emergency department and was subsequently admitted after medical clearance that included physical examination, laboratory assessment and drug screen.  Her assessment included no abnormal or remarkable laboratory findings including a negative drug screen consistent with her history.

The patient's treatment plan included safety monitoring and medication targeting mood disturbance and psychosis, as well as the opportunity for therapy and psycho-education provided in the therapeutic milieu.  The patient was cooperative but guarded.  The patient continued to display severe symptoms of psychosis with essentially no change in her mental status examination, and continued response to auditory hallucinations.  She had received 400 milligrams (mg) of Abilify Maintena on prior to admission, and there were plans for continued use of Abilify supplemented with antipsychotic medication with Cogentin and Prozac, with as needed (prn) use of Haldol and Ativan for agitation and Benadryl for insomnia.  The patient remained psychotic with continued evidence for affective instability with hopelessness, helplessness, and dysphoric mood, odd behavior, and responses to internal stimuli including command auditory hallucinations telling her to refuse medications and indicating that she was at risk for harm from others.  She continued to display guarded behavior and was restless requiring prn medications and medication changes including the use of olanzapine and trazodone at night.  She continued to attend to internal stimuli and was socially isolative.

Six days into the stay the patient gradually became more at ease and was more receptive to participating in educational groups and other group sessions focusing on social skills with ongoing monitoring and development of a relapse prevention plan focusing on medication compliance/adherence.  She received an injection of Abilify Maintena on with plans for continued treatment in the community with assertive community treatment (ACT).  Case management was involved in developing a safe and clinically appropriate discharge plan that included discharge to a women's shelter and continued social services, as well as resumption of ACT level treatment.  She was discharged, at which time she was no longer deemed to be a danger to herself or others and had resolved her auditory hallucination with improved mood and diminished anxiety and better control of impulses and ability to comply with treatment.

The health plan's determination is overturned, in whole.

The patient's continued hospital stay for treatment of an exacerbation of a psychotic and mood disorder (schizoaffective disorder, depressed type) associated with non-adherence and non-compliance with outpatient treatment and risk for suicidal behavior did warrant the continued stay through discharge.  The patient's severity of symptoms, and the treatment refractory nature of her psychotic and mood disorder, as well as the patient's inability to benefit from treatment at a lower level of care, functional decline, and safety issues related to persistent symptoms of psychosis and mood disturbance, were clinical factors and treatment dimensions that warranted the continued acute inpatient hospital care, structure, and monitoring as proposed through discharge.

The medication adjustments and safety monitoring together with attention to the compliance issues in this case were medically necessary in this case scenario; the intensity of services and safety issues related to erratic/catatonic behavior and affective instability could not have been effectively addressed or managed at a lower level of care during the time interval under review.  The additional inpatient treatments including medication adjustments, evidence-based psychosocial therapy and other therapeutic interventions to address reality testing and social skills were medically necessary in order to continued active treatment, and to develop a safe and clinically appropriate discharge plan and disposition.  Treatment also included monitoring the response to medication adjustments as well as the work with community providers for a step down to ACT level care and continued use of a long-acting injectable antipsychotic medication.  All of these were clinical factors and treatment dimensions that did require the continued inpatient mental health stay.  Thus, medical necessity is met in this case.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse

Treatment: Inpatient substance abuse treatment

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient substance abuse treatment. The denial is reversed. 

This patient is a male admitted to medically supervised inpatient detoxification treatment for alcohol and substance detoxification treatment. The patient reported drinking several beers per day with the last use on the day of admission and also using 2 mg Xanax bars several times per week with the last use prior to admission, and using tens of dollars' worth of cocaine per day with the last use on the day of admission. As inpatient, the patient was put on a Librium protocol for detoxification. The patient's past history was significant for past inpatient substance detoxification treatments.

The APA Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders report that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. In this case, this patient had been drinking large amounts of alcohol daily and taking Xanax 2 mg bars several times per week with tens of dollars' worth of cocaine use daily and was at risk for severe, complicated, and life threatening withdrawal symptoms and required 24 hour inpatient hospital detoxification treatment. The patient's polysubstance use was heavy. The patient drank large amounts of alcohol daily in addition to benzodiazepine use, which placed this patient at high risk for delirium tremens. Studies have shown that the risk of life complicated withdrawal such as delirium tremens can occur 4 days after alcohol use and even up to 1 week after Xanax use. Thus, the patient required the entire duration of the inpatient stay.

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), the patient required 24 hour hospital treatment as the patient could not safely and effectively be treated in outpatient detoxification settings and had past recent inpatient detoxification treatments prior to this admission. The patient could not stop use of alcohol, Xanax, and cocaine as the patient's history indicated that this patient lacked the coping skills for abstinence. Also, the patient required and received detoxification medication, Librium, from inpatient stay to prevent life threatening withdrawals. This inpatient care was needed for this patient due to the large amount of alcohol use in conjunction with other high risk drugs, which were cocaine and benzodiazepines. Thus, the inpatient hospital detoxification treatment was medically necessary to treat this patient's medical condition.   

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient.

The carrier's denial of coverage for the inpatient substance abuse treatment is reversed. The medical necessity is substantiated.

This case involves a female admitted from the emergency department for acute inpatient psychiatric treatment. The patient was brought in by police due to erratic behavior and aggressive behavior in the context of psychosis and mood disturbance. She has a history of bipolar disorder and co-occurring substance use disorder with use of alcohol and cannabis and tobacco. She was acutely agitated and paranoid and had stopped her psychotropic medications. 

The patient has a history of mood disorder best characterized as bipolar disorder, but a past diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type. She was receiving outpatient psychiatric treatment with medications but had been non-compliant with treatment and was actively using substances of abuse, as noted. There was a history of multiple past psychiatric hospitalizations. 

The mental status examination revealed a disheveled and poorly groomed female with labile affect and anxiety including apprehension, nervousness, tension, irritability, and excessive worry together with irritable dysphoria and motor agitation with screaming. Sleep, appetite, energy levels and volition were disturbed. The patient exhibited irritable mood with paranoid thought content and delusions that neighbors were cooking weird things and up to no good. There was faulty reality testing and cognitive impairment and perceptual disturbance characterized by slow processing of information with impaired executive functioning. Judgment was markedly impaired; insight was poor/limited; and risk for violence and aggression was judged to be high with poor control of impulses. 
There were no acute general medical conditions. The patient had a history of hypertension and dyslipidemia with associated treatments. Physical examination and laboratory assessment and EKG were normal or negative or unremarkable. 

The patient is married, unemployed and high school educated. There are no legal issues or trauma issues in this case. The patient was involuntarily admitted to inpatient level care with plans for close observation and safety monitoring, structured milieu therapy, and resumption of pharmacotherapy with antipsychotic and mood stabilizing medication supplemented with as needed (prn) medications for anxiety and agitation with nicotine replacement therapy, and, monitoring for any withdrawal symptoms. The patient had the opportunity to participate in group, individual, and milieu therapy; she received counseling for the substance use disorders and declined smoking cessation. 

The patient had a stormy clinical course characterized by agitation, psychosis, and erratic behavior requiring staff intervention. The patient was prescribed Latuda, Depakote and Klonopin, titrated as clinically appropriate. She remained socially isolated with persistent symptoms of psychosis and irritability. The patient remained apprehensive, nervous, tense, irritable and agitated with deficient social skills and labile affect requiring prn medications and ongoing interventions from staff with monitoring. She did show improving mood and diminished levels of anxiety with improving insight. She was medication adherent but declined an injectable medication. By the date of discharge, the patient had participated in family meetings with her husband and case management had worked on a discharge plan. Again, the patient's anxiety diminished with improved mood and functioning and resolution of any safety concerns. She had participated passively in milieu activities and groups. She was discharged with clinically appropriate aftercare and medication that had been titrated to therapeutic dosages with tolerability. 

The health plan's determination is overturned. 

The patient did require the continued acute inpatient level care and the continued structure of an acute inpatient level setting in order to remain safe and to administer treatment for her psychiatric disturbance and co-occurring substance use disorder while conducting an evaluation, and while observing her functioning with the resumption/adjustment of clinically appropriate medications. 

The medical necessity for the continued inpatient level structure and monitoring is reasonable and in the patient's best interest in view of the patient's severe symptoms of mood disorder and psychosis; and need for safety monitoring in the context of persistent symptoms of psychosis and agitation, and the deteriorated functioning requiring staff interventions to address agitation and impulsive aggression. Additionally, the inpatient stay during this time interval is medically necessary in order to monitor the response to medications, to ensure that the patient will have a sustained response to treatment, and to continue to address the acute risk of aggressive or erratic behavior in the context of severe symptoms of bipolar mood disorder and co-occurring substance use disorder with active use of tobacco and cocaine. 

The patient's presentation and clinical features included severe symptoms of a mood disturbance with psychosis, risk for impulsive aggression, and deterioration in functioning with inability to care for self in the context of substance use disorder with multiple substances of abuse and medication non-adherence. The patient could not have been expected to participate in treatment at a lower level of care in this case scenario for the time interval under review. The medical necessity for intensive services and monitoring did warrant the continued acute inpatient psychiatric admission, as proposed.
The necessity for the continued inpatient level services is in keeping with prevailing standards of professional practice, and with the published practice guidelines and American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, referenced below, as well as NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Guidelines.

Several medications in hospital were tried and found to be ineffective or worsened the patient's symptoms; therefore, a longer time was necessary for treatment as an inpatient.

This is a patient referred for residential mental health treatment to address behavioral disturbances in the context of a mood disturbance and co-occurring substance use disorder associated with impaired functioning and problematic behavior. The patient was diagnosed with a moderately severe and unspecified depressive disorder; and moderately severe cannabis use disorder, as well as disruptive behavioral disorder. The patient has longstanding issues with self-esteem, confidence, and relationship problems together with stressors within the primary support, educational and social environment domains; the patient has been in past treatment settings with continued symptoms of depression together with a history of social withdrawal, and mood instability associated with substance use primarily with cannabis, but also use of tobacco and alcohol. The patient was referred to residential treatment in order to address the core symptoms of depression and relationship problems including parent-child relational problems and his lack of motivation and the moderately severe substance use disorder with cannabis. He presented with a history of violent behavior, and bouts of rage and impulsive aggression with threats toward others including his mother.
The patient has a history of outpatient treatments and other intensive treatment including attending a therapeutic preparatory school without sustained benefit. The patient has conflict with his parents including problematic behavioral disruptions and abuse of tobacco, alcohol and cannabis.
Initial evaluation upon admission for residential care revealed a mental status examination that was free of severe psychiatric symptoms such as psychosis, thought disorder, severe cognitive impairment or active suicidal ideation. His mood was dysphoric and affect was anxious together with a history of problematic behaviors that included academic failure due to truancy and conflict with parents, and other behaviors that were self-destructive or reflective of severe mood disturbance including social withdrawal and self treatment with cannabis. The patient's anxiety included social anxiety associated with problematic interpersonal functioning at school and at home. He was described as depressed with anxious demeanor, but cooperative and calm during the assessment. Insight was limited and judgment impaired with poor control of impulses.
The patient had no acute general medical conditions or abuse of other substances.
The patient is supported in his treatment effort by family. He is a student. There is no trauma history or legal issues in this case.
Diagnoses included the unspecified depressive disorder associated with oppositional behavior, unspecified disruptive disorder and cannabis use disorder, as well as parent-child relational problems, and, the problematic behaviors affecting educational and social and family functioning.
The patient was referred and admitted to the Residential Program. The patient underwent comprehensive evaluation with treatment planning that included therapeutic interventions to improve coping skills and self-esteem, as well as cognitive behavior therapy to address the mood disorder. The treatment plan included the goals of improved coping; breaking the cycle of self-destructive behaviors including anger issues and impulsive aggression; and, the development of healthy relationships and functioning.
The program focused on organizational skills; self-care; peer relationships; and other life skills as well as behavioral and emotional regulation with milieu, individual, group, family, and outdoor therapies/sport, as well as other interventions aimed at improving life skills. The patient actively participated in the treatment plan and worked on therapeutic, social, and emotional functions in the context of a therapeutic milieu with a residential level of structure and monitoring in a behavioral health program and setting that included educational services and ongoing medication management.
The patient was noted to gain insight and showed improve control of impulses. He remained dysphoric with anxiety that included social anxiety, apprehension, nervousness, tension, sleep disruptions, irritability and excessive worry. Family-focused sessions were provided with steady improvement going forward that was modest. The patient was treatment plan compliant and had started to work earnestly with regard to cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and other evidence-base therapies while participating in milieu and activity therapies designed to build self-confidence and life skills.
The patient was noted to be increasingly more at ease with peers and staff, and better engaged with group and individual sessions including the beginning incorporation of therapy skills. He worked on therapeutic assignments, and had frequent family focused sessions to address issues within the family constellation. He consistently denied suicidal ideation or urges to be aggressive or act in angry impulses. He achieved mood regulation and became better motivated to participate in treatment including involvement in recovery groups and other therapeutic interventions to support abstinence from cannabis and other substances of abuse. The patient was subsequently referred for clinically appropriate aftercare at the time of discharge. The correspondence and case summaries indicates that he steadily participated in mental health services with better functioning and improved mood. He was at risk for regression upon return home prompting the recommendations for continued mental health and family focused treatment. Again, the treatment team recommendations for clinically appropriate aftercare were to have continued involvement with intensive and structured therapy, as well as psychiatric aftercare.
The health plan's determination is overturned.
In this case, the patient could not have been effectively managed in a less restrictive environment for the dates of service under review. The residential structure, monitoring and intensity of services were warranted in this case scenario in view of the treatment factors and presenting clinical features that included safety risks, and severe symptoms of multiple psychiatric disorders including mood related disorder and substance use disorder that were associated with affective instability and impaired functioning, as well as the treatment failure at lower levels of care. The patient continued to require residential structure and monitoring until he had achieved stability with regard to the mood disturbance and was engaged in treatment for the co-occurring disorders with improved functioning with the remaining issues to include relationship and interpersonal functioning with authority figures, peers, and family, and continued need for clinically appropriate aftercare, as noted in the clinical summary.
He continued to display clinical features and symptoms that necessitated the continued residential level services as he struggled to engage in treatment and had intermittent bouts of affective instability that did require residential level structure and monitoring with active treatment. He had a history of treatment failure with lower level services and had displayed dangerous and problematic behaviors with maladaptive coping, emotional regulation problems, distress problems, interpersonal functioning problems and day-to-day functioning problems in the context of severe mood, disruptive and substance use disorders complicated by aggressive and violent behaviors. He continued to represent a safety risk and relapse risk, and could not have been effectively managed in a less restrictive treatment environment during the time interval under review through discharge.

summary:
Diagnosis: Overdose
Treatment: Inpatient admission
The insurer denied the inpatient admission.
The denial is upheld.

The proposed treatment was not medically necessary. The patient was clinically stable and had a limited plan of care anticipated for him.

Following this patient's ED evaluation, he was clinically stable. He was lethargic but had normal vital signs. There was no concern that he could not protect his airway. At no point was hypotensive. His symptoms were attributed to drug overdose. His testing in the ED had been unremarkable. The patient was kept in the hospital because he remained lethargic in the ED. The admission note for this patient indicates that he would be kept on a cardiac monitor until his mental status normalized. He would be observed for signs of drug withdrawal. No other testing was anticipated for the patient according to the admission note. At the time this patient was kept in the hospital, it would have been reasonable to believe that this limited plan of care could be accomplished for a stable patient with a short stay in the hospital. For this reason, an observation level of care would have been appropriate.

The patient had no severity of illness to warrant an inpatient admission. He had alteration of mental status, but a CT scan was normal and his blood work was normal. His altered mental status was attributed to drug overdose. No additional testing was planned to look for other potential causes of altered mental status. He had stable vital signs and was protecting his airway.

The patient had no intensity of services to warrant an inpatient admission. He would be kept on a cardiac monitor until his mental status normalized. No additional testing was planned for the patient. He ultimately required a psychiatric evaluation due to agitation that was likely related to drug withdrawal.

In conclusion, the patient was clinically stable following his ED evaluation. A limited plan of care was anticipated for him. An observation level of care would have been appropriate for the patient. The Health Plan acted reasonably in denying coverage for this inpatient admission.

This patient is a female who was admitted inpatient mental health treatment after a suicide attempt by taking 60 Benadryl pills and having a subsequent seizure. The patient reported severe depressive symptoms including depressed mood, suicidal thoughts, anhedonia, poor energy, concentration problems, and guilt. The patient's history was significant for suicide attempt by cutting self. The patient had a diagnosis of Depressive Disorder. The patient had multiple stressors including poverty, victimization of bullying, lack of supports, adverse childhood events, and disrupted attachments. The patient was started on Fluoxetine during her inpatient stay, and the medication was increased several times due to continued depressive symptoms. The patient was transferred to the adolescent unit with 1:1 observation. A 72 hour letter reportedly was submitted and she was discharged.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Suicidal Behaviors reports that patients with suicidal intent or plan or attempts are in need of inpatient treatment. It also reports that patients with past suicide attempts are at high risk for suicide. In this case, this patient had a very serious suicide attempt by taking 60 Benadryl pills with intent to die and she had a seizure on way to the hospital. The patient also had a past suicide attempt less than a year ago by cutting, which put this patient at high risk for suicide. The patient continued to report severe depressive symptoms including depressed mood, suicidal thoughts, low energy, isolation, and during her inpatient stay, the patient required multiple changes to her anti-depressive medications to appropriately treat and stabilize her symptoms.

Notes reported that the patient was started on Fluoxetine for depression. Other notes reported that the patient's Fluoxetine had to be increased due to continued significant depressive symptoms including dysphoric mood, suicidal thoughts, and low energy. The patient was noted to be lying in bed, exhibiting social isolation and withdrawal, poor participation, and irritable mood. Still other notes reported that the patient's Fluoxetine again had to be increased to 30 mg per day for continued depressive symptoms. Notes reported that the patient's Fluoxetine was then again increased to 40 mg per day to target continued depressive symptoms. Subsequent notes reported that the patient was transferred to the adolescent unit with 1:1 observation and precautions for her sexual acting out. Notes reported that a 72 hour letter was submitted and the patient was discharged.  

Based on the review of the medical record, this patient was a high risk patient for self-harm and danger. The patient was admitted with a serious suicide attempt, and during her inpatient stay, her depressive symptoms were difficult to control with anti-depressant medication. The patient also required 1:1 observation and precautions for sexually acting out and affecting other peer patients.  Given this patient's psychiatric history as well as her persistent unstable symptoms and behavioral activity, continued inpatient stay was medically necessary to treat this patient's medical condition. 

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient.

The carrier's denial of coverage for the inpatient admission should be reversed. The medical necessity is substantiated.

He had active withdrawal symptoms including sweats, nausea, agitation, visual disturbance, anxiety, depression, numbness, and headache, and he had a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) score of 5 that went to 10. He reportedly had a seizure history with the last reported seizure having been a couple of days before admission. He was drinking shots of vodka and several tall boys per day and had a decade long history of alcohol use. He reportedly was homeless and unemployed. He reportedly had a positive toxicology for benzodiazepines and ethylglucuride. He reportedly was started on a Librium protocol. He reportedly was transferred to a substance inpatient rehabilitation treatment.

This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient hospital treatment for detoxification as this was a high risk patient in need of 24 hour detoxification hospital treatment for several days prior to going to the substance inpatient rehabilitation treatment. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. In this case this patient had been drinking large amounts of alcohol daily and had active withdrawal symptoms with a recent seizure several days prior to admission. His CIWA score increased from 5 to 10 and he required detoxification medications. He also was homeless and lacked supports and could not safely be in detoxification outside of this hospital. 

According to the LOCADTR he did require 24 hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated in outpatient detoxification settings as he continued to use large amounts of alcohol despite medical issues including seizures, homelessness, lack of finances, family and friend discord, and emotional and health issues, and he required and needed detoxification medication to modify withdrawal and needed 24 hour treatment then as he was at risk for worsened withdrawal symptoms if not in this 24 hour setting. He was at risk for severe, complicated, and life threatening withdrawal symptoms. The risk of life complicated withdrawal such as delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use so he required the entire time in this hospital with several days detoxification prior to attending inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment. It was unlikely that he would remain abstinent while still having withdrawal symptoms also. He reportedly could not stop drinking without a 24 hour setting so he likely also could not have been safely and effectively detoxified in a less restrictive setting other than this 24 hour hospital setting.  As a result, the recommendation is to reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for inpatient substance detoxification. It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably or in the best interests of the patient then. 

Based on the above, the medical necessity for the inpatient admission for substance abuse is substantiated.  The insurer's denial is reversed.

His onset of withdrawal symptoms had initially included anxiety, irritability, insomnia, agitation with tremors, gastrointestinal upset and body aches. The patient was admitted to detoxification treatment with a comprehensive detoxification protocol with tapering dosages of methadone, and prn medications for comfort including clonidine, as well as vitamin replacement therapy. The program provided for case management with referral to sober housing and access to rehabilitation treatment that included comprehensive evidence-based treatments. During detoxification the patient engaged in counseling sessions focusing on education about the disease model of addiction, and, involvement with counseling and milieu activities including peer support and education sessions to motivate the patient to proceed to rehabilitation treatment. Vital signs remained normal during his brief stay. 

The patient engaged with detoxification treatment; he was cooperative with the tapering dosages of methadone. Withdrawal symptoms remained mild and resolved after the first two days of treatment. The patient completed the detoxification treatment and accepted referral for rehabilitation treatment. There were no complications during his inpatient stay.

This is a patient with a past medical history of bipolar disorder who presented to the emergency department after taking Ativan, Trazadone, and Lithium in a suicide attempt.
On presentation, the patient was afebrile with blood pressure 99/59, heart rate 85, respiratory rate 20, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Her exam otherwise noted the patient to be alert and oriented without neurologic deficits or nystagmus, to have a depressed affect, and to have lice. Lab results revealed white blood cell count (WBC) 8.2, hemoglobin (HGB) 13.2, platelets (PLT) 392, sodium (Na) 138, potassium (K) 4.4, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) 6, creatinine 0.64, lithium level 1.1, Tylenol and salicylate levels negative, alcohol level negative, and venous blood gas with potential hydrogen (pH) 7.34/ partial pressure of carbon dioxide (pCO2) 50.9/ bicarbonate (HCO3) 26.7. A urine drug screen was negative. An electrocardiogram (EKG) showed normal sinus rhythm without QTc prolongation. The patient was brought into the hospital with plans for telemetry monitoring, serial labs every 6 hours, serial EKGs, IV fluids, and a 1:1 sitter, and permethrin.
The patient was hemodynamically stable and alert and oriented without nystagmus or neurologic deficits. Her renal function remained normal, her lithium level decreased to 0.8, and she had no arrhythmias on telemetry. She remained on 1:1 sitter given ongoing depression and expression of suicidal thoughts with plans to transfer to an inpatient psychiatry bed once she was medically clear.
The patient was ultimately transferred to inpatient psychiatry.
The health plan's determination is upheld.
This patient presented with an intentional overdose on Lithium, Trazadone and Ativan in the setting of suicidal ideation. She was noted to be alert and oriented on presentation, hemodynamically stable, with normal renal function and otherwise unremarkable lab results, lithium level of 1.1, and with an EKG that showed no evidence of QtC prolongation or other arrhythmia. In this setting, she was appropriate to bring into the hospital for intravenous (IV) fluids, serial labs, monitoring of her mental status, and telemetry monitoring. She required care for her ongoing suicidal ideation and unstable psychiatric illness, but admission was not medically necessary for medical issues; therefore, the inpatient level of care was not medically necessary.

summary:
Diagnosis:  Bipolar disorder.
Treatment:  Continued inpatient mental health treatment.
 
The insurer denied the continued inpatient mental health treatment.  The denial is overturned.

The patient is an adult male admitted for acute inpatient evaluation and treatment of bipolar disorder with most recent episode of major depressive disorder, severe and recurrent with psychotic features.  The patient presented with a history of worsening symptoms of depression with agitation and aggressive behavior in the context of psychosis and deteriorating.  He reported poor appetite with weight loss to 98 pounds down from 140 pounds at five feet and eight inches of height; in the emergency department he expressed worry that he was going to be harmed and had sleep disturbance.  He had stopped his medications and was not following up with his outpatient psychiatrist.

The patient has a history of bipolar disorder with most recent episodes depressed with psychotic features and past history of mania or hypomania.  He had one prior psychiatric hospitalization and outpatient aftercare with medication management.  The patient has a history of an eating disorder with anorexia.  He has a remote history of alcohol and tobacco use.

His mental status examination included depressed mood and flat affect with motor agitation.  He had no evidence for internal stimuli, but had paranoid thought content with persecutory delusions, as well as the mood disturbance with morbid thoughts and ruminations and severe anxiety and agitation.  He was guarded, uncooperative and disheveled.  His insight was limited, and judgment impaired with inability to care for self.  He denied suicidal ideation or aggressive impulses and was notably withdrawn though agitated, due to his psychotic thought content.  He had decreased appetite, concentration, energy, sleep and volition with the weight loss.

Yes, the proposed treatment, continued inpatient mental health treatment, was medically necessary for this patient.

The patient required the admission and the continued acute inpatient level care and the structure and monitoring of an acute inpatient level setting in order to remain safe and to receive treatment for his psychiatric disturbances, bipolar mood disorder and comorbid eating disorder, while conducting an evaluation and while observing his functioning with the resumption/adjustment of clinically appropriate medications.  The clinical course was complicated by medication non-adherence, a lack of insight, and functional impairment being addressed during the time interval under review.  Additionally, the treatment team was planning for a safe and clinically appropriate disposition with aftercare arrangements in concert with the patient's mother, with whom he lived.

The medical necessity for the continued inpatient level structure and monitoring is reasonable and in the patient's best interest, in view of the patient's severe symptoms of mood disorder, risk for relapse, and co-morbid eating disorder.  And, in view of these clinical features and the complicated presentation with psychosis and deterioration in functioning, the patient's continued active treatment with safety monitoring was warranted in the context of the patient's deteriorated functioning and stressors involving primary support and general medical domains.  Additionally, the inpatient stay was medically necessary in order to monitor the response to medications, to insure that the patient will have a sustained response to treatment, and to continue to address the acute risk of relapse or non-compliance or rehospitalization in the context of severe symptoms of bipolar mood disorder in a patient with impaired judgment and a lack of insight.  The necessity for continued inpatient level services reflects sound medical judgment in keeping with prevailing standards of professional practice and with the published practice guidelines and criteria, referenced below, as well as New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews.

summary:

Treatment: Inpatient Mental Health Treatment for Adults with diagnosis code F32.9.
The insurer is denied coverage for Inpatient Mental Health Treatment for Adults with diagnosis code F32.9.
The denial is upheld.
 
This is a female patient who was admitted to inpatient mental health treatment due to depressive symptoms including suicidal ideation with a plan to jump off a train. She has a history of a past suicide attempt and a psychiatric hospitalization. The patient reported having flashbacks and nightmares of past reported sexual abuse victimization. The patient's reported symptoms included sad mood, low energy, and sleeping problems. The patient reportedly took Cymbalta and clonazepam. The patient was discharged.

There were no reports of suicidal ideation, plan, or intent, severe depressive symptoms, inability to care for basic needs, aggressive or self -injurious behavior, psychotic symptoms, substance use problems or substance withdrawal, or acute medical instability. Notes reported that the patient denied suicidal or homicidal ideation, had goal directed thoughts, improved sleep, better mood, was calm and cooperative, and had only mild anxiety. Notes reported that the patient had good sleep, no suicidal ideation, and was feeling more stable overall, had minimal anxiety, and was able to tolerate stressors better, and she was feeling more optimistic about her future. Notes reported that the patient had no aggression, impulsivity, or hopelessness, and denied suicidal or homicidal ideation, hallucinations; the patient reported good sleep and appetite. Notes reported that the patient had okay mood, denied hallucinations, suicidal or homicidal ideation, and had logical and linear thoughts, fair insight and judgment. The patient reportedly was discharged.

According to the American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Major Depressive Disorders, the least restrictive level of care for safe and effective treatment is appropriate and that patients with suicidal plan or intent or behaviors, or inability to adequately care for basic needs are candidates for hospitalization.

Based on the review of the medical record the patient had no reports of suicidal or homicidal ideation, intent, or plan, inability to adequately care for basic needs, manic episodes, and psychotic symptoms, self-injurious, aggressive, threatening, or agitated behavior. The chart notes did not provide enough specific evidence that the patient was an imminent danger to self or others or unable to adequately care for her basic needs. Also, as of then, there were no reports of specific identifiable or quantifiable treatment goals or objectives that could only be achieved in a 24 hour acute psychiatric hospital setting or that could not be achieved in a less restrictive setting. Thus, continued inpatient mental health treatment was not medically necessary.

The health plan acted reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient.

The carrier's denial of coverage for the continued Inpatient Mental Health Treatment for Adults with diagnosis code F32.9 to discharge should be upheld. The medical necessity is not substantiated.

He had legal issues due to use including assault charges due to use. He reportedly was homeless. He reportedly had a positive toxicology for opiates, cocaine, benzodiazepines, THC, and methadone. He reportedly had multiple past inpatient substance detoxification treatments and also rehabilitation treatments including a detoxification treatment days prior to this admission. He reported that he feared he would overdose due to use and he reported withdrawal symptoms such as runny nose, teary eyes, and nausea. He reportedly was put on 2 detoxification medications including Librium and Methadone which he took from but he signed out AMA.

The APA Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. 

In this case this patient had use of large amounts of multiple serious substances of use and alcohol putting him at very high risk for overdose or severe, complicated, and life threatening withdrawal. He reportedly was using up to 40 bags of heroin per day, drinking 2 1/2 pints of liquor per day, 20 mg of Xanax 1-2 times per week, 4-6 blunts of cannabis per day, and 1/2 gram of cocaine IV 3-6 times per week.

According to the LOCADTR he did require 24 hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive setting as he continued to use multiple serious substances of use and alcohol despite multiple past inpatient detoxification and rehabilitation treatments including a detoxification treatment several days prior to this admission and despite negative consequences including legal issues due to use. Also, he needed 2 detoxification medications (Librium and Methadone) to modify withdrawal and prevent severe, complicated, and life threatening withdrawal. He also lacked coping skills, ability to identify triggers, and he was homeless and did not have a sober support system as well. It was unlikely that he would remain abstinent outside of this hospital setting and he was a high risk for severe and life threatening withdrawal due to the large amount of serious substances of use and alcohol and also at high risk for overdose. His environment was not conducive to recovery as evidenced by his continued use. This was a high risk patient in need of hospital detoxification treatment. 

It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably, with sound medical judgment, or in the best interests of the patient then.

The patient was using up to two pints of liquor plus 40 ounces of beer daily with use of crack cocaine, as well as intermittent use of cocaine at a cost of $1000 when using. The patient had presented with mild alcohol withdrawal at the time of admission including gastrointestinal upset, tremors, headache, and anxiety with a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) scale score of 4. Patient had alcohol in system as well as cocaine. The patient had a history of substance-related treatment episodes including detoxification and rehabilitation treatment with relapses.  There were no acute medical issues, but was in treatment for coronary artery disease with a stent, congestive heart failure, automatic implantable cardioverter defibrillator (AICD) implant, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease, as well as pre-diabetes. The patient was tobacco dependent at one pack per day. There was a history of shoulder and back surgery. Physical examination, laboratory assessment, Chest X-Ray, and electrocardiogram (EKG) were consistent with history of cardio-metabolic disease including elevated liver functions and evidence for alcoholic liver disease. The patient was admitted to acute inpatient level care and placed on a detoxification regimen with a five-day Librium taper, vitamin replacement therapy, fluid replacement, and medical monitoring; the patient was offered smoking cessation treatment and nicotine replacement. summary:

Inpatient Hospital

This case involves a female with a history of alcohol dependence and anxiety disorder who presented to the hospital with a chief complaint of shaking and palpitations. Symptoms started the morning of the presentation. She did consume two shots of whiskey in the morning, but the shaking persisted. She denied nausea, vomiting, or dizziness. She also reported no chest pain or shortness of breath. The patient was admitted to the hospital with a principal diagnosis of alcohol withdrawal. Alcohol withdrawal scale on admission was three, and the blood alcohol level was 243. The patient was started on intravenous (IV) thiamine folic acid and intramuscular injections of Ativan, both scheduled and as needed. In addition, the laboratory studies revealed the presence of elevated liver function tests

The health plan's determination is overturned. The inpatient stay was medically necessary. This patient presents with clear signs of alcohol withdrawal, as evidenced by tachycardia, tremors, and palpitations. The patient has a clearly established history of alcoholism, with a slightly positive blood alcohol level. It is clinically evident that the patient is undergoing alcohol withdrawal, and requires prompt and aggressive treatment to prevent delirium tremens. The patient was appropriately admitted under inpatient status and started on the scheduled treatment of benzodiazepines, which is the standard of care for alcohol withdrawal. The patient rapidly improved because of the appropriate treatment that was started. These types of presentations require close monitoring of vital signs, and frequent assessment of CIWA scores to determine the dosing of benzodiazepine medications. This is not something that can be evaluated and treated under an observation level of care or outpatient status. An inpatient level of care was medically necessary.

The proposed treatment, intensive outpatient substance use treatment, was medically necessary for this patient.

The requested benefit of Intensive outpatient substance user treatment could not have been effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario.  The patient in this case presented with a mood disturbance with suicidal risk and was using large quantities of alcohol on a daily continuous basis with severe psychosocial stressors and functional impairments that did warrant continued IOP level structure, monitoring and services.  The treatment for the co-occurring disorders diagnosed in this case could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment that was provided at the time of admission.  Moreover, the patient's social environment was not conducive to lower level treatment, and the patient struggled with craving in the context of the mood disturbance and associated symptoms of anxiety with limited insight, impaired judgment and poor control of impulses.

Thus, the clinical features and treatment dimensions did necessitate the continued structure of an IOP level setting with intensive treatment, structure, supports, and safety monitoring.  The patient's history of substance use (frequency and quantity) together with the severe psychosocial stressors and co-occurring psychiatric disorders do reflect a complicated clinical picture and do support and the need for a safe and effective treatment setting, especially in regard to recent suicidal threats while using alcohol and the potential for high risk behaviors while under the influence of alcohol.  The documentation clearly indicated that the patient was at high risk for treatment failure if treatment were to be attempted at a lower level of care.  Therefore, medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published practice guidelines, the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and the scientific literature, referenced below, and it is consistent with New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews including the appropriate application of NY OASAS LOCADTR 3.0 Criteria.

The requested benefit of continued intensive outpatient substance use treatment is clinically appropriate, medically necessary and warranted, and, therefore, a covered benefit in this case scenario.  The treatment of the patient's co-occurring mental health and substance use disorders could not have been safely or effectively provided with lower level services, as notes above. summary:
Diagnosis: Psychiatric/Substance abuse
Treatment: Inpatient Detoxification

The patient requested detoxification treatment for polysubstance use in the context of severe psychosocial stressors including unemployment and diagnosis of hepatitis C, with multiple past substance use disorder treatments. The patient had been using up to 12 bags of heroin daily with intravenous (IV) administration with one pint of cognac plus beer and one gram of cocaine three to six times weekly. The substance use disorder had its onset in adolescence and progressed into adulthood with diagnoses of opioid, stimulant (cocaine) and alcohol use disorders. Patient presented with mild symptoms of withdrawal with Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) and Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) scale scores of 2 and 4 with sweats, gastrointestinal upset, and anxiety and insomnia with normal vital signs. There were no acute general medical or psychiatric issues. Patient had a history of unspecified depressive disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder with report of one psychiatric hospital stay. Patient was taking no psychotropic medications. Patient was admitted and placed on a detoxification regimen with methadone and Librium taper, comfort medications, as well as vitamin replacement therapy. Detoxification was uncomplicated regarding withdrawal management though the patient did have an untimed CIWA and COWS scale score of 12 and 10, respectively with no complaints or apparent distress. Patient received counseling and education from staff. The clinical course was uncomplicated with continued normal vital signs, and the patient was discharged against medical advice upon completion of detoxification with clinically appropriate recommendations for aftercare. The patient refused immediate referral/admission to inpatient rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment. The requested detoxification treatment, withdrawal management and medical services could have been safely and effectively provided at a lower level. There were no co-morbid medical issues or psychiatric disorders warranting inpatient admission. Withdrawal symptoms were not reported as severe, and clinical symptoms were not serious enough to necessitate inpatient level detoxification treatment/monitoring. There were no safety concerns or history of complicated withdrawal from drugs or alcohol. The patient was considered to be motivated for detoxification treatment and had access to substance use disorder services in the community. The health plan's determination is upheld, as medical necessity has not been established for the services in keeping with prevailing standards of professional practice, and consistent with the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria and scientific literature. Additionally, medical necessity for the requested inpatient detoxification and other medical services is not met in keeping with NY State OASAS LOCADTR 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines.

Substance Abuse Inpatient

The patient is a male who presented  for inpatient rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment to address substance use disorder with stimulants (crack cocaine) and alcohol. The patient had no history of withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens or other episodes of severe withdrawal symptoms. He had a history of substance use disorder that had begun in adolescence with multiple prior treatments with relapses though he had achieved a long period of sobriety in the past with up to four years of abstinence. His relapse was precipitated by the death of a friend. He was using cocaine in large quantity with up to $100 worth in a day and daily use of alcohol with up to two pints of liquor.

The patient was admitted to inpatient rehabilitation treatment following detoxification with vitamins and nicotine replacement to address tobacco dependence. He was provided comprehensive evaluation and treatment that included focus on coping skills, relapse prevention techniques with identification of triggers, education about the disease model of addiction, and, involvement with groups and individual therapy, as well as 12-step recovery groups and other therapeutic activities. He was prescribed Campral to address craving and the alcohol use disorder.
Throughout the inpatient stay, the patient was engaged in treatment with intensive services, sober housing, monitoring, and structure provided within the residential treatment program. The patient was enthusiastically participating actively in treatment with continued risk for relapse; the patient had no severe withdrawal symptoms or post-acute withdrawal symptoms; he was participating actively in treatment, and had no complications with respect to biomedical, general medical, emotional or other treatment domains. Mental status examinations/progress notes reflected stable mood with sleep, appetite and energy that were okay. He was social with peers. He was discharged with referral to outpatient aftercare as clinically appropriate.

The health plan's determination is upheld.

The requested health service/treatment of inpatient rehabilitation was not medically necessary for this patient. The proposed inpatient level treatment noted in the clinical summary could have been safely and effectively provided at a lower level of care.
The clinical features and indicated treatment dimensions of this patient's alcohol and cocaine use disorders did not require or warrant the structure of an inpatient setting or 24-hour monitoring. The patient displayed no serious disturbance of mental status despite having a history of ongoing substance use disorder with alcohol and cocaine and a history or schizoaffective disorder. Moreover, the patient had been evaluated and cleared with regard to safety concerns and did not show evidence for suicidal or aggressive behavior or risk, or severe cognitive impairment or psychosis, or perceptual disturbance, or general medical concerns that would have warranted an inpatient level admission and treatment. Any indicated treatment for the cocaine and the alcohol use disorders in this case could have been provided, as clinically appropriate, at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment and stabilization that occurred during his detoxification treatment immediately prior to entering rehabilitation treatment.
Thus, the requested inpatient rehabilitation was not medically necessary in this case. summary:
Mental Health
Depression


The patient is a female with a diagnosis of recurrent and severe major depressive disorder without psychotic features. The patient has co-morbid psychiatric disorders that include anxiety disorders (agoraphobia and social phobia), post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), borderline personality disorder, and mild alcohol use disorder, as well as documentation of bipolar II disorder and history of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). The patient received transcranial magnetic therapy, thirty deep transcranial magnetic stimulation (dTMS) treatments with an initial Beck Depression Inventory score of 13 with a decrease to 9. There is information provided to document treatment with antidepressants and augmentation with other classes of medications, and combined use of cognitive behavioral therapy and supportive psychotherapy. Failed antidepressant trials due to lack of efficacy or adverse effects include fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline, venlafaxine and mirtazapine. Augmentation has occurred with Seroquel, Zyprxa, Risperdal and Latuda, as well as use of Provigil to address daytime sedation with the Seroquel and alprazolam to address associated symptoms of anxiety. The patient has reportedly not been provided treatment with electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), and the documentation does not note whether ECT was offered or received in this case. The clinician and patient are requesting additional dTMS therapy with 14 additional sessions. The health plan has denied authorization for coverage of additional dTMS on the basis of coverage exclusion and that the requested treatment is considered not medically necessary in view of the apparent lack of a robust response to the initial treatments with 30 TMS treatment sessions and/or the health plan's assertion that other treatment with therapy/counseling is more likely to address the patient's multiple mental disorders. Issue under review: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) with 14 additional sessions for the treatment of recurrent and severe major depressive disorder. The health plan's determination of medical necessity is upheld. Yes, the health plan, in its determination of medical necessity, did act reasonably, with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. There are other clinically appropriate approaches available for treatment of depressive disorder, including combination therapy or another established augmentation therapy, as well as mood stabilizers. Moreover, electroconvulsive therapy may be offered. Thus, alternative, standard therapeutic options known to be effective in the treatment of Major Depressive Disorder and the multiple co-morbid psychiatric conditions are available to this patient to address the recrudescence of depressive symptoms or to continue efforts to achieve a remission of symptoms of the mood disorder. Thus, the health plan has acted reasonably and should not cover the proposed treatment, as requested. The requested Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation treatment is not "medically necessary" for this patient. Repetitive TMS therapy as a primary or adjunctive therapy for treatment of depression has generally been evaluated in patients who have treatment refractory depression, as defined by one or more, antidepressant medication treatment failures with or without augmentation. TMS therapy for depressive disorder has been established by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as a safe treatment; and, the data, as reflected in peer reviewed medical literature, supports this assertion. Specifically, when treatments with antidepressant medication with or without augmentation, electroconvulsive therapy, and/or psychotherapy, especially cognitive behavioral therapy, have failed, then TMS may be an appropriate consideration. This assertion is also noted in the American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorder, referenced below. The documentation in this case does not meet those guidelines with regard to the use of TMS for maintenance therapy in this case scenario largely due to the lack of a robust response to 30 dTMS treatments and the presence of multiple co-morbid mental disorders. Thus, in this case, the proposed repetitive and deep TMS therapy is not likely to be more beneficial for the patient than other available standard therapy/treatments, and medical necessity is not met. This answer is consistent with practice guidelines concerning major depressive disorder and the scientific literature pertaining to TMS therapy for major depressive disorder.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance  Abuse/Addiction.
Treatment: Substance  Abuse Inpatient.
The insurer denied the Substance Abuse Inpatient stay.
The health plan's determination is upheld in whole. 

The inpatient substance abuse admission was not medically necessary for this patient. The patient is an adult  who received inpatient rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment of opioid (heroin) use disorder; the patient had been using 3 bags of heroin per day with intravenous (IV) administration, and history of use of up to 20 bags of heroin in the past. Patient was also tobacco dependent at one-half pack per day. The referral was prompted by a decline in functioning with severe psychosocial stressors involving the primary support (family), occupational, housing, economic and social environment domains. The patient had acute general medical issues with infection at the injection sites and antibiotic treatment. Chronic medical conditions included hepatitis C positivity and musculoskeletal pain addressed with gabapentin and analgesics. Medical screening at the time of admission was negative and unremarkable except for a drug screen consistent with history. The patient denied the current use of other substances of abuse.
There are co-occurring psychiatric disorders in this case with unspecified anxiety disorder and bipolar mood disorder with the most recent episode depressed, and a history of at least one psychiatric hospitalization in the past. The patient was prescribed olanzapine and mirtazapine for his mental disorders, as well as the gabapentin, muscle relaxers and Benadryl to address insomnia. The patient was admitted to inpatient rehabilitation treatment with inpatient level substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment including the opportunity to participate in groups, individual counseling, education, and 12-step recovery groups with peer support. Comfort medications were available as needed, and patient was prescribed vitamins with the availability of nicotine replacement therapy. Patient was continued on psychotropic medications in order to address psychiatric disorders. The clinical course was benign, and patient engaged with treatment. The patient was discharged against medical advice with recommendations for continued substance use disorder rehabilitation services and continued treatment for general medical co-morbidity and co-occurring psychiatric disorders.
The structure and intensity of services necessary for a successful rehabilitation/substance use disorder treatment can be and could have been effectively provided at a lower level of care in a less restrictive treatment setting with sober supports. There is no evidence that inpatient level structure and 24-hour monitoring is medically necessary for a successful outcome in this case. And, there were no biomedical, psychiatric, or general medical issues that warranted the admission for inpatient level treatment.
The inpatient substance abuse rehabilitation treatment, in this case scenario, was amenable to treatment at a lower level of care. The patient was generally motivated and capable of effectively engaging in substance use disorder treatment in a less restrictive treatment setting with sober supports and/or housing. The patient did not need the structure or 24-hour monitoring of an inpatient setting in order to participate in rehabilitation substance abuse treatment safely and effectively. This answer is consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and the scientific literature, as well as New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews together with the NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines, referenced below and applicable in this case.

summary:
Diagnosis:  Substance abuse.
Treatment:  Residential Rehabilitation.

The insurer denied the residential rehabilitation.  The denial is overturned. 

The patient is a adult male admitted for residential rehabilitation and substance use disorder treatment of alcohol, opioid and stimulant (cocaine) use disorders.  His rehabilitation treatment included the continued use of medication assisted treatment with methadone.  The patient has no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens.  He was admitted with persistent withdrawal or post-acute withdrawal symptoms (PAWS) with craving at the time of admission.  He has a history of poly-substance use disorder with more recent daily continuous use of heroin, alcohol and cocaine.  The patient has a history of past treatment episodes including past involvement with Alcoholics and Narcotics Anonymous, as well as medication assisted treatment.  Despite the best efforts of community providers, the patient had relapsed with use of heroin, alcohol and cocaine.

The patient is homeless and relies on others for housing.  He is unemployed.  There is no report of current legal issues or trauma history in this case.

The patient received comprehensive treatment that included focus on coping skills, relapse prevention techniques with identification of triggers, education about the disease model of addiction, and, involvement with groups, as well as involvement in 12-step recovery groups and other therapeutic activities. 

Yes, the proposed treatment, residential rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment, was medically necessary for this patient and is consistent with NY State OASAS LOCADTR 3.0 Criteria.

The requested benefit of residential rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment is considered clinically appropriate and medically necessary in order to address the immediate needs for rehabilitation of the severe substance use disorders diagnosed in this case, and to work toward relapse prevention in a patient with high risk for relapse.  The admission and continued inpatient rehabilitation treatment was warranted in order to address the patient's lack of awareness of the seriousness of his illnesses with psycho-education and evidence-based psychosocial interventions, in order to address issues within the social environment, in order to work on coping skills that will be necessary in building a sober support system, and necessary for continued recovery efforts with community providers and re-engagement with peer-supported recovery groups that had been effective in the past.  The counseling, educational sessions, and the development of a relapse prevention plan were critical in this case, together with the motivational techniques that served to facilitate gains with insight and acquisition of better coping skills - all important components of the treatment that were provided with clinically appropriate structure, intensity of services, and monitoring.  It was clinically appropriate and medically necessary that the patient have 24-hour monitoring and inpatient level services prior to step down to lower level treatment and that he be provided continued inpatient level services for the duration of the proposed treatment in order to prepare the patient for a safe and clinically appropriate disposition and discharge to the community.  None of this therapeutic work could have been effectively provided at a lower level of care in view of the multiple, complicating factors in this case for the time interval under review.

On presentation to the emergency department, the patient reported past history of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) / human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), high cholesterol, substance abuse, bipolar disorder, diabetes. Vital signs were initially within normal limits with a heart rate of 78. The patient reported  drinking "3 pints with some beer." It was unclear from the initial documentation what type of alcoholic drink was quantified by the phrase "3 pints." Patient stated that her last drink had been a few hours prior to coming to the hospital. Patient reported alcohol withdrawal with detoxification some months ago. Patient reported having seizures in the past. There were no initial medical complaints.
Subsequent documentation indicated that the patient was drinking "3-4 pints of liquor daily." Patient reported that her maximum period of sobriety had been 4 months in the past. Also reported a history of seizures and delirium tremens during prior detoxification admissions. Patient also reported a history of heroin, cocaine, and marijuana abuse. Patient reported being sober for more than 20 years, though was unclear from documentation to which substance this referred. Medications included Seroquel, Lexapro, Ambien, Klonopin/Ativan, Truvada, Isentress.
Initial Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) score was 13. Patient was admitted for detoxification on an Ativan protocol. 
The health plan's determination of medical necessity is overturned in whole. The patient was drinking heavily prior to admission, had a significantly elevated alcohol withdrawal score, and had a history of alcohol withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens and needed inpatient detoxification. The patient did not require immediate hospitalization for life-threatening medical conditions or for a severe psychiatric crisis. Alcohol was the substance most likely to cause harm. The patient clearly met criteria for an alcohol use disorder. The patient was not in full remission from the substance use disorder. The patient was using a substance with the risk of medical complications from withdrawal. The patient did have serious medical symptoms of withdrawal that would require medical management and a hospital setting. Vital signs would need to be monitored at least every 6 hours and likely more. Detoxification medications were needed to prevent or modify withdrawal and the client's needs needed to be monitored to adjust medication. The patient had a history of seizures and delirium tremens and there was a long term history of substance abuse that would eventually lead to serious medical problems.
