summary:
Diagnosis: Acute psychotic symptoms 

Treatment: Inpatient hospital admission

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient hospital admission. The denial reversed.

This patient is a male who was admitted to this hospital as he had a heart rate of 149 and blood pressure of 134/108 with a BUN of 42 and creatinine of 2.65 and he was on telemetry and received intravenous (IV) fluids and was on 1:1 as he was psychotic.  He had a positive toxicology for cocaine and Methadone.  He had auditory and visual hallucinations, disorganized thinking and behavior, agitation, persecutory delusional thinking, irrational behavior, and reportedly was using IV cocaine and heroin, Methadone, pills off the street, and alcohol.  He had a diagnosis of Schizoaffective Disorder and substance use disorders.  He was seen by the Psychiatry consultant who recommended psychiatric hospitalization when medically cleared but there were no beds available until when he was transferred to the Psychiatric unit. The insurer denied coverage for inpatient hospital treatment.

This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient hospital treatment as he had acute psychotic symptoms reported from a specified range requiring 24 hour hospital treatment.  He was not safe to be treated outside of a 24 hour hospital as he was not able to function or care for his basic needs.  He had reports of auditory and visual hallucinations, disorganized thinking and behavior, agitation, persecutory delusional thinking, irrational behavior, and reportedly was using intravenous (IV) cocaine and heroin, Methadone, pills off the street, and alcohol.  

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Schizophrenia report that patients with hallucinations, delusional thinking, disorganized thinking or behavior, severe agitation, or aggression are in need of hospital treatment.  In this case he had reports of hallucinations, delusional and disorganized thinking and behavior, and inability to care for his basic needs. Notes on a specified date reported auditory and visual hallucinations, disorganized thinking and behavior, agitation, persecutory delusional thinking, and irrational behavior. Notes on another date reported that he was agitated overnight and pulled out his IV as he was hallucinating with delusions and psychiatry recommended physical and chemical restraints. Notes on the day after reported that he still had auditory hallucinations and delusions. Notes on the next day reported that he had auditory hallucinations and was talking to himself and still had paranoid delusions.  Notes on the following day reported that he had hallucinations, delusional thinking, and needed inpatient psychiatric hospital treatment when the bed was available.  He had command auditory hallucinations telling him to go.  He still had reports of paranoid delusional thinking, internal preoccupation, and Risperidone was increased.    
Other notes reported that he was very disorganized, trying to get out of bed and drink toilet water, had a thought disorder, was agitated, and IM Ativan was given and mitten restraints and he still required 24 hour psychiatric hospital treatment. Notes on the final date reported that he was still having auditory hallucinations, paranoid delusional thinking, internal preoccupation, and was isolative, and he was transferred to the psychiatric unit.  He had acute psychotic symptoms requiring 24 hour hospital treatment then. 

As a result, the recommendation is to reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for inpatient hospital treatment.  It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably or with sound medical judgment or in the best interests of the individual then.

The carrier's denial of coverage for the inpatient hospital admission is reversed.  The medical necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse

Treatment: Medically Supervised Inpatient Withdrawal and Stabilization Services
 
The insurer denied the medically supervised inpatient withdrawal and stabilization services.

The denial was overturned.

This is a female patient who was admitted to this inpatient hospital for detoxification treatment from alcohol and heroin.  She had withdrawal symptoms and had a Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) score of 6 and a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment of Alcohol (CIWA) score of 4.  She reported drinking 3-4 liters of vodka and wine per day, using 5-15 bags of intranasal heroin per day, and using 1-2 grams of intranasal cocaine; she had two prior overdoses.  She had prior inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatment and still was unable to stop use.  She had depressive symptoms and self-injurious behavior including cutting herself.  It was reported that she stopped her psychotropic medications.  She was put on two detoxification medications.  She was discharged to the Emergency Department when she expressed suicidal plans to overdose or cut a vein. 

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment.  It states patients with past complicated or life-threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens are in need of inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal.  They report that patients with co-morbid medical conditions that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification.  The US Department of Health and Human Services-Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) Center for Substance Abuse Treatment reports that inpatient treatment is necessary if the ability to attend outpatient treatment daily is a problem, one is unable to follow up in outpatient treatment, if medical conditions complicate the treatment of withdrawal, if one has previous withdrawal seizures of delirium tremens, or if one does not have the capacity for informed consent.  According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), she required 24-hour treatment as she could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive setting.  She was put on two detoxification medication protocols to modify withdrawal from alcohol and heroin, and she had active reported withdrawal symptoms and was at risk of severe, complicated, and life-threatening withdrawal, as well as overdose.  She had two past overdoses; therefore, she was a high risk for another overdose.  She had self-injurious behavior including cutting herself and had comorbid depression with suicidal ideation.  She had two suicidal plans including overdose and cutting her vein.  She was discharged to the Emergency Department (ED) for psychiatric assessment.  She needed 24-hour treatment as she was at risk for worsened withdrawal symptoms if not in this 24-hour setting, including more severe, complicated, and even possible life-threatening withdrawal such as delirium tremens.  The risk of delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use.  She did require 24-hour medically supervised inpatient withdrawal treatment.  It was considered unsafe for her to have detoxification at a less restrictive level of care.  

The health care plan did not act reasonably, or sound medical judgment, or in the best interests of the patient.

The carrier's denial of coverage for the Medically Supervised Inpatient Withdrawal and Stabilization Services is overturned.  The medical necessity is substantiated.

Mental health inpatient

The case involves an adult who was admitted on early 2019 to acute inpatient psychiatric services for mood disturbance and psychosis. The patient was brought in by police and emergency medical services due to threatening behavior towards  mother and sister's boyfriend with whom the patient  lived. Patient had been acting bizarre in the two months prior to presentation and had been discharged from inpatient level psychiatric treatment just two days prior to presentation. The patient reported increasing symptoms of depression in the context of symptoms of psychosis that included paranoid thought content and the belief that the mother had stolen  money. The patient had become increasingly depressed following a divorce 3 months earlier. Moreover, the patient reported not taking medication, Latuda, that had been prescribed. And,  mother had kicked him out of the home and filed a restraining order leaving the patient homeless.
The patient presented to the emergency department, and was subsequently admitted after medical clearance that included physical examination, laboratory assessment and electrocardiogram (EKG).  Assessment included normal laboratory findings and a positive drug screen consistent with  intermittent use of cannabis (marijuana). Patient had co-occurring alcohol use disorder and had spent nine months in rehabilitation treatment in the previous year with a reduction of alcohol use, but continued daily use of two beers.
The patient has a history of psychiatric treatment and hospitalizations for schizophrenia and depressive disorder. Also had a history of medication non-adherence and co-occurring substance use disorders with alcohol and cannabis, as noted. Patient had been using one blunt of marijuana intermittently.  The patient was psychotic and cognitively impaired with thought blocking and paranoid thought content and depressive ruminations with regard to the ex-spouse. Patient was guarded, but cooperative with poor eye contact, displayed depressed mood with anxiety, nervousness, apprehension, tension, irritability, and excessive worry, and, indicated that patient was having aggressive impulses, but denied active suicidal or homicidal intent. Again, patient demonstrated paranoid delusions and intense ruminations including grief related to the recent divorce. Patient had decreased concentration, energy, sleep, and volition. The patient's treatment plan included safety monitoring and medication targeting mood disturbance and psychosis, as well as therapy and psychoeducation provided in the milieu. Haldol and as needed (prn) Ativan were prescribed for acute agitation and anxiety. Other medications included Atarax and Benadryl for anxiety and insomnia. The patient refused medications indicating did not need them except for Benadryl which the patient did take to enhance sleep. Discharge planning occurred and disposition to the community with intensive services had been arranged with therapeutic shelter and assertive community treatment. The patient was discharged with follow-up for the co-occurring psychiatric and substance use disorders with disposition to the shelter and recommendations for follow up for general medical care of obesity and smoking cessation. The HP determination of medical necessity is overturned in whole. The patient's continued inpatient mental health treatment is reasonable and in the best interest of the patient; Patient had severe symptoms of depression and psychosis complicated by substance abuse and medication non-adherence and decline in functioning. Patient had deteriorated to the point that he was a safety risk with intrusive thoughts that included aggressive impulses. Moreover, the patient's co-occurring substance use disorder was significant, and the patient had clinical features and continued mental status findings that posed a serious safety risk during the time interval under review. The patient could not have been safely or effectively managed during the time interval under review at a lower level of care.
The patient's severity of symptoms, and inability to benefit from treatment at a lower level of care, functional decline, and safety issues related to persistent symptoms of psychosis and mood disturbance were clinical factors and treatment dimensions that necessitated acute inpatient hospital care, structure, and monitoring as proposed through discharge. The medication management and safety monitoring together with attention to the precipitating issues in this case were medically necessary; the intensity of services and safety issues in this case could not have been effectively addressed or managed at a lower level of care.

summary:
This is a patient who presented for detoxification and substance-related services. The patient has a history of severe substance use disorders with alcohol and opioid class substances of abuse, as well as use of prescribed and non-prescribed benzodiazepines. He had recent substance use disorder treatment in the previous year, but had left treatment prematurely and relapsed and was using large quantities of alcohol and opioids on a continuous daily basis. He had multiple prior substance use disorder treatments with a chronic relapsing course, and history of two prior overdoses with one requiring the use of Narcan. His substance use disorder history was associated with escalating use and progression of the disease.
At the time of presentation, the patient was also requesting referral for rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment. He was unemployed and reported severe psychosocial stressors within the primary support, social environment, occupational and housing domains with homelessness. The patient reported functional decline as the substance abuse/disease had progressed together with homelessness which prompted his self-referral for detoxication treatment and request for assistance with rehabilitation services.
The patient provided no past history of withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens or severe alcohol or drug withdrawal symptoms. He was medically screened and admitted for inpatient level detoxification with plans for a five day detoxification treatment with Librium and methadone and supportive measures. His Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) / Clinical Institute Narcotic Assessment (CINA) scale scores showed mild withdrawal symptoms with a score of 8. Withdrawal symptoms and signs included sweats, tremor, diaphoresis, restlessness, and anxiety, as well as insomnia. A drug screen was consistent with history.
The patient has no history of psychiatric disorders or treatment or suicidal or self-harming behaviors. There were no acute medical issues in this case other than the alcohol and opioid withdrawal, and the healing abdominal wound requiring continued antibiotic treatment. The patient was tobacco dependent and declined nicotine replacement therapy.
On Mental Status Examination, there were no severe symptoms on mental status examination and no safety concerns with regard to risk of harm to self or others. The patient displayed fair to good insight despite his history, and impaired, but good judgment and control of impulses. He demonstrated symptoms of anxiety with generalized symptoms including insomnia, and dysphoric affect together with somatic symptoms related to the alcohol and opioid withdrawal, as noted.
The patient was admitted for inpatient treatment with detoxification protocol. He received tapering dosages of Librium and methadone and replacement of vitamins with the availability of nicotine replacement and smoking cessation counseling and comfort medications and as needed (prn) medications prescribed for pain, anxiety, agitation, and insomnia. The patient's hospital course progressed without incident. Vital signs remained normal during the hospital stay, and the patient reported persistently mild symptoms of withdrawal that diminished and responded to use of prn medications administered through discharge. He was participating in counseling and educational sessions.
Arrangements were being made for a direct referral to rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment including arrangements for sober housing in a ¾ house. Again, the patient received active treatment together with monitoring that had occurred without incident while receiving a detoxication protocol with Librium and methadone and vitamin replacement therapy, and the patient attended groups sessions and received counseling with recommendations and planning for clinically appropriate aftercare.
The health plan's determination is overturned. The requested inpatient detoxification treatment could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. The patient in this case was using large quantities of substances that did warrant the admission and the continued inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring. Detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments pertinent to the detoxification treatment episode could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment that was provided at the time of admission. Moreover, the patient's social environment was not conducive to an effective detoxification, and the patient had struggled with withdrawal symptoms (tremor, sweats, anxiety, irritability, restlessness and insomnia) which were being effectively addressed with Librium and methadone and supportive measures. The patient had associated clinical features that included lack of sober supports and severe psychosocial stressors including homelessness. Thus, the adult inpatient admission and continued detoxification treatment of this patient's substance use disorders did necessitate the structure of an inpatient level setting with withdrawal management and psychosocial supports, and 24-hour monitoring. The patient's history of substance abuse (frequency and quantity) together with the severe psychosocial stressors and functional impairments do reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder and the need for a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management as the patient was at high risk for treatment failure or general medical complications such as seizures if detoxification and withdrawal management were to be attempted at a lower level of care. summary:
Diagnosis:  Substance abuse 

Treatment: Inpatient substance abuse treatment

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient substance abuse treatment. The denial reversed.

This patient is a male who reportedly was admitted to this inpatient substance detoxification treatment due to heroin detoxification.  He reportedly had anxiety and insomnia.  He had four past inpatient substance detoxification treatments, two past inpatient substance rehabilitation treatments, and one past substance outpatient treatment and could not stop heroin use.  He reportedly was using 8-10 bags per day of intranasal heroin.  He reportedly had past vomiting, tremors, and lightheadedness.  He reportedly was put on a Methadone protocol and took Methadone for detoxification for a specified number of days. He reportedly left against medical advice (AMA). The insurer denied coverage for inpatient substance detoxification treatment.

This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient substance detoxification treatment as the chart notes did provide enough specific evidence to support that he required this level of treatment then.  The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders report that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment.  This was the case with this patient.  This patient had four past inpatient substance detoxification treatments and two past inpatient substance rehabilitation treatments, and one past substance outpatient treatment and could not stop heroin use as he was still using large amounts of heroin daily.  It was reported that he needed better coping skills and identification of relapse triggers and could not stop heroin use without a 24 hour treatment so he could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in an outpatient setting.  It was not likely that he could attend an outpatient substance detoxification treatment due to his continued use despite past inpatient substance treatments so he required only inpatient substance detoxification treatment then.  He also was at risk for accidental overdose.  

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) he did require 24 hour treatment as he needed detoxification medication, Methadone, to modify withdrawal and could not stop heroin use despite multiple past treatments so outpatient treatment for detoxification was not considered enough or safe as he needed 24 hour treatment for detoxification. 

As a result, the recommendation is to reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for inpatient acute hospital treatment for substance detoxification treatment as he was reportedly left AMA after his Methadone dose. It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably or in the best interests of the patient then.  

The carrier's denial of coverage for inpatient substance abuse treatment is reversed.  The medical necessity is substantiated

summary:
Diagnosis: Depression; Anxiety
Issue under review: Inpatient admission

Determination:
The Inpatient admission was medically necessary.

The patient is an adult male with a history of mental illness who received inpatient psychiatric treatment at the hospital.

The patient has a history of mental illness including diagnosis of depression and anxiety.  He had previously been evaluated in the emergency room for symptoms of anxiety and a panic attack.  There is a medical history of diabetes mellitus, obesity, and high blood pressure.  There is no prior history of psychiatric treatment and no outpatient treatment providers in place.

On the dates of admission, he presented with a family member to the emergency room for evaluation.  He was noted to have depression and anxiety with poor appetite, inability to sleep and "no drive."  He was noted to be scared and withdrawn.  There was impaired reality testing, and he was noted to have had "blood glucose levels running high."  He was evaluated by a psychiatrist who recommended inpatient psychiatric hospitalization.  He was admitted with a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder, Single Episode, Severe.  

On the unit, the patient was treated by a multidisciplinary team including nursing, psychiatry, and therapy staff.  He received individual and milieu treatment.  He received a psychopharmacology evaluation and was treated with Mirtazapine 15mg PO (by mouth) QHS (nightly) and Lorazepam as a PRN (as needed) medication.

The following day, the patient's family arrived and the patient and his family requested discharge.  He was noted to be safe for discharge and was released from the inpatient unit with a plan to follow up in the outpatient setting.

The patient represented an acutely elevated risk of dangerous behaviors, and there was no less-restrictive treatment environment appropriate.  The acute risk factors of inability to function as well as depression and anxiety with the chronic risk factors of potentially dangerous behaviors suggest that the patient would have been at an acute risk of self-injurious behaviors (including but not limited to suicide) were he to have been discharged from the inpatient hospital setting.  The patient was discharged from the inpatient psychiatric hospital setting as soon as a less-restrictive treatment setting was appropriate.  

The patient represented an elevated risk of dangerous behaviors including self-injury, and suicide, and there was no less-restrictive treatment environment appropriate.  Therefore the treatment was medically necessary.  While the patient was not endorsing active suicidality or homicidality, the patient remained depressed, anxious and had demonstrated inability to function in the outpatient setting.  The patient had multiple static risk factors for potentially dangerous behaviors including depression, medical illness, and diagnosis with a severe mental illness.  Therefore the patient represented a chronic risk of potentially dangerous behaviors.  Furthermore, the fact that there was no less-restrictive environment of care appropriate suggests that ongoing inpatient psychiatric hospitalization was medically necessary and should be covered by the patient's health plan.

summary:
Diagnosis: OCD
Issue under review: Transcranial magnetic stimulation

Determination:
The Transcranial magnetic stimulation is not medically necessary.

The patient is an adult male. He was treated with multiple sessions of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) for OCD (obsessive compulsive disorder). 

The provider's assertion that there is a wealth of evidence of supporting OCD as an indication for dTMS (Deep Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation), and his referring to it as the "gold standard" are not accurate. Studies to date are suggestive, but at times contradictory and inconclusive, regarding the efficacy of dTMS in the treatment of OCD. 

Also, the provider's citing approval by the FDA is misleading, as the FDA approval of dTMS for OCD is specifically as a Humanitarian Use Device (HUD), which clearly means the FDA considers there to be inadequate evidence of efficacy at this time. The FDA HUD approval was based on a single study involving 99 patients. Other published studies implying FDA approval are reprints by the manufacturer of the device and fail to note the HUD status.

While the patient's YBOCS (Yale Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale) score has improved, there is insufficient evidence to attribute this to the specific treatment as opposed to other factors, such as patient expectations, placebo, observer bias, unknown changes in the patient's life, etc. 

Therefore, given the above, the TMS is not medically necessary for the patient at this time.

summary: The patient with alcohol use disorder, bipolar disorder, and a history of traumatic brain injury (TBI) was admitted to inpatient rehabilitation following inpatient detox at an affiliated facility.  The patient reported a serious TBI  for which alcohol intoxication was a contributing factor.  Patient reported that this accident was motivating him to get clean from alcohol.  Patient had no withdrawal symptoms on arrival.  Urine was positive for benzodiazepines, presumably from recent withdrawal management.  Patient was not on medication assisted treatment (MAT), and there is no documentation that this was discussed or offered.  Patient reported taking Prozac and olanzapine regularly but was not in outpatient mental health treatment for the last year; patient indicated these medications were helpful for him and denied any acute psychiatric complaints. He denied pain.  The course on the rehab unit appears uncomplicated.  Patient requested to meet with psychiatry to request an increase in olanzapine back to a previously helpful dose.  The patient reported having labile moods to the psychiatrist. Fluoxetine and olanzapine were increased as a result of this evaluation.  However, this evaluation does not coincide with any notes from staff citing labile mood or any psychiatric concerns.  Patient was assigned to attend groups and individual therapy and weekly progress notes from Credentialed Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Counselor (CASAC), and nursing indicated the patient was attending treatment without issue.  Patient worked with the team to arrange appropriate outpatient follow-up appointments/linkages for psychiatric, SUD and medical needs.  For the period in question, nursing notes do not indicate any clinical change or concern.  Vital signs were normal.  Patient was being discharged to a stable residence.  There is no discussion of MAT during this time period. The CASAC discharge note indicates the patient denied cravings for the last few days of the admission.  The health plan's determination of medical necessity is upheld in whole.  There is no documented discussion of MAT for alcohol use disorder in the chart and no rationale documented for why this was not done.  MAT is part of the standard of care for treatment of alcohol use disorders.  The presence of strong supports in the community was not clear; however, the treatment plan had addressed the building of supports and outpatient follow-up.  There is no documentation that the patient has been using in hazardous situations.  A completed concurrent review LOCADTR resulted in a recommendation for a lower level of care.  This was not updated by the facility during the admission to evaluate the ongoing stay.

summary:
This is a patient with a chronic psychotic disorder best characterized as schizoaffective disorder, depressed type. The patient has a history of co-occurring substance use disorder with an opioid class substance of abuse. The patient presented to emergency services and was admitted for acute inpatient treatment of an exacerbation of the psychotic and mood disorder with anxiety, paranoia, and worsening symptoms of depression with suicidal ideation.
The mental status examination revealed suicidal ideation, suspiciousness with paranoid delusions, depressed mood, motor agitation, and disorganized thought processing. He had markedly impaired judgment together with limited insight and poor impulse control. He had morbid preoccupations indicating fear that he was in a movie and being filmed and was at risk to be harmed. He was anxious with irritability, nervousness, tension and worry. He had decreased concentration, energy, appetite and volition.
The patient has a past treatment history for schizoaffective disorder, depressed type; he had multiple prior psychiatric hospitalizations including one suicide attempt with an intentional heroin overdose. There were no acute general medical conditions in this case.
The patient was admitted to acute inpatient psychiatric services with close observation and safety monitoring; structured psychosocial programming; and pharmacotherapy with mood stabilizer and antidepressant and antipsychotic medications. His hospital course was complicated by severe symptoms of psychosis and persistent suicidal ideation with little progress. His medications were titrated, as clinically appropriate with a regimen of lithium, quetiapine, fluoxetine and clonazepam with adherence and tolerability.
The patient remained depressed with withdrawn behavior and continued psychosis and suicidal ideation. The treatment team focused on coping skills, attention to self-care and reality testing with active treatment of the mood and psychotic disorder with the medication and therapy and safety monitoring.
Ten days later, the patient was noted to be calm and cooperative with improved sleep, appetite and functioning. His mood was improved with only passive suicidal ideation. The patient was increasingly cooperative with care, compliant with milieu therapeutic activities, and, medication adherent with tolerability. He had been started on clozapine with the addition of Wellbutrin which produced improved mood that was subsequently okay despite persistent symptoms of anxiety. Going forward, the patient remained calm but anxious, cooperative and engaged in treatment with medication adherence and tolerability. Discharge planning had occurred with regard to a safe and clinically appropriate discharge plan and disposition.
 
The health plan's determination is overturned in part.
The proposed inpatient treatment is medically necessary, in part, as the patient required the structure of an inpatient level of care in order to remain safe and to administer continued treatment for his psychiatric disturbance while conducting an evaluation, and observing his functioning with titration and monitoring of his medication including tolerability and response to antipsychotic/mood stabilizing medication, clozapine together with lithium and antidepressant medications. It was medically necessary for the patient to continue to receive 24-hour monitoring in view of residual symptoms of psychosis, the mood disturbance, and risk for affective instability, and continued disturbance of thought.
However, acute inpatient mental health treatment was not medically necessary once the patient no longer required the structure of an inpatient level of care in order to remain safe or to administer continued treatment for the psychiatric disturbance, including administration and monitoring of medication that could have been arranged without the need for continued acute inpatient level services. It was not medically necessary for this patient to have 24-hour monitoring in view of his relative lack of impulsive behaviors, diminished symptoms of psychosis, and improvements in mood and daily functioning. There were no general medical issues or co-occurring substance use disorder complicating this case that would have required continued acute inpatient level services. Additionally, the inpatient stay during this time interval forward was not medically necessary in order to monitor the patient for at-risk behaviors, or to address the acute risk of relapse or medication non-adherence. The patient had access to services and treatment that could safely and effectively continue at a lower level of care with intensive services and a safety plan.

summary: This is a patient with bipolar affective disorder (BPAD) admitted to Inpatient Hospital Admission (IHA). Case notes document that the patient had been chronically ill with BPAD, with worsening of depression. He developed suicidal ideation with a plan to hang himself. He felt helpless and hopeless. He experienced insomnia. He had been experiencing several high stressors in his life, including the death of his mother before admission, arrest of his wife for opiate use disorder, care of his children, and loss of his job. On admission to the emergency room, he was noted to be sad, depressed, with a constricted affect, feeling hopeless and helpless. He had a history of self-cutting. He had been treated as an outpatient with Prozac, lithium, Wellbutrin, oxycodone, and Xanax. It is not known if he was compliant or not with his medications. He had a strong family history of affective disorders, including BPAD, depressive disorders, and suicides. On admission, he was treated with Wellbutrin, Lithium, Prozac, trazodone and Xanax. He also received psychotherapy and discharge planning. His psychotropic medications were adjusted according to his clinical progress. For example, Pamelor was later added. In addition, he was evaluated and treated for his multiple medical conditions. The health plan's determination is overturned. The patient was depressed, anxious, with a constricted mood, isolate, feeling hopeless and helpless, but with improved reality testing. He was deemed not safe for discharge. He was anxious, sleeping better and partially improved in depressive symptoms. He was highly stressed by his wife's imprisonment, feeling anxious, with impaired concentration and attention.  The patient suffered from a severe, chronic, life-threatening mental disorder, BPAD, with a suicidal plan. He faced overwhelming stressors including loss of his wife to prison, the care of three children and the loss of his job. Partial improvement was not an adequate standard for discharge.

This patient is a male was admitted to this inpatient substance detoxification treatment due to alcohol and opiate detoxification. He reportedly had a CIWA of 10 and had reports of withdrawal symptoms including tremors, diaphoresis, nausea, vomiting, anxiety and insomnia. He was drinking several 24 ounce beers daily and had alcohol use since adolescence. He was using cannabis and benzodiazepines. He had 2 past inpatient substance detoxification and inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment and left the rehabilitation treatment and relapsed. He was homeless. He was put on an Ativan taper and Methadone maintenance; he was discharged.

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient substance detoxification treatment. This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient substance detoxification treatment as the chart notes did provide enough specific evidence to support that he needed this level of care. The APA Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. In this case this patient had been drinking large amounts daily including drinking 8-10 24 ounce beers daily. 

According to the LOCADTR he did require 24 hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated in the outpatient detoxification setting as he continued to use alcohol daily despite reports that he failed previous outpatient treatment for recovery and 2 past inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatments including leaving a rehabilitation treatment and then relapsing so he needed more inpatient substance detoxification treatment then. He also required and needed detoxification medications including an Ativan taper and protocol then to modify withdrawal and needed 24 hour treatment then as he was at risk for worsened withdrawal symptoms including severe, complicated or life threatening withdrawal if not in this 24 hour setting then. He also took Methadone for maintenance to prevent a relapse with heroin as he had a history of past use months prior to admission.

He likely would have relapsed again as evidenced by relapsing after past treatments including 24 hour treatment. Also, he was reportedly homeless and lacked sober supports.  It was unlikely that he would remain abstinent while having withdrawal symptoms so he required the admission and remaining time in this treatment setting to stop withdrawals and prevent more serious withdrawal including possible life threatening withdrawal and decrease the chance that he would relapse again when not in this 24 hour setting.  The risk of life complicated withdrawal such as delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use so he required the entire time.

Continued inpatient substance detoxification was medically necessary. It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably or in the best interests of the patient then.  

Based on the above, the medical necessity for the inpatient detoxification admission is substantiated.  The insurer's denial is reversed.

From notes toward the end of his admission, it appears that some degree of confusion was present during baseline functioning. He also received psycho-education about his medications and risk management strategies for falls.

The health plan's determination is overturned. The inpatient level of care was medically necessary for this patient. The dates of service (DOS) at the IMHL of care were medically necessary through discharge. The patient was unable to answer questions adequately, was anxious, ruminated, appeared confused, with impaired memory, and was disorganized. Days of service at the IMHL through the remaining hospital days were examined. 
Two points need to be addressed: First, he did not show a continuing improvement in crucial areas necessary for functioning in a group home up until discharge. This means he had not attained a baseline before this time. So, there is no evidence that he was kept after he had reached a baseline. Secondly, for him to function in a group home, he needed to be able to interact with staff and act is a less impaired way than when he was admitted. This was gradually achieved during hospitalization. The mild anxiety he had at discharge was either a baseline mood or could be addressed as an outpatient. Discharge before the date would have a high likelihood of resulting in rehospitalization or harm to himself by neglect and poor functioning.

He had a decline in functioning and marital problems though he maintained his employment. He reported co-occurring depression and anxiety in the past that was treated off and on. There was no history of suicidal behavior or psychiatric hospitalization. He had no prior substance use disorder treatment and reported no periods of sobriety. Evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination that was free of severe psychiatric symptoms. He was cooperative and superficially motivated for treatment. He displayed anxiety and euthymic mood and a full range of affect with fluent, articulate speech. There was no evidence for psychosis, thought disorder, cognitive impairment or perceptual disturbance. He denied suicidal or homicidal ideation and had no aggressive impulses. He displayed anxiety and dysphoria. He reported sleep disturbance. He had support from family (sibling), but reported anxiety and stress related to his spouse. His insight and judgment were characterized as limited and impaired with poor control of impulses. The patient received detoxification and slow engagement with residential rehabilitation treatment that included focus on coping skills, relapse prevention techniques with identification of triggers, education about the disease model of addiction, and involvement with 12-step recovery groups as well as family-focused sessions. The patient was judged to be in the precontemplative stage of change and received treatment with intensive services, sober housing, monitoring, and structure provided within the residential treatment program. He struggled to engage with treatment due to cravings and ongoing stress related to the marriage with affective disturbance/anxiety and insomnia treated with supportive measures and trazodone.The patient he continued to struggle with post-acute withdrawal symptoms and craving. He was prescribed vitamin replacement therapy and supplements. The patient had no complications of rehabilitation treatment, nor did general medical problems emerge. He participated in the rehabilitation program with full participation and became increasingly motivated, gaining insight and additional knowledge of a recovery process. He was committed to continued involvement with 12-step recovery groups with sober supports. His sibling/family participated in focused sessions near the end of his residential stay including focus on the development of sober supports and an aftercare plan.
During his stay, the patient was considered at high risk for relapse due to the limited supports and lack of a reasonable recovery environment. His discharge diagnosis was severe alcohol use disorder and he had been diagnosed with an unspecified anxiety disorder during his stay with resolution of the symptoms of anxiety and continued use of trazodone to address his insomnia. The health plan's determination is overturned. The patient was considered at high risk for relapse due to the limited supports and lack of a reasonable recovery environment. The patient's lack of insight and coping skills as well as co-morbid psychiatric condition are factors that support the continued necessity for residential level services through discharge. The need for continued treatment with sober supports and family-focused therapy to address the issues within the family constellation are other factors that support the necessity for continued residential level services and the requested benefit through discharge. The patient could not have been effectively treated at a lower level of care during the time interval under review in keeping with prevailing standards of medical practice, American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and the Scientific Literature, referenced below. Based upon the diagnoses, mental status and clinical course, the patient did warrant the continued structure and monitoring and intensity of services provided by the residential program through discharge. The residential level rehabilitation treatment provided was reasonable, in the best interest of the patient, and was provided with sound medical judgment in keeping with evidence-based and empirical based practice. The patient's lack of insight and coping skills, the need for family-focused sessions to develop sober supports, as well as co-morbid psychiatric condition with unspecified anxiety, are other factors that support the necessity for continued residential level services through discharge. The need for an appropriate and safe disposition is another factor that supports the necessity for continued residential level services and the requested benefit through discharge.

The question is whether dates of service (DOS) at the Inpatient Hospital Level (IHL) are medically necessary, Case notes document that the patient suffers from chronic psychiatric symptoms with the most recent exacerbation leading to emergency department evaluation and discharge. The recent exacerbation began two to three weeks prior to admission. The patient was referred to the emergency department (ED) for overwhelming anxiety, suicidal ideation with a plan, and auditory hallucinations as well as paranoia. The patient was then admitted to the IHL. The treatment included psychopharmacological medications of Abilify, Celexa, Neurontin, and Klonopin. Her risperidone was discontinued. Additionally, the patient received psychotherapy and discharge planning.

The health plan's determination is upheld. Case notes documented that while the patient was experiencing anxiety, the patient had no delusions or hallucinations, was not suicidal, and had organized reality-based thoughts. The patient was cooperative with the health care team and showed good insight and judgment. The patient could therefore be discharged to a lower level of care. The patient no longer required an inpatient level of care on the dates in question.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
 
Treatment: Inpatient Admission

The insurer denied the Inpatient Admission. The denial was reversed.  

This is a female patient who presented to a rehabilitation facility for detoxification treatment. Her presenting withdrawal symptoms included chills, cravings, headache, lethargy, tremors, sweats, nausea, vomiting, body aches, increased heart rate, restlessness, irritability, anxiety, fatigue, and depressed mood. The patient reported that she had a history of opioid abuse and traumatic brain injury, depression, self-injury behavior; cutting herself. Her initial Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) for Alcohol Scale scores were: 6 and 13 and at the time of discharge it was a 4. She was placed on Methadone protocol. While at rehabilitation she attended individual and group therapy. The patient was safely discharged after completing her detoxification. 

The APA Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. This was the case with this patient. 

According to the LOCADTR she did require 24 hour treatment throughout her admission as she needed and received detoxification medication of Methadone to modify withdrawal and prevent severe withdrawal. She had continued withdrawal symptoms during the denial period including chills, cravings, headache, lethargy, tremors, sweats, nausea, vomiting, body aches, increased heart rate, concentration problems, restlessness, irritable mood, anxiety, fatigue, and depressed mood.

Based on the above, the medical necessity for medically supervised inpatient withdrawal and stabilization services is substantiated. The insurer's denial is reversed.

1) The APA Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders

2) LOCADTR

summary:
Diagnosis: Depression and suicidal plans

Treatment: inpatient mental health residential treatment. 

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient mental health residential treatment. The denial was reversed.

This patient is a female child who was admitted to this inpatient mental health residential treatment after two recent psychiatric hospitalizations for depression and suicidal plans. It was reported that she was psychiatrically hospitalized in mid- 2018 and again several weeks later. It was reported that her depression worsened, including an inability to get out of bed and not eating or showering. She had multiple suicidal plans, including overdose and strangling herself and had recent text messages to an ex-girlfriend about a plan for suicide with a knife. She was not able to contract for safety then. It was recommended upon discharge from her last psychiatric hospitalization that she attend a supervised and structured therapeutic inpatient mental health residential treatment to try to improve coping and problems solving skills, better deal with regulating her emotions and not acting out her negative emotions and depression in a self-destructive way. She had past reports of self-injurious behavior, including cutting herself. She reported social anxiety, isolation and loneliness and was feeling overwhelmed. She had diagnoses of Major Depressive Disorder and Borderline Personality Disorder. She attended individual, group and family therapy and was discharged.

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient mental health residential treatment as not medically necessary treatment. They stated that she did not require 24-hour treatment then, and they recommended a less restrictive level of care.

This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient mental health residential treatment as the chart notes provided enough specific evidence to support that she required this 24-hour supervised and structured therapeutic inpatient mental health residential treatment. The American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry's Practice Parameter for the Assessment and Treatment of Children and Adolescents with Depressive Disorders provides that the decision for level of care will depend primarily on level of function and safety to self and others. 

In this case, this patient was considered to be a potential danger to self if not in a 24-hour supervised and structured therapeutic inpatient mental health residential treatment, as she had two recent psychiatric hospitalizations for worsened depression with multiple suicidal plans; therefore, she was considered a high risk patient. She had poor coping and problem solving skills and difficulty regulating her emotions. It was reported that she needed this supervised and structured therapeutic inpatient mental health residential treatment to try to learn better coping and problem solving skills and healthy strategies when dealing with negative emotions, so as not to internalize them resulting in depression with suicidal plans. Other goals included learning how to better deal with frustrations, verbalize feelings, increase awareness of family dynamics, identify maladaptive control patterns, and increase her sense of capability and responsibility.

The insurer did not act reasonably, or with sound medical judgment, or in the best interests of the patient.
	
Based on the above, the medical necessity for the mental health residential treatment services is substantiated.  The insurer's denial is reversed.

summary:
The patient is a male who presented for inpatient detoxification treatment in order to address severe substance use disorder with opioid (heroin) class substance of abuse. The patient has participated in a medication assisted treatment (MAT) program with Suboxone in the past without benefit or sustained sobriety; he indicated that he wanted detoxification treatment for his use of heroin with up to two bundles used daily with intranasal administration (snorting). He has an 18 year history of opioid use with limited treatment episodes and serious legal issues that resulted in a decline in functioning and incarceration for various offenses beginning at an early age.

The patient was admitted to detoxification treatment with a comprehensive detoxification protocol with a methadone taper, and as needed (prn) medications for comfort including medication to address pain and aches, anxiety and insomnia and diarrhea/abdominal cramps. He was prescribed Lexapro and Seroquel as well as prn doses of Vistaril. The patient had persistent symptoms of withdrawal scoring a 15 on the COWS scale on hospital days two, with persistent symptoms on day three and four when his withdrawal symptoms diminished; he tolerated the taper of methadone and was able to participate in counseling and educational group sessions. The day following his last dose of methadone, the patient was immediately referred to rehabilitation treatment which had followed the use of motivational techniques by the treatment team and case manager. Again, while in detoxification treatment the patient continued to receive counseling and education and attended groups and was adherent to his medication regimen with the Seroquel and Lexapro as well as hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) that was continued to address his hypertension.
The patient completed the detoxification protocol and was discharged with referral for rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment, and with recommendations for smoking cessation, as well as recommended involvement with recovery groups and follow-up for clinically appropriate treatment of his co-occurring psychiatric disorders and primary care.

The health plan's determination is overturned, in whole. 

The continued inpatient treatment of this patient's substance use disorder with detoxification and withdrawal management did require the continued structure of an inpatient level setting and 24-hour monitoring in view of the patient's clinical presentation and course of treatment and risk factors for relapse and lack of a reasonable treatment/recovery environment. Withdrawal symptoms were appropriately managed with tapering dosages of methadone requiring monitoring and supportive measures including the availability of nicotine replacement therapy and comfort medications, as noted in the clinical summary. The patient's history of opioid use despite receiving medication assisted treatment with Suboxone, limited psychosocial supports and psychosocial stressors within several psychosocial domains did reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder. Moreover, the patient presented with co-occurring mood and anxiety disorders and recent general medical problems resulting in a surgical procedure one month prior to admission. The case was therefore complicated with co-occurring disorders and co-morbidity.
Thus, the patient did require a safe and effective detoxification treatment with Continued Inpatient Detoxification and Withdrawal Management for the time interval under review thru discharge, as it was unlikely that the patient was unable to abstain from use of heroin, or maintain abstinence if detoxification were to be attempted at a lower level of care. Moreover, using the NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines, the continued inpatient level care through discharge is supported as medically necessary with the clinically appropriate application of the LOCADTR Guidelines.

summary:
Diagnosis: Psychotic symptoms

Treatment: Inpatient mental health treatment 

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient mental health treatment. The denial was modified.

This patient is a male who was admitted to this inpatient mental health treatment due to psychotic symptoms including command auditory hallucinations suicidal in nature telling him to kill himself and stab himself. He reportedly had past suicide attempts, substance use history including cocaine and cannabis, past legal issues, past aggression/violence, and he was non-compliant with medications. He reportedly had past psychiatric hospitalizations. He had a diagnosis of Schizoaffective Disorder. He took Risperidone, Lithium, and Clozapine. He was discharged.

The insurer denied coverage for continued inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital as not medically necessary treatment. They stated that he improved and did not require 24 hour hospital treatment then, and they recommended a less restrictive level of care then.

This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for continued inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital for certain days but agrees with the decision to deny coverage for continued inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital for other specified days thereafter. 

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Schizophrenia reports that patients with hallucinations, delusional thinking, disorganized thinking or behavior, suicidal or homicidal plan or intent, agitation, or aggressive behavior, or inability to adequately care for basic needs are candidates for hospitalization. In this case this patient still had psychotic symptoms until a specific date as it was reported that he was febrile and started antibiotics and then his psychotrophic medication was stopped for 24 hours and he had reports of command auditory hallucinations telling him to bang his head. He required Haldol and Ativan IM and was on 1:1 observation. After one day of observation without further reported psychotic symptoms the day after the specified date referenced above, there was no further reported evidence that he had psychotic symptoms or required further acute psychiatric hospital treatment. It was appropriate to observe him for one day without reported symptoms in this hospital setting due to his recent serious psychotic symptoms of command auditory hallucinations to hurt self.

As of a certain date there were no further reports of significant psychotic symptoms, severe depressive symptoms, homicidal or suicidal ideation, plan or intent, and there were no reports of specific identifiable or quantifiable treatment goals or objectives that could only be achieved in a 24 hour acute psychiatric hospital setting or that could not be achieved in a less restrictive setting. As a result, the recommendation is to modify the previous decision and approve coverage for continued inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital for a few days but deny coverage for continued inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital thereafter.

Based on the above, the insurer's denial is modified. The inpatient behavioral health hospital admission for a few days was medically necessary. It was not medically necessary thereafter.
references: 1) The APA Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Schizophrenia

summary:
This is a patient who presented for detoxification and substance-related services. The patient has a history of severe substance use disorders with alcohol, opioid (heroin), stimulants (crack cocaine), and cannabis (marijuana) class substances of abuse. He has a history of prior substance use disorder treatment including detoxification treatment with relapse. The patient was using large quantities of alcohol on a continuous daily basis together with 16 grams of crack cocaine and intermittent and occasional use of heroin with intranasal administration.
At the time of presentation, the patient was requesting referral for rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment. He denied current legal issues or other external factors prompting his presentation for treatment. He was homeless and unemployed and reported severe psychosocial stressors within the primary support, social environment, occupational and housing domains. The patient reported functional decline as the substance abuse/disease had progressed which prompted his self-referral for detoxification treatment and request for rehabilitation services.
The patient provided a past history of withdrawal seizures and severe alcohol withdrawal symptoms. He was medically screened and admitted for inpatient level detoxification with plans for a four day detoxification treatment with Librium and supportive measures. Withdrawal symptoms and signs included tremor, nausea and vomiting, diaphoresis, malaise and fatigue, anxiety, and irritability, as well as insomnia. A drug screen was consistent with his history, but was positive for cannabis as well as cocaine. The patient has a history of psychiatric disorders (schizophrenia and/or bipolar disorder and anxiety disorder) and treatment including inpatient psychiatric hospitalization, but no history of overdose or suicidal or self harming behaviors.
There were no acute medical issues in this case other than the alcohol withdrawal, but the patient was medically ill with type II diabetes mellitus and chronic leg pain and dysplipidemia, as well as peripheral neuropathy. The patient was tobacco dependent.
The health plan's determination is overturned.
The patient was using large quantities of alcohol on a daily continuous basis together with other substances of abuse that did warrant the admission and the continued inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring. Moreover, the patient's social environment was not conducive to an effective detoxification, and the patient had struggled with withdrawal symptoms (tremor, nausea and vomiting, diaphoresis and malaise, anxiety, irritability, restlessness and insomnia) which were being effectively addressed with Librium and comfort medications and with supportive measures that included seizure precautions in a patient with seizure history. The patient had associated clinical features that included lack of sober supports and limited insight, impaired judgment and poor control of impulses.
Thus, the adult inpatient stay and continued detoxification treatment of this patient's substance use disorders did necessitate the admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level setting with withdrawal management and psychosocial supports, and 24-hour monitoring. The patients history of substance abuse (frequency and quantity) together with the severe psychosocial stressors and functional impairments do reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder and the need for a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management as the patient was at high risk for treatment failure or general medical complications such as seizures if detoxification and withdrawal management were to be attempted at a lower level of care.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
 
Treatment: Continued Inpatient Detoxification Services

The insurer denied the Continued Inpatient Detoxification Services. The denial was reversed. 

This is a male patient who presented to a rehabilitation facility for detoxification for multiple substances. He had withdrawal symptoms that included tremors, joint pain, sweats, runny nose, irritability, anxiety and elevated heart rate of 108. He had a Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) of 14 and a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) of 2. He has a history of drinking 1 pint of alcohol per day, using multiple bags of intravenous (IV) heroin and IV cocaine daily, smoking multiple bags of methamphetamine, smoking blunts of cannabis, and using 80 mg of Methadone. He also had a history of inpatient substance detoxification. He was treated with a Methadone protocol and was discharged to substance inpatient rehabilitation when medically indicated.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. 

According to the LOCADTR he did require 24 hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive setting as he continued to use substances despite past inpatient substance detoxification treatment and negative consequences including legal problems, and he needed two detoxification medications to modify withdrawal and prevent severe, complicated, and life threatening withdrawal as he took Librium and took Methadone. He still had withdrawal symptoms reported including tremors and anxiety and still required Methadone detoxification medication. Also, the risk of life complicated withdrawal such as delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use so he required the entire time. It also was necessary to get detoxification treatment prior to inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment and he could not successfully be detoxified in an outpatient setting.

Based on the above, the medical necessity for the continued inpatient detoxification services is substantiated. The insurer's denial is reversed.

1) The APA Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders

2) LOCADTR

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance abuse
Treatment:Continued residential rehabilitation treatment 

The requested benefit of continued residential rehabilitation treatment is not medically necessary for this patient.

The patient presented with substance use disorders with the past use of heroin and medication assisted treatment with Suboxone, with continued use of large quantities of alcohol on a daily continuous basis with decline in functioning and psychosocial consequences/stressors. He received stabilization treatment transitioning to residential level rehabilitation treatment. He readily engaged in treatment with continued use of Suboxone and medications to address mood, trauma-related and attentional disorders including medication to assist with smoking cessation. 

During the time interval under review, the patient was noted to be in no apparent distress with improved functioning and active participation in treatment including positive interactions with staff and peers. From the time period under review and forward, there were no remaining treatment issues or biomedical or co-occurring psychiatric issues that would have warranted continued residential level of care. The application of NY State OASAS LOCADTR Criteria (referenced below) did indicate that the patient was clinically appropriate for treatment with lower level care in a less restrictive treatment setting, as the health plan asserts. Thus, medical necessity for the continued residential rehabilitation treatment is not met in this case scenario consistent with ASAM Criteria, the scientific literature and published guidelines, referenced below.

The patient in this case scenario is not clinically appropriate for the continued residential level of care during the time interval under review. The patient had reached a level of stability by the time period under review that he no longer warranted residential level care and could have been effectively managed in a less restrictive treatment setting with sober supports and monitoring. He no longer needed 24-hour monitoring or the intensity of residential level treatment to address the co-occurring psychiatric disorders of remaining symptoms related to his substance use disorders. He was engaged with treatment and involved with peer supported recovery groups while continuing medication assisted treatment with Suboxone and his psychotropic medications, as noted in the clinical summary. Thus, the health plan's determination is reasonable in this case scenario. This answer is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice for the conditions diagnosed and under treatment in this case, and entirely consistent with the NY State instruction and OASAS LOCADTR Guidelines applicable in this case.

summary:
This is a patient who was admitted for acute inpatient psychiatric services due to an overdose of his pain medications together with alcohol in the context of worsening symptoms of depression. He was in treatment for depressive disorder in the context of substance abuse with alcohol and general medical problems that included chronic pain associated with multiple surgical procedures and past injuries. He has a history of multiple psychiatric hospitalizations and emergency department visits for depression and general medical concerns and had recently been discharged from hospital level treatment. The patient was stabilized in the emergency department and medically cleared prior to his admission for acute inpatient psychiatric services. He had persistent complaints of pain in the context of overuse of his oxycodone. His alcohol use had escalated that contributed to his depression and hopelessness.
The patient has a history of alcohol use disorder with prescribed opioids, as noted. There was no other use of substances of abuse though he was tobacco dependent.
The health plan's determination is upheld. The patient was medically stabilized prior to his admission for psychiatric care. He did not present with acute general medical complications, or severe withdrawal symptoms or complications of co-occurring alcohol use disorder. Following admission, the patient had been treated for the mood disturbance and associated symptoms of anxiety/insomnia and functional impairments with improvement in symptoms and functioning; he did not require continued acute inpatient level structure or monitoring during the time interval under review. There was no further risk for suicidal behavior or documented symptoms that would have warranted continued assessment, safety monitoring and treatment in an acute inpatient setting.

summary:
Other
Inpatient Mental Health 
The patient is a woman with a diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder (SCZAD). Case notes document that the patient was experiencing auditory hallucinations (AH) for about two weeks prior to admission. She received an intramuscular (IM) dose of Haldol from her outpatient provider and was started on lithium. Despite the outpatient treatment, she continued to experience AH as well as depressed mood, insomnia, self-talk, low energy, and dysphoria. She went to the emergency room in distress and was admitted. She had required at least two prior psychiatric admissions due to her SCZAD, with at least one admission due to cannabis use disorder (CUD). The patient's illness under review apparently began 2 weeks prior when she again smoked Cannabis which precipitated her AH. Her treatment included increasing doses of Haldol as well as lithium. At one point in her treatment, she was given trazodone for sleep. In addition, she was treated with psychotherapy and milieu management.

Diagnosis: Suicidal thoughts, plans, intent, and attempts

Treatment: Continued inpatient mental health treatment. 

The insurer denied coverage for continued inpatient mental health treatment. The denial was upheld.

This patient is a male was admitted to this inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital due to; suicidal thoughts, plans, intent, and attempts as it was reported that he had a suicide attempt the night prior to admission by taking an overdose of his girlfriend's blood pressure medications and tried to stab himself in the throat with a knife five days prior to this admission. He had depressed and irritable mood, poor impulse control, sleeping problems, paranoia, visual hallucinations, and outbursts. He had a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder. He was prescribed the following medication: Lexapro, Remeron, and Zyprexa. He was discharged.

The insurer denied coverage for continued inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital as not medically necessary treatments. They stated that he did not require 24 hour hospital treatment, and they recommended a less restrictive level of care.

This reviewer agrees with the decision to deny coverage for continued inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital as the medical records did not provide enough specific evidence to support that he still only required this acute psychiatric hospital level of care or that he could not be safely and effectively treated in a less restrictive level of care. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Major Depressive Disorders indicates that the least restrictive level of care for safe and effective treatment is appropriate and that patients with suicidal plan or intent or behaviors, or inability to adequately care for basic needs are candidates for inpatient level of treatment.

He reportedly had suicidal thoughts, plans, intent, and attempts prior to admission and required and received 24 hour acute psychiatric hospital treatment. However, the medical records for a specified service date did not report further suicidal ideation, intent, plan, or behavior. The notes on a specified date reported that he denied suicidal ideation, was eating and sleeping better, and stated that if he were to have suicidal thoughts or worsened depression that he would tell someone.  The notes reported that he was calm and compliant, withdrawn, guarded, with poverty of speech, but denied suicidal or homicidal ideation, plan, or intent, or hallucinations. The notes reported that he no longer was endorsing suicidal ideation.  He was discharged.  

As of a specified date there were no reports of suicidal or homicidal ideation, intent, or plan, inability to adequately care for basic needs, manic episodes, psychotic symptoms, self-injurious, aggressive, threatening, or agitated behavior. As of a specified date the chart notes did not provide specific evidence that he was an imminent danger to self or others or unable to adequately care for his basic needs. Also, there were no reports of specific identifiable or quantifiable treatment goals or objectives that could only be achieved in a 24 hour acute psychiatric hospital setting or that could not be achieved in a less restrictive setting.  

As a result, the determination is to uphold the previous decision and deny coverage for inpatient mental health treatment at this hospital. It appeared that the health care plan acted reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interests of the patient.

Based on the above information, the medical necessity for the continued inpatient admission is not substantiated.  The insurer's denial is upheld.

This is a male patient who presented to a detoxification facility for inpatient alcohol and substance detoxification treatment. He had a history of drinking 1-2 pints of alcohol a day, intravenous heroin 3-6 times per week, and smoking hundreds of dollars worth of crack daily. He had a positive toxicology screening for cocaine, benzodiazepines, and THC. It was reported that he had past inpatient detoxification and rehabilitation treatments, and that his longest sobriety had been 8 months. His withdrawal symptoms include body aches, headache, strong urges and cravings, and lethargy. For the first several days of treatment his CIWA score ranged from 12 down to 11. He was put on a Librium protocol and left against medical advice (AMA) several days after his admission. 
According to the LOCADTR he did require 24 hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated in outpatient detoxification settings as he continued to use multiple serious substances daily. He had past inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatments, and he also required and needed detoxification medication, including Librium, to modify withdrawal. Furthermore, he needed 24 hour treatment at the time because he was at risk for worsened withdrawal symptoms including severe, complicated, and life threatening withdrawal. He was at high risk for overdose and reportedly had a near overdose 2 weeks prior to admission, so at the time he required this 24 hour inpatient detoxification setting. 

The risk of life complicated withdrawal such as delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use, so he required the entire time including the first 4 days in this inpatient detoxification setting, even as he was discharged on the 5th day. Also, he likely would have relapsed again as evidenced by relapsing after past treatments. So it was not likely that he could safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in an outpatient setting. It was unlikely that he would remain abstinent while having withdrawal symptoms, which he still had. He continued to use alcohol and substances despite negative consequences including losing jobs and relationships and past legal problems. He also had medical issues. 

Based on the above, the medical necessity for the inpatient substance abuse services is substantiated.  The insurer's denial is reversed.
