summary:
This is a patient who presented for inpatient detoxification treatment to address severe substance use disorder with opioid and stimulant (Cocaine) class substances of abuse. The patient has a longstanding history of cocaine use with subsequent use of heroin. He reported a past history of severe withdrawal symptoms when attempting to curtail his use, and his substance use was interfering with his ability to work and take care of his family. He was using heroin with up to two bundles/twenty bags daily with intravenous (IV) administration together with $100 worth of cocaine also administered IV. Thus, he presented for detoxification treatment in the context of severe opioid and stimulant use disorders.
The patient has no history of a psychiatric disorder or treatment. He has no acute comorbid general medical issues other than a history of hepatitis C and cellulitis of the hand treated with antibiotics. His drug screen was positive and consistent with his history, but also included positivity for oxy (prescription opiates) which he denied using. He was medically screened and cleared for detoxification treatment including laboratory assessments that were negative or unremarkable.
The patient is high school educated with a vocational degree and employed, and lives with his family with three young children. There were no legal issues in this case.
Evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination that was free of severe psychiatric symptoms except for symptoms of anxiety and irritability associated with opioid withdrawal that included headache, nausea, and joint pain together with anxiety, irritability and insomnia reflecting mild withdrawal symptoms, and scoring a 10 on the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) and 9 on the Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) scales. He was generally motivated for treatment and described as cooperative with speech that was clear and organized thoughts that were free of delusions. There was no evidence for a thought disorder or cognitive impairment. The patient denied suicidal or homicidal ideation. Insight was limited with impaired judgment and poor control of impulses due to the addiction to heroin and cocaine.
The patient was admitted to detoxification treatment with comprehensive detoxification protocol with a five day methadone taper, and as needed (PRN) medications for comfort including medication to address pain and aches, anxiety and insomnia and nausea. The patient initially had mild symptoms of withdrawal that diminished in intensity but persisted throughout his inpatient stay until the last day when he felt better. While in detoxification treatment, the patient received counseling and education and attended groups, and received motivational enhancement therapy to encourage him to proceed to rehabilitation treatment.
The patient almost completed the detoxification protocol and was discharged against medical advice with referral for outpatient program (IOP) level substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment and recommendation for medication assisted treatment for the opioid use disorder, as well as recommended involvement with self-help recovery groups. He was discharged to home with family with plans to return to work.
The health plan's determination is overturned.
The treatment of this patient's substance use disorder did require the structure of an inpatient level setting and 24-hour monitoring in view of the patient's clinical presentation and course of treatment. Withdrawal symptoms were appropriately managed with tapering dosages of methadone requiring monitoring and supportive measures including the availability of comfort medications, as noted in the clinical summary.
The patient's history of opioid use and use of cocaine with daily use with IV administration, limited psychosocial supports and psychosocial stressors within several domains did reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder and a complicated case with regard to the ongoing struggle with achieving abstinence from opioid and cocaine use.
Thus, the patient did require the requested services, as it was foreseeable that the patient was unable to abstain from use of opioid or cocaine, or maintain abstinence if detoxification were to be attempted at a lower level of care. Moreover, the application of NY State OASAS LOCADTR 3.0 Criteria did warrant the admission and did also warrant the continued inpatient level care through discharge.

summary:
Diagnosis:  Alcohol abuse/addiction.
Treatment:  Mental Health Residential Treatment.
The insurer denied the residential mental health treatment.  The denial was overturned.  

The patient presented for residential substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment to address severe alcohol use disorder.  The patient was not using other substances of abuse; she had no past history of withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens, or severe withdrawal symptoms, but she did report frequent blackouts in the context of alcohol use.  Her alcohol use had increased with more recent use of up to one-half water bottle of vodka daily including use while working.  She had a decline in functioning and family problems related to the alcohol use.  She was in treatment for co-occurring generalized anxiety and depressive disorders.  There was no history of suicidal behavior or psychiatric hospitalization.  She had prior substance use disorder treatment and had failed to remain abstinent while in outpatient treatment, including involvement in peer-supported recovery groups.

Evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination that was free of severe psychiatric symptoms.  She was fidgety and cooperative and superficially motivated for treatment in the contemplative stage of change.  She displayed mood disturbance with affective lability and with anxiety, as well as hopelessness, shame and guilt.  She had soft spoken speech and circumstantial and tangential thought processing with racing thoughts.  There was no evidence for psychosis, thought disorder, severe cognitive impairment or perceptual disturbance.  She denied suicidal or homicidal ideation, and she had no aggressive impulses.  She reported sleep disturbance.  She had support from family, but reported anxiety and stress related to her family, especially in her relationship with her mother.  Her insight and judgment were characterized as limited and impaired with poor control of impulses.

The patient had no acute general medical conditions, and had chronic medical conditions that included a history of traumatic brain injury, polycystic ovary disease, obesity and type II diabetes mellitus, and her laboratory assessment showed elevated liver enzymes and dyslipidemia.  Urine drug screen was consistent with history.

The patient is single, college educated, and employed with job stress.  The patient lives alone.  Stressors included primary support, occupational, and social environment domains, as well as other psychosocial stressors associated with the alcohol use disorder and her general medical problems.

The patient received residential rehabilitation treatment that included focus on coping skills, relapse prevention techniques with identification of triggers, education about the disease model of addiction, and involvement with 12-step recovery groups, as well as family-focused sessions.  The patient engaged in treatment with intensive services, sober housing, monitoring, and structure provided within the residential treatment program.  She struggled to engage with treatment due to cravings and ongoing stress related to the family and to her affective disturbance/anxiety and insomnia.

She continued to struggle with craving addressed with anxiolytic medications and naltrexone and topiramate.  She was placed on a regimen of as needed (PRN) Seroquel and melatonin and trazodone, as well as vitamin and nicotine replacement therapy and supplements.  The patient had no complications of rehabilitation treatment, nor did general medical problems emerge.  She engaged with the rehabilitation program with full participation and became increasingly motivated, gaining insight and additional knowledge of a recovery process.  She was committed to continued involvement with 12-step and Self-Management and Recovery Training (SMART) recovery groups with sober supports.  Her family participated in family focused sessions near the end of her residential stay including focus on the development of sober supports.  During her stay, the patient was considered at high risk for relapse; the risk diminished near the time of discharge, though she continued to display anxiety and dysphoric mood with insomnia.  She was stepped down to lower level services with plans for continued rehabilitation treatment, family-focused therapy, and continued involvement with recovery groups including the obtainment of a sponsor.  Her anxiolytic/antidepressant medications were continued, as well as naltrexone and topirimate for anti-craving.  At issue is the medical necessity of the residential treatment.

The health plan's determination is overturned.

The patient's severity of alcohol use disorder, risk of relapse, and lack of sober supports do support the medical necessity for an admission and continued treatment at the residential level of care.  The patient could not have been effectively treated at a lower level of care during the time interval under review in keeping with prevailing standards of medical practice, American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and the Scientific Literature, referenced below.

The need for a disposition to intensive outpatient rehabilitation and mental health treatment with sober supports are other factors that support the necessity for continued residential level services toward the end of her residential stay, and these factors and treatment dimensions support the requested benefit through discharge in order to effect a safe and appropriate disposition.

The patient's severity of substance use disorder, risk of relapse, and lack of sober supports do support the medical necessity for an admission and continued treatment at the acute residential level of care.  The patient could not have been effectively treated at a lower level of care during the time interval under review and does meet medical necessity for the continued residential level services in keeping with prevailing standards of medical practice, ASAM Criteria, and the Scientific Literature, referenced below. Treatment:  Residential Substance Use Treatment.

The insurer denied coverage for Residential Substance Use Treatment.  The denial is overturned.

This is a male patient, who was admitted for inpatient substance residential treatment for 24-hour therapeutic inpatient treatment, due to his significant alcohol, heroin, and cocaine use.  The patient reportedly was drinking 12 beers per day, using 4-5 bags of intravenous (IV) heroin per day, and smoking 2-3 grams of cocaine per day.  The patient reportedly had past legal issues and jail time.  The patient also had marital discord.  The patient reported having 9-10 inpatient detoxification or rehabilitation treatments in the past.  His longest reported recent abstinence was 16 months.  The patient also had medical conditions, such as hepatitis C viral infection, and lacked coping skills for recovery.  The patient was in a recent inpatient substance setting and was then admitted for this 24-hour alcohol and substance rehabilitation treatment.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that residential treatment is indicated primarily for individuals who do not meet clinical criteria for hospitalization but whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting.  Residential facilities provide a safe and substance-free environment in which residents learn individual and group living skills for preventing relapse.  

In this case, this patient was considered in need of 24-hour residential treatment then with his recent relapse after receiving 9-10 inpatient substance treatments in the past.  The patient was at a high risk for overdose and life-threatening withdrawal symptoms with his polysubstance use.  According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), the patient met criteria for inpatient substance residential rehabilitation treatment, as he continued to use multiple serious substances of use despite multiple past inpatient substance treatments and despite negative consequences of substance use including legal problems and past jail time, medical consequences to use including hepatitis C, and marital discord.  The patient reportedly did not have the ability to make behavioral changes with the reported structure and supervision of this residential treatment.  The patient also had a history of past victimization issues.  The patient's clinical presentation required more than the one week in his previous inpatient setting to learn better coping skills, identification of relapse triggers, work on relapse prevention skills, improving impulse control and decision making, and increase sober supports.  Considering this patient's past substance history and current use of multiple substances despite legal, health and marital issues, inpatient substance residential treatment was medically necessary for this patient's safety and to provide effective treatment care.

The health plan did not act reasonably, with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient.

The carrier's denial of coverage for Residential Substance Use Treatment should be overturned.  The medical necessity is substantiated.

The patient is an adult male who presented for residential substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment to address severe opioid, stimulant (cocaine and Adderall), alcohol, and cannabis use disorders, as well as intermittent use of non-prescribed benzodiazepines. The patient had no past history of withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens, or severe withdrawal symptoms, but did report frequent blackouts in the context of alcohol use with a binge pattern of use together with other substances. His substance use began in adolescence and had increased with more recent use resulting in family conflict and other psychosocial consequences; he had a decline in functioning and family problems related to the substance use. He was in treatment for co-occurring generalized anxiety and depressive disorders. There was no history of suicidal or self-harming behavior, but his substance use did result in high risk behaviors due to intoxication and blackouts. He had prior substance use disorder treatment and had failed to complete treatment or remain abstinent.
Evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination that was free of severe psychiatric symptoms. He was fidgety/restless and cooperative and superficially motivated for treatment in the contemplative or pre-contemplative stage of change. He displayed mood disturbance with affective lability and anxiety. He had soft spoken speech and circumstantial and tangential thought processing with racing thoughts. There was no evidence for psychosis, thought disorder, severe cognitive impairment or perceptual disturbance. He denied suicidal or homicidal ideation, and he had no aggressive impulses. He reported sleep disturbance. He had support from family, but reported anxiety and stress related to his family. His insight and judgment were characterized as limited and impaired with poor control of impulses.
The patient had no acute general medical conditions, and an electrocardiogram (EKG) and laboratory assessment were unremarkable or normal. A urine drug screen was consistent with the history.
The patient received residential rehabilitation treatment that included focus on coping skills, relapse prevention techniques with identification of triggers, education about the disease model of addiction, and involvement with 12-step recovery groups as well as family-focused sessions. The patient engaged in treatment with intensive services, sober housing, monitoring, and structure provided within the residential treatment program. He struggled to engage with treatment due to cravings and ongoing stress related to the family and to his affective disturbance/anxiety and insomnia.
He continued to struggle with craving and post-acute withdrawal symptoms that were addressed with anxiolytic medications. He was placed on a regimen of venlafaxine, Seroquel and melatonin and trazodone, as well as vitamin replacement therapy and supplements. The patient had no complications of rehabilitation treatment, nor did general medical problems emerge. He gradually engaged with the rehabilitation program with full participation and became increasingly motivated, gaining insight and additional knowledge of a recovery process. She was committed to continued involvement with recovery groups and effort to develop sober supports. During his stay, the patient was considered at high risk for relapse; the risk diminished near the time of discharge/step down though he continued to display anxiety and dysphoric mood with insomnia and Post-Acute Withdrawal Syndrome (PAWS). He was stepped down to lower level services with plans for continued rehabilitation treatment, family-focused therapy, and continued involvement with recovery groups including the obtainment of a sponsor. 
The issue under review is the medical necessity of residential substance use disorder treatment.

The requested services are medically necessary for this patient.

The need for a disposition to intensive day rehabilitation and mental health treatment with sober supports are other factors that support the necessity for continued residential level services toward the end of his residential stay. These factors and treatment dimensions support the requested benefit through discharge in order to effect a safe and appropriate disposition.
The patient could not have been effectively treated at a lower level of care during the time interval under review, and does meet medical necessity for the residential level services in keeping with prevailing standards of medical practice, ASAM Criteria, and the Scientific Literature, referenced below.
The patient's lack of insight and coping skills as well as co-morbid psychiatric conditions are factors that warranted the admission and the continued necessity for residential level services through discharge/step down. The need for a disposition with sober supports and family-focused therapy to address the issues within the family constellation are other factors that support the necessity for continued residential level services and the requested benefit through discharge with step down for continued services.

This is a male patient with a history of schizophrenia and depression. He was admitted to the hospital for inpatient management of his alcohol withdrawal symptoms that included abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, tremors, chills, and headache. He had a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) for an Alcohol score of 11. The patient reported drinking 2 pints of vodka per day. The patient's medical treatment included intravenous fluids, a proton pump inhibitor, Serax taper, and Ativan.  It was noted that the patient had severe pruritus due to lice/scabies. He was consulted by Dermatology and empirically treated for lice and scabies with whole-body permethrin. It was also reported that the patient had alcohol-induced thrombocytopenia. The patient was stabilized and discharged. 

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders report that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment.  It also states that patients with past complicated or life-threatening withdrawal symptoms, including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens, are in need of inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal and reports that patients with a comorbid medical condition that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification. In this case, this patient could not have been safely treated in a less restrictive detoxification treatment level of care as he was at risk for severe, complicated, and life-threatening withdrawal due to his large amount of daily alcohol use. The patient also had comorbid medical issues, such as colitis and alcohol-induced thrombocytopenia that could complicate the management of his alcohol withdrawal.

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), the patient required 24-hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated in an outpatient detoxification settings as he continued to use large amounts of alcohol despite medical issues. He required and needed detoxification medication to modify his withdrawal symptoms and to prevent more severe withdrawal symptoms. Also, at the time of hospital presentation, the patient had active withdrawal symptoms that included nausea and vomiting, tremors, chills, headache, and a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment of Alcohol (CIWA) score of 11. The patient required as needed Ativan and a Serax 4-day taper to treat his alcohol withdrawal and detoxification needs.  The patient needed to be in the inpatient hospital setting for detoxification treatment as he was at risk for life-threatening withdrawal.  Studies indicate that the risk of life complicated withdrawal such as delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use, so this patient required inpatient detoxification protocol treatment.  

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. 

The carrier's denial of coverage for the inpatient hospital admission should be overturned.  The medical necessity is substantiated.

The patient was admitted for alcohol intoxication and withdrawal. However, patients who exhibit suicidal or homicidal ideation, plans, or intent require close assessment and monitoring and inpatient treatment is generally indicated for patients who are considered to pose a serious threat of harm to themselves or others.

This is a male patient who was admitted for inpatient detoxification treatment. His withdrawal symptoms included tremors, nausea, vomiting, agitation, anxiety, sleeping problems, headache, and irritable mood. He was reportedly drinking 1 pint of alcohol, smoking crack/cocaine, and smoking cannabis daily. The patient reportedly had multiple past inpatient substance detoxification treatments including a recent one in which he relapsed on the day of discharge. He also had comorbid bipolar disorder. The patient's Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) for Alcohol score on admission was 13. He was admitted and treated via a Librium taper protocol. He was stabilized and discharged to aftercare rehabilitation program on day 5 of admission.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. In this case, this patient had active withdrawal symptoms on admission including a CIWA for Alcohol score of 13 and he continued to have withdrawal symptoms during the inpatient course. 

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), the patient required 24-hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated in an outpatient detoxification setting as he continued to use alcohol daily as well as crack/cocaine and cannabis despite reports that he had multiple previous inpatient substance detoxification treatments and still relapsed (i.e. the day of discharge after his last admission for detoxification). The patient also required and needed detoxification medication to modify his withdrawal symptoms, and needed 24-hour treatment and monitoring as he was at risk for complicated and life-threatening withdrawal with his heavy polysubstance use. Notes on admission reported that the patient's CIWA for Alcohol score was 13 with withdrawal symptoms including tremors, nausea, vomiting, agitation, anxiety, sleeping problems, headache, and irritable mood, for which the patient was put on a Librium taper. In addition to withdrawal symptoms, the patient had a comorbid diagnosis of bipolar disorder. It was unlikely that the patient would remain abstinent while still having withdrawal symptoms. Thus, the patient required the time in this inpatient detoxification treatment setting to treat his withdrawal symptoms and decrease the chance of relapse again. The risk of life complicated withdrawal such as delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use so this patient required the entire admission course.

The inpatient substance detoxification was medically necessary for this patient.

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. 

Based on the above, the medical necessity for the inpatient hospital admission is substantiated. The insurer's denial should be overturned.

summary:
Diagnosis:  Substance Use.
Treatment:  Inpatient admission.

The insurer denied coverage for the inpatient admission.  The denial is overturned. 

This is a male patient who was admitted for inpatient substance detoxification. The patient reportedly had withdrawal symptoms including tremors, anxiety, sleeping problems, and had a systolic blood pressure of 138.  The patient reported drinking alcohol daily, smoking crack/cocaine daily, and using 2 bags per day 1-2 times per week of marijuana/hashish.  The patient's history was significant for multiple past inpatient substance detoxification treatments.  In this case, the patient was admitted for inpatient substance detoxification and was put on a Librium protocol and received Librium.  He was discharged to a substance inpatient rehabilitation treatment.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment.  It also states that patients with past complicated or life threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens are in need of inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal and reports that patients with comorbid medical conditions that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification.  Also, the United States Department of Health and Human Services-Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) Center for Substance Abuse Treatment reports that inpatient treatment is necessary if the ability to attend outpatient treatment daily is a problem, one is unable to follow-up in outpatient treatment, if medical conditions complicate the treatment of withdrawal, if one has previous withdrawal seizures of delirium tremens, or if one does not have the capacity for informed consent.  In this case, this patient could not safely be treated in a less restrictive setting than an inpatient medical hospital detoxification treatment, as he reportedly was at risk for severe, complicated, and life threatening withdrawal if not in this setting.  

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), the patient required 24-hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive setting, as he continued to use large amounts of alcohol and crack/cocaine almost daily, and cannabis/hashish despite multiple past inpatient substance detoxification and inpatient substance rehabilitation treatments including past inpatient substance detoxification treatments.  Also, the patient required and received detoxification medication, Librium protocol to modify his withdrawal, and he had active reported withdrawal symptoms on admission including tremors, anxiety, sleeping problems, and had a systolic blood pressure of 138.  The patient needed 24-hour treatment then, as he was at risk for worsened withdrawal symptoms if not in this 24-hour setting, including more severe, complicated, and even possible life threatening withdrawal such as delirium tremens.  The risk of delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use, so this patient was considered at risk for this.  The patient also was considered at risk medically, due to his large use of crack/cocaine with alcohol use.  It would have been unsafe to treat this patient at a less restrictive level of care. 

The inpatient admission was medically necessary for this patient.  The health plan did not act reasonably, with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient.

The carrier's denial of coverage for the inpatient admission should be overturned.  The medical necessity is substantiated.

This is a male patient who was admitted for substance intensive, outpatient program treatment after an inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment. He reportedly had severe opioid and severe alcohol use disorder. He attended 3 days per week of intensive outpatient program treatment and attended 32 sessions, after which he was referred to substance outpatient program treatment.

According to the American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders , intensive outpatient programs provide an intensive, structured treatment experience for individuals with substance use disorders who require more services than those generally available in traditional outpatient settings. These programs are sometimes used as step-down programs for individuals leaving hospital or residential settings who are at a high risk of relapsing because of: problems with motivation, the presence of frequent cravings or urges to use a substance, poor social supports, immediate environmental cues for relapse and/or availability of substances, and co-occurring medical and/or psychiatric disorders. The goal of such a step-down approach is to stabilize patients by retaining them in treatment and providing more extended intensive outpatient monitoring of relapse potential and co-occurring disorders. The aim is to prepare the individual for transition to less intensive outpatient services and increased self-reliance through the practice and mastery of relapse prevention skills and the active use of self-help programs. The National Institute on Drug Abuse: Principles of Addiction Treatment: A Research Based Guide reports that the best treatment outcomes occur with longer durations of treatment. Recovery from drug addiction is a long term process. It also states that treatment techniques to increase motivation for treatment are necessary to prevent dropout rates. 

In this case, this patient's daily significant opiate and alcohol use impaired his functioning interpersonally and occupationally so this patient required substance intensive outpatient program treatment at least 3 hours per day 3 days per week. The patient met the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) criteria for intensive outpatient program (IOP) treatment. This patient met criteria for IOP treatment as he had been unable to maintain more than 3 weeks of abstinence and that was only after past inpatient detoxification treatment and inpatient rehabilitation treatment. He continued to report urges and cravings to use and was associating with his brother who was actively drinking alcohol. The patient was in an inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment and needed to transition from that setting to at least this intensive level of care. The patient reportedly had positive toxicology during the denial period and continued to struggle which indicated that he required at least this intensive outpatient program treatment then. 

The patient needed time in this structured and supervised IOP setting to further progress and improve further in coping skills, identifying triggers, interpersonal relations and communication, working on better identifying and accepting his addiction, building a sober support and not associating with active users, and better dealing with cravings. The patient was at high risk of relapse if he were stepped down too quickly to outpatient substance treatment as he could not maintain abstinence even after past inpatient substance treatments. 

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient.

The medical necessity for substance use disorder services is substantiated. The insurer's denial should be overturned.

Diagnosis:  Phencyclidine (PCP) induced psychosis.
Treatment:  Inpatient Mental Health Stay.

The insurer denied the inpatient mental health stay.  The health plan's determination is overturned in part. Two additional days were medically necessary. 

The patient is a male with a diagnosis of hallucinogens (phencyclidine) (PCP) induced psychosis.  Case notes document that the patient was admitted via the Emergency Department (ED) because of his aggressive and dangerous behavior in the community.  When he could not be stabilized in the ED, he was admitted.  The patient has a history of substance use disorder, primarily PCP.  He has two prior arrests, one for domestic abuse and one for substance use.  He had functional impairment and high social stressors prior to admission, specifically lack of family support, residing in a shelter, and no college education.

In the ED, he was noted to be responding to internal stimuli.  He was screaming and making inappropriate sexual gestures.  He had poor impulse control, disorganized behavior, paranoid delusions, as well as poor insight and poor judgment.  On the inpatient unit, he was treated with Haldol, Cogentin, risperidone, trazodone, and Ativan as needed (prn).  In addition, he received supportive psychotherapy and discharge planning.

The Adult Inpatient Mental Health Treatment for Adults (AIMHTA) for 2 additional days is medically necessary for this patient. 

Based on a review of hospital progress notes, the patient could not be safely discharged and with good medical judgment on day 2 recommended by the health plan.  The patient had clearly improved in several parameters, but was still experiencing auditory hallucinations as he had also experienced prior.  PCP produces schizophrenia type symptoms.  PCP induces psychotic symptoms and needs to be treated as a psychosis.  PCP psychosis is treated with neuroleptics and anti-anxiety agents, as was done with this patient.  The experience of continuing auditory hallucinations supports the fact that the patient was still under the influence of his PCP use disorder.  This symptom would entail a high probability that he would need to be readmitted, or would be of risk to others, and possibly to himself, if discharged on the date in question.  The lack of new clinical information would support the probability that there was no new adverse symptomatology in the patient.  Therefore, the patient could be safely discharged on the 2nd day with good medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.

Diagnoses were listed as cocaine dependence, alcohol dependence with withdrawal, opioid dependence with intoxication, anxiety, bipolar, depression. The patient reported a history of substance use disorder difficulties and past treatment on five occasions. He reported some extended periods of sobriety. On admission, the patient reported drinking 2 pints of liquor and 140-ounce beer per day. He also used six bags of heroin intranasally and $50 of crack cocaine daily. He was additionally taking Methadone pills that were not prescribed to him one to three times over the prior 30 days. His blood alcohol level was zero on admission and urine drug screen was positive for opiates, cocaine, and Methadone. Initial alcohol withdrawal score was 8 and opioid withdrawal score was 12.
An appeal letter states that he did not have any prior clean time, though medical records indicate that he reported episodes of clean time in the past of up to seven years. The patient reported multiple prior treatment episodes at various levels of care including residential and outpatient. Clinical records indicate that the patient was adherent to prescribe treatments and took advantage of various treatment modalities offered.
At issue is the medical necessity of the inpatient stay.

The health plan's determination of medical necessity is upheld, in whole.

No. The patient did not require immediate hospitalization for a life-threatening medical condition or severe psychiatric crisis. The substance with the greatest potential for harm to self or others was alcohol. The patient clearly met criteria for diagnosis with multiple substance use disorders including alcohol, cocaine, and opiates. The patient did not meet criteria for full sustained remission from a substance use disorder. There was no evidence of serious medical symptoms that needed to be managed in an inpatient rehabilitation setting. Diagnosis: Neurocognitive Disorder
Treatment Inpatient Mental Health Treatment
The insurer denied the Inpatient Mental Health Treatment
The determination is overturned.

This is a patient with a neurocognitive disorder best characterized as traumatic brain injury with behavioral disturbance arising from complications of encephalopathy. The patient has a moderately severe mood disorder associated with affective instability and aggressive outbursts with destruction of property, self-harming behavior that has included banging her head and swallowing objects, and aggression towards others and property in severe instances of impulsive aggression.
The complications of the brain injury occur together with past diagnoses of neuro-developmental disorder, mild intellectual disability/disorder, attention deficit disorder, and impulse control disorder with other disruptive and problematic behaviors requiring safety monitoring and one-to-one observation. The patient has received mental health treatment with various levels of care including extensive treatment in the past that included therapy and medication with family support and involvement. Despite the best efforts of her community, the patient remains symptomatic and requires direction with basic care and disturbances of behavior that include impulsive aggressive, self-destructive and oppositional behaviors with family and peers.
The patient is judged to be at moderate risk for self-harm and risk for impulsive and aggressive behaviors and has experienced functional impairments and deterioration with regard to relationship functioning, together with safety concerns and the continued need for intensive services with intensive therapy and safety monitoring and efforts to address life skills and social functioning. Prior to referral for neuro-rehabilitation services, the patient was participating in an Adult Day Program and living in a residential facility for individuals with autism (autism spectrum disorder and/or intellectual disability).
The patient presented with anxiety, depression, hopelessness, and affective instability with limited insight and impaired judgment associated with anxiety symptoms that were prominent; she exhibited coping and personality traits that reflected poor control of impulses with high risk for repeated violations of boundary issues and problems with maintaining emotional control in the context of the neurocognitive disorder, mood disturbance, and impulse control problems associated with the underlying traumatic brain injury (TBI).
There were no acute general medical conditions or substance use disorders in this case. The patient did not have a history of disordered eating. The patient had been prescribed mood stabilizing and antidepressant medications to address anxiety, depression, and her aggressive outbursts: Depakote, Invega, Tegretol, Topamax, Lamictal, Latuda Vyvanse and trazodone, as well as vitamin supplements and melatonin.
The patient's inpatient treatment is to include neuro-rehabilitation services and continued mental health services with intensive therapy services and safety monitoring together with the intensity of treatments and structure of an inpatient (or high-intensity residential level of care) with additional services to include speech and language assessments, nutritional assessments and behavior modification techniques targeting the impulsive aggression. She received comprehensive psychiatric evaluations with the development of a treatment plan including continuing medication management. The treatment plan included therapeutic interventions to improve coping skills and self-esteem, and the treatment plan included the goals of breaking the cycle of self-destructive behaviors including self-harm; and, the development of healthy relationships and functioning. The program focused on organizational skills; self-care; peer relationships; and other life skills, as well as behavioral and emotional regulation with milieu, individual, group, family, and activity therapies, and other interventions aimed at improving life skills.
The patient is to actively participate in the treatment plan and work on therapeutic, social, and emotional functions in the context of a therapeutic milieu with an inpatient rehabilitation level of structure and monitoring with a behavioral health program and setting that provided structure, intensive and evidence-based therapy, and safety monitoring, as well as ongoing interventions to address impulsivity. Life skills and other age-appropriate therapeutic interventions are provided, as the program will allow. Additionally, the patient is to receive ongoing rehabilitation and therapy to assist her to process the issues associated with her tendency for dysregulated mood and disruptive behaviors including problematic behavior related to the impulsive aggression and persistent mood disorder. Processing therapy occurs individually and in groups. The patient will also work with a life coach/counselor to address educational and vocational needs with hands on experience. The goal of the treatment plan is to allow this patient to become more independent and transition to a transitional living environment with continued treatment as a step down followed by more independent living in a less restrictive treatment setting than the previous/current treatment setting.
The appeal documentation and case records and health plan documents were reviewed including correspondence and case summaries provided by the referring clinicians and parent. The health plan's rationale for the denial of authorization for the admission and the coverage of the requested services was reviewed together with reference to the plan level of care guidelines/medical necessity criteria. 
The issue under review is the medical necessity of inpatient mental health treatment. 

The requested health service/treatment of Inpatient Mental Health Treatment is medically necessary for this patient.
The patient's clinical history and presenting features and persistent symptoms together with safety concerns warrant the admission and the continued structure and monitoring of an inpatient (neuro-rehabilitation) setting with the intensity, scope, and duration of inpatient level services in order to effectively address the patient's risk of self-harm, continue to learn adequate coping skills to engage in an ongoing therapeutic process, and prevent treatment failure, while the treatment team and family worked toward a clinically appropriate disposition with continued mental health services to address the severe and persistent symptoms of the multiple diagnosed disorders and the associated disturbances of mood, attention and functioning.
The inpatient level services are medically necessary in order to effectively address the patient's risk of aggressive and problematic behaviors, continue to learn adequate coping skills to achieve better control of impulses and boundaries with peers and family, and prevent treatment failure as she had previously experienced, while the treatment team and family worked toward a clinically appropriate disposition with continued mental health services to address the co-occurring mood and attentional and anxiety and neurocognitive disorders including the use of behavioral techniques to address the aggressive and disruptive behaviors in this patient.
The patient had a history of failing to benefit from prior treatment episodes and demonstrated residual symptoms and behaviors that had persisted despite multiple treatment episodes; and, the patient lacked the insight and control of impulses to remain engaged in treatment in a less restrictive setting during the time frame under review. The serious behavioral disturbances have persisted in the context of severe symptoms of mood disorder with co-morbid traumatic brain injury/neurocognitive disorder and mild intellectual disability that complicates the case and warrants the treatment with neuro-rehabilitation and behavioral interventions targeting neurocognitive disorder and comorbid psychiatric disorders including aggressive behavior and mood disturbance with affective instability. The treatment plan also serves to modify or eliminate high risk behaviors that represent imminent and ongoing risk for harm to self or others. These factors support the assertion that the patient could not have been effectively treated at a lower level of care until which time the patient is working on the psychological issues associate with brain injury with improved insight and impulse control and coping skills as outlined in the goal of treatment for improved independence and ability to live in a less restrictive treatment setting as opposed to her prior living situation.
This answer is in keeping with prevailing standards of medical practice and consistent with the scientific literature and guidelines, referenced below.

The patient is a female with a history of obsessive-compulsive disorder and co-morbid major depressive disorder associated with chronic suicidal ideation with plan and severe symptoms of anxiety and functional impairments. She has co-occurring alcohol use disorder with a binge pattern of use; she has engaged in high-risk behaviors when using alcohol and due to impulsivity. Additionally, the patient has an unspecified personality disorder with cluster B and other personality traits that are maladaptive. She was referred and admitted for residential psychiatric services after failing to respond to ongoing treatment in the community including a past history of multiple psychiatric hospitalizations and suicidal behavior. Despite intensive treatments with varying psychiatric services, the patient continued to have severe symptoms of anxiety, compulsive behaviors/rituals and intrusive thoughts; and, she had a significant decline in functioning such that he was unable to work, or effectively do basic self-care, spending excessive time with compulsive rituals associated with isolation and depressive symptoms. She had a history of self-harming with cutting and hitting self and persistent suicidal thoughts with a past history of suicide attempt putting her at high risk for suicide. The subject under review is the medical necessity for the residential level of care. 

The health plan's determination is upheld in part. 

Part of the patient's continued residential level treatment is reasonable and in the best interest of the patient; she continued to display severe symptoms of obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) and associated symptoms of depression in the context of a diagnosis of recurrent and severe major depressive disorder with past suicide attempt and persistent suicidal ideation. And, the patient had presented with significant functional impairments, as well as problems with emotional regulation reflected in her self-harming behaviors, distress problems, interpersonal functioning problems and continued impairment of functioning that had previously deteriorated to the point that she was unable to benefit from treatment at lower levels of care. During this time the patient had not made enough progress in these treatment domains or with regard to these clinical features to warrant a step down to lower level services. Step down would not have been clinically appropriate until the patient was fully engaged in treatment and showing definitive improvements. Thus, the patient warranted the continued intensity of services, structure, and ongoing monitoring of a residential program for part of the time period reviewed.
However, for the remainder of the time, the patient was doing better clinically with improved mood, diminished anxiety and gained insight, as well as improved functioning that included socialization with peers and involvement with the therapeutic interventions. The patient was doing well with daily functioning and was showing successful interactions with staff and other patients and showed cooperation with staff and compliance with treatment. Thus, the patient could have been safely and effectively managed with lower level services, for the remainder of the time.

The patient was admitted to inpatient chemical dependency detoxification and hospitalization for a primary diagnosis of alcohol dependence with withdrawal uncomplicated. He additionally had psychiatric diagnoses of cocaine dependence, uncomplicated, and depression not otherwise specified. Records reflect that he was admitted for inpatient detoxification and was placed on a Librium protocol. 
According to a comprehensive evaluation, the patient reported daily oral use of up to one fifth a day of alcohol, along with six 16-ounce bottles over a long duration. Additionally, he endorsed smoking cocaine daily  at the amount of $60 per day. His drug screens were negative for opiates, amphetamines, hallucinogens (phencyclidine) (PCP), tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), and OxyContin and methamphetamine. He was positive for benzodiazepines, reported to have been given to him at the inpatient psychiatric hospitalization, as well as being positive for cocaine.
A psychiatric evaluation reflects that he reported a chief complaint of depression and noted psychiatric care lasts through inpatient rehabilitation services approximately two years prior in which he was prescribed Lexapro 10 milligrams (mg) every morning. He endorsed no recent psychiatric hospitalizations with the psychiatric evaluation identifying him not to be at risk of harm to self or others. The diagnostic impression was depression not otherwise specified with a recommendation to begin Lexapro 10 milligrams (mg) every morning and then for aftercare placement and would follow up with psychiatry upon completion of rehabilitation services.
A Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment of Alcohol Scale Revised (CIWA-AR) was completed. In this scale, he achieved an overall score of 5 out of a maximum possible of 67. He was noted to endorse the presence of anxiety at a rating of 2 between a scale of 0 to 7, paroxysmal sweats at a rating of 1 on a scale of 0 to 7, and tremors on a rating of 2 on a scale of 0 to 7.
According to the nursing progress notes, he attended five days of inpatient detoxification services for alcohol dependence and was placed on a Librium taper. All documentation based on the nursing progress notes over the days of service, as well as documentation from the clinical progress notes reflects that he engaged in no concerning behaviors, actively participated, complied with medication and progressed well. The assessment interpretive summary documented within the clinical progress notes reflect that he has a long history of alcohol use and notes that when he binges, he uses a fifth of vodka and 12 cans of beer. The patient is married, has two children and reports stable housing. He reportedly has diabetes type 2 due to his alcohol consumption and reports no mental health or legal problems.
At the time of the patient's presentation, the staff completed a detox Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) to assist with a level of care determination. He was identified to be incapacitated, evidencing no risk of physical harm, no risk of severe withdrawal, no risk due to complications or abnormalities, but presenting with risk of moderate withdrawal and a lack of support for early abstinence. As a result, they determined inpatient medically supervised withdrawal was appropriate. At issue is the medical necessity of an inpatient mental health stay.

The patient was medically stable, did not have a history of seizures or delirium tremors and did not have a history of complicated withdrawal. He was not suicidal, homicidal or psychotic. He was motivated to be in treatment, had access to sober support and determined that treatment at a substance use residential rehabilitation level of care would appear more appropriate. He was not experiencing symptoms of functional impairment that created an imminent risk of harm to self or others. These findings are supported by the medical records provided and available. Documentation reflects that the patient had completed two days of some form of inpatient care identified at one point as being for psychiatric care and another point at being for detoxification services in the two days prior to admission for inpatient detoxification for the dates in question.
Furthermore, drug screening reflected the patient had not presence of alcohol in his system. Additionally, the completion of the CIWA identified the claimant achieved a score of 5 out of a possible total of 67, suggesting that the patient was experiencing minimal symptoms associated with withdrawal. The completion of the detoxification Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) that the hospital staff used to support medically supervised inpatient detoxification was erroneously indicated and based on the findings provided within the medical records would have been more appropriate to support medical detoxification at an outpatient level of care.
The patient did not present based on findings available within the medical records with symptoms that warranted the need for inpatient care. The patient did not present through examination findings at acute risk and evidenced minimal symptoms of withdrawal associated with his substance use. Furthermore, he was not noted to be an imminent risk of harm to self or others based on his psychiatric evaluation. Given the totality of the findings provided, the requested service/treatment of inpatient mental health stay was not medically necessary. The medical records provided for review in this case do not support the patient as functionally impaired or requiring medically necessary for the patient to receive inpatient detoxification or inpatient psychiatric care.

summary:
Diagnosis: Symptoms Of Depression.
Treatment: Inpatient Mental Health Treatment.
The insurer denied the Inpatient Mental Health Treatment. The denial is overturned.

The patient is an adult female. She was admitted for acute inpatient evaluation and treatment of an exacerbation of bipolar disorder with most recent episode of major depressive disorder, severe and recurrent with psychotic features. The patient presented with worsening symptoms of depression in context of psychosis and deteriorating function. She reported poor appetite and had sleep disturbance. Her medications had recently been changed and she had not followed up with outpatient mental health aftercare after being discharged from intensive outpatient program (IOP) one month prior to her presentation.  

A comprehensive evaluation was conducted/completed with testing that had included laboratory assessments and physical examination. The patient had a history of hypertension, dyslipidemia, coronary artery disease, COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), seizures, hypothyroidism and degenerative joint disease, as well as orthopedic procedures that had included bilateral knee replacement. Associated treatment included amlodipine, propranolol, oxcarbazepine, Keppra, Plavix, Breo Ellipta and a rescue inhaler.

The patient has a history of bipolar disorder, as noted, with most recent episodes depressed and worsening symptoms since discharge from IOP level care with psychotic features and past history of mania or hypomania. She has a remote history of prescription opioid and marijuana use, but denied current substance use. Drug screen was negative and consistent with her history.

The patient's mental status examination included depressed mood and constricted affect with motor retardation and underproductive thought. She had evidence for auditory and visual hallucinations, as well as the mood disturbance with morbid thoughts and ruminations and severe anxiety and diminished energy and volition. She presented as unkempt and disheveled. Her insight was limited and judgment impaired with inability to care for self. She denied suicidal ideation or aggressive impulses and was notably withdrawn due to her morbid thought content. She had decreased appetite, concentration, energy, sleep and volition with poor attention and concentration.

The patient is widowed and college educated with disability. She lives with her family that includes her oldest daughter and son-in-law and four children with guardianship of the two older children age ten and seven years. There were no legal issues or trauma-related issues. 

The patient was admitted to acute inpatient level services with close observation, safety monitoring, and pharmacotherapy supplemented with PRN (pro re nata-as needed) medications to enhance sleep and to address anxiety. The patient was withdrawn and socially isolated with severe symptoms of anxiety-apprehension, tension, worry, nervousness, and somatic concerns that persisted during her initial stay. She was started on Seroquel at a daily dose of 400 mg (milligrams) together with Cymbalta, Lexapro and Buspar, and had the opportunity to participate in group, individual and educational sessions, as well as family focused sessions that were addressing appropriate aftercare and need for compliance with treatment. Throughout her brief inpatient stay, the patient isolated in her room and had to be encouraged to participate in milieu activities. 

The patient's hallucinations had resolved and she reported a positive outlook with better functioning. She was medication adherent with tolerability. Thus, she was deemed to be capable of treatment with lower level care and was discharged to home with clinically appropriate aftercare and continued use of her psychotropic medications with plans for resumption of IOP care. On the day of discharge, she was more spontaneous and well-groomed with improved mood and diminished anxiety. She had consistently denied suicidal ideation or aggressive impulses. Her family supported the discharge plan and had remained supportive throughout her inpatient stay.

Yes, the Inpatient Mental Health Treatment was medically necessary for this patient.

The patient required the admission and the continued acute inpatient level care and the structure and monitoring of an acute inpatient level setting in order to remain safe and to administer treatment for her psychiatric disturbance, bipolar mood disorder with severe depression and psychotic features. The admission was warranted in order to conduct an evaluation and observe her functioning with the resumption/adjustment of clinically appropriate medications. The clinical course was complicated by the presence of psychosis and functional impairment being addressed during the time interval under review. Additionally, the treatment team was planning for a safe and clinically appropriate disposition with aftercare arrangements in concert with the patient's family with whom she lived and with community providers.

The medical necessity for the admission and the continued inpatient level structure and monitoring is reasonable, and in the patient's best interest in view of the patient's severe symptoms of mood disorder, risk for relapse, and co-morbid medical conditions. In view of these clinical features and the complicated presentation with psychosis and deterioration in functioning, the patient's continued active treatment with safety monitoring was warranted in the context of the patient's deteriorated functioning and stressors involving primary support and general medical domains. Additionally, the inpatient stay was medically necessary in order to monitor the response to medications, to insure that the patient would have a sustained response to treatment, and to continue to address the acute risk of relapse or non-compliance or rehospitalization in the context of severe symptoms of bipolar mood disorder in a patient with impaired judgment and a limited insight and deteriorated functioning. The necessity for the admission and continued inpatient level services is in keeping with prevailing standards of professional practice, and with the published practice guidelines, referenced below, as well as New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews.

The patient could not have been expected to participate in treatment at a lower level of care during the time interval under review in this case scenario.

summary:
Diagnosis: Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome, Transaminitis
Treatment Inpatient Hospital Stay
The insurer denied the Inpatient Hospital Stay
The determination is overturned.

The patient has a past medical history significant for alcoholism, hypertension, tobacco abuse, opioid abuse on Suboxone, and depression who presented to the emergency department with complaints of feeling "I'm going to explode." Reportedly, he reported shaking in his hands and the entire body, lightheadedness, left lower quadrant pain with nausea, vomiting. He also complained of some palpitations. The review of systems was positive for diarrhea for 2 months, blood in the vomitus. The rest of the review of systems was negative.
Reportedly, the patient was previously seen in the emergency department for similar symptoms and was admitted to a psychiatric facility because of a major depressive disorder that was associated with suicidal ideations. When the patient was seen by the admitting physician, he was afebrile, heart rate was 60 beats per minute (bpm), respiratory rate 16 breaths/minute, blood pressure 156/94, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
The patient was a well-developed, well-nourished, and well-groomed male who was diaphoretic and had tremors in his hands. He looked anxious. His head, eyes, ears, neck, throat (HEENT) exam was within normal limits. He had dry oral mucosa. The patient had a regular heart rate and rhythm, without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. The lungs were clear to auscultation without wheezes, rales, or rhonchi. The abdomen was soft, nontender to palpation, with normal bowel sounds, without guarding or rebound.
The neurological exam was unremarkable except for the tremor in the hands. The rest of the physical exam was within normal limits.

The patient was admitted to the hospital with a diagnosis of alcohol withdrawal syndrome, alcohol intoxication, and transaminitis. Other admitting diagnoses included opioid abuse, tobacco abuse, and hypertension. In the hospital, the patient was seen by a psychiatrist who suggested that there were no indications for psychiatric hospitalization.
During the hospital stay the patient was monitored closely and given medications based on Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) protocol. Since his clinical condition improved, he was transitioned to outpatient care. At issue is the medical necessity of an inpatient stay.

Yes, the inpatient stay was medically necessary. Medically supervised alcohol withdrawal is indicated for patients with or at risk of withdrawal symptoms. For patients with mild symptoms and no history of seizures or delirium tremens, supervised withdrawal can be managed safely and effectively in the ambulatory setting.
Patients with more severe symptoms and/or at risk of delirium tremens, seizures, or hallucinations require closer monitoring and intervention, typically in an inpatient setting.
Additional circumstances prompt medically supervised withdrawal in an inpatient setting, llowing for more careful monitoring and more aggressive treatment. These include:
Fever
Disorientation
Drenching sweats
Severe tachycardia
Hypertension
Pregnancy
Concurrent substance use that could lead to withdrawal symptoms (eg, benzodiazepines)
Markedly abnormal laboratory values

In this clinical case, the patient had a history of multiple substance abuse and was at risk of withdrawal from opioids. It was clearly indicated that he had hypertension. He had moderate alcohol withdrawal symptoms since his Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) score was documented at 16. In addition, the patient had significant risk factors for developing delirium tremens (DTs).
Taking into consideration all of this information, the admission at the acute inpatient level of care was medically necessary. The admission to the acute inpatient level of care was justified since the patient had moderate alcohol withdrawal symptoms (CIWA score of 16) in addition to multiple medical conditions including hypertension and polysubstance abuse that would increase the severity of withdrawal.
In addition, the patient had significant risk factors to develop DTs. Therefore, he required very close monitoring, and administration of medications in a timely manner to treat his alcohol withdrawal symptoms, prevent dehydration, as well as prevent DTs. This kind of care could be provided in the most effective way at the inpatient level.

summary:

The patient is a male who completed detoxification treatment and was converted to inpatient rehabilitation and substance use disorder treatment to address a seven-year history of severe substance use disorders with alcohol and opioid (heroin and buprenorphine) class substances. The patient has no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens. He had extensive treatment experience with at least six detoxification episodes and two rehabilitation treatment episodes that included one outpatient and one residential level treatment. His substance use included one pint of vodka daily, and 20 to 30 bags of heroin with inhalation, and intermittent use of buprenorphine when unable to obtain heroin.

The patient has no history of psychiatric disorder and denied history of psychiatric hospitalization or suicidal behavior.

The patient has no acute general medical issues; he was medically screened upon admission with laboratory assessment and physical examination that were grossly normal or unremarkable. He had a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with emphysema with at least one hospitalization related to his lung disease. He was tobacco dependent.

The patient is divorced and retired with a pension and lives with family who were supportive. There was no history of legal issues or trauma history in this case.

Evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination that reflected reasonable motivation for rehabilitation treatment, but limited insight, impaired judgment, and poor control of impulses. The patient was described as cooperative with fluent speech and organized thought processing. He displayed euthymic mood, and, diminished focus or concentration with no severe symptoms such as mania, formal thought disorder, psychosis, perceptual disturbance or severe cognitive impairment. He did not report suicidal ideation or aggressive impulses. There were no significant or severe withdrawal symptoms or post-acute withdrawal symptoms upon completion of his detoxification.

Upon admission to inpatient level services, the patient received comprehensive evaluation and treatment that included focus on coping skills, relapse prevention techniques with identification of triggers, education about the disease model of addiction, and, involvement with groups, as well as 12-step recovery groups and other therapeutic activities. Psychiatric evaluation had been provided and affirmed that the patient had no co-occurring psychiatric disorders. The patient engaged in substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment. He was noted to participate in the therapeutic activities, was social with peers and was actively participating in recovery groups, and, adherent with medication that included vitamin supplements and the availability of nicotine replacement to address tobacco dependence, as well as 'as needed' (PRN) use of Vistaril and trazodone for anxiety and insomnia. He was sleeping and eating okay with steady gait and functioning with daily activities.

Throughout his brief inpatient stay, the patient remained stable and engaged with the treatment regimen. He received intensive rehabilitation services, monitoring, and structure provided within the inpatient treatment program including 24-hour monitoring. The patient was discharged against medical advice with recommendations for clinically appropriate aftercare of his substance use disorders and a reminder that he had left treatment prematurely two previous times and would not be converted to inpatient rehabilitation services with future detoxification treatments. 

No, the requested inpatient stay is not medically necessary for this patient.

The patient presented following detoxification treatment with substance use disorders, diagnosed with alcohol and opioid and tobacco use disorders. He briefly received inpatient level rehabilitation treatment and left treatment against medical advice. He did engage in treatment and he had no biomedical or psychiatric treatment issues that warranted inpatient level care. During the time interval under review, the patient was noted to be in no apparent distress with reasonable functioning and active participation in treatment including positive interactions with staff and peers. Throughout his brief inpatient stay, there were no complicating treatment issues or biomedical or co-occurring psychiatric issues that would have warranted inpatient level of care, structure or 24-hour monitoring. The application of NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria (referenced below) did indicate that the patient was clinically appropriate for treatment with lower level care in a less restrictive treatment setting, as the health plan asserts. Thus, medical necessity for the inpatient level treatment for substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment is not met in this case scenario, consistent with the American Society of Addicition Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, the scientific literature and published guidelines, referenced below.

The patient in this case scenario is not clinically appropriate for an inpatient level of care during the time interval under review. The patient had presented with a level of stability that included no significant withdrawal symptoms or biomedical issues and no co-occurring psychiatric disorders or safety concerns that would have warranted inpatient level care. He did not need the monitoring or the structure of an inpatient setting in order to receive effective substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment. He readily engaged with treatment and was involved with treatment interventions and peer-supported recovery groups that could have been provided in a less restrictive treatment setting with sober supports or living. Thus, the health plan's determination is reasonable in this case scenario. summary:
Diagnosis: Alcohol, Cocaine, and Cannabis Use Disorder
Treatment: Inpatient admission
The insurer denied coverage for the inpatient admission.
The denial is overturned. 

This is a male patient who was admitted to inpatient substance detoxification treatment for treatment of withdrawal symptoms. He reportedly had tremors, anxiety, irritable mood, and teary eyes. He reportedly was drinking 1 pint per day, smoking crack daily, and using cannabis. He reportedly continued to use alcohol and substances despite a recent inpatient substance detoxification treatment. He had diagnoses of Alcohol, Cocaine, and Cannabis Use Disorder.  He was put on a Librium protocol and required and received Librium. He left Against Medical Advice (AMA) on day 4 of admission.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. It also states that patients with past complicated or life threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens are in need of inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal and reports that patients with comorbid medical conditions that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification. The United States Department of Health and Human Services-Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) Center for Substance Abuse Treatment reports that inpatient treatment is necessary if the ability to attend outpatient treatment daily is a problem, one is unable to follow up in outpatient treatment, if medical conditions complicate the treatment of withdrawal, if one has previous withdrawal seizures of delirium tremens, or if one does not have the capacity for informed consent. In this case, this patient had been drinking large amounts of alcohol daily as it was reported that he was drinking 1 pint of alcohol per day and using crack daily which put him at risk medically and also for severe, complicated, and life threatening withdrawal.  

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), he did require 24 hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated in outpatient detoxification settings as he continued to use large amounts of alcohol and crack/cocaine despite a recent past inpatient substance detoxification treatment and he required and took detoxification medication, Librium, to modify withdrawal and prevent more severe, complicated, or life threatening withdrawal. He signed out AMA on day 4 of admission. It was unlikely that he would remain abstinent so he required the time in this treatment setting to stop withdrawals and also to decrease the chance that he would relapse again when not in this 24 hour setting as well as to prevent possible life threatening withdrawal symptoms. The risk of life complicated withdrawal such as delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use, so he required the time in this inpatient substance detoxification setting. 

Inpatient substance/alcohol detoxification was medically necessary. It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably or in the best interests of the patient then.  

The carrier's denial of coverage for the inpatient admission is overturned. The medical necessity is substantiated.
