1)	American Psychiatric Association Practice Guidelines For The Treatment Of Patients With Substance Use Disorders.

2)	US Department of Health and Human Services-Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) Center for Substance Abuse Treatment.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance use

Treatment: Admission to the substance abuse inpatient detoxification level of care

The insurer denied coverage for the admission to the substance abuse inpatient detoxification level of care.

The denial is overturned. 

This is a male patient with a history of substance use including cocaine use disorder, nicotine dependence, and opiate dependence who presented to the hospital with a chief complaint of withdrawal symptoms. He was admitted to this inpatient hospital for substance detoxification treatment. He had withdrawal symptoms including chills, flushing, tremors, dilated pupils, nasal congestion, diffuse aches, gastrointestinal upset, yawning, and anxiety. He reportedly had a Clinical Opioid withdrawal Scale (COWS) score of 11 which then increased to 13 on day 2 of admission. He was using 10-12 bags of heroin daily, cocaine, and 4 milligrams (mg) of benzodiazepines (Klonopin) daily. He also reportedly was using methadone 50 mg per day a few times per week. He reportedly had a positive toxicology for cocaine, fentanyl, opiates, and methadone. He had multiple past inpatient substance detoxification treatments. He was unemployed, single and had no children. He was put on a methadone detoxification protocol due to his withdrawal symptoms for detoxification. He also had a Psychiatry consultation and had a past history of major depressive disorder and past psychiatric hospitalizations and he was prescribed Trazodone. He reportedly left Against Medical Advice (AMA) on day 3 of admission.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. This was the case with this patient. This patient had multiple past substance detoxification treatments and still was using heroin daily and cocaine as well as Klonopin which put him at risk of overdose and severe withdrawal. It was not likely that he could be treated in a less restrictive substance detoxification treatment due to his continued use despite past inpatient substance detoxification treatments so he required inpatient substance hospital detoxification treatment. He also had reports of worsened withdrawal as his COWS score increased from 11 to 13 so he was more at risk for severe withdrawal and in need of 24 hour hospital detoxification treatment. 

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), the patient did require 24 hour treatment from day 1 to day 3 of admission as he needed detoxification medication, methadone, to modify withdrawal and prevent more severe withdrawal. He reportedly was using large amounts of heroin including 10-12 bags per day with cocaine, and Klonopin, so he was considered a high risk medically for overdose and more severe withdrawal. He was considered at risk for complicated and life threatening withdrawal due to his large amount of daily Klonopin use in addition to his large amount of heroin and cocaine use. 

Inpatient acute hospital treatment for substance detoxification was medically necessary.  It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably or in the best interests of the patient.  

The medical necessity for the admission to the substance abuse inpatient detoxification level of care is substantiated. The insurer's denial is overturned.

summary:

Treatment: Mental Health In-Patient.

The patient did not have a diagnosis of co-occurring substance use disorder or acute general medical issues though she did have a diagnosis of scoliosis and past orthopedic problems. Her symptoms of mood disturbance were associated with chronic suicidal behavior for which she had been hospitalized multiple times followed by outpatient treatment with medication and therapy. She had received multiple medication trials and varying levels of treatment without sustained benefit or a remission of symptoms. More recently, she had attempted suicide earlier in the year with subsequent leave from college and return home where she was monitored by her family. She was subsequently referred to the residential treatment facility with admission. The patient's presenting clinical features prompted the referral to residential treatment to address the psychosocial issues and behavioral disturbances associated with the mood and personality disorder. Her referral for residential treatment was also prompted by her clinical providers with safety concerns and the persistent depressive disorder and recurrent episodes of major depression. Thus, the patient was admitted to residential level care in the context of worsening symptoms of mood disturbance with chronic suicidal and self-destructive behaviors associated with poor control of impulses together with maladaptive coping and emotional dysregulation. Evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination with severe psychiatric symptoms in the context of chronic depressive disorder (dysthymic disorder or persistent depressive disorder) associated with severe and recurrent major depressive disorder and the personality disorder. The patient was cooperative with evaluation. There was no acute suicidal ideation, but she had reported suicidal behaviors and attempts, as well as a history of self-harm. There was no evidence of frank psychosis, mania, thought disorder, or severe cognitive impairment. Insight was limited. The patient is single and a college student; she is characterized as a good student. There are no prominent family problems, but the patient has relationship problems, but no specified trauma history or legal problems. She reports being bullied in high school. Throughout the residential stay, the patient was engaged in therapy and participating in sessions to address the mood and personality disturbance. The health plan's determination of medical necessity is upheld. The requested health service/treatment of Residential Treatment Center (RTC) Mental Health Services was not medically necessary for this patient. The health plan's decision to deny coverage for the requested residential treatment is reasonable in this case scenario. The patient was cooperative and motivated to engage in treatment. The patient had no complicating general medical or clinical or psychiatric features that would necessitate 24-hour monitoring or residential level of care. The patient did not exhibit aggressive or impulsive behaviors and denied suicidal plan or intent of self-harm. Her suicidal ideation was chronic in nature and the patient was capable of engaging in treatment in a less restrictive treatment setting. She was compliant with the treatment plan and adherent with medications and attending to daily activities and attending groups and other therapeutic activities. Participation in treatment at a lower level of care was reasonable and was in the patient's best interest in this case scenario.

summary:
Diagnosis: Alcohol withdrawal.

Treatment: Inpatient hospital admission.

The insurer denied coverage for the inpatient hospital admission.

The denial is overturned.

This is a male patient with prior history of bipolar disorder, depression, schizoaffective disorder, crack cocaine use and alcohol dependency who was admitted for inpatient hospital detoxification treatment for alcohol and substance detoxification. He had withdrawal symptoms including tremors, difficulty sleeping, anxiety, and he was started on a Librium protocol. On day 3 of admission, the patient left Against Medical Advice (AMA) instead of completing detoxification. He also did not agree with the referral for inpatient alcohol/substance rehabilitation after the detoxification treatment. He reportedly had multiple past inpatient substance/alcohol detoxification treatments and also had past inpatient substance/alcohol rehabilitation treatment. He reportedly was drinking 2-3 pints of liquor per day and also drinking 40 ounces of beer, and using crack/cocaine and alcohol for many years, and using 2 joints per day 1-2 times per week.  He reportedly had past psychiatric hospital treatment for a suicide attempt and depression. He did not have stable housing.

The insurer denied coverage for the inpatient hospital detoxification treatment. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. It also reports that patients using large amounts of alcohol or benzodiazepines are at a higher risk of having delirium tremens 3-4 days after cessation of use. It also states that patients with comorbid medical conditions complicating that management of withdrawal are candidates for inpatient hospital treatment.  

In this case this patient had active alcohol withdrawal symptoms including tremors, anxiety, and insomnia and was at risk for worsened withdrawal symptoms including severe, complicated, or life threatening withdrawal and he required and received detoxification medication including Librium to modify withdrawal and prevent worsened withdrawal. He reportedly was at risk for severe, life threatening, and complicated withdrawal including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens as delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after cessation of alcohol use.  

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) he did require 24 hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated in outpatient detoxification settings as he continued to use large amounts of alcohol, crack/cocaine, and cannabis despite multiple past inpatient detoxification and inpatient rehabilitation treatment. Also, he required and needed detoxification medication to modify withdrawal and to prevent more serious withdrawal. He also did not agree with the referral for inpatient alcohol/substance rehabilitation after the detoxification treatment. It was not likely that he could safely be managed in an outpatient setting or a less restrictive setting other than a hospital detoxification setting as he was a high risk patient. He lacked stable housing and supports. He needed 24 hour treatment as he was at risk for worsened withdrawal symptoms if not in this 24 hour setting, including severe and life threatening withdrawal symptoms, and this risk is high from 3-4 days after alcohol use. 

The health care plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment in the best interests of the patient.  

The carrier's denial of coverage for the inpatient hospital admission is overturned. The medical necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Use

Treatment: Inpatient rehabilitation admission

The insurer denied coverage for the inpatient rehabilitation admission.

The denial is overturned.

This is a male patient who was admitted to inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment after being referred from his men's residential treatment. The patient reportedly was drinking 24 ounces of alcohol daily and smoking 2 blunts of cannabis daily. The patient reportedly had a past substance detoxification. The patient reported past legal issues including cannabis possession. The patient lacked supports and was unemployed after losing his job. The patient reportedly minimized his addiction. As an inpatient, the patient was compliant to treatment, and attended individual and group therapy. 

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that residential treatment is indicated primarily for individuals who do not meet clinical criteria for hospitalization but whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. Residential facilities provide a safe and substance-free environment in which residents learn individual and group living skills for preventing relapse. In this case, this patient was considered in need of 24-hour residential treatment then as he lacked insight into the seriousness of his addiction and continued to use alcohol and cannabis daily despite past legal issues due to this use and despite past inpatient substance treatment. According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), the patient met criteria for inpatient substance residential rehabilitation treatment as he continued to use alcohol and cannabis daily despite past legal issues due to this use and despite past inpatient substance treatment. The patient reportedly had legal issues in the past related to his use and lacked supports. The chart notes reported that the patient was working on trying to confront his denial and minimization of use, improve coping skills and relapse prevention skills, and better identify triggers to use while improving insight into use. The patient still reportedly was working on identification of triggers and working on improving his sober support system as reported in the second week of treatment. 

Also, the National Institute on Drug Abuse: Principles of Addiction Treatment: A Research Based Guide, reports that research indicates that the best treatment outcomes occur with longer durations of treatment and states that recovery from drug addiction is a long term process. It also states that treatment techniques to increase motivation for treatment are necessary to prevent dropout rates. In this case, this patient needed the entire time in this 24-hour therapeutic supervised and structured treatment setting to learn better coping skills and relapse prevention skills, decrease impulsivity, increase supports, improve insight, confront denial and minimization. Thus, the 3 weeks of treatment was considered medically necessary to further progress and sustain any gains and to better ensure abstinence upon discharge to a less restrictive level of care.  Without this structured and supervised therapeutic residential treatment, the patient likely would have relapsed again. As a result, the recommendation is to overturn the previous decision and approve coverage for inpatient substance residential treatment.

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient. 

Based on the above, the medical necessity for the inpatient rehabilitation admission is substantiated. The insurer's denial should be overturned.

Treatment: Substance abuse inpatient admission

The denial is overturned. 

The patient is male with a longstanding history of alcohol use disorder and subsequent use of benzodiazepines (Xanax and Klonopin). He was also receiving medication assisted treatment with Suboxone to treat opioid use disorder. The patient was admitted to inpatient level care for detoxification treatment following medical screening. He reported drinking multiple shots of vodka with a binge pattern of use together with daily use of a benzodiazepine with up to four milligrams (mg) (two sticks) of Xanax or Klonopin. He had frequent blackouts but denied history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens despite his longstanding use of alcohol and subsequent use of benzodiazepines in the context of severe symptoms of anxiety and depression. Additionally, the patient had an inadvertent overdose one month prior to admission. The patient was admitted for monitoring and detoxification and withdrawal management of severe alcohol and sedative-hypnotic-anxiolytic use disorder, and continued treatment for general medical conditions including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), and cardiac valve regurgitation, as well as a history of hepatitis B and C. 

The patient has a history of mental disorder and mental health treatment for anxiety and depression that resulted in job loss and disability and homelessness.

Mental status examination included evidence for poor coping skills with fair insight, judgment and impulse control. He presented as cooperative with good eye contact. Speech was clear with organized thought processing. There were no severe symptoms such as mania, psychosis, thought disorder, or perceptual disturbance, and, the patient denied suicidal ideation or aggressive impulses. He was anxious with withdrawal symptoms that included chills, sweats and restlessness with a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) scale score of eight. 

The patient is single and lives with his girlfriend. He is college educated and unemployed and receiving disability support. There were no legal issues or trauma history in this case.

The patient was admitted to inpatient level care and placed on a detoxification regimen with vitamins replacement therapy and a detoxification protocol with benzodiazepine and medical monitoring with seizure and fall precautions. The patient gradually improved with better ability to perform basic activities of daily living by the day of discharge. The patient's metabolic state, laboratory functions, and vital signs normalized or remained normal. He received counseling and education together with peer support and group sessions offered within the therapeutic milieu. There were no general medical complications during the inpatient stay. He had continued use of Suboxone at eight milligrams (mg) twice daily in order to address the treatment of opioid use disorder. 

The patient was discharged with completion of the detoxification protocol with recommendations for continued substance-related treatment including outpatient services for the mental health follow up and involvement in 12-step recovery groups, and continued medication-assisted treatment for the opioid use disorder, as well as follow up for his general medical conditions.

The proposed treatment, Inpatient Admission for Detoxification and Withdrawal Management was medically necessary for this patient.

The requested benefit of detoxification treatment and withdrawal management and other medical services could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. The patient in this case was using large quantities of alcohol together with benzodiazepines that did warrant inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring. The patient's social environment was not conducive to an effective detoxification, and the patient struggled with withdrawal symptoms. There was a history or frequent blackouts and a recent overdose reflecting the seriousness of his use of alcohol and benzodiazepines. 

Thus, the adult inpatient stay for detoxification treatment of this patient's substance use disorders did necessitate the structure of an inpatient level setting with 24-hour monitoring. The patient's history of substance abuse (frequency and quantity) together with the severe psychosocial stressors and functional impairments and a co-occurring psychiatric disorder do reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder and co-occurring disorder with persistent anxiety and depression that served to trigger the patient's substance use. Again, the clinical features and treatment dimensions in this case do warrant and support the need for a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management as the patient was at high risk for treatment failure or general medical complications such as seizures if detoxification and withdrawal management were to be attempted at a lower level of care. Therefore, medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published practice guidelines, American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and the scientific literature, referenced below, and, consistent with New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews including the appropriate application of NY (New York) State State Office of Addiction Services and Supports (OASAS) Level of Care Determination (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines, referenced below. 

The requested benefit of Inpatient Admission for Detoxification and Withdrawal Management is clinically appropriate, medically necessary and warranted, and is therefore a covered benefit in this case scenario. The substance abuse detoxification and continued inpatient level treatment through discharge could not have been safely or effectively provided with lower level services, as noted above. Thus, the requested benefit is not excluded under the plan, and should be covered in keeping with prevailing standards of care pertaining to substance use disorder services including American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria and the application of NY State Office of Addiction Services and Supports (OASAS) Level of Care Determination (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines, referenced below.

The patient's VS (vital signs) were as follows: Temperature 98, Pulse 77, Respiration rate 19, Blood pressure 135/91, Pulse oximetry 96%. His exam was unremarkable. The patient was admitted. Plan of care included CIWA (clinical institute withdrawal assessment) protocol. 

Admission day 1, the patient's vital signs were stable. He was feeling better. CIWA (clinical institute withdrawal assessment) 1 - 12. CPK (creatine phosphokinase) was 285. He was requesting Suboxone, as he was feeling withdrawal starting. He was continued on CIWA (clinical institute withdrawal assessment) protocol. He was continued IVF (intravenous fluids) at 100 cc/hr (cubic centimeters per hour). CXR (chest x-ray) revealed NAD (no active disease).

summary:
Diagnosis: Unspecified psychotic disorder

Treatment: Continued inpatient hospital admission

The insurer denied coverage for the continued inpatient hospital admission.

The denial is upheld. 

This is a male patient with no prior psychiatric history who was admitted for inpatient mental health treatment due to threatening, aggressive, and agitated behavior, and psychotic symptoms. The patient reportedly was involved in a physical altercation with his brother and threw a hammer that broke a printer. The patient reportedly had odd behavior, was smiling and laughing inappropriately, had frequent anger outbursts, and exhibited labile affect and mood fluctuations, sleeping problems, impulsivity, frequent arguments, and poor anger control. The patient had been smoking 2 joints of cannabis per day and had past use of synthetic cannabinoid and crack/cocaine. The patient was admitted and was treated with Abilify. The patient had a reported diagnosis of unspecified psychotic disorder. The patient lived with his parents and was unemployed.  The patient was stabilized and was discharged to home on day 5 of admission.

The Milliman Care Guidelines (MCG) Behavioral Health Inpatient Level of Care Adult criteria guidelines report that a patient needs to present as an imminent danger to self, imminent danger to others with severe psychiatric or behavioral symptoms, have a severely dysfunctional living situation including inability to care for self, unwillingness to participate voluntarily, or a less restrictive level of care is not feasible to meet criteria for inpatient behavioral health level of care. 

In this case, there were no reports of suicidal ideation, plan, or intent, psychotic symptoms, manic episodes, major depressive episodes, aggressive, self-injurious, or agitated behavior, inability to adequately care for his basic needs, acute medical instability, or withdrawal symptoms as of day 4 of admission. Notes on day 4 of admission reported that the patient denied suicidal or homicidal ideation, hallucinations, and the patient was counseled about cannabis for which he was agreeable. The patient reported regret for the incident prior to admission with his brother, and other than some mood fluctuations, impulsivity, and anger, the patient had no other manic or depressive symptoms. The patient was then discharged home on day 5 of admission. Also, as of day 4 of admission, there were no reports of specific identifiable or quantifiable treatment goals or objectives that could only be achieved in a 24-hour acute psychiatric hospital or that could not be achieved in a less restrictive level of care. There was no further specific evidence that the patient was still considered an imminent danger to self or others then. Thus, continued behavioral health inpatient admission was not medically necessary for this patient from day 4 of admission to day 5 of admission.  

The health plan acted reasonably with sound clinical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.  

The carrier's denial of coverage for the continued inpatient hospital admission should be upheld. The medical necessity is not substantiated.

The patient's inpatient treatment included intramuscular (IM) Haldol, Ativan and Benadryl, and oral Lithium. The patient clinically improved and was discharged on day 15 of admission.

The patient was discharged on day 15 of admission.

The health plan acted reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient.

summary:

Treatment: Substance Abuse: Inpatient.

The patient is an unemployed adult male who was admitted following medical screening to acute inpatient level services for detoxification and withdrawal management of severe alcohol, sedative-hypnotic-anxiolytic (Xanax) and stimulant (cocaine) use disorders. The patient was using up to two pints of vodka daily together with frequent use of 4 milligrams (mg) of Xanax (two bars up to 6 times per week) and with use cocaine with a quantity of 2 grams per day with intranasal administration.

The patient was admitted to acute inpatient level care and placed on a detoxification regimen with a five-day Librium taper, vitamin replacement therapy, fluid replacement, and medical monitoring; the patient was tobacco dependent and offered smoking cessation treatment and nicotine replacement. Following his first day of treatment, the patient began to participate in counseling and educational sessions. Vitamins were continued, as well as comfort medications with monitoring and assistance with daily activities. He was maintained on fall and seizure precautions. His demeanor improved as he underwent detoxification treatment, and he was social with peers. Again, he participated in educational sessions and counseling during the remaining hospital stay through discharge. The patient was discharged with plans to start a rehabilitation treatment the following day with recommendations involvement in 12-step recovery meetings.

The health plan's determination is overturned in whole.

The patient in this case presented with a diagnosis of severe alcohol, sedative-hypnotic-anxiolytic, and stimulant use disorder. The presenting clinical features and history and risk for withdrawal seizures and other psychosocial complications of the substance use disorders did warrant the admission and continued inpatient level services with medical monitoring in this case. The patient's admission and continued inpatient stay with detoxification, withdrawal management, and other medical services through discharge could not have been effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario.
The adult inpatient treatment of this patient's substance use disorders did require the admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level setting and 24-hour monitoring in view of the severity of the substance use disorders, and the presentation with withdrawal symptoms despite use on the day of presentation. Withdrawal symptoms were managed with tapering dosages of benzodiazepine/Librium requiring monitoring, as well as comfort medications and vitamin replacement therapy. Thus, the patient did require a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management during the time frame under review, as it was reasonable that the patient would have been unable to abstain from the substances of abuse if detoxification and treatment were to be attempted at a lower level of care. Medical necessity for the admission and the continued inpatient services, is met in this case, and is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice, published practice guidelines, and American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, referenced below. This answer is also consistent with the application of NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria and Guidelines.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance abuse
Treatment: Inpatient admission for substance use disorder
The insurer denied coverage for the inpatient admission for substance use disorder.
The denial is overturned. 

This is a male patient with a history of substance abuse who was admitted to inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment after a step down from inpatient substance detoxification treatment. The patient reportedly was drinking 30, 12-ounce beers daily and using crack/cocaine 1-3 times per week. It was reported that the patient could not stop the large amount of alcohol use and crack/cocaine use despite past inpatient substance detoxification treatments. The patient lacked supports and was homeless and unemployed. The patient also lacked coping skills and had difficulty identifying triggers. The patient left Against Medical Advice (AMA) on day 3 of admission.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that inpatient treatment is indicated primarily for individuals whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. In this case, this patient was considered in need of 24-hour substance rehabilitation treatment and a step down from inpatient detoxification treatment as he was considered a high risk patient medically due to past alcohol withdrawal seizures. The patient was more at risk for life-threatening withdrawal such as delirium tremens. The patient was using large amounts of alcohol daily including up to 30 beers per day as well as crack/cocaine use which put him at risk medically especially with his history of cardiac disease. The patient lacked the coping skills and ability to identify relapse triggers to stop use.  

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), the patient met criteria for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment as he continued to use large amounts of alcohol and also crack/cocaine despite past inpatient substance treatments including past inpatient substance detoxification treatments. The patient lacked sober supports to maintain abstinence outside of this 24-hour substance rehabilitation treatment as he was homeless and unemployed, lacked coping skills and ability to identify relapse triggers so he was a high risk to continue use. The patient reportedly lacked coping skills, needed to better identify relapse triggers, and needed to learn relapse prevention skills. The patient was unable to stop substance use without being in a sober and supervised therapeutic inpatient substance rehabilitation setting then. Without this structured and supervised therapeutic rehabilitation treatment, the patient likely would have relapsed quickly.  

Thus, based on the review of the medical record and literature, inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment was medically necessary for this patient.

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient.

The carrier's denial of coverage for inpatient admission for substance use disorder should be overturned. The medical necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Partial Hospitalization Substance Use Treatment 
The insurer denied the Partial Hospitalization Substance Use Treatment.
The denial is upheld. 

The patient is a male. He presented for partial hospital program (PHP) level substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment to address substance use of alcohol. The patient had no past history of delirium tremens or withdrawal seizures, but had chronic medical conditions including hypertension, gout and GERD (gastroesophageal reflux disease) with associated treatments. He had a history of substance use disorder with onset in adolescence, escalating to daily continuous use of approximately 12 to 18 beers per day. The patient self-referral for treatment was prompted by a family intervention and the admission for PHP (partial hospitalization program) level care had immediately followed a seven-day detoxification treatment. The patient had not previously engaged in substance use disorder treatment. 

There was a history of psychiatric disorder diagnosed as an unspecified anxiety disorder and major depressive disorder. The patient denied history of psychiatric hospitalization or suicidal or self-harming behavior. He indicated that he had trauma history with physical abuse at the hands of his in-laws.

The patient was motivated for rehabilitation treatment. The patient exhibited fair, but limited insight and fair judgment and control of impulses. There were no severe symptoms on mental status examination; the patient had no symptoms of mania, psychosis, perception, cognition, or thought disorder. The patient was described as "neat" and "cooperative" with good eye contact. He was depressed with sad affect and exhibited anxiety and complained of insomnia. He presented with post-acute withdrawal symptoms including sweats, tremor, chills and fatigue, as well as the depression, anxiety and insomnia. 

The patient was married with children, and he lived with his spouse who was sober. He was employed. He had trauma/abuse history as noted, and there were no legal issues in this case.

The patient's rehabilitation treatment included focus on coping skills, relapse prevention techniques with identification of triggers, education about the disease model of addiction, and involvement with 12-step recovery groups. The patient engaged in treatment and intensive services, sober housing, monitoring, and structure provided within the rehabilitation treatment program. The patient participated actively with treatment, and showed no severe symptoms or signs of withdrawal, and had no complications of rehabilitation treatment during his brief PHP (partial hospitalization program) stay earlier in the year. summary:
Diagnosis: Substance use disorders
Treatment: Inpatient admission
The insurer denied the inpatient admission.
The denial is overturned. 

The patient is a male who was admitted to acute inpatient level of care for detoxification and withdrawal management and stabilization in order to address substance use disorders with opioid (heroin), alcohol, and stimulant (cocaine) class substances, as well as intermittent use of sedative-hypnotic-anxiolytic class drugs of abuse. The patient had been using up to four bags of heroin with intravenous (IV) administration while participating in a methadone maintenance treatment program (MMTP) receiving 105 milligrams (mg) of methadone daily. He was using one pint of brandy daily together with intermittent use of six milligrams (mg) of Xanax one to two times per week. He was using $20 worth of crack cocaine daily and was tobacco dependent at ½ pack per day. He has no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens. He had a history of prior detoxification and substance use disorder treatments including MMTP (methadone maintenance treatment program) and exposure to 12-step recovery groups. His self-referral for treatment was prompted by multiple stressors including housing, primary support, social environment and other psychosocial domains.

The patient has a history of psychiatric disorder with unspecified bipolar disorder treated with Depakote. He has a history of psychiatric hospitalization with a clinical course best characterized as severe and persistent mental illness. He denied recent suicidal behavior or overdose.

The patient presented with acute co-morbid general medical issues that included diabetes mellitus and poor dentition, missing most of his teeth. Laboratory assessments were unremarkable or normal with a positive drug screen consistent with history.

Evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination that was free of severe psychiatric symptoms. He was generally motivated for treatment and described as cooperative with a full range of affect with apprehension, nervousness, tension, irritability, sleep disturbance, and aches due to the onset of opioid and alcohol withdrawal. Clinical opiate withdrawal scale (COWS) and Clinical Insitute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) scale scores were at nine reflecting mild to moderate withdrawal symptoms. Speech was clear with organized thoughts that were free of delusions. There was no evidence for a formal thought disorder, mania, psychosis or cognitive impairment. The patient denied suicidal or homicidal ideation and did not have perceptual disturbances. Insight was limited with impaired judgment and poor control of impulses. His onset of withdrawal symptoms included anxiety, irritability, insomnia, agitation, nausea, sweats, chills, tremor and body aches.

The patient was admitted to detoxification treatment with a comprehensive detoxification protocol with tapering dosages of Librium and continued use of methadone, and clonidine as needed, and as needed (PRN) medications for comfort, as well as vitamin replacement therapy and use of Depakote for seizure prophylaxis and maintenance treatment of the bipolar mood disorder. He received trazodone to address insomnia. The program provided for case management with referral to sober housing and access to rehabilitation treatment that included comprehensive evidence-based treatments. During detoxification the patient engaged in counseling sessions focusing on education about the disease model of addiction, and, involvement with counseling and milieu activities including peer support and education sessions to motivate the patient to proceed to rehabilitation treatment. Vital signs remained normal during his brief inpatient stay. 

The patient engaged with detoxification treatment; he was cooperative with the tapering dosages of Librium. Withdrawal symptoms remained mild, but persisted with aches, pain, anxiety and insomnia requiring prn (as needed) medications and monitoring. The patient completed his detoxification treatment protocol and was immediately transitioned to rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment. 

Yes, the proposed treatment, Inpatient Admission was medically necessary for this patient.

The requested Inpatient admission and continued treatment could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. The patient in this case was using heroin while participating in a methadone program, together with alcohol and crack cocaine on a daily continuous basis with intermittent use of large amounts of Xanax that did warrant inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring for the duration of the protocol; detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments pertinent to the detoxification treatment episode could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment that was provided at the time of admission.  Moreover, the patient had a positive drug screen that included opioids and benzodiazepines, as well as methadone and cocaine. He had mild and persistent withdrawal symptoms, and, the patient's social environment was not conducive to detoxification in the context of limited insight, impaired judgment and poor control of impulses.

Thus, the adult inpatient detoxification treatment and withdrawal management of this patient's substance use disorder did warrant the inpatient admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level detoxification setting with 24-hour monitoring and use of as needed (PRN) medications. The patient's history of substance abuse (frequency and quantity) reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder and the need for a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management, as the patient was at high risk for treatment failure if the continued detoxification and withdrawal management were to be attempted at a lower level of care. Additionally, the patient presented with a history of severe and persistent mental illness, unspecified bipolar disorder. Therefore, medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published practice guidelines, the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and the scientific literature, referenced below, and, New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews including the appropriate application of the NY (New York) State Office of Addiction Services and Supports (OASAS) Level of Care Determination (LOCADTR) Tool required that the patient in this scenario default to the higher level of care.

The requested benefit of Inpatient Admission was medically necessary and clinically appropriate in this case scenario and is therefore a covered service. The patient's clinical features and treatment dimensions did warrant inpatient level detoxification services thru discharge and did necessitate the monitoring that is provided with inpatient level treatment including the use of comfort medications, together with counseling and educational sessions and peer support. Case management services were critical in this case to motivate the patient to proceed to rehabilitation treatment and formal substance use disorder treatment with a safe and clinically appropriate disposition. Moreover, the admission and the continued substance abuse detoxification treatment through discharge could not have been safely or effectively provided with lower level services, as noted above. Thus, the requested benefit is not excluded under the plan, and should be covered in keeping with prevailing standards of care pertaining to substance use disorder services including the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria and the New York State Office of Addiction Services and Supports (OASAS) Level of Care Determination (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines, referenced below.

summary:
Diagnosis:  Substance Abuse.
Treatment:  Inpatient admission.

The insurer denied the inpatient admission.  The denial is upheld. 

The patient is a male, who received detoxification treatment and presented for inpatient level substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment to address use of stimulants (cocaine), cannabis (marijuana), and alcohol class substances.  The patient was tobacco dependent at one-half pack per day; he had no past history of delirium tremens or withdrawal seizures.  He reported onset of alcohol and marijuana use at a very early age, escalating to daily continuous use together with crack cocaine with up to $100 per day, and alcohol with up to sixteen 24-ounce beers, and daily use of up to $30 worth of marijuana that had resulted in past legal issues and other current psycho-social problems. 

The patient had previously engaged in substance use disorder treatment with relapses.  He had a history of being incarcerated.  He was unemployed and disabled with chronic conditions that included back pain, asthma, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), arthritis and glaucoma with associated treatments.

There was a history of psychiatric disorder and treatment for depression, and the patient has a history of psychiatric hospitalization, but he denied suicidal or self-harming behaviors.

The patient was motivated for rehabilitation treatment.  The patient exhibited fair, but limited insight and fair judgment and control of impulses except when using substances. 

There were no severe symptoms on mental status examination; the patient had no symptoms of mania, psychosis, perception, cognition, or thought disorder.  The patient was described as "groomed" and "cooperative" with good eye contact.  He was depressed and exhibited anxiety and complained of insomnia.  He did not present with post-acute withdrawal symptoms. 

The rehabilitation treatment included focus on coping skills, relapse prevention techniques with identification of triggers, education about the disease model of addiction, and involvement with 12-step recovery groups.  The patient engaged in treatment and intensive services, sober housing, monitoring, and structure provided within the inpatient treatment program.  The patient participated actively with treatment, and showed no significant symptoms or signs of withdrawal, and had no complications of rehabilitation treatment.  The patient participated in activity therapies and other therapeutic interventions to improve insight and life skills.  He received vitamins, and psychotropic medications, Lexapro and trazodone.  Again, the patient was engaged in rehabilitation treatment, and a discharge plan was in place including involvement with 12-step recovery groups and work on a relapse prevention plan.  However, he requested discharge against medical advice due to a dispute over his property. 

No, the proposed treatment of Inpatient Admission was not medically necessary for this patient.

The substance abuse rehabilitation services in this case scenario were amenable to treatment at a lower level of care.  The patient was motivated and able to effectively engage in rehabilitation services, and the patient did not need the structure or monitoring of an inpatient setting or 24-hour monitoring in order to safely and effectively participate in rehabilitation substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment.  There were no biomedical or psychiatric complications, or severe psychiatric symptoms in this case that would have required continued inpatient level services and rehabilitation treatment.  Moreover, the patient had support for the substance use disorder treatment with access to sober housing and peer support, and he was motivated to participate in rehabilitation treatment, as noted.  Thus, the requested benefit of Inpatient Admission was not medically necessary.

This answer is consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published practice guidelines, American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and the scientific literature, referenced below, as well as New York State instruction regarding medical necessity reviews and the application of NY (New York) State OASAS Office of Addiction Services and Supports Level of Care Determination (OASAS LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria, referenced below.

The patient had received detoxification treatment and he was motivated to actively engage in rehabilitation treatment without biomedical complications or significant withdrawal or post-acute withdrawal symptoms.  He had prior exposure to substance use disorder treatment and 12-step recovery principles and was able to engage and participate actively in the treatment plan without complication.  There were no severe psychiatric disturbances or general medical concerns that required inpatient level services, structure or monitoring.  The patient was noted to benefit in all aspects of his treatment plan throughout his stay despite his decision to leave treatment against medical advice.  He had access to sober housing from which substance use disorder treatment could be received.  Thus, the patient's substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment could have been effectively provided at a lower level of care including sober housing, and other supportive services in the community including peer support through 12-step recovery groups such as Alcoholics Anonymous (AA).  Moreover, the application of NY State Office of Addiction Services and Supports Level of Care Determination (OASAS LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines does not support treatment at the inpatient level of care, as the health plan asserts.

without psychotic features)

Progress notes throughout the first two weeks of the last approved month show that the patient and her family participated in an outdoor physical activities program in order to enhance family communication. The patient had passes home during that time. There was no evidence of significant out of control behavior or danger to self.

No, the proposed treatment, Continued Mental Health Residential Level of Care is not medically necessary.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder, recurrent, severe, Generalized Anxiety Disorder, and Cluster B Personality Disorder. 
Treatment: Continued Residential Mental Health Services. 

The insurer denied the Continued Residential Mental Health Services. 
The denial is overturned. 

The patient is a female. She was admitted to a residential treatment center for the treatment of Major Depressive Disorder, recurrent, severe, Generalized Anxiety Disorder, and Cluster B Personality Disorder. The patient's parents wrote letters of appeal. Her history of symptoms and treatments are reported. They state that her treatment at Solstice is saving her life. Prior to admission earlier in the year, she ran into the road and almost killed herself.  Medical records indicate that the patient's inpatient admission was after she ingested 30 to 40 Motrin and Aleve with the intent to commit suicide. She was regretful that the attempt was not successful. She was discharged to a PHP (partial hospitalization program). A counselor writes an email to the patient's parents stating that her level of distress and fluctuating commitment to safety is very significant and she would like to look into programs such as residential, wilderness or therapeutic boarding schools. 

Other hospital records indicate that the patient is seen for worsening suicidal ideation with a plan and is admitted inpatient. A residential program records indicate admission. The patient is diagnosed with Generalized Anxiety Disorder with panic attacks, and Major Depressive Disorder, recurrent, severe. On discharge she is noted to have made gains but demonstrated ongoing difficulty accessing her emotional regulation skills. She struggles with social skills and has a tendency to become overwhelmed by stress. She has pervasive urges to self-harm. She requires a 24-hour clinical milieu and structure. A psychologist conducted a psychological evaluation. The patient has had four inpatient and one PHP (partial hospitalization program) admissions since and has been seen in outpatient therapy and psychiatric medication management. She is diagnosed with Major Depressive Disorder and Generalized Anxiety Disorder. Continued care in a therapeutic/residential setting was recommended. 

Facility records indicate on admission that the patient is transitioning from a wilderness program where she was admitted after a dramatic decline in behavioral and emotional regulation. In that program she was on and off safety for self-harm and tried to run at one point. She would become dehydrated to get attention. Her parents report that she has had depression for a couple of years prior, with suicidal ideation with occasional plans, lack of motivation, insomnia, isolation and poor self-care. She was hospitalized and was in a PHP (partial hospitalization program). She was rehospitalized. She was then sent to wilderness therapy. Unless otherwise indicated, records describe the patient engaging appropriately in treatment. 

At the wilderness therapy program, the patient is put on safety for self-harm with a staple. She stated that she may need to go inpatient because she is not safe and does not trust herself. She had very low water intake and may be sent to the ER (emergency room) for rehydration. She says she thinks about dying all the time. The patient reported a plan to run into traffic to kill herself. She states that she is actively making plans and efforts to kill herself. She stateed that she is seriously contemplating suicide and is very anxious. She becomes agitated and reports suicidal ideation. She presented as highly dysregulated. She eventually had gone for two weeks without acting out. The following month she is seen for urination and incontinence. It is noted that she has not been hydrating sufficiently. She had continued to struggle with physical complaints. Her therapist says she is doing better in therapy. 

A month later, the patient has been refusing to go to bed or go with the team and has been making suicidal gestures. She has struggled since coming back from a home visit. She became dysregulated, and she ran out of the campus and into the street where a car swerved out of her way. She has been on suicide precautions. She reported ongoing suicidal ideation but brighter affect. She complains of depression and is focused on her body image. She presents as emotionally reactive and upset, complaining about her team, saying that she is finding it upsetting to the point of her entertaining suicidal thinking. She is responsive to treatment efforts but is highly reactive. 

The patient had been diagnosed with polycystic ovarian syndrome two months into admission. She also has trench foot and incontinence. She has gained 40 pounds in the past six months. She is doing well with an increase in Lamictal. Abilify will continue to be titrated down. She was noted to take a more measured approach to her medical concerns, demonstrating concern but with more proportion. She was seen by a doctor for a fungal infection on her foot, excessive sweating and possible asthma. Her Abilify is decreased. She was noted to be demonstrating increased stability. A few days later, she is dysregulated in a family meeting regarding some medical issues. She is tearful and complains that she is tired of not knowing what is going on. Her parents are empathic, and she takes comfort. 

The patient is seen for bladder issues. Physical therapy is recommended. She flew home for a pass for a week. Upon return, she is frequently tearful and reports suffering from intolerable depression that she is afraid will not stop. She reports an increase in self harm urges and suicidal ideation. She says that she does not intend to act on them but states that it is really hard, and she is scared. She is very tearful. 

Approximately two weeks later, she presents as being in much better spirits. A few days after she reports ongoing severe depression, distressing enough that at some point she feels she will reattempt suicide. She reports feeling disconnected and hopeless and with a lot of dark thinking. She states that suicidal thoughts have reemerged. She states that she is worried about her thinking, that last night she was thinking about suicide. She reports that she has frequent thoughts of suicide with no specific plan. She is concerned about making it through the weekend without clinical support. She presents as depressed and is tearful. She reports hopelessness and states that life is not worth living. She reports being very depressed. She is prickly, evasive and rude in therapy. She reports having had more suicidal ideation than previously indicated. She did not take her PRN medication (as-needed) last night because she wanted to commit suicide and thought if she felt better, she would decide not to. She stated that she does not have a plan but often muses about ways she could do it. She presents as highly depressed and also gamey. She is on safety for a suicide attempt last weekend. She refuses to go to class, saying that this program is not working, and she needs to go somewhere else. She lies on the floor, saying that she is queasy and refuses to go to the rest room, instead throwing up three times while lying on the floor. Her parents express frustration that she is on too many medications. It is once more explained to them that while the program would like to reduce her medications that cannot happen when she is actively reporting suicidal ideation. She flies home for a pass. 

Upon return, the patient has continued to struggle with motivation, not caring about going up levels. She reports suicidal ideation as recently as the day before, at an intensity of 5, when she can tolerate a 5 or 6. She had self-harm thoughts last week. She is not taking care of her trench foot at night. 

The patient has turned a corner in the last month, taking on leadership roles. She feels good acting under pressure and being a good example. Her energy is lower, likely related to a peer leaving. Some significant changes have happened in terms of family dynamics, taking her out of the role of the acting out child. She has stabilized and is no longer actively suicidal. This would be a good time to undergo medication simplification. She flies home for a pass. 

The patient continues on a Neurontin taper. She feels more anxious and paranoid at times, feeling that everyone is out to get her. She returns from a home visit which she states was great. A discharge summary indicates that at admission the patient reported a history of frequent suicidal ideation with planning. She would reportedly refuse to attend school, was socially withdrawal and had few healthy peer relationships. On admission she was highly suicidal and this continued on and off through much of her stay, As late as the spring, she admitted to saving Tide Pods "just in case," so that if things were to become bad enough she would have an out. She was able to throw them away and acknowledge she no longer felt that way. She initially relied on pathology for identity and connection. She has made the most gains in this area, no longer identifying with her pathology. 

In terms of prognosis, the patient has historically engaged in cycling mood disruptions in which she becomes depressed enough not to try, which is a concern. She will be discharged home and to remote schooling. She was tapered off of Neurontin and Abilify. A decrease In Zoloft led to spikes in anxiety and a suicide attempt. 

Yes, the Continued Resident Mental Health Services was medically necessary. 

Records indicate that the patient continued to require the intensity, safety and restrictiveness of a residential treatment program after her admission. She continued to express and exhibit suicidal ideation and behavior, including stockpiling detergent to ingest, running in front of a car, and keeping a PRN (as-needed) medication so that she would continue to have suicidal ideation. Her history had included a serious overdose with intent and disappointment that she had not succeeded. Previous hospital, PHP (partial hospitalization program) and wilderness therapy admissions, as well as outpatient treatment, had not led to an increase in her ability to keep herself safe. During this admission, she additionally continued to exhibit significant difficulty with self-care, including not adequately hydrating herself leading to urinary issues, not taking adequate care of a fungal infection, and lying on the floor as she repeatedly vomited. It is not until summer that her suicidal ideation and behavior have stabilized enough so that her medications could begin to be simplified, which had been a treatment goal for the treatment team and the patient's parents; an earlier attempt to lower a medication had led to her running into traffic. By the time of discharge, while the patient continued to have issues requiring less intensive treatment, she had made significant gains in her identification as being a sick person who was destined to kill herself, leading to her being able to be safely discharged. The residential admission was medically necessary and provided treatment which led to significant improvement in her condition.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse/Addiction
Treatment: Substance Abuse: Inpatient rehabilitation-Chemical Dependency
The health plan denied the Inpatient chemical dependency rehabilitation stay as not medically necessary. 

The patient was admitted to inpatient rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment to address substance use disorder with stimulants (methamphetamine); cannabis, alcohol; and opioids (heroin). The patient had no history of withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens or other episodes of severe withdrawal symptoms, but did report an inadvertent overdose. The patient had a history of substance use disorder treatment with  most recent prior treatments following the overdose (detoxification only) and detoxification treatment with relapses. The patient was using one and one-half pints of liquor plus beer on a daily basis, and $60 worth of methamphetamine together with a small amount of heroin with intranasal (snorting) administration up to three times per week, and also reported intermittent use of marijuana/cannabis. Substance use had escalated with significant decline in functioning and other consequences within social, occupational, and other psychosocial domains. The patient has no history of psychiatric disorder or treatment. There was no history of psychiatric hospitalization or suicidal or self-harming behavior. The patient had normal vital signs and no severe withdrawal or post-acute withdrawal symptoms. Laboratory assessment was negative or unremarkable. Evaluation on admission for residential level services revealed a mental status examination that was free of severe psychiatric symptoms. Throughout the inpatient stay, the patient was engaged in treatment with intensive services, sober housing, monitoring, and structure provided within the residential treatment program. The patient was discharged against medical advice despite plans to immediately begin residential level treatment. 

The requested health service/treatment of Inpatient Chemical Dependency Rehabilitation Admission is not medically necessary for this patient. The inpatient treatment and other inpatient medical services  could have been safely and effectively provided at a lower level of care. The clinical features and indicated treatment dimensions of this patient's alcohol use disorder, and other substance use disorders, did not require or warrant the structure of an inpatient setting or 24-hour monitoring. summary:
Diagnosis: Alcohol dependence, Nicotine dependence, Cannabis dependence

Treatment: Inpatient hospital stay

The insurer denied coverage for the inpatient hospital stay.

The denial is overturned. 

This is a male patient with a history of alcohol dependence, nicotine dependence, cannabis dependence and hypertension who was admitted for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment due to alcohol, crack/cocaine, and cannabis addiction. The patient reportedly wanted to stop substance use and work on relapse prevention skills. The patient had multiple past inpatient substance detoxification treatments as well as a 14-day inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment.  

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that inpatient treatment is indicated primarily for individuals whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. In this case, this patient reported that it was difficult for him to stop his alcohol, cannabis, and crack/cocaine addiction, and the patient was asking for help in this 24-hour therapeutic substance rehabilitation treatment setting. A few months prior to this admission, the patient reportedly had a 14-day inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment and still was unable to maintain abstinence so he required even more time than the 14 days at this inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment level of care at this admission.  

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), the patient met the criteria for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment as he continued to use large amounts of alcohol, cannabis, and crack/cocaine despite multiple past inpatient substance detoxification. The patient was unable to comply with treatment outside of a 24-hour structured treatment setting. The patient also wanted to work on housing issues and possible employment, and he needed to work on having more sober supports, improve coping skills, work on relapse prevention skills, better identification of triggers, and improve his insight into his addiction. It was reported that after his first week, the patient was looking for long-term treatment after this. It was reported that after the second week, the patient had a drug dream and agreed to the Vivitrol shot to try to curb his cravings. It was reported that after the third week, the patient had a couple of drug dreams, and was trying to work on improving his social supports. It was reported that after the fourth week, the patient was prepared to undertake more long-term treatment.  

The National Institute on Drug Abuse: Principles of Addiction Treatment: A Research Based Guide, reports that research indicates that the best treatment outcomes occur with longer durations of treatment and states that recovery from drug addiction is a long term process.  It also states that treatment techniques to increase motivation for treatment are necessary to prevent dropout rates. In this case, this patient did not learn enough in two weeks of past inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment to maintain abstinence so he required the entire stay in this inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment. Without this structured and supervised therapeutic inpatient rehabilitation treatment setting, the patient likely would have relapsed again quickly.  

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient. 

The carrier's denial of coverage for the inpatient hospital stay should be overturned. The medical necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance use
Treatment: Inpatient substance abuse detoxification
The insurer denied coverage for the inpatient substance abuse detoxification.
The denial is overturned. 

This is a male patient, who was admitted for alcohol detoxification.  He reportedly had withdrawal symptoms including tremors, nausea, vomiting, agitation, anxiety, irritable mood, sweats, headaches, disorientation to time, and tactile disturbances with a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) score as high as 18.  He reportedly was drinking beer daily, and using crack/cocaine and cannabis/hashish.  He reportedly had a positive toxicology for cocaine and benzodiazepines.  He reportedly was put on a Librium protocol for detoxification.  He also had reports of psychiatric hospitalizations, as he had diagnoses of post-traumatic stress syndrome (PTSD) and bipolar disorder.  He reportedly was taking Seroquel.  He was discharged on day 6 of admission with a referral for outpatient treatment.
  
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, currently abuse other substances, or who have very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment.  In this case this patient had been drinking alcohol daily and was also using crack/cocaine, and cannabis/hashish daily, and his toxicology was positive for cocaine and benzodiazepines, as well, which put him at risk for overdose as well as severe, complicated, and life threatening withdrawal.  He also had psychiatric comorbidity with PTSD and bipolar disorder, as he had reports of severe trauma.  

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), the patient did require 24-hour treatment, as he could not safely and effectively be treated in outpatient detoxification settings, as he continued to use alcohol daily and had active withdrawal symptoms including tremors, nausea, vomiting, agitation, anxiety, irritable mood, sweats, headaches, disorientation to time, and tactile disturbances with a CIWA score as high as 18, which put him at high risk for complicated and life threatening withdrawal, which required 24-hour hospital detoxification treatment then.  It was reported that he had the detoxification medication, Librium.  He continued to have reports of alcohol withdrawal as notes on day 3 of admission reported tremors, agitation, and anxiety. 

Notes on day 4 of admission reported tremors and sweats.  Notes on day 5 of admission reported tremors, agitation, anxiety, irritable mood and a CIWA score still as high as 9.  The patient was considered at high risk while still reporting alcohol withdrawal symptoms during the denial period and while still being treated with Librium for detoxification treatment.  He had psychiatric comorbidities and was using other serious substances daily including crack/cocaine.  It was unlikely that he would remain abstinent while still having withdrawal symptoms, so he required the time in this treatment setting to stop withdrawals and decrease the chance that he would relapse again when not in this 24-hour setting and also to prevent possible life threatening withdrawal symptoms.  The risk of life-complicated withdrawal, such as delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use, so he required the entire time in this hospital. 

Inpatient substance detoxification was medically necessary.  It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably or in the best interests of the patient.  

Based on the above, the medical necessity for the inpatient substance abuse detoxification is substantiated.  The insurer's denial is overturned.

summary:
Diagnosis:  Substance Abuse.
Treatment:  Inpatient admission.

The insurer denied the Inpatient admission.  The denial is overturned. 

The patient is a male requesting detoxification treatment and admitted to acute inpatient level care in order to address substance use disorder with opioids (heroin), alcohol, and stimulant (cocaine) class substances, as well as use of sedative-hypnotic-anxiolytic class drug of abuse (Xanax).  The patient had been using up to five bags of heroin together with six to eight beers and occasional use of crack cocaine.  He was using up to 6 mg (milligrams) of Xanax on a daily continuous basis.  He denied history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens or blackouts and denied history of accidental overdose.  He had a history of prior detoxification and substance use disorder treatment with Suboxone/medication assisted treatment of the opioid use disorder.  His self-referral for treatment was prompted by multiple stressors including occupational, primary support, social environment and other psychosocial domains.

The patient has no history of psychiatric disorder and presented without acute co-morbid general medical issues.  Laboratory assessments were unremarkable or normal with a positive drug screen consistent with history.  He has a history of hepatitis C positivity.  The patient is an every-day smoker and tobacco dependent with one pack per day use and 30 pack years.

The patient is single and unemployed with housing.  He did not report trauma or abuse history, or legal issues.  He had social supports from family.

Evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination that was free of severe psychiatric symptoms.  The patient was generally motivated for treatment and described as cooperative with a full range of affect with apprehension, nervousness, tension, irritability, sleep disturbance, and aches due to the onset of opioid and benzodiazepine withdrawal.  Speech was clear with organized thoughts that were free of delusions.  There was no evidence for a thought disorder, mania, psychosis or cognitive impairment.  The patient denied suicidal or homicidal ideation and did not have perceptual disturbances.  Insight was limited with impaired judgment and poor control of impulses.  His withdrawal symptoms included anxiety, irritability, nausea, rhinorrhea, sweats, hot and cold flashes, yawning, tremor and body aches.  COWS (clinical opiate withdrawal scale) score was at 17 indicating moderately severe withdrawal symptoms.

The patient was admitted to detoxification treatment with a comprehensive detoxification protocol with tapering dosages of Suboxone, and clonidine as needed, and prn (as needed) medications for comfort, as well as vitamin replacement therapy.  He had the availability of nicotine replacement and smoking cessation education.  The program provided for case management with referral to sober housing and access to rehabilitation treatment that included comprehensive evidence-based treatments.  During detoxification the patient engaged in counseling sessions focusing on education about the disease model of addiction, and involvement with counseling and milieu activities including peer support and psycho-educational sessions to motivate the patient to proceed to rehabilitation treatment.  Vital signs remained normal during the stay. 

The patient engaged with detoxification treatment; he was cooperative with the tapering dosages of Suboxone.  Withdrawal symptoms gradually diminished, but persisted throughout the stay with aches, pain, anxiety and insomnia.  By the time of discharge, the patient reported mild withdrawal symptoms.  He did not complete the detoxification protocol and was discharged from inpatient level care against medical advice (AMA), and was given a prescription for Suboxone with referral for substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment and continued medication assisted treatment and recommendation for involvement in peer-supported recovery groups.

Yes, the Inpatient admission  was medically necessary for this patient.

The requested Inpatient admission and continued treatment could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario.  The patient in this case was using heroin and Xanax on a daily basis together with alcohol and crack cocaine that did warrant inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring for the duration of the protocol; detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments pertinent to the detoxification treatment episode could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment that was provided at the time of admission.  Moreover, the patient had persistent withdrawal symptoms, and the patient's social environment was not conducive to detoxification, and the patient struggled with withdrawal symptoms during the time interval under review in the context of limited insight, impaired judgment and poor control of impulses.

Thus, the adult inpatient detoxification treatment and withdrawal management of this patient's substance use disorder did warrant the admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level detoxification setting with 24-hour monitoring and use of prn (as needed) medications.  The patient's history of substance abuse (frequency and quantity) together with the severe psychosocial stressors and functional impairments reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder and the need for a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management, as the patient was at high risk for treatment failure if the continued detoxification and withdrawal management were to be attempted at a lower level of care.  Therefore, medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published practice guidelines, ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) Criteria, and the scientific literature, referenced below, and this answer is in keeping with New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews including the application of the NY (New York) State OASAS (Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services) LOCADTR (level of care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) Tool in this case that requires the patient in this scenario default to the higher level of care.

The requested benefit of Inpatient Admission is medically necessary and clinically appropriate in this case scenario and is therefore a covered service.  The patient's clinical features and treatment dimensions did warrant the admission and continued inpatient level detoxification services through discharge and did necessitate the monitoring that is provided with inpatient level treatment including the use of comfort medications, together with counseling and educational sessions and peer support.  Case management services were critical in this case to motivate the patient to proceed to rehabilitation treatment and formal substance use disorder treatment with a safe and clinically appropriate disposition.  Moreover, the admission and the continued substance abuse detoxification treatment through discharge could not have been safely or effectively provided with lower level services, as noted in the answer earlier. Thus, the Inpatient Admission should be covered in keeping with prevailing standards of care pertaining to substance use disorder services including ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) Criteria and the New York State OASAS (Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services) LOCADTR (level of care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines, referenced below.
