The insurer denied coverage for the inpatient detoxification treatment services.
The denial is overturned. 

This is a male patient who was admitted to inpatient alcohol detoxification treatment for alcohol detoxification.  He had withdrawal symptoms including tremors.  He was drinking large amounts of alcohol daily.  He had past inpatient detoxification and inpatient rehabilitation treatment and continued to relapse.  He had past blackouts.  It was reported that he had a sad mood, fatigue, and poor insight.  His alcohol use reportedly interfered with family relationships and finances.  He was put on a Librium taper protocol and given Ativan as needed for alcohol detoxification treatment, as well as Campral, thiamine, folic acid, and multivitamin.  He was discharged with a referral to outpatient rehabilitation treatment. 

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment.  In this case, this patient had been using large amounts of alcohol daily and had active withdrawal including tremors which put him at risk for severe, complicated, and life threatening withdrawal. 

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) he did require 24 hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive setting as he continued to use very large amounts of alcohol daily despite past inpatient detoxification and inpatient rehabilitation treatment, needed detoxification medications including Librium and Ativan for detoxification,  and  continued to drink large amounts of alcohol daily despite negative consequences from alcohol interfering with relational issues, finances, and medical issues.  He reportedly lacked the coping skills to stop alcohol use and needed 24 hour hospital detoxification as he was considered a high risk medically.  He needed 24 hour treatment then as he was at risk for worsened withdrawal symptoms if not in this 24 hour setting then including possible life threatening withdrawal such as delirium tremens which could occur 4 days after alcohol use so he required the entire hospital treatment.  This was a high risk patient who had withdrawal symptoms and was considered a high risk medically for severe, complicated, and life threatening withdrawal.   

Inpatient hospital detoxification treatment was medically necessary.  It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably, with good clinical judgment, or in the best interests of the patient then.

The carrier's denial of coverage for the inpatient detoxification treatment services is overturned.  The medical necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder.

Treatment: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation.

The insurer denied coverage for Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation.

The denial is overturned. 

This male patient has Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). He had depressive symptoms including depressed and irritable mood, low energy and interest, decreased speech, feelings of guilt and remorse, sleeping problems, increased eating, poor concentration, despair, loneliness, and ruminating. He also had a decline in functioning. He tried multiple antidepressant medications including Zoloft, Lexapro, Effexor, Cymbalta, and Wellbutrin, and took antidepressant augmenting medication including Abilify and Seroquel. He also took Depakote. He was taking Vyvanse for ADHD and Klonopin for anxiety. He also tried cognitive behavioral therapy and psychotherapy. Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) therapy (codes 90867 and 90868) was recommended.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved Neurostar TMS therapy for the treatment of depression in October 2008, indicated for the treatment of MDD in patients who failed or who did not have satisfactory improvement from 1 past antidepressant medication at or above minimal effective dose and duration in the current episode. The study did not report that one needed to fail more than 1 antidepressant medication trial. In this case it was reported that he had side effects or lack of efficacy 5 total antidepressant medications with reports including minimal improvement, sexual side effects, partial response, sexual side effects, weight gain, worsened anxiety. Of the medications tried, Zoloft and Lexapro are serotonin reuptake inhibitors, Effexor and Cymbalta are norepinephrine serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and  Bupropion is a dopamine norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor. He also had reports of cognitive behavioral therapy and individual psychotherapy. 

Neurostar TMS Therapy System was the largest multisite (23 centers) randomized sham controlled trial ever conducted with TMS therapy. This was the principal study for the FDA's approval. 

According O'Reardon, patients that had failed to benefit from prior antidepressant drug medications and demonstrated a level of treatment resistance similar to patients treated in studies of electroconvulsive therapy. It also showed clinical efficacy and safety for the treatment of TMS therapy for MDD. 

The 2011 Federally Funded Effective Health Care Program of the Agency for Health Care Research and Quality published comparative effectiveness reviews entitled, "Nonpharmacological Intervention for Treatment Resistant Depression in Adults." It concluded that there was a substituted and well replicated body of evidence for randomized sham controlled clinical trials providing high strength of evidence that TMS therapy procedures were significantly greater in decreasing depression severity and resulting in a greater response rate and remission rate when compared to sham treatment condition and peer reviewed published clinical trials. 

In addition, the American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Major Depressive Disorders considers TMS therapy as an appropriate acute phase option for patients who do not respond adequately to pharmacotherapy or psychotherapy and were considered treatment resistant. 

In this case this patient had a current diagnosis of MDD which is an FDA approved diagnosis for TMS therapy and had depressive symptoms. He was considered a candidate for TMS therapy as he had taken multiple different antidepressant medications with reports of side effects or lack of efficacy. 

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment in the best interest of the patient.

The medical necessity for Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) treatment (codes 90867 and 90868) for major depressive disorder is substantiated. The insurer's denial is overturned.

The patient is a adult male who presented to the emergency department requesting detoxification treatment and was medically screened and admitted to acute inpatient level care in order to address substance use disorder with opioid, alcohol, and sedative-hypnotic-anxiolytic class substance use disorders. The patient had been using up to six shots of vodka together with two sticks of Xanax or Klonopin. He has no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens. He had a history of prior detoxification and substance use disorder treatments and was receiving medication assisted treatment of opioid use disorder with Suboxone. His self-referral for treatment was prompted by multiple stressors and general health concerns.

The patient presented with acute co-morbid general medical issues that included history of hepatitis C and B positivity with normal liver functions and other chronic conditions including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), chronic venous stasis of a lower extremity and mitral valve regurgitation. He was prescribed aspirin (ASA) and pantoprazole. Laboratory assessments were unremarkable or normal with a positive drug screen consistent with history, as well as positivity for tetrahydrocannabinol (THC).

Evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination that was free of severe psychiatric symptoms. He was generally motivated for treatment and described as cooperative with a full range of affect. Speech was clear with organized thoughts that were free of delusions. There was no evidence for a thought disorder, mania, psychosis or cognitive impairment. The patient denied suicidal or homicidal ideation and did not have perceptual disturbances. Insight was limited with impaired judgment and poor control of impulses. His onset of mild withdrawal symptoms included anxiety, motor agitation, nausea, sweats, and tremor, scoring an 8 on the CIWA (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment) scale.

The patient engaged with detoxification treatment; he was cooperative with the tapering dosages of Klonopin and received vitamin replacement therapy. Withdrawal symptoms remained mild, but persisted, requiring PRN (as needed) medication and monitoring. The patient completed the detoxification treatment and was discharged with clinically appropriate aftercare.

Yes, the proposed treatment was medically necessary for this patient.

The requested Inpatient admission and continued treatment could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. The patient in this case was using alcohol and a benzodiazepine on a daily continuous basis that did warrant inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring for the duration of the protocol; detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments pertinent to the detoxification treatment episode could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment that was provided at the time of admission. The patient had mild and persistent withdrawal symptoms, and, the patient's social environment was not conducive to detoxification in the context of limited insight, impaired judgment and poor control of impulses. Additionally, the patient presented with significant medical conditions and was in treatment for opioid use disorder with Suboxone.

Thus, the adult inpatient detoxification treatment and withdrawal management of this patient's substance use disorders did warrant the admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level detoxification setting with 24-hour monitoring and use of PRN medications. The patients history of substance abuse (frequency and quantity) together with the severe psychosocial stressors and functional impairments reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorders and the need for a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management, as the patient was at high risk for treatment failure if the detoxification and withdrawal management were to be attempted at a lower level of care. The patient is a homosexual transgendered female to male. The patient was admitted to the hospital.

The hospital records indicate that the patient was seen in the Emergency Department. The patient had been attending the hospital's Partial Hospital Program (PHP) due to suicidal ideation. The patient stated that the patient had suicidal ideation for a month, and that the patient tried to kill the patient's self two days prior, but it did not work. The patient overdosed on Melatonin. The patient has a history of suicidal ideation and multiple suicide attempts via overdose, hanging and cutting. The patient reported that the patient's first attempt was in the fifth grade. The patient also reported having been sexually assaulted a year ago by a male classmate and having been verbally abused by the patient's father. Prior to the patient's PHP (partial hospitalization program) admission the patient had been treated inpatient for a month. The patient also has a history of non-suicidal cutting, eating disorder and body dysmorphia. The patient reported that the patient's family does not support the patient's being transgender. The patient reported having constant suicidal ideation, and stated that the patient will eventually be successful in killing the patient's self. The patient had not told anyone while the patient was in the PHP (partial hospitalization program) about the patient's suicidal ideation so that the patient could just "off [the patient's self]," but the patient had sent a message about it to a friend who told the patient's parents. The patient did not want to be admitted inpatient, but stated that the patient would definitely kill the patient's self on discharge.

Discharge records indicate that the patient is diagnosed with Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder. The patient felt ready for discharge and denied self-harm or suicidal thoughts. The patient was discharged to a transitional living program.

A letter of appeal states that the patient was accepted to a residential treatment program prior to this admission, but it was denied by insurance. The patient's mood worsened without this level of support, leading to a suicide attempt. The patient was again hospitalized and another attempt at securing residential placement was made. The patient was, however, no longer suited to the initial residential program due to the patient's suicide attempt. The patient was eventually accepted to another residential treatment program. Discharging the patient without the appropriate resources and supports in place would likely have resulted in decompensation, possibly leading to a suicide attempt.

No, the Continued Inpatient Mental Health Treatment was not medically necessary.

The patient did not display behavior requiring inpatient level of treatment. The patient was no longer suicidal, and the patient denied any thoughts of self-harm, homicidal ideation or psychotic symptoms. The patient did not engage in, or express ideation to engage in, any behaviors threatening the patient's or others' safety. The patient did not require intensive staffing and structure to remain safe: the patient did not require any staff escorts, holds or restraints or any PRNs (as needed) or IMs (intramuscular) medications. While the patient was noted to require monitoring for eating disorder behaviors, there was no information indicating that these behaviors were threatening the patient's health or daily functioning at this time; there were no reported concerns about the patient's weight or physical condition. The patient's medications were stable and the patient reported no side effects. The patient was able to engage in program treatment and activities, and did not need intensive staffing in order to engage in treatment. The patient used coping skills when necessary.

The patient's stay was reported to be due to the patient's needing to wait for a residential program bed to open up. There is no information provided to indicate that the patient could not have safely waited for this bed in a less restrictive environment. The patient indicated that the patient could remain safe in any environment except the patient's home. There is no evidence that the patient could not be maintained safely in an alternative placement, such as a group home or short term residential placement, while the patient waited for placement in the longer term treatment setting the patient's team has determined was necessary. There is no indication that the patient could not be safely contained in a setting less restrictive than inpatient during this time.

There is no evidence that the patient required continued inpatient care or that the patient could not be safely maintained during this time in a less restrictive setting.

safe
effective
generally accepted national standard of medical practice
not provided primarily for convenience of the patient or the practitioner
the least intensive and/or most appropriate alternatives among diagnostic and treatment option.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder.
Treatment: Mental health inpatient admission.
The insurer denied coverage for the mental health inpatient admission.
The denial is overturned. 
	   
This is male patient who was admitted to inpatient mental health treatment after going to the Emergency Department (ED) the day before.  He reportedly presented with severe depressive symptoms including depressed mood, 35 pounds (lbs.) of weight loss in one month, poor sleep, hopelessness, anhedonia, poor functioning, and suspicion of non-compliance with medication.  He reportedly had eight panic attacks in one week along with anxiety.  It was reported that he could not handle his worsened depression and anxiety.  He was in outpatient Psychiatric treatment and had worsened depressive symptoms and poor functioning.  He had a reported history of a past psychiatric hospitalization and three prior inpatient rehabilitation treatments.  He reportedly had diagnoses of Major Depressive Disorder, Panic Disorder, and Generalized Anxiety Disorder.  He reportedly took Paxil and was discharged on day 3 of admission.

The Milliman Care Guidelines (MCG) Behavioral Health Inpatient Level of Care Adult-Geriatric criteria reports that patients who present as an imminent danger to self, imminent danger to others, with severe psychiatric or behavioral symptoms, have severely dysfunctional living including inability to care for self, unwillingness to participate voluntarily, or a less restrictive level of care is not feasible, meet criteria for inpatient behavioral health level of care.  

The InterQual  Behavioral Health Adult and Geriatric Psychiatry Inpatient medical necessity criteria reports that if one has assaultive behavior within 24 hours, catatonia, command hallucinations to harm self or others, destruction of property with poor impulse control within 24 hours, disorganized behavior, unstable eating disorder, fire setting, homicidal or suicidal attempt within 24 hours, suicidal or  homicidal ideation with high risk for an attempt, mania, risk of harm to self or others, non-suicidal self-injury and continued danger to self, positive psychotic symptoms with risk of harm to self or others, posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) with risk of harm to self or others, psychomotor agitation and potential for violence, severe social withdrawal and refusing treatment, unavailable support or inability to provide needed care and supervision and there is acute deterioration in functioning then criteria is met for inpatient treatment.  

This patient had an acute deterioration in functioning.  He had severe depressive symptoms in addition to difficulty functioning and significant weight loss.  He was noted to be overwhelmed and had recent stressors.  He had past psychiatric hospitalization and past alcohol and cocaine use so he was considered in need of 24 hour hospital treatment due to severe depressive symptoms and poor functioning with a weight loss of 35lbs. in one month.  He reportedly was in outpatient psychiatric treatment and his depressive symptoms were worsening.  

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Major Depressive Disorders reports that the least restrictive level of care for safe and effective treatment is appropriate and that patients with inability to adequately care for basic needs are candidates for hospitalization. This patient reportedly had significant weight loss in one month so that was specific evidence that he had inability to care of his needs and also had severe depressive symptoms also reported including depressed mood and feelings of hopelessness.  

It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably or in the best interests of the patient then.  

The carrier's denial of coverage for the mental health inpatient admission is overturned.  The medical necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance abuse.
Treatment: Inpatient substance abuse treatment.
The insurer denied the inpatient substance abuse treatment.
The denial is overturned.

The patient is a adult male. He presented to the emergency department requesting detoxification treatment and was admitted to acute inpatient level care in order to address substance use disorder with opioid (heroin) and stimulant (cocaine) class substances. The patient had been using up to 10 bags of heroin with IV (intravenous) administration as well as four bags of cocaine daily. His use of heroin had escalated and he was unable to cut down due to severe withdrawal symptoms.

The patient had a history of prior detoxification and substance use disorder rehabilitation treatments with relapses. His self-referral for treatment was prompted by multiple stressors including occupational, primary support, housing, social environment and other psychosocial domains, and he had somatic complaints that included abdominal cramps and nausea with withdrawal symptoms from heroin including anxiety, irritability, body aches, joint pain, gastrointestinal upset (nausea and diarrhea), rhinorrhea and tremors.

The patient has no history of a psychiatric disorder and denied past history of suicidal or self-harming behaviors.

The patient presented without acute co-morbid general medical issues. He had a history of asthma with a rescue inhaler and stage 3 chronic kidney disease. Laboratory assessments were unremarkable or normal with a positive drug screen consistent with history.

The patient is married and unemployed with family support that included living with his spouse. There were no current legal issues but the patient has a history of incarceration and legal arrests. He denied trauma history or family history of substance use or mental disorder.

The patient's evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination that was free of severe psychiatric symptoms. He was generally motivated for treatment and described as cooperative with a full range of affect. Speech was clear with organized thoughts that were free of delusions. There was no evidence for a thought disorder, mania, psychosis or cognitive impairment. The patient denied suicidal or homicidal ideation and did not have perceptual disturbances. Insight was limited with impaired judgment and poor control of impulses. His onset of withdrawal symptoms had initially included anxiety, irritability, agitation with tremors, sweats, gastrointestinal upset and body/muscle aches.

The patient was admitted to detoxification treatment with a comprehensive detoxification protocol with tapering dosages of methadone, and prn (as needed) medications for comfort including clonidine, as well as vitamin replacement therapy. The program provided for case management with referral to sober housing and access to rehabilitation treatment that included comprehensive evidence-based treatments. During detoxification, the patient engaged in counseling sessions focusing on education about the disease model of addiction and involvement with counseling and milieu activities including peer support and education sessions to motivate the patient to proceed to rehabilitation treatment. Vital signs remained normal during his brief stay.

The patient engaged with detoxification treatment; he was cooperative with the tapering dosages of methadone. Withdrawal symptoms remained mild and resolved after the first two days of treatment. The patient completed the detoxification treatment and accepted referral for rehabilitation treatment. There were no complications during his inpatient stay. 

Yes, the inpatient substance abuse treatment was medically necessary for this patient.

The requested inpatient admission and continued treatment could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. The patient in this case was using heroin, together with cocaine with IV (intravenous) administration of heroin in large quantities on a daily continuous basis that did warrant the admission for inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring for the duration of the protocol. Detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments pertinent to the detoxification treatment episode could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment that was provided at the time of admission. Moreover, the patient had a positive drug screen that was consistent with history. He had mild and persistent withdrawal symptoms through day 2. The patient's social environment was not conducive to detoxification in the context of limited insight, impaired judgment and poor control of impulses.

Thus, the adult inpatient detoxification treatment and withdrawal management of this patient's substance use disorder did warrant the admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level detoxification setting with 24-hour monitoring and use of prn (as needed) medications and other medical services. The patient's history of substance abuse (frequency and quantity) together with the severe psychosocial stressors and functional impairments reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder and the need for a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management, as the patient was at high risk for treatment failure if the detoxification and withdrawal management were to have been attempted at a lower level of care. Therefore, medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published practice guidelines, ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) Criteria, and the scientific literature, referenced below, and with New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews including the appropriate application of the NY (New York) State OASAS (Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (level of care determination) Tool that requires the patient in this scenario default to the higher level of care.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance use and Shortness of breath. 

Treatment: Inpatient admission.

The insurer denied coverage for the inpatient admission.

The denial is overturned. 

This is a male patient who was admitted to the hospital due to shortness of breath, severe pain, and it was reported that he was retching, was an active cocaine user, and also had alcohol use.  The patient had multiple medical issues including poorly controlled immunocompromising illness, anemia secondary to alcohol induced bone marrow suppression, severe malnutrition including being cachectic, alcohol gastritis, and a history of multiple hospitalizations for falls.  It was reported that the patient had a Medical Intensive Care Unit (MICU) stay for severe cellulitis which required surgical intervention.  The patient reportedly had a recent substance rehabilitation treatment and left against medical advice (AMA).  It was reported that the patient's wife brought the patient to this hospital.  The patient was put on an Ativan protocol for detoxification, intravenous (IV) thiamine, seizure precautions, and antacids.  However, the patient left against medical advice (AMA) on day 2 of admission.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment.  It also states that patients with past complicated or life threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens are in need of inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal and reports that patients with comorbid medical condition that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification.  

In this case, this patient could not safely be treated in a less restrictive detoxification treatment level of care other than an inpatient hospital treatment as he was at risk for severe, complicated, and life threatening withdrawal due to alcohol use, and he reportedly had comorbid medical issues complicating the management of withdrawal as he had a significant medical history of poorly controlled immunocompromising illness, anemia secondary to alcohol induced bone marrow suppression, severe malnutrition including being cachectic, alcohol gastritis, and had a history of multiple hospitalizations for falls, as well as a past medical intensive care unit (MICU) stay for severe cellulitis which required surgical intervention.  The patient reportedly presented with shortness of breath, retching, and severe pain.  The patient was considered a medical risk due to his multiple medical issues and was considered in need of 24-hour hospital treatment for detoxification as he was put on an Ativan protocol and seizure precautions.  The patient relapsed shortly after leaving inpatient substance rehabilitation against medical advice (AMA).  The patient could not maintain abstinence outside of a 24-hour setting for detoxification treatment.  The risk of life complicated withdrawal such as delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use so this patient required inpatient detoxification protocol treatment.

Based on the review of the medical record and literature, inpatient admission was medically necessary for this patient. 

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient. 

The carrier's denial of coverage for the inpatient admission should be overturned.  The medical necessity is substantiated.

The requested benefit of inpatient substance use disorder treatment is medically necessary and clinically appropriate in this case scenario, and should therefore be covered in this case scenario. Indeed, the patient's clinical features and treatment dimensions did warrant inpatient level detoxification and other medical services thru discharge, and did necessitate the monitoring that is provided with inpatient level treatment including the use of comfort medications, together with counseling and educational sessions and peer support. Case management services were critical in this case to motivate the patient to proceed to rehabilitation treatment and formal substance use disorder treatment with efforts to achieve a safe and clinically appropriate disposition with sober housing.

Moreover, the admission and the continued substance abuse detoxification treatment through discharge could not have been safely or effectively provided with lower level services, as noted in the answer to question 2. Thus, the requested benefit is not excluded under the plan, and should be covered in keeping with prevailing standards of care pertaining to substance use disorder services including ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) Criteria and the New York State OASAS (Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (level of care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) 3.0 Criteria, referenced below.

summary:
Diagnosis: Obsessive Compulsive Disorder and emotional dysregulation.
Treatment: Partial Hospitalization Mental Health Treatment, Service Code F42.2.
The insurer denied coverage for the Partial Hospitalization Mental Health Treatment, Service Code F42.2.

The denial is overturned. 

This patient, who identifies as a transgender male, was admitted to mental health partial hospital program due to severe obsessive compulsive symptoms and emotional dysregulation. The patient reportedly had intrusive thoughts, compulsive ritualistic and checking behavior including sometimes taking 4 hours prior to work which resulted in inability to work and also to have medical leave of absences at school. The patient also reportedly had self-injurious behavior, and physical aggression and anger; and had police escorts to the Emergency Room (ER) in restraints. The patient had reports of gender and body image issues which worsened obsessive compulsive symptoms and emotional dysregulation. The patient reportedly had a diagnosis of Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD), as well as Autism Spectrum Disorder and Body Dysmorphic Disorder. The patient reportedly had psychiatric hospitalizations including 3 days while in this partial hospital program. The patient had medication management and intensive treatment 5 days per week while living in a supportive living facility. The patient was referred to this specialized partial hospital program by the outpatient psychologist who reportedly was doing 2 sessions per day of treatment and recommended more intensive treatment. 
 
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Obsessive Compulsive Disorders reports that the least restrictive level of treatment for safe and effective treatment is appropriate and that longer durations of treatment are often necessary to treat OCD as this is a difficult disorder to treat. This was the case for this patient. 

In this case, this patient required at least this level of care and for the allotted duration as the patient had severe obsessive compulsive symptoms, emotional dysregulation, self-injurious behavior including head banging, physical aggression, gender and body image issues contributing to worsened symptoms, poor functioning including inability to work or remain in school, and also required multiple psychiatric hospitalizations. It also was reported that the patient was attending outpatient sessions and required more intensive daily treatment. This patient had severe obsessive compulsive symptoms significantly interfering with functioning and also putting self and others at risk of danger. The patient had reports of suicidal statements. It was reported that while in this partial hospitalization program setting, the patient had such severe intrusive thoughts and gender dysphoria and sexual orientation issues that the patient began head banging on the counter, crying, and yelling and required a police escort and 3-day hospital stay. The patient reportedly had extreme guilt and shame which exacerbated emotional dysregulation leading to self-destructive behaviors. There was a family history of suicide which also increased the suicidal risk for this patient. The patient reportedly was discharged to another facility for further intensive mental health treatment. This was a high risk patient with severe obsessive compulsive symptoms, gender issues, emotional dysregulation, and self-destructive behaviors with inability to function. The patient also required a 3-day hospital stay during partial hospitalization program treatment. Thus, the patient required at least this partial hospital program level of care treatment.

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient. 

The medical necessity for the Partial Hospitalization Mental Health Treatment, Service Code F42.2 is substantiated.  The insurer's denial should be overturned.

summary:
Diagnosis: Overdose
Treatment: Inpatient admission
The insurer denied the inpatient admission.
The denial is upheld. 

The patient is a female teen with medical history significant for cannabis use disorder, adjustment disorder with depressed mood, disruptive mood dysregulation, self-harming behavior, and possible major depressive disorder. She presented to the ED (emergency department) after having ingested an unknown amount of risperidone in an attempt at suicide six hours earlier.

The patient's vital signs included temperature 97.8, heart rate 132, respiratory rate 18, and blood pressure 126/87. She was noted to be somnolent. Lab work was obtained including toxicology, an electrocardiogram was obtained read as normal by the on-call cardiologist, and Poison Control was contacted with recommendations for admission for observation. Concerns included cardiac arrhythmia, hypotension, somnolence, extrapyramidal symptoms, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome. She was admitted to the PICU (pediatric intensive care unit). Admission orders included 1:1 observation, monitoring for complications of the ingestion, continuous cardiopulmonary monitoring, IV (intravenous) fluids at 1.5 maintenance, repeat lab studies including creatine kinase, Social Work consultation, and Psychiatry consultation.

Approximately twelve hours after the ingestion, the patient remained somnolent but denied suicidal/homicidal ideation, serial electrocardiogram studies were normal, and labs were unremarkable. She was evaluated by Psychiatry, with recommendations to restart her risperidone routinely at night and refer to outpatient mental health services. Inpatient psychiatric admission was not deemed necessary. After having been cleared medically and by Psychiatry, as she was preparing to discharge home, she had an episode of suspected dystonia with retrocollis and oculogyric crisis while remaining fully conscious and able to follow commands.

The discharge was canceled, and the patient returned to continuous cardiopulmonary monitoring and neurochecks every two hours. She did well overnight with no further episodes of dystonia. She was deemed stable for discharge with appropriate outpatient follow-up.

No, the Inpatient admission was not medically necessary. The patient could have been safely managed at lower level of care such as observation.

Risperidone is an atypical, or second-generation, antipsychotic that is used for both psychotic and non-psychotic disorders such as disruptive disorders. The main features of acute toxicity include tachycardia and dystonic reactions, with other cardiac and neurologic reactions less likely. Extrapyramidal symptoms may be severe, typically resolving following treatment with an anticholinergic agent. For patients with acute toxicity, recommendations include observation following extrapyramidal symptoms in case of recurrence. Overall, outcomes from overdose are typically favorable, with minimal risk of major toxicity.

In the case of this patient, she had been observed in the hospital setting following her ingestion of an unknown amount of risperidone and was preparing for discharge when she developed an acute dystonic reaction. She remained in the hospital overnight for further monitoring with no recurrence of dystonia. The care that the patient was given, including continuous cardiopulmonary monitoring and frequent neurologic evaluation, did not merit acute inpatient hospitalization. She could have been safely managed at lower level of care, including the overnight stay after the acute dystonia.

summary:
Diagnosis: Depression And Substance Abuse.
Treatment: Continued Residential Mental Health Treatment.
The insurer denied the Continued Residential Mental Health Treatment.
The denial is upheld. 

The patient is an adolescent male. He was referred for residential mental health treatment in order to address behavioral disturbances in the context of a history of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)-inattentive type, parent-child relational problems, and co-occurring cannabis and alcohol and tobacco/nicotine use disorders associated with impaired functioning and problematic behaviors at school and home.

The patient presented with longstanding and worsening issues with self-esteem, confidence, and relationship problems together with stressors within the primary support, educational and social environment domains; the patient has been in past treatment settings with lower-level treatment with continued behavioral disturbance and high-risk behaviors that included stealing from his parents, lying, defiance of authority figures and bouts of anger.

The patient was referred to the residential treatment following Wilderness Treatment. The referral and admission to residential treatment was recommended in order to address the core symptoms of the co-morbid psychiatric disorders of ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) and mood disorder and co-occurring substance use disorders, and to address relationship problems including parent-child relational problems and his lack of boundary control and problematic behaviors that had persisted despite the best effort of his parents and community providers.

The patient was referred and admitted to the Residential Treatment. The patient underwent comprehensive evaluation with treatment planning that included therapeutic interventions to improve coping skills and self-esteem, as well as individual and group and family therapy to address the co-morbid disorders, and programming that would target his substance use disorder. The treatment plan included the goals of improved coping; breaking the cycle of self-destructive behaviors including anger issues and impulsive aggression; and the development of healthy relationships and functioning.

The program focused on organizational skills; self-care; peer relationships; and other life skills as well as behavioral and emotional regulation with milieu, individual, group, family, and other interventions aimed at improving life skills. The patient struggled with treatment and was dismissive at first, but gradually participated actively in the treatment plan and worked on therapeutic, social, and emotional functions in the context of a therapeutic milieu with a residential level of structure consistent with a behavioral health program and setting that included ongoing medication management with a psychiatrist.

No, the Continued Residential Mental Health Treatment was not medically necessary for this patient.

The patient was noted to be engaged in treatment and capable of working with the clinical providers and family to address the remaining issues to include relationship and interpersonal functioning with authority figures, peers, and family, as well as continued treatment with Medication Management and other clinically appropriate therapeutic interventions to address the co-occurring psychiatric and substance use disorders. Therefore, the residual symptoms of the psychiatric disorders; and problems with psychosocial, educational and daily functioning were amenable to treatment in a less restrictive environment with lower level services and the monitoring, structure and intensity of residential services were no longer medically necessary, as indicated by the patient's progress and engagement in the ongoing treatment of his co-occurring disorders.

In summary, the patient's treatment could have been reasonably and effectively provided with lower level services in a less restrictive treatment environment. The patient's psychosocial stressors were not so severe to prevent ongoing assessment and treatment at a lower level of care in this case scenario. Moreover, there are no general medical issues, no co-occurring substance use disorder treatment issues, and no other clinical features that would have warranted continued residential level treatment or 24-hour monitoring in this case scenario.

summary:
Diagnosis: Suicidal Ideation With Impairment In Functioning
Treatment: Mental Health Residential Treatment
The insurer denied the Mental Health Residential Treatment.
The denial is overturned. 

The patient is a male. He was admitted residential treatment center. The patient's parents write an undated letter of appeal stating that any services provided cannot be safely and satisfactorily provided at home or through the use of a virtual PHP (partial hospitalization program) model. During this week alone, they witnessed their son have a severe panic attack during a family therapy session, requiring the session to be stopped and his being removed from programming for the rest of the day. These panic attacks have resulted in past hospitalizations. The parents are not equipped to handle them at home.

The patient's current medication has recently been modified and his diagnoses are still unmanaged. He has also struggled greatly with his academics, resulting in a significant setback. Virtual models would require him to isolate in his room for at least eight hours per day, which would only exacerbate his symptoms of anxiety and depression. He also has a 504 plan around him being blind in one eye: long periods of screen time are detrimental to his visual health.

Another undated letter states that since the last letter, the patient has had several significant struggles, particularly with his medication. He has been experiencing dissociative feelings which leave him unable to do schoolwork or participate in some of the programming. It has brought back anxiety, OCD (obsessive compulsive disorder) and suicidal ideation. His Zoloft has been lowered twice over the past two weeks and a medication change is being considered. He is not stable.

Facility records indicate that the patient reports that his intrusive thoughts continue to be intense and constant and difficult to reframe. He states that he had a panic attack in the last family session, with sweating and hyperventilation. His mother's yelling affected him and he felt awful. The patient's therapist points out that the patient is now doing things differently and expressing himself instead of bottling things up. He has recently described dissociating more. The patient tries to control his mother's responses which perpetuates crippling anxiety. He struggles to stay present.

Yes, the Mental Health Residential Treatment is medically necessary.

Records indicate that the patient continues to display behaviors which are concerning for his ability to maintain safety, appropriately interact with others, and use treatment for further progress to be made. He discloses new information regarding Obsessive Compulsive Disorder symptoms which requires reassessment, changes his treatment plan and has a negative impact on his ability to function. He reports a pattern of unmanageable obsessive thoughts/ruminations tied to suicidal ideation. He is noted to be in danger of uncontrolled suicidal ideation until these symptoms are better controlled. He also reports apparent medication side effects which leave him struggling with dissociation, depersonalization and derealization.  At this time he also reports suicidal ideation. He is unable to engage in a family session due to his symptoms. The patient reports continuing dissociative symptoms and is unable to engage in an EMDR (eye movement desensitization and reprocessing) session.

The patient displays and reports significant symptoms, some newly disclosed, which require the intensity, structure and safety of residential treatment to be adequately assessed, monitored and treated.

The patient requires the intensity and safety of residential treatment in order to monitor him for suicidal ideation and behavior; provide a consistent, structured and intensive treatment environment for him to begin to acknowledge, address and stabilize significant symptoms, some newly disclosed, including obsessions, compulsions, suicidal ideation, dissociation, depersonalization and derealization; be monitored for medication changes which have led to significant symptoms and treatment disruption; and prepare him and his parents for understanding and coping with these symptoms/conditions prior to discharge.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse/Addiction. 
Treatment: Substance Abuse: Inpatient. 
The insurer denied inpatient substance abuse treatment for medical necessity. 
The denial was upheld.

The patient is a male referred for detoxification of alcohol use disorder. The patient was using alcohol with use of one liter of liquor and use of cocaine. He reported at least seven prior substance use treatments with detoxification episodes with relapse. 
The patient provided no history of severe alcohol withdrawal symptoms. His vital signs were normal, and his Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) scale score was 5 with mild symptoms. His chronic conditions included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with asthma/bronchitis, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), Lumbago, and hypertension. He was medically screened and cleared for admission to detoxification treatment. 
There was psychiatric comorbidity diagnosed in this case best characterized as unspecified schizophrenia. He had a history of inpatient mental health stays with non-adherence to his medications. 
The patient was admitted for inpatient detoxification following the assessment for safety issues and medical clearance. He received vitamin replacement therapy, and other supportive measures including as needed (PRN).He was discharged with completion of the detoxification treatment with referral for appropriate aftercare and rehabilitation.
At issue is the medical necessity of Inpatient Substance Abuse Treatment: Medically Supervised Inpatient Detoxification.
The health plan's determination of medical necessity is upheld in whole.
The requested health service/treatment of Inpatient Substance Abuse Treatment: Medically Supervised Inpatient Detoxification was not medically necessary for this patient.
The patient in this case presented with continuous daily use of alcohol and cocaine. He did not have a history of complications from withdrawal or present with severe symptoms of withdrawal or a co-occurring psychiatric disorder or show abnormal findings on examination. He did not pose a safety risk that would have warranted the admission and continued inpatient level services.
The patient displayed no disturbance of mental status. The patient had been evaluated and cleared with regard to safety concerns in the emergency department and did not show evidence for suicidal or aggressive behavior or risk, severe cognitive impairment or psychosis, perceptual disturbance, or general medical concerns that would have warranted an inpatient level admission and treatment.
Thus, the requested health service/treatment of Inpatient Substance Abuse Treatment: Medically Supervised Inpatient Detoxification, was not medically necessary.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Use. 
Treatment: Residential Treatment Center Care.

The insurer denied coverage for the Residential Treatment Center Care.  The denial is overturned. 

This is a male patient who was admitted to inpatient substance residential treatment for alcohol rehabilitation. He reportedly was drinking more alcohol with increased frequency. He had hypertension, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), and diabetes. He reportedly continued to drink increased amounts and frequency of alcohol despite his reports of past outpatient substance treatment. He attended individual, group, and family therapy prior to discharge. 

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that inpatient treatment is indicated primarily for individuals whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. 

In this case, this patient was considered in need of 24-hour substance rehabilitation treatment for the time period under review as he was using larger amounts of alcohol more frequently and it interfered with both occupational and interpersonal functioning.  He reportedly was observed to be slurring his speech at work and was suspended for reports of alcohol intoxication while at work. It was reported that he was drinking alcohol late the night before. He also had a marital separation and was living separate from his young son due to alcohol use. He reportedly could not stop use on his own although he tried. 

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), he met criteria for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment as he continued to use larger amounts of alcohol more frequently despite negative consequences including being suspended from his occupation and also was separated from his wife and child. He reportedly lacked coping skills to maintain abstinence, needed to better identify relapse triggers, needed motivation for change, needed sober supports, better decision making and impulse control, and needed to develop relapse prevention skills. He was unable to stop alcohol use without being in a sober and supervised therapeutic inpatient substance residential setting then. Without this structured and supervised therapeutic inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment he likely would have relapsed quickly and had more negative consequences due to use. The National Institute on Drug Abuse: Principles of Addiction Treatment: A Research Based Guide - reports that the best treatment outcomes occur with longer durations of treatment. It also states that recovery from drug addiction is a long term process and that treatment techniques to increase motivation for treatment are necessary to prevent dropout rates. 

This patient required this 24-hour rehabilitation treatment, as he was at high risk to continue use of alcohol and at higher amounts. He required this 24-hour therapeutic substance rehabilitation treatment setting to develop the necessary skills for abstinence. He continued to be at high risk for relapse and required the structured and supervised therapeutic rehabilitation setting then. 

Inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment for the time period under review was medically necessary. It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably or in the best interests of the individual.

The carrier's denial of coverage for the Residential Treatment Center Care is overturned. The medical necessity is substantiated.

There was no documented change in the member's condition overall that had prompted the transfer, other than the closing of her residence.  There were no documented recent hospitalizations, emergency room visits, health care provider encounters or other encounters that prompted the change in placement.

Hearing has been noted to be adequate.  She has been verbal and able to communicate her needs.  She was noted to be a little anxious, which was attributed to the change to a new environment. She has been continent of bowels.  There has been no leg edema.  There have been no significant pain issues.  X-rays of her left knee showed no acute findings.  She has been risperidone, sertraline, aspirin, famotidine, atorvastatin, eye drops, topical analgesics, oral acetaminophen and vitamins.

summary:
Diagnosis: Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and Marijuana abuse

Treatment: Inpatient residential treatment

The insurer is denied coverage for inpatient residential treatment.

The denial is upheld. 

This male patient has a history of nicotine abuse, marijuana abuse, and oppositional defiant disorder (ODD). He presented to the rehabilitation facility because of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and marijuana abuse. His parents noted that he had trouble making and keeping friends. He was also verbally violent towards his mother. The patient was admitted to receive residential treatment services. During the admission the patient participated in group and individual therapy sessions. A psychological assessment was performed. The patient was diagnosed with generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), unspecified depressive disorder, a nonverbal learning disorder, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). He was on 150 milligrams (mg) of oral Wellbutrin a day. The patient was able to function well in the program. He did make some errors with judgement and decision making but was able to gain insight to improve decision making. The patient was discharged to another residential treatment facility for further care.

The American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry (AACAP) Practice Parameters for the Assessment and Treatment of Children, Adolescents, and Adults with Oppositional Defiant Behaviors reports that one can consider other out of home community based alternatives to residential treatment such as therapeutic foster care or respite care but there is no mention of wilderness programs. Wilderness programs are an adventure based therapy with use of wilderness for purpose of therapeutic interventions often using the survival approach which this facility used. The aim is to become more self-reliant and have more self-respect. This is not considered a standard treatment for children with oppositional defiant behaviors. Also, the American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that residential treatment is indicated primarily for individuals who do not meet clinical criteria for hospitalization but whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. For these individuals, residential facilities provide a safe and substance-free environment in which residents learn individual and group living skills for preventing relapse. The duration of residential treatment should be dictated by the length of time necessary for the patient to meet specific criteria that would predict his or her successful transition to a less structured, less restrictive treatment setting.  In this case it appeared that this patient required a sober therapeutic residential treatment setting to learn better coping skills, improve identification of relapse triggers, improve insight and relapse prevention skills, increase sober supports, improve decision making, have better impulse control, decrease behavioral and mood symptoms as he was at risk for dangerous behavior if not in a residential treatment setting as evidenced by selling cannabis and purchasing fake money to buy substances from drug dealers and he reportedly had threatening behavior. However, this wilderness program was not considered a clinically licensed residential treatment due to lack of nursing staff and lack of psychiatric assessments on site.  

The health plan did act reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient.

The carrier's denial of coverage for the inpatient residential treatment is upheld.  The medical necessity is not substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Alcohol/substance Detoxification

Treatment: inpatient substance abuse treatment

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient substance abuse treatment

The denial is overturned

This patient is a male who was admitted for inpatient hospital treatment for alcohol/substance detoxification treatment.  The patient reportedly had alcohol withdrawal symptoms including agitation, sweats, nausea/vomiting, headache, tactile and auditory hallucinations, light sensitivity, elevated heart rate, disorientation to date, and had a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment of Alcohol (CIWA) of 14.  The patient reportedly was drinking 1 pint of vodka per day and started alcohol use at an early age.  The patient reportedly was using $200 worth of crack/cocaine per day and also using Xanax.  The patient reportedly had a recent inpatient detoxification.  The patient was put on a Librium protocol.  The patient had alcohol withdrawal symptoms again with a CIWA score of 14.  The patient was disruptive on the floor, noncompliant with rules and regulations including not wearing a mask and walking barefoot.  The patient left against medical advice (AMA). 

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment.  In this case, this patient had been drinking large amounts of alcohol daily with daily crack/cocaine use and Xanax use putting him at high risk for life threatening withdrawal and also for overdose or worsened medical issues.  

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), the patient required 24-hour hospital treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated in a less restrictive detoxification setting as he continued to use large amounts of alcohol daily despite medical issues and he required and needed detoxification medication to modify withdrawal and needed 24-hour treatment then as he was at risk for worsened withdrawal symptoms if not in this 24-hour setting. It was reported that the patient was put on a Librium protocol for detoxification. The risk of life-complicated withdrawal such as delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use so this patient required the entire time as he had Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment of Alcohol (CIWA) scores of 14 on both days and has active symptoms of moderate withdrawal. 

The patient also had comorbid medical issues.  The patient was considered a high medical risk.  The Office of Addiction Services and Supports (OASAS) criteria also for medically managed detoxification includes a CIWA of 12 or more and hallucinations within 24 hours; this patient had both of these criteria as his CIWA score was 14 and he had tactile hallucinations and auditory hallucinations.  The patient continued to use large amounts of alcohol daily and large amounts of crack/cocaine daily as well as Xanax despite a recent inpatient hospitalization.  The patient was considered a high risk patient medically and required 24-hour hospital treatment. 

The coverage for inpatient alcohol/substance detoxification is considered medically necessary for this patient. 

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient.  

Based on the above, the medical necessity for the inpatient alcohol/substance detoxification is substantiated. The insurer's denial should be overturned.

He was admitted to acute inpatient level services with severe symptoms of depression and suicidal ideation with plans to hang or shoot himself. The patient's admission had been precipitated by the worsening symptoms of depression with nonadherence with his medication and increasing use of alcohol with onset of suicidality.
The patient has a history of multiple prior admissions for psychiatric treatment for schizoaffective disorder and/or major depressive disorder with suicidal behavior, and had been in outpatient treatment with non-compliance with treatment in the community.
There were no acute general medical issues in this case, and laboratory assessments, a chest x-ray and an electrocardiogram (EKG) were normal or unremarkable with a negative drug screen consistent with his history. There was evidence of malnutrition or anemia with a low hemoglobin.
The patient is single, unemployed, and homeless living in a men's shelter. There was no mention of trauma history or legal issues in this case. He had two children that he had not seen in seven years which was a prominent clinical feature of his depression. He had no social supports.
On Mental Status Examination on admission, the patient was motor retarded, guarded with poor eye contact, and dysphoric mood and flat affect. He displayed depressed mood with slowed mentation with thought blocking. He had decreased concentration, energy, appetite, sleep, and volition. His speech was coherent with mental confusion and disorganized thought processing and morbid thought content with hopelessness, helplessness, worthlessness and suicidality. Insight and judgment were limited and impaired.
The patient was admitted to acute inpatient level care after medical screening in the emergency department. The patient's treatment plan included safety-monitoring, access to group and milieu therapies, and resumption of medication to address mood disturbance and the thought disorder. He had the availability of nicotine and vitamin replacement therapy. The patient was initially depressed and socially withdrawn. However, he was increasingly cooperative with staff and became medication adherent with use of Depakote, Prozac and Abilify, titrated as clinically appropriate. The patient tended to isolate with minimal participation in the therapeutic activities. His depression and thought disorder persisted, and he remained anxious and depressed requiring as needed (PRN) medication for anxiety and agitation. The patient remained restless, motor agitated and anxious with irritable dysphoria and labile affect requiring ongoing re-direction from staff and safety monitoring. His thoughts were disorganized with persistent depressive ruminations focused on his children. He had not had significant withdrawal symptoms and was not interested in referral for rehabilitation treatment of the alcohol use disorder or smoking cessation.
The patient was noted to exhibit improving mood and diminished anxiety. He was increasingly better with his functioning including less resistance to returning to his shelter.
A discharge plan was completed including plans for after care and return to the community. At the time of discharge, the patient was better focused, calmer, and displaying better judgment with improved mood and brighter affect without evidence for suicidal intent or plan. Discharge occurred with clinically appropriate aftercare in collaboration with community providers to include mental health services with a safety plan, as well as recommendations to address the co-occurring substance use disorders with tobacco and alcohol.
The health plan documents including case notes and criteria  and appeal documents were reviewed, as well as correspondence from the health plan and the treatment facility. The dates under review were denied certification of coverage by the health plan for continued inpatient level treatment on the basis of medical necessity. This case is a New York mandated review.
The issue under review is continued inpatient mental health stay.
The requested health service/treatment of the continued inpatient mental health stay is medically necessary for this patient.
The patient's symptoms of mood and thought disorder together with continued risk of impulsive behavior and suicidal risk prompted the necessity for continue acute inpatient level structure and monitoring through discharge. The case is complicated by active substance use and non-compliance with treatment and medication adherence problems in the context of alcohol use and a history of suicidal behavior. The residual symptoms of mood disorder and thought disorder; risk for suicidal behavior and non-compliance, co-occurring substance use disorder, and treatment issues related to arranging a safe and appropriate discharge plan warranted the continued services at an acute inpatient level of care to include safety monitoring and maintaining abstinence from alcohol. The inpatient continued stay through discharge was therefore clinically appropriate and medical necessary for continued inpatient level structure and 24-hour monitoring through the day of discharge, when the patient had reached a level of stability that he could return to the community shelter with clinically appropriate follow-up and aftercare.

Treatment: 5 Days/Units of Inpatient Substance Abuse Services.

The insurer denied coverage for 5 Days/Units of Inpatient Substance Abuse Services.

The denial is overturned. 

The patient is a male who was admitted to inpatient hospital treatment for alcohol detoxification. The patient reportedly had withdrawal symptoms including tremors, nausea, decreased appetite, sleep disturbance, malaise, muscle cramps, low energy, and he had a past reported alcohol withdrawal seizure 6 months prior to admission. The patient reportedly had been drinking multiple pints of hard liquor per day and had alcohol use since a young age. The patient also had visual hallucinations and reported them when drinking alcohol. The patient's psychiatric history was significant for schizophrenia and past reported psychiatric hospitalization. The patient had multiple past inpatient detoxification and rehabilitation treatments as well as outpatient alcohol treatments; yet, still the patient relapsed. The patient was recently incarcerated and released from jail, one week prior to admission. The patient was homeless, unemployed, and lacked supports. The patient had a positive toxicology for benzodiazepines. The patient was admitted and was placed on Ativan for detoxification throughout the hospitalization. The patient also had medical issues. The patient also took Zoloft, Depakote, and Seroquel, as well as thiamine, folic acid, and Campral.
  
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. It also states that patients with past complicated or life threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens are in need of inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal and reports that patients with comorbid medical condition that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification. Also, the US Department of Health and Human Services-Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) Center for Substance Abuse Treatment reports that inpatient treatment is necessary if the ability to attend outpatient treatment daily is a problem, one is unable to follow up in outpatient treatment, if medical conditions complicate the treatment of withdrawal, if one has previous withdrawal seizures of delirium tremens, or if one does not have the capacity for informed consent. In this case, this patient had reported alcohol withdrawal seizures which require inpatient medical detoxification treatment.   

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), the patient did require 24-hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive setting as he continued to use large amounts of alcohol daily, required and received detoxification medication (Ativan) to modify withdrawal from alcohol and prevent another withdrawal seizure or more complicated or life threatening withdrawal such as delirium tremens. The risk of delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use so this patient was considered at high risk for severe, complicated, and life threatening withdrawal. It was still reported that the patient took Ativan throughout the hospitalization and it was reported that he took Ativan 1 milligram (mg) still due to withdrawal. The patient also continued to use large amounts of alcohol despite multiple past inpatient detoxification and rehabilitation treatments as well as outpatient alcohol treatments and despite negative consequences including incarceration. The patent also lacked supports and was homeless. The patient required 24-hour inpatient medical hospital treatment for alcohol detoxification and it was considered unsafe for the patient to be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive level of care. Thus, inpatient substance abuse services were medically necessary for this patient.

The health plan did not act reasonably, with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.

Based on the above, the medical necessity for 5 Days/Units of Inpatient Substance Abuse Services is substantiated. The insurer's denial should be overturned.

The patient was diagnosed with obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) associated with anxiety and depression, and with severe symptoms and impaired functioning. The patient scored 27/40 on the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (YBOCS) reflecting moderately severe symptoms of OCD.
The patient has a history of co-morbid major depressive disorder, generalized or unspecified anxiety disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)with associated treatments, and co-occurring cannabis use disorder. There is no other substance use disorder in this case and no acute general medical issues.
The patient has received medication trials with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) (Prozac and Luvox), Cymbalta and stimulants with the latter targeting ADHD. She has also received treatment with cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) without substantial improvement in symptoms of OCD or functioning. She has attended mentalizing group sessions.
The patient's clinician has recommended treatment with repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) therapy with a clinically appropriate number of sessions and with a protocol to address the patient's OCD.
The case summary and case records provided by the clinician, health plan documents, correspondence from the health plan and patient's clinician and the patient were reviewed, as well as appeal documents, and the plan's Behavioral Health Policy pertaining to TMS procedures and the Summary Plan Description were reviewed.

Repetitive TMS therapy as a primary or adjunctive therapy for treatment of major depression and for OCD has generally been evaluated in patients who have treatment refractory or pharmaco-resistant symptoms, as defined by one or more, antidepressant medication treatment failures with or without augmentation, and with or without psychotherapy, especially cognitive behavioral therapy, as in this case.
Transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy, as applied in OCD, is considered to be a safe treatment by the FDA(Food and Drug Administration). The data as reflected in peer reviewed medical literature supports this assertion.
Specifically, when treatments with antidepressant medication with or without augmentation, and/or psychotherapy (especially cognitive behavioral therapy) have failed, then TMS is an appropriate treatment for OCD with the application of protocols as outlined in the scientific literature. According to the Gold et al. (2019), the literature states that TMS is a promising approach for treatment of depression in bipolar disorder who failed to respond to pharmacological or psychosocial treatment.  Also, according to Nahas et al. (2003), the literature states that daily left prefrontal TMS appears safe in bipolar depression subjects and the risks of inducing mania is small. 

In this case, this patient had multiple trials of antidepressants and mood stabilizer medications including serotonin reuptake inhibitors, serotonin norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, dopamine norepinephrine inhibitor, antidepressant with unique mechanism of increasing serotonin and norepinephrine, and tricyclic antidepressants. The patient also tried mood stabilizers. The patient either had reports of lack of sustained efficacy or medication side-effects that made the medication intolerable. With this patient's history of past suicidal ideation, depressed mood, hopelessness, and past hypomanic symptoms including restlessness, hypersexuality, and sleeping problems, TMS appeared to be an appropriate treatment option and medically necessary treatment. It was reported that the patient had 2 past hospitalizations for serotonin syndrome and bipolar depression so he was considered a high risk patient if not treated for his depression. 

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted breakthrough device designation for TMS for the treatment of bipolar disorder and with some other literature supporting its efficacy and safety for treatment of depression in bipolar disorder. This breakthrough device designation is intended to help patients and providers receive more timely access to breakthrough technology that has potential to provide more effective treatment. This is considered medically appropriate for this patient's case. 

Based on the review above, TMS is considered medically necessary for this patient.

The patient was worried about getting COVID. Notes indicated that when the patient had self-harm thoughts, the patient thought about going home and trying to cope in different ways. The patient had poor frustration tolerance and high rejection sensitivity. The patient had worsened suicidal thoughts and anxiety, and worsened feeling of hopelessness and tried to jump out the window but was stopped by the staff. It was reported that the patient then tried to jump out again but was stopped. The patient had worsened reported symptoms of depression. This was specific evidence that the patient was still considered a danger to self and was in need of 24-hour inpatient treatment. The patient required Thorazine as needed (PRN).  

As per medical records submitted for this review, the patient had worsened suicidal thoughts, depression, anxiety, and hopelessness and made a suicide attempt while in this inpatient mental health treatment setting. This indicated that this patient was considered a danger to self and in need of at least 24-hour inpatient mental health residential treatment.  There were no further notes for review. As a result, continued mental health residential treatment services provided was medically necessary for this patient.

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient.

summary:
