Treatment: Continued Inpatient Admission 
The insurer denied the Continued Inpatient Admission.
The denial is upheld. 

This was the first psychiatric admission for this patient with a history of major depressive disorder who was referred for admission due to new-onset psychotic symptoms and chronic headache. She had initially been evaluated in the emergency department and discharged home.  For the previous two or three months the patient complained of worsening fatigue, dizziness, headaches, memory problems and "no longer being allowed to take care of the kids." She complained of trouble concentrating and remembering things. She admitted that she at times forgot if she took her medications or that she left the stove on. She spent most of her time sitting in a chair or in her room. 

The patient had multiple psychosocial stressors including financial problems, joblessness, and the responsibility of caring for her husband who had a history of strokes. She had difficulty sleeping and reported being able to sleep only three or four hours a night. She reported nightmares of choking and of snakes trying to catch her. She was alert and oriented, but when asked if she could name the current president, she asked the psychiatrist if she passed her citizenship test. She denied suicidal intent but admitted to passive suicidal ideation. She did however admit to auditory hallucinations with multiple voices calling her nicknames and telling her to hit herself. Her outpatient psychiatrist told her to discontinue her medications the day before admission. They had included Lexapro 10 milligrams (MG) daily, omeprazole 40MG daily, sumatriptan 50MG as needed, and topiramate 25MG twice daily.

The patient was provided reassurance, support and pharmacotherapy. Over the course of her stay she showed improvement in mood and anxiety. A psychiatry progress note reported that the patient was cooperative and appropriate. There was no further evidence of psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations or delusions. Her mood remained depressed and her affect was constricted.

No, the proposed continued inpatient admission was not medically necessary. 

The patient's mood had improved significantly. She described her mood as being good and staff described her affect as bright. There was never any question of suicidal plan or intent or behavioral dyscontrol. She had no further psychotic symptoms. She tolerated her medications without difficulties. Nothing in the documentation reviewed indicates that treatment could not have continued equally safely and effectively in a less restrictive setting.

summary:
Diagnosis: Suicide attempt
Issue under review: Continued inpatient admission

Determination:
The Continued inpatient admission was not medically necessary.

The patient is an adult male. He was admitted with a primary diagnosis of major depressive disorder after he attempted suicide by taking an overdose of 180 0.5 mg clonazepam tablets. He was initially stabilized at another hospital and then transferred to this facility. A secondary diagnosis was PTSD (posttraumatic stress disorder). He had a possible history of alcoholism, but he denied drinking for the last nine years. He had hepatic steatosis, probably secondary to hyperlipidemia. 

At admission, the patient stated that he was disappointed that he failed in his attempt and felt betrayed by God that his attempt was unsuccessful. He has been going through a separation from his wife for three years and stated that he quit his job earlier in the year. He stated that he had the intention of trying to kill himself again if he had the opportunity. He had been seeing his psychiatrist and therapist less and less frequently, as he felt that they did not understand him. The patient's brother reported that the patient had a long history of anhedonia, depression, feelings of hopelessness, and feelings of despair.

The patient was treated with Effexor, Abilify, and ECT (electroconvulsive therapy), which was begun while his medications continued to be titrated. He received a total of 10 ECT treatments while hospitalized, including four treatments after the last authorized date.

A progress summary reported that the patient was alert and verbally responsive. He denied suicidal or homicidal ideation, and no distress was noted. He reported "feeling good." 

A progress note reports that the patient was agreeable to referrals to a partial hospital program. He denied suicidal ideation, was pleasant and cooperative, and stated that he continued to feel that the ECT was helping him. He reported his mood as a 7 out of 10. He noted that his family and others had been very supportive of him and this was helping him as well.

On the first date of service under review, the patient stated, "I feel good and I want to live my life. I would never try to kill myself again." 

The patient was scheduled for his seventh ECT the following day. He planned to stay with his parents for a few weeks after discharge. His affect was brighter. The patient stated, "I am looking forward to going back to work and going on with my life." He rated his mood as 8 out of 10. There was a reference to difficulties with transportation for outpatient ECT. 

Two days later, the treatment plan was for the patient to remain in the hospital for medication and ECT for 11 days and then to be discharged to a partial hospital program.

The patient's mood had improved significantly, and he consistently denied suicidal ideation for at least a week preceding the last authorized date for inpatient care. He cited numerous examples of future orientation. His family was supportive. The only stated rationale for continued inpatient care was transportation difficulties for outpatient ECT. It is not clear if further ECT treatments were indicated, and in any case, no details were provided regarding the stated transportation problems. As noted above, the patient had several supportive family members.

Therefore, given the above, the Continued inpatient admission was not medically necessary.

The patient is a female who was admitted to inpatient psychiatric unit.

Emergency Department records indicate that 911 was activated by the neighborhood due to a verbal altercation between the patient and her mother. Her mother reports that her daughter has been regressing in terms of her self care for several years: she has been eating less, and is scared to wash her face or hands. She has been washing her hands one to two times an hour which gradually subsided until the pandemic started. It reemerged then and became worse in the past one to two months. She starts thinking about being dirty and needs a lot of reassurance from her mother. She showers every three days and resists brushing her teeth because she feels that the bathroom is dirty. She avoids touching her shoes. She did not leave the house for two months because of contamination fears. She has been seeing an outpatient therapist twice a week but refuses psychiatric treatment. She is transferred for inpatient admission. 

Inpatient records indicate that the patient is calm and cooperative. She attends school and group activities and participates. She interacts well with peers. She denies suicidal and self harm ideation. She is in good behavioral control. She has a good visit with her mother. She showered and attended groups with no behavioral dysregulation. She maintained safe behavior. She was calm and cooperative. She was visible in the milieu and was more engaged, verbal and interactive. She denied suicidal ideation and contracted for safety. No agitation was noted. Her affect was fair. The patient was calm and cooperative. She listened to staff and followed unit routines. She showered and was visible and interactive in the community. By report she continued to spend excessive amounts of time washing her hands in the bathroom. She has been responding to redirections from staff. She denies suicidal ideation, dysphoric mood, anhedonia and hopelessness. She is eating and sleeping well and participating appropriately. There are no medication side effects. No medication changes were made. Her affect was bright. A visit with her mother went well. She showered. She was in good behavioral control. It was noted that during that week she has remained in good behavioral control with no aggressive or self harm behaviors. She continued to attend daily groups although she did not verbally share her feelings. She was calm in the community but was mainly to herself. She achieved level II. She stated that she was continuing to avoid touching a toothbrush after it fell on the ground two days go. She was unwilling to use this as an exposure opportunity. She continued to display minimal insight into her issues. Her affect was bright. She has been accepted at a Partial Hospital Program (PHP). 

The patient was calm, cooperative and compliant. She showered. She interacted minimally with peers. She interacted well with others and attended groups. She denied suicidal ideation. Lexapro would be increased. She was noted to continue to spend excessive amounts of time washing her hands in the bathroom. She was sleeping and eating without difficulty. She participated appropriately in groups. There are no medication side effects.  She showered and attended groups. She interacted well with peers. A visit with her mother went well. She showered. She maintained good behavioral control. No excessive washing of hands was noted. She was calm and cooperative. She showered. She maintained good behavioral control. She talked about her history of compulsive behaviors. She stated that she continues to have difficulty washing her hands in the shower. She is receptive to placing limits on the amount she washes her hands in the sink She has been tolerating the increased Lexapro dose well. She continues to express worries about contamination and some compulsive handwashing but is able to respond to them with redirection. She has no difficulty eating or sleeping. She engages in groups and interacts appropriately. The patient is calm and in good control. She showered. She was complaint. She attended school and participated. A discharge summary states that during her stay she gradually opened up to the team, consistently participated in daily individual therapy and groups, and maintained good behavioral control. She consistently denied suicidal and homicidal ideation. She was looking forward to discharge home and continuing treatment in a partial hospital program (PHP).

No, the proposed treatment is not medically necessary.

There is no evidence that the patient requires the restrictiveness, intensity and safety of inpatient treatment. She does not engage in any unsafe behavior toward herself or others and denies suicidal and homicidal ideation. She does not require intensive staffing to keep her safe or engaged in treatment. She has no medical issues and no medication side effects. She engages consistently in treatment and activities. While she reports that she continues to struggle with some obsessions and compulsions, they are not affecting her ability to engage in daily activities or self care. She showers regularly. Her sleep and appetite are good. There is no indication that she misses any activities due to engaging in compulsive behaviors or that she is harming herself or anyone else in any way due to these behaviors. There is minimal evidence of Exposure Response Prevention treatment being applied during her admission; treatment in a less restrictive environment would be safe and could be more effective in treating her condition.

The patient did not require inpatient level of care and could have been safely and effectively treated in a lower level of care.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major depressive disorder; Generalized anxiety
disorder
Treatment: Continued Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Treatment (TMS) 20 additional units
The insurer denied the Continued Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Treatment (TMS) 20 additional units
The denial is upheld. 

The patient is an adult male. He has a diagnosis of recurrent and severe major depressive disorder without psychotic features and generalized anxiety disorder. The patient has a history of depressive disorder with worsening and persistent symptoms of depression despite past treatments with SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) and SNRIs (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor), as well as augmentation with ketamine. The patient's symptoms recurred and/or persisted with deterioration in functioning socially and occupationally, including a declined in ability to maintain activities of daily living. He was subsequently referred for repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) therapy to include thirty-six treatment sessions with tapering over a three-week time frame per protocol.

The patient's PHQ-9 (Patient Health Questionnaire-9) improved to a score of 9 or 6; he was calm and cooperative. Mood was anxious and depressed with brighter affect and animated demeanor. Speech was normal and clear with organized thought patterns. There were no severe symptoms such as psychosis, cognitive impairment, perceptual disturbance or suicidal ideation.

In this case, there is no report of substance use disorder or other mental disorders. The patient has sleep disorders including restless leg syndrome and obstructive sleep apnea with history of PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder)-like sleep disturbance. The patient has reportedly not been provided treatment with electro-convulsive therapy (ECT), and the documentation does not note whether CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) or other evidence-based psychotherapy is ongoing or provided by a skilled and certified therapist.

The patient's current medications include Wellbutrin, Lamictal, Deplin, trazodone and Klonopin.

The health plan has denied authorization for coverage of rTMS (repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation) on the basis of coverage exclusion and indicated that the requested treatment is considered as not medically necessary because the patient has improved with regard to symptoms of depression and functioning with a return to work. Additionally, the health plan notes that additional TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy is not indicated in view of the current rating of depression as mild and in view of other treatments that are available and referenced in the peer review submitted for review.

No, the Continued Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Treatment (TMS) 20 additional units is not medically necessary.

In this case, alternative therapeutic trials with augmentation, combination therapy, or these treatments together with other therapeutic measures are indicated and reasonable in order to address the residual symptoms of depression and PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder)-like symptoms/sleep disturbance. Examples of other therapeutic measures for patient such as this include a course of cognitive behavioral therapy or a course of ECT (electroconvulsive therapy). Thus, in this case, the additional repetitive TMS transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy is not likely to be more beneficial for the patient than any other available standard therapy, and medical necessity is not met in keeping with the instruction for this review. This answer is consistent with practice guidelines concerning major depressive disorder and the scientific literature pertaining to TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy for major depressive disorder, and this answer is consistent with New York State instruction for this review.

Clinically appropriate approaches are available for continued treatment of depressive disorder in this case, including combination therapy or an established augmentation therapy, as well as specific forms of psychotherapy that would establish that the patient is treatment refractory. Moreover, the patient's symptoms are mild, and the patient's functioning has improved as outlined in the clinical summary. As noted in the answer to question 2, alternative, standard therapeutic options known to be effective in the treatment of Major Depressive Disorder are available to this patient to address the recrudescence or persistence of depressive symptoms. Thus, the health plan should not cover the Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) with twenty additional treatments, and the health plan did act reasonably, with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient in this case scenario.

This answer is consistent with practice guidelines concerning major depressive disorder and the scientific literature pertaining to TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy for major depressive disorder, and this answer is consistent with New York State instruction for this mandated and binding review.

His presentation for mental health and substance use disorder treatment was prompted by a relapse that included binge drinking alcohol and a manic episode with psychotic features. He had experienced a precipitous decline in functioning in the context of escalating use of substances including alcohol, cannabis and stimulant class substances together with co-occurring psychiatric disorders, bipolar I disorder and history of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and obsessive- compulsive disorder (OCD). The patient presented with associated symptoms mood disorder with paranoid thinking, grandiose delusions, auditory hallucinations and mixed mania together with binge drinking up to 12 beers and six shots of tequila, as well as daily use of cannabis/marijuana. He had also misused his Vyvanse in the past.

The patient provided a history of psychiatric treatment for bipolar mood disorder or schizoaffective disorder with history of psychotic features and obsessive-compulsive related symptoms that were unspecified. He had prior suicidal behavior and treatment at varying levels of care including inpatient, partial hospital program (PHP) and intensive outpatient program (IOP) treatment. His onset of mental disorder was in his early years with subsequent use of substance use as an adolescence. The patient has a history of mental health and substance use disorder treatments going back to childhood including recent inpatient and residential level treatment with step downs to PHP (partial hospital program) and IOP (intensive outpatient program) levels of care, respectively. Nonetheless, the patient resumed binge drinking triggered by the mood disturbance and resulting in re-admission to residential level care with 24-hour safety monitoring and intensive residential treatment.

The patient had no acute medical issues. Laboratory assessments were normal or unremarkable with a positive drug screen consistent with history.

The patient is single and unemployed and a student. He lives with family. He has not had legal issues or trauma history.

The patient's mental status examination included mixed features of mania and dysphoric irritability. Speech was clear and thoughts were disorganized and erratic with grandiose delusions and paranoid thought content, as well as religiosity. He denied suicidal thoughts or ideas. There was perceptual disturbance with auditory hallucinations or severe cognitive impairment (executive function deficits) with concentration difficulties. He reported low energy and sleep disturbance. Insight was limited and judgment impaired due to the substance use disorder and psychosis, and he had poor control of impulses.

The residential level treatment provided structure, monitoring, and the intensity of residential level services. The residential program included intensive rehabilitation services with sober housing and monitoring for abstinence. Treatment included group, individual, family-focused, and educational services with emphasis on coping skills, and with the goal of the development of a relapse prevention plan. He received vitamin replacement therapy and psychotropic medications included Risperdal Consta and Wellbutrin with the latter targeting the ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder). There was the opportunity to participate in 12-step recovery groups with assignments, and he worked with peers to address relapse issues and identification of triggers to use alcohol and cannabis. The patient struggled with PAWS (post-acute-withdrawal syndrome) that diminished with persistent craving, and sleep disturbance, as noted with prn (as needed) medications. During his brief inpatient residential stay, the patient continued to display co-occurring symptoms of the mood disorder with psychosis and struggles with maintaining abstinence and the lack of coping skills. The patient made steady progress, but required ongoing monitoring to assure abstinence and therapeutic interventions to address interpersonal problems and anger issues best characterized as borderline personality disorder; he was exposed to dialectical and cognitive-behavioral therapy (DBT & CBT), as well as continued involvement in 12-step groups.

Again, the patient focused on the development of better coping skills, and participated in mindfulness training, DBT (dialectical behavioral therapy) and CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) treatment, and continued working on a relapse prevention plan, and was increasingly engaged and active in group sessions. His family was supportive of his efforts and the patient had the opportunity for family-focused sessions with regard to discharge planning that occurred a step down to PHP (partial hospital program) level care and IOP (intensive outpatient program) level care with focus on the need for sober supports and arrangements for step down to lower level care in the community with continued substance use disorder and psychiatric services, and encouragement to participate in recovery groups with the obtainment of a sponsor.

Yes, the Residential Mental Health Treatment Services were medically necessary.

The admission and continued inpatient residential rehabilitation treatment were medically necessary in order to address issues related to relapse with focus on a relapse prevention plan and additional work on developing coping skills in a case that poses high risk for relapse; in order to address co-morbid psychiatric disorders with medication and evidence-based therapy; in order to address the patient's lack of awareness of the seriousness of his illness with psycho-education and evidence-based psychosocial interventions; in order to address the social environment including use of multiple substances of use with high risk for relapse; and in order to work on coping skills that will be necessary in building an effective sober support system and continued recovery efforts with community providers while maintaining his abstinence with peer supported recovery groups. None of this therapeutic work could have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in view of the multiple, complicating factors in this case, the high risk for relapse, the treatment history with relapses and continued use of substances and mood disturbance/disorder and comorbid psychiatric disorders despite access to treatment, and the lack of a reasonable recovery environment that includes high risk behaviors including use of dangerous combinations of substances (alcohol and stimulant medication), and the patient's initial ambivalence towards treatment or lack of commitment to a recovery process, and treatment refractory nature of his bipolar mood disorder complicated with psychotic features.

This answer is consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice and ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) Criteria and scientific literature and published practice guidelines referenced below, and with NY (New York) State instruction for this review including the application of NY (New York) State OASAS (Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (level of care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) 3.0 Criteria.

summary:
Diagnosis: Generalized anxiety disorder. 
Treatment: Extended outpatient treatment services (code 90837). 

The insurer denied coverage for extended outpatient treatment services (code 90837). 

The denial is upheld. 

This is a female patient who reportedly was in outpatient psychotherapy treatment with a Licensed Clinical Social Worker (LCSW). The provider stated, in letters, that the patient was being treated with eye movement desensitization reprocessing (EMDR) for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and that the patient had flashbacks of trauma, memories interfering with functioning including work ability, concentration problems, and sleep. She also reportedly had chronic medical problems. The diagnosis submitted on the bills in the records for review reported a diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder. There were no medical records for review of the dates of denial for the extended session of 60 minutes for outpatient mental health treatment services. 

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Acute Stress Disorder and Posttraumatic Stress Disorder reports that EMDR is a form of psychotherapy that includes an exposure-based therapy with multiple brief, interrupted exposures to traumatic material, eye movement, and recall and verbalization of traumatic memories of an event or events. It therefore combines multiple theoretical perspectives and techniques, including cognitive behavior therapy. 

According to the APA Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Post Traumatic Stress Disorder, trauma exposure cognitive behavioral therapy is a treatment of choice for PTSD and EMDR is considered a form of cognitive behavioral therapy and exposure therapy. Some point to the use of directed eye movements as a feature markedly distinguishing this form of therapy from other cognitive behavior approaches. Like many of the studies of other cognitive behavior and exposure therapies, most of the well-designed EMDR studies have been small, but several meta-analyses have demonstrated efficacy similar to that of other forms of cognitive and behavior therapy. 

The only medical records provided for review reported a diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder. There were no specific documented medical records stating that the patient had a diagnosis of PTSD or documented treatment of EMDR for extended sessions of 60 minutes duration with a Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) code of 90837 in clinical medical records for review. Without medical records for review stating specifically that the patient required and received EMDR for the treatment of PTSD during the denial dates, there was not sufficient medical records provided to support the medical necessity for extended sessions of 60 minutes for outpatient mental health treatment services for the dates of service under review. 

The health plan acted reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. 

The insurer's denial of coverage for extended outpatient treatment services (code 90837), is upheld. Medical necessity is not substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). 
Treatment: Psychological testing. 

The insurer denied psychological testing. The health plan's determination is overturned. 

The patient is a female who reported having problems with attention, concentration, and short-term memory. Her primary care physician referred her for evaluation. She was sent for psychological testing. The evaluation resulted in a diagnosis of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), Combined Presentation and mild anxiety. 
Under review is the medical necessity of the psychological testing. 

Psychological Testing is medically necessary for this patient. There are complexities to the case that warranted a more thorough assessment. 
ADHD diagnostic criteria require a detailed interview and history gathering to determine the developmental nature of symptoms (i.e., onset in early childhood and before adolescence). In this patient, such a process is necessarily more time intensive and requires carefully ruling out other related causes of symptoms that may mimic ADHD. 
Most physicians are hesitant to prescribe stimulant medication (which is usually the front line treatment for ADHD) because it is a controlled substance and has abuse potential. As such, this fact makes it more necessary to screen for other problems (such as a substance abuse history) and to increase one's confidence that it is, in fact, ADHD that is driving the patient's symptoms (versus (vs). numerous other related conditions). 
ADHD is becoming increasingly malingered, or its symptoms exaggerated, in routine clinical care for the purpose of obtaining medication that is known to improve the performance of otherwise normal, healthy people and/or to obtain accommodations in one's educational or employment setting. A simple clinical interview and brief rating scales are not sufficient to rule out these other considerations. 

Psychological testing is medically necessary for this patient.

summary:
Diagnosis: Polysubstance use disorder
Treatment: Substance use disorder services
The insurer denied substance use disorder services.
The determination is overturned.

The patient was admitted for partial hospital program (PHP) level services for continued treatment of polysubstance use disorder (opioid, cannabis and tobacco), and co-occurring psychiatric disorders including generalized anxiety disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and other obsessive-compulsive related disorder. The patient has a history of escalating substance use; he reported daily of use of opioids (heroin and oxycodone) in large quantities and use of cannabis (marijuana). He had a binge pattern of use; daily use of opioids; and, he reported use and experimentation with other substances of abuse. He was using tobacco on a daily basis. There was conflict in the home due to his substance use including a decline in functioning and high-risk behaviors that included multiple inadvertent overdoses requiring emergency medical services, as well as coma for several days. The patient's referral for substance use disorder and mental health treatment was prompted by his continued use of substances and complications of the psychiatric disorders together with failure to achieve a sustained response to treatment at lower levels of care characterized by a chronic relapsing course.
There were no acute general medical issues in this case, and physical examination and laboratory assessments were normal or unremarkable. He had medications for the psychiatric disorders including Paxil, Buspar and Vyvanse, and he had received Suboxone.
Mental status examination included casual dress, cooperative but guarded stance, and, motor agitation/fidgeting. His speech was clear and fluent with normal tone and volume. Thoughts were produced in a linear fashion and were goal direct. The patient did not have evidence for mania, psychosis, cognitive impairment, or homicidal ideation. His mood was depressed with anxiety and irritability. He reported low interest with anhedonia, sleep disturbance and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD)-related symptoms. His Insight was limited and judgment impaired due to the substance use disorder, and the patient had poor control of impulses with craving for opioids.
The patient was poorly motivated to engage in rehabilitation treatment that prompted his treatment with PHP structure and use of a 24-hour sober living environment with supervision and random drug screens. He had family support from his family with whom he lived. There were no legal issues in this case. The patient was unemployed and had dropped out of school. Stressors included primary support, occupational, social environment (peers), and, other psychosocial domains with severe functional impairments.
The patient was admitted to partial hospital program (PHP) level services with a comprehensive evaluation and treatment plan. The treatment provided included individual and group counseling sessions, education, and other interventions to support a recovery effort including participation in age-appropriate recovery groups focusing on relapse prevention and development of life skills and better coping.
The patient was superficially cooperative during the initial PHP stay. His involvement in groups was appropriate. However, he remained anxious and depressed with irritability, anhedonia and limited insight impacting his stage of change. He participated in groups and individual sessions, as well as educational sessions and continued medication to address mood and anxiety with the use of Vyvanse for ADHD. Activity therapies were provided to improve life skills and healthy living.
He made incremental improvement with regard to mood and anxiety such that he was better able to participate in treatment for the co-occurring substance use disorders and mood disorder. His Suboxone was tapered.
The patient worked on the development of better coping skills with regard to emotional regulation and control of impulses, and with regard to distress tolerance (modified DBT). His affect was more stable though he remained at high risk for relapse reporting anxiety at 5/10 and depression at 3/10. He had begun working on a relapse prevention plan with identification of triggers. The treatment team was planning to have the patient proceed to intensive outpatient program (IOP) level services, when ready in order to provide continued intensive "dual diagnosis" treatment and safety monitoring, as well as medication management, as noted. He insight and judgment were only fair with a guarded to fair prognosis and risk for relapse that was significant. He was able to complete PHP level treatment with discharge.
The health plan documents, appeal documents, and correspondence were reviewed, as well as the health plan's certificate of coverage and rationale for the denial . This is a New York State review with the application of NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria, also reviewed.
The issue under review is Continued Partial Hospitalization Substance Use Disorders and Mental Health Treatment.
The requested health service/treatment of substance use disorder services is medically necessary for this patient.
The patient could not have been safely or effectively managed with lower level services during the time frame under review. The patient had risk for relapse that warranted PHP level services with boarding, as provided in this case. The continued PHP level services were provided with a treatment plan that was reasonable, clinically appropriate and necessary in keeping with prevailing standards of medical practice for the conditions under treatment in this case. The patient had demonstrated that he needed the structure and monitoring and intensity of treatment provided with PHP level services.
The application of ASAM Criteria and NY State LOCADTR Criteria support the expert opinion provided in this case. The patient's documentation is replete with evaluations reflecting high risk for relapse, affective instability, poor control of impulses in the context of impaired judgment, and and anxiety and attentional disturbance with history of multiple inadvertent overdoses and high-risk use of substances in the context of co-occurring psychiatric disorders.
Therefore, the requested benefit of continued PHP substance abuse rehabilitation services and mental health treatment through discharge and step down to IOP level services was medically necessary in order to manage the co-morbid psychiatric conditions; in order to address the patient's lack of awareness of the seriousness of the substance use disorders (multiple substances with large quantity and frequent use); in order to continue psycho-education and evidence-based psychosocial interventions; in order to address the social environment and severe psychosocial stressors; and, in order to work on relapse prevention skills that are necessary in building/working toward the development of a sober support system and continued recovery efforts with community providers and the patient's family. None of this therapeutic work could have been effectively provided for this patient at a lower level of care, especially in view of the multiple, complicating factors in this case. These clinical factors and treatment dimensions are the reason that the patient could not have been effectively managed at a lower level of care for the time frame under review.
This answer is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice and is in keeping with ASAM and NY State LOCADTR Criteria, as well as the published guidelines and scientific literature, referenced below.

summary:
Diagnosis: Bipolar disorder.
Treatment: 6 units of continued inpatient mental health treatment.

The insurer denied coverage for 6 units of continued inpatient mental health treatment.  
The denial is overturned. 

This is a female patient with a history of bipolar disorder, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and hypothyroidism. She was admitted to the hospital due to psychotic symptoms including paranoid delusional thinking, religious preoccupation, disorganized thinking and speech, threatening statements including saying it is all going to end today, restlessness, perseverative speech, grandiosity, and she reportedly was brought in by police. She reportedly had past inpatient psychiatric hospitalizations. She reportedly took Seroquel, Clonazepam, and Trazodone, and then Lithium and Gabapentin. She continued to have reported psychotic symptoms until discharge.
  
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Bipolar Disorders reports that the least restrictive level of care for safe and effective treatment is appropriate and also that patients with severe agitation, aggression, psychotic symptoms, suicidal or homicidal plan or intent or attempts, manic episodes, severe major depressive episodes, or inability to adequately care for basic self-care needs are in need of hospital treatment. In this case this patient had continued reports of psychotic symptoms during the denial period and had manic symptoms also and was still considered not at baseline and not able to care for her basic needs while still presenting with these symptoms. 

She continued with psychotic and manic symptoms requiring psychiatric hospitalization during the denial period. She also had medications added including Lithium and Gabapentin in addition to Seroquel, Clonazepam and Trazodone. She also had medical issues including low blood glucose. She lacked support and was reportedly homeless after her mother's death. Prior to admission she was unable to function in the community or care for basic needs, so she was considered still in need of psychiatric hospital treatment while reporting psychotic and manic symptoms.  

It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably or in the best interests of the patient.

The insurer's denial of coverage for 6 units of continued inpatient mental health treatment is overturned. Medical necessity is substantiated.

His substance use had escalated over several years after a relapse to continuous daily use in the context of severe stressors including loss of employment and housing, and a decline in functioning. He did not have a history of seizures or delirium tremens or other severe withdrawal issues in the past.

The patient has a history of significant psychiatric disorders including major depressive disorder and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). He denied history of psychiatric hospitalization or suicidal behavior.

The patient is divorced and separated from a significant other, and unemployed and homeless with limited family support and sober supports that were not working. There is legal history of incarceration and parole for drug-related crime. He reported trauma-related problems best characterized as unspecified and persistent or chronic.

Mental status examination revealed no evidence for severe cognitive impairment, psychosis, dissociation, perceptual disturbance or thought disorder. Insight and judgment were limited and impaired due to the substance use with high risk for relapse due to the recovery environment and lack of coping skills necessary for a recovery effort. He exhibited symptoms of anxiety with dysphoric mood. He denied suicidal and homicidal ideation. He did not have significant drug withdrawal symptoms or post-acute withdrawal symptoms as he presented for residential level treatment. However, he had intense craving despite receiving medication assisted treatment with Suboxone.

The patient was admitted to residential level rehabilitation services. The patient engaged superficially in substance use disorder treatment including group and milieu interventions, as well as educational sessions. He had the opportunity to participate in recovery groups with peer support. Psychiatric management was provided with use of lithium and the subsequent addition of Adderall at 300 and 20 milligrams (mg) per day respectively, as well as medication assisted treatment with Suboxone at 16 milligrams per day. The patient gradually engaged in treatment that included evidence-based psychosocial interventions-dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT) and Seeking Safety and therapist-led recovery groups. Case management worked to include his significant other and/or ex-spouse in the treatment for support, as well as addressing psychosocial needs with housing and vocational supports. 

The patient was engaged in treatment and committed to a recovery process. He was calm and cooperative and groomed/kempt. His mood had improved and his concentration was better, with improved motivation. He gained insight together with better judgment. He was medication adherent with tolerability. The residential substance abuse rehabilitation treatment, in this case scenario, was amenable to treatment at a lower level of care. There were no biomedical or psychiatric complications, or severe psychiatric symptoms/disorders in this case that would have warranted continued residential level services and treatment. Moreover, the patient demonstrated his motivation for continued involvement in the substance use disorder treatment, as noted above. Thus, the requested benefit of continued residential substance use disorder treatment was not medically necessary for this patient.

The patient is an adult male. He was admitted to partial hospital program (PHP) level substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment to address severe opioid (Percocet) and cannabis use disorders. The patient has a history of substance use beginning in adolescence with cannabis, and subsequent misuse of Percocet following exposure after a medical procedure. He denied use of other substances of abuse. He reported progression to daily continuous use of marijuana and regular use of up to 15 mg (milligrams) of Percocet. The patient carried a diagnosis of schizophrenia with history of affective instability and psychosis that included paranoid-driven behavior and hyper-religiosity for which he was prescribed lithium and quetiapine. His referral for substance-related treatment was prompted by the failure to remain sober despite access to treatment in the community together with family encouragement.

The patient had no prior history of formal substance use disorder treatments or involvement in peer-supported recovery groups, but he had received mental health treatment, including three prior inpatient psychiatric admissions for mood disturbance and psychosis.

The patient's evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination with severe psychiatric symptoms, including mania, psychosis, thought disorder and cognitive impairment (mental confusion). At the time of admission for PHP (partial hospitalization program) level care, the patient was not clearly motivated for rehabilitation treatment due to minimization and lack of insight. The patient was described as having questionable judgment and limited insight with poor control of impulses. He denied active suicidal ideation or aggressive impulses, but did report paranoid thought and was preoccupied with religious themes, talking directly with God. His energy and volition were impaired. Also, he had experienced and reported symptoms of anxiety and insomnia, as well as the grandiose and paranoid-driven behaviors that were identified upon entering treatment with residual anxiety and psychotic turmoil together with post-acute withdrawal symptoms and intense craving. He was generally cooperative, but guarded in the pre-contemplative stage of change.

The patient had no significant general medical conditions. He had been medically cleared for PHP (partial hospitalization program) level treatment. He was tobacco-dependent at one pack per day use. He was prescribed vitamin and nicotine replacement therapy.

The patient is single, high school-educated, and employed with family. He lives with his parents, who were supportive of his efforts to obtain treatment. Stressors included primary support, occupational, economic and social environment, as well as the severe and persistent mental illness. There are no prominent legal issues or trauma history in this case.

The patient underwent comprehensive psychiatric evaluation following admission to PHP (partial hospitalization program) level care.  Substance Use Disorder Rehabilitation Treatment included focus on coping skills, relapse prevention with identification of triggers, education about the disease model of addiction, and involvement with peer-support recovery groups, as well as plans for family-focused sessions when clinically appropriate. He received treatment with intensive services, sober housing, monitoring and structure provided within the rehabilitation treatment program and therapeutic milieu including five day per week programming and services, and the opportunity to attend daily 12-step recovery groups.

During the time interval, the patient was attending groups and participating in recovery groups and working on steps to facilitate his recovery. He continued to demonstrate cravings and continued PAWS (post-acute-withdrawal syndrome). He continued to display erratic behavior that was disruptive, and he was distractable with strange mannerisms. He proved to be non-compliant with his treatment plan despite exposure to educational, group and peer supported recovery sessions in order to work on development of coping skills, a relapse prevention plan, and efforts to enhance his motivation to continue a recovery effort. During treatment, the patient was deemed to be at high risk for relapse with variable levels of motivation due to the craving and lack of insight and co-occurring psychotic and mood disorder.

The treatment team was recommending a higher level of care in a more restrictive treatment setting that could address the schizoaffective disorder. His family arranged for a transfer to inpatient residential treatment with discharge.

Yes, the Substance Use Disorder Partial Hospital Program (PHP) level treatment and services were medically necessary for this patient.
The patient's persistent symptoms of psychosis and mood disturbance together with continued risk of erratic behavior, and risk for non-adherence to medication prompted the necessity for PHP (partial hospitalization program) level structure and monitoring through discharge. The case is complicated by active substance use disorder with prescription opioids and marijuana; and non-compliance with treatment and medication non-adherence. The residual symptoms of mood and psychotic disorder (schizoaffective disorder); co-occurring substance use disorder and treatment issues related to medication adjustments and arranging a safe and appropriate discharge plan warranted the continued services at a PHP (partial hospitalization program) level of care in keeping with ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) Criteria and NY (New York) State OASAS (Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR  (level of care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines.

The Substance Use Disorder Partial Hospital Program (PHP) level treatment and services were therefore clinically appropriate and medical necessary, as the patient warranted the PHP (partial hospitalization program) level structure and monitoring through the day of discharge when the patient was transferred to a higher level of care and more restrictive treatment setting with clinically appropriate follow-up and aftercare.

This answer is consistent with the scientific literature and published guidelines, and the ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) Criteria referenced below, as well as New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews and the application of NY (New York) State OASAS (Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR  (level of care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) 3.0 Criteria.

The Substance Use Disorder Partial Hospital Program (PHP) level treatment and services could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care. Thus, the requested benefit of Substance Use Disorder Partial Hospital Program (PHP) level treatment and services is reasonable and in the patient's best interest, and is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice for the treatment of the conditions diagnosed in this case.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance use. 
Treatment: Inpatient substance abuse residential rehabilitative services.

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient substance abuse residential rehabilitative services.  The denial is overturned. 

This is a male patient who was admitted to inpatient substance residential treatment due to alcohol rehabilitation and initially also detoxification from alcohol. He reportedly had a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment of Alcohol (CIWA) of 4 and then 7 and had tremors, sweats, anxiety, and headache and was prescribed Ativan for withdrawal. He had no reports of withdrawal seizures or complicated withdrawal. He reportedly was drinking 20 ounces of vodka per day and had past blackouts. He reported that alcohol interfered with his relationships and ability to work. He reportedly stated that life was out of control, unmanageable, and that he was unable to stop using alcohol on his own. He reportedly had comorbid anxiety and depressive symptoms including diagnoses of Generalized Anxiety Disorder and Major Depressive Disorder and was treated with Zoloft. He reportedly lived by himself. He reportedly lacked coping skills and was self-medicating his anxiety and depression with alcohol. He reportedly had no past substance/alcohol treatment.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that inpatient treatment is indicated primarily for individuals whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. 

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) the patient met criteria for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment as he continued to use large amounts of alcohol daily despite negative consequences, including it interfering with relationships and ability to work. He reportedly lacked coping skills to maintain abstinence, needed to better identify relapse triggers, needed motivation for change, needed sober supports, better decision making and impulse control, and needed to develop relapse prevention skills. He was unable to stop alcohol use without being in a sober and supervised therapeutic inpatient substance residential setting then. Without this structured and supervised therapeutic inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment he likely would have relapsed quickly and had more negative consequences due to use.  

According to the National Institute on Drug Abuse: Principles of Addiction Treatment: A Research Based Guide, the best treatment outcomes occur with longer durations of treatment. It also states that recovery from drug addiction is a long term process and that treatment techniques to increase motivation for treatment are necessary to prevent dropout rates. 

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. 

The insurer's denial of coverage for inpatient substance abuse residential rehabilitative services is overturned. Medical necessity is substantiated.

The health plan's determination is overturned.

The patient is a female with a history of major depressive disorder, recurrent and severe without psychotic features. The patient has comorbid conditions that include eating disorder not specified, generalized anxiety and borderline personality traits. The patient has a documented history of multiple medication treatments for depression including treatment with more than two disparate classes of medication and at least four or more trials with antidepressant medications (SSRIs-Luvox, Zoloft and Lexapro, SNRI-Cymbalta, Trazodone, and Wellbutrin), as well as use of other medications including Topamax, Vyvanse and Prazosin. Additionally, the patient has been treated with Ketamine infusions, and with psychotherapy including cognitive behavioral therapy and dialectical behavioral therapy (CBT & DBT), as well as counseling and supportive psychotherapy.
Due to adverse effects or lack of efficacy, the patient has continued to experience severe symptoms of depression and functional impairments that impact quality of life and day-to-day responsibilities.
The patient has reportedly not had psychiatric hospitalization or suicide attempts. She has had partial hospital treatment with three treatment episodes and ongoing DBT group sessions to address borderline personality traits. There is no report of other co-morbid psychiatric disorders or co-occurring substance use disorders in this case. The patient has no significant general medical issues except for gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and history of migraine headaches. Issue under review:  Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) Therapy for Major Depressive Disorder and Treatment Refractory Depression.

The health plan's determination of medical necessity is overturned, in whole.

The requested benefit of Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) is reasonable, clinically appropriate, medically necessary, and in the patient's best interest. The requested TMS service is backed by credible scientific study and is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice for the condition under treatment in this case, recurrent major depressive disorder and treatment refractory depressive disorder.
The proposed treatment can reasonably be expected to provide the patient with greater net health benefit than any other available standard therapy in this case scenario. Repetitive TMS therapy as a primary or adjunctive therapy for treatment of depression has generally been evaluated in patients who have had treatment resistant or treatment refractory depression, as defined by one or more, treatment failures with or without augmentation. TMS therapy for depression is established as a safe treatment by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and the data as reflected in peer reviewed medical literature supports this assertion. Specifically, when treatments with antidepressant medication with or without augmentation, electroconvulsive therapy, and/or psychotherapy (especially cognitive behavioral therapy) have failed, then TMS is an appropriate treatment option. This assertion is also noted in the American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorder, referenced below.

The patient presented to the emergency department (ED) with the complaint of withdrawing form opiates and benzodiazepines. Exam was remarkable for being anxious. summary:
Diagnosis: Suicide attempt. 
Treatment: Continued inpatient mental health treatment. 

The insurer denied coverage for the continued inpatient mental health treatment. 

The denial is modified. 

This is a transgender female (male-to-female) patient who was admitted to inpatient mental health treatment due to suicide attempt by overdose and she reportedly had depressed mood, poor impulse control and coping skills, and multiple past psychiatric hospitalizations. She was unemployed. She had a diagnosis of Bipolar Disorder II-depressed and took Quetiapine. She was discharged on day 59 of admission. 
  
The insurer denied coverage for continued inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital from day 48 of admission to day 59 of admission as not medically necessary treatment then. They stated that she did not present as an imminent danger to self or others and did not require further hospital treatment. They recommended a less restrictive level of care then. This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for continued inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital from day 48 of admission to day 50 of admission but agrees with the decision to deny coverage for continued inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital from day 51 of admission to day 59 of admission as the medical records provided reported that she still had suicidal ideation and self-harm thoughts and depression until day 50 of admission but not as of day 51 of admission. 

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Suicidal Behaviors reports that patients with suicide attempts are at high risk for suicide. Past suicide attempts are the single most reliable predictor of suicide. This patient was considered an at risk patient while still reporting suicidal ideation due to her serious suicide attempt on admission. The medical records from day 51 of admission no longer provided enough specific evidence to support that the patient still required 24 hour hospital treatment after that. As of day 51 of admission there were no reports of suicidal or homicidal ideation, intent, or plan, inability to adequately care for basic needs, manic episodes, psychotic symptoms, self-injurious, aggressive, threatening, or agitated behavior, specific evidence that she was an imminent danger to self or others or unable to adequately care for her basic needs. Also, as of then there were no reports of specific identifiable or quantifiable treatment goals or objectives that could only be achieved in a 24 hour acute psychiatric hospital setting or that could not be achieved in a less restrictive setting. 

As a result, the determination is to modify the previous decision and approve coverage for continued inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital from day 48 of admission to day 50 of admission but deny coverage for continued inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital from day 51 of admission to day 59 of admission.  It appears that the insurer acted reasonably, with good clinical judgment, and in the best interests of the patient from day 51 of admission to day 59 of admission but not from day 48 of admission to day 50 of admission. 

The insurer's denial of coverage for the continued inpatient mental health treatment from day 48 of admission to day 59 of admission is modified as noted above. Medical necessity is partially substantiated.

Treatment: Continued Residential Treatment Level of Care stay

The patient is an adult male. He has a chronic psychotic disorder best characterized as schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type. The patient had co-occurring substance use disorder with recent use of cannabis that was mild. There was a past history of use of other substances of abuse including MDMA (Ecstasy) and cocaine. The patient is diagnosed with co-morbid generalized anxiety disorder.

The patient presented for residential treatment due to persistent symptoms of anxiety, depression with ruminations, and guilt and shame regarding his sexual behavior that had been problematic. Despite extensive outpatient level treatments, the patient had deteriorated in the context of a mood disturbance and cognitive decline associated with the schizoaffective disorder. The exacerbation of the psychotic and mood disorder resulted in significant consequences with regard to family, social, and occupational functioning and relationships, as well as his own identity despite having family support and being well-educated.

The patient's mental status examination at the time of presentation for residential level services revealed dysphoric mood with sad and anxious affect and disorganized thought processing that included poor executive functioning with regard to decision-making, organizing, and problem solving. He had a history of markedly impaired judgment related to his sexuality together with limited insight and poor impulse control. At the time of admission for residential level treatment, the patient had no evidence of psychosis (delusions or hallucinations), mania, or other symptoms reflecting bipolar disorder. He denied suicidal ideation or intent despite the depressive ruminations with shame, guilt, and a profound sense of hopelessness. Concentration was impaired and volition and motivation were diminished, impacting his ability to function.

The patient has a past treatment history for mood and psychotic disorder; he had multiple prior psychiatric hospitalizations but no history of suicide attempt. He was prescribed antipsychotic medications and mood stabilizers including the use of Depakote, Seroquel, and propranolol.

There were no acute general medical conditions. The patient had a history of concussion and chronic back pain with possible traumatic brain injury related to a motor vehicle accident. He reported 85 pounds of weight gain over 12 months.

The patient is well-educated, single, and unemployed, with past work as an attorney. There is a possible history of trauma or abuse in this case. The patient had severe impairment of functioning with stressors involving occupational and other psychosocial domains.

The patient was admitted to residential services with safety monitoring, structured psychosocial programming, and resumption of pharmacotherapy. His clinical course was complicated by severe symptoms of mood and anxiety that persisted with modest progress. Adjustment of the patient's medications had occurred as clinically appropriate with a regimen of Lamictal, Seroquel, and Vyvanse, and a tapering of the Depakote. He had lost weight and was feeling better with regard to his general health; laboratory assessment was normal or unremarkable. He was receiving treatment for the back pain including ablation therapy. The patient's adherence with medications was variable and uneven.

The patient was noted to have made gains with therapy including family focused sessions and he displayed improvement with clearer thinking and improved concentration. He continued to have anxiety, depression, and hopelessness with shame, guilt, and ruminations with regard to past behavior and his current circumstances. However, the patient has made significant progress and was more hopeful and forward-looking with regard to prospects for the future. He had stopped family focused sessions and was more optimistic in his thinking. He continued to deny suicidal ideation or intent and his mood was not cycling. Thought was disorganized with improved ability to think. concentrate, and execute his functions. The treatment team was planning for continued and extended residential treatment going forward as indicated by the submitted documentation that revealed engagement in treatment, no safety concerns, and improved function while working to address struggles with identity and relationships including intimacy.

The Continued Residential Treatment Level of Care stay was medically necessary, in part.

Specifically, for the first part of the residential stay, the requested health service was medically necessary. However, for the second part of the residential stay, the requested health service was not medically necessary for this patient.

In accordance with prevailing standards of medical practice and the NY (New York) State instruction for review, the patient did require the continued structure, monitoring, and treatment with residential level of care during the interval under review in order to administer the continued treatment for the psychiatric disturbance in this case while conducting ongoing evaluations and observing the patient's functioning with intense therapy and monitoring for response to medications that had been adjusted accordingly. It was medically necessary for this patient to continue with 24-hour monitoring and remain in residential level structure in view of the persistent symptoms of chronic psychosis and mood disturbance, the continued disturbance of thought with depressive ruminations, guilt, shame, and hopelessness that represented a safety risk, as well as high risk for relapse with co-occurring substance use disorder and impulsive and inappropriate sexual behavior. Additionally, the residential stay during this time interval was medically necessary in order to monitor the response to medications as noted, especially in view of a recent history of multiple past hospitalizations together with limited insight and judgment, and substance abuse while receiving outpatient services prior to his referral to residential treatment.

However, the continued residential level treatment beyond a certain point was not medically necessary in this case. The patient had made progress with the treatment, and was noted to be functioning better with more optimism, clearer thinking and concentration and completion of family-focused sessions, all of which were indicative of the patient's ability to continue treatment in a less restrictive treatment setting. The patient could have been effectively managed with lower-level care based upon the submitted documentation and in keeping with prevailing standards of medical practice and published guidelines pertaining to appropriate levels of care. There were no remaining treatment issues or clinical features that would have required the continued residential level services, structure, or monitoring.

This answer is consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, and with the published practice guidelines, referenced below.

summary:
Diagnosis: Unspecified schizophrenia
Treatment: Continued Inpatient Mental Health Services
The insurer denied the continued inpatient mental health services.
The denial is overturned.

The case involves an adult female diagnosed with unspecified schizophrenia. She was admitted to acute inpatient level services after presenting to the emergency department with severe symptoms reflecting an exacerbation of the chronic psychotic disorder. She had stopped her psychotropic medications and was lost to follow-up with her outpatient providers. Her presentation to the emergency department included bizarre behavior and impulsive aggression with grossly disorganized thought content.

The patient has a history of schizophrenia and psychiatric treatment, including multiple hospitalizations and use of long-acting injectable antipsychotic medication. She did not have a history of suicidal or self-harming behavior.

There were no acute general medical issues in this case, though the patient had presented with chronic medical conditions that included hypertension, diabetes mellitus and chronic bronchitis. Medical screening in the emergency department was unremarkable or normal.

Mental Status Examination on admission: The patient was agitated with poor eye contact and mental confusion. She was uncooperative, guarded and hypervigilant, with irritable mood and anxiety. She had decreased concentration, energy, appetite, sleep, and volition. Her speech was rapid and illogical, with disorganized thought processing. She denied suicidal ideation or aggressive impulses despite her presentation with hostility, anger, tension, and excitability. Insight and judgment were limited and impaired, and she had poor control of impulses. 

The patient is single, homeless, unemployed, and disabled. She had no social supports. There were no legal issues or trauma history in this case.

The patient was admitted to acute inpatient level care after medical screening in the emergency department, as noted. The patient's treatment plan included safety and resumption of medication to address an exacerbation of the chronic psychotic disorder. The patient remained acutely psychotic, requiring frequent re-direction and safety monitoring. She was started on Depakote and risperidone, titrated as clinically appropriate together with as needed (PRN) medications for anxiety, agitation, and insomnia including trazodone. General medical consultation was provided and she had laboratory assessment, an electrocardiogram (EKG), and chest x-ray that were abnormal with first degree atrioventricular (A-V) block, hypertrophy of the left ventricle, and a granuloma of the right lung. She refused a computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest.  

The patient remained with persistent symptoms of psychosis that were slowly improving in response to her medications; she continued to display poor attention to self-care with continued evidence for impaired insight and judgment. Medications were titrated as clinically appropriate, with an injection of Risperdal Consta with plans for continued use. The treatment included efforts to address the lack of insight (anosognosia) and risk for medication non-adherence with psychoeducation and encouragement to attend groups focusing on social skills and relapse prevention.

The patient showed improved functioning, she had been increasingly cooperative with staff, and continued to be medication adherent; she was able to receive psychoeducation with discharge planning with assistance of the case manager. By the time of discharge, the patient was approaching baseline with goal directed thought and improved mood and functioning with activities of daily living (ADLs). Her medications had effectively addressed the exacerbation and acute symptoms of schizophrenia that had persisted. Case management developed a safe and clinically appropriate discharge plan with plans for follow up with community providers and referral to a women's shelter. The patient reported feeling better and denied suicidal ideation, morbid thoughts, or perceptual disturbance. Mood was okay. Sleep and appetite were okay.  She did continue to have minimal interaction with peers and did not attend group sessions, staying in her room during much of the stay. Discharge occurred with clinically appropriate aftercare in collaboration with community providers to include mental health services with a safety plan, as well as recommendations to address the general medical conditions.

Yes, the proposed treatment is medically necessary for this patient.

The admission and the continued inpatient stay for the dates of service under review could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care. Thus, the requested benefit of the inpatient stay for mental health treatment through discharge is reasonable, clinically appropriate, and is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice for the treatment of the condition diagnosed in this case. Medical necessity is met, which means or describes a health care service that a health care Provider, exercising his/her prudent clinical judgment, would provide to a Covered Person for the purpose of evaluating, diagnosing, or treating an illness, injury, disease, or its symptoms and that is: in accordance with the generally accepted standards of medical practice; clinically appropriate, in terms of type, frequency, extent, site and duration, and considered effective for the Covered Person's illness, injury or disease; not primarily for the convenience of the Covered Person or the health care Provider; and not more costly than an alternative service or sequence of services at least as likely to produce equivalent therapeutic or diagnostic results as to the diagnosis or treatment of that Covered Person's illness, injury, or disease. "Generally accepted standards of medical practice", as used above, means standards that are based on: 1) credible scientific evidence published in peer-reviewed medical literature generally recognized by the relevant medical community;  2) physician and health care Provider specialty society recommendations; 3) the views of physicians and health care Providers practicing in relevant clinical areas; and 4) any other relevant factor as determined by the independent expert reviewer assigned to this New York mandated case review.

The patient's continued symptoms of schizophrenia together with continued risk of erratic and unsafe behavior, as well as issues with non-compliance with treatment prompted the necessity for the admission and warranted the continued acute inpatient level structure and monitoring through discharge when the patient was nearing her baseline functioning. The case is complicated by severe psychosocial stressors (homelessness and a lack of support), non-compliance with treatment, and medication adherence problems. The residual symptoms of the chronic psychotic disorder, risk for erratic behavior or response to continued disturbance of thought and reality testing, and treatment issues related to non-compliance/non-adherence with medications, and the need for arranging a safe and clinically appropriate discharge plan all warranted the acute inpatient level services to include safety monitoring and assistance with activities of daily living (ADLs). The continued inpatient stay through discharge was therefore clinically appropriate and medical necessary in order to provide the necessary and the continued inpatient level structure and 24-hour monitoring through the day of discharge when the patient had reached a level of stability such that she could return to the community with the arrangement of outpatient level services and with clinically appropriate follow-up and aftercare, as well as referral to a women's shelter where she would receive social supports.

The patient's acute symptoms of schizophrenia together with continued risk of impulsive or erratic behavior and safety concerns, as well as the presenting feature of non-compliance with treatment, prompted the necessity for the continued acute inpatient level structure and monitoring through discharge. The acute symptoms of psychosis, risk for problematic or unsafe behavior, and treatment issues related to non-compliance/non-adherence with medications, and the need for arranging a safe and clinically appropriate discharge plan, warranted the admission and continued services at an acute inpatient level of care to include safety monitoring and medication monitoring. The continued inpatient stay through discharge was therefore clinically appropriate and medically necessary in order to provide the necessary and the continued inpatient level structure and 24-hour monitoring through the day of discharge when the patient had reached a level of stability that she could return to the community with outpatient level services, housing, and with clinically appropriate follow-up and aftercare.

These answers are consistent with prevailing standards of care and the scientific literature and guideline, referenced below, and is in keeping with New York State instruction for this medical necessity review.

summary:
Diagnosis: Drug overdose.
Treatment: inpatient admission.

The insurer is denied coverage for inpatient admission.  The denial is overturned. 

This female patient has a history of anxiety and major depressive disorder.  She presented to the Emergency Room (ER) after taking 24 pills of Lexapro-10 milligrams (mg) each and 8 pills of Ambien- 5 mg each.  Heart rate was 120 beats per minute.  An electrocardiogram (EKG) revealed sinus tachycardia.  White blood cell count was 10.2, hemoglobin was 14.8, hematocrit was 43.2, platelet count was 236, and neutrophils were 84.9%.  Basic metabolic panel was within normal limits (WNL).  A urinalysis revealed s specific gravity of 1.018, trace leukocyte esterase, negative ketones, blood, and nitrites.  Acetaminophen level and acetylsalicylic acid level were WNL.  Poison control was contacted.  They recommended observing the patient for 24 hours post-ingestion for seizures, altered mental status, serotonin syndrome, and hypoglycemia.  The patient was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) for further care.  She was initially kept on nothing by mouth (NPO) status. Strict intake and output (I&O) was monitored.  An intravenous (IV) normal saline bolus and continuous IV fluids were given.  The patient was given 20 mg of IV Famotidine every 12 hours (Q12H).  EKGs were done Q6H and neurological checks were done Q1H.  The patient was monitored for seizures and serotonin syndrome. IV Lorazepam was ordered as needed (PRN) for seizures. Psychiatry and Social Work consultations were ordered.  The patient's diet was advanced to a regular diet. She was given 600 mg of oral Ibuprofen for headache.  The patient was placed on 1:1 constant observation, and suicide precautions were maintained.  Her diet was advanced to a regular diet. She was transferred to an inpatient psychiatric unit.    

MCG Drug Ingestion or Overdose criteria states that one of the following needs to be met: hemodynamic instability, dangerous arrhythmia, respiratory abnormalities, hypertension requiring inpatient treatment, specific finding indicating severe and prolonged drug toxicity, or inpatient admission is required other than observation care.  In this case this patient had an overdose from 24 Lexapro and 8 Ambien and needed to be observed for serotonin syndrome, possible seizures, was on 1:1 suicide observation and suicide precautions as she was considered a high suicide risk due to her recent suicide attempt with intent to end her life in the context of worsened depression and hopelessness which also is a risk factor for suicide, had continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring, EKG's every 6 hours, and neuro checks every 1 hour.  She was considered an imminent danger to self and in need of 24-hour psychiatric hospitalization in addition to medical treatment due to her overdose, so this was considered a severe drug toxicity and not observation care as she was a high suicide risk.  She was considered an imminent danger to self and in need of inpatient hospital treatment then.  This patient required and received active psychiatric treatment in this hospital even though she was on a medical unit as she was followed by Psychiatry and Social Work consultants and was transferred to the Psychiatric Unit for further psychiatric hospital treatment she required hospital treatment even in this medical hospital with psychiatric consultation as she had severe psychiatric symptoms putting herself in imminent danger.  

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient.

The carrier's denial of coverage for the inpatient hospital admission is overturned.  The medical necessity substantiated.
