summary:
Diagnosis: Suicidal ideation. 
Treatment: Continued Inpatient Mental Health Services. 

The insurer denied the Continued Inpatient Mental Health Services. 
The denial is upheld. 

The patient is a female with major depression and generalized anxiety disorder. She was admitted to inpatient psychiatric hospitalization. She presented after reporting a suicide attempt by hanging herself soon after discharge from her previous hospital stay. The patient made a prior suicide attempt by overdosing approximately two years prior. 

The patient's medications included Wellbutrin, Seroquel, Lexapro and Vistaril. Custody issues were present, with a reported court hearing involving the patient's father and CPS (child protective services) involvement. Continued inpatient treatment is the subject of the review. 

No, the Continued Inpatient Mental Health Services was not medically necessary. 

The documentation provided did not indicate ongoing acute safety concerns that would have necessitated 24 hours a day 7 days a week mental health treatment. This is because there was no documented persistent pervasive suicidal or homicidal ideation. 

The patient reported "fleeting thoughts" of suicide, but no documentation of any suicidal intent or plan, so the patient was not an imminent risk of harm to herself. There were no psychotic symptoms. The patient did not engage in any significant self-injurious behaviors, as skin scratching episodically would not require 24 hour nursing supervision. She did not need to be placed in restraints or seclusion for any physical aggression. She was capable of doing ADLs (activities of daily living). She was medically stable and tolerated the medications prescribed. There were no documented drug-related issues such as withdrawal symptoms needing 24 hour supervision. The progress notes documented "She made no reports of SI [suicidal ideation]/HI [homicidal ideation] or thoughts of self harm" and she was "social with both peers and staff." She rated her depression as 4/10 and anxiety 1/10, and: SI [suicidal ideation] 0/10; she "appears bright with congruent affect. She is an active participant in her treatment plan and is future-oriented." 

As a result, the patient's treatment did not require the intensity of inpatient level of care, but instead would have been more appropriate for continuation of treatment in a less restrictive setting. Continued residential treatment was not medically necessary. 

The clinical documentation did not indicate any persisting pervasive severe mental health symptoms that necessitated 24-hour inpatient treatment. As such, denial of this intensity of level of care was appropriate. There were also issues of patient placement documented regarding custody court procedure and CPS (child protective services) involvement. This indicated that custodial issues were more salient during the dates of service under review. This provides additional clinical support for the denial decision by the health plan.

summary:
Diagnosis: Severe eating disorder symptoms.

Treatment: Inpatient mental health child services request of 3 days/units. 

The insurer denied coverage for the inpatient mental health child services request of 3 days/units. 

The denial is overturned. 

This patient is a female child who was admitted to inpatient hospital treatment due to severe eating disorder symptoms. She reportedly was restricting food intake, purging as it was reported that her mother found bags of chewed food hidden as she was chewing and spitting out food into bags and hiding them, excessive exercise, sad mood, increased anxiety, and loss of 13% of her body weight 1 month prior to admission. Her admission body weight reportedly was 47.9 kilograms (kg) with a height of 61 inches. She reportedly had a history of self-injurious behavior. She reportedly had past bradycardia due to her eating disorder symptoms. She reportedly had 2 past hospitalizations due to eating disorder symptoms and returned to maladaptive eating behaviors upon discharge from the hospital. She reportedly had weight restoration and nutritional stabilization. She reportedly took Prozac, was working on a safety plan for discharge, still lacked insight into her illness, and required hospital treatment until discharge after a discharge meeting with her mother who agreed to better supervise the patient and help make every effort to help the patient maintain her weight.

The American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (AACAP) Practice Parameters for the Assessment and Treatment of Children, Adolescents, and Adults with Eating Disorders reports that the least restrictive level of treatment for safe and effective treatment is appropriate. 

In this case it was reported that the patient required the entire hospital stay. It was reported that during the denial period she still had poor insight into her eating disorder illness and was still attempting to hide food while in this 24 hour unit, was limited into her difficulties that she may have when returning home without this intense supervision and structure. It also was reported that she quickly returned to her maladaptive eating behaviors after 2 hospital discharges, so she required more time in the hospital this time to work on a safety plan for discharge and to improve insight into the triggers to her eating disorder symptoms so as not to return to them when not as supervised. She also needed the safety plan and strong focus on ability to maintain gains while in the community with outpatient providers. It was reported that during the denial period the health care team remained concerned about the patient's status and ability to maintain behavioral changes if outside of the hospital setting with significantly less supervision and level of support. After the discharge meeting with her mother, it was reported that her mother stated that she would make every effort to help maintain the patient's weight and provide more supervision regarding meals and to observe for maladaptive eating behaviors. Discharging this patient prematurely would likely have increased her chances of returning to maladaptive eating behaviors upon discharge as evidenced by her doing this upon her past 2 hospitalization discharges for eating disorder symptoms. She also had past medical issues related to her eating disorder including bradycardia and had significant weight loss prior to this hospitalization so she was at risk medically if discharged prematurely.  

Continued inpatient hospital treatment was medically necessary as the medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that the patient required continued hospital treatment until discharge. It did not appear that the health care plan acted in the best interests of the patient.  

The insurer's denial of coverage for the inpatient mental health child services request of 3 days/units is overturned. Medical necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance use disorder
Treatment: Inpatient substance abuse services
The insurer denied inpatient substance abuse services.
The determination is overturned.


The patient received inpatient substance use disorder level of care related to his opioid use disorder. On earlier dates of service, he had been receiving inpatient detoxification level of care with a Valium taper of 5 milligrams (mg), two by mouth (PO) twice a day (BID) and buprenorphine of 4 mg PO BID. The patient also reported using three joints of marijuana daily and "two sticks" of Xanax on a daily basis. He reportedly completed detoxification and was scheduled to go to inpatient rehabilitation.

The clinical history indicated that he was positive on a urine drug screen for cannabis and opiates, though notably not benzodiazepines or other substances. He reported a diagnosis of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and being stable on medications. He took antihypertensive medications many years ago, but was taken off of the medications. He was reported to have high blood pressure at times during this admission. He denied any diagnosis of psychiatric issues formally in the past, though he reported some history of depression.

A clinical note indicates that he was a "consistent behavioral problem" on the unit. He had cursed out staff multiple times and was resistant to following facility policy. The patient did report an interest in medication-assisted treatment. He was judged to be at low risk for harm to self or others. The clinical notes are primarily nursing notes in a tabular format. There are relatively few narrative clinical descriptions from a physician or other provider. Additionally, some pages did not copy well such that the dates are difficult to discern. The patient had a modestly elevated blood pressure at various times during his admission, consistent with the prior history of hypertension. The patient was participating in therapeutic offerings, though at times he was irritable and agitated towards staff members.

At issue is the medical necessity of inpatient substance abuse services.

The inpatient substance abuse services were medically necessary.

Responses to the questions on the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) tool for concurrent review are as follows. The patient had no change in status requiring a higher level of care. The patient did have a diagnosis of opioid use disorder. He was not yet receiving medication-assisted treatment during the dates of service in question, though had indicated interest in this treatment. The patient was no longer experiencing significant withdrawal symptoms. The patient did note urges to use medications. The treatment plan did not appear to indicate specific strategies for dealing with cravings. The patient did not have serious medical problems that were not stable and continued to be requiring inpatient rehabilitation management. The patient did not have serious psychiatric symptoms that were active during the dates of service in question. The patient was at risk for using substances and hazardous situations. Based on review of the provided criteria, the patient did meet criteria for continued inpatient rehabilitation level of care. The LOCADTR result was Concurrent Review Level of Care: Inpatient Rehabilitation. Therefore, the requested services were medically necessary.

Treatment: Mental health Residential.

The patient is a male with history of attention deficit disorder combined type, generalized anxiety disorder, specific phobias, and oppositional defiant disorder. He was also felt to have misuse of substance and features of conduct disorder and personality disorder. His psychiatrist recommended admission to Residential Treatment for his increasing symptoms. summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse.
Treatment: Substance use disorder services-residential.

The insurer denied substance use disorder services-residential.  The determination is upheld

The patient was admitted to residential level services for treatment of substance use disorder (alcohol and cannabis); the patient had been using marijuana on a daily continuous basis with alcohol use on an intermittent basis. He had a history of substance use beginning in 8th grade. The patient was motivated to enter substance abuse rehabilitation treatment and was supported in his effort by his family with whom there was stress over his use.

The patient had no past history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens. He had no past history of formal substance use disorder treatment other than outpatient counseling.
The patient was diagnosed with generalized anxiety and unspecified depressive disorders. He was taking Zoloft 50 milligrams (mg) daily, which had been switched from Lexapro.

The patient had no acute or chronic general medical issues. There is a history of concussions incurred during sports. He was medically screened prior to admission, and his laboratory assessment was normal or unremarkable with drug screen positive for tetrahydrocannabinol (THC)-consistent with his history. He was tobacco dependent.
The patient is single and attends college and lives with family. There is no report of legal issues or trauma history.

A Mental Status Examination revealed symptoms of depression and anxiety without suicidal ideation or psychotic features. His speech was clear; thoughts were disorganized, but logical and goal directed; and insight was fair with impaired judgment. Post-Acute Withdrawal Symptoms were mild with craving.

The inpatient level substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment included the opportunity to participate in groups, individual counseling, education and peer-supported recovery groups. Medications included continued use of Zoloft titrated to 100 mg and nicotine replacement therapy, and comfort medications as needed. The patient engaged in substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment with active involvement in group and educational sessions, as well as other therapeutic interventions to support healthy living and the development of sober supports. In this regard, the patient worked on coping skills and a relapse prevention plan with the identification of triggers including the negative influence of depression and anxiety. He participated in dialectical behavioral interventions including mindfulness training.

The patient reported feeling better and was engaged in treatment. He was described as motivated. He was tolerating the Zoloft and was sleeping and eating okay. He was making progress with the treatment plan and was noted to be committed to a recovery process. He did report craving for tobacco but was otherwise without withdrawal symptoms. The patient continued with the residential program without complication. He was discharged with referral for outpatient aftercare for the co-occurring substance-related and mental health conditions, and recommendation to participate in family-focused or peer-supported recovery groups as clinically appropriate. He returned to his home with family supports with the goal of returning to college.

Case records and the health plan documents, appeal documents, correspondence from the health plan and advocate, as well as the health plan's case notes and rationale for denial of the requested inpatient rehabilitation services were reviewed. Additionally, the Certificate of Coverage with the schedule of benefits and plan language and health plan's Behavioral Health Services Policy was reviewed, as submitted. This is a New York State mandated review including the application of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria 3.0.

The issue under review is the medical necessity of Residential Rehabilitation Substance Use Disorder Treatment.

The requested health service/treatment of substance use disorder services-residential treatment was not medically necessary for this patient.

The services could have been safely and effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. The patient was using marijuana regularly with intermittent use of alcohol; and the patient exhibited symptoms of anxiety and depressive disorders without severe symptoms such as psychosis or suicidality. There were no co-morbid general medical problems, or psychiatric symptoms/disorders in this case, that would have warranted the continued residential level services, structure or monitoring. The patient was motivated to remain engaged in treatment, had responded well to the initial treatment following an evaluation and medical screening, and the patient had access to sober supports/sober living and peer-supported recovery groups in the community. The patient had a sober home and family support; and the patient had successfully engaged in substance use disorder treatment in view of the motivating factors in this case. The psychosocial stressors and co-occurring psychiatric disorders were not so severe to prevent effective and safe treatment in a less restrictive environment with lower level care and sober housing or supports.
 
The structure and intensity of services necessary for a continued and successful rehabilitation treatment can be effectively provided at a lower level of care in a less restrictive treatment setting; moreover, the patient had not previously been exposed to formal and intensive rehabilitation treatment; thus, there is no evidence that residential level structure and monitoring was medically necessary for a successful outcome. There were no biomedical, psychiatric or general medical issues that necessitated continued residential level treatment following the initial evaluation and treatment.

These answers are consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, published practice guidelines, and the scientific literature, referenced below, as well as the New York State OASAS LOCADTR Criteria applicable in this case.

This is the case of a male patient who was in inpatient substance residential rehabilitation treatment and had an initial psychiatric evaluation. The patient had a diagnosis of alcohol use disorder and cannabis use disorder. He reportedly was homeless and had been unemployed for a long period of time. He reportedly had limited supports and was isolative. He reportedly had trust issues due to trauma and losses including recent deaths of his father and brother. He had negative urine toxicologies. The patient reportedly had depression, sleeping problems, low energy, and had some medication noncompliance with his diabetes medication. He was taking Bupropion, Seroquel, Trazodone, Amitriptyline, and Hydroxyzine. The patient was attending groups. 

The insurer denied coverage for continued inpatient substance residential rehabilitation treatment as not medically necessary treatment. They stated that he was actively participating in treatment, had no severe urges or cravings, or withdrawal symptoms, and had no acute medical or psychiatric conditions requiring 24 hour inpatient residential treatment.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance abuse.
Treatment: Inpatient admission.

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient admission.  The denial is overturned.

This adult male patient was admitted to inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment due to daily use of synthetic cannabinoid (K2). He was using 2-4 joints per day. He reportedly was in intensive outpatient program (IOP) substance treatment and still could not stop substance use. He also continued to use this substance despite negative consequences including past legal problems including for robbery, medical consequences due to substance use including liver damage and a diagnosis of hepatitis C, and he reportedly lacked coping skills and relapse prevention skills for abstinence. He also was homeless and was living with friends for the past few months, so he lacked supports. The patient also had a medical history of hypertension, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), glaucoma, left knee replacement, in addition to liver damage and hepatitis C. He attended group and individual therapy and had cognitive behavior therapy (CBT), dialectical behavior therapy (DBT), and rational emotive behavioral therapy (REBT), as well as medication adjustments. The patient was discharged with a referral back to IOP.
    
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that residential treatment is indicated primarily for individuals who do not meet clinical criteria for hospitalization but whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. Residential facilities provide a safe and substance-free environment in which residents learn individual and group living skills for preventing relapse. 

In this case this patient was considered in need of 24-hour residential treatment as he needed time in this 24-hour inpatient therapeutic structured and supervised setting to learn coping skills, relapse prevention skills, improve insight, better identify triggers, improve motivation, improve relapse prevention skills and build sober supports. 

The Institute on Drug Abuse: Principles of Addiction Treatment: A Research Based Guide- reports that research indicates that the best treatment outcomes occur with longer durations of treatment and states that recovery from drug addiction is a long-term process. It also states that treatment techniques to increase motivation for treatment are necessary to prevent dropout rates. 

In this case, the patient required the treatment time in this residential treatment setting. He needed the entire time in this sober therapeutic 24-hour residential rehabilitation treatment in order to develop relapse prevention skills, strengthen coping skills, decrease impulsivity, better identify triggers, improve relapse prevention skills and insight, and sober supports. He also reportedly had psychiatric issues including depression, anxiety, panic attacks, and sleeping problems, as well as medical issues including liver damage and hepatitis C due to substance use. He reportedly was homeless and had limited sober supports. Without this structured and supervised therapeutic residential treatment, he likely would have been unable to maintain abstinence, so he required this 24-hour therapeutic inpatient substance residential treatment. 

This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment as the medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that he required this level of care. It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably, with good clinical judgment, or in the best interests of the individual.

The insurer's denial of coverage for the inpatient admission is overturned. Medical necessity is substantiated.

The case involves a male patient who presented to an emergency department requesting detoxification and substance use disorder treatment, and who was screened and admitted to acute inpatient level care beginning in order to address substance use disorder with opioid (heroin), alcohol, cannabis and stimulant (cocaine) class substances. 

The patient had been using up to one pint of liquor and 12 beers per day together with up to one gram of cocaine daily, and up to twelve bags or two bundles of heroin with intranasal administration (snorting), as well as one marijuana blunt per day. He denied history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens, but reported blackouts.

This patient had a history of prior detoxification and rehabilitation treatments with treatment episodes and relapses with his longest period of sobriety at 36 months. His self-referral for treatment was prompted by multiple stressors including occupational, primary support, social environment and housing domains.

Evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination that was free of severe psychiatric symptoms. He was generally motivated for treatment and described as cooperative with a full range of affect with anxiety related to withdrawal symptoms and okay sleep. Speech was clear with organized thoughts that were free of delusions. There was no evidence for mania, acute symptoms of psychosis or severe cognitive impairment (delirium or dementia). The patient denied suicidal or homicidal ideation and did not have perceptual disturbances. Insight was limited with impaired judgment and poor control of impulses. His withdrawal symptoms included anxiety, irritability, pain, and aches with a Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) score of six (mild) and elevated blood pressure.

The patient was admitted to detoxification treatment with a comprehensive detoxification protocol with five-day tapering dosages of methadone and valium, and as needed (PRN) medications for comfort, as well as vitamin and nicotine replacement therapy. The program provided for case management with referral to sober housing and access to rehabilitation treatment that included comprehensive evidence-based treatments. 

During the brief detoxification the patient engaged in counseling sessions focusing on education about the disease model of addiction, and, involvement with milieu activities including peer support and sessions to motivate the patient to proceed to rehabilitation treatment. The patient was placed on a pain management protocol. Withdrawal symptoms persisted, but diminished with continued aches and pain at a seven out of ten (7/10) day one, mental confusion and persistent aches, pain and elevated blood pressure on days two and three, with improvement noted on day four. The patient completed the detoxification protocol and was discharged with immediate step down for rehabilitation treatment and with recommendations for continued involvement with self-help recovery groups, and consideration of medication assisted treatment and smoking cessation.

Yes, the proposed treatment, continued inpatient substance use disorder treatment with detoxification and withdrawal management was medically necessary for this patient.
The patient in this case was using heroin and cocaine together with large quantity of alcohol on a daily continuous basis; and use of other substances of abuse that did warrant continued inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring; detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments pertinent to the detoxification treatment episode could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment that was provided at the time of admission and during the time interval under review.  Moreover, the patient had persistent withdrawal symptoms, and, the patient's social environment was not conducive to detoxification, and the patient struggled with symptoms of anxiety in the context of limited insight, impaired judgment and poor control of impulses.

Thus, the continued adult inpatient detoxification treatment and withdrawal management of this patient's substance use disorder did warrant the continued structure of an inpatient level detoxification setting with 24-hour monitoring and use of as needed (PRN) medications. The patient's history of substance use (frequency and quantity) together with the drug-infested social environment, and severe psychosocial stressors and functional impairments reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder and the need for a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management, as the patient was at high risk for treatment failure if the continued detoxification and withdrawal management were to be attempted at a lower level of care. Therefore, medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published practice guidelines, American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria and Level of Care Utilization System (LOCUS) Guidelines, and the scientific literature, referenced below, and, New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews including the appropriate application of the NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Tool that requires the patient in this scenario default to the higher level of care.

This female patient has a history of hypertension and presented to the emergency department for opioid detox.  She disclosed snorting up to eight bags of heroin per day and being noncompliant with antihypertensives for one month.  

The patient's blood pressure (BP) in emergency department (ED) was 213/118 associated with headache.  Exam was unremarkable.  Labs revealed: white blood cell (WBC) 10.4, hemoglobin/hematocrit (H/H) 14.6/43.6, and platelets (Plt) 214.  Her Clinical Opioid Withdrawal Assessment Score (COWS) was four.  Her basic metabolic panel (BMP) was normal.  Urine toxicology was negative.  Electrocardiogram (EKG) showed normal sinus rhythm with a QTc (corrected QT interval) of 440.  The patient's chest x-ray revealed nothing abnormal detected (NAD).  Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed nothing abnormal detected (NAD).  Head computed tomography (CT) revealed nothing abnormal detected (NAD).  The patient's blood pressure remained elevated at 206/102 despite medications including clonidine, chlorthalidone, and hydralazine.  The patient was admitted on 04/21/2021 with hypertensive urgency.  A nicardipine drip was started.  Repeat blood pressure (BP) was 179/106.  Plan was to start amlodipine.  

The patient's blood pressure was 156/90.  The nicardipine drip was discontinued.  Amlodipine and labetalol were resumed.  The following day, the patient's blood pressure was 151/92.  The patient was cleared for discharge.

No, the proposed treatment was not medically necessary.
Medically necessary services are those which are:
- safe 
- effective
- generally accepted national standard of medical practice 
- not provided primarily for convenience of the patient or the practitioner 
- the least intensive and/or most appropriate alternatives among diagnostic and treatment option.

The requested inpatient admission was not medically necessary because it was not in accordance with generally accepted national standard of medical practice.

This patient with a history of hypertension, medical noncompliance and opioid abuse was admitted with hypertensive urgency.  She presented to the emergency department with a blood pressure of 203/118 and for opioid detox.  After receiving several medications in the emergency room, her blood pressure was 206/102.  Her Clinical Opioid Withdrawal Score (COWS) score was four, which is consistent with no signs of withdrawal.  She did not have altered mental status.  Renal function was normal.  Electrocardiogram (EKG) did not show ischemic changes.  Exam did not show findings of end organ damage.  There were no physical signs of withdrawal.  The patient was treated with a nicardipine drip on day #1 and transitioned to home medications on day #2.  Patients without end organ damage have not been shown to benefit from aggressive antihypertensive therapy at an acute inpatient level of care.  Studies show that rapid lowering of blood pressure in these patients offers no benefit, especially if the patient has longstanding severely elevated blood pressure.  These patients can be started on oral antihypertensives with the goal of lowering the blood pressure slowly over 24 to 48 hours.  In addition, she did not have findings of severe withdrawal that required management at an acute inpatient level of care.  Therefore, the inpatient hospital admission was not medically necessary.

The insurer denied coverage for continued inpatient substance use rehabilitation treatment, revenue code 0128

This adult male patient was admitted to this inpatient mental health substance rehabilitation due to alcohol use problems. He reportedly was drinking up to 1.5 liters of alcohol per day. He reportedly had past blackouts and suspicion of delirium tremens (DT's). He reportedly had withdrawal symptoms including tremors, restlessness, agitation, and high blood pressure and a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) of 11. The patient had Valium for detoxification and attended individual and group therapy for alcohol rehabilitation treatment. He reportedly had seen his primary care provider (PCP) who prescribed Vivitrol intramuscular (IM) for alcohol use problems. He reportedly had depressed mood, anxiety, and hopelessness. The patient reportedly had auditory and visual hallucinations when under the influence of alcohol. He reportedly lacked coping skills and insight for recovery. The patient had past inpatient substance/alcohol treatment for inpatient alcohol/substance rehabilitation treatment. He attended group and individual therapy and was discharged.
  
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that inpatient treatment is indicated primarily for individuals whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting.  

In this case this patient was considered in need of 24-hour substance rehabilitation treatment for the entire inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment stay as he could not stop drinking alcohol and reportedly was at risk for severe, complicated, and life-threatening withdrawals as there was suspicion of past DT's and he had active withdrawal symptoms on admission. He reportedly continued to use alcohol despite past inpatient alcohol treatments and Vivitrol IM shots and still relapsed and could not maintain abstinence. He reportedly lacked enough sober supports to maintain abstinence outside of this 24-hour substance rehabilitation treatment. 

The patient required more than just 2 days in this 24-hour alcohol inpatient treatment for detoxification and rehabilitation and required the full amount of time there until discharge. He reportedly needed time to try to improve coping skills, better identify relapse triggers, and needed to learn relapse prevention skills. He was unable to stop alcohol use without being in a sober and supervised therapeutic inpatient substance rehabilitation setting and required the entire stay including as he was discharge. Without this structured and supervised therapeutic rehabilitation treatment he likely would have relapsed quickly. 

This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for continued inpatient mental health substance as the medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that he required this level of care. It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably, with sound clinical judgment, or in the best interests of the individual.

The insurer's denial of coverage for continued inpatient substance use rehabilitation treatment, revenue code 0128 is overturned. Medical necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Severe Depression, obsessive compulsive disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). 
Treatment: Mental Health Residential Treatment. 

The insurer denied the Mental Health Residential Treatment. 
The denial is overturned. 

The patient is a female who was referred for residential mental health treatment for a severe and recurrent mood disorder, obsessive-compulsive related disorder, and trauma-related symptoms resulting from sexual assaults and triggered by recent workplace trauma witnessing the death of COVID-19 cases. The patient has no co-occurring substance use disorder. The patient is described as having an anergic depression with vegetative symptoms impacting energy, interest and volition. Mood is dysphoric and affect is anxious together with a history of trauma and social anxiety disorder or avoidant behaviors and obsessive-compulsive related symptoms with checking and ordering rituals. 

The patient has had suicidal behavior including three inpatient psychiatric hospitalizations, as well as partial hospital program (PHP) and outpatient treatment with a recurrence and worsening symptoms of depression in the year prior to admission. Despite treatment with outpatient therapy and antidepressant medications, the patient's mood and comorbid disorders had worsened with persistent and intermittent suicidal ideation with a plan to overdose, self-harm with scratching arms and impairment of functioning. She had dropped out of school and was socially isolated with no or little supports. There is no mention of mania, thought disorder or psychosis. However, the patient does dissociate when experiencing trauma-related symptoms. Insight and judgment are limited and fair due to the multiple psychiatric conditions and treatment resistance or recurrence of symptoms. 

The program focuses on organizational skills; self-care; peer relationships; and coping skills as well as behavioral and emotional regulation with stress management, cognitive behavioral or dialectical behavioral techniques (CBT & DBT). Nutritional supports were provided to facilitate health eating. 

The patient struggled during the first several weeks of treatment and then began to actively participate in the treatment. The patient was noted to be flat with blank stares with high anxiety and little interaction with peers. She appeared tired and depressed, and apprehensive and tense with self-harming behavior and persistent suicidal thoughts. She continued to have urges to self-harm with was at high risk for suicide. 

The patient was prescribed medications that were being titrated as clinically appropriate, including Effexor XR, Prozac, Rexulti, Lithium, Neurontin, Prazosin and Seroquel withas needed (PRN) use of Vistaril for anxiety and insomnia, as well as supplements and vitamins. The patient was noted to be non-adherent to medications at times requiring monitoring and encouragement. 

The patient was increasingly engaged in treatment, but tended to isolate socially often reading or staying to herself. She made slow progress and struggled to achieve emotional regulation. The patient was engaged with the continued use of dialectical behavioral techniques (DBT) and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) while maintaining a therapeutic alliance and focus on the disordered eating with more intensive treatment. Medications were continued and had been titrated with monitoring with the addition of Cytomel and Modafinil. The patient made steady progress with discharge and step down to lower level care with a treatment plan that called for continued intensive treatment to address the multiple comorbid psychiatric disorders with safety monitoring and family support/involvement as clinically appropriate. 

Yes, the proposed treatment was medically necessary for this patient. 

The admission and continued residential services were clinically appropriate and not amenable to treatment at a lower level of care, and therefore, are not excluded under the plan, as medical necessity is met under the plan. During the time interval under review the patient was working to learn improved coping skills and life skills together with the development of improved insight and motivation, as well as family involvement. She did need the admission and did warrant the continued structure and monitoring of a residential setting in order to safely continue mental health treatment and services while maintaining safety with high risk for self-harm or suicide. There were severe psychiatric symptoms including complications related to trauma history, as noted in the clinical summary. Thus, the requested services are clinically appropriate and consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice and consistent with published practice guidelines (best practice) referenced below, as well as the plan coverage language and NY State instruction for this review. 

The patient needed the continued structure and monitoring of a residential setting in order to effectively address the risk of relapse, continue to learn adequate coping skills to engage in therapy, and prevent treatment failure, while the treatment team worked toward a clinically appropriate disposition, as well as working on trauma and obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD)-related symptoms with evidence-based interventions. The patient has demonstrated nihilistic behaviors including medication non-adherence and self-harming behavior that did require ongoing residential structure and monitoring with active treatment to address coping skills and symptoms related to the trauma/injury and the mood and obsessive compulsive disorder and anxiety disorders. The patient's lack of awareness or limitations of insight and impulse control, together with the seriousness of her mental health disorders are pertinent treatment factors that warranted the continued residential level services, despite having access to treatment in the community. The psychiatric symptoms of trauma, depression, anxiety, and stress within the social environment including a significant trauma history complicates this case, as the patient has symptoms that are triggering the risk for suicidal or self-harming behaviors. These factors support the assertion that the patient could not have been/cannot be effectively treated with a lower level of care going forward. These clinical factors needed to be effectively addressed prior to step down to a lower level of care.

The patient is a male who was admitted for residential treatment of a mood disorder diagnosed as bipolar I disorder and comorbid attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), predominantly hyperactive type; and, other behavioral problems associated with impulsive, conduct and disruptive behaviors (stealing, lying, self-harming and suicidality), as well as problems with school related to his unspecified disruptive, conduct and impulse behaviors that were also experienced at home. The patient had received prior outpatient, partial hospital program (PHP) and inpatient level services; he had received Wilderness Therapy immediately prior to the referral for residential level services, as well as past involvement in psychotherapy including family focused sessions. The admission to residential services followed a progression of disruptive and problematic and high-risk behaviors that had included mental health issues; impulsive aggression towards self; and impulsive behaviors driven by affective instability and emotional dysregulation / dysregulated mood despite treatment in the community. He also had a history of school refusal. There was substance use with cannabis as a drug of choice, and with tobacco / nicotine use. 

The patient presented with the mood, attention and impulse disturbances with limited insight and impaired judgment; he exhibited coping and personality traits that reflected boundary issues and poor control of impulses in the context of the attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and bipolar disorder. He related conflict with peers and family problems with interpersonal relation problems with peers and a decline in functioning over the course of four to five years when his mental disorder was initially diagnosed. 

No, the proposed treatment, continued residential mental health treatment billed and depicted as intensive outpatient program (IOP) level of care was not medically necessary for this patient. 

The residential mental health services billed as intensive outpatient program (IOP) level of care going forward would have been reasonably amenable to treatment at a lower level of care and therefore excluded from coverage under the plan, as not medically necessary. During this time interval, the patient had effectively engaged in mental health treatment and services; he was able to learn and demonstrate improved coping skills and impulse control, gain insight with respect to his behavior, and develop life skills, as well as ongoing family focused sessions and support. He demonstrated improved sleep, concentration and volition with mood stabilization and improved control over symptoms related to the attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and impulse / disruptive behavior. He did not need the continued structure or monitoring of a residential setting billed as intensive outpatient program (IOP) level care in order to safely continue the mental health treatment and services with lower level care in the community. There were no remaining biomedical or psychiatric complications, or severe psychiatric symptoms that would have required continued residential level or intesnive outpatient program (IOP) level services beyond the initial approved timeframe. Thus, the requested services are not consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice (best practice), and the scientific literature, and practice guidelines referenced below. Additionally, medical necessity is not met for the continued residential mental health treatment billed and depicted as intensive outpatient program (IOP) level of care in keeping with New York instruction for this review. 

Moreover, the appeal is not valid in this case scenario (see below) and the health plan's reason for denial is reasonable and appropriate in this case scenario indicating as follows: the patient is in residential treatment and not intensive outpatient program (IOP); the patient is engaged in treatment and has family support; the patient has had multiple home passes without incidence; self-harming behavior is under control and safety concerns are at lower risk and can be managed with lower level of care, as can medication management and adjustments of medications. 

In Summary, the health plan should not cover services as medical necessity is not met and the continued residential mental health treatment billed and depicted as intensive outpatient program (IOP) level of care is not warranted as the health plan asserts with the stated reasons for denial and in keeping with the practice guidelines referenced below including the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (AACAP) Child and Adolescent Service Intensity Instrument (CASII) service intensity instructions pertaining to risk of harm, functional status, co-occurring disorders, the recovery environment, psychosocial stressors, response to treatment and level of participation and engagement with the treatment.

The patient is an adult male re-admitted to partial hospital program (PHP) level substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment to address severe opioid and moderately severe cannabis use disorders. The patient has a history of substance use beginning in adolescence with cannabis and subsequent misuse of oxycodone escalating to use of heroin together with cannabis and tobacco. He denied use of other substances of abuse. The patient carried a diagnosis of obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and a depressive disorder with associated treatments. His referral for substance-related treatment was prompted by the failure to remain sober despite access to treatment in the community and a relapse while in sober living with outpatient treatment.

The patient had a prior history of formal substance use disorder treatments and involvement in peer-supported recovery groups, and he had received mental health treatment including recent partial hospital program level services and involvement with self-help recovery groups. He had a history of several hospitalizations for heroin overdoses.

Evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination without severe psychiatric symptoms including mania, psychosis, thought disorder and cognitive impairment (mental confusion). At the time of admission for partial hospital program level care, the patient was not clearly motivated for rehabilitation treatment due to minimization and lack of insight. The patient was described as having questionable judgment and limited insight with poor control of impulses. He denied active suicidal ideation or aggressive impulses, but did report energy and volition that were impaired. Also, he had experienced and reported symptoms of anxiety and insomnia, as well depression and anxiety identified upon entering treatment with residual anxiety and depressive turmoil together with post-acute withdrawal symptoms and intense craving. He was generally cooperative, but guarded in the pre-contemplative or contemplative stage of change. 

The patient had no significant general medical conditions. He had been medically cleared for partial hospital program level treatment. He was tobacco dependent. He was prescribed vitamin and nicotine replacement therapy, as well as a regimen of Paxil, gabapentin, and Vyvanse.

The patient is single with a General Education Development (GED); he lives with his parents who were supportive of his efforts to obtain treatment. Stressors included primary support, occupational, economic and social environment, as well as the severe and persistent mental disorders with the co-occurring disorders. There are no prominent legal issues or trauma history in this case though there is a remote history of 'driving under the influence' (DUI) arrest.

The patient underwent comprehensive psychiatric evaluation following admission to partial hospital program level care.  Substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment included focus on coping skills, relapse prevention with identification of triggers, education about the disease model of addiction, and, involvement with peer-support recovery groups, as well as plans for family-focused sessions when clinically appropriate. He received treatment with intensive services, sober housing/boarding, monitoring that included random drug screens, and structure provided within the rehabilitation treatment program and therapeutic milieu including five day per week programming and services, and the opportunity to attend daily 12-step recovery groups.

During the time interval in question, the patient was attending groups and participating in recovery groups and working on steps to facilitate his recovery. He continued to demonstrate cravings and was started on medication assisted treatment with buprenorphine (Sublocade). He continued to display anxious demeanor, and he was distractible with adjustments of his psychotropic regimen and a switch from buspirone and doxepin to gabapentin and zaleplon. During partial hospital program level treatment, the patient was deemed to be at high risk for relapse with variable levels of motivation due to the craving and lack of insight, and co-occurring attentional and mood disorders and obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) requiring active psychiatric management. 

The patient had reached 80 percent of his goals and the treatment team was recommending step down to less restrictive treatment setting and a sober living environment. He proceeded to intensive outpatient program (IOP) level care with continued plans for involvement with recovery groups and medication assisted treatment and treatment of the comorbid psychiatric disorders with monitoring for abstinence. Records show that he was discharged to the community.

The reason for denial by the health plan: the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Guidelines are not met including no comorbidity, no post-acute withdrawal syndrome (PAWS) or craving, no compliant issues, and no safety concerns/risk in a patient who was compliant with treatment and participating in treatment.

Appeal documents assert that patient has serious safety concerns with history of overdoses, significant comorbidity with obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and depression, requires medication assisted treatment for craving, and has a history of treatment failure and relapses despite in sober living and treatment in the community. Additionally, the appeal documents indicate that Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Guidelines are met.

Yes, the proposed treatment was medically necessary for this patient.
The patient's relapse and treatment failure in the community and safety concerns prompted the necessity for partial hospital program  level structure and monitoring and intensity of treatment through discharge/step down. The case is complicated by active substance use disorder with opioids/heroin and marijuana; and non-compliance with treatment in the community. The residual symptoms of mood and other psychiatric co-occurring disorders; co-occurring substance use disorders and treatment issues related to medication adjustments and starting medication assisted treatment and arranging a safe and appropriate discharge plan warranted the admission and the continued services at a partial hospital program (PHP) level of care in keeping with the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria and NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines as the appeal documents assert. 

Thus, contrary to the health plan's denial and inappropriate application of the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Guidelines, the substance use disorder partial hospital program (PHP) level treatment and services was therefore clinically appropriate and medically necessary, as the patient warranted the partial hospital program level structure and monitoring through the day of discharge when the patient was transferred to a lower level of care and less restrictive treatment setting with clinically appropriate follow-up and aftercare.

This answer is consistent with the scientific literature and published guidelines, and the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria referenced below, as well as New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews and the application of Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines.

Diagnosis: anorexia nervosa

Treatment: inpatient mental health services

The insurer is denied coverage for inpatient mental health services

The denial is overturned. 

This female patient has a history of constipation, gastroparesis, seizure disorder and anorexia nervosa.

Anorexia nervosa has a high mortality rate if untreated and is a chronic and difficult disorder to treat. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Eating Disorders reports that patients that need supervision at all meals need 24-hour inpatient treatment. It also states that patients with acute weight decline with food refusal, preoccupation with intrusive repetitive thoughts, NG tube placement, or being uncooperative while in a highly structured environment need inpatient treatment.
The medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that she required at least this level of care. The patient had continued difficulty with both severe eating disorder symptoms and depressive symptoms including suicidal thoughts with plans to jump in front of traffic if not in this 24-hour setting. During the denial period she had poor meal compliance and severe malnutrition with inability to restore weight.  There were also reports of physically aggressive behavior including attacking staff. 
The patient lost 5.8 pounds and had a body mass index (BMI) as low as 14.66. She continued to refuse oral intake at times, continued to hide and crumble food, refused the request for nasogastric (NG) tube placement, and eventually had involuntary tube feedings. The patient also had poor activities of daily living (ADLs), and would not get out of bed at times to eat breakfast. She reported suicidal ideation and plans to jump into traffic if discharged. She was considered a high suicide risk due to multiple past suicide attempts including Tylenol overdose and running into traffic and she still reported suicidal thoughts and plans. 
She continued to refuse NG tube placement. Notes reported that she had increased suicidal thoughts since involuntary tube feedings. Notes reported that she was transferred to a medical inpatient hospital setting due to severe malnutrition and inability for weight restoration. 
This was a very high risk patient who required this 24-hour inpatient setting until her transfer to a more intensive inpatient medical hospital setting. Without this structured and supervised inpatient setting, she likely would have continued to restrict and lose weight, and compromise herself further both medically and psychiatrically, as she was also a high suicide risk. Based on the above, the continued inpatient mental health services at Walden Behavioral Care were considered medically necessary treatment for the patient's condition.

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient.

The carrier's denial of coverage for the inpatient mental health services is overturned.  The medical necessity is substantiated.

Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Continued Intensive Outpatient Care
The insurer denied the Continued Intensive Outpatient Care
The denial is overturned. 

The patient is a male who presented as a step down for intensive outpatient program (IOP) level treatment for co-occurring disorders including severe alcohol use disorder, bipolar affective disorder and generalized anxiety disorder in the context of severe psychosocial stressors and trauma history with a diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). The patient has a history of using alcohol since adolescence with progression of the disease and escalating use resulting in his self-referral for treatment with detoxification and partial hospital program level services with step down to intensive outpatient program (IOP) level services. Thus, the patient's presentation for intensive outpatient program (IOP) treatment followed partial hospital program treatment and he had received detoxification treatment with immediate transfer for substance use disorder rehabilitation and dual diagnosis treatment of the co-occurring psychiatric disorders.

The patient presented with mood disturbance, anxiety and severe substance-related problems that had resulted in functional impairments and inability to maintain abstinence. He had no prior substance use disorder treatment. The patient provided no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens. He was medically screened prior to intensive outpatient program (IOP) level treatment  with three day per week and three hours per day programming, as well as sober living and involvement in recovery groups, and intensive treatment of the mood, anxiety and trauma-related disorders.

The patient was admitted with step down for intensive outpatient program (IOP) treatment having had the detoxification and partial hospitalization program (PHP) level care. His clinical course progressed slowly without incident. However, he continued to display affective disturbance and reported intense craving during the initial weeks of intensive outpatient program treatment. While in intensive outpatient program level care, the patient's health plan changed with Medicare part A&B. The patient participated in intensive outpatient program (IOP) sessions including therapies with cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT) techniques, and he was regularly attending 12-step recovery groups with plans for obtainment of a sponsor. He received medication assisted treatment with gabapentin for anxiety/post-acute withdrawal symptoms (PAWS). He was prescribed Prozac, Seroquel and trazodone with as needed (PRN) use of Vistaril. Vistaril and trazodone/Seroquel were effective in addressing symptoms of anxiety and insomnia. He also was participating actively in group and educational sessions with the goal of developing improved coping skills which were notably deficient. He gradually participated more actively in treatment with increasing levels of engagement despite persistent anxiety, craving and sleep disturbance that were present. He remained in the treatment program with subsequent step down to outpatient level care with plans for trauma recovery and eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR), as well as continued dual diagnosis treatment for the co-occurring disorders. He completed the program and was discharged with referrals and recommendations for clinically appropriate aftercare and consideration of a sober living environment (or supports) and continued participation in peer-supported recovery groups.

Reason for Denial was indicated on the basis of the plan's Behavioral Health Services administrative policy, and also with the indication by the health plan that the New York State Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) was no longer met for the intensive outpatient program  level care and dates of service under review.


The appeal documents reference the change in health care coverage with the addition of Medicare triggering the denial for continued intensive outpatient program (IOP) services, and as the primary reason for the denial, and the appeal asserts that the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) tool continued to support intensive outpatient program level care thus supporting the clinical judgment to have the patient remain at the intensive outpatient program level of care for the dates of service under review.

Yes, the proposed treatment, continued intensive outpatient substance use and dual diagnosis treatment, is medically necessary for this patient.
The requested benefit of continued intensive outpatient substance use treatment for the dates of service could not have been effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. The patient in this case presented with a mood and anxiety disturbance with trauma history and he was using large quantities of alcohol on a daily continuous basis with severe psychosocial stressors and functional impairments that did warrant the continued intensive outpatient program level structure, monitoring and services. The treatment for the co-occurring disorders diagnosed in this case could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment that was provided at the time of admission to the treatment program. Moreover, the patient's social environment was not conducive to lower level treatment, and the patient struggled with craving in the context of the mood disturbance and associated symptoms of anxiety with limited insight, impaired judgment and poor control of impulses.

Thus, the clinical features and treatment dimensions outlined in the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria did necessitate the continued structure of an intensive outpatient program level setting with intensive treatment, structure, supports, and safety monitoring. The patient's history of substance use (frequency and quantity) together with the severe psychosocial stressors and co-occurring psychiatric disorders do reflect a complicated clinical picture, and does support and the need for a safe and effective treatment setting, especially in regard to recent suicidal threats while using alcohol and the potential for high-risk behaviors while under the influence of alcohol. The documentation clearly indicated that the patient was at high risk for treatment failure if treatment were to be attempted at a lower level of care. Therefore, medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published practice guidelines, American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and the scientific literature, referenced below, and, consistent with New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews including the appropriate application of the New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria.

The requested benefit of continued intensive outpatient substance use disorder and dual diagnosis treatment is clinically appropriate, medically necessary and warranted, and is therefore a covered benefit in this case scenario. The treatment of the patient's co-occurring mental health and substance use disorders could not have been safely or effectively provided with lower level services, as noted above. Thus, the requested benefit is not excluded under the plan, and should be covered in keeping with prevailing standards of care and the guidelines and scientific literature, referenced below, as well as meeting New York State instructions for this case review and the appropriate application of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Guidelines and Criteria, asserted by the appeal.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major Depressing Disorder. 
Treatment: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS). 

The insurer denied coverage for TMS. 
The denial is overturned. 

This is the case of an adult female with history of depressive symptoms including sad mood, suicidal ideation, feelings of hopelessness, poor sleep, low energy, and not feeling good for an entire day. She reported a long history of depression. The patient has a diagnosis of major depressive disorder- severe-recurrent type, generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). She reportedly was taking Escitalopram 25 mg (milligrams). She reportedly had tried Fluoxetine up to 60 mg with no response, Mirtazepine and had reported sedation, and had side effects to Bupropion including feeling wired, and also took intravenous (IV) Ketamine. The patient reportedly also took Quetiapine, Aripiprazole, Lamotrigine, Lithium, Topiramate, and Gabapentin. She also reportedly had  trials of weekly psychotherapy for years, as well as cognitive behavioral therapy, Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) therapy, and phototherapy. The patient had a psychiatric evaluation who recommended transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) therapy. 
    
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved NeuroStar TMS Therapy for the treatment of depression. TMS therapy was cleared by the FDA and indicated for the treatment of major depressive disorder in patients who failed or who did not have satisfactory improvement from 1 past antidepressant medication at or above minimal effective dose and duration in the current episode. NeuroStar TMS Therapy System was the largest multisite (23 centers) randomized sham-controlled trial ever conducted with TMS therapy. This was the principal study for the FDA's approval of TMS therapy for major depressive disorders. 

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Major Depressive Disorders considers TMS therapy as an appropriate acute phase option for patients who do not respond adequately to pharmacotherapy or psychotherapy and were considered treatment resistant. 

In this case this patient had a documented diagnosis of major depressive disorder-severe recurrent which is an FDA approved diagnosis for TMS therapy treatment. She has tried and failed several antidepressant medications in different classes including Fluoxetine, a serotonin reuptake inhibitor, and it was an adequate dosage of 60 mg and adequate duration; Escitalopram, currently at a high dosage of 25 mg per day; Bupropion, which is a dopamine norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, which is FDA approved for major depressive disorder, and she reportedly had a side effect of feeling wired; and Mirtazepine which has a unique mechanism of increasing serotonin and norepinephrine, and she took it. She also tried ketamine for depression. This is more than an adequate trial of antidepressant medications. She also reportedly took Quetiapine, Aripiprazole, Lamotrigine, Lithium, Topiramate, and Gabapentin which are mood stabilizers. She also had 2 trials of weekly psychotherapy for years, cognitive behavioral therapy, EMDR, and phototherapy. 

The standard recommendation for TMS therapy treatment is for patients who failed or who did not have satisfactory improvement from 1 past antidepressant medication at or above minimal effective dose and duration in the current episode. The patient was considered a candidate for TMS therapy treatment, and it was considered medically necessary treatment and also is an FDA approved treatment for her diagnosis. 

The health care plan did not act reasonably, with sound clinical judgment, or in the best interests of the patient. The medical records provided enough specific evidence to support the medical necessity for TMS.

The insurer's denial of coverage for the Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) is overturned. Medical necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Thoughts of Self Harm.
Treatment: Continued Inpatient Mental Health Treatment.
The insurer denied the Continued Inpatient Mental Health Treatment.
The denial is upheld. 

The patient is a male who received inpatient mental health treatment. The patient was initially admitted due to thoughts of self-harm. On initial admission, the patient expressed a plan to overdose on medications. He stated "I don't want to kill myself but I did consider shooting myself or cutting myself." He was described by his family as being delusional and paranoid and being without sleep for many days.

Clinical history indicates a prior diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder, previously being Covid 19 positive, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, renal stones. He also had a history of hernia repair. He had a history of cataract surgery. He had continuing problems with his vision after this surgery. The patient had been started on Lexapro by a neurologist prior to admission though stopped it after two weeks because he felt it was not helping. He later took Klonopin, but it made him tired. He went to another psychiatrist and was started on an antipsychotic medication but stopped taking it several weeks later.

On initial mental status examination, the patient was described as suspicious, dysphoric, tearful, anxious, illogical with perseveration, impaired reality testing, hopeless, helpless, visual hallucinations, Persecutory delusions, suicidal ideation and impaired concentration, attention, insight, and judgment. He was initially started on Klonopin and Haldol PRN (as needed) as well as PRNs (as neededs) for anxiety with Vistaril and lorazepam.

The patient was described as withdrawn and isolative with paranoid ideations. There was no evidence of suicidal or homicidal ideation. He was said to be less perplexed than on admission but with continuing paranoid delusions. He was stated to have noticeable improvement in mood, eye contact, and participation in unit activities, while denying suicidal thoughts. By the date of discharge, he was stated to be feeling better, denying suicidal or homicidal ideation and with no agitation. 

No, the Continued Inpatient Mental Health Treatment was not medically necessary.
Essentials for a continued hospitalization include the diagnosis of a psychiatric disorder as defined by both the criteria of the American Psychiatric Association's Diagnostic and Statistical Manual (DSM)-5 (5). Among many others, these guidelines include as requirements:

1) The psychiatric disorder must be of such severity as to cause significant impairment of daily functioning in at least two important areas of the person's life such as work performance, social interactions, or family relationships.
2)  The treatment proposed must be relevant to the problems diagnosed and adjudged likely to benefit the patient.
3) Other available less restrictive treatment resources must have been considered and determined to be not available or not appropriate to the patient's needs or have been attempted and proven unsuccessful. Examples of less restrictive treatment resources would include, but are not limited to, residential treatment, day treatment, or intensive outpatient care.

With the application of these principles, inpatient psychiatric hospital treatment should be used only when necessary and avoided when other, more appropriate alternative treatments are available.

For the dates under review, it is not clear what the treatment rationale was that kept the patient in the hospital.  The patient had experienced significant improvement in psychotic symptoms and no longer evidenced dangerousness to self or others. The patient was compliant with treatment and there is nothing in these records to support the need for inpatient treatment for issues that could have been effectively managed at a lower level of care (1, 2, 3, 4). Therefore, based on the evidence-based literature, the inpatient stay on the dates of service in question cannot be established as medically necessary.

He had comorbid PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder) and bipolar disorder. The patient was put on a 5-day Ativan and Methadone taper but left AMA (against medical advice) prior to completing treatment.
    
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. 

According to the LOCADTR [Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral] , the patient did require 24-hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated in less restrictive detoxification settings, as he continued to use large amounts of multiple serious substances of use. He reportedly had been using large amounts of multiple serious substances of use including heroin, cocaine, alcohol, Xanax, and cannabis and had active withdrawal symptoms. He reportedly had withdrawal symptoms including diarrhea, tremors, nervousness, irritable mood, agitation, insomnia, chills/flushing, dilated pupils, diffuse discomfort, nasal stuffiness, nausea, and loose stools, and had a COWS of 12 and CIWA of 9 and required and received 2 detoxification medications including Ativan and Methadone. He was at risk for worsened withdrawal symptoms if not in this 24-hour setting, including severe and life-threatening withdrawal symptoms. He reportedly could not maintain any abstinence despite multiple past inpatient substance detoxification treatments including 4 inpatient detoxification treatments. The risk of life complicated withdrawal such as delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol/benzodiazepine and he was at risk for severe withdrawal as well due to the large amount of substance use, so he required the entire time in this medical inpatient detoxification setting when he left AMA despite the recommendation for a 5-day inpatient detoxification treatment in this hospital setting. As a result, the recommendation is to reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for inpatient substance/alcohol detoxification in this hospital setting.

detoxification treatment was provided in a less restrictive treatment setting.
