summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse.
Treatment: Inpatient Rehabilitation Services.
The insurer denied the Inpatient Rehabilitation Services.
The denial is upheld. 

The case involves a male who self-referred with admission to inpatient rehabilitation and substance use disorder treatment beginning to primarily address substance use disorder with alcohol and crack cocaine. The patient has no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens. He was also diagnosed with opioid use disorder and in medication assisted treatment with methadone 100 milligrams daily. He had been using up to 40 ounces of beer and $50 worth of crack cocaine daily, as well as taking his methadone prescribed with a methadone maintenance treatment program (MMTP). He had past treatment experience with at least seven detoxification treatment episodes and the ongoing methadone maintenance treatment program. His drug screen was positive for cocaine, benzodiazepines and methadone.

Upon admission to inpatient level services, the patient received comprehensive evaluation and treatment that included focus on coping skills, relapse prevention techniques with identification of triggers, education about the disease model of addiction, and, involvement with groups, as well as peer-supported recovery groups and other therapeutic activities. Psychiatric evaluation had been provided and affirmed that the patient had no co-occurring psychiatric disorders. The patient engaged in substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment. He was adherent with medication that included vitamin supplements and the availability of nicotine replacement to address tobacco dependence, as well as 'as needed' (PRN) use of medications for pain and insomnia and elevations in blood pressure. Amlodipine and metformin were continued, as well as methadone at 100 milligrams per day.

Throughout her brief inpatient stay, the patient remained stable and engaged with the treatment regimen. He received intensive rehabilitation services, monitoring, and structure provided within the inpatient treatment program including 24-hour monitoring. The patient was discharged and transferred to a sister program for continued rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment.

The Issue under Review is the Inpatient Rehabilitation Services.  The denial was on the basis of New York State Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria indicating that outpatient level care was appropriate. Additionally, the denial indicated that the patient had no significant general medical issues requiring inpatient level care, or psychiatric comorbidity and had reasonable motivation for an effort at substance use disorder treatment with Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria indicating that outpatient level referral and treatment was clinically appropriate.  The appeal was on the basis of multiple past treatment episodes with no "clean" time and a lack of coping skills, indicating that New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria were met for inpatient level rehabilitation treatment. The appeal also indicated that the lack of psychotic features was not a valid reason to deny the requested level of care.

No, the requested inpatient stay for rehabilitation treatment was not medically necessary for this patient.
The patient received inpatient level rehabilitation treatment. He self-referred for treatment with family support and had not received multiple past substance use disorder treatments including at least seven detoxification treatments with relapses. He was receiving methadone maintenance treatment. As the health plan asserts, the patient had no significant general medical or psychiatric comorbidity and presented with no complicated withdrawal or safety concerns such as suicidality or aggressive impulses. He was motivated to engaged in rehabilitation treatment and had no biomedical or psychiatric treatment issues that warranted inpatient level care. Thus, the patient did not meet Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria as the health plan asserts in the denial.

During the time interval under review, the patient was noted to be in no apparent distress with reasonable functioning and active participation in treatment including positive interactions with staff and peers. During his brief inpatient stay prior to transfer, there were no complicating treatment issues that would have warranted inpatient level of care, structure or 24-hour monitoring. The application of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria (referenced below) did indicate that the patient was clinically appropriate for treatment with lower-level care in a less restrictive treatment setting, as the health plan also asserts. Thus, the argument on appeal noted below is not consistent with Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria and medical necessity for the inpatient level care for substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment and is not met in this case scenario, consistent with the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, the scientific literature and published guidelines, referenced below.

Note: The appeal was on the basis of multiple past treatment episodes with no "clean" time and a lack of coping skills, indicating that New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria were met for inpatient level rehabilitation treatment. The appeal also indicated that the lack of psychotic features was not a valid reason to deny the requested level of care.

The patient in this case scenario is not clinically appropriate for an inpatient level of care for the time interval under review. The patient had presented with a level of stability that included no significant withdrawal symptoms or biomedical issues and no co-occurring psychiatric disorders or safety concerns that would have warranted inpatient level care. He did not need the monitoring or the structure of an inpatient setting in order to receive effective substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment. Moreover, he was motivated for treatment and was already involved with methadone maintenance treatment and peer-supported recovery groups that could have been provided in a less restrictive treatment setting in order to address the comorbid cocaine and alcohol use disorders. Thus, the health plan's determination is reasonable in this case scenario-noted below. This answer is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice for the conditions diagnosed and under treatment in this case, and consistent with the application of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Guidelines/Criteria, referenced below.

summary:
Diagnosis: Alcohol Use and Alcohol Withdrawal

Treatment: continued hospital admission

The insurer is denied coverage for continued hospital admission

The denial is overturned. 

This patient was admitted to this inpatient hospital due to multiple medical problems related to alcohol use and alcohol withdrawal. It was reported that he had high Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) and a past history of delirium tremens (DT's). It was reported that he had Ativan for detoxification initially as well as marked electrolyte imbalance due to malnutrition from alcohol use, thrombocytopenia due to alcohol use, and severe depletion of Mg [magnesium], and K [potassium], and required supplementation. He reportedly had racing heart and palpitations and bloody stools, as well as neuropathic pain due to alcohol use. He reportedly had nephrology, gastroenterology, and psychiatry consultations. It was reported that the psychiatry consultant stated that the patient did not have the capacity to make decisions due to alcohol dementia and was considered not only a high risk for relapse, but also unsafe and unable to care for his basic needs. He reportedly was drinking 1 bottle of wine daily. He reportedly was living alone and unemployed. He reportedly continued to have medical issues and was accepted to a rehab and discharged later.
  
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. It also states that patients with past complicated or life threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens are in need of inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal and reports that patients with comorbid medical condition that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification. This patient could not safely be treated in a less restrictive setting as he reportedly had multiple medical issues related to alcohol use including marked electrolyte imbalance due to malnutrition from alcohol use, thrombocytopenia due to alcohol use, and severe depletion of Mg, and K and required supplementation, and also had racing heart and palpitations and bloody stools, as well as neuropathic pain due to alcohol use, and a history of DT's. This was a very high risk medical patient who required hospital treatment. Psychiatric evaluation was provided and he was restarted on quetiapine titrated to 600 mg (milligrams) daily with tolerability, as well as vitamin and nicotine replacement therapy, and amlodipine to address hypertension, and comfort meds.

The patient readily engaged in substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment. He actively received intensive rehabilitation services, monitoring, and structure provided within the inpatient treatment program including 24-hour monitoring. He completed approximately two weeks rehabilitation treatment and was discharged with recommendations and referrals for continued and clinically appropriate aftercare of the mental health, general medical and substance use disorders.

The denial is overturned. 

This male patient has a history of major depressive disorder and schizophrenia.

Transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy was cleared by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in October 2008 and was indicated for the treatment of major depressive disorder in patients who failed or who did not have satisfactory improvement from 1 past antidepressant medication at or above minimal effective dose and duration in the current episode. Neurostar TMS Therapy System was the largest multisite (23 centers) randomized sham controlled trial ever conducted with transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy. This was the principal study for the FDA's approval of transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy for major depressive disorders. In addition, the American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Major Depressive Disorders considers TMS therapy as an appropriate acute phase option for patients who do not respond adequately to pharmacotherapy or psychotherapy and who are considered treatment resistant. The standard recommendation for TMS treatment is for patients who failed or who did not have satisfactory improvement from 1 past antidepressant medication at or above minimal effective dose and duration in the current episode.
The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient.

The carrier's denial of coverage for the transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) treatment with treatment planning (code 90867) treatment delivery and management per session (code 90868), and redetermination of resting motor threshold and TMS session delivery (code 90869) is overturned.  The medical necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Alcohol Dependence, Cocaine Dependence

Treatment: Medically supervised inpatient detoxification

The insurer denied coverage for medically supervised inpatient detoxification.

The denial is overturned.

This patient was admitted to the inpatient hospital detoxification treatment for a medically supervised inpatient detoxification treatment. He reportedly had withdrawal symptoms including tremors, sweats, agitation, anxiety, elevated heart rate, diffuse discomfort, nasal stuffiness, and had a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Alcohol (CIWA) of 10 and Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Score (COWS) of 6. He reportedly had a positive toxicology for cocaine and benzodiazepines. He reportedly was drinking 1 pint of liquor per day and using 2 mg (milligrams) of Xanax per day, as well as smoking $80 worth of crack per day. He reportedly had hepatitis C and hypertension. He reportedly had comorbid bipolar disorder. He reportedly had a diagnosis of Alcohol Use Disorder. He reportedly had multiple past inpatient detoxification treatments and past inpatient rehabilitation treatment, as well as a past psychiatric hospitalization. He reportedly could not maintain any prolonged period of abstinence. He reportedly was unemployed. He reportedly was put on an Ativan taper for detoxification and started Ativan and received multiple doses including 3 doses, and also still had another does but left against medical advice (AMA).
   
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. In this case this patient had been drinking large amounts of alcohol daily including up to 1 pint per day and also was using 2 mg of Xanax per day which put him at risk for severe, complicated, and life-threatening withdrawal so he required 24 hour inpatient hospital detoxification treatment then as he was at risk medically. 

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) he did require 24 hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated in less restrictive detoxification settings as he continued to use large amounts of alcohol daily despite medical issues and bipolar disorder and he required and needed detoxification medication, Ativan, to modify and treat withdrawal and needed 24 hour treatment then as he was at risk for worsened withdrawal symptoms if not in this 24 hour setting then including severe and life threatening withdrawal symptoms. Also, he reportedly had active withdrawal symptoms including tremors, sweats, agitation, anxiety, elevated heart rate, diffuse discomfort, nasal stuffiness, and had a CIWA of 10 and COWS of 6 so it was unlikely that he would remain abstinent while still having withdrawal symptoms. He reportedly could not maintain any prolonged abstinence despite multiple past inpatient substance detoxification treatments and an inpatient rehabilitation treatment. The risk of life complicated withdrawal such as delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use so he required the entire time in this medical inpatient detoxification setting including when he left against medical advice (AMA) despite the recommendation for a 5-day inpatient detoxification treatment in this hospital setting. 

Inpatient substance/alcohol detoxification was medically necessary. It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably, with good clinical judgment, or in the best interests of the patient.  

The insurer's denial of coverage for medically supervised inpatient detoxification is overturned. Medical necessity is substantiated.

The patient is a male who presented for detoxification and withdrawal management. The patient has a history of severe substance use disorders beginning in early adolescence with daily use of alcohol, stimulants (crack cocaine), and cannabis (marijuana) class substances of abuse, as well as use of phenylcyclohexyl piperidine (PCP). He has a history of multiple detoxification and rehabilitation treatment episodes with relapses. He was using up to four pints of various liquors on a continuous daily basis together with twelve blunts of marijuana and $200 worth of cocaine daily.

The patient was admitted for inpatient treatment with detoxification protocol. He received tapering dosages of Librium and replacement of vitamins with the availability of counseling and comfort medications and as needed (PRN) medications prescribed for pain, anxiety, and insomnia, as well as medication assisted treatment with Campral. 

The patient's hospital course progressed without incident. Vital signs remained normal with occasional variability, and the patient reported mild nausea, anxiety, restlessness and insomnia with persistently mild symptoms of withdrawal that diminished throughout his hospital course. He was participating in counseling and educational sessions. During the last two days of his treatment, the patient was participating more readily in group, educational and counseling sessions, and was receiving individual counseling with case management to enhance motivation to proceed to rehabilitation treatment. Arrangements were being made for a direct referral to rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment. He was discharged with recommendations for continued medication assisted treatment and involvement with alcoholics anonymous (AA) and narcotics anonymous (NA) self-help groups for support of a recovery.

At the time of presentation to the emergency department, the patient was requesting detoxification and subsequent referral for rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment. He denied current legal issues. He was unemployed with limited family support, and homeless living with his mother; he reported severe psychosocial stressors within the primary support, social environment, and housing domains with unemployment-as noted. The patient reported functional decline as the substance abuse/disease had progressed which again prompted his self-referral for detoxication treatment in the context of at least four prior detoxification treatment episodes and several rehabilitation treatments with a pattern of relapses functional impairments.

Yes, the proposed treatment and requested services were medically necessary for this patient in keeping New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria and prevailing standards of medical practice.

The requested benefit of inpatient detoxification treatment, withdrawal management, monitoring and other medical services could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. The patient in this case was using large quantities of alcohol and other drugs of abuse (crack cocaine and marijuana) on a daily continuous basis together with intermittent use of PCP (phenylcyclohexyl piperidine) that did warrant the admission and the continued inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring. Detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments pertinent to the detoxification treatment episode could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment that was provided at the time of admission. Moreover, the patient's social environment was not conducive to an effective detoxification, and the patient had struggled with withdrawal symptoms which were being effectively addressed with a Librium protocol and supportive measures. The patient had associated clinical features that included lack of sober supports and functional impairments. Thus, the adult inpatient stay and detoxification treatment of this patient's substance use disorders did warrant the hospital admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level setting with withdrawal management and psychosocial supports, and 24-hour monitoring. The patient's history of substance abuse (frequency and quantity) together with the severe psychosocial stressors and functional impairments do reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder and the need for a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management as the patient was at high risk for treatment failure or general medical complications such as seizures if detoxification and withdrawal management were to be attempted at a lower level of care. The health plan's denial on the basis of New York LOCADTR Criteria is not reasonable, and attempting detoxification with residential or lower-level treatment, as the health plan recommended, is not in the best interest of the patient or safe in this case scenario. summary:

The patient is a adult male. He presented to the emergency department with a request for detoxification services. The patient was using alcohol on a continuous daily basis with up of two pints of liquor plus beer, and use of cannabis with daily use of 1-2 marijuana joints. He presented with mild symptoms of withdrawal in the context of the alcohol use disorder. He had a positive drug screen for PCP (phenylcyclohexyl piperidine) and cannabis. The patient has a history of detoxification treatments including a recent treatment episode six months prior to presentation. 

The patient had a history of a co-occurring anxiety disorder and denied past history of suicidal or self-harming behavior. The patient provided no history of withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens or severe alcohol or drug withdrawal symptoms, but did report history of blackouts. The patient had no acute general medical problems. He had low back pain treated with Robaxin and Tylenol. He was tobacco dependent. He was medically screened and admitted for inpatient level detoxification with plans for a five-day detoxification treatment episode with Librium, vitamin replacement therapy and comfort medications, as well as the availability of nicotine replacement therapy. Laboratory assessment showed a slightly low hematocrit and was otherwise unremarkable. EKG (electrocardiogram) and chest X-Ray were normal. 

The patient was admitted for inpatient detoxification. He was placed on a Librium taper with vitamin therapy and comfort medications as noted. He received counseling and education and motivational enhancement therapy, and had the opportunity to participate in recovery groups. He was placed on Campral for medication assisted treatment. The patient's hospital course progressed without incident. The patient slept and received meals. His monitoring occurred without incident, and he had the opportunity to attend group sessions and receive counseling and education with planning for clinically appropriate aftercare. 

His CIWA (clinical institute withdrawal assessment) scale increased from 1 to 2. Thereafter, he refused Librium and continued to have mild withdrawal symptoms. He completed the detoxification treatment and was discharged. He was advised on further treatment as clinically appropriate. 

The requested inpatient treatment was considered by the health plan as not medically necessary under the plan in keeping with LOCADTR (level of care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) 3 Guidelines. The health plan recommended rehabilitation treatment in a residential treatment setting. 

The treatment facility appealed the denial on the basis that the patient had immediately relapsed after his last detoxification treatment episode, and had severe withdrawal symptoms. The appeal also noted that the patient was not appropriate for outpatient level detoxification treatment. 

No, the Inpatient Substance Abuse Rehabilitation Services was not medically necessary.
The inpatient stay and detoxification treatment and other medical services noted in the clinical summary could have been safely and effectively provided at a lower level of care, as the health plan asserts. The treatment of this patient's substance use disorder did not require the structure of an inpatient setting or 24-hour monitoring. The patient displayed no serious disturbance of mental status despite having a history of ongoing substance use disorder with alcohol and cannabis and a comorbid anxiety disorder. Moreover, the patient did not show evidence for suicidal or aggressive behavior or risk, or severe cognitive impairment or psychosis, or perceptual disturbance that would have warranted an inpatient level admission and treatment. There were no severe/objective symptoms of withdrawal or biomedical issues in this case, and the patient had received detoxification treatments recently with knowledge of substance use disorder treatment protocols, as noted in the clinical summary. The patient had fair insight and control of impulses, and a working knowledge of substance use disorder treatment with a past treatment, as noted. 

Thus, the inpatient admission for detoxification treatment and 24-hour monitoring, and the requested inpatient level services were not medically necessary in this case scenario, contrary to the appeal from the treatment facility that argued that the patient had immediately relapsed after his last detoxification treatment episode, and had severe withdrawal symptoms. The appeal also noted that the patient was not appropriate for outpatient level detoxification treatment; the health plan indicated that the appropriate level of care was residential treatment per LOCADTR (level of care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) 3 Guidelines.

The health plan reasonably asserted that the requested inpatient treatment was considered not medically necessary under the plan in keeping with LOCADTR (level of care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) 3 Guidelines. The health plan appropriately recommended rehabilitation treatment in a residential treatment setting. In this case scenario, the patient was amenable to treatment with lower-level care in a less restrictive setting. The patient displayed no serious disturbance of mental status and no general medical complications or co-occurring disorders that would have warranted inpatient level services. There were no severe symptoms of withdrawal or biomedical issues in this case. The admission for detoxification treatment and 24-hour monitoring, and the requested inpatient level services were therefore not medically necessary in this case scenario, as the health plan asserts. summary:

The insurer denied the inpatient substance abuse admission
The denial is overturned.

The patient is an adult male who presented to an emergency department
requesting detoxification and substance use disorder treatment. He was screened
and admitted to acute inpatient level care in order to address substance use disorders with opioid, alcohol, cannabis and stimulant class substances. The patient was concerned for his health and stressed by his responsibilities at home, as well as several pending legal issues.

The patient has a history of psychiatric disorder, schizophrenia, and multiple
psychiatric hospitalizations in the past. He was not currently in treatment for his
mental disorder.

The patient presented without acute co-morbid general medical issues. Laboratory
assessments, EKG (electrocardiogram) and Chest X-Ray were unremarkable or
normal with a positive drug screen consistent with history. The patient has chronic
medical conditions including GERD (gastroesophageal reflux disease), gastritis and
arthritis treated with pantoprazole and analgesics.

The patient was admitted to detoxification treatment with a comprehensive
detoxification protocol with five-day tapering dosages of Methadone, and prn (as
needed) medications for comfort. The program provided for case management and
access to rehabilitation treatment that included comprehensive evidence-based
treatments.

During the brief detoxification, the patient did not readily engage in counseling
sessions focusing on education about the disease model of addiction, and,
involvement with milieu activities including peer support and sessions to motivate
the patient to proceed to rehabilitation treatment. His stage of change was
precontemplative and he tended to isolate indicating that he was meditating.
Withdrawal symptoms persisted and increased to a COWS (clinical opiate withdrawal scale) scale score of 9, and subsequently diminished with continued with improvement noted with discharge planning. The patient completed the detoxification protocol and was discharged with immediate step down for rehabilitation treatment and with plans for medication assisted treatment and recommendations for involvement with self-help recovery groups, and consideration of treatment for his co-occurring mental disorders and general medical conditions. At the time of his discharge, he remained with poor
insight and in a pre-contemplative or contemplative stage of change.

Yes, the inpatient substance abuse admission was medically necessary.

The insurer states that the patient did not meet New York State OASAS (New York
Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (level of care for alcohol and
drug treatment referral) 3.0 Criteria, and was medically stable and had mild
withdrawal symptoms at the time of presentation with normal vital signs, as well as
not having psychiatric symptoms that required inpatient level care. However, the
denial did not take into account the treatment dimensions in a patient who was
using heroin up to the date of presentation, had frequent relapses despite treatment
and little history of abstinence in the context of comorbidity with deficient coping
skills and a lack of insight and motivation, as well as a severe and persistent mental
disorder impacting the patient's ability to sustain a recovery effort. Thus, the
treatment facility notes in the appeal that the patient did meet LOCADTR (level of
care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) 3.0 Criteria and published guidelines

treatment dimensions that required inpatient level structure and monitoring with
treatment and withdrawal management. Moreover, the history of relapses and
comorbidities complicated the case, as well as the lack of insight and poor impulse
control and impaired judgment associated with poly-substance use and comorbid
schizophrenia that was generally untreated in the context of substance use. Thus,
the appeal indicated that the requested inpatient level treatment was appropriate
with regard to structure, setting, intensity of treatment and length of treatment.

In this case, New York State LOCADTR (level of care for alcohol and drug
treatment referral) 3.0 Criteria are met for inpatient level treatment that was
appropriate with regard to structure, setting, intensity of treatment and length of
treatment. The patient in this case was using heroin and cocaine together with
large quantity of alcohol on a daily continuous basis; and use of other substances of
abuse that did warrant continued inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal
management and monitoring; detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments
pertinent to the detoxification treatment episode could not have been safely or
effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive
assessment that was provided at the time of admission and during the time interval
under review. Moreover, the patient had persistent withdrawal symptoms, and, the
patient's social environment was not conducive to detoxification, and the patient
struggled with symptoms of anxiety in the context of limited insight, impaired
judgment and poor control of impulses.

The patient's history of substance use (frequency and quantity) together with the
high drug-use social environment, and severe psychosocial stressors and functional
impairments reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder and the need for
a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management, as the patient was
at high risk for treatment failure if the continued detoxification and withdrawal
management were to be attempted at a lower level of care.

Therefore, inpatient substance abuse admission was medically necessary in this
case and is consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published
practice guidelines, ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) Criteria and
LOCUS (Level of Care Utilization System)

Day one, the patient's vital signs were as follows: temperature 36.7 Celsius, pulse 70, respiratory rate 12, and blood pressure 117/72.  The patient reported minimal tremors. The patient was admitted with a plan for Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) protocol.  During his hospital stay, he did not have findings of acute alcohol withdrawal. summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse.
Treatment: Inpatient admission.
The insurer denied the inpatient admission.
The denial is upheld. 

The patient is a male referred for inpatient rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment in order to address use of a cannabis class substance with use of two to three joints per day. The patient has no reported history of withdrawal seizures or delirium. The patient was self-referred and indicated that he was tired of feeling unwell.

The patient has a history of psychiatric disorder and treatment for schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type and comorbid anxiety disorder. The patient has a history of psychiatric hospitalizations with ongoing outpatient treatment with clozapine and Haldol Decanoate and Depakote. There is a history of formal substance use disorder treatment with no evidence for outpatient follow up or involvement with 12-step recovery groups.

There were no acute general medical issues and he was medically screened prior to admission. Vital signs were normal and laboratory assessments were normal or unremarkable with a drug screen consistent with history.

Evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination that reflected motivation for rehabilitation treatment, but limited insight, impaired judgment, and poor control of impulses. The patient was described as cooperative with fluent speech and disorganized thought processing with referential thought content that was bizarre. Mood was anxious and congruent affect. He had no severe symptoms such as mania, psychosis, perceptual disturbance or severe cognitive impairment. He did not report suicidal ideation or aggressive impulses. Sleep and appetite were okay.

Upon admission to inpatient level services, the patient received comprehensive evaluation and treatment that included focus on coping skills, relapse prevention techniques with identification of triggers, education about the disease model of addiction, and, involvement with groups, as well as peer supported recovery meetings, and other therapeutic activities within the treatment milieu. Psychiatric evaluation was provided and he was continued on his psychotropic regimen. Other medications included lisinopril, metformin, Lipitor and alogliptin, as well as a rescue inhaler to address chronic medical conditions.

No, the proposed Inpatient Admission was not medically necessary for this patient.
The health plan's determination is appropriate in keeping with NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria. In this case, the patient could have been reasonably managed with lower-level care in a less restrictive treatment setting. The patient presented with substance use disorder, diagnosed with cannabis use disorder. He was medically screened and had no acute general medical issues. He received inpatient level rehabilitation treatment and readily engaged in treatment and had no significant biomedical (withdrawal symptoms or signs) or psychiatric treatment issues and resumed treatment for the co-occurring psychiatric disorders. During the time interval under review, the patient was noted to be in no apparent distress with reasonable functioning and active participation in treatment including positive interactions with staff and peers. Throughout his stay, there were no complicating treatment issues or biomedical or co-occurring psychiatric issues or safety concerns that would have warranted inpatient level of care, structure or 24-hour monitoring for the time interval under review. The application of NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria, as well as Level of Care Utilization System (LOCUS) and American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria referenced below, did indicate that the patient was clinically appropriate for treatment with lower-level care in a less restrictive treatment setting, as the health plan asserts, and contrary to the appeal indicating that the health plan's rationale for denial was "invalid." summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Use Disorder
Treatment: Inpatient substance abuse treatment
The insurer denied inpatient substance abuse treatment.
The determination is overturned.

The patient presented for detoxification and substance-related services. He has a history of severe substance use disorders with alcohol, opioid (heroin), stimulants (crack cocaine), and cannabis (marijuana) class substances of abuse. He has a history of multiple detoxification treatment episodes with the more recent with a brief rehabilitation treatment and relapse. He was using one-fifth of cognac on a continuous daily basis together with up to ten bags of heroin, as well as tobacco (½ pack per day), two blunts of marijuana, and $100 worth of cocaine daily.

At the time of presentation, the patient was also requesting referral for rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment. He denied current legal issues. He was unemployed with limited family support and reported severe psychosocial stressors within the primary support, social environment, and housing domains with unemployment and social security disability. The patient reported functional decline as the substance abuse/disease had progressed which again prompted his self-referral for detoxication treatment in the context of at least twenty prior detoxification treatment episodes and a pattern of back-to-back admissions.

The patient provided no past history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens, but did report severe alcohol withdrawal symptoms. He was medically screened and admitted for inpatient level detoxification with plans for a five-day detoxification treatment with Valium and Suboxone and supportive measures. Withdrawal symptoms were mild to moderate with a clinical opiate withdrawal (COWS) and Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) scale scores up to 15 and 21, respectively, on day two of his inpatient stay. He displayed a headache, tremor, nausea and bone aches with restlessness and anxiety.

The patient has no history of psychiatric disorder or treatment, and no history of suicidal or self-harming behaviors. There were no acute medical issues in this case other than the alcohol and opioid withdrawal. The patient was tobacco dependent at one-half pack per day, as noted, and he had a history of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) positivity with no active signs of HIV.

On mental status examination, there were no severe symptoms and no safety concerns with regard to risk of harm to self or others. The patient displayed poor insight despite his extensive treatment history, impaired judgment due to the substance use, and poor control of impulses. He demonstrated symptoms of anxiety with generalized symptoms including insomnia and labile affect, together with symptoms related to the alcohol and opioid withdrawal, as noted.

The patient was admitted for inpatient treatment with a detoxification protocol. He received tapering dosages of Valium and Suboxone and replacement of vitamins with the availability of nicotine replacement and smoking cessation counseling and comfort medications and as needed (prn) medications prescribed for pain, anxiety, and insomnia.

The patient's hospital course progressed without incident. His vital signs remained normal with occasional variability and the patient reported mild nausea, anxiety, restlessness and insomnia with persistently mild symptoms of withdrawal that diminished throughout his hospital course. He was socially withdrawn initially, but participating in counseling and educational sessions. The patient was participating more readily in group, educational and counseling sessions, and was receiving individual counseling with case management to enhance motivation to proceed to rehabilitation treatment. Arrangements were being made for a direct referral to rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment. He received case management services and planning for clinically appropriate aftercare with discharge.

The case records, health plan documents, appeal documents, correspondence from the treatment facility, correspondence from the health plan, as well as the health plan's rationale for the denial of certification for coverage of the requested treatment were reviewed. This review is a New York State review with the application of NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines.

The issue under review is inpatient substance abuse treatment.

The requested health service/treatment of inpatient substance abuse treatment is medically necessary for this patient.

The patient was using large quantities of alcohol and heroin on a daily continuous basis together with cocaine and cannabis that did warrant the admission and the continued inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring. Detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments pertinent to the detoxification treatment episode could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment that was provided at the time of admission. The patient's social environment was not conducive to an effective detoxification and the patient had struggled with withdrawal symptoms which were being effectively addressed with Valium and Suboxone protocols and supportive measures. The patient had associated clinical features that included a lack of sober supports and limited insight, impaired judgment and poor control of impulses.

The adult inpatient stay and continued detoxification treatment of this patient's substance use disorders did necessitate the hospital admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level setting with withdrawal management, psychosocial supports, and 24-hour monitoring. The patient's history of substance abuse (frequency and quantity) together with the severe psychosocial stressors and functional impairments do reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder and the need for a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management, as the patient was at high risk for treatment failure or general medical complications such as seizures if detoxification and withdrawal management were to be attempted at a lower level of care. Therefore, medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published practice guidelines, ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) Criteria, and the scientific literature, referenced below, and New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews including the appropriate application of NY OASAS LOCADTR 3.0 Criteria referenced below.

summary:
Diagnosis: Suicide attempt, substance abuse
Treatment: Continued Inpatient Mental Health Stay
The insurer denied the continued inpatient mental health stay.
The determination is upheld.


The patient was brought in by the police after a suicide attempt with an overdose of Xanax and one bottle of Nyquil. The patient's sister had notified police of the suicide attempt. The patient's mood had recently worsened with increased anxiety, depression and sleep disturbance in the context of substance use and a pending divorce. The patient has co-occurring substance use disorder with cocaine, cannabis, and alcohol with benzodiazepine use and tobacco dependence. The patient's reported ongoing stress with regard to primary support, social, occupational and daily functions. He reported a history of a myocardial infarction and atrial fibrillation and other chronic medical conditions including obesity and metabolic syndrome, as well as a recent injury to his left foot. He was medically screened and admitted to inpatient psychiatric care.

His past history included psychiatric hospitalizations and substance use disorder treatment with a chronic relapsing course. He had a longstanding mood disturbance together with marital problems and a past history of legal problems.

Mental status examination on admission included a disheveled male, appearing older, and with poor eye contact and a cooperative stance. His mood was depressed and irritable with anxious affect and sleep disturbance. His thought processing was linear with no evidence of psychosis, mania, thought disorder, or severe cognitive impairment. The patient denied suicidal ideation despite the attempt and subsequent calls to his mother threatening suicide with fair to poor insight and impaired judgment.

The patient was assessed with a comprehensive psychiatric and psychosocial evaluation. Medications were provided to include Zoloft and Remeron with adjustments to address insomnia and anxiety-related symptoms with as needed (prn) use of hydroxyzine for insomnia. The patient had the opportunity to participate in group, educational and milieu activities including educational sessions aimed at assisting the patient with improved coping skills and abstinence from substances. The patient received a tapering regimen of Librium with mild withdrawal symptoms and the patient had the availability of comfort medication and was prescribed supplements including vitamins and nicotine replacement.
The patient was compliant with his treatment plan and adherent with medications with tolerability. The patient remained depressed with irritability. He had attempted to elope on the day of admission and subsequently had called his mother threatening suicide, as noted. He also attacked another patient for reasons unknown.

He displayed improved mood with brighter affect and better sleep and functioning. He had fair insight, but impaired judgment, as before. He was future oriented with a more positive outlook, and was receiving support from his mother. He was attending groups and considering treatment for the substance use disorders. He remained on Zoloft 50 milligrams (mg) and Remeron was increased to 30 mg. An orthopedic consultation had been obtained with recommendation for a boot on his left foot.

There were no further complications of treatment or the clinical course during his inpatient stay. By the date of discharge, he was noted to be calm and cooperative, still with improved mood and diminished anxiety and better sleep. Insight was improved. Throughout the inpatient stay, he had denied suicidal ideation and there were no remaining safety concerns. He was discharged with clinically appropriate aftercare including referral to his community provider of services for medication management and recommendations for substance use disorder treatment. The health plan documents, the case records, and correspondence from the health plan and treatment facility were reviewed. The rationale for denial of the requested benefit of inpatient level mental health stay was reviewed.

The issue under review is continued inpatient mental health stay.

The requested health service/treatment of inpatient mental health stay was not medically necessary for this patient.

Continued inpatient level monitoring for safety and the structure of the residential setting was not medically necessary in this case scenario. The patient could have received intensive mental health services with lower level care in keeping with prevailing standards of medical practice. His family was supportive and the marital issues and other psychosocial issues as well as the substance use disorders could have been effectively addressed at a lower level of care. The patient's psychosocial stressors were not so severe to prevent treatment from continuing at a lower level of care with more intensive services. The patient had access to 12-step recovery groups and medication-assisted treatment for the substance use disorders. Thus, the requested benefit of inpatient level mental health stay was not medically necessary in keeping with prevailing standards of medical practice and the guidelines and American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria referenced below, as well as the application of NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria, also referenced below.

summary:
Diagnosis: Acute pancreatitis due to alcohol use

Treatment: Inpatient hospital admission

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient hospital admission.

The denial is overturned.

This patient was admitted to this hospital with acute pancreatitis due to alcohol use and had alcohol detoxification treatment as he had reports of alcohol withdrawal including nausea, multiple episodes of vomiting, shakes, fatigue, insomnia, loss of appetite, weakness, and elevated heart rate. He reportedly had 4-5 drinks but was averaging 7-9 drinks of bourbon per day. He reportedly had multiple medical issues due to alcohol use including pancreatitis, acute transaminitis, low potassium (K) of 2.7 and low magnesium (MG) requiring supplementation and intravenous (IV) fluids. He reportedly had hepatomegaly and thrombocytopenia with a platelet level of 57 and also had a prolonged QT (interval on electrocardiogram [EKG]) interval. He was started on Librium for detoxification which was then changed to Ativan for detoxification. He reportedly required and received Ativan for alcohol detoxification treatment and then was discharged with referral to outpatient treatment. 

This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient hospital treatment, for the medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that he required this hospital level of care. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports "that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal" are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. It also states that patients with past complicated or life-threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens are in need of inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal and reports that patients with comorbid medical condition that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification. Also, the United States (US) Department of Health and Human Services-Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) Center for Substance Abuse Treatment reports that inpatient treatment is necessary if the ability to attend outpatient treatment daily is a problem, one is unable to follow up in outpatient treatment, if medical conditions complicate the treatment of withdrawal, if one has previous withdrawal seizures of delirium tremens, or if one does not have the capacity for informed consent. In this case this patient had comorbid medical conditions complicating the management of withdrawal, as he had past reported alcohol withdrawal seizures which requires inpatient medical detoxification treatment. 

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) he did require 24 hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive setting, as he continued to use large amounts of alcohol daily, required and received IV detoxification medication (Lorazepam and Librium initially) to modify withdrawal from alcohol and prevent more complicated or life threatening withdrawal such as delirium tremens. The risk of delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use, so he was considered at high risk for this. He also had multiple medical issues due to alcohol use including acute pancreatitis, acute transaminitis, low K of 2.7 and low MG requiring supplementation, hepatomegaly, thrombocytopenia with a platelet level of 57 and also had a prolonged QT interval. These multiple medical issues complicated the management and treatment of withdrawal and he required inpatient medical hospital detoxification treatment. He did require 24 hour medical hospital treatment for alcohol detoxification and it was considered unsafe for him to be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive level of care then. He required at least the entire duration of stay, as he was at risk for life threatening and complicated withdrawal including delirium tremens. As a result, the recommendation is to overturn the previous decision and approve coverage for inpatient hospital treatment. 

It did not appear that the health care plan decision was reasonable, considering medical evidence, or in the best interests of the patient.

The insurer's denial of coverage for the inpatient hospital is overturned. Medical necessity is substantiated.

The case involves an adult male admitted to acute inpatient psychiatric services for treatment of an exacerbation of a chronic psychotic disorder best characterized as schizophrenia, unspecified type, and comorbid general medical conditions with hyperglycemia and metabolic acidosis. The patient has other co-morbid mental health condition best characterized as an unspecified anxiety disorder; general medical comorbidities include type II diabetes mellitus and hypertension. The patient presented to the emergency department brought in by his spouse. He had worsening symptoms of psychosis attributed to the recent second dose of the COVID-19 (coronavirus) vaccine; he presented with a serum glucose above 500 and other laboratory abnormalities including elevated creatine phosphokinase (CPK), low sodium and blood gases indicating a metabolic acidosis and consistent with an acute worsening of the diabetes. 

The patient had been to an emergency department four days earlier with agitation, psychosis and aggressive behavior associated with mood swings. At the time of presentation for evaluation and treatment, the patient was acutely psychotic and demonstrated disorganized thought processing with content that was illogical and incoherent with paranoid thinking impacting his functioning. He reported auditory hallucinations hearing voices in the walls and windows, and anxiety and apprehension with sad affect and suicidal ideation. He also reported somatic sensations indicating that his skin felt "artificial."

He was admitted to acute inpatient level care with combined medical and psychiatric treatment for the comorbid conditions, an exacerbation of the schizophrenia and diabetes. He received one-to-one observation, medication adjustments per the psychiatric consultant and general medical support. He was prescribed intravenous insulin and olanzapine, as well as "as needed" (PRN) use of Haldol for agitation and psychosis. Other medications included enalapril, enoxaparin and metoprolol. During his brief stay, the patient's mental status and functioning had not changed significantly, despite ongoing treatment with antipsychotic medications and other therapeutic interventions to address the hyperglycemia and metabolic disturbance. He continued to display perceptual disturbances and delusions prompting him to call 911 that involved fears that the family pets were at risk. He was intermittently hyper-religious and paranoid with compulsive behaviors associated with motor agitation. He required staff intervention for daily care; he was cooperative with staff and medication adherent. He was deemed to be medically cleared and was transferred for acute inpatient psychiatric services.

The dates under review were denied certification of coverage by the health plan for inpatient level treatment on the basis of medical necessity with reference to InterQual Criteria and the assertion that the patient could have been effectively treated as an outpatient. 

The treatment facility indicated that the inpatient admission and stay was medically necessary on the basis of Milliman Care Guidelines (MCG) Criteria for inpatient level care: Other Psychotic Disorders and Endocrinology/Diabetes, respectively for Inpatient Care (B-011-IP and M-130). Additionally, the appeal letter indicated that the inpatient level care was reasonable and medically necessary in view of the exacerbation of schizophrenia with acute symptoms and decline in functioning, and the general medical comorbidity.

Yes, the proposed treatment was medically necessary for this patient.

The patient's admission and continued hospital stay for treatment of an exacerbation of a psychotic disorder (schizophrenia) and treatment to address the metabolic disturbance (diabetes) did require the admission and continued inpatient level services, structure, and monitoring through discharge/transfer. The patient's severity of symptoms, and inability to effectively participate in treatment at a lower level of care, persistent functional impairment, and treatment issues related to persistent symptoms of acute psychosis with general medical complications were clinical factors and treatment dimensions that necessitated the acute inpatient hospital care, structure, and monitoring. The medication treatment and safety monitoring, the support of functioning and the continued application of general medical treatments for the diabetes and hypertension, as well as assurance of medication adherence, were factors that did warrant the admission and the continued inpatient level treatment through discharge/transfer. 

As the treatment facility asserts in the appeal, the inpatient admission and stay was medically necessary and the inpatient level care was reasonable and medically necessary in view of the exacerbation of schizophrenia with acute symptoms and decline in functioning, and the general medical comorbidity. The health plan's denial is not reasonable in that the patient could not have been safely or effectively managed with lower level services such as outpatient treatment.

Specifically, the patient's admission and continued treatment through discharge/transfer is reasonable and in the best interest of the patient; he had severe symptoms of psychosis complicated by an acute general medical disturbance, a decline in functioning and safety issues together with a high risk for medication non-adherence due to persistent symptoms of psychosis. He had deteriorated to the point that he was a safety risk with disorganized and perceptual disturbance/paranoid thinking and poor insight and impaired judgment that persisted throughout his stay. Again, the patient could not have been safely or effectively managed during the time interval under review at a lower level of care or in a less restrictive treatment environment. The admission and continued stay was necessary to develop a safe and clinically appropriate discharge plan and disposition that would effectively support his continued treatment.

summary:
Diagnosis: Depression
Treatment: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS), Pre-service
The insurer denied the Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS), pre-service.
The denial is overturned. 

The patient is an adult male. He has a history of major depressive disorder, recurrent and severe without psychotic features. The patient has a documented history of multiple medication treatments for depression including treatment with more than two disparate classes of medication and at least three or more trials with antidepressant medications (SSRI [selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor], SNRI [serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor] and trazodone), as well as augmentation with Abilify and Rexulti, in keeping with FDA (United States Food and Drug Administration) indicated use. Additionally, the patient has had treatment with an evidence-based psychotherapy for over five years combined with medication. Due to the lack of efficacy with those treatments, the patient was referred for TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy and underwent repetitive TMS therapy for 3 months with an initial robust clinical response.

The patient's clinician has recommended treatment with another course of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) therapy with up to 36 treatment episodes. The recommendation is in the context of the recurrent episode of depression that is known to be treatment-resistant/refractory and had been ongoing for several years without sustained benefit from treatment and without a response of remission until the first course of TMS therapy.

Coverage of the TMS therapy is therefore requested on appeal from the denial by the health plan in view of the robust response to TMS therapy. The health plan has denied authorization for coverage of rTMS on the basis of coverage exclusion and indicates that the requested treatment is not a covered benefit with reference to the plan's InterQual medical necessity criteria and medical coverage policy/plan guidelines concerning TMS therapy for depressive disorder referencing that the patient did not have his course of TMS therapy 6 months prior to the request for another course of TMS therapy and that during the first course of TMS therapy, the patient did not show a significant reduction of 50% or greater on the measures of depression - as required in order to be approved for coverage. Moreover, the plan denial indicated that no information was submitted to suggest a recurrence of the major depressive disorder.

Yes, the requested transcranial magnetic stimulation is medically necessary for this patient.

In this case, the patient has a diagnosis of treatment refractory major depression, and at least three or more alternative therapeutic trials with augmentation together with other therapeutic measures have been provided without clinical benefit. The patient had a prior response to TMS therapy. He subsequently experienced a recurrent episode of major depression, scoring a 19 on the PHQ-9 (patient health questionnaire) as before.  Thus, in this case, the proposed TMS therapy is considered clinically appropriate and medically necessary in view of the scientific literature and guidelines for the evaluation of treatment of refractory major depressive disorder. Additionally, the proposed rTMS therapy is reasonable and in the best interest of the patient. The decision to proceed with another course of TMS therapy reflects sound medical judgment based upon the current scientific literature and American Psychiatric Association practice guideline concerning the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorder. The patient in this case has demonstrated that his depressive disorder is treatment refractory or resistant, and the proposed treatment of recurrent major depressive disorder with TMS therapy with a clinically appropriate number of sessions is reasonable and warranted in this case scenario, and is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice and the definition of medical necessity.

Moreover, the plan reason for denial of coverage is not valid indicating on the basis of coverage exclusion that the requested treatment is not a covered benefit with reference to the plan's InterQual medical necessity criteria and medical coverage policy/plan guidelines concerning TMS therapy for depressive disorder referencing that the patient did not have his course of TMS therapy 6 months prior to the request for another course of TMS therapy and that during the first course of TMS therapy, the patient did not show a significant reduction of 50% or greater on the measures of depression - as required in order to be approved for coverage. Moreover, the plan denial indicated that no information was submitted to suggest a recurrence of the major depressive disorder. Indeed, as the treating clinician argues on appeal, the recommended treatment with another course of rTMS therapy with up to 36 treatment episodes is in the context of the recurrent episode of depression, as supported with submitted information is reasonable in a case that is known to be treatment-resistant/refractory and had been ongoing for several years without sustained benefit from other standard treatments and without a response of remission until the first course of TMS therapy, as well as the evidence for a robust response to TMS therapy with a 68% reduction in measures of depression as noted in the clinical summary.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Inpatient Rehabilitation Services
The insurer denied the inpatient rehabilitation services.
The denial is overturned.

This case involves an adult female with severe alcohol use disorder who was admitted to inpatient residential level substance use disorder services following detoxification treatment and withdrawal management and after medical screening with plans for rehabilitation treatment and continued treatment of co-occurring mental disorders with anxiety and depression. Her presentation for residential level care was prompted by a break up with her fiancé/significant other in the context of longstanding and continued use of alcohol with use of up to two bottles of wine daily. The alcohol disorder had onset in adolescence with progression of the disease and escalating use in the five years prior to admission. The increasing use of alcohol occurred in the context of a co-occurring anxiety disorder and grief related to the death of family members and severe psychosocial stressors including the break up with the fiancé. The alcohol use had resulted in impairment of functioning with regard to social, occupational and daily functions with use throughout the day, putting her health at risk. The patient had no other significant past substance use disorder treatment. 

The patient presented with associated symptoms of anxiety and dysphoric mood with sad affect in the context of grief. There was no recent history of psychiatric hospitalization, and no mention of suicidal behavior except for one hospital stay as a teen. Psychotropic medications included Paxil 40 milligrams and as needed use of trazodone for sleep. She reported low energy and appetite.

The patient had no acute general medical issues. She had hypertension treated with amlodipine and metoprolol. Her exam and laboratory assessment and electrocardiogram (EKG) were otherwise normal or unremarkable except for markedly elevated liver functions and mean corpuscular volume (MCV) and cholesterol. The patient presented with acute withdrawal symptoms with a Clinical Institute for Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) scale score of four, having just completed formal detoxification with vitamin replacement. She reported intense craving and tremor/shakes with elevated blood pressure.

Mental status examination included a kempt appearance with anxiety, dysphoria, and sad affect. Speech was clear and thoughts were circumstantial and tangential, but goal directed. She denied suicidal thoughts or ideas. There was no evidence for psychosis, mania, thought disorder, or severe cognitive impairment despite concentration difficulties. Insight was limited and judgment impaired due to the alcohol use disorder.

The patient had received detoxification treatment, and immediately transferred to inpatient residential level treatment with the structure, monitoring, and the intensity of residential level services. Treatment included group, individual, and educational services with the addition of non-pharmacologic interventions to address the anxiety disturbance, and emphasis on coping skills with the goal of the development of a relapse prevention plan and planning for a safe and appropriate discharge back to the community with partial hospital level care. She was prescribed Paxil and Acamprosate for craving (medication assisted treatment) with vitamin and nicotine replacement. 

The patient had engaged in treatment and was improving; she had received evidence-based interventions, and the patient's insight and mood had improved, as she was calm with euthymic mood with persistent reports of anxiety and less craving. The treatment team was recommending intensive treatment in the community with continued involvement in peer-supported recovery groups and sober supports or a sober living environment, and recommendations for the obtainment of a sponsor. Prognosis was guarded to fair and she was deemed to be at high risk for relapse unless continued treatment was to be provided. Discharge planning occurred as treatment continued with discharge and return to the community/home and plans for continued substance use disorder treatment and involvement in recovery groups with sober supports, as well as treatment from her primary care physician (PCP), and referral for psychotherapy. Medications were to be continued as noted.

Yes, the proposed treatment was medically necessary for this patient.

The continued inpatient residential level of services, structure, and monitoring provided in this case are warranted in view of the severity of the alcohol use disorder and associated symptoms of anxiety and depression, and complications of the alcohol disorder, as well as the intense craving that persisted up until the time of discharge. The patient could not have been effectively managed with lower-level services during the time interval under review contrary to the plan's reasoning for denial.

The continued residential level services through discharge were clinically appropriate and consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice, as well as the appropriate application of NY State Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria that are meant to serve for determining an appropriate level of care, and indeed, the health plan covered the admission and inpatient residential stay for a certain time period. The services were provided with evidence-based treatments that are known to benefit patients with severe alcohol use disorder, as well as providing services to address treatment issues in a patient who presented with persistent withdrawal symptoms and craving, and general medical complications of an alcohol disorder and with high risk for relapse and continued liver damage. Thus, the patient's severity of alcohol use disorder and associated symptoms of  anxiety and depression in the context of severe psychosocial stressors did warrant and necessitate the continued inpatient residential level services, as proposed, and with the plan for step down to lower level services once the patient had stabilized with the ability to achieve abstinence with sober supports in working toward discharge plans and considering a safe and appropriate transition to the community with appropriate aftercare to include involvement with recovery groups and medication assisted treatment to address craving. 

Moreover, the patient presented with high risk for relapse in view of an inadequate recovery environment, a relative lack of coping skills and readiness to change, and a lack of sober supports despite some exposure to recovery groups. The additional time spent with motivational techniques and other interventions were essential to a successful therapeutic outcome in this case, especially since the patient was making progress and engaged in treatment and adherent to medications which the health plan had determined as reasons for not needing continued residential treatment. These clinical features and treatment dimensions did support the necessity for the continued inpatient level services and the continued structure and monitoring and intensity of services provided at the inpatient residential level of care through discharge.

This answer is consistent with the application of  New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria, and with Level of Care Utilization System (LOCUS) Guidelines and the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and with the published guideline and the scientific literature, referenced below.

The application of Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria were not appropriately applied in this case; the health plan denied services  indicating that continued inpatient residential treatment is not necessary because there were no withdrawal symptoms, that the patient was medically stable with no psychiatric disorders requiring continued inpatient level care and that the patient was taking medications including medication assisted treatment (MAT) and was motivated for treatment and engaged in treatment with access to sober living and/or sober supports, as well as making progress. None of these reasons would support the level of care determination for the dates of service under review. The continued inpatient residential level of care in this case was medically necessary and consistent with the application of  New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria, and with Level of Care Utilization System (LOCUS) Guidelines and the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and with the published guideline and the scientific literature, referenced below, as the appeal document asserts.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder-severe-recurrent. 
Treatment: Continued stay at an acute mental health inpatient level of care. 

The insurer denied coverage for continued stay at an acute mental health inpatient level of care. 

The denial is overturned. 

This teenage male was admitted to this inpatient mental health residential treatment after a psychiatric hospitalization due to a suicide attempt by cutting himself. He had major depressive symptoms including suicidal intent, plans, behaviors, depressed mood, emotional dysregulation, feelings of hopelessness, anxiety symptoms, delays in social interaction and communication and in social relationships. He reportedly had difficulties with affect regulation, relationship difficulties, academic difficulties, and also substance use issues including alcohol and cannabis use. The patient had diagnoses of Major Depressive Disorder-severe-recurrent, Autism Spectrum Disorder, Generalized Anxiety Disorder, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). He reportedly had past other inpatient treatments following a serious suicide attempt by overdose of 50 Tylenol pills and Aleve with a large amount of vodka which resulted in a psychiatric hospitalization. He reportedly was in a wilderness program. He then went to a boarding school due to more hopelessness and self-injurious behavior by cutting self. He also went to the Emergency Room (ER) for another suicide attempt by cutting. He was in psychiatric hospitalization and then went residential treatment, a mental health residential treatment. 
    
The American Psychological Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Major Depressive Disorders reports that the least restrictive level of care for safe and effective treatment is appropriate. The APA Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Suicidal Behaviors reports that patients with past suicide attempts are at high risk for suicide. 

This patient had 2 past suicide attempts by overdose resulting in hospitalizations. He was considered a high-risk patient with difficulty in coping skills and had multiple psychiatric problems and multiple past suicide attempts with continued suicidal plan and intent and depressive symptoms. This supervised and structured 24-hour inpatient therapeutic residential treatment setting was considered still medically necessary treatment during the denial period. 

It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably, with sound clinical judgment, or in the best interests of the patient. 

The medical records provided enough evidence to support that he required this level of care. This was a very high-risk patient with multiple past suicide attempts who still reported suicidal intent and made threatening suicidal statements such as he will sign out of this facility and then kill himself. He continued to report depressive symptoms including depressed mood and hopelessness during the denial period while still struggling with social interactions, relationships, and communication. 

The insurer's denial of coverage for the continued stay at an acute mental health inpatient level of care is overturned. Medical necessity is substantiated.
