summary:
Diagnosis: Substance use disorder
Treatment: Inpatient admission
The insurer denied the inpatient admission
The denial is upheld

The case involves a male who was admitted to inpatient rehabilitation and substance use disorder treatment beginning to address substance use disorder with opioid, alcohol and stimulant class substances. The patient has no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens, but did report blackouts. He was receiving medication assisted treatment with methadone 50 milligrams daily. He had been using up to five bags of heroin and cocaine with intravenous (IV) administration, and using up to three pints of liquor per day, as well as taking his methadone prescribed from a methadone maintenance treatment program (MMTP). His drug screen was positive for cocaine, opiates, Fentanyl and methadone.

The patient has a history of psychiatric disorder best characterized as schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type; he denied history of suicidal behavior and had been lost to follow up with his mental health care. He reported being hospitalized a couple years prior.

The patient had no acute general medical issues other than left shoulder pain; he had chronic conditions that included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with bronchitis and history of hepatitis C, as well as malnutrition with weight loss. He was medically screened upon admission with laboratory assessment and physical examination that were grossly normal or unremarkable. Shoulder x-ray did not reveal a fracture. He was tobacco dependent at one-fourth pack per day.

The patient is single and unemployed. There was no history of legal issues or trauma history in this case. Psychosocial stressors included primary support, economic, occupational, social environment and general medical domains.

Evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination that reflected reasonable motivation for rehabilitation treatment, but limited insight and coping skills. The patient was described as cooperative with fluent speech and organized thought processing. He displayed euthymic mood with no severe symptoms such as mania, psychosis, perceptual disturbance or severe cognitive impairment. He did not report suicidal ideation or aggressive impulses. There were withdrawal symptoms or post-acute withdrawal symptoms with a Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) score of 17 including chills, tremors, muscle aches and joint pain, piloerection, rhinorrhea, yawning, and restlessness with anxiety.

Upon admission to inpatient level services, the patient received comprehensive evaluation and treatment that included counseling, group sessions, education, and other therapeutic activities. Psychiatric evaluation had been provided and affirmed that the patient had no acute symptoms of the co-occurring psychiatric disorder(s). The patient engaged in substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment. He was adherent with medication that included vitamin supplements and the availability of nicotine replacement to address tobacco dependence, as well as as-needed (PRN) use of medications for pain and insomnia and elevations in blood pressure. He received methadone at 500 milligrams per day.

Throughout his brief inpatient stay, the patient remained stable and engaged with the treatment regimen. He received intensive rehabilitation services, monitoring, and structure provided within the inpatient treatment program including 24-hour monitoring. The patient was discharged and referred to a residential program for continued rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment, as well as recommendation for follow up with his primary care physician. 

No, the requested inpatient stay for rehabilitation treatment is not medically necessary for this patient.
The patient received inpatient level rehabilitation treatment. He was receiving methadone maintenance treatment in the community. As the health plan asserts, the patient had no significant general medical or psychiatric comorbidity that would have warranted acute inpatient level care, and presented with no complicated withdrawal or safety concerns such as suicidality or aggressive impulses. He was motivated to engage in rehabilitation treatment. Thus, the patient did not meet New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria, as the health plan asserts in the denial.

During the time interval under review, the patient was noted to be in no apparent distress or mild distress with reasonable functioning and active participation in treatment including positive interactions with staff and peers. During his brief inpatient stay prior to discharge, there were no complicating treatment issues that would have warranted inpatient level of care, structure or 24-hour monitoring. The application of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria (referenced below) did indicate that the patient was clinically appropriate for treatment with lower-level care in a less restrictive treatment setting, as the health plan also asserts and contrary to the appeal. Thus, the argument on appeal noted below is not consistent with New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria, and medical necessity for the inpatient level care for substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment is not met in this case scenario, consistent with the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, the scientific literature and published guidelines, referenced below.

Yes, the health plan has acted reasonably, with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.
The patient in this case scenario is not clinically appropriate for an inpatient level of care for the time interval under review. The patient had presented with a level of stability that included no complicated withdrawal symptoms or biomedical issues, and no co-occurring psychiatric disorders or safety concerns that would have warranted inpatient level care. He did not need the monitoring or the structure of an acute inpatient setting in order to receive effective substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment. Moreover, he was motivated for treatment and was already involved with methadone maintenance treatment and peer-supported recovery groups that could have been provided in a less restrictive treatment setting in order to address the comorbid opioid, cocaine and alcohol use disorders. Thus, the health plan's determination is reasonable in this case scenario. 

This answer is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice for the conditions diagnosed and under treatment in this case, and consistent with the application of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Guidelines/Criteria, referenced below.

The patient is an adult male. He was brought by emergency services to the emergency department after he was found unconscious in an apartment building. He was revived with 8 mg (milligrams) of Narcan. He had likely overdosed on Fentanyl, as he described using a white substance that he thought was cocaine. Incidentally, his wife had also used the same drug and reportedly had required ICU (intensive care unit) treatment.

In the emergency department, an evaluation revealed abnormal laboratory findings of transaminitis and leukocytosis reflecting kidney injury with an initial BUN (blood urea nitrogen) of 26 and creatinine of 2.5. He had elevated liver functions and WBC (white blood count) at 20.7 initially, then 13.3. Troponin was initially elevated at 0.499 with subsequent value at 0.198. Chest X-Ray showed bilateral evidence of pneumonitis and/or edema with right greater than left. Cardiology consult was obtained with EKG (electrocardiogram) showing no ischemic changes and an ejection fraction at 45-50% with acute heart failure. Psychiatric consultation was obtained indicating that the patient had no safety concerns such as suicidal ideation with diagnoses of the substance use disorders and recommendation for outpatient treatment. In this regard, the patient had a positive drug screen for cocaine and cannabis consistent with history. He was also using alcohol and tobacco.

The patient was treated in the emergency department with Lasix and Zosyn with IV (intravenous) administration and started on antibiotics to address the provisional diagnosis of pneumonitis. He was admitted for inpatient level monitoring of EKG (electrocardiogram), serial cardiac enzymes, CK (creatine kinase), BMP (basic metabolic panel), CBC (complete blood count), and LFTs (liver function tests), as well as continued use of Zosyn and antibiotics together with vitamin replacement therapy and comfort medications, as well as the availability of nicotine replacement therapy and comfort medications, and oxygen at 3 liters with nasal cannula. COWS (clinical opiate withdrawal scale) monitoring with withdrawal protocol was employed and was not significant.

The inpatient hospital course was generally benign with improving status. Discharge diagnosis was pneumonitis and drug overdose likely due to Fentanyl. He was discharge with recommendations for clinically appropriate follow up per recommendations of the psychiatric and cardiology consultants. He was advised on further treatment as clinically appropriate.

The patient's underlying treatment for cocaine, alcohol and cannabis use disorders was amenable to treatment in a less restrictive treatment setting, as indicated by the psychiatric consultant. As the health plan asserts in the denial determination, the patient had no hemodynamic instability, no altered mental status, no arrhythmias, and no respiratory distress, as well as no psychiatric or neurologic signs or symptoms that would have required inpatient hospital level of care. Any indicated cardiac monitoring and serial monitoring of laboratory assessments and other assessments of the kidney injury, cardiac status and treatment of the pneumonitis could have been appropriately managed with observation level care with referral for the underlying substance use disorders.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse

Treatment inpatient substance abuse rehabilitation admission

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient substance abuse rehabilitation admission

The denial is overturned

This female that was admitted to inpatient substance rehabilitation for alcohol and substance rehabilitation treatment. She reportedly was drinking a fifth of alcohol per day, smoking 2 blunts of cannabis per day, and using cocaine. Her toxicology was positive for cocaine, benzodiazepines, and THC (tetrahydrocannabinol). The patient had multiple past inpatient substance detoxification treatments and rehabilitation treatments. She also had comorbid schizophrenia-bipolar diagnosis and past inpatient psychiatric hospitalizations. She reportedly had no clean time and lacked coping skills, ability to identify relapse triggers, insight into use and the consequences of use, lacked relapse prevention skills and sober support, and was homeless. She had 4 past arrests in 6 months. The patient attended group and individual therapy and took Zyprexa, Quetiapine, Trazodone, and Neurontin. She reportedly was supposed to be discharged to residential treatment but was combative and refused to go so she was discharged to a shelter.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that inpatient treatment is indicated primarily for individuals whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. 

In this case this patient was considered in need of 24-hour substance rehabilitation treatment as she reportedly was using large amounts of alcohol daily and using serious substances daily including cocaine in addition to daily cannabis use and she could not maintain abstinence despite multiple inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatments. She reportedly lacked the coping skills and ability to identify relapse triggers to stop use and lacked sober supports and relapse prevention skills as she was homeless. She also had comorbid psychiatric conditions including a diagnosis of schizophrenia-bipolar and was noncompliant with psychotropic medications due to her substance use. 

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) she met criteria for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment as she continued to use large amounts of alcohol and cannabis and also was using cocaine despite multiple past inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatments. That was specific evidence that inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment was medically necessary treatment then. She needed to improve her coping and relapse prevention skills, identification of relapse triggers, insight into use and the consequences of use, and increase sober supports. She was unable to stop alcohol substance use without being in a sober and supervised therapeutic inpatient substance rehabilitation setting. Without this structured and supervised inpatient therapeutic rehabilitation treatment she likely would have relapsed very quickly. Also, she could not stop use for this therapeutic treatment without being in a 24-hour inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment. 

The medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that she required this level of care. The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment in the best interest of the patient.

The insurer's denial of coverage for the inpatient substance abuse rehabilitation admission is overturned. Medical necessity is substantiated.

The patient's vital signs were as follows: temperature 98.6, pulse 117, respiratory rate 20, blood pressure 162/110, and oxygen saturation 95%. His Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol Scale (CIWA) score was 15.  The patient's exam was remarkable for mild tremors.  Labs revealed the following: complete blood count (CBC) and basic metabolic panel (BMP) was unremarkable.  The patient's electrocardiogram showed new onset atrial fibrillation with no ischemic changes.  He was given Ativan and Tygan in the emergency department.  

The patient was admitted for alcohol withdrawal.  Cardiology was consulted.  Day two, vital signs were stable.  The patient's Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) scale score was seven.  Cardiology recommended echocardiogram and medications - Toprol for atrial fibrillation.  The patient was to continue the Ativan taper.  Day three, the patient's Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) scale score was seven. The patient signed out against medical advice (AMA).

No, the proposed inpatient hospital admission was not medically necessary.
This patient, with a history of alcohol abuse, was admitted for alcohol withdrawal.  He was not acutely intoxicated.  The patient was hemodynamically stable and afebrile.  He had tachycardia with new onset atrial fibrillation.  He was noted to have mild tremors but did not have findings of severe alcohol withdrawal.   The patient was admitted with plan for Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) protocol.  During his hospital stay, he did not have findings of severe alcohol withdrawal.  He was being managed with oral medication assisted treatment as well as medications for control of heartrate.  He did not have symptoms that required an acute inpatient level of care and he had not failed a lesser level of care.

Yes, the health plan acted reasonably with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.

The medical records did not provide enough specific evidence to support that he required only this wilderness treatment program or that this wilderness program provided weekly psychiatric evaluations. 

The health plan did act reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient. 

The carrier's denial of coverage for residential inpatient care is upheld.  The medical necessity is not substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse. 
Treatment: Substance Abuse Residential Treatment. 

The insurer denied substance abuse residential treatment. 
The determination is upheld. 

The patient was admitted to residential level services for treatment of severe cannabis use disorder. The patient has a history of escalating use with up to twelve grams of marijuana at most. The patient reported no history of withdrawal seizures or blackouts or severe withdrawal such as hyperemesis; he did not report erratic behavior or high-risk behaviors such as driving under the influence. The patient has one prior substance use disorder treatment. 

The patient presented with a comorbid psychiatric disorder diagnosed as unspecified anxiety disorder, but no history of psychiatric hospitalization, and no history of suicidal or self-harming behaviors. He has good social supports from family. 

On mental status examination, he was groomed and cooperative with anxious demeanor and good eye contact. He exhibited apprehension, nervousness, tension and worry. His mood was euthymic. He endorsed bouts of boredom that served to trigger his substance use. There was no evidence of mania, thought disorder, psychosis, perceptual disturbance or severe cognitive impairment though he did have concentration and attention problems. Insight and judgment were fair. He was judged to be in the contemplative stage of change. 

There were no acute general medical issues in this case. The patient's medical screening revealed a drug screen consistent with history but no other abnormalities. He has a history of asthma with a rescue inhaler. 

The patient was admitted for residential level rehabilitation treatment of the comorbid substance use disorders and co-occurring psychiatric disorder. The rehabilitation program provided for comprehensive treatment that included focus on coping skills, plans for the development of a relapse prevention plan with identification of triggers, education about the disease model of addiction, and involvement with groups and individual therapy, as well as family focused sessions and involvement in recovery groups and other therapeutic activities to improve coping skills and develop sober supports. 

The patient engaged in treatment with intensive services, sober housing, monitoring, and structure provided within the residential treatment program. Psychiatric evaluation was provided with use of Lexapro, Buspar and as needed (prn) Vistaril to address the unspecified anxiety symptoms. The patient was participating in treatment without incident or complications with respect to biomedical, general medical, emotional or other treatment domains. The patient was attending groups and completing assignments despite ongoing symptoms of anxiety which had improved. The patient was deemed to be sufficiently motivated for continued treatment with a fair prognosis. There was no evidence for significant withdrawal symptoms or biomedical complications. 
 
The case summary and records, health plan documents, appeal documents, correspondence from the health plan and treatment facility, and, the rationale for the denial of certification for coverage of the requested treatment, were reviewed. The plan medical necessity criteria and guidelines, New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria were reviewed. This review is New York State mandated in consideration of the LOCADTR Criteria/Guidelines. 

At issue is the medical necessity of continued residential substance use disorders treatment. 

The requested health service/treatment of continued stay in the substance use residential rehabilitation treatment setting is not medically necessary for this patient. 

The requested benefit of continued residential mental health stay is not reasonable in this case scenario, as patient is amenable to treatment in a less restrictive environment that addresses both the mental health and co-occurring substance use disorders. The patient has stabilized to the extent that safe and effective treatment could be provided at a lower level of care with intensive services and a safety plan and sober supports. The patient's symptoms of anxiety had improved, and there was no imminent risk of suicide or self-harm in this case, or severe symptoms such as psychosis, mania/mood cycling, perceptual disturbance or thought disorder that would have required residential level services. The patient is engaged in treatment with external and internal motivating factors, cooperative with staff, and medication adherent, and the patient is future oriented with regard to a commitment to a recovery effort. His family is supportive and involved in the treatment planning and treatment. Thus, the proposed continued residential level services did not meet prevailing standards of practice with regard to continued care at the residential level and is not in keeping or consistent with New York State LOCADTR 3 Criteria. Moreover, the denial determination including application of LOCADTR Criteria is appropriate and reasonable in this case scenario. 

The patient no longer required the continued structure and monitoring and intensity of a residential level service. Effective treatment could have been provided at a lower level of care in keeping with prevailing standards of medical practice, American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria and the scientific literature, referenced below, as well as NY State instruction for this review and the application of NY State OASAS LOCADTR 3.0 Criteria.

The patient is a male who presented to an emergency department with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain in the context of severe alcohol use disorder. The patient has a history of severe substance use disorder with daily use of alcohol and intermittent use of cannabis (marijuana). He has a history of prior detoxification and rehabilitation treatment episodes with relapses and no recent sober time. 

At the time of presentation to the emergency department, the patient reported functional decline as the substance use/disease had progressed. The patient provided no past history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens, but did report severe alcohol withdrawal symptoms in the past. He was admitted for inpatient level care with plans for withdrawal management and detoxification and stabilization with an Ativan protocol with Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) monitoring and supportive measures. 

The medical screening had revealed evidence for acute pancreatitis, elevated liver functions and a drug screen that was positive for tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), consistent with history. His examination revealed abdominal tenderness with complaints of epigastric pain, as well as withdrawal symptoms including nausea, vomiting, tremors and chills with a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) scale score in the mild range. 

The patient was admitted for inpatient treatment with detoxification protocol, supportive measures, and withdrawal management. He received tapering dosages of Ativan and replacement of vitamins and fluids with the availability of nicotine replacement for tobacco dependence, as well as comfort medications and as needed (PRN), medications prescribed for pain, anxiety, and insomnia. He was prescribed pantoprazole, and gabapentin to serve as an anti-craving medication or medication assisted treatment.

The patient's hospital course progressed without incident. Vital signs remained normal with occasional bradycardia and sinus rhythm on electrocardiogram-- that was present on his initial presentation. The patient reported mild nausea, anxiety, restlessness and insomnia with persistently mild symptoms of withdrawal that diminished throughout his brief hospital course. He quickly stabilized and arrangements were being made for a referral to rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment and follow up. He was discharged with recommendations for continued medications as noted, and involvement with self-help groups for support of a recovery, as well as recommendations for clinically appropriate aftercare.
The health plan denied coverage for the requested services on the basis of New State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria indicating that the patient could have been sufficiently managed with lower-level care and stabilization in a residential setting. The denial determination indicated that the withdrawal symptoms were mild, that the patient had no general medical or psychiatric symptoms requiring inpatient level care, and, that the patient was stable with employment and housing.

In appeal, the treatment facility indicated that the requested services were medically necessary in keeping with New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria and guidelines. The appeal argued that the admission to hospital inpatient care was medically necessary and that the patient required detoxification and stabilization in keeping with Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) guidelines and in view of the severity of the alcohol use disorder that included general medical complications.

Yes, the proposed treatment, inpatient hospital level care for detoxification treatment and withdrawal management and stabilization with monitoring and other medical services was medically necessary for this patient in keeping New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria and prevailing standards of medical practice.
The requested benefit of inpatient admission for detoxification treatment and withdrawal management and monitoring and other medical services could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. The patient in this case was using large quantities of alcohol with daily use, and one other drug of abuse (marijuana) with a presentation and history that did warrant the admission and the continued inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring.

Inpatient hospital level care with detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment that was provided in the emergency department and continued at the time of admission. Moreover, the patient's social environment was not conducive to an effective detoxification, and the patient had struggled with withdrawal symptoms and maintaining abstinence which were being effectively addressed with inpatient level monitoring with an Ativan protocol and supportive measures. The patient had associated clinical features that included lack of sober supports and functional impairments with unemployment and general medical complications of the alcohol use disorder-contrary to the denial determination. 

Thus, the appeal did appropriately indicate the necessity for the adult inpatient stay and detoxification treatment of this patient's substance use disorders that did warrant the hospital admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level setting with withdrawal management and psychosocial supports, and 24-hour monitoring. The patient's history of substance use (frequency and quantity) together with the severe psychosocial stressors and functional impairments do reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder and the need for a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management and stabilization, as the patient was at high risk for treatment failure or general medical complications such as seizures if detoxification and withdrawal management were to be attempted at a lower level of care. Moreover, the stage of change was contemplative at best and the patient's lack of awareness or insight regarding the severe alcohol use disorder and risk for medical complications. 

Medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published practice guidelines, the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and the scientific literature, referenced below, and, New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews including the appropriate application of New York Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria-referenced below. The health plan's denial on the basis of New York Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria is not reasonable and attempting detoxification and other treatment in the emergency department or with lower-level treatment is not in the best interest of the patient or safe in this case scenario.

No, the health plan, in its determination of medical necessity, did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.
The health plan's denial on the basis of New York State Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria is not reasonable, and attempting appropriate treatment with lower-level services, as the health plan recommended, is not in the best interest of the patient, or safe in this case scenario. The requested benefit of Inpatient Hospital detoxification treatment and withdrawal management and monitoring and other medical services is clinically appropriate, medically necessary and warranted, and is therefore a covered benefit in this case scenario.

summary:
Diagnosis: Alcohol use disorder. 
Treatment: Residential Substance Use Disorder Services. 

The insurer denied the Residential Substance Use Disorder Services. 
The denial is overturned. 

This case involves an adult female, with severe alcohol use disorder who was admitted to residential rehabilitation treatment and who received treatment of co-occurring mental disorders. Her presentation for residential level care was prompted by a relapse after two years of sobriety; her alcohol use quickly escalated to two liters of wine per day with a rapid decline in functioning and inability to maintain work as a nurse. The alcohol disorder had its onset in adolescence with a chronic relapsing course in the context of a co-occurring anxiety disorder best characterized as generalized anxiety disorder, an unspecified depressive disorder, and severe psychosocial stressors within the primary support, social environment and occupational domains. The alcohol use resulted in impairment of functioning with regard to social, occupational and daily functions putting her health and job at risk. The patient had prior past substance use disorder treatment primarily with the use of peer-supported recovery groups and mental health treatment. Her self-referral for treatment was prompted by her supervisor who was supportive of her seeking treatment. 

The patient presented with associated symptoms of anxiety and dysphoric mood in the context of moderately severe post-acute withdrawal symptoms related to the alcohol use. 

The patient began residential level treatment with the structure, monitoring, and the intensity of inpatient level services. Treatment included group, individual, and educational services with the addition of non-pharmacologic interventions to address the anxiety disturbance, and emphasis on coping skills with the goal of the development of a relapse prevention plan and planning for a safe and appropriate discharge back to the community. She was prescribed sertraline and gabapentin at appropriate dosages with vitamin replacement and continued use of as needed (PRN) Vistaril and trazodone and melatonin to address anxiety and insomnia. She had received evidence-base interventions, and the patient's insight and mood improved in response to the treatments, as she was calmer with euthymic mood with persistent reports of anxiety during her stay. 

The patient was more active in her treatment and increasingly engaged in group sessions. Family wellness and other wellness activities were provided together with mindfulness, yoga, meditation and continued medication management with the addition of propranolol to address anxiety. By the last week of treatment, the treatment team was recommending intensive treatment in the community with continued involvement in peer-supported recovery groups and sober supports, and recommendations for the obtainment of a sponsor including a nurse-to-nurse program. Prognosis was guarded to fair and she was deemed to be at high risk for relapse unless continued treatment was to be provided. Discharge planning occurred with discharge and return to the community/home and plans for continued substance use disorder treatment and involvement in recovery groups with sober supports, as well as treatment from her primary care physician  and referral for psychotherapy/mental health services. The patient was not interested in medication assisted treatment and was discharged on sertraline, propranolol and melatonin at clinically appropriate dosages. 

Yes, the proposed treatment was medically necessary for this patient. 

As the appeal from the patient and treatment facility indicated, the residential level treatment was needed and medically necessary in that the patient had no alternative level of care treatment available in the plan network, thus prompting the admission to residential level care after detoxification treatment. Medical necessity is therefore met, as residential level treatment was provided as clinically appropriate with the least restrictive treatment setting and level of care. Moreover, in view of the clinical features in this case that included limited supports (living alone), a decline in functioning putting her and her job at risk (job jeopardy) and the severity of alcohol use; the residential level of care did meet the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria contrary to the health plan's denial and determination on the basis of American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria. 

The residential level of services, structure, and monitoring provided in this case are warranted in view of the severity of the alcohol use disorder and associated symptoms of anxiety and complications of the alcohol disorder. The patient could not have been effectively managed with lower-level services during the time interval under review. 

The residential level services through discharge were clinically appropriate, and consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice. The services were provided with evidence-based treatments that are known to benefit patients with severe alcohol use disorder, as well as providing services to address treatment issues in a patient with moderately severe post-acute withdrawal symptoms and complications of an alcohol disorder that included liver damage, and with high risk for relapse. Thus, the patient's severity of alcohol use disorder and associated symptoms of anxiety, did warrant and necessitate the admission and the continued residential level services, as proposed, with the plan for step down to lower-level services once the patient had stabilized with the ability to achieve abstinence with sober supports in working toward discharge plans and considering a safe and appropriate transition to the community with appropriate aftercare. 

Moreover, the patient presented with high risk for relapse in view of an inadequate recovery environment, a relative lack of coping skills and readiness to change, and a lack of sober supports despite some past exposure to recovery groups. The time spent with motivational techniques and other interventions throughout the residential stay were essential to a successful therapeutic outcome in this case. These clinical features and treatment dimensions did support the necessity for the continued inpatient level services and the continued structure and monitoring and intensity of services provided at the residential level of care through discharge. 

This answer is consistent with the application of the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and with the published guidelines and the scientific literature, referenced below. 

No, the health plan did not act reasonably, with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. 

The residential level treatment was needed and medically necessary; moreover, the patient had no alternative level of care treatment available within the plan network, thus prompting the clinically appropriate admission to residential level care after detoxification treatment. 

This answer is consistent with the application of the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and with the published guidelines and the scientific literature, referenced below, as well as New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews and the application of NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria, referenced below.

summary:
Diagnosis: Alcohol Detoxification. 
Treatment: Continued Inpatient Hospital Treatment. 

The insurer denied coverage for continued inpatient hospital treatment.

The denial is overturned.

This patient presented to the ED (emergency department) of this hospital and was admitted to this inpatient hospital for alcohol detoxification as he reportedly had active alcohol withdrawal symptoms including headache, vomiting, tremors, abnormal skin sensations, and had a past alcohol withdrawal seizure 1 1/2 weeks prior to this admission. He reportedly had low potassium of 2.7 and low magnesium of 1.3 and had elevated AST [Aspartate transaminase]/ALT [Alanine transaminase] of 350/106. He reportedly was given Ativan 2 mg (milligram) intravenous push (IVP) and then put on a detoxification protocol of Ativan 2 mg intramuscular (IM) every (q) 6 hours and Ativan 1 mg q (every) 8 hours prn (as needed) alcohol withdrawal. He also received IV potassium, thiamine, folic acid, and IV (intravenous) fluids. He also was managed for alcohol steatohepatitis. He was discharged home after refusing alcohol inpatient rehabilitation treatment. 
    
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. It also states that patients with current or past complicated or life threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens are in need of inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal and reports that patients with comorbid medical condition that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification. 

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) he did require 24 hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive setting as he required and received detoxification medication including intravenous (IV) Ativan to modify withdrawal from alcohol and prevent another withdrawal seizure or more complicated or life threatening withdrawal such as delirium tremens. The risk of delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use so he was considered at high risk for this.  He did require 24 hour medical hospital treatment for alcohol detoxification and it was considered unsafe for him to be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive level of care then. He required at least the entire days as it was reported that he had a Clinical Institute of Withdrawal (CIWA) protocol with Ativan detoxification.  This was a high risk patient who had a recent withdrawal seizure which requires medical hospital detoxification treatment, and he had active comorbid medical conditions. He reportedly refused the recommendation for inpatient alcohol rehabilitation treatment and was discharged. This patient was considered high risk for delirium tremens. 

As a result, the recommendation is to overturn the previous decision and approve coverage for continued inpatient hospital treatment. It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably, with sound medical judgment, or in the best interests of the patient then. 

Based on the above, the medical necessity for the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) level of care is substantiated. The insurer's denial is overturned.

summary:
Diagnosis: Mild Alcohol Withdrawal Symptoms
Treatment: Inpatient admission
The insurer denied the inpatient admission
The denial is overturned

The patient is a female. She presented to an emergency department with nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and abdominal pain in the context of severe alcohol use disorder. The patient has a history of severe substance use disorder with daily use of alcohol and intermittent use of cannabis (marijuana). She has a history of multiple detoxification and rehabilitation treatment episodes with relapses and no sober time. She also had a history of alcohol-related pancreatitis, and peripheral neuropathy related to longstanding use of alcohol.

At the time of presentation to the emergency department, the patient reported functional decline as the substance abuse/disease had progressed. The patient provided no past history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens, but did report severe alcohol withdrawal symptoms and frequent blackouts. She was admitted for inpatient level care with plans for withdrawal management and detoxification and stabilization with Librium and supportive measures. The medical screening had revealed evidence for bacteria and blood in the urine, elevated liver functions and a drug screen that was positive for THC (tetrahydrocannabinol) and consistent with history. Her examination revealed abdominal tenderness with complaints of epigastric pain.

The patient has a history of psychiatric disorder, anxiety, and past treatment with Zoloft, but no history of suicidal or self-harming behaviors.

On Mental Status Examination, there were no severe symptoms, and no safety concerns with regard to risk of harm to self or others. The patient displayed limited insight, and intact judgment. She demonstrated symptoms of anxiety with generalized symptoms including insomnia, and anxious affect together with symptoms related to the alcohol use associated with a blood alcohol level of 388 on admission. She was cooperative with normal speech and linear thought processing. There were no severe symptoms of cognition, or psychosis, perceptual disturbance or mood cycling.

The patient was admitted for inpatient treatment with detoxification protocol, supportive measures, and withdrawal management. She received tapering dosages of Librium and replacement of vitamins and fluids and magnesium with the availability of counseling and comfort medications and prn (as needed) medications prescribed for pain, anxiety, and insomnia. She was started on Celexa to address anxiety and gabapentin for neuropathy and to serve as an anti-craving medication or medication assisted treatment.

The patient's hospital course progressed without incident. Vital signs remained normal with occasional tachycardia that was present on her initial presentation. The patient reported mild nausea, anxiety, restlessness and insomnia with persistently mild symptoms of withdrawal that diminished throughout her brief hospital course. She quickly stabilized and arrangements were being made for a referral to rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment and outpatient mental health services or follow up. She was discharged with recommendations for continued medications as noted, and involvement with self-help groups for support of a recovery, as well as recommendations for clinically appropriate aftercare.

The health plan denied coverage for the requested services on the basis of MCG (Milliman Care Guidelines) Criteria indicating that the patient could have been sufficiently managed in the emergency department and discharged with lower-level care.

The treatment facility indicated that the requested services were medically necessary in keeping with MCG (Milliman Care Guidelines) level of care guidelines for alcohol and psychoactive substance withdrawal and common complications and conditions (MCG [Milliman Care Guidelines]-035). The appeal argued that the admission to hospital inpatient care was medically necessary and that the patient required IV (intravenous) replacement with fluids and magnesium, psychiatric consultation, and stabilization in keeping with MCG (Milliman Care Guidelines) guidelines.

Yes, the Inpatient admission was medically necessary.
The inpatient admission was medically necessary for this patient in keeping New York State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (level of care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) 3.0 Criteria and prevailing standards of medical practice.

The requested benefit of Inpatient Hospital Admission for detoxification treatment and withdrawal management and monitoring and other medical services could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. The patient in this case was using large quantities of alcohol with daily use, and one other drug of abuse (marijuana) with intermittent use with a presentation and history that did warrant the admission and the continued inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring.

Inpatient hospital level care with detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment that was provided in the emergency department and continued at the time of admission. Moreover, the patient's social environment was not conducive to an effective detoxification, and the patient had struggled with withdrawal symptoms and maintaining abstinence which were being effectively addressed with inpatient level monitoring with a Librium protocol and supportive measures. The patient had associated clinical features that included lack of sober supports and functional impairments.

Thus, the adult inpatient stay and detoxification treatment of this patient's substance use disorders did warrant the hospital admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level setting with withdrawal management and psychosocial supports, and 24-hour monitoring. The patient's history of substance use (frequency and quantity) together with the severe psychosocial stressors and functional impairments do reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder and the need for a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management and stabilization, as the patient was at high risk for treatment failure or general medical complications such as seizures if detoxification and withdrawal management were to have been attempted at a lower level of care.

In summary, medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published practice guidelines, ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) Criteria, and the scientific literature, referenced below, and, New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews including the appropriate application of NY OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (level of care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) 3.0 Criteria-referenced below. The health plan's denial on the basis of New York LOCADTR (level of care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) Criteria is not reasonable and attempting detoxification and other treatment in the emergency department or with lower-level treatment is not in the best interest of the patient or safe in this case scenario.

No, the health plan, in its determination of medical necessity, did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.
The health plan's denial on the basis of MCG (Milliman Care Guidelines) Criteria is not reasonable, and attempting appropriate treatment with lower-level services, as the health plan recommended, is not in the best interest of the patient or safe in this case scenario. The requested benefit of Inpatient Hospital detoxification treatment and withdrawal management and monitoring and other medical services is clinically appropriate, medically necessary and warranted.

The admission and the continued inpatient level treatment through discharge could not have been safely or effectively provided with lower-level services. Thus, the requested benefit should be covered in keeping with prevailing standards of care pertaining to substance use disorder services including consideration of ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) Criteria, LOCUS (Level of Care Utilization System) Guidelines, and application of NY State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (level of care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) 3.0 Criteria, referenced below.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder

Treatment: residential behavioral health level of care, adult

The insurer denied coverage for residential behavioral health level of care, adult

The denial is overturned.

This patient was admitted to this inpatient mental health residential treatment after being admitted to the crisis center. She reportedly was involved in a physical altercation with her mother an kicked out of the house and charged with a misdemeanor domestic assault and was incarcerated over that weekend. She reportedly had depressive symptoms including depressed mood, suicidal ideation and plans to hurt self, hopelessness, decreased interest and pleasure, sleeping and appetite problems, concentration problems, and was drinking alcohol to numb herself, had post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms as she was the reported victim of assault, had worthlessness, and low self-esteem. She reportedly had emotional dysregulation and poor coping skills. She reportedly had multiple past suicide attempts by overdose resulting in psychiatric hospitalizations. She had diagnoses of Major Depressive Disorder, PTSD, Generalized Anxiety Disorder, Borderline Personality Disorder, Alcohol Use Disorder, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). She reportedly was unemployed and homeless. She reportedly took Venlafaxine and Trazodone, attended group and individual therapy. It was reported that she was discharged and transferred to another inpatient residential treatment for further inpatient therapeutic residential treatment.
    
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Major Depressive Disorders reports that the least restrictive level of care for safe and effective treatment is appropriate. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Suicidal Behaviors reports that patients with past suicide attempts are at high risk for suicide and this patient had 2 past suicide attempts by overdose resulting in hospitalizations. She was a high-risk patient with poor coping skills and poor insight with multiple psychiatric problems and conditions including depression, anxiety, PTSD, ADHD, poor interpersonal and poor coping skills, emotional dysregulation, multiple past suicide attempts by overdose, and increased alcohol use. She reportedly continued to exhibit poor coping skills and lack of responsibility as she did not learn and sustain the necessary coping skills to function outside of a 24-hour inpatient residential treatment setting. Also, the InterQual 2020 Psychiatry Mental Health residential treatment guidelines reports that criteria are still met if one still has psychiatric or behavioral symptoms that put the patient at high risk for hospitalization if not in this 24 hour treatment, that they still have psychiatric or behavioral symptoms that are improving or expected to improve but they are not clinically stable yet, or have persistent symptoms that are unable to be managed without this intensity of services. It also states that one has symptoms including disorganized thinking or behavior, hallucinations, angry outbursts, assaultive behavior, delinquent acts, poor impulse control, psychomotor agitation, sexually inappropriate or high-risk behavior, suicidal ideation, or threatening behavior requiring 24 hour treatment. 

In this case, this patient did have continued reported psychiatric symptoms that would put her at high risk for harm to self if not in this 24 hour treatment and she still had psychiatric and behavioral symptoms that were improving or expected to improve but were not clinically stable yet, and she reportedly required continued 24 hour residential treatment to learn better coping skills, better regulate emotions, better problem solve, improve insight, better deal with trauma issues so as to decrease depressive and anxiety symptoms and decrease the risk of another suicide attempt as well as addressing her increased alcohol use as self-medication to these symptoms. She still presented as a high risk for hospitalization if not in a 24-hour residential treatment setting and was transferred to another inpatient residential treatment setting. She required this 24-hour therapeutic mental health residential treatment including the denial days. This was a complex and high-risk patient with multiple psychiatric issues and an alcohol use problem who had past suicide attempts by overdose, so she was considered high risk and in need of improving coping skills and taking responsibility for her behaviors and actions. 

Inpatient mental health residential treatment was medically necessary. 

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment in the best interest of the patient.

The insurer's denial of coverage for residential behavioral health level of care, adult is overturned. Medical necessity is substantiated.

The patient is a male with a history of polysubstance abuse. He presented to the ED (emergency department) requesting detox. He last used heroin the day before. He complained of irritability, anxiety, chills, nausea, joint pains and abdominal cramps.

The patient's vital signs were as follows: Temperature 98.2, pulse 78, respiration rate 18. His exam was remarkable for bumps at injection site with warmth, redness and tenderness. The patient's labs were as follows: WBC (white blood count) 10.68, H/H (hemoglobin/hematocrit) 13.5/41.8, Plt (platelets) 346, Na (sodium) 128, K (potassium) 4.0, BUN/Cr (blood urea nitrogen/creatinine) 21/1, VBG (venous blood gas) 7.4/59/34/35, and Lactate 1.2. Urine toxicology was positive for benzodiazepines and opiates. Chest x-ray revealed no active disease. EKG (electrocardiogram) revealed NSR (normal sinus rhythm) and QTc (corrected QT interval) 422. His COWS (clinical opiate withdrawal scale) score was 7. His CIWA (clinical institute withdrawal assessment) score was 4.

The patient was admitted. Plan of care included Lorazepam, methadone protocol, IVF (intravenous fluids), and IV (intravenous) antibiotics for arm cellulitis.

On day two, the patient's vital signs were stable. Vomiting was reported. The plan was to continue current management.

On day three, the patient's vital signs were stable. He denied symptoms of withdrawal. His COWS (clinical opiate withdrawal scale) score was 0. His CIWA (clinical institute withdrawal assessment) score was 0. The plan was to continue current management.

On day four, the patient's vital signs were stable. His Na (sodium) was 136. He signed out AMA (against medical advice).

No, the Inpatient admission was not medically necessary.
This patient with a history of polysubstance use was admitted for opiate and benzodiazepine withdrawal. The patient was hemodynamically stable and afebrile. He did not have tachycardia, arrhythmia, or prolonged QTc (corrected QT interval). He complained of nausea. He did not have vomiting, tremor, or perspiration. There were no physical signs of withdrawal. Labs were remarkable for hyponatremia positive urine toxicology. His COWS (clinical opiate withdrawal scale) score was 7. His CIWA (clinical institute withdrawal assessment) score was 4. He was found to have upper extremity cellulitis. He did not have bacteremia. He did not have a limb threatening infection. The patient was admitted with planned COWS (clinical opiate withdrawal scale) and CIWA (clinical institute withdrawal assessment) protocols and management with lorazepam and methadone as well as IV (intravenous) antibiotics for cellulitis.

The patient's hyponatremia corrected during his hospital stay. He remained hemodynamically stable and afebrile, and with no signs of severe withdrawal. The patient signed out AMA (against medical advice). He did not have symptoms that required an acute inpatient level of care. He had not failed management in a lesser level of care.

Therefore, given the above, inpatient admission was not medically necessary.

Yes, the health plan acted reasonably, with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.

Diagnosis: Substance Abuse. 
Treatment: Inpatient Stay. 

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient stay. 

The denial is overturned. 

The patient was admitted due to alcohol withdrawal symptoms. She reportedly had tremors, elevated heart rate of 107, high blood pressure, agitation, sleeping problems, concentration problems, and was falling and hitting her head due to alcohol use. She reportedly had diagnoses of major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder in addition to alcohol use disorder. She reportedly increased drinking alcohol after a friend's death. She reportedly was drinking 3 drinks daily. She also reportedly was abusing cocaine. Her longest reported abstinence was a few weeks. She reportedly was in psychiatric treatment and taking Lexapro, Olanzapine, Gabapentin, Xanax, and Lamictal. She reportedly was living with her husband and children and had reported discord with her husband. She was started on a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Alcohol (CIWA) protocol with Librium, given a banana bag and then thiamine and folate. She was discharged but declined the recommendation for inpatient alcohol/substance treatment. 
  
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. It also states that patients with past complicated or life-threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens are in need of inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal and reports that patients with comorbid medical conditions that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification. Also, the US Department of Health and Human Services - Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) Center for Substance Abuse Treatment reports that inpatient treatment is necessary if the ability to attend outpatient treatment daily is a problem, one is unable to follow up in outpatient treatment, if medical conditions complicate the treatment of withdrawal, if one has previous withdrawal seizures of delirium tremens, or if one does not have the capacity for informed consent. 

In this case this patient had active alcohol withdrawal symptoms including tremors, elevated heart rate of 107, high blood pressure, agitation, sleeping problems, concentration problems, and was falling and hitting her head due to alcohol use. She reportedly increased her alcohol use and was drinking daily which put her at risk for more severe, complicated, and life-threatening withdrawal. 

The medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that the patient required 24-hour hospital treatment. 

The health plan did not act reasonably, with sound medical judgment, or in the best interest of the patient. 

The insurer's denial of coverage for the inpatient stay is overturned. Medical necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse. 
Treatment: Substance Abuse Treatment. 

The insurer denied coverage for substance abuse treatment. 

The denial is overturned. 

This patient was admitted to a substance residential treatment as a self-referral due to crack/cocaine and marijuana use. He reportedly had increased frequency of use and this reportedly was his 6th substance treatment. He was not allowed to live with his wife while using so he was considered homeless. He reportedly spent 100 days in the county jail prior to admission. He also had comorbid psychiatric issues including anxiety and depression and had trauma issues including childhood trauma. 

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that residential treatment is indicated primarily for individuals who do not meet clinical criteria for hospitalization but whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. Residential facilities provide a safe and substance-free environment in which residents learn individual and group living skills for preventing relapse. In this case this patient was considered still in need of 24 hour residential treatment then as he needed time in this 24 hour inpatient therapeutic structured and supervised setting to learn better coping skills, relapse prevention skills, improve insight into his addiction including how his psychiatric comorbidities contributed to his addiction, better identify relapse triggers, improve motivation, and increase sober supports. 

The Institute on Drug Abuse: Principles of Addiction Treatment: A Research Based Guide- reports that research indicates that that the best treatment outcomes occur with longer durations of treatment and states that recovery from drug addiction is a long-term process. It also states that treatment techniques to increase motivation for treatment are necessary to prevent dropout rates. In this case this patient required more treatment time in a 24-hour inpatient therapeutic residential treatment setting including. Notes reported that he was making progress and would benefit from further inpatient substance residential treatment, and that he needed to work on aftercare goals and barriers to obtaining them. Notes reported that he was still working on trying to better understand how his emotions and thoughts triggered his use. Notes reported that cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) was used to try to connect thoughts and feelings with his behaviors and use and that he still had housing issues and was considered at risk for another relapse due to past relapses after 5 other substance treatments, so he required more time in this setting. It was reported that he was making progress and would benefit from further inpatient substance residential treatment. Notes reported that he still had insomnia despite taking Melatonin and he also took Sertraline for anxiety and depression.  This was a complex patient who could not stop crack/cocaine or marijuana use despite 5 other substance treatments and needed at least the entire time in this sober therapeutic 24-hour residential rehabilitation treatment to develop relapse prevention skills, strengthen coping skills, decrease impulsivity, better identify triggers, improve insight into how his comorbid psychiatric and trauma issues contributed to his use and addiction, and increase sober supports. He had multiple relapses despite past substance treatments and required this level of care including during the denial period and needed to learn how to make better decisions and not self-medicate his psychiatric and trauma issues. At the time of the denial, he still had not obtained the skills needed to remain sober and was still working on them. Due to his difficulties with expressing emotions in a healthy manner, if he were discharged prematurely, he was considered a high risk for relapse.  Without this structured and supervised therapeutic residential treatment, he likely would have relapsed quickly. 

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment in the best interest of the patient. 

The insurer's denial of coverage for the substance abuse treatment is overturned. Medical necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Bipolar mood disorder.
Treatment: Continued Inpatient Mental Health Treatment.

The insurer denied the Continued Inpatient Mental Health Treatment.  The denial is overturned.

The patient is an adult male. He was admitted for acute inpatient psychiatric treatment for an exacerbation of bipolar mood disorder. The patient had stopped his medications with subsequent recrudescence of mood disturbance and erratic and aggressive behavior requiring emergency medical services. He was threatening towards other while carrying a metal rod and making sounds as if he was shooting a gun. The patient had become acutely manic without overt psychotic features. He has a history of psychiatric hospitalizations with past episodes of mood disturbance that are often in the context of stopping his medications or medication non-adherence resulting in increased activity and dysphoric or irritable mood.

The patient had co-occurring substance use disorders including cannabis and alcohol use disorders with unspecified frequency and quantity of use.

The patient's mental status examination revealed motor agitation with irritable mood and labile affect, disorganized thoughts with pressured speech and racing thoughts, and with limited insight and impaired judgment and poor control of impulses. He was superficially cooperative and guarded and uncooperative. Sleep, energy levels and volition were disturbed. He was internally preoccupied with aggressive impulses together with poor impulse control.

The patient was admitted to inpatient level services with close observation and safety monitoring, structured milieu with programming, and resumption of pharmacotherapy with Abilify, and PRN (as needed) medications for agitation and anxiety and safety emergencies. He refused to resume treatment with Depakote or Abilify Maintena or Vraylar.

The patient was initially uncooperative with agitation and resistance to taking medication, and a difficult clinical course. The mental status examination remained unchanged.  He was hyperverbal, irritable, and had been labile with respect to mood and behavior and remained at risk for impulsivity due to limited insight and impaired judgment. He had become medication adherent with Abilify titrated to 15 mg (milligrams), and his family remained supportive but not actively involved in the treatment with regard to treatment planning and consideration of clinically appropriate aftercare.

The patient was deemed appropriate for discharge, and was improved with regard to mood and impulse control. The patient was discharged with plans to live with his friend and sublet an apartment, and continue treatment with PHP (partial hospitalization program) level care and intensive case management services (ICMS).

The health plan's denial was on the basis of InterQual Behavioral Health Criteria and plan coverage indicating that the patient had no safety issues (homicidal of suicidal ideation or intent) for the denied dates of service.

The appeal was on the basis of medical necessity and continued need for inpatient level structure, monitoring and the need to develop a safe and clinically appropriate discharge plan and disposition.

Yes, the Continued Inpatient Mental Health Treatment was medically necessary.

The patient's presentation and clinical features included an acute manic episode in the context of bipolar mood disorder and deterioration in functioning with safety issues and medication non-adherence, as well as severe cannabis use disorder and unspecified alcohol use disorder. The patient had failed to benefit from treatment with lower-level care, and was engaging in problematic and aggressive behaviors. The patient exhibited cognitive impairment (disorder thought processing and executive function) with deterioration in functioning in the context of impaired judgment, aggressive behavior, and limited insight. He had required intervention and emergency services to address his erratic and problematic behavior associated with severe symptoms of mania and disturbance of mood including homicidal threats.

The additional days/units of inpatient level service were warranted in order to effectively provide treatment and to work toward a safe and clinically appropriate disposition in accordance with prevailing standards of medical practice. Moreover, the additional days/units of inpatient level services were medically necessary in view of the history of relapse and non-compliance with his outpatient treatment and medication non-adherence and safety concerns with continued risk for harm to others or self. Thus, the time necessary for additional stabilization of mood and to arrange a clinically appropriate discharge from acute inpatient care is critical in this case to prevent another relapse and to safely provide for the transition/step down from acute inpatient level care to the community. The patient could not have been safely or effectively transitioned to a lower level of care during the time interval under review due to persistent symptoms of the mood disturbance, risk for substance use, and continued deficits with regard to insight and judgment.

In summary, medical necessity is met in this case consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, and with published practice guidelines and the scientific literature, referenced below, as well as NY (New York) State instruction for this medical necessity review including the application of New York State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (level of care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) 3 Criteria. The denial reasons are not consistent with standards of care in this case in view of the clinical features and treatment dimensions necessary for effective management of the patient's co-occurring psychiatric and substance use disorders.

No, the health plan did not act reasonably, with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.

The requested service could not be safely or effectively provided with lower level care services in this case scenario, and, the patient was receiving active treatment that continued to be consistent with prevailing standards of professional medical practice. Thus, in keeping with NY (New York) State instruction for medical necessity reviews and LOCADTR (level of care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) Criteria, the requested benefit of continued inpatient admission through discharge should be covered under the plan. The continued inpatient admission is reasonable, clinically appropriate, and in the best interest of the patient, and was consistent with sound medical judgment and standards of medical practice, as well as New York State instruction for this review.

summary:
Diagnosis: Mental Health 
Treatment: Outpatient Mental Health 
The insurer denied psychological testing. 
The denial is partially overturned.

At the time of service, the patient was a female referred for comprehensive psychological evaluation due to suspected bipolar disorder. She reported a very complex history of psychological problems, including depression, anxiety, substance abuse, obsessive-compulsive behavior, and disordered eating. She reported a history of sexual abuse. She also reported a history of trauma in both childhood and adulthood (e.g. [for example], father shot in the neck with resultant quadriplegia). Additionally, she endorsed current problems with insomnia. The health plan denied coverage for the evaluation due to a lack of medical necessity. The subject under review is the medical necessity for the psychological testing.

The requested service of psychological testing is medically necessary for this patient, in part. The patient has a very complex presentation with multiple historical and current problems and symptoms. A standard clinical interview would not be sufficient to address her multiple issues. Comprehensive psychological testing was clearly needed to differentiate among several diagnostic possibilities. Moreover, the diagnosis of bipolar disorder requires a careful review of the history, symptoms, course, and potential overlap with related disorders.

The records provided clearly establish the medical necessity for comprehensive psychological evaluation due to the complexity of the case and need to rule in/rule out related disorders in order to arrive at a proper diagnosis and treatment plan.
However, establishing the medical necessity of comprehensive psychological evaluation does not necessarily imply that this psychological evaluation was entirely medically necessary. The provider employed a broad array of measures, but not all of them are clearly necessary to arrive at a diagnosis and treatment plan. For example, there does not appear to be a sufficient rationale for inclusion of the following cognitive measures:

1) California Verbal Learning Test - Third Edition (CVLT-3) 2) Delis-Kaplan Executive Functioning System (D-KEFS) - selected subtests 3) Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale - Fourth Edition (WAIS-IV)

This was not a neuropsychological evaluation, and a comprehensive assessment of cognitive functioning was not clearly supported by the history and referral questions. It is fairly common for some of these measures to be included in a comprehensive psychological evaluation, but the present one did not clearly provide a rationale for cognitive assessment, and these measures were not medically necessary to rule in or rule out plausible alternative diagnoses.

This patient clearly needed a comprehensive psychological evaluation, and this is fully supported. 

As such, it would be reasonable and medically necessary to overturn the portion of the psychological evaluation medically necessary to arrive at a proper diagnosis and treatment plan.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse. 
Treatment: Inpatient hospital admission. 

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient hospital admission. 

The denial is upheld. 

According to the documentation submitted, this patient has a history of post-traumatic stress disorder, gastritis, constipation, and marijuana abuse. She presented to the emergency room (ER) with complaints of abdominal pain. Imaging of the abdomen revealed a slight prominence of extrahepatic biliary ductal system. In the ER the patient was given intravenous (IV) Protonix, IV morphine, IV Tylenol, IV Toradol, IV Reglan, IV fluids, and Zofran. She was admitted with intractable abdominal pain related to marijuana use. The patient was given around the clock pain medication and IV fluids. Serial abdominal examinations were done. Signs and symptoms were monitored. The patient was discharged after a period of medical stability. 
  
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. It also states that patients with past complicated or life-threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens are in need of inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal and reports that patients with comorbid medical condition that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification. 

In this case this patient did not have reports of active severe substance withdrawal symptoms, past complicated withdrawal such as alcohol withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens, and there were no reported acute medical issues requiring only 24-hour hospital treatment then.  The medical records stated that the patient had abdominal pain, small bowel obstruction, and gastritis, nausea and vomiting, diffuse abdominal tenderness, distress, and sinus bradycardia with fusion complexes and had occasional cannabis use. 

There were no reports of clinical institute of withdrawal scale (CIWA) protocol or detoxification medications given, and the patient had abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting but she reportedly did not have unstable stable vital signs and there no reports of severe substance or alcohol withdrawal or the need for withdrawal detoxification treatment. There were no reports of acute psychiatric symptoms requiring inpatient hospital treatment as there were no reports of suicidal or homicidal ideation, intent or plan, hallucinations, delusional or disorganized thinking, aggressive or self-injurious behavior, substance or alcohol withdrawal symptoms that would have required inpatient hospital treatment then, manic or major depressive episodes, inability to adequately care for basic needs, or evidence that he was considered an imminent danger to self or others then.  She reportedly was being treated for abdominal pain with IV Morphine, Tylenol, Protonix, Toradol, Reglan, Zofran, and IV fluids. There were no reports of specific identifiable or quantifiable treatment objectives or goals that could only be achieved in a 24-hour inpatient medical, psychiatric, or detoxification hospital setting. 

It appeared that the health care plan acted reasonably and with sound medical judgment. 

Based on the above, the medical necessity for the inpatient hospital admission is not substantiated. The insurer's denial is upheld.
