summary:
Diagnosis: Depression, Suicidal Behavior
Treatment: Inpatient Psychiatric Stay
The insurer denied the Inpatient Psychiatric Stay.
The determination is overturned.

The patient was admitted to acute inpatient level psychiatric services with severe symptoms of depression and anxiety associated with psychosis, suicidal behavior/risk and impaired functioning. The patient experienced a mental breakdown previously prompted by workplace stress and culminating in a suicide attempt by overdose. His breakdown followed a change in medication without benefit and with worsening symptoms of depression. He became paranoid with delusions thinking that he would be arrested for mistakes made at his workplace. His delusions resulted in persistent suicidal ideation with plans to electrocute himself or overdose or cut his wrists.
Despite ongoing treatment in the community with his primary and specialty care physicians, the patient's mood worsened with associated symptoms of depression and profound hopelessness with morbid preoccupations together with the delusions and treatment refractory depression that did not respond to medication or transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) therapy. He was focused on the fear of being incarcerated with thoughts that he would be better off dead. He was admitted to inpatient level psychiatric services for a comprehensive psychiatric evaluation and treatment and safety monitoring.
The patient has a history of general medical co-morbidities that includes gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and headaches with associated treatments. Laboratory assessments were normal or unremarkable with a negative drug screen. There is no active substance use disorder in this case.
The patient is married and lives with his spouse. There were no legal issues in this case and no history of trauma or abuse. The patient is employed with workplace stress and declining performance prior to his breakdown.
On Mental Status Examination on admission, the patient was cooperative and tearful with motor retardation and slowed mentation. He displayed depressive demeanor and expressed morbid ruminations with delusions, as noted. He displayed depressed mood with anxiety and cognitive clouding. He had decreased concentration, energy, appetite, sleep, and volition. His speech was coherent with linear thought processing and morbid content with active suicidal ideation and auditory hallucinations of dogs and police helicopters overhead searching for him. Insight and judgment were limited and fair with minimization. He displayed hopelessness, helplessness, guilt, shame and low self-worth indicating that he was exhausted and unable to function.
The patient was admitted to acute inpatient level care with safety-monitoring, access to group and milieu therapies, and medication adjustments in order to address the anxiety, depression, psychosis and sleep disturbance. The patient was initially noted to be severely depressed and socially withdrawn. Medications were adjusted to include Zoloft, risperidone, and trazodone with as needed (prn) use of Vistaril for anxiety.
The patient continued to display delusional thinking and indicated that he was soon to be arrested; he was unable to be reassured that this would not happen despite ongoing treatment. He received cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) interventions, as well as family sessions with his spouse. He did gradually improve with regard to mood and anxiety such that he was able to deny the delusions involving workplace and was more hopeful with a forward-looking outlook. His medications had been adjusted during this time frame with an increase in risperidone resulting in gradual reduction in his psychotic thought content. Discharge planning had occurred; he declined step down to Partial Hospitalization Program (PHP) level care, but was referred to outpatient aftercare. Discharge diagnoses included severe and recurrent major depressive disorder with psychotic features and unspecified anxiety disorder. Discharge medications included Zoloft 100 milligrams (mg), risperidone 1 milligrams (mg) in the AM and 1.5 mg at bedtime together with 250 mg of trazodone and continued use of Vistaril as needed for anxiety or agitation.
During the time interval under review, the patient remained psychotic, but by the date of discharge had gradually responded to treatment with diminished intensity of depressive symptoms including diminished anxiety and better functioning; the patient was better focused and displaying better judgment with improved mood and brighter affect. He no longer felt overwhelmed or hopeless, and he was medication adherent with tolerability. A discharge conference had occurred with discharge planning, and he was discharged to home with clinically appropriate aftercare in collaboration with community clinicians to include continued therapy and medications.
At issue is the medical necessity of Acute Inpatient Psychiatric Services.
The requested health service/treatment of psychiatric disorder treatment- acute inpatient level of care was medically necessary for this patient.
The patient's symptoms of depression and anxiety together with impaired functioning and risk for suicide warranted the admission and the continued acute inpatient level structure and monitoring through discharge. The case is complicated by severe psychosocial stressors related to the patient's preoccupation with workplace performance with a breakdown that included psychosis and suicidal ideation in the context of treatment refractory depression. The symptoms of mood disorder and associated symptoms of anxiety; continued risk for suicide, psychosocial stressors; and, treatment issues related to medication adjustments and need for monitoring, and the need for arranging a safe and appropriate discharge plan warranted the continued services at an acute inpatient level of care. The patient had worsened and declined in functioning despite having access to treatment in the community with outpatient level services. These clinical factors support the medical necessity for the continued acute inpatient level structure and 24-hour monitoring through the day of discharge when the patient had reached a level of stability that he could return home with family with clinically appropriate follow-up and aftercare.
This answer is consistent with the scientific literature and published guidelines, referenced below, as well as prevailing standards of medical practice.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder, Suicidal Behavior
Treatment: Inpatient Mental Health Stay
The insurer denied the Inpatient Mental Health Stay.
The determination is upheld.

The patient was admitted to acute inpatient psychiatric services for treatment of recurrent and severe major depressive disorder associated with acute suicidal behavior and an attempt to commit suicide by cutting his wrists. The patient was evaluated at the time of presentation and was subsequently admitted and was treated with inpatient mental health/psychiatric services. There were no substance use disorders in this case, other than past use of alcohol and "edibles;" a drug screen was negative and consistent with his history. He was medically screened in the emergency department and cleared for admission to acute inpatient mental health services.
The patient has a history of a mood disorder treated with Paxil and Wellbutrin. He was receiving outpatient treatment with therapy/counseling. There was a history of one prior psychiatric hospitalization. He had no substance use disorder diagnoses, and no general medical issues other than pre-diabetes and the laceration of his wrist.
The patient is married, college educated, employed and lives with his wife and two daughters. There is a family history of depression and completed suicide reflecting genetic predisposition.
Mental status examination on admission included mood that was depressed with anxiety. He was cooperative with good eye contact and clear speech that was soft. There was no evidence for psychosis, thought disorder, severe cognitive impairment, or perceptual disturbance. There were no somatic concerns other than sleep disturbance. Insight and judgment were fair and poor, respectively and the patient had anhedonia, hopelessness and low self-worth with depressive ruminations.
The patient was admitted to the acute inpatient psychiatric level of care with a diagnosis of major depressive disorder. He was continued on his psychotropic medications, titrated as clinically appropriate with adjustments. He had the opportunity to participate in individual and group therapy, group activities, and participate in other milieu interventions. He actively attended groups and other milieu activities. The patient's mood had improved with diminished anxiety and better sleep addressed with low-dose quetiapine and melatonin. He continued to deny suicidal ideation and was feeling better. The patient was maintained on the psychotropic regimen that included Wellbutrin, Paxil, and the addition of Abilify for augmentation with adherence and tolerability.
The treatment team and attending physician were discharge planning in concert with the patient's spouse who was reluctant to have the patient home. The patient received continued inpatient treatment. During this time interval, records indicate that the patient's mood was "fine" with congruent affect and denial of suicidal thoughts. He was future focused and remorseful for his suicide attempt, and his judgment was considered good. A discharge plan was developed in concert with the patient's spouse with immediate transfer for residential level services and a safety plan.
Throughout the hospital course the patient had not exhibited severe psychiatric symptoms including psychosis, severe cognitive impairment, mania, or thought disorder; he had not shown active suicidal ideation or aggressive impulses or violent intent. Discharge medications included Paxil 40 milligrams (mg), Wellbutrin 300 mg and Abilify 2 mg.
The health plan documents were reviewed including case notes and level of care guidelines/medical necessity criteria, as well as correspondence from the health plan and the treatment facility, and the patient's appeal documents. The dates under review were denied certification by the health plan for continued acute adult inpatient level psychiatric treatment on the basis of medical necessity indicating that the patient could have been safely managed with lower-level care such as partial hospital program treatment. This is a New York State mandated review.
At issue is the medical necessity of continued Inpatient Mental Health Treatment.
The requested health service/treatment of inpatient mental health treatment is not medically necessary for this patient.
The intensive treatment for the depressive disorder including safety monitoring did not require the continued structure of an acute inpatient level of care or 24-hour monitoring. The patient did not display continued evidence of a suicidal ideation, plan or intent, and did not engage in self-harm during the hospital course; other symptoms such as severe cognitive impairment (dementia or delirium), thought disorder, mania or psychosis were not present in this case, nor was there psychiatric co-morbidity or co-occurring substance use disorders that would have warranted the continued acute inpatient level care. The patient was generally cooperative with treatment and he was medication adherent with tolerability and engaged in treatment with family support.
The psychosocial stressors in this case were not so severe to require continued acute inpatient care or 24-hour monitoring during the time interval under review in this case. Additionally, the patient had access to services in the community with the availability of continued treatment for his mood disorder.
Medical necessity for continued acute inpatient level care is not met in this case for the time interval under review. These answers are consistent with published practice guidelines, the scientific literature as well as prevailing standards of medical practice.

The patient was admitted for acute inpatient level care with symptoms of depression and self-harming behavior. She had an argument with her husband with fear that he was cheating which resulted in the patient cutting her wrist. She was brought to the emergency department for treatment of the wrist laceration and a psychiatric evaluation in the context of severe psychosocial stressors. The patient presented with a history of depressive disorder and prior treatment with antidepressant medications. She indicated that the medications were not working and were not well tolerated.
At the time of presentation, the patient was tearful with symptoms of anxiety and depressive demeanor and preoccupation with her situational stressors. She had depressed mood with sadness, anger, and anxiety and reported low energy with decreased concentration and volition. There were no symptoms of mania, thought disorder, psychosis or severe cognitive impairment though she did display lethargy and fatigue. Insight was limited and poor, judgment was impaired, and impulse control was questionable. The patient denied prior hospitalization or suicidal or self-harming behaviors. There were no acute general medical problems or current substance use disorders in this case.
The patient is married and employed on a part time basis, and lives with her mother and husband. There was no trauma history or legal issues in this case. There is a family history of depression. The patient's father had recently died which was a perpetuating factor for the depression, and there was conflict with the husband, as noted.
The diagnoses included major depressive disorder, recurrent and unspecified, history of social anxiety disorder, and severe deterioration in functioning that included suicidal risk and severe psychosocial stressors.
The patient had received a comprehensive medical evaluation prior to admission. She received eight stitches to address the laceration. Laboratory assessments and an electrocardiogram (EKG) were normal. She was admitted with subsequent safety monitoring and treatment with milieu therapy that included group, educational and activity therapies. She received medication with the use of Effexor with plans to titrate as clinically appropriate, and as needed (prn) medications to address anxiety and insomnia. She engaged in therapeutic interventions with safety monitoring and support from her mother. The treatment team and case manager were working to develop a safe and clinically appropriate discharge plan and disposition in concert with the patient's mother.
By the last day of her brief inpatient stay, the patient was noted to be adherent to medication and participating in the therapeutic interventions. She was calmer with normal speech that was clear and thoughts that were linear and logical, as before. She denied suicidal ideation or any urges to self-harm. Discharge planning had occurred and the patient was discharged with clinically appropriate aftercare and continued medication (Effexor titrated to 75 milligrams (mg) daily), as well as the safety plan developed in concert with her mother with whom she lived and follow up appointments for continued mental health services.
At issue is the medical necessity for acute inpatient treatment for dates of service.
The health plan documents and appeal documents were reviewed, as well as correspondence from the health plan and treatment facility, health plan medical necessity criteria, certificate of coverage were reviewed, as submitted. This review is New York State mandated review.
At issue is the medical necessity of an inpatient stay.
The requested health service/treatment of inpatient stay was medically necessary for this patient.
The patient's acute inpatient treatment was clinically appropriate, reasonable, and in the best interest of the patient. She had severe symptoms of depression, she was a safety risk with the need to address the mood disorder and precipitating factors resulting in the impulsive self-harming behavior, and outpatient treatment had failed to prevent the worsening symptoms of depression with the onset of severe symptoms in the context of severe psychosocial stressors and the conflict with her husband. The patient remained a safety risk and functionally impaired with a high risk for relapse or self-harm or suicide; and the patient needed to reach a stable baseline of functioning with assurance of medication tolerability with a solid disposition and safety plan prior to discharge from inpatient level care.
Thus, it was medically necessary for this patient with major depressive disorder and safety concerns to remain in the acute inpatient setting in order to continuously assess her risk of suicidal or impulsive behaviors, and to address the acute risks of a return to the community with the noted functional impairments and treatment issues, as well as the need to develop a safe and clinically appropriate discharge plan and disposition with clinically appropriate aftercare.

He was later transferred to Residential Mental Health treatment level of care. During his treatment he was started on Wellbutrin and participated in group, family, and individual therapy. He was not having suicidal ideation and was noted to not have vegetative symptoms such as disrupted sleep or appetite. The medical necessity of ongoing residential mental health treatment is currently under review. 

The requested Residential Mental Health Treatment is not medically necessary for this patient. The patient was participating well, was not a danger to self and was not agitated, manic or psychotic during his residential mental health treatment. He has good support from his family. He tolerated Wellbutrin and showed improvement on this medication. Guidelines have been established looking at medical necessity of residential level of care which were not met in this case (InterQual guidelines). The patient was not an imminent danger to himself and had family support and involvement. He was able to attend to activities of daily living and did participate in treatment. He was not agitated during his residential treatment.  He does not meet the established InterQual guidelines for continued residential treatment.

In this case, the patient was not a danger to himself and not acutely manic or psychotic. He was engaged in treatment and willing to attend treatment. He was tolerating medications.

This patient was admitted to this hospital as she had an ulcer with cellulitis and maggots in her heel which needed debridement and was washed out. She reportedly was put on intravenous (IV) antibiotics. She reportedly was immunecompromised and had a past medical history of hepatitis C, asthma, endocarditis, and had a toe amputation. summary:
Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder.
Treatment: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS).

The insurer denied Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation.  The determination is overturned.

The patient has a longstanding history of major depressive disorder, recurrent and severe without psychotic features. The patient has a documented history of multiple medication treatments for depression including treatment with more than two disparate classes of medication and at least four or more trials with antidepressant medications (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), serotonin norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI), trazodone, and Wellbutrin), as well as combination treatment with an SSRI and Wellbutrin and augmentation with Ketamine nasal spray without a positive response. Additionally, the patient has received combined treatment with psychotherapy including cognitive behavioral therapy.

Due to adverse effects or a lack of efficacy, the patient has continued to experience severe symptoms of depression and functional impairments that impact her quality of life and day-to-day functioning. The patient's psychiatric evaluation indicated ethyl alcohol (ETOH) use and that the patient used to be a social drinker but states she is drinking more than she should be, typically drinks like 2-3 shots of Southern Comfort 5-6 nights per week. She has sought out treatment with Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) in the past and just feels like if she could address the depression she doesn't feel the alcohol would be an issue. Despite this history, the evaluation concluded that there is no diagnosed co-morbid psychiatric disorders or co-occurring substance use disorders in this case with the evaluation that only diagnosed major depressive disorder of moderate severity. The psychiatric evaluationdid not affirm a diagnosis of alcohol use disorder. Case records also characterize the patient as a "social drinker." The patient has no significant or acute general medical issues.

Mental status examination reveals depressed mood, sad affect with anxiety, and anhedonia together with negative thoughts/depressive ruminations. She has loss of interest and low energy and motivation with decreased concentration and bouts of insomnia. Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ)-9 score was at 18 at the time of evaluation for TMS therapy reflecting moderately severe symptoms of depression. The PHQ-9 has been as high of 21 reflecting severe depression. The patient is divorced and employed and lives alone. There are no legal issues or trauma history in this case.
The patient's clinician recommended treatment with a course of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) therapy that would generally include up to 36 treatment episodes/TMS sessions. The recommendation is in the context of the ongoing episode of depression that is treatment-resistant/refractory despite current treatment with Prozac and Wellbutrin together with cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and as needed (prn) use of lorazepam.

The case summary and records were reviewed including the psychiatric evaluation provided by the clinician, health plan documents, correspondence from the patient's mental health clinicians and the health plan , as well as appeal documents and case notes from the health plan, the health plan's coverage policy pertaining to transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) therapy and excerpts from the Certificate of Coverage. 
At issue is the medical necessity of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) therapy for major depressive disorder.

The requested health service/treatment of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is medically necessary for this patient.

The requested benefit of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is reasonable, clinically appropriate, medically necessary, and in the patient's best interest. The patient has demonstrated that her depressive disorder is treatment refractory with multiple failed trials of antidepressant medications of disparate mechanisms of action with augmentation, as noted in the clinical summary. The patient has also failed to achieve a sustained clinical response or remission of symptoms with combined treatment with psychotherapy (CBT) and medication regimens including current treatment. Thus, the proposed treatment of recurrent moderately severe to severe major depressive disorder using rTMS therapy with a clinically appropriate number of sessions of adequate dose including a maintenance taper is medically necessary in this case.
The requested TMS service is backed by credible scientific study and is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice for the condition under treatment in this case, recurrent major depressive disorder and treatment refractory/resistant depressive disorder.

The proposed treatment can reasonably be expected to provide the patient with greater net health benefit than any other standard therapy in this case scenario. Repetitive TMS therapy as a primary or adjunctive therapy for treatment of depression has generally been evaluated in patients who have had treatment resistant or treatment refractory depression, as defined by one or more, treatment failures with or without augmentation. TMS therapy for depression is established as a safe treatment by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and the data as reflected in peer reviewed medical literature supports this assertion. Specifically, when treatments with antidepressant medication with or without augmentation, or electroconvulsive therapy, and/or psychotherapy (especially cognitive behavioral therapy) have failed, then TMS is clinically appropriate. This assertion is also noted in the American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorder, referenced below.
This answer is consistent with the scientific literature and published guidelines, referenced below.

summary:
Diagnosis: Mental Health. 
Treatment: Mental Health: Inpatient. 
The insurer denied Inpatient mental health services. 
The denial was upheld in whole.

The patient is a male admitted to acute inpatient psychiatric services for treatment of major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder associated with severe anxiety and concentration difficulties, as well as interrupted sleep resulting in daytime fatigue and irritability. The patient was referred for emergency care by his outpatient psychiatrist. The patient was evaluated at the time of presentation and was subsequently admitted for treatment with inpatient mental health/psychiatric services due to concern for suicidal risk and the worsening symptoms of anxiety and depression. There were no active substance use disorders, but the patient had a past history of cannabis and alcohol use disorders which were determined to be in early full remission. The patient also reported a history of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). He was medically screened in the emergency department and cleared for admission to acute inpatient mental health services.
The patient was admitted to the acute inpatient psychiatric level of care with a diagnosis of major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder and the past history of substance use disorder and OCD. He actively attended groups and other milieu activities receiving evidence-based psychotherapeutic interventions.
He continued to have intermittent passive suicidal ideation but was feeling better and denied a suicidal plan or intent. The patient was maintained on the psychotropic regimen with adherence and tolerability.
The patient wanted to remain in the hospital until he was 100% better according to progress notes, and there was concern for a relapse if discharged prematurely. Thus, the patient received continued inpatient treatment. A discharge plan had been developed in concert with the patient's spouse. He was discharged to home with a safety plan and with outpatient follow up arranged.
At issue is the medical necessity of Inpatient mental health services.

The health plan's determination of medical necessity is upheld in whole.

The requested health service/treatment of Inpatient mental health services is not medically necessary for this patient.
The continued treatment for the mental disorders in this case did not require the continued structure of an acute inpatient level of care or 24-hour monitoring. Specifically, the patient did not present with acute general medical complications, or active substance use. Following admission, the patient was treated for the mood disturbance and associated symptoms of anxiety/insomnia and functional impairments with clinically appropriate titration psychotropic medications with augmentation and other treatment that resulted in improvement in symptoms and functioning; he did not require continued acute inpatient level structure or monitoring during the time interval under review, as he was showing improvement and no longer considered a serious risk for suicidal behavior that would have warranted continued assessment, safety monitoring and treatment in an acute inpatient setting. The patient did not display continued evidence of active suicidal ideation, plan, or intent, and did not engage in self-harm during the hospital course; other symptoms such as severe cognitive impairment (dementia or delirium), thought disorder, mania or psychosis were not present in this case, nor was there symptoms of the psychiatric co-morbidity or co-occurring substance use disorders that would have warranted the continued acute inpatient level care. The patient had access to services in the community with the availability of continued treatment for his psychiatric disorders, and the patient had family supports and a discharge plan that was appropriate. 
Therefore, the requested health service/treatment of Inpatient mental health services is not medically necessary.

summary:
Diagnosis: Alcohol Withdrawal

Treatment: Inpatient hospital admission

The insurer denied coverage for the inpatient hospital admission.

The denial is overturned.

This patient was admitted to this hospital due to medical complaints and withdrawal symptoms. He had severe epigastric pain 10 out of 10, vomiting, nausea, dizziness, tremors, tongue fasciculations, elevated heart rate and elevated blood pressure, and fever with lactate. He had alcohol pancreatitis and hepatomegaly. Bloodwork showed low potassium (K), low Magnesium (Mg), elevated lipase and elevated blood alcohol level. He reportedly was given Ativan intravenously (IV) for withdrawal and put on an Ativan Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for alcohol (CIWA) protocol. Gabapentin was also prescribed as needed for withdrawal. He had intravenous (IV) fluids, thiamine, folic acid, and vitamin B12 (Cobalamin). He was in rehabilitation treatment prior to this hospitalization. He did not want to return for alcohol rehabilitation treatment at that facility, so he was given other alcohol rehabilitation treatment options and was discharged. 
   
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. It also states that patients with past complicated or life-threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens are in need of inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal and reports that patients with comorbid medical conditions that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification. 

This patient could not safely be treated in a less restrictive detoxification treatment level of care as he was at risk for severe, complicated, and life-threatening withdrawal due to large amounts of alcohol use and had comorbid medical issues complicating the management of withdrawal. He had alcohol withdrawal symptoms and medical conditions including severe epigastric pain 10 out of 10, vomiting, nausea, dizziness, tremors, tongue fasciculations, elevated heart rate, elevated blood pressure, and fever with lactate. He had alcohol pancreatitis. He also reportedly had low K and low Mg, elevated lipase, and hepatomegaly. According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) he did require 24-hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated in a less restrictive treatment setting. He continued to use large amounts of alcohol despite medical issues and past inpatient alcohol rehabilitation treatment as he was in an inpatient alcohol rehabilitation treatment prior to this admission and still relapsed. He required and needed detoxification medication to modify withdrawal including Ativan intravenous push (IVP) and Ativan CIWA protocol and Gabapentin as needed for withdrawal. The risk of complicated withdrawal such as delirium tremens can occur 3 to 4 days after alcohol use so he required inpatient detoxification protocol treatment, The patient was at risk medically for more severe, complicated, and life-threatening withdrawal with active medical issues putting him at risk and required 24- hour hospital treatment. 

It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably or in the best interests of the patient then.

Based on the above, the medical necessity for the inpatient hospital admission is substantiated. The insurer's denial is overturned.

summary:
Diagnosis: major depressive disorder, autism spectrum disorder, social pragmatic communication disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder

Treatment: Continued inpatient mental health residential treatment

The insurer denied coverage for continued inpatient mental health residential treatment

The denial is overturned

The patient has a history of major depressive disorder (MDD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), social pragmatic communication disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), anxiety, and social media addiction. She presented to the RTC [Residential Treatment Center] for treatment due to suicidal ideation, aggression, self-injurious behavior including cutting, poor emotional regulation, poor decision making and insight, extreme impulsivity, dangerous behavior including sexting adults,  extremely poor boundaries, poor social cues and communication including social pragmatics, poor attention, hyperactivity, racing thoughts, inability to assess risks of danger to self, disorganization, inability to function appropriately independently, and difficulty processing and understanding language. She was in intensive outpatient (IOP) and outpatient mental health treatment including dialectical behavior therapy and still had significant struggles and behaviors, putting herself and others at risk of danger. The patient received individual, group, family therapy, and pharmacotherapy and was taking Sertraline, Vyvanse, Clonidine, and Prazosin. 

The Milliman Care Guidelines (MCG) Inpatient Acute Residential Behavioral Health Level of Care-Child and Adolescent medical necessity guidelines report that one needs to have continued danger to self or others, moderately or severe psychiatric or behavioral symptoms requiring 24-hour daily treatment, or serious dysfunction in daily living. For discharge it states that there needs to be sufficient support at a lower level of care, and absence of suicidal or homicidal thoughts or thoughts of harm to self or others.

In this case, the medical records provided did support that the patient did not have sufficient support at a lower level of care as her family could not manage her due to her extremely impulsive and risky behaviors. She reportedly put herself at risk of danger due to sexting and poor insight as well as self-injurious and aggressive behavior. The patient lacked the social and coping skills to care for her needs and was unable to identify dangerous situations and behaviors. She had poor emotional regulation and disorganization and poor attention and executive functioning. This was a complex patient with complex needs and would have been considered a risk to self and others if not in this residential treatment setting. 

This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for continued inpatient mental health residential treatment as the medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that without this level of 24-hour supervision and structure, the patient was at risk of putting herself in more danger. She had functional impairment, risk of danger to self, and mood and behavioral symptoms supporting intensive therapeutic 24-hour residential treatment during the denied dates of service.  She needed to learn better social and adaptive and coping skills to help keep herself safe and function more independently. She also required this therapeutic intensive, structured, and supervised level of care to address social, emotional, behavioral, and educational needs. The patient needed to remain in this 24-hour setting for safety while trying to learn better coping and social skills and emotional regulation, decision making, and impulse control.

It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably, with sound clinical judgment, or in the best interests of the patient.

The insurer's denial of coverage for continued inpatient mental health treatment is overturned. Medical necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
	
Treatment: Continued Residential Substance Use Treatment Services

The insurer denied the continued residential substance use treatment services.

The denial was overturned.

This is a male patient who was admitted to inpatient substance residential treatment who reportedly eloped and relapsed with alcohol use and a nicotine vaporizer. The patient's diagnoses included Severe Cocaine Use Disorder, Opiate Use Disorder, Severe Hallucinogen Use Disorder, Inhalant Use Disorder, Amphetamine Use Disorder, Alcohol Use Disorder, Cannabis Use Disorder, Major Depressive Disorder and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). In early 2019 the patient reported having had multiple attempts of drug overdoses. His mood symptoms included depression, hopelessness and helplessness. His history also included of homicidal threats, self-injurious behavior that included cutting self, running away, property destruction, and multiple school suspensions. The patient reportedly eloped with the intent of stealing medications and overdosing. The patient was brought to the psychiatric hospital.
 
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that residential treatment is indicated primarily for individuals who do not meet clinical criteria for hospitalization but whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. Residential facilities provide a safe and substance-free environment in which residents learn individual and group living skills for preventing relapse. This patient was considered in need of a 24-hour residential treatment because of his history of relapsing immediately after receiving 24-hour inpatient substance residential treatment in the past and was even relapsing during this current stay in this substance residential treatment as he reportedly eloped twice to use alcohol and substances. The patient was also a high-risk patient as he was using multiple, serious substances of use and had a few instances of serious overdoses recently in early 2019. The patient had suicidal plans and intent, and could not stop substance use without being in at least a 24-hour inpatient substance residential treatment setting. 

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), the patient met criteria for inpatient substance residential rehabilitation treatment as he continued to use multiple serious substances of use despite past inpatient substance treatments and despite negative consequences of substance use including violence, self-injurious behavior, overdoses, homelessness, property destruction, homicidal threats, running away, and more severe depression. The patient could not stop using multiple substances without the 24-hour therapeutic supervised and structured programming of this therapeutic residential treatment setting; the patient even eloped a few times to use alcohol and substances. The patient was a significant risk of danger to self and others, and required at least this 24-hour therapeutic inpatient substance residential treatment. 
The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient.

Based on the above, the medical necessity for continued Residential Substance Use Treatment services is substantiated.  The insurer's denial should be overturned.

summary:

Treatment: Inpatient Stay
The insurer denied the Inpatient Stay.
The determination is upheld.

The patient presented to the emergency department with a request for detoxification treatment. The patient reported nausea and intermittent vomiting of bright red blood together with intractable hiccups. He reported drinking alcohol in a large quantity on a daily basis for the past 25 years. He was medically screened with supportive measures on the emergency department and admitted to inpatient level services for detoxification of alcohol and stabilization and other medical services.
The patient reported using cocaine as well as alcohol. The patient had no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens. His self-referral was prompted by his desire to stop using alcohol due to concerns about his health. He presented with mild symptoms of withdrawal with a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) scale score of 9-12 with sweats, gastrointestinal upset, headache, tremor, anxiety and restlessness/agitation together with normal vital signs or mildly elevated pulse at 101 and a blood alcohol level of 90.
There were no acute general medical issues other than the report of vomiting and nausea and other symptoms of alcohol withdrawal, and no psychiatric issues in this case with a past history of unspecified anxiety disorder. Laboratory assessment was unremarkable except for elevated liver functions and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT), and a urine drug screen that was positive and consistent with history including the presence of cocaine and the blood alcohol level reflecting recent use. He was tobacco dependent.
The mental status examination was free of severe symptoms such as thought disorder, mood disturbance, psychosis, cognitive impairment or perceptual disturbance. The patient was deemed to be motivated to enter detoxification treatment and he had mild symptoms of withdrawal at the time of admission, as noted, as well as the report of intermittent vomiting.
The patient was admitted and placed on a CIWA detoxification regimen with intravenous (IV) Fluids, Ativan, and supportive measures with comfort medications including Zofran, as well as vitamin and nicotine replacement therapy. The detoxification was uncomplicated with regard to withdrawal management in that he was noted to be in no apparent distress on the next day, his liver functions were trending down. The patient received counseling and education from the staff. His clinical course was uncomplicated with normal vital signs and electrocardiogram (EKG). He had no withdrawal signs or symptoms, and was stable and in distress. He had resumed treatment with his home medications including citalopram, trazodone and as needed (prn) hydroxyzine, as well as methyl prednisone and azathioprine. The patient was discharged with clinically appropriate aftercare and immediate referral to outpatient rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment and recommendation for follow up with his primary care physician (or provider) (PCP).
 
The case records, health plan documents including case notes, appeal documents, correspondence from the health plan and treatment facility, and the rationale for the denial of certification for coverage of the requested services were reviewed. This case is a New York State mandated review with the application of NY State OASAS LOCADTR 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines.
At issue is the medical necessity of the inpatient stay.

The requested health service/treatment of inpatient stay is not medically necessary for this patient.
The requested detoxification treatment and withdrawal management and other medical services could have been safely and effectively provided with lower-level services. There were no co-morbid general medical problems or co-occurring psychiatric disorders that would have warranted admission for inpatient level services. Moreover, the withdrawal symptoms were not reported to be severe, and the patient's clinical symptoms were not serious enough to necessitate inpatient level detoxification treatment or monitoring. There were no safety concerns in this case and no history of complicated withdrawal from drugs or alcohol. The patient was considered to be motivated for detoxification treatment, and had access to substance use disorder services in the community. The denial determination reasonably indicated that lower-level treatment with an observation level of care with monitoring was an appropriate alternative to inpatient admission and in the best interest of the patient. Thus, medical necessity is not met in this case for the requested benefit of an admission and continued inpatient detoxification and other medical services in keeping with prevailing standards of professional practice, and consistent with the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria and scientific literature, referenced below, as well as NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Guidelines, referenced below.

summary:
Diagnosis: Delusions of Persecution.
Treatment: Inpatient mental health treatment. 

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient mental health treatment. 

The denial is overturned. 

This patient was admitted to inpatient mental health hospital treatment with involuntary status due to worsened psychotic and manic symptoms. He reportedly had delusions of persecution, grandiosity, and religious delusions, internal preoccupation, disorganized thinking, agitation, lack of insight and judgment, noncompliance with medication, racing thoughts, labile affect and irritable mood, poor sleep, poor concentration, reckless decisions with money, mood changes, arguing, physical fights, and he felt unsafe. He reportedly had a diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder-Bipolar type and Alcohol Dependence. He reportedly had past psychiatric hospitalizations. He reportedly had past ACT [acceptance and commitment therapy] and AOT [assisted outpatient therapy]. He had a history of alcohol, cocaine, and cannabis use. He reportedly refused medications still and had poor insight and acute psychotic and manic symptoms, so a court hearing was done for medication over objection and he then was started on Lithium and Aripiprazole po (oral) as well as Aripiprazole IM [intramuscular]. He reportedly was discharged when he improved enough. 
  
The InterQual Behavioral Health-Adult Psychiatry-Inpatient medical necessity criteria reports that if one has assaultive behavior within 24 hours, catatonia, command hallucinations to harm self or others, destruction of property with poor impulse control within 24 hours, disorganized behavior, unstable eating disorder, fire setting, homicidal or suicidal attempt within 24 hours, suicidal or homicidal ideation with high risk for an attempt, mania, risk of harm to self or others, non-suicidal self-injury and continued danger to self, positive psychotic symptoms with risk of harm to self or others, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) with risk of harm to self or others , psychomotor agitation and potential for violence, severe social withdrawal and refusing treatment, unavailable support or inability to provide needed care and supervision and there is acute deterioration in functioning then meet criteria for inpatient treatment. In this case the chart notes did report continued severe psychiatric symptoms during the denial period including acute psychotic and manic symptoms. The Milliman Care Guidelines (MCG) Behavioral Health Inpatient Level of Care Adult criteria reports that a patient needs to present as an imminent danger to self, imminent danger to others, with severe psychiatric or behavioral symptoms, have a severely dysfunctional living including inability to care for self, unwillingness to participate voluntarily, or a less restrictive level of care is not feasible meet criteria for inpatient behavioral health level of care. 

This patient had severe psychiatric symptoms on admission requiring 24 hour hospital treatment including psychotic and manic symptoms including delusions of persecution, grandiosity, and religious delusions, internal preoccupation, disorganized thinking, agitation, lack of insight and judgment, noncompliance with medication, racing thoughts, labile affect and irritable mood, poor sleep, poor concentration, reckless decisions with money, mood changes, arguing, physical fights, and he felt unsafe. He refused psychotropic medications and lacked insight. He was psychiatrically hospitalized on an involuntary admission. 

He reportedly improved enough and was discharged. The medical records provided enough specific evidence that he was acutely psychotic and manic until discharged. 

It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably, with sound clinical judgment, or in the best interests of the patient. 

The insurer's denial of coverage for the inpatient mental health treatment is overturned. Medical Necessity is substantiated.

He had a history of alcohol and marijuana use beginning in late adolescence with use of cocaine beginning in early adulthood. He reported 12 or more prior substance use disorder/detoxification treatments, the most recent with a two-day stay and against medical advice (AMA) discharge with relapse; his treatment history included no rehabilitation treatments or involvement in self-help recovery groups. 

The patient was admitted for inpatient detoxification and other medical services following the assessment for safety issues and medical clearance. He received vitamin replacement therapy, and other supportive measures including as needed (prn) Benadryl for insomnia. The patient's hospital course progressed without incident. He was placed on an Ativan taper over a five-day time frame. The patient slept and received meals without complications. The patient received counseling with recommendation for clinically appropriate aftercare including ongoing involvement with counseling and educational groups. He declined medication assisted treatment. He was discharged with completion of the detoxification treatment with referral for clinically appropriate aftercare and rehabilitation substance-related treatment. The subject under review is the medical necessity inpatient for the substance abuse detox.

The patient's admission and continued inpatient stay with detoxification, withdrawal management, and other medical services through discharge could have been safely provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Inpatient Detoxification Admission

The insurer denied the Inpatient Detoxification Admission.
The denial is upheld.

The appeal documentation describes the patient as a female who presented having been using cocaine, heroin, and alcohol each day. She had already been enrolled in a methadone program where she received 190 milligrams (mg) of methadone each day. She tested positive for cocaine, opiates, and methadone. Blood alcohol level (BAL) was zero. There was also a diagnosis of bipolar disorder for which she was prescribed Prozac, Abilify, and Neurontin. 

The medical records are consistent with the above information. On intake, there was no medical acuity present. Three was no history of blackouts or seizures, nor of overdose. Blood pressure was 108/68 with pulse of 62. Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) score was eight. No opioid withdrawal symptoms were documented. The patient was placed on Librium, but this was noted to make her "drowsy." Mental status exam did not reveal dangerousness to self/others or psychotic symptoms. The patient remained stable throughout her stay, sleeping well, and showing no signs of acuity.

No, the proposed treatment, inpatient detoxification admission, was not medically necessary.
The patient was demonstrating only mild symptoms of withdrawal, with a Clinical Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) score of less than ten and no Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) score present. This is consistent with the need for ambulatory withdrawal management without extended on-site monitoring. There was no physical or psychiatric acuity present and the patient was not suicidal, homicidal, or psychotic. Inpatient detox was therefore not medically necessary.

Yes, the health plan acted reasonably, with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.
The health plan denied the admission to inpatient detox. The patent had mild withdrawal symptoms and was at minimal risk of severe imminent withdrawal symptoms. The patient had adequate support services to ensure commitment to completion of withdrawal management as she was already engaged in an opioid treatment program which would have available both counseling and increased intensity of ambulatory services. The patient could have been safely and effectively treated within an ambulatory setting.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse. 
Treatment: Inpatient admission. 

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient admission. 
The denial is overturned. 

The patient was admitted to this inpatient hospital for suspected acute coronary syndrome due to cocaine use or alcohol pancreatitis as he had reports of severe and worsened abdominal pain of maximal intensity, chest pain, nausea and vomiting, and inability to tolerate oral intake while using cocaine. He had a positive toxicology for cocaine. It was reported that he used cocaine 2 days prior to admission and also was binge drinking including the night prior to admission. His troponin was elevated at 96.6 and lipase was elevated at 239. He had severe concentric left ventricular hypertrophy. He was given intravenous (IV) hydration, pain management, aspirin 324 mg (milligrams), and had cardiology and gastrointestinal consultations. When cardiology and gastrointestinal consultants deemed him ready for discharge, the patient was discharged. 
  
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that patients with comorbid medical condition that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification and patients with acute medical conditions related to alcohol or substance use are candidates for inpatient hospital treatment. This patient reportedly had both alcohol and cocaine use, and it was reported that his admission and medical symptoms including severe and worsened abdominal pain of maximal intensity, chest pain, nausea and vomiting, and inability to tolerate oral intake were likely due to acute coronary syndrome due to cocaine use or from alcohol pancreatitis as he had elevated lipase of 239 with severe and maximal abdominal pain and also had elevated troponin levels with chest and abdominal pain. He was treated with IV hydration, IV pain medications, and aspirin and had cardiology and gastrointestinal consultations. He was not deemed ready for discharge outside of this hospital setting when both cardiology and GI (gastroenterology) consultants deemed him safe for discharge. Untreated acute alcohol pancreatitis or untreated acute coronary syndrome due to cocaine use would have put this patient at high medical risk and possibly could have been life threatening so he required 24-hour hospital treatment. 

According to the American Heart Association (AHA) the management of patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome requires inpatient hospital treatment. It was reported that his cocaine use was the likely etiology or alcohol pancreatitis, and this required hospital medical treatment and work up. 

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment in the best interest of the patient. 

The insurer's denial of coverage for the inpatient admission is overturned. Medical Necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis:  Severe major depressive disorder.
Treatment:  Additional 15 Sessions of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS), Pre-service.

The insurer denied the  Additional 15 Sessions of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS), Pre-service.  The denial is upheld.

The patient is a adult female with a diagnosis of severe major depressive disorder without psychotic features. The patient has a history of treatment refractory depression. She was subsequently referred for repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) therapy to include up to thirty-six treatment sessions per protocol. Progress notes indicate a patient health questionnaire (PHQ)-9 scale score of 24 at the time of starting transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) therapy sessions, and a decline to 11 or 12 with a score of 12 at the time of her 35th therapy session, reflecting at least 50 percent improvement in the patient health questionnaire (PHQ)-9 score and indicating a clinical response to the transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) therapy. The treating clinician has recommended continuation therapy with transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) with up to 15 additional transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) therapy sessions in order to achieve a remission and additional benefit from transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) treatment.

No, the proposed treatment, an additional 15 sessions of transcranial magnetic stimulation, is not medically necessary for this patient.

In this case, the patient reached a plateau scoring an 11 or 12 on the patient health questionnaire (PHQ)-9 scale following a 50 percent reduction in scoring. Continued treatment did not produce additional benefit with regard to patient health questionnaire (PHQ)-9 scoring. Thus, the proposed continuation of treatment with repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) therapy is not likely to be more beneficial for the patient than any other available standard therapy, and medical necessity is not met in keeping with the plan denial determination. This answer is consistent with practice guidelines concerning major depressive disorder and the scientific literature pertaining to transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) therapy for major depressive disorder, and this answer is consistent with New York State instruction for this review.

Yes, the health plan did act reasonably, with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.

summary:
Diagnosis: Anxiety, Depression, Self-harming behaviors
Treatment: Residential Treatment
The insurer denied Residential Treatment.
The determination is overturned.

The patient has diagnoses of Asperger's disorder, anxiety and depression. She has had severe self-harming behaviors and has had multiple suicide attempts. Prior to residential treatment she failed outpatient treatment on a weekly basis as well as therapeutic boarding schools. Her providers recommended a higher level of care and she was rejected from programs at an intensive outpatient level of care due to her self-harming behaviors and prior history of suicide attempts. The patient was unable to function in multiple school setting due to the severity of her mental illness. At issue is the medical necessity for residential treatment.
The requested residential treatment is medically necessary.
The patient has struggled with incessant suicidal thoughts. She has shown that with a less restrictive environment she is unable to cope with activities of daily living such as returning to school. Her mental illness is severe and impedes her judgement and activities of daily living. She meets criteria for residential treatment per Milliman Care Guidelines (MCG) and InterQual guidelines as she is a danger to herself, has a pattern of self-destructive behaviors and would not be able to safely be treated at a lower level of care.
The patient arrived to residential treatment with hopelessness, dysphoria, low self-esteem and suicidal ideation. She also endorsed mood lability, racing thought and crying spells. She was reluctant to engage in some groups regarding coping skills  and required prompting. She was noted to struggle with emotional dysregulation and particularly with expression of her emotions to her family. While in treatment she continued to demonstrate mood lability, hopelessness and uncontrolled impulsive behaviors (ripping a stuffed animal in half). Her providers in residential treatment felt that she needed 1:1 supervision in the restroom out of fears that the patent would self-harm. Given the above, the residential treatment is warranted and medically necessary.

The health plan's determination of medical necessity is overturned.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse.
Treatment: Full hospital admission.

The insurer denied coverage for full hospital admission.  The denial is overturned.

This patient was brought in by emergency medical services (EMS) after being found confused and vomiting on a ferry. It was reported that he was nauseous and confabulating also. He reportedly drank 3 pints of vodka, and there was concern for Wernicke's encephalopathy. The neurology consult was questioning whether the altered mental status was the result of a seizure due to alcohol withdrawal. The patient had multiple medical issues including elevated liver enzymes. There was concern for liver failure as well. He had reports of worsened cirrhosis and varices secondary to portal hypertension and acute hepatitis. He reportedly had acidosis with an anion gap of 21.9. He reportedly also had ketones in the urine. He also had pancytopenia and dehydration. He reportedly was put on a CIWA (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol) protocol of Ativan 2 mg (milligrams) q (every) 6 hours prn (as needed) and seizure precautions. He reportedly was given IV (intravenous) fluids, folic acid, and thiamine. He also had diabetes and hypertension. He reportedly was discharged.
  
Also, the US (United States) Department of Health and Human Services-Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) Center for Substance Abuse Treatment reports that inpatient treatment is necessary if the ability to attend outpatient treatment daily is a problem, one is unable to follow up in outpatient treatment, if medical conditions complicate the treatment of withdrawal, if one has previous withdrawal seizures of delirium tremens, or if one does not have the capacity for informed consent. In this case this patient had several comorbid medical conditions complicating the management of withdrawal and he had past reported alcohol withdrawal seizures which requires inpatient medical detoxification treatment.  

According to the LOCADTR (Level of Care Determination) he did require 24-hour treatment, as he could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive setting, as he continued to use a large amount of alcohol including 3 pints of vodka the day prior to admission, and he had active withdrawal symptoms including nausea and vomiting and a possible withdrawal seizure as per neurology consultation with altered mental status with confusion and confabulation. He reportedly had multiple medical issues including elevated liver enzymes, and there was concern for liver failure, and he had reports of worsened cirrhosis and varices secondary to portal hypertension and acute hepatitis as well as acidosis with an anion gap of 21.9, ketones in the urine, pancytopenia and dehydration. The risk of delirium tremens (DT) can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use, so he was considered at risk for DT's, and there was concern for Wernicke's encephalopathy due to his confusion and altered mental status, so he required 24-hour hospital treatment. He reportedly could not function and could not care for basic needs as well. He did require 24-hour medical hospital treatment for alcohol detoxification and monitoring and treatment of multiple medical issues. It was considered unsafe for him to be treated in a less restrictive level of care then and also unsafe for him to be treated medically outside of a hospital setting due to his acute medical issues requiring hospital treatment then as well as the need for detoxification monitoring and CIWA treatment protocol in the hospital setting.

Inpatient hospital treatment was medically necessary. It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably, with sound medical judgment, or in the best interests of the patient.

The insurer's denial of coverage for the full hospital admission is overturned. Medical Necessity is substantiated.

The patient has a history of mood and anxiety disorders and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) with co-occurring poly-substance abuse beginning in adolescence with use of multiple substances of abuse including cannabis, anxiolytics (benzodiazepines), and stimulants (amphetamines) with the latter two classes of substances as drugs of choice. The patient was referred for residential level services with the threat of eviction from the family home due to continued escalating use of substances.
The patient has history of psychiatric hospitalization (seven-day inpatient stay) and suicidal ideation in the context of ongoing treatment for major depressive disorder of moderate severity, social anxiety, and ADHD. He was abusing or misusing prescribed Clonazepam and Etizolam, and was using amphetamines including 4-FMPH, a methylphenidate analogue.
The substance use disorder progressed with a dramatic decline in functioning that was related to the severe substance use disorders and perpetuated by the psychiatric comorbidities. Despite treatment efforts in the community and the effort by parents to address the mental health and substance use disorders, the patient remained resistant to treatment resulting in the subsequent referral for residential level treatment under threat of eviction from his parent's home. Thus, his referral for treatment was prompted by the failure to remain sober despite treatment in the community and the co-occurring psychiatric disorders, as well as parent child relational problems or conflict.

The health plan's determination of medical necessity is overturned, in whole.

Yes, the requested health service/treatment of Residential substance use treatment is medically necessary for this patient.
The patient's lack of awareness or limitations of insight together with the seriousness of his depressive and anxiety disorders and co-occurring substance use disorders is illustrated by his continued risk for suicide in view of the past history of suicidal ideation and psychiatric hospitalization; and, in view of the continued use of high-risk substances of abuse including designer stimulants together with benzodiazepines with blackouts and functional decline despite having access to treatment in the community, and despite having sober support from the family, and in the context of parent-child relational problems with the threat of homelessness. The presence of high-risk behaviors does complicate this case to a great extent, as does the negative influence of peers or the social environment. Additionally, the patient had serious mental health issues (along with the family stress) that were triggering the patient's use of substances and were associated with a relapsing course. These factors are the reason that the patient could not have been/could not be safely or effectively treated at a lower level of care during the time interval under review. 
None of this therapeutic work could have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in view of the multiple, complicating factors in this case for the time interval under review, and in view of the treatment history and history of treatment failure with lower levels of care and/or brief inpatient services.

It also states that patients with past complicated or life-threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens need inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal and reports that patients with comorbid medical condition that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification.

The risk of delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use and he reportedly was drinking large amounts of liquor including an entire bottle of whiskey a few days per week and reported drinking one bottle just prior to this admission. summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse. 
Treatment: Inpatient Admission. 

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient admission. 

The denial is overturned. 

This is the case of a male admitted to this inpatient hospital due to acute distress with new onset chest pain. He was diagnosed with bilateral pulmonary embolism and concern for new infarct. He also had hypertension, increased heart rate of 114, and was drinking 3-4 doses of alcohol per day for many years and had mild withdrawal symptoms. The patient was put on a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment Alcohol (CIWA) protocol with Librium 25 mg (milligrams) every 8 hours and Ativan 2 mg every 6 hours as needed and was given intravenous (IV) morphine, IV heparin, supplemental oxygen, and aspirin. He was discharged. 
 
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. It also states that patients with past complicated or life-threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens need inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal and reports that patients with comorbid medical condition that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification. 

The US (United States) Department of Health and Human Services-Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) Center for Substance Abuse Treatment reports that inpatient treatment is necessary if the ability to attend outpatient treatment daily is a problem, one is unable to follow up in outpatient treatment, if medical conditions complicate the treatment of withdrawal, if one has previous withdrawal seizures of delirium tremens, or if one does not have the capacity for informed consent. 

In this case this patient had several comorbid medical conditions including a pulmonary embolism complicating the management of withdrawal which required 24-hour hospital treatment. He was considered at risk of worsened withdrawal also due to his daily alcohol use and current withdrawal and he was put on a CIWA protocol with Librium. The risk of delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use and the patient was drinking alcohol daily with a 50-year history of use and had significant medical issues including bilateral pulmonary embolism which complicated the management of withdrawal and put him at risk medically. He had hypertension, elevated heart rate of 114, fell after drinking alcohol and was considered in acute distress with new onset chest pain. He was considered a high medical risk and in need of 24-hour hospital treatment including CIWA protocol and detoxification management. It was considered unsafe for him to be treated in a less restrictive level of care and also unsafe for him to be treated medically outside of a hospital setting due to his medical issues and alcohol treatment issues needed which required hospital treatment. 

The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. 

The insurer's denial of coverage for the inpatient admission is overturned. Medical Necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Mood Disorder
Treatment: Continued Residential Mental Health Treatment
The insurer denied Continued Residential Mental Health Treatment.
The determination is overturned.

The patient was referred to residential treatment by her outpatient clinician with severe symptoms of a treatment refractory mood and trauma related disorder and co-occurring substance use disorder. The patient had become increasingly anxious and depressed with suicidal ideation and deterioration in functioning despite several treatment episodes that included psychiatric hospitalizations and multiple medication trials, as well as electroconvulsive therapy and ketamine infusions without sustained benefit or response. She had received ongoing psychotherapy which had failed to produce a response or remission. She was diagnosed with bipolar I mood disorder with psychotic features including paranoid thought content, posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and co-occurring substance use disorder with alcohol and tobacco class drugs. The patient presented with a clinical course that included multiple psychiatric hospitalizations, suicide attempts and severe substance use disorder with ongoing and escalating use of alcohol, especially after quitting her job. Her functioning had deteriorated in the context of severe psychosocial stressors that included marital stress and unemployment, and limited psychosocial support. Thus, she was referred for residential treatment to provide for more intensive treatment with monitoring and further evaluation.

The mental status examination on admission revealed a patient with sad affect and anxiety including apprehension, nervousness, tension, and excessive worry. Sleep, appetite, energy levels and volition were disturbed. The patient exhibited a depressed mood with passive suicidal ideation, hopelessness, guilt and worthlessness. There was no overt psychosis or cognitive impairment or perceptual disturbance though the patient was prone to paranoid thinking. Judgment was fair, and suicidal risk was judged to be moderate to low with fair insight.

There was active substance use disorder with alcohol and tobacco, as noted. The patient had no sober supports. There were no acute general medical conditions. Physical examination and laboratory assessment were normal or negative or unremarkable. She had chronic conditions including hypothyroidism with low-normal parameters and an essential treatment with associated treatments including Lamictal, lithium, quetiapine, Wellbutrin, Primidone, propranolol and Cytomel. She had been placed on vitamins and supplements, as clinically appropriate, and was prescribed lorazepam as needed for anxiety.

The patient was married, unemployed and was living with spouse with a conflicted relationship, as noted. There are no legal issues and a complicated trauma history.

The patient was admitted with plans for a comprehensive evaluation with safety monitoring structured milieu therapy, and resumption of pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy The patient initially had a difficult clinical course with severe symptoms of anxiety and mood disturbance that limited her ability to engage with treatment. Her medications were adjusted included downward titrations or discontinuation of medications to simplify her psychotropic regimen. Psychological testing was provided to affirm her diagnoses and inform treatment.

During her continued stay, the patient became increasingly cooperative and receptive with treatment and social with peers with continued mood disturbance, affective instability and sleep disturbance. She received motivational interviewing and enhancement with regard to the substance use disorder, and dynamic and behavioral therapy with focus on mindfulness and distress tolerance, as well as emotional regulation, and trauma recovery. She denied active suicidal ideation, plan or intent during this time interval, but had continued evidence for passive suicidal ideation with continued risk. Insight, judgment and impulse control remained fair.

The treatment plan going forward included continued therapy with focus on the mood disturbance and trauma recovery, family-focused sessions to address issues within the marital/family constellation, and other interventions within the therapeutic milieu with the intensity of services, structure and monitoring of a residential program including sustained abstinence from alcohol and efforts at smoking cessation.

The issue under review is the medical necessity of Continued Residential Mental Health Treatment.

The requested health service/treatment of mental health residential treatment is medically necessary for this patient.

In this case scenario, the patient required the admission and the continued residential level care in order to remain safe and to administer treatment for her psychiatric disturbances while conducting an evaluation, and while observing her functioning with the resumption/adjustment of clinically appropriate medications to address the mood disturbance and stabilize mood while implementing evidence-based treatments to address the comorbid conditions, PTSD and the co-occurring substance use disorder. The clinical course is complicated by her past history of suicide attempts and suicidal risk during the time interval under review. Additionally, the treatment team was planning for an extended stay with intensive treatment targeting mood with trauma recovery in order to develop a safe and clinically appropriate disposition and discharge plan that would allow for a safety plan and efforts to address the co-occurring substance use disorders with alcohol and tobacco.

The medical necessity for residential level structure and monitoring is reasonable and in the patient's best interest in view of the patient's severe symptoms of mood disorder and comorbid mental and substance use disorders including continued risk for suicidal behavior; in view of these clinical features and the complicated presentation with comorbidities, continued active treatment with safety monitoring was warranted in the context of the patient's deteriorated functioning and severe psychosocial stressors. Additionally, the residential stay during the time interval under review is medically necessary in order to monitor the response to medications, to assure that the patient will have a sustained response to treatment, and to continue to address the risk of suicidal behavior in the context of severe symptoms of bipolar mood disorder and severe psychosocial stressors including marital conflict. The necessity for the admission and the continued residential mental health services reflects sound medical judgment in keeping with prevailing standards of professional practice, and with the published guidelines and criteria, referenced below.. This answer is consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, and with the published guidelines and criteria, referenced below, including the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria and Level of care utilization system for psychiatric and addiction services (LOCUS) Guidelines, as well as the scientific literature referenced below.
