He had a positive drug screen for cocaine and cannabis consistent with history, and a blood alcohol level of zero. The patient has a history of multiple detoxification treatments including a recent discharge. He reported two prior attempts at rehabilitation treatment with "no clean time."

The patient was admitted for inpatient detoxification. The patient's hospital course progressed without incident. However, his blood pressure was elevated requiring use of clonidine. The patient slept and received meals. His monitoring occurred without incident, and he had the opportunity to attend group sessions and receive counseling and education with planning for clinically appropriate aftercare. He completed the detoxification protocol and was discharged with referral for further treatment as clinically appropriate including inpatient rehabilitation services and follow up with primary care.

No, the proposed treatment, Inpatient Admission was not medically necessary for this patient.
The proposed inpatient stay and detoxification treatment and other medical services noted in the clinical summary could have been safely and effectively provided at a lower level of care. The patient displayed no serious disturbance of mental status despite having a history of ongoing substance use disorder with alcohol, cocaine and cannabis. Moreover, the patient did not show evidence for suicidal or aggressive behavior or risk, or severe cognitive impairment, or psychosis, or perceptual disturbance that would have warranted an inpatient level admission and treatment. This patient was admitted to this inpatient mental health residential treatment due to post traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) trauma related symptoms, depressive symptoms, anxiety, eating disorder symptoms, and substance use, and past self-injurious behavior and multiple past suicide attempts. She reportedly had depressed mood, hopelessness, low self-esteem, guilt, anhedonia, poor appetite, past suicide ideation and multiple past suicide attempts including overdose of pills and alcohol, hanging, drowning, suffocating, and slitting wrists. She reportedly had self-injurious behavior, dangerous behavior including impulsive sexual behavior, and PTSD symptoms including flashbacks, nightmares, dissociative symptoms, shame, self-blame, as well as anxiety, worrying, panic attacks, and obsessive-compulsive symptoms. She also reportedly had eating disorder symptoms including restricting, purging, separating food, weight fixation, eating quickly, body image distortion, hiding and throwing away food, body checking, calorie counting, food rituals, and thinking about food more than 5 hours per day. She was using cannabis to get numb. She had past hospitalization and a past inpatient eating disorder residential treatment. She took Zoloft and Abilify, attended group, individual, and family therapy. She reportedly was discharged. 
  
The Milliman Care Guidelines (MCG) Residential-Behavioral Health Level of Care- Psychiatry guidelines report that one needs to have continued danger to self or others, moderately or severe psychiatric or behavioral symptoms requiring 24-hour daily treatment, or serious dysfunction in daily living. For discharge it states that there needs to be sufficient support at a lower level of care, absence of suicidal or homicidal thoughts or thoughts of harm to self or others. In this case this patient continued to have moderate psychiatric symptoms and did not have the coping skills to deal with her multiple psychiatric issues, eating disorder issues, and substance use. She was a complex patient with multiple psychiatric diagnoses including PTSD, Major Depressive Disorder, Generalized anxiety Disorder, Unspecified Eating Disorder, and Cannabis Use Disorder. She reportedly had maladaptive coping skills, poor communication, feelings of shame and guilt, multiple past suicide attempts including  overdose of pills and alcohol, hanging, drowning, suffocating, and slitting wrists, self-injurious behavior, poor insight into how her trauma and psychiatric symptoms affected her poor coping skills of self-injurious behavior and suicide attempt6s, substance use, eating disorder symptoms, sexual behavior, impulsivity, poor boundaries, difficulty dealing with parental conflict including the parental divorce, and difficulty identifying triggers to her maladaptive behaviors and cognitive distortions. She had past recent hospitalization and residential treatment for eating disorders but needed more residential treatment to try to better process and deal with trauma and PTSD symptoms, depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, and substance use. This patient was admitted to this inpatient hospital in the medical unit due to altered mental status and inability to care for basic needs. She was severely dehydrated with rhabdomyolysis. She reportedly was overusing Ambien. She had intravenous (IV) fluids, Trazodone, Haldol as needed, corrective insulin, Gabapentin, and a lidocaine patch. She had uncontrolled hypertension, diabetes, gangrene, and spastic diplegia. She had psychiatric and neurological consultations and had delirium. The disposition was for her to be discharged to an inpatient rehabilitation facility but left against medical advice (AMA). 

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient hospital treatment as not medically necessary treatment. They stated that she had no brain infarction or a new stroke. They stated that she did not require 24-hour hospital treatment and they recommended a less restrictive level of care.
  
The MCG - Milliman Criteria Guidelines for Psychiatric Disorder: Common Complications and Conclusions reports that one meets criteria for hospitalization if one is a danger to self or others and not manageable at a lower level of care, if they have severe behavioral health issues such as hallucinations, or if a less restrictive level of care is not considered feasible until acute intervention is done. This was the case with this patient as she was considered to have severe psychiatric symptoms. She was severely dehydrated with rhabdomyolysis. She had psychiatric and neurological consultations and had a diagnosis of delirium and still had multiple medical issues including severe dehydration, rhabdomyolysis, uncontrolled hypertension, needed corrective insulin, IV fluids, and medications for agitation and pain. Also, the American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Delirium reports that delirium frequently heralds a medical emergency and patients are usually managed in an acute-care hospital setting and patients with altered mental status are candidates for inpatient hospital treatment. This patient had a change in mental status and could not care for her basic needs and was considered a danger to self as a result as she was not eating or drinking or taking medications appropriately and was found in the street naked lying-in feces, and she had a diagnosis of delirium. 

Notes reported that she had recent proximal muscle weakness and mechanical falls and the neurology consult recommended a brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and also stated that she had cerebral palsy. Notes reported that the disposition was for substance abuse rehab (SAR) placement, and she was no longer considered to have acute care needs and was placed on alternate level of care (ALOC) status awaiting placement to the SAR placement. Notes reported that she was psychiatrically cleared for discharge as well. Notes reported that she left AMA prior to placement in an SAR placement. 

The patient presented with acute mental status changes and inability to function. It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably or in the best interests of the patient for the initial days but did act reasonably and with sound medical judgment for the extended stay.

The health plan acted reasonably in part with sound medical judgment in the best interest of the patient.

The insurer's denial of coverage for the inpatient admission is modified. Medical necessity is partially substantiated.

Treatment: Mental Health Outpatient. 
The insurer denied transcranial magnetic stimulation. 
The denial is overturned. 

The patient is a male diagnosed with major depressive disorder, recurrent and severe without psychotic features and treatment refractory/resistant depression. The patient has a documented history of multiple medication treatments for depression including treatment with more than two disparate classes of medication and at least three or more trials with antidepressant medications (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor [SSRIs] and Wellbutrin). Due to adverse effects or lack of efficacy, the patient has continued to experience severe symptoms of depression. 

Co-morbid psychiatric disorders include unspecified mental disorder best characterized as other mental health or behavioral health disorder, and the patient has no co-occurring substance use disorder.
The patient's clinician recommended treatment with a course of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) therapy that would generally include up to 36 treatment episodes/transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) sessions. The recommendation is in the context of the ongoing episode of depression that is treatment-resistant/refractory despite treatment with three antidepressant medications, Prozac, Celexa and Wellbutrin.
The subject under review is the medical necessity for Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) Therapy for recurrent and severe major depressive disorder without psychotic features and treatment refractory/resistant depression.

The health plan's determination is overturned.

Yes, the requested health service/treatment of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is medically necessary, reasonable, clinically appropriate, and in the patient's best interest. The requested TMS service is backed by credible scientific study and is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice for the condition under treatment in this case, recurrent major depressive disorder, and treatment refractory/resistant depressive disorder.
The proposed treatment can reasonably be expected to provide the patient with greater net health benefit than any other standard therapy in this case scenario. Repetitive TMS therapy as a primary or adjunctive therapy for treatment of depression has generally been evaluated in patients who have had treatment resistant or treatment refractory depression, as defined by one or more, treatment failures with or without augmentation. TMS therapy for depression is established as a safe treatment by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and the data as reflected in peer reviewed medical literature supports this assertion. Specifically, when treatments with antidepressant medication with or without augmentation, or electroconvulsive therapy, and/or psychotherapy (especially cognitive behavioral therapy) have failed, then TMS is clinically appropriate. Treatment: Inpatient Detoxification Admission
The insurer denied the Inpatient Detoxification Admission
The denial is overturned

The patient is an adult male. He presented to an emergency department with request for detoxification treatment in the context of severe alcohol use. The patient has a history of severe substance use disorder with daily use of alcohol, Xanax and cannabis (marijuana). He was using up to three pints of vodka and six 16-ounce beers, one marijuana blunt, and one bar of Xanax daily. He has a history of prior detoxification treatment episodes with relapses and no recent sober time. His last detoxification treatment was approximately a few months earlier.

At the time of presentation to the emergency department, the patient reported functional decline as the substance use/disease had progressed. The patient provided no past history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens, but did report severe alcohol withdrawal symptoms in the past. He was screened and admitted for inpatient level care with plans for withdrawal management and detoxification and stabilization with a 5-day Librium protocol with CIWA (clinical institute withdrawal assessment) monitoring and supportive measures.

The medical screening had revealed evidence for elevated liver functions and a drug screen that was positive for THC (tetrahydrocannabinol), consistent with history. The patient's examination revealed withdrawal symptoms including diarrhea, sweats, tremors and chills together with anxiety and irritability with a CIWA (clinical institute withdrawal assessment) scale score in the mild range at 8-9 and a BAL (blood alcohol level) of 0.014 reflecting recent alcohol consumption. Vital signs were normal and laboratory assessment was normal or unremarkable other than the elevated AST (aspartate aminotransferase). Chronic conditions included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, GERD (gastroesophageal reflux disease), asthma, coronary heart disease and history of stroke. He was tobacco dependent at one pack per day. Medications included ASA (aspirin), amlodipine, atorvastatin, Depakote and albuterol inhaler that were continued.

The patient's hospital course progressed without incident. Vital signs remained normal. The patient reported mild nausea, anxiety, restlessness and irritability with persistently mild symptoms of withdrawal that diminished throughout her brief hospital course. He quickly stabilized and arrangements were being made for a referral to rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment and follow up. He completed the protocol and was discharge with recommendations for continuing his prescribed medications and involvement with self-help groups for support of a recovery, as well as recommendations for clinically appropriate aftercare with immediate transfer for inpatient rehabilitation treatment and services.

The health plan denied coverage for the requested services on the basis of New State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (level of care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) 3 Criteria indicating that the patient could have been sufficiently managed with lower-level care. The denial determination indicated that the withdrawal symptoms were mild, that the patient had no general medical or psychiatric symptoms requiring inpatient level care, and, that the patient had no history of complicated withdrawal and had access to support.

Yes, the Inpatient Detoxification Admission for detoxification treatment and withdrawal management and stabilization with monitoring and other medical services was medically necessary for this patient in keeping New York State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (level of care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) 3.0 Criteria and prevailing standards of medical practice.
The requested inpatient admission for detoxification treatment and withdrawal management and monitoring and other medical services could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. The patient in this case was using large quantities of alcohol with daily use, and two other drugs of abuse (marijuana and Xanax) with a presentation and history that did warrant the admission and the continued inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring.

Inpatient hospital level care with detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment that was provided in the emergency department and continued at the time of admission. Moreover, the patient's social environment was not conducive to an effective detoxification, and the patient had struggled with withdrawal symptoms and maintaining abstinence which were being effectively addressed with inpatient level monitoring with a Librium protocol and supportive measures. The patient had associated clinical features that included lack of sober supports and functional impairments with unemployment and serious general medical complications of the alcohol use disorder-contrary to the denial determination.

Thus, the appeal did appropriately indicate the necessity for the adult inpatient stay and detoxification treatment of this patient's substance use disorders that did warrant the hospital admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level setting with withdrawal management and psychosocial supports, and 24-hour monitoring. The patient's history of substance use (frequency and quantity) together with the severe psychosocial stressors and functional impairments do reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder and the need for a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management and stabilization, as the patient was at high risk for treatment failure or general medical complications such as seizures if detoxification and withdrawal management were to be attempted at a lower level of care. Moreover, the stage of change was contemplative at best and the patient's lack of awareness or insight regarding the severe alcohol use disorder and risk for medical complications.

Medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published practice guidelines, ASAM Criteria, and the scientific literature, referenced below, and, New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews including the appropriate application of NY (New York) OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (level of care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) 3.0 Criteria-referenced below. The health plan's denial on the basis of New York LOCADTR (level of care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) Criteria is not reasonable and attempting detoxification and other treatment in the emergency department or with lower-level treatment is not in the best interest of the patient or safe in this case scenario.

No, the health plan, in its determination of medical necessity, did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.
The health plan's denial on the basis of NY (New York) State LOCADTR (level of care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) Criteria is not reasonable, and attempting appropriate treatment with lower-level services, as the health plan recommended, is not in the best interest of the patient, or safe in this case scenario. The requested Inpatient Hospital detoxification treatment and withdrawal management and monitoring and other medical services is clinically appropriate, medically necessary and warranted, and therefore should be covered in this case scenario.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse/Addiction-Alcohol Abuse/Addiction/withdrawal. 
Treatment: Inpatient hospital stay. 

The health plan denied the inpatient stay as not medically necessary. 
The reviewer has overturned in whole the health plan's determination. 

The patient presented to the emergency department with complaints related to alcohol withdrawal. The patient was admitted to acute inpatient level services for detoxification and withdrawal management of severe alcohol use disorder and comorbid sedative-hypnotic-anxiolytic use disorder and co-occurring substance induced anxiety and depressive disorder, unspecified bipolar disorder, and acute stress disorder. The patient was using alcohol in large quantities on a daily basis together with prescribed temazepam. At the time of presentation, she scored a 9 on the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) scale reflecting mild withdrawal symptoms with a blood alcohol concentration of 0.265. She was tobacco dependent at ½ to 1 pack per day. She had limited treatment history with five detoxification treatment episodes without appropriate follow up. She reported psychiatric hospitalizations, ongoing treatment with psychotropic medications not consistently used due to heavy alcohol use. General medical issues included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with asthma, morbid obesity, neuropathy of the feet and gait problems with vascular insufficiency in her lower extremities prompting use of a wheelchair. Prescribed medications included a rescue inhaler and gabapentin, as well as duloxetine, risperidone, bupropion, and temazepam. The patient was admitted to acute inpatient level care and placed on a detoxification regimen.The patient continued to have mild to moderate withdrawal symptoms throughout the stay with CIWA scale scores from 9 to 19 peak and declining thereafter to a 12 at the time of discharge on despite receiving Valium with 5 to 10 milligrams (mg) dosages. The withdrawal symptoms included headache, tactile and visual hallucinations/sensations, agitation and anxiety, restlessness, and tremors. Treatment was continued through discharge/transfer with monitoring and assistance with daily activities with fall and seizure precautions. 

The requested health service/treatment of continued inpatient stay is considered medically necessary for this patient. 

The continued inpatient services and detoxification treatment and withdrawal management for severe alcohol and anxiolytic use disorder could not have been safely and effectively provided at a lower level of care. The adult inpatient treatment of this patient's substance disorders did require the continued structure of an inpatient level setting and 24-hour monitoring in view of the severity of the alcohol use disorder, and the presentation with withdrawal symptoms and co-occurring psychiatric and general medical disorders. Withdrawal symptoms were managed with benzodiazepine/Valium with a CIWA protocol requiring monitoring, as well as comfort medications and vitamin and nicotine replacement therapy together with fall and seizure precautions. Thus, the patient did require a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management during the time frame under review, as it was reasonable that the patient would have been unable to abstain from the substances of abuse if detoxification and treatment were to be attempted at a lower level of care. Medical necessity for the continued inpatient stay is met in this case, and is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice, published practice guidelines, and American Society of Addiction Medicine  Criteria. This is consistent with New York State instruction concerning medical necessity reviews including the application of NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria and Published Guidelines.

summary:
Diagnosis: Social anxiety.
Treatment: Mental Health: Residential.
The insurer denied continued mental health residential stay. 
The health plan's determination is upheld. 

The patient is a male with history of severe social anxiety, unspecified depression and attention deficit disorder inattentive subtype. Prior to residential treatment, the patient failed outpatient treatment, intensive outpatient treatment and had a history of social avoidance and school refusal. He was admitted to residential care.

The continued stay at the residential care facility was not medically necessary for the patient. The records were reviewed including letters from previous providers, history of non-attendance in his high school and prior failures of lower levels of care. The patient showed significant improvement while at Ironwood. He attended and participated in treatment willingly. He was not agitated, aggressive, manic or psychotic. He did not require any standing medications for his depression or his anxiety. He was not engaging in self harm behaviors or having thoughts of harm to himself or others. He was willing to participate in groups and engage in individual, group and family therapy. He was looking forward to returning home. He did not require medical monitoring for any co-morbid conditions and tolerated his treatment without issues. He has a supportive family and access to treatment providers in his home environment and was willing to engage on the dates in question. He did show signs of anxiety and some mild avoidance but was able to be redirected. He does not meet CALOCUS (Child and Adolescent Level of Care Utilization System) guidelines for residential treatment on the dates in question for the reasons stated above and could have been safely treated in a lower level of care.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse. 
Treatment: Inpatient Detoxification Admission. 

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient detoxification admission. 

The denial is overturned. 

The patient is a male reportedly was admitted to inpatient detoxification treatment for detoxification treatment. He reportedly had withdrawal symptoms including nausea, tremors, sweats, anxiety, irritable mood, agitation, diffuse discomfort, and had a clinical institute withdrawal assessment (CIWA) of 12 and clinical opiate withdrawal scale (COWS) of 11. He reportedly was drinking 3 pints of wine per day, using 7-10 bags of heroin intranasally per day, and using $50 per day of crack/cocaine. His toxicology was positive for opiates, cocaine, and benzodiazepines. He reportedly had multiple past inpatient substance detoxifications. He reportedly had no clean time and was homeless and unemployed. He reportedly was started on 2 detoxification medications including Librium and Methadone. He left against medical advice (AMA) after his doses of these medications despite the recommendation to complete detoxification and then go to an inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment. 
  
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. It also states that patients with past complicated or life-threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens are in need of inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal and reports that patients with comorbid medical condition that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification. 

According to the level of care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), he did require 24-hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive setting as he continued to use large amounts of alcohol daily including up to 3 pints of wine daily and he had active withdrawal symptoms including nausea, tremors, sweats, anxiety, irritable mood, agitation, diffuse discomfort, and had a CIWA of 12 and COWS of 11. He reportedly lacked coping skills and ability to identify relapse triggers which resulted in no abstinence time. He did require 24-hour medical hospital treatment for alcohol detoxification, it was considered unsafe for him to be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive level of care. The plan was to go to inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment after completion of this inpatient substance detoxification treatment. He reportedly left AMA after taking Librium and Methadone.  As a result, the recommendation is to overturn the previous decision and approve coverage for inpatient hospital treatment. 

It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably, with sound medical judgment, or in the best interests of the patient then. 

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment in the best interest of the patient. 

The insurer's denial of coverage for the inpatient detox admission is overturned. Medical Necessity is substantiated.

Therefore, the health plan was noted to have acted reasonably, with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, and alcohol abuse. 
Treatment: Residential mental health admission. 

The insurer denied coverage for residential mental health admission. 

The denial is overturned. 

This case involves a female diagnosed with Major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, and alcohol abuse. 

The patient was admitted to residential treatment due to depressive symptoms, suicidal thoughts, anxiety, alcohol use, eating disorder symptoms, past suicide attempts and self-injurious behavior, and trauma related symptoms. She reportedly had depressed mood, suicidal thoughts, hopelessness, worthlessness, shame, concentration problems, sleeping problems, crying, decreased interest, pleasure and energy, amotivation, self-blame, high anxiety, impulsive behaviors, victimization of rape at school, 3 past suicide attempts including an overdose with alcohol and opiates, an overdose with Benadryl and an overdose with Klonopin. She reportedly was restricting fluids and food intake and had cognitive distortions. She reportedly had impairment in functioning as she attended class intoxicated or missed class due to alcohol sue and psychiatric symptoms. She also reportedly had family conflict as her father reportedly came back from military deployment with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and traumatic brain injury (TBI). She reportedly was drinking 3-4 whiskey drinks daily. She reportedly had a past psychiatric hospitalization. She reportedly took Abilify and Bupropion, attended individual and group therapy, family therapy, dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT), cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), yoga, adventure and equine therapy, music therapy, and horticulture. She reportedly eventually improved enough for discharge with step down to a partial hospitalization program (PHP). 
  
The insurer denied coverage for continued inpatient behavioral health residential treatment as not medically necessary treatment. They stated that she was no longer at risk of serious harm to self, did not require 24-hour residential treatment, and they recommended a less restrictive level of care. 
  
This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for continued inpatient behavioral health residential treatment as the medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that she required that level of care. The Milliman Care Guideline (MCG) Residential-Behavioral Health Level of Care- adult guidelines report that one needs to have continued danger to self or others, moderately or severe psychiatric or behavioral symptoms requiring 24-hour daily treatment, or serious dysfunction in daily living. For discharge it states that there needs to be sufficient support at a lower level of care, absence of suicidal or homicidal thoughts or thoughts of harm to self or others. In this case this patient continued to have moderate psychiatric symptoms and did not have the coping skills to deal with her multiple psychiatric issues, eating disorder issues, and substance use. She was a complex patient with multiple psychiatric diagnoses including Major Depressive Disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, and alcohol abuse and had eating disorder symptoms and trauma issues who continued to report suicidal thoughts and limited coping skills in dealing with her psychiatric symptoms and still had urges to drink. She required more time in this therapeutic structured and supervised residential treatment to learn more coping skills so as not to act in maladaptive ways in dealing with her psychiatric symptoms. 

Notes reported increased suicidal ideation and that she was struggling with reasons to live and not ready to leave this facility yet. Notes reported that she still struggled with suicidal ideation multiple times per day, had urges to self-harm, depression still, and with her 3 past suicide attempts and history of impulsive behavior, she was considered still at risk for suicide and alcohol relapse. Notes show that she was doing Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) and reported that she was struggling with shame, had suicidal ideation, cravings and urges, impulse control problems, racing thoughts, and somatic distortions. Notes reported high anxiety and rapid speech. It also reported that she was at great risk for relapse due to rigid and intrusive thinking, and she still had impulse control issues as well as cravings and urges. She reportedly had shame which increased suicidal thoughts, and also had depression still. She reportedly was struggling to develop and implement effective coping skills that allow normal interaction with others without irrational fears or intrusive thoughts controlling behavior. Notes reported that she still had moderate depression and anxiety, suicidal thoughts, and was struggling to reestablish hope. Notes reported cravings, and she was working on depression and anxiety treatment, independent living skills, interpersonal effectiveness, and she had cravings and working on self-acceptance and hope but had less overall depression and anxiety. 

She reportedly was discharged with referral to PHP treatment. She had multiple psychiatric diagnoses and symptoms and required more time in a 24-hour inpatient therapeutic residential treatment to learn sustained improved coping skills to decrease dangerous and maladaptive behaviors and use health coping skills. Also, the American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Suicidal Behaviors reports that patients with past suicide attempts are at high risk for suicide and this patient had 3 past serious suicide attempts by overdose of pills, alcohol, and opiates so she was considered a high-risk patient for suicide and self-injury if she did not learn better coping skills while in a 24 hour therapeutic supervised and structured residential treatment setting. This was a high risk patient with 3 past suicide attempts, self-injurious behavior, moderate depressive and anxiety symptoms, trauma related issues, eating disorder symptoms, alcohol abuse, poor coping skills, impairment in functioning who still had reports of moderate psychiatric symptoms, suicidal thoughts, and cravings during the denial period  who required more time in this therapeutic structured and supervised residential treatment to learn more coping skills so as not to act in maladaptive ways in dealing with her psychiatric symptoms. As a result, the recommendation is to reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for inpatient mental health residential treatment. 

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment in the best interest of the patient. 

The insurer's denial of coverage for the residential mental health admission is overturned. Medical Necessity is substantiated.

The patient is an adult male. He self-referred for inpatient rehabilitation and substance use disorder treatment. The patient has a history of longstanding substance use disorder with cocaine. The patient has no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens. He indicated difficulty with the social environment with peers using substances of abuse and coping problems related to the substance use disorder which had adversely impacted his health and functioning. His history of substance use included up to $100 worth of cocaine on a daily continuous basis. He denied use of other substances except for tobacco. 

Throughout his inpatient stay, the patient remained stable with mental status and engaged with the treatment regimen, as noted. He received intensive rehabilitation services, monitoring, and structure provided within the inpatient treatment program including 24-hour monitoring. The patient was discharged with plans for clinically appropriate aftercare of his substance use disorders with referral for outpatient services and return home. 

The health plan denied coverage of the patient's stay on the basis of New York State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (level of care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) 3 Criteria indicating that there were no acute symptoms that would have required inpatient level services and suggesting that lower-level treatment was the appropriate level of care. The case records and health plan documents were reviewed including correspondence and case notes and New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3 medical necessity criteria. The health plan's rationale for the denial of the requested services was reviewed together with the appeal for the dates of service under review. The review is New York State mandated with the application of NY State OASAS LOCADTR 3 Criteria.
At issue is the medical necessity of continued residential substance use disorder and mental health treatment.

The services were medically necessary in part.

The patient required the admission and warranted the continued structure and monitoring of a residential setting that was medically necessary in order to effectively address the patient's risk for impulsive and problematic behaviors including risk for self-harm, continue to learn adequate coping skills to achieve better control of impulses and work on relapse prevention, while the treatment team and family worked toward a clinically appropriate disposition with continued mental health services to address the co-occurring mood and anxiety symptoms associated with PTSD and to effectively address the co-occurring substance use disorders. The patient had residual symptoms and behaviors that had persisted despite past treatment prompting the referral to residential care and the patient continued to lack the insight and control of impulses to remain engaged in treatment in a less restrictive setting during this time frame.

The clinical presentation and acuity of symptoms and complicated psychosocial factors in this case together with the treatment dimensions with regard to American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria are the reasons that the admission and continued residential level services do meet medical necessity with the application of New York State OASAS LOCADTR Criteria, as well as prevailing standards of medical practice and in keeping with the guidelines referenced below. Again, the patient's admission and treatment is reasonable and in the best interest of the patient; she presented with severe symptoms of depression and anxiety, suicidal ideation and behaviors associated with unresolved grief/trauma triggering the substance use, and outpatient treatment had failed to prevent increasing symptoms of depression and suicidal ideation and self-harming behavior in the context of severe psychosocial stressors and substance use.

The patient could not have been effectively treated at a lower level of care until the patient was stable with euthymic mood and was effectively working on the remaining psychological issues with improved insight and impulse control and coping skills per the health plan's case notes and case records. Thus, the requested services of residential level treatment for 27 days are reasonable and consistent with prevailing standards of medical care, and with the application of NY State OASAS LOCADTR 3 Criteria, referenced below. Services after that are not medically necessary.

Diagnosis: Substance Abuse.
Treatment: Inpatient Rehabilitation Admission.
The insurer denied the Inpatient Rehabilitation Admission.
The denial is upheld.

The patient is male with diagnoses of cannabis dependence, uncomplicated, and nicotine dependence, cigarettes, uncomplicated.  The question is whether inpatient rehabilitation treatment was medically necessary.

During his inpatient rehab admission, patient's treatment included a medication regimen of comfort medications. A psychiatric evaluation note notes that patient endorsed symptoms of anxiety and insomnia and was prescribed Vistaril and trazodone to help with these symptoms. He denied any hallucinations or other psychotic symptoms in spite of reportedly having been observed smiling to himself on the unit. In a progress note, he also admitted to a history of depression but denied current symptoms. Group notes indicate that the patient participated in groups focusing on developing coping skills, managing stress, and preventing relapse.  He continued to deny any safety concerns, SI/HI (suicidal ideation/homicidal ideation), or withdrawal symptoms throughout admission. Progress notes indicate that the patient did admit to marijuana cravings but was able to identify relapse triggers. Nursing notes indicate that the patient was alert and oriented throughout admission.

At issue is inpatient rehabilitation level of care.  The health plan used Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) for Substance Abuse Inpatient Rehabilitation criteria for the determination and concluded that medical necessity for an inpatient rehab level of care was not met due to the patient's lack of medical instability, being able to participate in or comply with treatment outside of a 24-hour strutted treatment setting, did not have social, emotional, or developmental barriers to participating in treatment outside of an inpatient level of care, did not have a co-occurring medical or psychiatric condition that required inpatient care, was not at risk from complications from withdrawal, was not suicidal, homicidal, or psychotic at the time of admission and initial evaluation, had access to social support, and was not experiencing symptoms or functional impairment that created an imminent risk of harm to self or others.

This decision was appealed by the facility with the managed care coordinator noting that medical staff evaluated the patient and deemed him appropriate for inpatient level of care at admission based on OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) guidelines. It also notes that the patient required evaluation by the facility's psych NP (nurse practitioner) after being observed pacing and laughing to himself and admitted to a history of self-injurious behavior. It notes that the patient was prescribed Vistaril and trazodone. It states that the patient lacked coping skills to remain sober and needed help to identify triggers and stress, and that he had never had any sober time (although this is contradicted elsewhere in the record).  It also states that the OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) tool does not state that a patient with a lack of psychotic symptoms should not be admitted to substance abuse treatment and that residential level of care would have required a referral.

No, the Inpatient Rehabilitation Admission was not medically necessary.
The patient's American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Patient Placement Criteria Rating was as follows:
(Dimension 1) Risk: 0-Individual fully functioning with good ability to tolerate, cope with withdrawal discomfort -No signs or symptoms of withdrawal present-No signs or symptoms of intoxication.
(Dimension 2) Risk: 0-Fully functioning with good ability to cope with or tolerate physical discomfort-No biomedical signs or symptoms are present.
(Dimension 3) Risk: 1-Subclinical mental disorder.
(Dimension 4) Risk: 0-Willingly engaged in treatment as a proactive participant, is aware of/admits to having an addiction problem and is committed to addiction treatment and changing substance abuse and adherence with psychiatric medications-Willing to cut negative influences.
(Dimension 5) Risk: 1-Some craving with ability to resist -Needs support and counseling to maintain abstinence, deal with craving, peer pressure, and lifestyle and attitude changes-Minimal risk of relapse.
(Dimension 6) Risk: 0-Has supportive environment Based on patient's risk ratings,  a lower level of care would have been appropriate for treating the patient's substance.

Additionally, the patient does not meet criteria for inpatient level of care using LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) criteria. The patient was not experiencing a life-threatening medical condition or severe psychiatric crisis, was not experiencing significant functional impairment due to his substance abuse, and was not experiencing acute withdrawal symptoms from marijuana. He did not have a history of life-threatening withdrawal syndromes. He was not experiencing a severe medical problem or serious psychiatric symptoms that needed to be managed in an inpatient rehab setting in order for treatment for his substance abuse to be effective. He did not endorse using substances in hazardous situations or in amounts or frequencies likely to imminently cause severe physical or emotional harm to self or others. He did not have any personal or interpersonal skills deficits. He was not documented to have been exhibiting predatory behavior that would have likely caused harm to others in a congregate setting. He did not report strong cravings or urges to use that were unmanageable or behavioral or emotional instability that would require stabilization with medical oversight in a residential setting. Based on LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) guidelines, the patient could have been appropriately managed at the residential rehabilitation level of care.

Yes, the health plan acted reasonably, with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.
As noted above, the severity of patient's symptoms based on ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) patient placement criteria and LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) patient placement guidelines show that the patient's condition could have been managed at a lower level of care than inpatient rehabilitation. There is no documentation of moderate or severe acute withdrawal symptoms, he did not have an acute medical condition that required inpatient treatment, and he did not endorse SI (suicidal ideation), HI (homicidal ideation), or any other severe psychiatric symptom that would require inpatient treatment. He also denied any history of any serious psychiatric diagnoses. His symptoms could have been managed at a lower level of care.

He reportedly lacked coping skills, ability to identify relapse triggers, insight into use, and could not maintain any abstinence despite multiple inpatient substance treatments. This patent was admitted to this inpatient hospital for alcohol detoxification. She reportedly had active withdrawal symptoms including nausea, tremulousness, sweats, and had a CIWA (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol) as high as 10. She reportedly was put on a Librium A CIWA protocol and had 2 doses of Librium 50 mg (milligrams) and one dose of Librium 25 mg for detoxification. She reportedly had been drinking 1 liter of vodka per day. She reportedly had multiple inpatient detoxification treatments and also a 4-month inpatient alcohol rehabilitation treatment and still could not maintain abstinence. She had a heart rate of 45. She reportedly had depressed mood and suicidal ideation as well and had a past psychiatric hospitalization. She reportedly had diagnoses of Major Depressive Disorder in addition to Alcohol Dependence with withdrawal. She reportedly lived alone. She reportedly was seen by the psychiatric consultant who ordered Sertraline in addition to Mirtazepine and also recommended inpatient voluntary psychiatric hospitalization, but the patient refused. She also took Disulfiram and Naltrexone. She reportedly was discharged.
   
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that patients with failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. It also states that patients with past complicated or life-threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens are in need of inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal and reports that patients with comorbid medical condition that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification. 

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), she did require 24-hour treatment as she could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive setting as she continued to use large amounts of alcohol daily, required and received detoxification medication, Librium, including 2 doses of 50 mg and 1 dose of 25 mg, to modify withdrawal from alcohol and prevent more complicated or life-threatening withdrawal such as delirium tremens. The risk of delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use so she was considered at high risk for this. She reportedly was being monitored in the telemetry unit. She also continued to use large amounts of alcohol despite multiple past inpatient detoxification treatments and also a 4-month inpatient alcohol rehabilitation treatment. She also took Disulfiram and Naltrexone due to her alcohol use problem. She also lacked supports and lived alone. She also had comorbid psychiatric symptoms including depressed mood and suicidal ideation with a diagnosis of major depressive disorder and the psychiatric consultant recommended voluntary psychiatric hospital treatment to which she declined.  She was considered at high risk for more severe, complicated, and life-threatening withdrawal so she required this inpatient medical hospital detoxification treatment then. 

The health plan did not act reasonably, with sound medical judgment, or in the best interest of the patient.

The insurer's denial of coverage for the one-day hospital stay is overturned. Medical necessity is substantiated.

summary:

Treatment: Inpatient chemical dependency rehab stay.
The insurer denied inpatient chemical dependency rehab stay.
The determination is upheld.

The patient was to inpatient level services for treatment of cannabis use disorder; the patient had been using up to 3 blunts of marijuana per day in violation of his parole. The patient was referred for substance-related treatment after testing positive for tetrahydrocannabinol (THC); he also tested positive for phencyclidine (PCP) and cocaine though he denied use of these substances. The patient was externally motivated to enter substance abuse rehabilitation treatment in order to comply with his parole officer's recommendation.
The patient has no acute general medical issues. He is diagnosed with asthma treated with a rescue inhaler. Medical screening was negative and unremarkable except for a positive drug screen. He was tobacco/nicotine dependent with 13 years of use at a ½ pack per day. There are no co-occurring psychiatric disorders in this case.
The patient is unemployed and housed and undomiciled. He is on parole, as noted, and in jeopardy with regard to violating the terms of his parole. There is a report of unspecified trauma history in this case.
Mental Status Examination revealed no severe symptoms and the patient was pleasant, cooperative and euthymic with normal speech, linear thought processing and no disturbance of thought content such as paranoid thoughts or delusions. He lacked coping skills and demonstrated only fair insight.
The inpatient level substance disorder rehabilitation treatment included the opportunity to participate in groups, individual counseling, education and 12-step recovery groups with peer support. Comfort medications were available as needed, and he was prescribed vitamins.
The patient engaged in substance use disorder treatment with active involvement in group and educational sessions, as well as other therapeutic interventions to support healthy living and the development of sober supports. The patient was noted to adjust easily to the treatment program. In this regard, the patient worked on coping skills and a relapse prevention plan with the identification of triggers including peer support to address the negative influence of the social environment.
The patient remained engaged throughout the inpatient stay with satisfactory progress. The patient was administratively discharged for rules violation.
Case records and the health plan documents, appeal documents, correspondence from the health plan and treatment facility, as well as the health plan's rationale for denial of the requested inpatient rehabilitation services were reviewed. This is a New York State mandated review including the application of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria.

At issue is the medical necessity of inpatient chemical dependency rehabilitation (rehab) stay.
The requested health service/treatment of inpatient chemical dependency rehab stay was not medically necessary for this patient.

The inpatient substance abuse rehabilitation treatment, in this case scenario, was amenable to treatment at a lower level of care. The patient was externally motivated and able to effectively engage in rehabilitation services and, the patient did not need the structure or 24-hour monitoring of an inpatient setting in order to safely and effectively participate in rehabilitation substance abuse treatment.
There were no biomedical or psychiatric complications, or severe psychiatric symptoms/disorders in this case that would have warranted inpatient level services and treatment.
This answer is consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and the published guidelines and scientific literature, referenced below, as well as the NY State OASAS LOCADTR 3.0 Criteria, referenced below and applicable in this case.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse. 
Treatment: Hospital admission at a substance abuse inpatient level. 

The insurer denied coverage for hospital admission at a substance abuse inpatient level. 

The denial is overturned. 

This patient was admitted to inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment for substance rehabilitation treatment. For many years, he was using 5-10 bags of intravenous (IV) heroin daily, $20 of intranasal cocaine twice per week, and 2-3 joints of marijuana daily with. He had a positive toxicology for opiates, cocaine, THC (Tetrahydrocannabinol), and methadone. He reportedly had withdrawal symptoms including diarrhea, hot and cold sweats, sleeping problems, and anxiety symptoms. He reportedly had 5 past inpatient detoxification or rehabilitation treatments and reportedly had a recent inpatient detoxification treatment. He was unemployed. He reportedly had no abstinence. He left against medical advice (AMA). 

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that inpatient treatment is indicated primarily for individuals whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. 

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) he met criteria for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment as he continued to use large amounts of IV heroin daily, $20 of intranasal cocaine twice per week, and 2-3 joints of marijuana and cannabis daily and could not maintain any abstinence. He had no clean time. He reportedly continued to use large amounts of opiates putting him at high risk for accidental overdose. He had a positive toxicology for opiates, cocaine, THC, and methadone. He also had withdrawal symptoms including diarrhea, hot and cold sweats, sleeping problems, and anxiety symptoms. 

The National Institute on Drug Abuse: Principles of Addiction Treatment: A Research Based Guide- reports that the best treatment outcomes occur with longer durations of treatment. It also states that recovery from drug addiction is a long-term process and that treatment techniques to increase motivation for treatment are necessary to prevent dropout rates. In this case this patient required inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment setting but left AMA. He required this sober, structured and supervised therapeutic inpatient substance rehabilitation setting for substance rehabilitation. Without this structured and supervised therapeutic rehabilitation treatment he likely would have relapsed quickly again and been more at risk medically for overdose due to the large amount of heroin use daily as well as cocaine use. As a result, the recommendation is to overturn the previous decision and approve coverage for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment. It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably, with good clinical judgment, or in the best interests of the individual. 

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment in the best interest of the patient. 

The insurer's denial of coverage for a hospital admission at a substance abuse inpatient level of is overturned. Medical Necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Bipolar. 
Treatment: Acute mental health inpatient treatment. 

The insurer denied inpatient Mental Health Treatment. 
The health plan's determination is overturned. 

This case involves an adult male admitted for acute inpatient psychiatric treatment with a diagnosis of bipolar mood disorder, manic phase with psychosis. The patient was brought into the emergency department from jail with onset of delusions and erratic behaviors. He had been arrested for running in the street and threatening others with a machete. He had threatened his girlfriend's brother accordingly. He indicated that he was being persecuted and was at risk for harm. Additionally, he was not sleeping and had become increasing agitated in the 72 hours prior to his arrest. The patient had a history of a depressive disorder treated with Zoloft in the past, and a history of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) treated with Adderall in the past. He had no history of psychiatric hospitalization or suicidal behavior. 

Inpatient Mental Health Treatment was medically necessary for this patient. 

The continued inpatient services served to provide intensive treatment in a patient with high risk for relapse, and severe symptoms of bipolar disorder including psychotic features and poor insight and control of impulses. Thus, the continued acute inpatient level care was necessary in order to continue a safe and clinically appropriate treatment with monitoring and address any psychosocial stressors and other issues that could result in medication non-adherence. Moreover, the patient presented with safety issues with delusional thinking and erratic behavior, and had remained anxious with illogical and disorganized thinking and mood disturbance and sleep disturbance. There were continued safety concerns, residual mood disturbance, and paranoid thinking together with continued risk of impulsive behavior. 

Only by the date of discharge did the patient exhibit calm demeanor without evidence for delusions or with clear thinking that would support a discharge to the community under the care of his grandparents with a clear discharge plan.

summary:
Diagnosis: Bipolar Disorder, ADHD (Attention Deficit Hyperactive Disorder), and Learning Disorder.
Treatment: Mental health residential treatment.

The insurer denied coverage for mental health residential treatment.  The denial is overturned.

This male was admitted to inpatient mental health residential treatment due to disruptive behavior, impulsivity, poor frustration tolerance, emotional dysregulation, depressed mood, hopelessness, guilt, concentration problems, suicidal thoughts, restlessness, cannabis use, poor and maladaptive coping skills, poor insight, blaming of others and not taking responsibility for his behaviors and actions. He did not improve after past traditional substance treatments in multiple settings. He had past hallucinations and paranoia. He had diagnoses of Bipolar Disorder, ADHD, and Learning Disorder. His discharge medications were Bupropion, Cariprazine, Depakote, Propranolol, and Melatonin. 
  
The Milliman Care Guidelines (MCG) Residential-Behavioral Health Level of Care- Psychiatry guidelines for adults report that one needs to have continued danger to self or others, moderately or severe psychiatric or behavioral symptoms requiring 24 hour daily treatment, or serious dysfunction in daily living. For discharge it states that there needs to be sufficient support at a lower level of care, absence of suicidal or homicidal thoughts or thoughts of harm to self or others. In this case this patient continued to have moderate psychiatric symptoms and limited coping skills putting him at risk for worsened mood symptoms and continued self-medication with substances. He was considered at risk of decompensation and relapse of drugs if discharged, as he still did not have adequate enough coping skills to function safely outside of this residential treatment setting. In this case this was a high-risk patient with poor coping skills and poor insight with neurodevelopmental delays in learning, who had depressive symptoms and still struggled with accepting responsibility for his actions and maladaptive interactions and functioning. 

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patient's with Bipolar Disorder reports that the least restrictive setting for safe and effective treatment is appropriate. It also states that the general goals of bipolar disorder treatment are to assess and treat acute exacerbations, prevent recurrences, improve interepisode and provide assistance, insight, and support to the patient and family. It also states that subsequently, specific goals of psychiatric management include establishing and maintaining a therapeutic alliance, monitoring the patient's psychiatric status, providing education regarding bipolar disorder, enhancing treatment compliance, promoting regular patterns of activity and of sleep, anticipating stressors, identifying new episodes early, and minimizing functional impairments. In this case this patient benefitted from more time in a structured and supervised inpatient mental health therapeutic residential treatment to try to improve coping skills more, emotion regulation, anger control, social interactions and relations, insight, decision making, decrease impulsivity, and transition back into the community and home. It was reported that the staff and family did not feel that this patient was ready for discharge and needed more time to sustain past gains and have more gains to better ensure that he would be safe and not have suicidal thoughts, maladaptive behaviors or coping skills. He required more time in this mental health residential treatment setting as past traditional substance use settings were not effective. 

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment in the best interest of the patient.

The insurer's denial of coverage for mental health residential treatment is overturned. Medical Necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance abuse.
Treatment: Inpatient admission.
The insurer denied the inpatient admission.
The denial is upheld.

The patient is a male with diagnoses of alcohol use disorder (AUD), cocaine use disorder, benzodiazepine use disorder, and type 2 diabetes mellitus.  The question is whether inpatient rehabilitation treatment was medically necessary.

The patient's urine drug screen at the time of admission was positive for benzodiazepines and blood alcohol level was negative. Patient denied any history of SI (suicidal ideation) or HI (homicidal ideation). With regards to functional impairment, patient denied any difficulty with completing activities of daily living, reported that he has worked several jobs "off the books," and denies any legal history related to substance abuse. He reported that his family was supportive of his recovery.

During his inpatient rehab admission, patient's treatment included a medication regimen of comfort medications. A treatment plan lists a goal of establishing and maintaining total abstinence with objectives of developing coping skills to prevent relapse.  He continued to deny any safety concerns, SI/HI (suicidal ideation/homicidal ideation), or withdrawal symptoms throughout admission. Nursing notes indicate that the patient was alert and oriented throughout admission but frequently refused finger sticks and medications. It is noted that he did not bring his diabetes supplies with him to the facility.

The patient requested discharge against medical advice from the rehab facility, noting that he planned to return to his job. He planned to return home and it was noted that he has stable housing. He had an appointment for outpatient follow up to address his substance use disorder and vocational concerns. He was noted to be medically stable at the time of discharge, denied any withdrawal symptoms, and denied SI/HI (suicidal ideation/homicidal ideation), hallucinations, or any other severe psychiatric symptoms.

At issue is inpatient rehabilitation level of care for dates of service.  A physician reviewer used Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) for Substance Abuse Inpatient Rehabilitation criteria for the determination and concluded that medical necessity for an inpatient rehab level of care was not met due to the patient's lack of acute withdrawal symptoms, unstable acute medical conditions requiring 24 hour care, lack of history of psychiatric diagnosis, having presented voluntarily for treatment, having left AMA (against medical advice) due to needing to get back to work, and having supports for sobriety. It was also noted that the patient was able to participate in or comply with treatment outside of a 24-hour strutted treatment setting, did not have social, emotional, or developmental barriers to participating in treatment outside of an inpatient level of care, did not have a co-occurring medical or psychiatric condition that required inpatient care, and was not experiencing symptoms or functional impairment that created an imminent risk of harm to self or others.  As such, it was noted that rehabilitative services in a residential setting were appropriate.

No, the Inpatient admission was not medically necessary.
The following is the patient's American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Patient Placement Criteria Rating:
(Dimension 1) Risk: 0-Individual is fully functioning with good ability to tolerate, cope with withdrawal discomfort-No signs or symptoms of withdrawal present-No signs or symptoms of intoxication.
(Dimension 2) Risk: 1-Demonstrates good ability to tolerate and cope with physical discomfort-Mild symptoms may interfere with daily functioning, but would likely not interfere with recovery treatment nor create risk.
(Dimension 3) Risk: 0-No current/chronic psychiatric, psychological, behavioral, emotional, or cognitive problems that create risk or complicate treatment.
(Dimension 4) Risk: 1-Willing to enter treatment and explore strategies for changing alcohol use.
(Dimension 5) Risk: 2-Impaired recognition and understanding of substance use relapse issues-Regular use of alcohol-Moderate use of drugs.
(Dimension 6) Risk: 0-Has a supportive environment or is able to cope with poor supports.

Based on patient's risk ratings, a lower level of care would have been appropriate for treating the patient's substance use disorders.

Additionally, the patient does not meet criteria for inpatient level of care using LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) criteria. The patient was not experiencing a life-threatening medical condition or severe psychiatric crisis, was not experiencing significant functional impairment due to his substance abuse, and was not experiencing acute withdrawal symptoms from alcohol or benzodiazepines. He did not have a history of life-threatening withdrawal syndromes or withdrawal seizures. He was not experiencing a severe medical problem or serious psychiatric symptoms that needed to be managed in an inpatient rehab setting in order for treatment for his substance abuse to be effective. He did not endorse using substances in hazardous situations or in amounts or frequencies likely to imminently cause severe physical or emotional harm to self or others. He did not have any personal or interpersonal skills deficits. He was not documented to have been exhibiting predatory behavior that would have likely caused harm to others in a congregate setting. He did not report strong cravings or urges to use that were unmanageable or behavioral or emotional instability that would require stabilization with medical oversight in a residential setting. Based on LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) guidelines, the patient could have been appropriately managed at the residential rehabilitation level of care.

Yes, the health plan acted reasonably, with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.
As noted above, the severity of patient's symptoms based on ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) patient placement criteria and LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) criteria show that the patient's condition could have been managed at a lower level of care than inpatient rehabilitation. There is no documentation of acute withdrawal symptoms, he did not have an acute medical condition that required inpatient treatment, and he did not endorse SI (suicidal ideation), HI (homicidal ideation), or any other severe psychiatric symptom that would require inpatient treatment. He also denied any history of any serious psychiatric diagnoses. He stated that he has a good sober support system at home and was willing to continue his treatment on an outpatient basis as evidenced by his upcoming follow up appointment.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder.
Treatment: Admission for residential mental health treatment.

The insurer denied coverage for admission for residential mental health treatment.
The denial is overturned.

This is the case of a male who was transferred from another residential treatment facility due to high risk of harm to self and others, continued mood symptoms, and poor functioning including inability to function adequately at home or in the community. He had depressed mood, isolation, crying, decreased energy, poor activities of daily living (ADLs), impulsive behavior, and social delays. He reportedly had multiple past serious suicide attempts including stabbing self and 2 carbon monoxide poisoning attempts while drinking. He reportedly also stabbed and cut himself in the wrists and arms and also attacked his roommate at college while he was sleeping and stabbed him with a knife in the throat just missing his artery. He reportedly had a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder, Social Pragmatic Disorder, and Substance Use Disorder. He reportedly had social delays and there was question about a possible diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder. He reportedly was taking Wellbutrin, Lithium, Abilify, Zoloft, Cytomel, and Melatonin. He reportedly had past residential treatment 6 months, and also was in a boarding school. It was reported that he stabbed his roommate in the neck almost killing him and then stabbed himself in the wrists and arms. He reportedly went to the psychiatric hospital after that and was discharged and then sent to residential treatment. He reportedly is still in residential treatment. 
    
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Major Depressive Disorders reports that the least restrictive level of care for safe and effective treatment is appropriate. The MCG (Milliman Care Guidelines) Residential-Behavioral Health Level of Care- Psychiatry guidelines report that one needs to have continued danger to self or others, moderate or severe psychiatric or behavioral symptoms requiring 24-hour daily treatment, or serious dysfunction in daily living. For discharge it states that there needs to be sufficient support at a lower level of care, absence of suicidal or homicidal thoughts or thoughts of harm to self or others. 

In this case, the patient continued to have moderate-severe psychiatric symptoms and was considered at risk to self and others if discharged from a 24-hour therapeutic supervised and structured residential treatment setting. He still did not have adequate enough coping skills to function safely outside of this residential treatment setting. In this case this was a high-risk patient with poor coping skills and poor insight with developmental delays who had depressive symptoms, past serious dangerous behavior to others and self, multiple past suicide attempts who still did not have the necessary coping skills to function so he required continued 24 hour therapeutic residential treatment. 

He required a substantial amount of time in this setting. It was reported that he changed insurance and that that insurer approved mental health residential treatment. He was considered a high-risk patient in need of 24-hour mental health residential treatment. 

The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. 

The insurer's denial of coverage for an admission for residential mental health treatment, revenue code 1001 is overturned. Medical Necessity is substantiated.

His diagnosis was Psychotic Disorder. He also had reported developmental delays and a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder and Profound Intellectual Disability. The medical records did not provide enough specific evidence to support that he only required 24-hour inpatient hospital treatment then. The MCG (Milliman Care Guidelines) Behavioral Health Inpatient Level of Care Adult criteria reports that a patient needs to present as an imminent danger to self, imminent danger to others, with severe psychiatric or behavioral symptoms, have a severely dysfunctional living including inability to care for self, unwillingness to participate voluntarily, or a less restrictive level of care is not feasible to meet criteria for inpatient behavioral health level of care. In this case it was reported that he no longer had bizarre behavior, hallucinations, delusional thinking, and he was cooperative and compliant and at his baseline. It was reported that he remained until he was able to be discharged to a group home instead of going to his parent's home first and then the group home. It was reported that he had lived with his parents prior to this hospitalization. Notes reported that he had no paranoia or delusions, was in good behavioral control, cooperative, denied hallucinations, had normal speech and psychomotor activity, linear thought process, and denied suicidal or homicidal ideation. There was no specific evidence that he still had severe or moderate psychiatric symptoms or that he could not safely be discharged home until a bed became available. Also, there were no reports of specific identifiable or quantifiable treatment goals or objectives that could only be achieved in a 24-hour acute hospital setting then or that could not be achieved in a less restrictive level of care then.  As a result, the recommendation is to uphold the previous decision and deny coverage for continued inpatient mental health treatment in this hospital. 

The health plan acted reasonably with sound medical judgment in the best interest of the patient.

The insurer's denial of coverage for psychiatric inpatient hospitalization is upheld. Medical Necessity is not substantiated.

Treatment: Inpatient rehabilitation

This male reportedly was admitted to inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment for substance rehabilitation treatment due to cocaine and cannabis. He reportedly had diagnoses of bipolar disorder and PTSD and was taking Depakote and Vistaril. He reportedly had poor coping skills, difficulty identifying relapse triggers, cravings, lacked insight and judgment, and motivation issues. He reportedly attended individual and group therapy and 12 step groups.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that inpatient treatment is indicated primarily for individuals whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. In this case this patient was considered in need of 24-hour substance rehabilitation treatment from as he reportedly was using large amounts of cocaine and cannabis and had comorbid psychiatric bipolar disorder and PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder). He reportedly lacked the coping skills and ability to identify relapse triggers to stop use and reportedly could not maintain any abstinence. 

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) tool he met criteria for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment as he continued to use large amounts of substances daily putting him at risk medically and for withdrawal despite past treatment. He reportedly lacked coping skills to maintain abstinence outside of this 24-hour substance rehabilitation treatment and needed to better identify relapse triggers and to learn relapse prevention skills as well as increase sober supports. It was reported that his use of substances was interfering with his functioning and put him more at risk for worsened psychiatric symptoms and danger to self. He still reportedly had drug dreams and cravings for substances, difficulty maintaining housing and employment, and was spending more time and money on using substances. 

Also, the National Institute on Drug Abuse: Principles of Addiction Treatment: A Research Based Guide- reports that research indicates that that the best treatment outcomes occur with longer durations of treatment and states that recovery from drug addiction is a long-term process. summary:
