The patient is a adult male. He was referred with admission to inpatient rehabilitation and substance use disorder treatment beginning to primarily address substance use disorder with alcohol, opioid and cocaine use, as well as intermittent use of Xanax. The patient has no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens. He was in medication assisted treatment with Suboxone, but had continued to use 3 to 4 bags of heroin with IV (intravenous) administration. He had been using one pint of liquor and beer together with daily use of one gram of cocaine, as well as taking his Suboxone. He had past treatment experience with at least two detoxification treatment episodes and the ongoing MAT (medication-assisted treatment). His drug screen was negative and his blood alcohol level was zero with a CIWA (clinical institute withdrawal assessment) scale score of 0 and a COWS (clinical opiate withdrawal scale) scale score of 1 reflecting no withdrawal symptoms.

Upon admission to inpatient level services, the patient received comprehensive evaluation and treatment that included focus on coping skills, relapse prevention techniques with identification of triggers, education about the disease model of addiction, and, involvement with groups, as well as peer-supported recovery groups and other therapeutic activities. Psychiatric evaluation had been provided and affirmed that the patient had co-occurring psychiatric disorders with anxiety and insomnia as a focus of treatment.

Throughout the inpatient stay, the patient remained stable and engaged with the treatment regimen. He received intensive rehabilitation services, monitoring, and structure provided within the inpatient treatment program including 24-hour monitoring. He had been medically cleared for aftercare, a bed was secured for continued treatment with sober living and residential rehabilitation treatment. The patient was discharged for continued rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment with check in on the following day.

The health plan denied coverage of the admission on the basis of New York State LOCADTR (level of care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) 3 Criteria indicating that residential level care was appropriate. Additionally, the denial indicated that the patient had no significant general medical issues or drug or alcohol withdrawal requiring inpatient level care. The denial determination referenced the psychiatric comorbidity as not requiring inpatient level care, and indicated that the patient had reasonable motivation for substance use disorder treatment with lower level care indicated.

The appeal was on the basis of multiple past treatment episodes with no "clean" time and a lack of coping skills, indicating that New York State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (level of care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) Criteria were met for inpatient level rehabilitation treatment. The appeal also indicated that the lack of psychotic features was not a valid reason to deny the requested level of care.

No, the Inpatient rehabilitation admission was not medically necessary.
The patient received inpatient level rehabilitation treatment. He was referred for treatment after failing to remain abstinent while receiving Suboxone treatment and other services.  As the health plan asserts, the patient had no significant general medical or serious symptoms of psychiatric comorbidity, and presented with no complicated withdrawal or safety concerns such as suicidality or aggressive impulses. He was motivated to engage in rehabilitation treatment and had no biomedical or psychiatric treatment issues that warranted inpatient level care. Thus, the patient did not meet New York State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (level of care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) Criteria, as the health plan asserts in the denial.

During the time interval under review, the patient was noted to be in no apparent distress with reasonable functioning and active participation in treatment including positive interactions with staff and peers. During his inpatient stay, there were no complicating treatment issues that would have warranted inpatient level of care, structure or 24-hour monitoring. The application of New York State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (level of care for alcohol and drug treatment referral) 3.0 Criteria (referenced below) did indicate that the patient was clinically appropriate for treatment with lower-level care in a less restrictive treatment setting, as the health plan also asserts. Yes, the health plan has acted reasonably, with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.
The patient in this case scenario is not clinically appropriate for an inpatient level of care for the time interval under review. The patient had presented with a level of stability that included no significant withdrawal symptoms or biomedical issues and no co-occurring psychiatric disorders or safety concerns that would have warranted inpatient level care. He did not need the monitoring or the structure of an inpatient setting in order to receive effective substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment. Moreover, he was motivated for treatment and was already involved with Suboxone maintenance treatment and peer-supported recovery groups that could have been provided in a less restrictive treatment setting in order to address the comorbid cocaine and alcohol use disorders and co-occurring psychiatric disorders with anxiety and insomnia.

Thus, the health plan's determination is reasonable in this case scenario-noted below. summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Residential substance use treatment
The insurer denied the Residential substance use treatment.
The determination is overturned in part.

The patient was referred and admitted for residential level mental health and substance use disorder treatment to address a recurrent mood disturbance diagnosed as unspecified bipolar disorder with comorbid unspecified anxiety disorder in the context of substance use disorders with regular use of cannabis and alcohol. Prior to admission, the patient had received emergency medical services for alcohol poisoning and recently had required emergency services for running away with a facial injury and subsequent involvement of the child protective services (CPS). The patient's substance use had started in early adolescence and escalated with progression of the disease including frequent blackouts and affective instability with anger and persistent irritability resulting in behavioral disturbance and conflict with her adoptive mother.

The patient has a history of substance use disorder treatment episodes without sustained benefit, as well as escalating bouts of aggression/irritability with relationship problems with peers at school and her mother with whom she lived. The patient has had ongoing issues with family related to problematic and disruptive behavior, and ongoing use of substances despite having treatment in the community. The patient's symptoms of mood and anxiety disorders remained despite multiple medication trials and outpatient treatment with decline in social, family, and educational functioning resulting in the referral for residential level services and treatment.

The mental status examination at the time of admission for residential treatment was free of severe psychiatric symptoms such as psychosis, mania, thought disorder, severe cognitive impairment or perceptual disturbance (hallucinations). She was anxious with dysphoric affect and persistent irritability. She also presented with coping difficulties with peers and family, and was described as having limited insight, impaired judgment and poor impulse control. Additionally, she presented as fidgety, distractible with poor concentration and prominent sleep disturbance. The patient had no acute general medical conditions, or drug or alcohol withdrawal symptoms. She is tobacco dependent.
The patient is single and a student. She had significant stressors related to oppositional behaviors as well as irritability and affective instability. 
The patient underwent a comprehensive psychiatric evaluation with plans for safety monitoring and treatment planning that included therapeutic interventions to improve coping skills and address core symptoms of mood disorder together with interventions to address the substance use disorders with her primary drugs of choice as alcohol, as well as frequent use cannabis and tobacco. The treatment plan included the goals of improved coping; breaking the cycle of self-destructive behaviors; and the development of healthy relationships. Individual, group and family therapies were provided, as clinically appropriate. She also had the opportunity to participate in age-appropriate groups with peer support. The program focuses on organizational skills; self-care; peer relationships; and life skills as well as behavioral and emotional regulation with stress management, behavioral techniques and evidence-based therapy including medication management and focus on family functioning. The patient also received ongoing educational programming with assignments and vocational services pertaining to educational needs.

She continued to receive residential services with revisions of the treatment plan and clinically appropriate titration of her medications that included Seroquel, Cymbalta, gabapentin and Wellbutrin at therapeutic dosages.
The treatment course and case records/notes reflect a stormy course during the first six weeks of treatment with continued evidence of mood swings, irritability and disruptive behavior including conflict with peers and her mother. She made slow and uneven gains with several incidents involving female peers and her mother during therapeutic leaves and family-focused sessions. She displayed mood swings and conflict with relationship functioning requiring staff re-direction and the implementation of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). Nonetheless, the patient demonstrated increasing engagement with the treatment plan and no active oppositional or violent behavior, and abstinence from substances of abuse while in treatment.
She made steady progress that slowly resulted in stabilization of mood with titration of her medications that were at therapeutic or near-therapeutic dosages. She did continue to display persistent irritability, insomnia and bouts of affective instability that had resulted in an increase in her dose of Seroquel and the addition of Wellbutrin to address problems with mood and concentration including consideration of a diagnosis of Attention Deficit Disorder (ADD). Again, during the course of treatment prior to discharge, the patient had intermittent bouts of affective instability and ongoing relational problems consistent with history. However, she was using her coping skills and maintaining better impulse control. She was actively working on family issues especially with regard to the continued risk for boundary problems. She was completing assignments and was maintaining abstinence from substances of abuse. Therapeutic interventions were continued with appropriate monitoring to include continued family work and medication management and consideration of a safe and clinically appropriate disposition.

The issue under review is the medical necessity of Residential Mental Health Treatment.

The requested health service/treatment of residential substance use treatment was medically necessary for this patient, in part.

The patient continued to display clinical features and symptoms that necessitated residential level services as she struggled to engage in treatment and had intermittent bouts of affective instability with lack of emotional control that did require residential level structure and monitoring with active treatment. She had a history of treatment failure with lower level services and had recently displayed significant oppositional behavior with maladaptive coping, emotional regulation problems, distress problems, interpersonal functioning problems and day-to-day functioning problems that included combative behavior. She continued to represent a safety risk and could not have been effectively managed in a less restrictive treatment environment.
However, after 18 days, the patient was noted to be engaged in treatment with improved functioning, diminished levels of anxiety, and more appropriate behavior, as noted in the clinical summary. Therefore, the residual symptoms of mood and anxiety disorders and co-occurring substance use disorders; and problems with psychosocial, educational and daily functioning were amenable to treatment in a less restrictive environment  and the monitoring, structure and intensity of residential services were no longer medically necessary, as indicated by improved mental status and functioning and engagement in the treatment plan. In summary,  the patient's treatment could have been safely and effectively provided with lower level services in a less restrictive treatment environment, as noted in the answer to question 1 above. The patient's psychosocial stressors were not so severe to prevent ongoing assessment and treatment at a lower level of care in this case scenario. Moreover, there were no general medical issues, no co-occurring substance use disorder treatment issues, and no other clinical features that would have warranted continued residential level treatment.

summary:

The patient was admitted for residential mental health treatment to address recurrent and moderately severe major depressive disorder with a decline in functioning and alcohol use that was moderate. The patient presented with symptoms of depression, anxiety, and affective instability together with functional impairment resulting in the referral and admission to residential level treatment. He had severe psychosocial stressors and grief related to the death of his father, a pending divorce and his mother's diagnosis with terminal stomach cancer.
Initial evaluation revealed a mental status examination with severe psychiatric symptoms that included depression with hopelessness and passive thoughts of death. He did not display symptoms of mood cycling or mania, thought disorder, severe cognitive impairment or homicidal ideation. He denied active suicidal ideation, plan or intent. He was noted to be calm with an anxious demeanor that included dysphoric mood, and fair insight with intact judgment and cognition. He had disturbed sleep and daytime fatigue.
The patient had no acute general medical conditions or other substance use disorders. Medical screening was negative or normal with regard to examination and laboratory assessments except for a fatty liver. He was diagnosed with Wolf Parkinson White syndrome and sleep apnea.
The patient is supported in his treatment effort by family-his mother and sister. As noted, he was married with a pending divorce. He has two children with his wife. He was well-educated and employed. There was no trauma history or legal issues in this case.
The residential treatment focused on mood stabilization and communication within the family, as well as other services to address life skills, coping, and peer relationships. Residential structure and monitoring and programming were provided, and initially, the treatment plan included safety monitoring with suicide precautions. Individual, group and activity therapies were provided along with family conferences and therapeutic interventions to address grief, affective instability and substance use.
The treatment and clinical course including documentation with therapy and progress notes depicted good relations with staff and peers despite a tendency to not follow rules. The patient continued with active participation in treatment that included group and individual sessions together with other interventions within the residential setting, and discharge planning, as well as safety checks. He was prescribed Abilify, Lexapro and gabapentin initially with discontinuation of Ability and the addition of Wellbutrin, titrated as clinically appropriate. Additionally, he received trazodone for sleep and modafinil to address daytime fatigue. His clinical course remained uncomplicated with improved mood and diminished anxiety. He was discharged from residential care with recommendations for continued medication management and intensive outpatient level care with group dialectical behavior therapy (DBT).
At issue is the medical necessity of residential mental health treatment.
The requested health service/treatment of residential mental health treatment is not medically necessary for this patient.
Continued Residential Mental Health Treatment is not considered clinically appropriate and was not medically necessary in this case scenario. The patient's symptoms depression and anxiety were amenable to treatment with lower-level services in a less restrictive environment with intensive services including therapeutic interventions to address the recent use of alcohol. Continued treatment could have been effectively provided in a less restrictive treatment setting with evidence based psychosocial treatments and continued medication management. The psychosocial stressors were not so severe to prevent ongoing assessment and treatment at a lower level of care in this case scenario. Moreover, there were no general medical issues that were a focus of treatment, and no other clinical features that would have warranted the continued residential level treatment in this case scenario. The patient has family support and access to mental health and substance use disorder treatment and services in the community that further supports that the services were not medically necessary.
This answer is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice, and with the scientific literature, referenced below, as well as New York State instruction for this review including the application of NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3 Criteria.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Inpatient detoxification level of care
The insurer denied inpatient detoxification level of care.
The determination is overturned.


The patient was admitted, following medical screening, to acute inpatient level services for detoxification and withdrawal management of severe alcohol and stimulant (cocaine) use disorders. The patient was using up to twelve 24 ounce beers daily together with $100-$200 worth of crack cocaine six days per week.

The patient was referred from an outpatient substance use treatment center due to his continued use of substances despite involvement in treatment. He presented with mild alcohol withdrawal at the time of admission. Withdrawal symptoms included tremor, insomnia, irritability and anxiety with a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) scale score of 10. The patient has no history of a psychiatric disorder. He denied psychiatric hospitalization, or suicidal or self-harming behavior. He had an extensive history of substance-related treatment episodes including at least three detoxification treatment episodes. There were no acute medical issues or general medical concerns.
The patient was admitted to acute inpatient level care and placed on a detoxification regimen with a five-day Librium taper, vitamin replacement therapy, fluid replacement, and medical monitoring; the patient was tobacco dependent and offered smoking cessation treatment and nicotine replacement. Following his first day of treatment, the patient began to participate in counseling and educational sessions. Vitamins were continued, as well as comfort medications with monitoring and assistance with daily activities. He was maintained on fall and seizure precautions, but had no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens (complicated withdrawal). His demeanor improved as he underwent detoxification treatment, and he was social with peers. He participated in educational sessions and counseling during the remaining days with motivational interviewing with the goal of proceeding to rehabilitation treatment and/or accepting medication assisted treatment. The patient was discharged after completion of the detoxification protocol with plans/referral to start a rehabilitation treatment and with recommendations for involvement in 12-step recovery meetings.

The health plan documents, appeal documents, correspondence from the health plan and treatment facility, as well as the health plan's rationale for the denial of certification for coverage of the requested treatment were reviewed. The case records and case summary were reviewed. This review is a New York State mandated review, including the application of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines.

The issue under review is the medical necessity of inpatient detoxification level of care.

Yes, the requested health service/treatment of inpatient detoxification level of care was medically necessary for this patient.

The patient presented with a diagnosis of severe alcohol and stimulant use disorder. The presenting clinical features and history and risk for withdrawal seizures and other psychosocial complications of alcohol and stimulant use disorders did warrant the admission and continued inpatient level services with medical monitoring in this case scenario. The patient's admission and continued inpatient stay with detoxification, withdrawal management, and other medical services through discharge could not have been effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario.

The adult inpatient treatment of this patient's substance disorders did require the admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level setting and 24-hour monitoring in view of the severity of the alcohol use disorder, and the presentation with continued use of substances while receiving outpatient level substance-related services. Withdrawal symptoms were managed with tapering dosages of benzodiazepine/Librium requiring monitoring, as well as comfort medications and vitamin and nicotine replacement therapy. Thus, the patient did require a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management during the time frame under review, as it was reasonable that the patient would have been unable to abstain from the substances of abuse if detoxification and treatment were to be attempted at a lower level of care.

Medical necessity for the admission and the continued inpatient services is met in this case and is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice, published practice guidelines, and American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, referenced below. This answer is also consistent with the application of New York State OASAS LOCADTR 3.0 Criteria and Guidelines.

Diagnosis: Paranoid schizophrenia.
Treatment: Inpatient Mental Health Stay.
The insurer denied Inpatient Mental Health Stay.
The determination is partially overturned.


The patient was admitted to inpatient psychiatric care. He presented with agitation and aggressive behavior directed towards his mother with whom he lived. His mother activated emergency services who brought the patient to the emergency department. He was noted to have an exacerbation of his underlying psychotic disorder, paranoid schizophrenia, with a past history of comorbid autism spectrum disorder. The patient was disorganized, delusional, and motor agitated with irritable mood and labile affect, and with poor insight and impaired judgment together with aggressive impulses and delusional thinking. He had stopped his psychotropic medications and was known to be non-compliant with outpatient treatment.
The mental status examination revealed a disheveled appearance with poor hygiene and with motor agitation and uncooperative stance. He displayed disorganized and circumstantial thought processing and markedly impaired judgment together with a lack of insight. His speech was slow and fluent. Mood was dysphoric and irritable with labile affect. The patient was illogical and concrete.
There was no substance use disorder or acute general medical issues in this case. The patient was chronically ill with diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), as well as his functional impairments and exacerbation of the chronic psychotic disorder. He had a history of multiple inpatient psychiatric admissions and aggressive behavior.
The patient was admitted to inpatient level services with medical clearance. He received acute inpatient level psychiatric services with close observation and pharmacotherapy that included continued the use of Abilify. His hospital course was complicated by severe symptoms of psychosis and thought disorder that persisted throughout his stay. The patient was resistant to taking medication and refused long-acting antipsychotic medication. He tended to isolate socially with continued bouts of agitation and irritable mood.
The patient remained irritable with illogical thought and delusions, but the patient was medication adherent with oral medications that included Abilify, Metformin and Simvastatin. He rarely participated in milieu activities, but was increasingly more cooperative with staff.
He became increasingly calm and cooperative with improved mood and functioning, better sleep and appetite and self-care. Planning was in place for referral to an Assertive Community Treatment (ACT) team for intensive case management and services in the community, as well as safety measures in the home. The patient remained cooperative with more organized thought processing and fair impulse control. He denied suicidal ideation or aggressive impulses. He was medication adherent with tolerability though refusing long acting injectable (LAI) medication. There were no general medical complications during his inpatient stay. He was discharged to the home of his mother.
At issue is the medical necessity of Continued Inpatient Mental Health Stay.

The inpatient stay is medically necessary in part. The requested health service/treatment of inpatient mental health treatment is medically necessary for this patient, except for the last 7 days of the stay.

The continued acute inpatient mental health treatment was clinically appropriate and medically necessary for this patient. The requested benefit of acute inpatient psychiatric care was appropriate to the diagnosis, and was necessary with regard to the level of care, the structure, the intensity of services, and the monitoring required to safely and effectively manage the patient's acute psychosis and chronic psychotic disorder, problematic behaviors and general medical comorbidities.
The patient displayed psychotic symptoms in the context of functional impairment and bouts of hostility, anger, tension and excitability in the context of disorganized thought processing and illogical and delusion thought content, as well as mood disturbance with persistent irritability. He had impaired judgment and a lack of insight. The patient continued to require ongoing direction and assistance from staff while receiving active treatment that was being provided to support reality testing and improve his functioning and coping skills. He had not shown the improvement that would allow him to safely receive treatment with lower level of care services for the time interval. Thus, the patient did require continued acute inpatient level monitoring and structure while developing a plan for continued psychiatric care with a safe and clinically appropriate disposition.
However, for the last 7 days, the patient's mental status had improved and he was functioning better, as noted in the clinical summary and documentation provided, and recommendations for continued care had been finalized. The patient no longer required the structure of an acute inpatient level of care in order to remain safe or to receive ongoing support of daily activities and safety monitoring. It was not medically necessary for this patient to have continued acute inpatient level services  in view of his relative lack of impulsive behaviors and cooperation with staff with regard to daily functioning. Also, the patient had no plan or intent of self-harm, or persistent impulsive or erratic behaviors that placed him at imminent risk for harm to self or others.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse.
Treatment: Inpatient Detoxication Admission.
The insurer denied the Inpatient Detoxication Admission.
The denial is overturned, in part.

The patient is an adult male referred for substance use disorder treatment to address severe alcohol use disorder. The patient had recent substance use disorder treatment in the month and the week prior to his presentation with immediate relapses. His substance use history began in adolescence with escalating use of alcohol and subsequent use of cocaine in combination with opioids. He had stopped using opioids (remission) and used one hit of cocaine intermittently with inhalation. He was using up to three pints of alcohol daily with a history of legal complications and past history of incarceration. He had motivating factors related to psychosocial stressors involving primary support, occupational, social environment and legal domains including an upcoming court date for "drinking related problems."

The patient's treatment included intensive services, sober housing, monitoring, and structure provided within the treatment program. The patient participated in milieu activities designed to support sober living and life skills. He struggled to engage in a recovery process and was anxious with ambivalence towards maintaining abstinence due to craving in the context of a history of leaving against medical advice (AMA) and administrative discharges from past treatment. He was prescribed buspirone and trazodone to address anxiety and insomnia, as well as other sleep aids, vitamins, nicotine replacement for tobacco dependence, and comfort medications. 

The patient was noted to have no residual post-acute withdrawal symptoms. He remained anxious, but less so with improved sleep. He was participating in groups and educational sessions, and 12-step recovery groups, as well as other therapeutic interventions to improve motivation and coping skills. He declined medication assisted treatment. The patient had worked on coping skills and identification of triggers, and had shown diminished anxiety, and fair insight and judgement with better sleep and functioning. He was medication adherent with tolerability. His treatment plan indicated focus on coping skills and consideration of a relapse prevention plan upon return to the community. He continued with sub-acute level treatment with step down to a crisis center with plans for extended treatment and sober living and continued involvement with 12-step recovery groups and obtainment of a sponsor, as well as plans to seek employment.

The issue under review is inpatient residential (sub-acute level) substance use disorders treatment.

The health plan denied the requested treatment on the basis of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) III Criteria indicating that criteria were not met and that outpatient level care was appropriate.

Yes, in part; the first portion of the admission dates in question, the proposed treatment was medically necessary for this patient; however, the proposed treatment for the latter half of the admission dates in question was not medically necessary in this case scenario.

No, in part; the health plan did not act reasonably, with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient; however, the latter portion of the dates of admission in question, the health plan did act reasonably, with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.
As indicated above, the proposed services were warranted and medically necessary for a portion of the admission dates in question, and were not medically necessary for the latter portion including the application of New York State Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria. The patient could have been effectively managed with lower level care in a less restrictive treatment setting for the remaining dates of service in question.

The patient needed the admission and continued structure and monitoring of an inpatient residential service for the dates of service in order to effectively address the risk of relapse, continue to learn adequate coping skills to remain engaged in rehabilitation treatment, to address psychosocial issues pertinent to his substance use disorders including the need for sober supports, and develop a transition plan that would effectively prevent treatment failure. 

The patient remained at high risk for relapse during this time frame with active symptoms of anxiety requiring medication management with clinically appropriate monitoring. Moreover, the patient continued to struggle with readiness to change and remain abstinent, and, he initially had intense craving and other symptoms reflecting post-acute withdrawal symptoms that did necessitate the admission and continued structure and monitoring of an inpatient residential setting while considering the use of anti-craving medication and additional medications to address anxiety and insomnia. The patient's lack of awareness or limitations of insight and impulse control, together with the seriousness of his substance use disorder with combined stimulant and alcohol class agents is illustrated by his behavioral disturbances and deterioration in functioning with continued substance abuse, despite having access to treatment in the community. The psychiatric co-morbidity (anxiety disorder) initially complicated this case, as the patient had symptoms of anxiety that were triggering the substance abuse, as well as impulsivity related to the quantity of substances used, and lack of sober supports and a sober recovery environment. These clinical features and treatment dimensions support the assertion that the patient could not have been effectively treated at a lower level of care consistent with the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria and the appropriate application of New York State Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria. Therefore, these clinical factors needed to be effectively addressed with intensive services and monitoring in an inpatient residential (sub-acute) treatment setting, prior to step down to a lower level of care.

However, the sub-acute inpatient residential level substance-related treatment and services for the latter portion of the admission dates in question were amenable to treatment at a lower level of care and therefore not medically necessary. During this time interval the patient had effectively engaged in rehabilitation treatment, and the patient's co-occurring psychiatric disorder (unspecified anxiety disorder with insomnia) had been addressed with stabilization; and, the patient was able to effectively participate in rehabilitation services with steady progress, as well as consideration of transition to sober living with continued rehabilitation treatment. The patient did not need the continued structure or monitoring of an inpatient residential setting in order to effectively continue rehabilitation treatment and services. These services could have been provided at a lower level of care with sober supports and continued involvement in rehabilitation treatment, as well as treatment for the co-occurring psychiatric condition.

The requested services for the latter portion of the admission dates in question are not consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, or consistent with published practice guidelines (best practice) or the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, referenced below, as well as New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse.
Treatment: Medically Supervised Inpatient Detoxification Admission.
The insurer denied the Medically Supervised Inpatient Detoxification Admission.
The denial is overturned.

The patient is a male who presented voluntarily for detoxification treatment and was medically screened and admitted to acute inpatient level care in order to address substance use disorder with opioid, cannabis, and sedative-hypnotic-anxiolytic class substance use disorders. The patient had been using up to eight bags of heroin with intravenous (IV) administration together with daily misuse of prescribed Xanax or Klonopin, and one marijuana blunt.  He has no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens. He had a history of prior detoxification and substance use disorder treatments; he indicated that he had a history of leaving treatment prematurely and had at least four relapses with only eight months of sobriety since his onset of substance use in adolescence. His use of heroin had begun several years prior. His self-referral for treatment was prompted by multiple stressors and general health concerns.

The patient was admitted to detoxification treatment with a comprehensive detoxification protocol with tapering dosages of methadone and as needed (pro re nata - prn) medications for comfort, as well as vitamin replacement therapy and the availability of nicotine replacement. The program provided for case management with referral and access to rehabilitation treatment that included comprehensive evidence-based treatments. During detoxification the patient engaged in counseling sessions focusing on education about the disease model of addiction, and, involvement with unit activities including peer support and education sessions to motivate the patient to proceed to rehabilitation treatment. Vital signs were intermittently elevated and his withdrawal symptoms persisted with intense craving. The patient left against medical advice with referral for clinically appropriate follow up.

The denial determination was on the basis of New York State NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria indicating that the patient had no serious withdrawal symptoms, no safety issues, no psychiatric or general medical comorbidity and was motivated. The denial indicated that the patient could have been treatment with residential level care.

The appeal noted persistent withdrawal symptoms with elevated blood pressure determinations and intense craving in a patient with a history of relapses and high-risk use of intravenous (IV) opioids and benzodiazepines. The appeal argued that New York State NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria were met for inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management.

The issue under review is Inpatient Level Detoxification and Withdrawal Management and other medical services.

Yes, the proposed treatment is medically necessary for this patient.
The requested inpatient admission and continued treatment could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. The patient in this case was using heroin, together with other substances of abuse on a daily continuous basis that did warrant inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring for the duration of the stay.  Moreover, the patient had a positive drug screen that included opioids and benzodiazepines, as well as tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) indicating high-risk use. He displayed persistent withdrawal symptoms, and, the patient's social environment was not conducive to detoxification in the context of limited insight, impaired judgment and poor control of impulses.

Thus, the adult inpatient detoxification treatment and withdrawal management of this patient's substance use disorder did warrant the admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level detoxification setting with 24-hour monitoring and use of as needed (pro re nata - prn) medications with monitoring. The patient's history of substance abuse (frequency and quantity) together with the severe psychosocial stressors and functional impairments reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder and the need for a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management, as the patient was at high risk for treatment failure if the continued detoxification and withdrawal management were to be attempted at a lower level of care. Therefore, as the appeal asserts, the medical necessity is met for the proposed treatment and is consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published guidelines, American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and the scientific literature, referenced below; this answer is in keeping with New York State instruction for this medical necessity review including the appropriate application of the NY State NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) tool that requires the patient in this scenario default to the higher level of care.

No, the health plan did not act reasonably, with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.
The proposed inpatient treatment is medically necessary and clinically appropriate in this case scenario. The patient's clinical features and treatment dimensions did warrant inpatient level detoxification services through discharge and did necessitate the monitoring that is provided with inpatient level treatment including the use of comfort medications, together with counseling and educational sessions and peer support. Case management services were critical in this case to motivate the patient to proceed to rehabilitation treatment and formal substance use disorder treatment with a safe and clinically appropriate disposition though the patient did discharge against medical advice. Moreover, the admission and the continued substance abuse detoxification treatment through discharge could not have been safely or effectively provided with lower-level services, as noted in the answer to question 2. Thus, the requested benefit is not excluded under the plan, and should be covered in keeping with prevailing standards of care pertaining to substance use disorder services including ASAM Criteria and the New York State OASAS LOCADTR 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines, referenced below.

His referral for PHP level care occurred after being administratively discharged from another treatment program for fighting with a peer. Mental status examination on admission to PHP level services was free of severe psychiatric symptoms including mania, psychosis, perceptual disturbance and cognitive impairment. The patient had residual symptoms of anxiety with normal (euthymic) mood and organized thoughts and clear speech. He had no suicidal or homicidal ideation and was generally motivated for treatment, although he was prone to lose interest in treatment. Insight was limited and judgment impaired with poor control of impulses by history.

During the course of PHP level treatment, the patient was participating actively in his rehabilitation treatment. He had no biomedical complications or severe withdrawal symptoms during his treatment. He was working on coping skills and a relapse prevention plan together with individual, group and other therapeutic activities that included psycho-education. The patient was discharged abruptly against medical advice with no explanation of plans by the patient. In addition, there were no biomedical, psychiatric or general medical issues that warranted the PHP level of care.

Thus, the patient's substance use disorders and co-occurring disorders were amenable to treatment at a lower level of care in this case scenario.

The PHP level substance abuse rehabilitation treatment, in this case scenario, was amenable to treatment at a lower level of care. summary:
Diagnosis: Cocaine, cannabis, and alcohol use disorder

Treatment: Inpatient chemical dependency, rehabilitation admission

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient chemical dependency, rehabilitation admission.

The denial is overturned.

The patient is a male admitted to inpatient chemical dependency substance rehabilitation treatment. He reportedly was drinking 1 pint of rum and a 12-ounce beer several times per week and using 4 bags of crack/cocaine daily, and $40 of marijuana a few times per month. He reportedly had cocaine, cannabis, and alcohol use disorder. He had a positive toxicology for cocaine, tetrahydrocannabinol, and Methadone, and had a blood alcohol level of .056. He had a Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Score (COWS) of 11. He reportedly could not maintain abstinence and had no abstinent time despite 3 past inpatient rehabilitation treatments. He reportedly lacked coping skills and ability to identify relapse triggers. He reportedly lived at a shelter. He continued with post withdrawal and cravings. He attended individual and group therapy. He was discharged for continued inpatient substance treatment at a residential treatment for step down and continued treatment.
    
The American Psychological Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that inpatient treatment is indicated primarily for individuals whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. In this case, this patient was considered in need of 24-hour substance rehabilitation treatment as he reportedly was using large amounts of alcohol, crack/cocaine, and lacked the coping skills and ability to identify relapse triggers to stop use and reportedly could not maintain any abstinence at all. According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), he met criteria for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment as he continued to use large amounts of substances daily putting him at risk medically and for withdrawal despite multiple past inpatient substance rehabilitation treatments so it was not likely that a less restrictive level of care would be effective. It was reported that after his 28 days stay in this inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment setting, he was transitioned to the next least restrictive level of care, a substance residential treatment. Transitioning to the next least restrictive level of care is considered standard and appropriate treatment, which was the case with this patient. Also, the National Institute on Drug Abuse: Principles of Addiction Treatment: A Research Based Guide reports that research indicates that that the best treatment outcomes occur with longer durations of treatment and states that recovery from drug addiction is a long-term process. It also states that treatment techniques to increase motivation for treatment are necessary to prevent dropout rates. Without this structured and supervised therapeutic rehabilitation treatment, he likely would have relapsed quickly, as evidenced by relapses after multiple past inpatient substance rehabilitation treatments. It was not likely that he could maintain abstinence and safely and effectively be treated in a less restrictive level of care other than an inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment and he had medical risks if he were to continue using alcohol and cocaine. 

The health plan did not act reasonably, with sound medical judgment, or in the best interest of the patient.

The insurer's denial of coverage for inpatient chemical dependency, rehabilitation admission is overturned. Medical necessity is substantiated.

to care for her basic needs. The patient had fair insight and reasonable motivation with fair insight, and a working knowledge of substance use disorder treatment with past treatment, as noted. Thus, the inpatient admission for detoxification treatment and 24-hour monitoring, and the requested inpatient level services were not medically necessary in this case scenario. 

This answer is consistent with New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines and with established practice guidelines, the scientific literature, and the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, as referenced below.

Yes, the health plan did act reasonably, with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.

The patient displayed no serious disturbance of mental status and no general medical complications or symptoms of co-occurring disorders that would have warranted inpatient level services. He also had intermittent use of mollies, prescription narcotics, and tobacco with use of one pack per day. He admitted to also using alcohol socially and occasionally misusing Xanax. The patient was diagnosed with a co-occurring psychiatric disorder best characterized as substance induced mood disorder. The patient's substance use started in adolescence with escalating use in the context of high-risk behaviors and the mood disturbance.

The patient was medically screened with laboratory assessments, electrocardiogram (EKG) and chest x-ray which were normal or unremarkable. He was stabilized in the emergency department and admitted for inpatient mental health treatment. He was placed on safety checks and had the opportunity to participate in group and other therapies focusing on coping skills while maintaining abstinence from substances of abuse with monitoring. He was prescribed psychotropic medications, Effexor with use of clonidine and hydroxyzine for agitation and anxiety, and medication assisted treatment with Suboxone at clinically appropriate dosages and adjustments. He also received nicotine replacement.

Progress notes and documentation indicate that the patient engaged with treatment with persistent symptoms of anxiety and depression, but no suicidal ideation or aggressive impulses. The patient was noted to have improved with some degree of self-awareness and better insight, though he was deemed to be at high risk for relapse. And, the patient was working on an exit strategy with plans for discharge with referrals to community services and clinically appropriate aftercare, and continued medication assisted treatment with Suboxone and mental health treatments including the use of Effexor. He was successfully discharged with outpatient follow up.

The denial determination was on the basis of medical necessity and InterQual Criteria indicating that there were no safety concerns in this case and that the treatment could have been provided with lower-level care in a less restrictive treatment setting.

The treatment facility appealed on the basis of safety concerns with severe substance use and high-risk presentation and behaviors together with the mood disturbance and need for a safe and clinically appropriate discharge and disposition in keeping with standards of medical practice.

Inpatient mental health stay was warranted by the patient as well as continued structure and monitoring of the inpatient level services that were provided together with ongoing efforts to treat the mood disturbance and to address the patient's risk of relapse while the treatment team and patient worked toward a clinically appropriate disposition with continued mental health services to address the co-occurring mood disorder and poly-substance use disorder including the initiation of medication assisted treatment with Suboxone. 

The patient had a history of continuous use of substances in large quantities, and lacked the insight and control of impulses to remain sober and remain engaged in treatment during the time frame under review. The treatment team was working on motivation for the patient to remain abstinent and addressing mood and affect disturbances in the context of symptoms of the mental disorder that complicated the case. The patient's lack of awareness or limitations of insight and impulse control was a significant clinical feature of the patient's history, together with the seriousness of the substance use disorder with use of multiple substances of abuse with high risk for another overdose or impulsive behavior due to paranoia. These factors support the assertion that the patient could not have been effectively treated at a lower level of care until which time the patient was more stable with better self-awareness such that he was better able to continue working on the remaining psychological issues and development of better coping skills and motivation to remain in a recovery process with a solid relapse prevention plan.

Treatment: Inpatient admission.
The insurer denied coverage for inpatient admission.

This male was admitted to the hospital for detoxification treatment due to alcohol withdrawal symptoms. He was on telemetry initially as he had bradycardia with heart rate ranging from 48-65. He had alcohol withdrawal symptoms including tremors, nausea and vomiting, agitation, anxiety, moist palms, shaking, and also had chest tightness, dizziness, dyspnea, and arthralgia and had a rising Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) as high as 16. He had medical issues due to alcohol use including elevated liver function tests (LFT's) and thrombocytopenia. He was put on a Lorazepam taper CIWA protocol and given Lorazepam 2 milligrams (mg) intramuscular (IM) and 1 mg by mouth (po) on the day of admission and was given Lorazepam through discharge. He was homeless and had psychiatric diagnoses and was taking multiple psychotropic medications. He took Lorazepam 1 mg 3 times per day the day prior to discharge and then Lorazepam 0.5 mg twice per day on the day of discharge.
    
The medical records provided enough specific evidence to support the need for inpatient hospital treatment. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. It also states that patients with past complicated or life-threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens are in need of inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal and reports that patients with comorbid medical condition that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification. Also, the US Department of Health and Human Services-Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) Center for Substance Abuse Treatment reports that inpatient treatment is necessary if the ability to attend outpatient treatment daily is a problem, one is unable to follow up in outpatient treatment, if medical conditions complicate the treatment of withdrawal, if one has previous withdrawal seizures of delirium tremens, or if one does not have the capacity for informed consent. In this case this patient had active alcohol withdrawal symptoms including tremors, nausea and vomiting, agitation, anxiety, moist palms, shaking, chest tightness, dizziness, dyspnea, arthralgia and had a rising CIWA and was at risk for more severe, complicated, life-threatening withdrawals. He also had several comorbid medical conditions due to alcohol use including elevated LFT's and thrombocytopenia and also had bradycardia requiring telemetry monitoring. The risk of delirium tremens can occur 4 days after alcohol use so he was considered at risk and in need of 24-hour inpatient hospital detoxification treatment. 

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) he did require 24-hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive setting as he had active withdrawal symptoms including CIWA of 16 and was shaky with tremors, nausea and vomiting, agitation, anxiety, and sweaty palms and required and received detoxification medication (Lorazepam) to modify withdrawal from alcohol and more severe withdrawal, complicated or life-threatening withdrawal such as delirium tremens. 

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment in the best interest of the patient.

The insurer's denial of coverage for inpatient admission is overturned. Medical Necessity is substantiated.

This patient had multiple substance use and a past DUI and was unable to maintain abstinence. He also had serious comorbid multiple psychiatric issues and had unresolved severe trauma issues contributing to his use. summary:
Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder
Treatment: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) services (codes 90867, 90868)
The insurer denied coverage for TMS services (codes 90867, 90868)
The denial is overturned

This patient had depressive symptoms including sad and irritable mood, suicidal ideation, hopelessness and worthlessness, guilt, decreased energy, anhedonia, increased appetite, sleeping problems, concentration problems, isolation, and had a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder-severe-recurrent. His depressive symptoms were severe, and his Beck Inventory Scale II revealed a score of 31 which also is considered severe. It was reported that his symptoms interfered with his ability to function daily. He had past psychotherapy trials and past multiple medication trials with antidepressants including Prozac for approximately 23 years with lack of sustained efficacy, Wellbutrin for 1 year with a dosage of 300 milligrams (mg) with lack of sustained efficacy, Cymbalta for approximately 4 years with a dose of 60 mg with lack of sustained efficacy, Elavil over 48 years ago with reports of adverse effects, and Trazodone for 2 years and discontinued 28 years ago. He was treated with TMS treatments.

The medical records provided enough specific evidence that he required this treatment as he had a reported diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder-severe-recurrent and had treatment resistant depression and he still had reports of severe depression even after taking multiple antidepressant medications. His Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) was 31 which is indicative of severe depression as per notes. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved Neurostar TMS Therapy for the treatment of depression in October 2008. Neurostar TMS Therapy System was the largest multisite (23 centers) randomized sham-controlled trial ever conducted with TMS therapy. In addition, the American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Major Depressive Disorders considers TMS therapy as an appropriate acute phase option for patients who do not respond adequately to pharmacotherapy or psychotherapy and were considered treatment resistant. In this case this patient had a documented diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder-severe-recurrent with active severe depressive symptoms including sad and irritable mood, suicidal ideation, hopelessness and worthlessness, guilt, decreased energy, anhedonia, increased appetite, sleeping problems, concentration problems, and isolation. He also reportedly had past psychotherapy trials and past multiple medication trials with antidepressants. This is sufficient evidence to support that he had adequate antidepressant trials and even had different classes of medications including serotonin reuptake inhibitor, serotonin norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, tricyclic antidepressant, and a dopamine norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor. He had adequate durations of trials and adequate dosages. He also had a trial of psychotherapy without prolonged efficacy. The standard recommendation for TMS treatment is for patients who failed or who did not have satisfactory improvement from 1 past antidepressant medication at or above minimal effective dose and duration in the current episode and this patient met that criteria as he tried multiple antidepressant medications from different classes of medications also. 

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment in the best interest of the patient.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance use disorders
Treatment: Inpatient Detoxification Admission
The insurer denied the Inpatient Detoxification Admission
The denial is overturned.

The patient is an adult male who presented to the emergency department requesting detoxification treatment. He was medically screened and admitted to acute inpatient level care diagnosed with opioid (heroin) and alcohol class substance use disorders. The patient had been using up to two pints of liquor together with intermittent use of three bags of heroin in the context of methadone maintenance treatment at 40 milligrams per day. He has no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens. He had a history of prior detoxification and substance use disorder treatment. His self-referral for treatment was prompted by multiple stressors and general health concerns.

The patient has no history of psychiatric hospitalization or suicidal behavior and was not taking psychotropic medications. He had a history of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

The patient presented with acute co-morbid general medical issues that included history of hepatitis C and other chronic conditions including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with asthma, lung neoplasm, hypertension, atrial fibrillation and spinal stenosis of the cervical spine. He was prescribed lisinopril, amlodipine, albuterol inhaler, and baclofen. Laboratory assessments were unremarkable or normal with a positive drug screen consistent with history, as well as positivity for tetrahydrocannabinol (THC).

Evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination that was free of severe psychiatric symptoms. He was generally motivated for treatment and described as cooperative with a full range of affect. Speech was clear with organized thoughts that were free of delusions. There was no evidence for a thought disorder, mania, psychosis or cognitive impairment. The patient denied suicidal or homicidal ideation and did not have perceptual disturbances. Insight was limited with impaired judgment and poor control of impulses. 

The patient was admitted to detoxification treatment with a comprehensive detoxification protocol with tapering dosages of Librium and use of methadone and as needed (PRN) medications for comfort, as well as vitamin replacement therapy and the availability of nicotine replacement in the context of tobacco dependence. The program provided for case management with referral and access to rehabilitation treatment that included comprehensive evidence-based treatments. During the brief detoxification, the patient engaged in counseling sessions focusing on education about the disease model of addiction, and, involvement with unit activities including peer support and education sessions to motivate the patient to proceed to rehabilitation treatment. The patient did not complete the detoxification protocol and left treatment noted to be in "no apparent distress."

The appeal was on the basis of medical necessity indicating that the severity of substance-related disorders and comorbid general medical conditions did require inpatient level care and monitoring. 

The denial was on the basis of medical necessity indicating that there were no complicated withdrawal symptoms and no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens. The denial determination referenced the lack of acute medical or psychiatric symptoms and noted that the patient was motivated and engaged in treatment.

The issue under review is inpatient detoxification and withdrawal management and other medical services.

Yes, the proposed treatment was medically necessary for this patient.
The requested inpatient admission and continued treatment could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. The patient in this case was using heroin intermittently while in a methadone program together with large quantities of alcohol on a daily continuous basis that did warrant inpatient level detoxification, withdrawal management and monitoring for the duration of the inpatient stay.  Moreover, the patient had a positive drug screen that included opioids and tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), as well as the alcohol use. The patient's social environment was not conducive to detoxification in the context of limited insight, impaired judgment and poor control of impulses. Moreover, the patient presented with an array of general medical conditions.

Thus, the adult inpatient detoxification treatment and withdrawal management of this patient's substance use disorder did warrant the admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level detoxification setting with 24-hour monitoring. The patient's history of substance abuse (frequency and quantity) together with the severe psychosocial stressors and functional impairments reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder and the need for a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management, as the patient was at high risk for treatment failure if the detoxification and withdrawal management were to be attempted at a lower level of care. Medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published practice guidelines, American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria and the scientific literature as referenced below, and with New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews including the appropriate application of the New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Tool that requires the patient in this scenario default to the higher level of care.

No, the health plan did not act reasonably, with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.
The requested benefit of inpatient substance abuse treatment is medically necessary and clinically appropriate in this case scenario, and is therefore a covered service in this case scenario. The patient's clinical features and treatment dimensions did warrant inpatient level detoxification services thru discharge and did necessitate the monitoring that is provided with inpatient level treatment including the use of comfort medications, together with counseling and educational sessions and peer support. Case management services were critical in this case to motivate the patient to proceed to rehabilitation treatment and formal substance use disorder treatment with a safe and clinically appropriate disposition though the patient did discharge against medical advice prior to completion of the detoxification protocol. Moreover, the admission and the continued substance abuse detoxification treatment through discharge could not have been safely or effectively provided with lower-level services, as noted in the answer above. 

Thus, the requested benefit is not excluded under the plan, and should be covered in keeping with prevailing standards of care pertaining to substance use disorder services including the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria and the New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines, referenced below.

He had a positive drug screen for benzodiazepines and cannabis, and a blood alcohol level of zero. The patient has a history of multiple detoxification treatment episodes with relapses. The patient provided no history of withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens or severe alcohol or drug withdrawal symptoms, and he denied blackouts. The patient was medically screened and admitted for inpatient level detoxification with plans for a detoxification treatment episode with Valium, vitamin replacement therapy and comfort medications, as well as the availability of nicotine replacement therapy and comfort medications. He was continued on gabapentin for anxiety and medication assisted treatment and the insomnia was treated with trazodone at 150 milligrams. The denial was on the basis of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Guideline indicating that inpatient level treatment was not medically necessary as there were no biomedical or psychiatric concerns or complicated withdrawal symptoms in the case, and that the patient was motivated for treatment. The denial indicated that residential level treatment was clinically appropriate in this case. The appeal was on the basis that the detoxification was medically necessary and that the patient was at risk for withdrawal requiring inpatient medical monitoring, as well as linkage to rehabilitation services.  

The proposed treatment is not medically necessary for this patient.
The proposed inpatient stay and detoxification treatment and other medical services noted in the clinical summary could have been safely and effectively provided at a lower level of care. The treatment of this patient's substance use disorder did not require the structure of an inpatient setting or 24-hour monitoring. The patient displayed no serious disturbance of mental status despite having a history of ongoing substance use disorder with alcohol and cannabis. Moreover, the patient did not show evidence for suicidal or aggressive behavior or risk, or severe cognitive impairment, or psychosis, or perceptual disturbance that would have warranted an inpatient level admission and treatment. There were no severe/objective symptoms of withdrawal or biomedical issues in this case, and the patient had received detoxification treatments in the past with knowledge of substance use disorder treatment protocols, as noted in the clinical summary. The patient had fair insight and judgment, and control of impulses. Thus, the inpatient admission for detoxification treatment and 24-hour monitoring, and the requested inpatient level services were not medically necessary in this case scenario.

summary:
Diagnosis: Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder
Treatment: Mental health residential treatment 
The insurer denied the mental health residential treatment.
The determination is overturned.

The patient has a history of disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, Asperger's syndrome, post-traumatic stress disorder and borderline personality disorder. The patient was admitted to an inpatient level of care after a suicidal gesture. The patient admitted to frequent suicidal thoughts that were occurring on a daily basis. The patient was noted to have some self-harm behaviors while on the inpatient unit and initially was minimally engaged. Following discharge from inpatient treatment, the patient was admitted to residential treatment. The patient continued to self-harm while in residential treatment and frequently refused medications and visits with the psychiatrist. At issue is the medical necessity for residential treatment.

The requested mental health residential treatment was medically necessary. The patient continued to have suicidal ideation and was struggling with aggression, irritability and difficulty functioning. The patient had failed lower levels of treatment and was intermittently non-adherent with treatment despite structure of residential treatment. InterQual guidelines support residential level of care when patients are unable to be managed safely within the community and have serious emotional disturbance. In addition, American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry (AACAP) guidelines also support residential treatment when it is the least restrictive means to ensure safety (AACAP, accessed 2022). The patient was clearly a danger to self and struggled with aggression/impulse control. The patient had failed lower levels of treatment and required significant amounts of monitoring despite the structure of residential treatment. Records indicate that the patient was impulsive, agitated, endorsing self-harm and requiring significant redirection on the dates leading up to the dates in question and could not have safely been treated at a lower level of care.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Substance abuse inpatient rehabilitation stay
The insurer denied the substance abuse inpatient rehabilitation stay.
The determination is upheld.

The patient is an adult male who presented for inpatient level substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment to address substance use of cannabis (marijuana) and alcohol class substances. The patient had no past history of withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens or severe withdrawal symptoms. He had a history of substance use disorder with alcohol and subsequent use of marijuana, escalating to daily continuous use with subsequent use of three 24-ounce beers and three to four shots daily together with five to six blunts per day. His substance use had resulted in psychosocial problems and concern. He was medically cleared prior to his admission.

The patient had previously engaged in substance use disorder treatment with a relapsing clinical course. His last treatment was a detoxification treatment episode with relapse. There was no history of psychiatric disorder or treatment. He denied suicidal or self-harming behavior.

The patient was motivated for rehabilitation treatment. The patient exhibited limited insight and impaired judgment with questionable control of impulses. There were no severe symptoms on mental status examination; the patient had no symptoms of severe depression, mania, psychosis, perception, cognition, or thought disorder. He denied problems with energy, concentration or appetite though he was dysphoric with insomnia.
He had no acute general medical conditions except for elevated blood pressure with chronic medical conditions including hypertension and hyperlipidemia. He was tobacco dependent at ½ (half) pack per day.
The patient was divorced and housed. There was no report of trauma history or legal issues in this case. He reported having support from family and friends.
The rehabilitation treatment included a focus on coping skills, relapse prevention techniques with identification of triggers, education about the disease model of addiction, and involvement with recovery groups. The patient engaged in treatment and intensive services, monitoring and structure provided within the inpatient treatment program. The patient participated actively with treatment and showed no significant symptoms or signs of withdrawal or post-acute withdrawal symptoms though he had persistently elevated blood pressure that was a focus of treatment.

The patient readily engaged in rehabilitation treatment and he had no complications other than ongoing concern with the elevations of blood pressure treated with hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) and lisinopril. He was fully compliant with his treatment plan and received vitamin supplementation and nicotine replacement therapy, and he had the availability of comfort medications, as well as ongoing treatment for his blood pressure. He was prescribed melatonin for sleep. He was started on gabapentin and naltrexone for medication assisted treatment. He was actively participating in treatment, learning better coping skills and made efforts to develop a relapse prevention plan and sober supports. During the course of treatment, the patient's mood and sleep improved and he gained insight learning coping skills. He had positive interactions with staff and peers. He was discharged with referral for clinically appropriate aftercare and plans for continued medication assisted treatment.

The treatment facility case records and summary, health plan documents, appeal documents, and correspondence from the health plan and treatment facility were reviewed. The rationale for the denial of certification for coverage of the requested treatment was reviewed. This case is a New York State mandated review with the application of NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Guidelines/Criteria.

The issue under review is the medical necessity of substance abuse inpatient rehabilitation stay.

The requested health service/treatment of substance abuse inpatient rehabilitation stay was not medically necessary for this patient. The proposed inpatient substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment was amenable to treatment at a lower level of care. 
The patient was motivated to actively engage in rehabilitation treatment without biomedical complications other than an elevated blood pressure or significant withdrawal symptoms. He had prior exposure to substance use disorder treatment and was able to engage and participate actively in the treatment plan without complication. There were no psychiatric disturbances or general medical concerns that required inpatient level services, structure or monitoring. The patient was noted to benefit in all aspects of his treatment plan throughout his continued stay. He had a supportive family and access to sober housing from which substance use disorder treatment could be received. Thus, the patient's substance-related treatment and rehabilitation services could have been effectively provided at a lower level of care in a less restrictive treatment setting.
This answer is consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, the published societal guidelines, American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and the scientific literature, referenced below, as well as the application of NY State OASAS LOCADTR 3.0 Guidelines/Criteria, referenced below.

The health plan's determination of medical necessity is upheld in whole.
