summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse. 
Treatment: Inpatient Rehabilitation Services. 

The insurer denied: Inpatient Rehabilitation Services. 
The denial is upheld. 

The patient is an adult male self-referred through his employer and admitted for inpatient rehabilitation and substance use disorder treatment in order to address use of stimulant (cocaine) and cannabis (marijuana and hashish) class substances. The patient has no reported history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens, or severe withdrawal symptoms. His history of substance use included use of up to $100 worth of crack cocaine and $50 worth of marijuana or hashish on a daily basis. The patient was medically screened upon admission including laboratory testing that was normal or unremarkable and drug screening that was positive for cocaine. Evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination that reflected motivation for rehabilitation treatment, and fair to good insight and judgment. He had no severe symptoms such as mania or depression, psychosis, perceptual disturbance or severe cognitive impairment. He did not report suicidal ideation or aggressive impulses. Upon admission to inpatient level services, the patient received comprehensive evaluation and treatment that included focus on coping skills, relapse prevention techniques with identification of triggers, education about the disease model of addiction, and, involvement with groups, as well as peer supported recovery groups and other therapeutic activities within the treatment milieu. Psychiatric evaluation was provided and he was prescribed vitamins with the availability of nicotine replacement therapy, and comfort meds that included melatonin and Benadryl. The patient completed the rehabilitation treatment and was discharged with recommendations and referrals for continued and clinically appropriate aftercare of the substance use disorders with return home with family support. 
The health plan denied coverage of the stay on the basis of the New York State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines indicating that the criteria for inpatient level treatment was not met. The treatment facility asserted that LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) Criteria were met on the basis of the longstanding use of multiple substances and the patient's need for monitoring and the structure of an inpatient rehabilitation setting. 

The Inpatient Rehabilitation Services were not medically necessary. 

The patient presented with substance use disorders, diagnosed with cannabis and stimulant/cocaine use disorders. The patient readily engaged in treatment and had no biomedical (withdrawal symptoms or signs) or acute psychiatric treatment issues or past history of psychiatric disorder. During the time interval under review, the patient was noted to be in no apparent distress with reasonable functioning and active participation in treatment including positive interactions with staff and peers. Throughout the inpatient stay, there were no complicating treatment issues or biomedical or co-occurring psychiatric issues that would have warranted inpatient level of care, structure or 24-hour monitoring. The application of NY (New York) State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) Criteria did indicate that the patient was clinically appropriate for treatment with lower-level care in a less restrictive treatment setting, as the health plan asserted. Thus, medical necessity for the inpatient rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment is not met in this case scenario. This answer is consistent with ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) Criteria, the scientific literature and published guidelines.

summary:
Diagnosis: Treatment-Resistant Depression. 
Treatment: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS). 

The insurer denied: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS). 
The denial is overturned. 

The patient is an adult male with a diagnosis of major depressive disorder, recurrent and severe without psychotic features and treatment resistant depression. The patient has a documented history of multiple medication treatments for depression including treatment with two antidepressants with disparate mechanism of action and at least four or more trials with antidepressant medications (fluoxetine, escitalopram, sertraline, duloxetine, and bupropion), as well as augmentation of the bupropion with quetiapine and supplemental use of clonazepam to address severe symptoms of anxiety and insomnia. Due to adverse effects or lack of efficacy, the patient continued to experience severe symptoms of depression and functional impairments that impact quality of life and day-to-day responsibilities. Additionally, the patient had ongoing treatment with cognitive behavioral therapy and past treatment with dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT) provided by a skilled and certified therapist. Comorbid psychiatric conditions include posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and generalized anxiety disorder. The patient has reportedly not had psychiatric hospitalization or suicide attempts or suicidal behavior, but has been treated with partial hospitalization program (PHP) level care, as well as outpatient mental health treatment when he had the onset of his mood, anxiety and trauma-related disorders when he was younger. The Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ)-nine (9) score was 20 reflecting severe depression at the time of initial evaluation for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) therapy, and a Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale (GAD7) score of 19 reflecting severe anxiety. The patient's clinician initially deferred transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) treatment, but subsequently recommended treatment with a course of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) therapy with the usual treatment with up to 36 treatment episodes to include 30 sessions with six tapering sessions. The health plan has denied authorization for coverage of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) on the basis of coverage exclusion and indicates that the requested treatment is not a covered benefit with reference to the plan's Medical Policy - Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) for Treatment Resistant Depression. 

The requested health service, transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) services, is medically necessary. 

Per the health plan documents and submitted information, transcranial magnetic stimulation services are clinically appropriate and considered medically necessary as an adjunct and augmentation of the patient's antidepressant regimen in order to achieve a remission of symptoms related to severe major depressive disorder in the context of treatment refractory/resistant depression and failed trials with at least four antidepressants including antidepressant medications with disparate mechanisms of action and at least one appropriate augmentation strategy. Moreover, the coverage of transcranial magnetic stimulation services for a patient who meets criteria for treatment refractory depression and who is a reasonable candidate for the requested benefit of transcranial magnetic stimulation should be approved in this case scenario. Transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy for the treatment of major depressive disorder is a well-established treatment that is proposed for this patient in keeping with prevailing standards of medical practice for the condition under treatment in this case. The comorbid conditions do not contraindicate the use of transcranial magnetic stimulation, and the patient had past trials with combined treatments with evidence-based psychotherapy (CBT).

summary:

Treatment: Residential Substance Use Treatment
The insurer denied: Residential Substance Use Treatment
The denial is upheld.

The patient is an adolescent male. He was admitted to substance abuse residential treatment level of care. The patient's primary diagnosis was major depressive disorder, recurrent, severe without psychotic features, cannabis use disorder, severe, unspecified anxiety disorder, ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) combined type, and parent child relational problems. The patient said he started feeling overwhelmed, and told his therapist. The therapist recommended residential treatment. The patient said that he was depressed, and then the COVID pandemic occurred. He turned to online gambling, made money and started smoking weed. He has no history of psychiatric hospitalizations. He has a history of passive suicidal ideation and cutting with the last cutting episode having been two weeks prior. He says he has had wishes of wanting to be dead, but he never went to the plan stage. He identified problems with anxiety, cannabis abuse, and unresolved issues with his sister. He also wants to work on issues with his parents. Prior to admission, he drank vodka and Red Bull until he blacked out.

The Residential Substance Use Treatment was not medically necessary.
At the time of admission, the patient did not present with symptoms that require substance abuse residential treatment level of care. The patient did not present with active withdrawal symptoms or life-threatening withdrawal symptoms. The patient did not present with significant post-acute withdrawal symptoms. The patient did not have active suicidal or homicidal ideation with intent or plan. He did not have worsening aggression or self-injurious behavior. While the patient did present with symptoms of depression and anxiety, the patient did not require 24/7 treatment in a residential setting. The patient could have been treated at a lower level of care.

summary:
Diagnosis: Mental Health/Other/Delusions/Hallucinations.
Treatment: Mental health: Residential.
The health plan denied the requested inpatient stay. 
The health plan's determination is partially overturned.


The patient is an adult female receiving residential level mental health treatment to address schizophrenia and co-morbid unspecified anxiety disorder with a history of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and a history of poly-substance use with cannabis, alcohol, stimulant (cocaine), and other psychoactive class substances, as well as nicotine at ½ pack per day use. The patient was known to use cannabis or CBD (Cannabidiol) to address PTSD symptoms and sleep disturbance.
The patient was admitted in the context of severe and persistent mental illness characterized by delusions and hallucinations, and a lack of insight (anosognosia) that resulted in non-compliance with medications. Before the admission, the patient had been in another residential program with a transfer to an extended stay program. The patient did not tolerate the extended stay treatment environment due to an exacerbation of her delusions that she was being experimented upon and that her body was being invaded. Thus, she was admitted back to residential level treatment with plans for continued intensive treatment together with the structure and monitoring of residential level service.

The patient was noted to gain insight with a medication regimen that was stabilized. Nonetheless, her delusions and auditory hallucinations persisted. However, there were no safety concerns, and there had been no general medical issues other than persistent nausea and constipation. The patient was discharged with a return to her mother's home with plans for clinically appropriate aftercare.

The health plan's determination of medical necessity is overturned, in part. 

In accordance with prevailing standards of medical practice and the NY State instruction for his review, the patient did require the continued structure, monitoring, and treatment with a residential level of care during the interval under review to administer the continued treatment for the psychiatric disturbance in this case while conducting ongoing evaluations, and observing the patient's functioning with intense therapy and monitoring for response to medications that had been adjusted accordingly. It was medically necessary for this patient to continue with 24-hour monitoring and remain in a residential level structure given the persistent symptoms of chronic psychosis and dysregulated emotions, the continued disturbance of thought with active symptoms of psychosis that represented a safety risk, as well as high risk for relapse with a history of co-occurring substance use disorder and treatment failure with prior treatment efforts. Additionally, the residential stay during this time interval was medically necessary to monitor the response to medications-as noted, especially given limited insight and impaired judgment, and non-compliance with medications while receiving outpatient and residential and extended care services before her referral to residential treatment.
However, the continued residential level treatment was not medically necessary in this case. The patient had made progress with the treatment and was noted to be functioning better with clearer thinking and improved insight with continued support from family-focused sessions, all of which were indicative of the patient's ability to continue treatment in a less restrictive treatment setting. The patient could have been effectively managed with an alternate level of care, based upon the submitted documentation and in keeping with prevailing standards of medical practice and published guidelines pertaining to appropriate levels of care. There were no remaining treatment issues or clinical features that would have required the continued residential level services, structure, or monitoring. The health plan's determination of medical necessity is overturned, in par. Medical Necessity is medically necessary for the first portion of the say but upholds the denial for the last 5 days' stay as not medically necessary. Medical necessity is partially substantiated.

The case involves an adult male medically screened and admitted for inpatient rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment in order to address use of stimulant (cocaine) and cannabis (marijuana) class substances with a history of alcohol use disorder in full remission. The patient has no reported history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens, or severe withdrawal symptoms. His history of substance use included use of up to one gram of crack cocaine daily and intermittent use of marijuana. The patient has a history one or more prior treatment episodes with relapse.

The patient has no history of psychiatric disorder, or suicidal behavior or psychiatric hospitalization. The patient had no acute general medical issues other than dental pain; he was medically screened upon admission including laboratory testing that was normal or unremarkable and drug screening that was positive for cocaine and tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). He was tobacco dependent.

The patient is single and homeless and lives in a shelter with peers using drugs. 

He was diagnosed with a mood disorder in addition to the substance use disorders.

Upon admission to inpatient level services, the patient received comprehensive evaluation and treatment that included focus on coping skills, relapse prevention techniques with identification of triggers, education about the disease model of addiction, and involvement with groups, as well as peer supported recovery groups and other therapeutic activities within the treatment milieu. 

The patient readily engaged in substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment. He actively received intensive rehabilitation services, monitoring, and structure provided within the inpatient treatment program including 24-hour monitoring. His clinical course was complicated with persistent dental pain that resulted in his discharge against medical advice with referral for dental services and recommendations and referrals for continued and clinically appropriate aftercare of the substance use disorders.

The issue under review is inpatient substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment.

The health plan denial was on the basis of the New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 criteria/guidelines indicating that the criteria for inpatient level treatment was not met. Additionally, the health plan noted no general medical or psychiatric symptoms or issues that warranted inpatient level care indicating that the patient could have been safely and effectively treated in a less restrictive treatment setting with lower-level care such as partial hospital program (PHP) level care.

In the appeal, the treatment facility asserted that Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) criteria were met on the basis of the longstanding use of multiple substances and the patient's need for monitoring and the structure of an inpatient rehabilitation setting. The appeal referenced the patient's adverse living situation, lack of support, high risk for relapse and the presence of drug dreams and craving.

The proposed treatment and the requested benefit of inpatient substance abuse rehabilitation treatment was not medically necessary.

The application of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) criteria (referenced below) did indicate that the patient was clinically appropriate for treatment with lower-level care in a less restrictive treatment setting, as the health plan asserted. Thus, medical necessity for the inpatient rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment is not met. This answer is consistent with the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) criteria.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Continued Partial Hospital Program Substance Use Disorder Rehabilitation Treatment
Continued Partial Hospital Program Substance Use Disorder Rehabilitation Treatment.
The determination is overturned in part.

The patient was admitted to a partial hospital program (PHP) level-of-care for substance use disorder treatment with moderate to severe use of cannabis and tobacco/nicotine class substances. The patient is diagnosed with co-occurring depressive and anxiety disorders best characterized as an unspecified depressive and anxiety disorder with associated symptoms of insomnia. The patient's substance use had its onset at age twenty and then escalated as the coronavirus 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic occurred with progression of the disease and decline in functioning. A precipitating and perpetuating factor was conflict within the family of origin and the symptoms of anxiety and depression that triggered his substance use. The patient had no prior substance use treatment and no history of blackouts or withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens. He had a trauma history due to a toxic home environment while growing up. He had no legal issues, but was selling marijuana to support his addiction with his use of up to five joints per day. His substance use included a past use of ketamine and oxycodone, but he denied current use of substances other than cannabis and tobacco.
His mental status examination at the time of admission was free of severe symptoms such as mania, thought disorder, psychosis, perceptual disturbance, or cognitive impairment. He presented with depression, anxiety, insomnia, and restlessness. He was generally cooperative and generally calm, but anxious at times during the interview. He had limited insight and impaired judgment and poor control of impulses due to the substance use. He reported cravings and anxiety that represented a high risk of relapse. He had insomnia with only 3 hours of total sleep time, as well as poor appetite, low energy and problems of volition.
The patient is married and employed in the family business. He has four children. The marriage is described as supportive. There was no family history of substance use disorder or mental disorder.
The patient presented for Partial Hospitalization Program (PHP) level substance-related treatment. He had the opportunity for participation in group, individual, psycho-educational and other therapies with focus on the development of coping skills while maintaining abstinence from substances of abuse. Life skills and other therapeutic interventions including motivational enhancement therapy (MET) were provided, as well as continued treatment with evidence-based therapies and wellness activities with meditation, yoga, relaxation techniques, mindfulness and EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing).
The patient made unsteady progress with the rehabilitation treatment. He had thoughts of leaving the program against medical advice (AMA) but remained in treatment. The patient had made modest progress, but still struggled with treatment. He had problems with motivation at the contemplative stage of change, and continued to have insomnia and anxiety. Gabapentin and doxepin were prescribed with adherence and tolerability. He continued to receive and participate in individual, group, and educational sessions with addition of work to develop a relapse prevention plan with identification of triggers, the development of sober supports, and involvement in 12-step recovery groups with peer support.
By the last week of treatment, the patient was noted to be more hopeful and optimistic and better engaged in treatment. His Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) assessment was at a 1 with mild depression and his anxiety and insomnia had improved with a positive outlook for the future. He was nearing a euthymic state with persistence family issues that were being addressed with family-focused sessions and continued wellness activities including exercise. Case management had developed a plan for step down with no complications during this time interval. He continued in Partial Hospitalization Program (PHP) level treatment and was discharged with recommendations for clinically appropriate aftercare.
The health plan documents including case notes, schedule of benefits and excerpts from the Summary Plan Description were reviewed, as well as the health plan's Administrative Policy for Behavioral Health Services. Appeal documents were reviewed, as submitted, with correspondence from the treatment facility. The health plan's rationale for the denial of authorization for continued coverage of the requested services was reviewed together with reference to and review of the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria and the American Academy of Clinical Psychiatrists Level of Care Utilization System (AACP LOCUS) Guidelines. This review is New York (NY) State mandated with the application of NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines.
At issue is the medical necessity of Continued Partial Hospital Program Substance Use Disorder Rehabilitation Treatment.

The requested health service/treatment of Mental Health Partial Hospitalization Program was medically necessary for this patient in part.
The patient's PHP level services with the continued structure and monitoring of PHP level service for 25 days was necessary in order to effectively address anxiety and depression triggering his use of cannabis, to continually assess the risk for relapse, to develop a relapse prevention plan with motivational techniques and work on coping skills to remain engaged in a recovery process, to address family issues with a detailed psychosocial assessment, and consider other psychosocial issues pertinent to his substance use disorders including the need for sober supports, and develop a transition plan that would effectively prevent treatment failure. These treatment factors and clinical features did necessitate the continued structure and monitoring of a partial hospital setting while receiving substance abuse treatment with development of a discharge plan and determination of the clinically appropriate disposition. The patient could not have been effectively treated at a lower level of care for these dates of service consistent with ASAM Criteria and NY State LOCADTR 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines. However, the patient had reached a level of stability such that he was capable of continuing treatment with lower-level services in a less restrictive treatment.

summary:
Diagnosis:  Substance Abuse.
Treatment:  Inpatient Detoxification Treatment.

The insurer denied the Inpatient Detoxification Treatment.  The denial is overturned.

The patient is an adult male who presented requesting detoxification treatment. He was medically screened and admitted to acute inpatient level care in order to address substance use disorder with opioid, alcohol, stimulant (designer stimulant and cocaine) and sedative-hypnotic-anxiolytic class substance use disorders. The patient had been using one pint of alcohol, ten to 20 bags of heroin and $100 of crack cocaine daily, as well as benzodiazepines and designer stimulant. He has no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens. He had a history of at least ten prior detoxifications for substance use disorder with no report of rehabilitation treatment or significant outpatient follow up or aftercare.

The patient has a history of psychiatric disorder with unspecified post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and depressive disorder without current treatments. He had no history of psychiatric hospitalization or suicidal behavior and was not taking psychotropic medications.

Laboratory assessments were unremarkable or normal other than elevated liver functions with a positive drug screen consistent with history, as well as positivity for benzodiazepine and cocaine. The patient has a history of peripheral vascular disease and past treatment with anticoagulants, a gunshot wound to the head, and a positive purified protein derivative (PPD); he uses a cane to ambulate. The patient was tobacco dependent.

The patient's withdrawal symptoms included body aches, chills, abdominal cramping, nausea, sweats, and tremor, scoring a 15 on the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) scale and a 14 on the Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS).

The patient engaged with detoxification treatment; he was cooperative with the tapering dosages of methadone and Librium. Withdrawal symptoms remained mild and diminished with persistent irritability. The patient did not complete the detoxification treatment and was discharged against medical advice with referrals for clinically appropriate aftercare, which the patient declined.

The denial was on the basis of the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria indicating that the patient had no symptoms that warranted 24-hour monitoring suggesting outpatient level care as clinically appropriate.

The appeal was on the basis of the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria indicating that the patient needed the structure of an inpatient setting in order to be effectively managed, and that the patient was not clinically stable with reference to the Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) and Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) scoring and clinical features warranting the inpatient level of care.
The issue under review is inpatient detoxification and withdrawal management.

The proposed treatment was medically necessary.

The requested inpatient admission and continued treatment could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. The patient in this case was using heroin, together with alcohol and stimulants and other substances of abuse on a daily continuous basis that did warrant inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring for the duration of the protocol; detoxification, as necessary. Moreover, the patient had a positive drug screen that included opioids and amphetamine and benzodiazepines, as well as cocaine. He had moderate and persistent withdrawal symptoms, and the patient's social environment was not conducive to detoxification.

Therefore, medical necessity is met in this case.

summary:
Diagnosis: Withdrawal - Alcohol Abuse
Treatment: Residential Treatment Center
The health plan denied the requested Residential Treatment Center as not medically necessary. 
The health plan's determination is upheld.

The patient is an adult female who presented with a request for detoxification treatment and withdrawal management of severe alcohol use disorder. The patient reported a relapse four months earlier drinking alcohol in large quantity on a daily basis with up to ten hard seltzers and varying amounts of wine. The patient was medically screened. The patient had no acute medical issues. Her blood alcohol level was at 0.253. She had psychiatric comorbidity with anxiety and depression treated by her primary care physician (or provider) (PCP) with Gabapentin and Lexapro.

The patient was admitted to residential level care, and was placed on a detoxification regimen with Librium and supportive measures with comfort medications, as well as vitamin and nicotine replacement therapy. The detoxification was uncomplicated with regard to withdrawal management in that she was noted to be in no apparent distress, and her appetite and sleep normalized. The patient received counseling and education from the staff. Her clinical course was uncomplicated with normal vital signs. She had mild withdrawal signs or symptoms with a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) scale score of 6, and she was stable and in no distress. She had resumed treatment with his home medications including Lexapro and Gabapentin, and as needed (prn) Trazodone for sleep and prn use of Propranolol, as well as medication assisted treatment with Naltrexone. The patient continued to do well with treatment with family support despite a strained family relationship, and she was discharged with clinically appropriate aftercare and immediate referral to outpatient rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment though she was uncertain about Intensive Outpatient Program (IOP) or Partial Hospitalization Program (PHP) level services, and was not planning to attend 12-step meetings.

The health plan's determination of medical necessity is upheld, in whole.

The requested health service/treatment of Residential Treatment Center was not medically necessary for this patient.
The requested benefit of detoxification treatment and withdrawal management and other medical services could have been safely and effectively provided with alternate level services. 
There were no co-morbid general medical problems or co-occurring psychiatric disorders that would have warranted the continued residential level services. Moreover, the withdrawal symptoms were not reported to be severe, and the patient's clinical symptoms were not serious enough to necessitate continued residential level treatment or monitoring. There were no safety concerns in this case and no history of complicated withdrawal from alcohol. The patient was considered to be motivated for detoxification treatment, and had access to substance use disorder services in the community. The denial determination reasonably indicated that an alternate level treatment was an appropriate alternative to continued residential level services and was in the best interest of the patient.
Thus, medical necessity is not met in this case for the requested benefit of the continued residential level services in keeping with prevailing standards of professional practice, and consistent with the ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) Criteria and scientific literature, referenced below, as well as New York State OASAS (Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (Level of Care Determination) 3.0 Guidelines, referenced below. The requested continued residential level treatment for alcohol use disorder and co-occurring psychiatric disorders could have been effectively provided with an alternate level care, as the health plan asserts in the denial determination.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Substance Abuse: Residential/04/15/2022 forward
The health plan denied the requested residential treatment- substance use disorder services as not medically necessary. 
The health plan's determination is overturned.

The patient is a male who was referred for residential substance use disorder treatment to address polysubstance use and co-occurring psychiatric disorders in the context of impairment of functioning and bouts of psychosis. The patient has a history of polysubstance abuse beginning in late adolescence with the use of multiple substances of abuse. The patient was referred for residential level services after spending days in an acute inpatient setting with treatment of the delusional disorder including the use of Invega Sustena.
The patient has history of multiple psychiatric hospitalizations for psychosis in the context of polysubstance use and ongoing treatment for generalized anxiety disorder with elements of social anxiety and panic attacks and a history of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). There is no history of suicidality or self-harm.
The substance use disorder progressed with a dramatic decline in functioning that was related to the severe substance use disorder and perpetuated by the psychiatric comorbidities and the episodes of psychosis diagnosed as a delusional disorder. Despite treatment efforts in the community and the effort by his parents to address the mental health and substance use disorders, the patient remained resistant to treatment resulting in the subsequent referral for residential level treatment. Thus, the referral for treatment was prompted by the failure to remain sober despite the availability of treatment in the community and the co-occurring psychiatric disorders.

From the date of admission forward, the patient engaged in treatment with intensive services, sober housing, monitoring and structure provided within the residential treatment program and therapeutic milieu. He was not well motivated initially due to the maladaptive coping and the addictions. He was cooperative and did participate in the rehabilitation treatment with plans to continue with a clinically appropriate step down to include continued medication management, counseling and involvement in 12-step recovery groups. Case summary and group notes indicate that the patient made steady improvement while in treatment and remained abstinent from substances of abuse though had to be directed to complete assignments together with ongoing psychiatric management of the co-occurring delusional and anxiety disorders.

The health plan's determination of medical necessity is overturned, in whole.

Yes, the requested health service/treatment of residential treatment- substance use disorder services, was medically necessary for this patient.
The clinical features and treatment dimensions in this case warranted residential structure and monitoring while providing intensive treatment for the co-occurring substance-related and psychiatric disorders. The patient could not have been safely or effectively treated in a less restrictive treatment setting.

The requested admission and continued Residential Mental Health Treatment was medically necessary in order to address the immediate needs for rehabilitation of severe substance use disorders and to work toward relapse prevention; in order to address the patient's lack of awareness of the seriousness of his illnesses with psycho-education and evidence-based psychosocial interventions; and in order to address issues within the social environment, especially in working with the patient's family with whom he lived and in order to work on coping skills that will be necessary in building a sober support system and continued recovery efforts with community providers and engagement with age-appropriate 12-step recovery groups, and, services to address the psychotic and anxiety disorders.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Substance Use inpatient rehabilitation treatment (5 days) 
The insurer denied: Substance Use inpatient rehabilitation treatment (5 days) 
The denial is: Upheld

The patient is a male who was self-referred with admission to inpatient rehabilitation and substance use disorder treatment to address substance use disorders with alcohol and cocaine. The patient had no history of blackouts or withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens. He had been using up to 2 pints of liquor daily with intermittent use of $100 worth of cocaine with a frequency of three to six times per week with intranasal administration. He had multiple past treatments with residential and outpatient substance use treatment with the most recent detoxification and the most recent residential level treatment. His drug screen was positive for cocaine with no significant withdrawal symptoms. He reported craving and urges to use. He was also tobacco dependent and an every-day smoker.

Throughout the inpatient stay, the patient remained stable and engaged with the treatment. He was noted to be respectful of peers and staff. He received intensive rehabilitation services, monitoring, and structure provided within the inpatient treatment program including 24-hour monitoring. The rehabilitation treatment proceeded without incident or complication, and the patient was transferred to a sister program for continued rehabilitation services. The subject under review is the medical necessity for substance use inpatient rehabilitation treatment (5 days).

The health plan's determination is upheld.

The requested health service/treatment of Substance Use inpatient rehabilitation treatment (5 days) was not medically necessary for this patient. The patient's treatment could have been safely provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario.
The patient in this case presented with continuous daily use of alcohol and intermittent and weekly use of cocaine; he did not experience general medical complications or present with severe symptoms of a co-occurring psychiatric disorder, or abnormal findings on examination or laboratory assessments, or severe withdrawal symptoms that would have warranted inpatient level services. His risk for withdrawal complications including seizures and delirium tremens were minimal considering his history, and he did not pose a safety risk that would have warranted the requested level of care.
The patient displayed no serious disturbance of mental status despite having a history of ongoing substance use disorder with alcohol and cocaine. Moreover, the patient had been evaluated and cleared with regard to safety concerns and did not show evidence for suicidal or aggressive behavior or risk, or severe cognitive impairment or psychosis, or perceptual disturbance, or general medical concerns that would have warranted an inpatient level admission and treatment. 
Thus, the requested services were not medically necessary in this case scenario. Any indicated treatment for alcohol or cocaine use disorder in this case could have been provided, as clinically appropriate, at a lower level of care in keeping with the Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria. This answer is also consistent with published guidelines, the scientific literature, and American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) criteria.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse.
Treatment: admission to the substance abuse inpatient rehabilitation level of care.
The insurer denied coverage for admission to the substance abuse inpatient rehabilitation level of care.
The denial is overturned.

This adult male was admitted to this inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment for alcohol and substance rehabilitation treatment. He reported that he could not be managed in an outpatient setting. It was reported that he was unable to remain abstinent, lacked coping skills and ability to identify relapse triggers. The patient had a past history of inpatient long term rehabilitation treatment and still was unable to remain abstinent. He reportedly was drinking 4 nips of liquor and two 24-hour ounce beers per day, smoking $100 of crack/cocaine per day, and smoking $20 of cannabis per day. He was unemployed and not married though he had a child. He also was anxious and had a history of bipolar disorder. He attended groups and individual therapy, and the plan was to complete this inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment and then attend long term inpatient substance residential treatment after that. The patient left against medical advice (AMA) prior to completing this inpatient treatment.
    
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that inpatient treatment is indicated primarily for individuals whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. 
In this case this patient was considered in need of 24-hour substance rehabilitation treatment as he reportedly was using large amounts of alcohol daily and using serious substances daily including $100 of crack/cocaine in addition to cannabis daily which put him at risk of medical issues due to alcohol and cocaine use and also severe, complicated, and life-threatening withdrawals. He lacked the coping skills and ability to identify relapse triggers to stop use. 

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol & Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), he met criteria for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment as he continued to use large amounts of alcohol, crack/cocaine, and cannabis daily despite a past long term 100-day inpatient substance treatment. He reportedly still was unable to remain abstinence after that treatment and stated that he could not be managed in an outpatient setting. He also reportedly lacked sober supports and stable housing to maintain abstinence outside of this 24-hour substance rehabilitation treatment, so he was considered at high risk to continue use if not in a 24-hour therapeutic substance rehabilitation treatment. He reportedly lacked coping skills, needed to better identify relapse triggers, and needed to learn relapse prevention skills. He was unable to stop substance/alcohol use without being in a sober and supervised therapeutic inpatient substance rehabilitation setting. Without this structured and supervised therapeutic rehabilitation treatment he likely would have relapsed quickly. He also had a history of bipolar disorder as well which further increased his risk of relapse. He had a large amount of daily alcohol use and a large amount of daily significant crack/cocaine use putting at risk medically and also for withdrawal. The plan was for him to complete this inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment to learn better coping skills for sobriety and to better identify relapse triggers, but he left AMA. 

The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. 

The insurer's denial of coverage for an admission to the substance abuse inpatient rehabilitation level of care is overturned. Medical Necessity is substantiated

summary:

Treatment: Mental Health/Residential Treatment.
The health plan denied the requested residential treatment as not medically necessary. 
The health plan's determination is overturned.

The case involves an adult male who was admitted to residential level services with severe symptoms of depression and anxiety associated with severe psychosocial stressors and the inability to function. The patient's admission had been precipitated by worsening symptoms of depression and anxiety in the context of treatment refractory depression, a near-lethal suicide attempt resulting in a spinal cord injury and other medical complications and associated with moderately severe stimulant use disorder with prescription amphetamines.
The patient has a history of severe and recurrent major depressive disorder with anxious distress and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) inattentive type associated with stimulant use. The patient has a history of prior psychiatric treatment that failed to produce a sustained response including two psychiatric hospitalizations for depression, suicidal behavior and psychosis. The onset of stimulant use and occasional use of alcohol began in adolescence and escalated while in college. There were no acute general medical issues. However, the patient had a spinal cord injury after jumping from a parking garage with bladder problems and incontinence, as well as chronic pain with leg spasms treated with Baclofen. Prior treatment had included dual diagnosis Intensive Outpatient Program (IOP) and outpatient level treatment, as well as the hospitalizations.
The patient is single, a student and is on medical leave.
Mental Status Examination on admission: The patient was cooperative and guarded with anxious and depressive demeanor. He displayed depressed mood with anxiety and slowed mentation that included cognitive clouding. He had decreased concentration, energy, appetite, and volition with hypersomnia and a tendency to isolate socially. His speech was coherent with organized thought processing. Insight and judgment were limited and impaired. He displayed hopelessness, helplessness, and self-reproach indicating that he was having fleeting thoughts of suicide or urges to self-harm.
The patient was admitted to residential level care with a treatment plan that included safety-monitoring, access to group and milieu therapies, intensive individual dynamic therapy, and medications to address the mood disorder. The patient was initially noted to be severely depressed and socially withdrawn. He was increasingly cooperative with staff and was medication adherent; he tended to isolate with social withdrawal and modest, but reasonable participation in the therapeutic activities with a lack of motivation and neglect of basic self-care requiring reminders and monitoring. The patient was treated with Rexulti, Trintellix, and Wellbutrin at clinically appropriate dosages, with past genetic testing showing that he was slow metabolizer.

The health plan's determination of medical necessity is overturned, in whole.

Yes, the requested health service/treatment of residential treatment was medically necessary for this patient.
The patient could not have been safely or effectively managed within a less restrictive setting or with a lower level of care during the time interval under review. The appeal appropriately provided the application of LOCUS Guidelines indicating that the patient was at high risk for harm, had severe functional impairments, had significant medical and substance-related comorbidities, had a recovery environment that had failed to provide a sustained therapeutic response, and had treatment refractory depression with limited prior engagement with treatment, warranting the continued residential treatments.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder
Treatment: Continued residential mental health treatment
The insurer denied coverage for continued residential mental health treatment
The denial is overturned

This male reportedly was admitted to this inpatient mental health residential treatment due to depressive symptoms, anxiety, and cannabis use. He reportedly had depressed mood, suicidal ideation, poor motivation and concentration, lack of interest and pleasure, feelings of hopelessness, feeling overwhelmed, school refusal, and behavioral issues including poor impulse control, attention problems, distractibility, and difficulty with completion of tasks. He reportedly had past school suspension for vaping in school, was self-medicating with cannabis, had past property destruction when angry including kicking doors and breaking a phone, as well as aggression by pushing his father. He had reported diagnoses of Major Depressive Disorder, Generalized Anxiety Disorder, Social Phobia, and Cannabis Use Disorder. He reportedly had Zoloft increased, attended individual, group, and family therapy.

The reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for continued inpatient mental health residential treatment as the medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that he required this level of care then still. 

The MCG (Milliman Care Guidelines) Residential- Behavioral Health Level of Care- Psychiatry guidelines report that one needs to have continued danger to self or others, moderately or severe psychiatric or behavioral symptoms requiring 24- hour daily treatment, or serious dysfunction in daily living. In this case, this patient continued to have at least moderate psychiatric symptoms and did not have the coping skills to deal with his multiple psychiatric issues, eating disorder issues, and substance use. For discharge it states that there needs to be sufficient support at a lower level of care, absence of suicidal or homicidal thoughts or thoughts of harm to self or others. In this case, this patient did not have appropriate supervision or care as it was reported that his parent had COVID (coronavirus) and also had a flood in the house and were in a hotel, so they were unable to care for this child. This child was a minor and was not able to be discharged without appropriate supervision and care. He had poor impulse control, recent depressive symptoms, past aggression and property destruction, past suicidal ideation and hopelessness as well as major depressive symptoms, and he required 24-hour supervision, structure, and safety in this 24-hour therapeutic residential treatment until appropriate supervision and care was available. summary:
Diagnosis: Major depressive disorder
Treatment: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)
The insurer denied coverage for TMS.
The denial is upheld.

This patient reportedly had depressive symptoms and major depressive disorder and had tried multiple past medications for depression with lack of efficacy including Prozac, Zoloft, Lexapro, Viibryd, Cymbalta, and Wellbutrin, and tried augmenters Rexulti, Abilify, Lithium, Lamictal, and Latuda. She reportedly had difficult functioning in school and interpersonally. The request was for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) therapy.
  
The insurer denied coverage for TMS therapy for her, stating that she was under the age of 18 and that TMS therapy is FDA (food and drug administration) approved for major depressive disorder 18 years of age or older. 
  
The reviewer agrees with the decision to deny coverage for TMS therapy as there is not sufficient evidence in the medical literature to support its efficacy and long-term safety in patients under 18 years of age. The FDA approved Neurostar TMS Therapy for the treatment of depression in October 2008 in patients 18 years old and older and TMS therapy was cleared by the FDA in October 2008 and indicated for the treatment of major depressive disorder in patients who failed or who did not have satisfactory improvement from 1 past antidepressant medication at or above minimal effective dose and duration in the current episode. However, there is not sufficient evidence in the medical literature to support the efficacy and long-term safety for patients 18 years old and younger. According to Biology Psychiatry, NY (New York) May 2018, "Open Trial of Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation in Youth with Treatment-Resistant Major Depression" by MacMaster FP, Croarkin PE, and Wilkes TC it states that a single center open trial suggest TMS is safe and effective in youth with treatment resistant major depression, but larger randomized controlled trials are needed. Also, according to the Journal of Child Adolescent Psychopharmacology 2016 26 (7) 5820589, "Magnetic Resonance Imaging Guided Open Label High Frequency Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation for Adolescents with Major Depressive Disorder" by Croarkin PE, Marony-Smith MJ it states that TMS therapy is feasible, tolerable, and effective in adolescents with treatment resistant major depressive disorder but larger blinded sham controlled trials are needed for definitive safety and efficacy. It states that further efforts to understand optimal delivery, dosing, and biomarker development for repetitive TMS therapy treatment for adolescent depression is warranted. As a result, the recommendation is to uphold the previous decision and deny coverage for TMS therapy.

The health plan acted reasonably, with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient.

The insurer's denial of coverage for the for TMS is upheld. Medical necessity is not substantiated.

summary:

Treatment: Inpatient Admission
The insurer denied coverage for inpatient admission.
The denial is overturned.

This adult patient reportedly was admitted to this inpatient hospital treatment for alcohol detoxification treatment. He reportedly had active alcohol withdrawal symptoms including nausea, vomiting, tremors, sweats, elevated heart rate of 108-201, elevated blood pressure of 153/93, agitation, anxiety, and dry mucous membranes. He reportedly had low sodium, potassium, magnesium, chloride, and his QTc (interval on electrocardiogram (EKG)) was high at 494. He reportedly still had moderate withdrawal with a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) of 16. He reportedly had 2 detoxification medications including Diazepam and Phenobarbital. 
  
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. In this case this patient had been drinking large amounts of alcohol daily for several days in a binge and then experienced alcohol withdrawal including nausea, vomiting, tremors, sweats, elevated heart rate of 108-201, elevated blood pressure of 153/93, agitation, anxiety, and dry mucous membranes and had a CIWA of 16 the next day indicative of moderate withdrawal. He also had medical issues including low sodium, potassium, magnesium, chloride, and his QTc was high at 494.  According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), he did require 24-hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated in a less restrictive treatment setting as he continued to use and required and needed 2 detoxification medications to modify withdrawal, including Diazepam and Phenobarbital. It was reported that he had 2 doses of intravenous (IV) Diazepam totaling 12.5 mg (milligrams) and 130 mg of IV Phenobarbital and 2 doses of oral phenobarbital for a total of 194.4 mg in the first 24 hours. Notes reported a CIWA of 16 which is moderate withdrawal, and he still had an elevated heart rate of 104 and elevated blood pressure of 148/96 and additional Diazepam of 7.5 mg for detoxification was needed including the IV Phenobarbital every 8 hours. 

He needed 24-hour inpatient hospital treatment as he was at risk for worsened withdrawal symptoms if not in this 24-hour setting then including severe and life-threatening withdrawal symptoms such as delirium tremens. The risk of life complicated withdrawal such as delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use so he required at least the entire time in this 24-hour inpatient detoxification treatment. 

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment in the best interest of the patient.

The insurer's denial of coverage for the inpatient admission is overturned. Medical Necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse

Treatment: substance use - inpatient rehabilitation treatment, 20 days

The insurer denied coverage for substance use - inpatient rehabilitation treatment, 20 days

The denial is overturned

This patient was admitted to this inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment for alcohol and crack/cocaine rehabilitation treatment. He reportedly was drinking 2 pints of alcohol per day and smoking $200 worth of crack/cocaine per day and was spending all his money to support his use. He had diagnoses of Cocaine Use Disorder and Alcohol Use Disorder. He reportedly had multiple past treatment episodes with relapse and could not maintain abstinence with recent inpatient substance rehabilitation one (1) month prior to this admission, and an inpatient substance detoxification treatment three (3) months prior to this admission. He had comorbid mental health issues including a diagnosis of bipolar disorder and took Wellbutrin and Abilify. He reportedly attended group and individual therapy. He reportedly was discharged with follow up for long term substance/alcohol residential treatment.
    
This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment as the medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that he required this level of care. 

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that inpatient treatment is indicated primarily for individuals whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. In this case, this patient was considered in need of 24-hour substance rehabilitation treatment as he reportedly was using large amounts of alcohol daily including up to 2 pints per day and using serious substances including crack/cocaine up to $200 worth per day which put him at risk medically and at risk for severe, complicated, and life-threatening withdrawals. He lacked the coping skills and ability to identify relapse triggers to stop use. He reportedly had comorbid psychiatric issues including bipolar disorder diagnosis and mood symptoms which triggered use. 

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral 3.0 (LOCADTR3) he met criteria for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment as he continued to use large amounts of alcohol daily and also used crack/cocaine daily, despite multiple past inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatment, and inability to maintain abstinence. He reportedly had an unstable recovery environment, lacked coping skills and ability to identify relapse triggers.  The goal was for him to learn better coping skills, improve insight into use, better identify relapse triggers, and to learn how to better deal with drug cravings.  He was also considered at risk medically due to his large amount of alcohol and crack/cocaine use and required inpatient rehabilitation treatment.  He was unable to stop substance use without being in a sober and supervised therapeutic inpatient substance rehabilitation setting. Without this structured and supervised therapeutic rehabilitation treatment he likely would have relapsed quickly as evidenced by relapsing after multiple past inpatient substance/alcohol treatments.  Furthermore, he was discharged to a long-term inpatient substance residential treatment for further inpatient substance/alcohol rehabilitation treatment. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be overturned.   The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. The medical necessity for substance use - inpatient rehabilitation treatment, 20 days is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder
Treatment: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation

The insurer denied Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation. 
The denial is overturned.

The patient is a female with a history of major depressive disorder, recurrent and moderately severe without psychotic features. The patient has a documented history of multiple medication treatments for depression including treatment with more than two disparate classes of medication and at least four or more six-week or longer trials with antidepressant medications (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor [SSRIs] and Wellbutrin), as well as combination treatment with an SSRI and Wellbutrin. Additionally, the patient has received augmentation with lamotrigine, risperidone, stimulants and other treatments treatment targeting sleep disturbance and anxiety including guanfacine, clonidine, modafinil and prazosin. She has been treated with an evidence-based psychotherapy with weekly therapy sessions for over one year. She has not received electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) or vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) therapy. She underwent treatment with transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) for the treatment resistant depression with a robust clinical response resulting in a decrease in the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ)-9 scale score from 16 to 2 with a remission. However, she subsequently had a recrudescence of symptoms of depression with a PHQ-9 scale score of 16 in the moderately severe range. The patient is also diagnosed with a co-morbid generalized anxiety disorder with a generalized anxiety disorder (GAD-7) scale score of 16 reflecting severe symptoms of anxiety. The subject under review is the medical necessity for transcranial magnetic stimulation. 

The requested transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is medically necessary for this patient.
TMS therapy as a primary or adjunctive therapy for treatment of depression has generally been evaluated in patients who have treatment refractory/resistant depression, as defined by one or more, antidepressant medication treatment failures with or without augmentation. TMS therapy for depressive disorder has been established by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as a safe treatment; and, the data, as reflected in peer reviewed medical literature, supports this assertion. Specifically, when treatments with antidepressant medication with or without augmentation, or with electroconvulsive therapy, and/or psychotherapy, especially cognitive behavioral therapy, have failed to produce a response or remission, then TMS is an appropriate consideration. This assertion is noted in the American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorder, referenced below. Moreover, the scientific literature indicates that a second course of treatment is reasonable in cases that have shown a robust response to TMS as in this case.
In this case, at least four or more alternative therapeutic trials with augmentation together with other therapeutic measures have been provided, and TMS provided a robust clinical response in 2021. Thus, in this case, the proposed TMS therapy is considered clinically appropriate and medically necessary. Additionally, the proposed TMS therapy is reasonable, and in the best interest of the patient. The decision to proceed with TMS therapy reflects sound medical judgment based upon the current scientific literature and American Psychiatric Association practice guidelines concerning the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorder. The patient in this case has demonstrated that her depressive disorder is treatment refractory or resistant, and the proposed treatment of recurrent major depressive disorder using TMS therapy with a clinically appropriate number of sessions is reasonable and warranted in this case scenario and is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice.

summary:
Diagnosis: Alcohol Abuse and Suicidal Ideation
Treatment: Inpatient Hospital Stay
The insurer denied the inpatient hospital stay.
The determination is overturned.

The patient was admitted for acute inpatient hospital treatment. The patient had become increasingly depressed with suicidal ideation, plan, and intent in the context of heavy alcohol use and severe psychosocial stressors that included primary support and occupational, housing, and social environment domains. The patient was brought to the emergency department by Emergency Medical Services (EMS) with severe symptoms of depression including plan to walk in front of a bus or train; he was using up to a gallon of vodka daily. The patient was homeless beginning five weeks prior to admission in the context of the death of his girlfriend. In the emergency department, he received an evaluation, medical screening, stabilization, and admission for an inpatient level of treatment. At the time of admission, the patient was noted to be severely depressed with persistent suicidal ideation wanting to die, and he had prominent symptoms of alcohol withdrawal with tremors and sinus tachycardia.
The patient's mental status examination revealed a depressed mood with hopelessness, helplessness, anhedonia, and morbid thought content that included thoughts of death and suicidal ideation with the wish to be dead. He was anxious with apprehension, tension, sleep disturbance, irritability, and excessive worry as well as motor retardation and withdrawn behavior. The patient reported morbid thoughts with depressive ruminations and inability to function in the context of the suicidal ideation and hopelessness. There was no evidence of psychosis, perceptual disturbance, mania, or severe cognitive impairment. The patient's sleep, appetite, energy levels, concentration, and volition were disturbed. His insight was fair and his judgment was limited and impaired due to the severity of his depression and associated symptoms of anxiety and alcohol dependence/use.
There were no acute general medical issues in this case other than the alcohol withdrawal. Chronic conditions included fatty liver with hyperlipidemia due to longstanding alcohol use, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), and a history of asthma.
The patient is single, homeless, and had worked as a plumber. He had housing issues and financial strain. There is no history of trauma or legal issues in this case.
The patient was admitted to acute inpatient level services and maintained on close observation with a Librium Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) protocol and vitamin replacement therapy. He was treated with Carafate, Omeprazole, Fluoxetine and Quetiapine at therapeutic dosages with titration as clinically appropriate. He was placed on fall, aspiration, and seizure precautions. The patient received counseling and education with motivational techniques, as well as a psychiatric consultation with medication management and plans for transfer to inpatient psychiatric care when stable. He received case management services to address his many psychosocial needs. Discharge plans were made and the patient was transferred to inpatient psychiatric care for continued mental health and substance-related treatment.
The health plan documents, correspondence from the health plan and treatment facility, and the case records were reviewed. The health plan's rationale for denial of coverage of the acute inpatient level services was reviewed with the denial based on medical necessity criteria. This case is New York State mandated review with the application of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria.
At issue is the medical necessity of the inpatient level of care.

The requested health service/treatment of inpatient stay was medically necessary for this patient.

The inpatient level of care provided in the context of a severe mood disturbance, alcohol use disorder with acute withdrawal symptoms, and severe psychosocial stressors and high risk for suicidal behavior could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. These clinical features warranted inpatient level services and monitoring, as well as efforts to develop a safe and clinically appropriate discharge plan and disposition in concert with case management services and psychiatric consultation with appropriate safety monitoring. The admission and continued inpatient level care through discharge was reasonable in this case scenario and in the best interest of the patient reflecting sound medical judgment with regard to the co-occurring conditions under treatment in this patient.
The inpatient stay was clinically appropriate as he was at high risk for suicide with severe symptoms of depression in the context of a potential for a lethal suicide attempt while using large quantities of alcohol with acute grief and recent homelessness and deterioration in functioning. The patient remained a safety risk and functionally impaired with high risk for relapse if discharged from acute inpatient level care prior to his discharge and transfer. Moreover, the patient needed alcohol detoxification and withdrawal management with monitoring in view of the severity of the alcohol use disorder that included general medical complications (fatty liver and risk for withdrawal seizures).
These answers are consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, the scientific literature, and published guidelines, referenced below and the clinically appropriate application of NY State OASAS LOCADTR 3.0 Criteria, referenced below.[10]

Treatment: Inpatient Substance Rehabilitative Treatment With 24 Hours a Day Nursing Support
The insurer denied the Inpatient Substance Rehabilitative Treatment With 24 Hours a Day Nursing Support
The denial is upheld

The patient is a female. She was referred for inpatient rehabilitation and substance use disorder treatment in order to address opioid (heroin) and stimulant (cocaine) class substance use disorders. The patient had been using opioid and cocaine substances of abuse while receiving methadone in a methadone maintenance treatment program (MMTP). Her referral was prompted by her failure to remain abstinent. She incurred legal charges that included possession of controlled substances and burglary, and she had been incarcerated and released with mandatory treatment ordered. Her referral had been coordinated by an agency providing oversight for the patient.

The patient's evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination that reflected external motivation for rehabilitation treatment, but limited insight, impaired judgment, and poor control of impulses with questionable motivation. The patient was described as superficially cooperative with fluent speech and organized thought processing. She displayed okay mood with no severe symptoms such as mania, formal thought disorder, psychosis, perceptual disturbance or severe cognitive impairment (dementia or delirium). She did not report suicidal ideation or aggressive impulses. She was dysphoric and irritable with reports of mood swings and sleep disturbance.

Upon entering treatment with inpatient level services, the patient received comprehensive evaluation and treatment that included focus on coping skills, relapse prevention techniques with identification of triggers, education about the disease model of addiction, and involvement with therapy groups, as well as recovery groups and other therapeutic activities to support her efforts at rehabilitation treatment. The patient did not readily engage in substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment, but indicated that she was planning to cut treatment short in order to proceed to long-term treatment.

Throughout her brief inpatient stay, the patient remained unstable with regard to mental status and remained uncooperative with respect to the treatment regimen which had included focus on coping skills and plan for the development of a relapse prevention plan while providing motivational enhancement. She received methadone at 20 mg (milligrams) daily and vitamin supplements, and she was restarted on lithium and Abilify with prn (as needed) use of trazodone, as well as comfort medications.

The patient continued treatment with intensive services, monitoring, and structure provided within the inpatient treatment program including 24-hour monitoring. The patient was discharged against medical advice with refusal of a Narcan kit and declining recommendations for clinically appropriate aftercare. The patient was adamant that she would proceed to the long-term facility on her own.

The health plan's denial determination was on the basis of New York State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) Criteria and medical necessity indicating that the patient could have been treated with lower-level services suggesting residential level care. The denial determination referenced that the patient had no physiologic or general medical disturbance or other comorbidities that would have required an inpatient level of care.

The treatment facility appealed on the basis of New York State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) Criteria, as well as the need to complete treatment with development of better coping skills and identification of triggers to prevent relapse.

No, the requested  Inpatient Substance Rehabilitative Treatment With 24 Hours a Day Nursing Support was not medically necessary.
The patient presented with substance use disorders with use of opioid and stimulant class substances while participating in an outpatient substance use disorder treatment with medication assisted treatment with methadone which had been started while the patient was in a correctional facility. She was referred for mandatory treatment of the substance use disorders as an alternative to incarceration. Upon referral for substance use disorder treatment, the patient engaged superficially in treatment, but left against medical advice due to her desire to continue treatment in a long-term treatment program.

During the time interval under review, the patient was noted to be in no apparent distress with satisfactory daily functioning and participation in treatment including positive interactions and peers, but conflict with staff over the need to complete the 28-day rehabilitation program. Nonetheless, during the brief inpatient stay, there were no emerging treatment issues or biomedical or co-occurring psychiatric issues that would have warranted the inpatient level of care. The application of NY (New York) State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) Criteria (referenced below) did indicate that the patient was clinically appropriate for treatment with lower-level care in a less restrictive treatment setting, as the health plan asserted. Thus, medical necessity is not met in this case scenario. This answer is consistent with ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) Criteria, the scientific literature and published guidelines, referenced below.

Yes, the health plan has acted reasonably, with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.
The patient in this case scenario is not clinically appropriate for the admission or continued inpatient level of care during the time interval under review. The patient's clinical features did not include residual withdrawal symptoms, biomedical complications or co-occurring psychiatric symptoms or disorders that would have warranted inpatient level care and monitoring. The patient's treatment did not warrant the structure or intensity of inpatient level services. The patient could have been safely and effectively treated with lower-level care in a less restrictive setting with sober supports and clinically appropriate monitoring to assure abstinence. Thus, the health plan's determination is reasonable in this case scenario. This answer is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice, as well as the NY (New York) State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines, referenced below.

summary:
Diagnosis: Anxiety/Depression
Treatment: Psychiatric Acute Inpatient 
The insurer denied: Psychiatric Acute Inpatient
The denial is: Upheld

The patient is a female who presented to the emergency department with weakness, anorexia and a 20-pound weight loss in three months with anxiety and depression. The patient was 14 weeks status post face and neck lift. She complained of a tightness in her throat and was afraid to swallow. Her outpatient psychiatrist had prescribed Prozac and Ativan, but she had an intolerance with the Prozac, and had a history of intolerance with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). She was medically screened and admitted for inpatient level psychiatric treatment with mood, anxiety, and trauma-related disorders. Her mood had recently worsened with increased anxiety, depression and sleep disturbance, as well as the weight loss associated with anorexia and dysphagia. The patient's functional capacity had declined, and she reported that she was afraid to eat. She had chronic medical conditions including gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) treated with omeprazole and a history of pulmonary embolus; she was also prescribed Linzess.

The patient was generally compliant with her treatment plan and mostly adherent with medications with ongoing concern that the medications were affecting her neck tightness. There were no complications of treatment otherwise, or complications of the clinical course during her inpatient stay. The patient was improved and functioning better with sleep and eating. She was noted to be persistently depressed and anxious though mood was improving, and anxiety had diminished. The patient was requesting referral for assisted living services due to her continued worry about her neck and swallowing capacity. Throughout the inpatient stay, she had denied suicidal ideation and there were no safety concerns. She was discharged with clinically appropriate aftercare including referral to Intensive Outpatient Program (IOP) level services for medication management and continued psychiatric care while residing in an assisted living facility. The subject under review is the medical necessity for the acute inpatient psychiatric stay.

The health plan's determination is upheld.
