The patient is an adult female. She was admitted/transferred to intensive outpatient program (IOP) level substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment in order to continue treatment following inpatient level rehabilitation treatment. The patient has a history of longstanding use of prescription opiates with escalating use over the five years prior to presentation for treatment. She was using 8-10 30 or 40 mg (milligrams) Percocet daily with significant impact on functioning and relationships with friends and family including job loss and social isolation and strained relationships with her immediate family. 

The patient lives with her spouse and mother-in-law. Stressors includes primary support, occupational, and social environment domains. There are no legal issues in this case, and the patient has trauma history.

The patient was developing a relapse prevention plan together with continued work on coping skills, and efforts continued to enhance her motivation to continue a recovery effort. The patient was deemed to be at high risk for relapse due to a lack of insight and no prior history of substance-related treatment or exposure to recovery groups. She was discharged from IOP (intensive outpatient program) level care against medical advice having completed most of her treatment goals and with consideration of clinically appropriate aftercare.

The health plan denied coverage on the basis of LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) Guidelines indicating that the patient was improved with no general medical or psychiatric issues requiring IOP (intensive outpatient program) level care in the context of a supportive spouse. 

The Intensive Outpatient Substance Use Treatment was medically necessary.

The continued IOP (intensive outpatient program) substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment was medically necessary for this patient in order to effectively address the continuing clinical needs for rehabilitation treatment of severe opioid use disorders with evidence-based psychosocial treatments and to work toward relapse prevention; in order to address the patient's lack of awareness of the seriousness of her illnesses with psycho-education and recovery groups; and in order to address issues within the social and family environment including an appropriate disposition with sober supports, especially in working with the patient's community providers in developing a clinically appropriate disposition; and in order to work on coping skills that will be necessary in building a sober support system and continued recovery efforts with community providers and engagement with peer-supported groups in the community.

The continued IOP (intensive outpatient program) treatment through discharge was therefore medically necessary including continued monitoring for the duration of the proposed treatment in order to achieve a safe transition to lower-level treatment and transition to community level care. None of this therapeutic work could have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance use disorder.
Treatment: Inpatient Rehabilitation Admission.
The insurer denied the Inpatient Rehabilitation Admission.
The denial is overturned.

The patient is a female who presented for detoxification treatment and was medically screened and admitted to acute inpatient level care in order to address substance use disorder with opioid and sedative-hypnotic-anxiolytic class substance use disorders. The patient had been using heroin with intravenous administration together with Xanax. She has no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens. She had a history of multiple prior detoxification treatment episodes and had past exposure to substance use disorder treatments with relapses and continued use of heroin and Xanax. 

The patient has a history of psychiatric disorder with unspecified anxiety and depressive disorders. There was no mention of general medical issues except for hepatitis C related to the intravenous drug use. The patient's initial assessment included a Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) score of nine and a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) scale score of ten reflecting mild to moderate withdrawal symptoms that included tremor, chills, sweats, nausea and abdominal cramps, headache, joint pain and fatigue.

The patient was admitted to detoxification treatment with a comprehensive detoxification protocol with tapering dosages of methadone and detoxification protocol to address the comorbid use of Xanax and as needed (PRN) medications for comfort. The program provided for case management with referral and access to rehabilitation treatment that included comprehensive evidence-based treatments. During detoxification the patient engaged in counseling sessions focusing on education about the disease model of addiction, and, involvement with other therapeutic activities including initial work on relapse prevention, and educational sessions to motivate the patient to proceed to rehabilitation treatment. By the second day of detoxification treatment the patient continued to display withdrawal symptoms with a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) of nine and Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) score of eight despite receiving treatment including methadone. The patient completed the detoxification treatment without complication, and she was discharged with clinically appropriate aftercare and immediate transfer for rehabilitation treatment and plans to address the co-occurring anxiety and depressive disorders that were thought to be triggering her substance use.

The denial was on the basis of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria indicating that there was no severe withdrawal symptoms, no past severe withdrawal symptoms, no safety issues, and, access to sober supports as well as prior detoxification treatment, the month prior to presentation. The denial also indicated that residential level care was the appropriate in this case.

The appeal is on the basis of the clinical features of the case including the high-risk use of heroin, the evidence for moderately severe withdrawal from both substances of abuse with persistent withdrawal symptoms, and the need to develop a relapse prevention plan that included planning to address the anxiety and depression. The appeal was argued that the patient met New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria for inpatient level detoxification and monitoring and withdrawal management based on the presenting clinical features and history of substance use.

The issue under review is inpatient detoxification and withdrawal management and other medical services,

Yes, the proposed treatment, inpatient substance abuse treatment was medically necessary for this patient.
The patient in this case was using heroin, together with Xanax, on a daily continuous basis that did warrant inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring for the duration of the protocol; detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments pertinent to the detoxification treatment episode could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment that was provided at the time of admission.  Moreover, the patient persistent withdrawal symptoms, and, the patient's social environment was not conducive to detoxification in the context of limited insight, impaired judgment and poor control of impulses, as well as high-risk behaviors noted in the appeal.

Thus, the adult inpatient detoxification treatment and withdrawal management of this patient's substance use disorders did warrant the admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level detoxification setting with 24-hour monitoring and use of as needed (PRN) medications. The patient's history of substance abuse reflects the seriousness of the substance use disorders and the need for a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management, as the patient was at high risk for treatment failure or complications if the detoxification and withdrawal management were to be attempted at a lower level of care. Medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published guidelines, the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and the scientific literature, referenced below, and, New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews including the appropriate application of the New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Tool that requires the patient in this scenario default to the higher level of care.

No, the health plan did not act reasonably, with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.

The patient's clinical features and treatment dimensions did warrant inpatient level detoxification services thru discharge and did necessitate the monitoring that is provided with inpatient level treatment including the use of comfort medications, together with counseling and educational sessions and peer support. Case management services were critical in this case to motivate the patient to proceed to rehabilitation treatment and formal substance use disorder treatment with a safe and clinically appropriate disposition though the patient did discharge against medical advice. The requested benefit is not excluded under the plan, and should be covered in keeping with prevailing standards of care pertaining to substance use disorder services including the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria and the New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines, referenced below.

summary:
Diagnosis: Alcohol abuse and withdrawal. 
Treatment: Inpatient admission. 

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient admission. 

The denial is overturned. 

This patient was admitted to inpatient hospital treatment for reports of tremors including uncontrollable shakes, as well as abdominal pain, agitation, headache, and a medical issue including low potassium and magnesium. He went on a drinking binge of 7 shots per day of vodka for the past 2 weeks. He had hyperglycemia, thrombocytopenia, hypertension, asthma, elevated liver function tests (LFT's), alcohol hepatitis, alcohol esophagitis, and alcohol gastritis. He was given Ativan for detoxification treatment, intravenous (IV) fluids, potassium chloride (KCl) and magnesium (Mg) supplementation. His discharge diagnosis was alcohol abuse and withdrawal. 
  
The insurer denied coverage for inpatient hospital treatment as not medically necessary treatment. They stated that he did not require 24-hour hospital treatment and they recommended a less restrictive level of care such as observational level of care. 
  
The medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that he required 24-hour hospital treatment. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. It also states that patients with past complicated or life-threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens (DT's) are in need of inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal and reports that patients with comorbid medical condition that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification. Also, the United States Department of Health and Human Services-Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) Center for Substance Abuse Treatment reports that inpatient treatment is necessary if the ability to attend outpatient treatment daily is a problem, one is unable to follow up in outpatient treatment , if medical conditions complicate the treatment of withdrawal, if one has previous withdrawal seizures of DT's, or if one does not have the capacity for informed consent. In this case this patient had active alcohol withdrawal symptoms after going on a 2-week binge of drinking. He also had several comorbid medical conditions including low potassium and magnesium, alcohol hepatitis, alcohol esophagitis, alcohol gastritis, hyperglycemia, thrombocytopenia, hypertension, asthma, and elevated LFT's. 

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) he did require 24 hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive setting as he continued to use large amounts of alcohol daily and had active withdrawal symptoms, and he required and received detoxification medication (Ativan) to modify withdrawal from alcohol and more severe withdrawal, complicated or life threatening withdrawal such as DT's. The risk of DT's can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use so he was considered at high risk for DT's due to his large amount of alcohol use daily with active withdrawal symptoms. He also had medical problems due to alcohol use, so he was considered in need of 24-hour inpatient hospital treatment for detoxification. 

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment in the best interest of the patient. 

The insurer's denial of coverage for inpatient admission is overturned. Medical Necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Alcohol withdrawal
Treatment: Inpatient Admission
The insurer denied the inpatient admission.
The denial is upheld.

The patient is a male with a past medical history significant for alcoholism, anxiety, depression, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, eczema, and gastritis who presented to the emergency department with symptoms of withdrawal. He reported alcohol abuse for at least 4 months after a period of sobriety. He reported drinking 24 cans of 12-ounce beer daily. When seen by the admitting physician he complained of being anxious, diaphoretic, having paresthesias in the face and extremities, also vomiting. Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) score at the time of admission was 10. The patient was in mild distress. He had some skin lesions. The head, eyes, ears, nose, throat (HEENT) exam was within normal limits. The neck was supple without lymphadenopathy, masses, jugular vein distention (JVD), and carotid bruits. The patient had a regular heart rate and rhythm, without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. The abdomen was soft, non-tender to palpation, with normal bowel sounds, without guarding or rebound. The patient was alert, oriented times 3, and anxious. During the hospital stay, the patient's clinical condition gradually improved, he tolerated his diet and was discharged from the hospital.

The health plan's determination is upheld.

The inpatient stay was not medically necessary. The patient could have been managed at a lower level of care status. The review of the medical records clearly demonstrated that the patient initially had signs of alcohol withdrawal CIWA 10, however, his symptoms subsided relatively quickly. Specifically, there was no mention that the patient had sustained tachycardia, tremor, or increased perspiration beyond the observation period. Even though the patient initially complained of nausea and vomiting, these symptoms resolved relatively quickly, and he tolerated his diet. There was no evidence that the patient had sustained tremors.
Overall, the symptoms of alcohol withdrawal, which were present at the time of admission, improved relatively quickly. Nausea and vomiting were unlikely related to acute gastroenteritis but were part of alcohol withdrawal syndrome.

Diagnosis: Anxiety and Depressive Disorders.
Treatment: Continued Residential Mental Health Treatment.

The patient completed a Wilderness Program and was referred for residential treatment of co-occurring anxiety and depressive disorders (severe and recurrent major depressive disorder, persistent depressive disorder, social anxiety disorder, and generalized anxiety disorder); attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)-combined type; and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) together with academic and educational problems associated with emotional abuse including bullying by peers. The patient has had increasing symptoms related to the co-morbid psychiatric conditions in the context of high- risk behaviors that have included self-harm with cutting and suicidal behavior/attempts requiring emergency medical services and psychiatric hospitalization. The patient's autism spectrum disorder is associated with problems with social skills and sense of self with low self-worth and a tendency toward impulsive aggression towards self and emotional dysregulation. The patient's mental health disturbances emerged at an early age with an increasing severity of symptoms and behavioral disturbances that included high risk behaviors with bouts of self-harm and suicidality with associated interpersonal relationship problems resulting in loneliness and social isolation.
The mental status examination at the time of admission for residential treatment revealed severe symptoms of anxiety, depression, low self-worth, and affective instability together with suicidal ideation associated with guilt and shame. He had trauma-related symptoms, as well as disturbed sleep. There were prominent issues with regard to peer relationships and a lack of insight together with impaired judgment and poor control of impulses. He reported panic attacks and paralyzing anxiety when in a social setting including apprehension, nervousness, tension and irritability.
Past psychiatric treatment with inpatient, outpatient and intermediate levels of care had failed to provide benefit or remission or sustained benefit despite the best effort of clinical providers. Thus, he was referred to the Wilderness Program followed by the referral for extended residential level services.
There were no acute medical conditions or current substance use disorders in this case though the patient has a history of alcohol and cannabis use disorders (in remission). The patient is a student and lives with family. The patient's academic functioning had declined as well as his attention to self-care and daily activities.
The patient presented for residential treatment and received comprehensive evaluations that affirmed the comorbid diagnoses. Records show that the patient initially participated in group, individual, family and other therapies focusing on coping skills and maintaining safety with monitoring. He received milieu, therapeutic and academic programming. The patient made steady progress such that he was able to reduce his tendency to engage in self-destructive behaviors though he continued to report suicidal ideation driven by interpersonal relationship problems and moderately severe symptoms of depression with a Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ)-9 determination averaging at 15 in association with depressive ruminations. The patient continued to show relationship issues with peers and affective instability with associated symptoms of anxiety and depression-a focus of treatment. The patient received treatment with psychotropic medication that included ketamine treatment targeting depression and suicidality, and as needed (prn) use of propranolol for social anxiety and panic. He was working on coping skills and use of modified dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT) with distress tolerance, mindfulness and emotional regulation techniques. Going forward during this time interval, the treatment plan called for continued active treatment targeting life skills, social skills, and trauma recovery, as well as involvement with academic programming focused on obtaining his GED [General Educational Development] and with mentoring. The patient was also participating in more intensive illness recovery services and family-focused sessions. These additional services were provided, as well as other therapeutic interventions as the program would allow that were age appropriate. The treatment plan included educational and peer support sessions; psychotherapy, as noted; and other activity therapies to address relational functioning; and family-focused sessions with encouragement to include his primary source of support, his mother, in the sessions. Safety monitoring was provided within the structure of the residential program.
Because of developmental disorder and the childhood trauma due to bullying, the patient had not developed secure attachments that had affected the patient's core beliefs about the world and self. The treatment focused on the patient's belief that he was bad, and that is why he had been abused or was bullied. The treatment plan in this case provided for active treatment to remedy to this belief system and the painful situations that arise as a consequence leading to suicidal risk and self-harming behavior. Thus, the core treatment with the continued use of therapy and medication and activities focused more on a relationally based treatment model. As noted, the patient's family-focused sessions were evolving to address the plan for reunification with the family and ongoing support with clinically appropriate aftercare in the community. The patient was actively participating in a recovery process with focus on the development of better coping skills and relational functioning. There were no complications of treatment reported in this case with regard to safety issues or a recrudescence of high-risk behaviors in the context of 24-hour monitoring and a safety plan to continue following discharge.
The health plan documents were reviewed including correspondence, case notes, and health plan medical necessity criteria (InterQual). Letters from the treatment facility and parent were reviewed with appeal. The health plan's rationale for the denial of authorization for continued residential coverage was reviewed. The denial was on the basis of InterQual Criteria for Adult and Geriatric Patients indicating that the patient had no impairment of functioning, no moderately severe symptoms, no eating disorder, no interpersonal conflict and the ability to cooperate with treatment.
The appeal referenced the moderately severe symptoms of depression and comorbidities with high risk for suicide including active suicidal ideation and history of suicidal behavior, as well as the substantial interpersonal relationship problems and history of being bullied together the decline in academic functioning.
At issue is the medical necessity of Continued Residential Mental Health Treatment.
The requested health service/treatment of mental health residential stay  was medically necessary for this patient.
The patient's symptoms, clinical features and treatment dimensions did warrant continued residential level care. They could not have been safely or effectively managed with lower-level services or in a less restrictive treatment setting.
The patient remained symptomatic with the need for continued residential treatment and structure and monitoring in order to address residual symptoms of anxiety and depression, trauma-related symptoms, and the need for ongoing psychiatric management together with the family focused and relational-based interventions that were occurring to address the psychological factors in this case.
The patient had multiple co-occurring disorders and was at high risk for relapse. The patient has failed to benefit from clinically appropriate treatment at lower levels of care, and represented a safety risk to self. It is not reasonable to expect that the patient could have been safely or effectively managed with lower-level services in a less restrictive level of care for the time frame under review.
The diagnoses per the treatment plan and psychiatric evaluations included sufficient clinical information in the patient's medical records to support the diagnoses in this case including the relational problems, as well as the neurocognitive deficits, autism and ADHD. The patient's conditions are considered moderately severe, especially with regard to the anxiety and mood disorder; the trauma-related problems; and the social relational problems associated with high-risk behaviors including past episodes of self-harm and impulsivity and suicidal behavior. The safety concerns; risk for relapse; and risk factors with regard to the history of high-risk behaviors did necessitate that the patient receive the continued structure, intensity and monitoring provided within a residential treatment setting consistent with generally accepted standards of medical practice, and the societal guidelines referenced below and applicable to an adolescent, as in this case.

summary:
Diagnosis: Cannabis use.
Treatment: Residential substance use disorder treatment.

The insurer denied coverage for residential substance use disorder treatment.  The denial is overturned.

This patient was admitted to this inpatient substance residential treatment due to severe cannabis use. He was using large amounts of cannabis daily and had reports of hallucinations at times when using. He had cravings and could not cut down or stop use. His use also interfered with his ability to attend college as he was on a medical leave due to his use. He had withdrawal symptoms including irritable, anxious, and depressed mood, concentration and energy problems. He had comorbid suicidal ideation with a past plan to jump out a window. He had diagnoses of Major Depressive Disorder and Generalized Anxiety Disorder. He took Duloxetine for anxiety and depression. He attended group and individual therapy and also had pain management. He was discharged after treatment.
   
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that residential treatment is indicated primarily for individuals who do not meet clinical criteria for hospitalization but whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. In this case this patient was considered still in need of 24-hour residential treatment as he needed more time to learn better coping skills, relapse prevention skills, improve insight into his addiction including how his psychiatric comorbidities contributed to his addiction, identify relapse triggers, improve motivation, and increase sober supports.  

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) he met criteria for inpatient substance residential rehabilitation treatment as he continued to use increased frequency of marijuana despite negative consequences. He was having difficulty functioning as he had to take a leave of absence from college. He had comorbid psychiatric conditions including major depression and anxiety and past suicidal ideation with plan to jump out a window and he was taking Duloxetine to treat depression and anxiety. He also had comorbid pain contributing to his use. It was reported that he had poor concentration and memory issues as per notes. It was reported that the day prior to discharge he took Wellbutrin for depression and low motivation as well as executive functioning complaints. He was worried about legal proceedings which caused him to withdraw more in groups. He could not stop use or cut down use on his own. He had external motivation as his attorney recommended this treatment after his legal charges. He lacked accountability for his behavior and consequences to use. His longest reported abstinence was 45 days when he was with his parent during the beginning of the pandemic and quarantine. The Institute on Drug Abuse: Principles of Addiction Treatment: A Research Based Guide- reports that research indicates that that the best treatment outcomes occur with longer durations of treatment and states that recovery from drug addiction is a long-term process. It also states that treatment techniques to increase motivation for treatment are necessary to prevent dropout rates. In this case this patient required more treatment time in a 24-hour inpatient therapeutic residential treatment setting. At the time of the denial, he still had not obtained the skills needed to remain sober and was still working on them. If he were discharged prematurely, he was considered a high risk for relapse.  

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment in the best interest of the patient.

The insurer's denial of coverage for residential substance use disorder treatment is overturned. Medical Necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse.
Treatment: Inpatient Detoxification Admission.

The insurer denied the Inpatient Detoxification Admission.  The denial is upheld.

The patient is male who was admitted for detoxification services for alcohol use disorder. The patient was using alcohol on a continuous daily basis with up to two pints of liquor and three 24-ounce beers, and use of $50 worth of crack cocaine approximately three times per week. He presented with mild symptoms of withdrawal in the context of the alcohol use disorder with a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) scale score of 9/67. The patient has a history of multiple prior detoxification treatments with relapse. Onset of alcohol use was in adolescence with escalation of use and progression of the disease, and subsequent use of cocaine.

The patient had no history of co-occurring psychiatric disorder or history of suicidal behavior. Chronic medical conditions included gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with asthma in the context of tobacco dependence. He was purified protein derivative (PPD) (tuberculosis) positive with a negative chest x-ray. The patient provided no history of withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens or severe alcohol or drug withdrawal symptoms.

The patient was admitted for inpatient detoxification. The patient's hospital course progressed without incident, and, he had the opportunity to attend group sessions and receive counseling and education with planning for clinically appropriate aftercare. He completed the detoxification treatment and was referred for continued substance use disorder treatment with clinically appropriate aftercare. Progress notes indicated that the patient was in no apparent distress and generally calm, but anxious during his inpatient stay. He engaged in treatment and tolerated the Librium taper with vitamin replacement and comfort medications. He was noted to be sleeping and eating okay with no biomedical complications during his stay. At the time of discharge, the patient declined transfer for rehabilitation services, indicating that he would return to outpatient services for aftercare.

The issue under review is the inpatient admission with detoxification treatment and withdrawal management.

The denial was on the basis of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria indicating that inpatient level treatment was not medically necessary, as there were no biomedical or psychiatric concerns or complicated withdrawal in the case, and that the patient was motivated for treatment. 

The appeal was on the basis of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Guidelines, indicating that the detoxification was medically necessary and that the patient was at risk for moderate withdrawal had no sober supports.

No, based on the submitted information, the proposed treatment, inpatient admission was not medically necessary for this patient.

The proposed inpatient stay and detoxification treatment and other medical services could have been safely and effectively provided at a lower level of care, as the denial determination asserts. The treatment of this patient's substance use disorder did not require the structure of an inpatient setting or 24-hour monitoring. The patient displayed no serious disturbance of mental status despite having a history of ongoing substance use disorder with alcohol, cocaine and tobacco. Moreover, the patient did not show evidence for suicidal or aggressive behavior or risk, or severe cognitive impairment, or psychosis, or perceptual disturbance that would have warranted an inpatient level admission and treatment. There were no severe/objective symptoms of withdrawal or biomedical issues in this case, and the patient had received detoxification and substance use disorder treatment in the past with knowledge of substance use disorder treatment protocols, as noted in the clinical summary. The patient had fair insight and reasonable motivation and was in no apparent distress throughout his inpatient stay. Thus, the inpatient admission for detoxification treatment and 24-hour monitoring, and the requested inpatient level services were not medically necessary in this case scenario. 

This answer is consistent with New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines and with published guidelines, the scientific literature, and American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, as referenced below.

Yes, the health plan did act reasonably, with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.

In this case scenario, the patient was amenable to treatment with lower-level care in a less restrictive setting. The patient displayed no serious disturbance of mental status and no general medical complications or symptoms of co-occurring disorders that would have warranted inpatient level services. There were no severe symptoms of withdrawal or biomedical issues in this case. The admission for detoxification treatment and 24-hour monitoring, and the requested inpatient level services were therefore not medically necessary in this case scenario, as the health plan asserts. And, New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines are not met for the inpatient level of care, as referenced below.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse/Addiction
Treatment: Inpatient Substance Use Detoxification Treatment
The insurer denied Inpatient Substance Use Detoxification Treatment.
The health plan's determination is overturned.

The patient is a male who was evaluated and subsequently admitted to inpatient level services for detoxification and withdrawal management of opioid (heroin) and stimulant (cocaine) class use disorders. The patient was using up to one bundle per day with smoking. He presented with mild withdrawal symptoms at the time of admission with sweats and body aches, as well as anxiety, irritability, and restlessness.

The patient had prior exposure to substance-related treatment with no sustained abstinence. He has no history of a co-occurring psychiatric disorder. He denied psychiatric hospitalization, or suicidal or self-harming behaviors. The patient had been medically screened with drug testing that was consistent with his history and with elevated and labile blood pressures. There were no other acute medical issues and no chronic medical conditions in this case.

The patient was admitted to inpatient level care and placed on a detoxification regimen with buprenorphine together with the availability of comfort medications, and medical monitoring. Following his first day of treatment, the patient began to participate in counseling and educational sessions, as his withdrawal symptoms diminished, and he was feeling better with the use of buprenorphine. His mental status examination included persistent symptoms of anxiety and irritability with associated symptoms of insomnia addressed with quetiapine. He demonstrated no severe symptoms such as mania, psychosis, perceptual disturbance, or severe cognitive impairment. He did continue with detoxification treatment briefly and was provided education and counseling during the inpatient stay, as well as plans to proceed directly to rehabilitation services to include dialectical behavior therapy (DBT), cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), motivational techniques, and involvement in 12-step recovery groups, as well as work on coping skills and a relapse prevention plan with identification of triggers. The patient made steady progress with completion of detoxification treatment, though he had continued to display elevated and labile blood pressures requiring safety monitoring and use of clonidine.

The health plan's determination of medical necessity is overturned in whole. The Inpatient Substance Use Detoxification Treatment was medically necessary for this patient.

The patient presented with a diagnosis of severe opioid and stimulant use disorders with severe psychosocial stressors with limited support and functional impairments.
The presenting clinical features and history and general medical concerns did warrant the admission and continued inpatient level services with medical monitoring in this case scenario in keeping with the appeal. The patient's admission and continued inpatient stay with detoxification, withdrawal management, and other medical services through completion could not have been provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario.
 Withdraw symptoms were managed with buprenorphine requiring monitoring and as needed (PRN) medications, as well as the availability of comfort medications. Counseling and educational sessions with motivational techniques together with case management services were appropriately provided to motivate the patient's transition to rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment. Thus, the patient did require a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management during the time frame under review with associated substance use disorder treatments, as it was reasonable that the patient would have been unable to abstain from the substances of abuse if detoxification and treatment were to be attempted at a lower level of care.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse.
Treatment: Inpatient admission/inpatient substance abuse services.
The insurer denied the inpatient admission/inpatient substance abuse services.
The health plan's determination is upheld.

The patient is a male who presented for inpatient substance related services. The patient was using cannabis on a continuous daily basis with approximately five joints daily together with intermittent use of $20 worth of cocaine with snorting. He had a long standing history of substance use beginning in adolescence and had little or no substance use disorder treatment and has no history of achieving sobriety. He was not in active substance use disorder treatment or involved with 12 step recovery groups.
The patient provided no history of withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens or severe alcohol withdrawal symptoms. The patient's vital signs were normal with a normal or unremarkable laboratory assessment and a positive drug screen consistent with his history. He was tobacco dependent at two packs per day for 15 years.
There was psychiatric comorbidity in this case best characterized as unspecified depressive disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) related to police brutality 15 years prior with hospitalization. The patient denied current mental health treatment or recent psychiatric hospitalization or suicidal behavior. The patient's mental status examination revealed mild symptoms of anxiety and insomnia with no severe symptoms and limited insight and judgment. He exhibited withdrawal symptoms including tremors, anxiety, irritability and craving.

The patient was admitted for inpatient detoxification, withdrawal management and substance-related services with as needed (prn) use of Vistaril and comfort medications and other medical services following the assessment for safety issues and medical clearance. He received vitamin replacement therapy and other supportive measures.
The patient's hospital course progressed without incident. The patient slept and received meals without complications. His gait was normal and there was no evidence of severe withdrawal symptoms. His monitoring occurred without incident throughout the inpatient stay. The patient was feeling better on the day following his admission. The patient had received counseling with a recommendation for clinically appropriate aftercare. He became disgruntled and left against medical advice. His discharge diagnoses included the substance related disorders with the stimulants (cocaine) and cannabis (marijuana) and the co-occurring PTSD and depressive disorder. There were no biomedical or psychiatric issues during his stay and he was euthymic and cooperative with care up until his discharge date.

The patient's admission and continued inpatient stay with detoxification, withdrawal management, and other medical services through discharge could have been safely provided at a lower level of care.
The patient in this case presented with continuous daily use of cannabis/marijuana and intermittent use of cocaine; he did not experience serious complications or present with severe symptoms of a co-occurring psychiatric disorder/depressive disorder, or abnormal findings on examination, or severe withdrawal symptoms, as noted in the clinical summary. His risk for withdrawal complications including seizures and delirium tremens were minimal considering his history, and he did not pose a safety risk that would have warranted the admission and continued inpatient level services and monitoring, as requested.

The requested health service and treatment of the inpatient admission was not medically necessary for this patient.
The patient displayed no serious disturbance of mental status despite having a history of ongoing substance use disorder and history of an unspecified depressive disorder and PTSD.

summary:
Diagnosis: Progressive Cognitive Impairment, Persistent Depressive Disorder
Treatment: Daily Social Day Care (SDC) Services: Total of 3 Days per Week
The insurer denied Daily Social Day Care (SDC) Services: Total of 3 Days per Week.
The health plan's determination is overturned.

The patient is a female with a diagnosis of progressive cognitive impairment (neurocognitive disorder) with persistent symptoms of depression best characterized as persistent depressive disorder. The patient is forgetful with limited functioning related to her mental health issues. The patient does cooperate with self-care and receives Home Attendant Services to assist her with bathing, feeding, dressing, ambulation and toileting. She also receives assistance with general housework including laundry, shopping and meals. She needs some assistance with medications and with the use of transportation. She participates in groups, activities, and other therapeutic interventions at the Day Program including peer support.

The Day Care services occur three days per week and serve to provide socialization and intellectual stimulation. The Day Care services also provide therapeutic intervention for the patient's loneliness, social isolation, and symptoms of depression which include depression, anhedonia and loss of interest together with concentration difficulties in the context of the cognitive impairment.

The patient's health plan has denied coverage for the Day Care services indicating that the services are not medically necessary and that the Personal Care Assistance is sufficient to address the patient's needs. Moreover, the denial indicates that there is overlap with services provided through the Day Care program and Personal Care Attendant. The denial references New York State Department of Health Uniform Assessment System guidelines (UAS_NY).

The patient's adult children, social worker, and physician are requesting coverage for the Day Care Services at a frequency of three days per week together with the personal assistance provided through the Home Attendant Services. The appeal indicates that there is no overlap of these services with Day Care.

The case summary and correspondence from the patient's physician, clinician, adult children, and correspondence from the health plan were reviewed. Also reviewed was information on the extent of the functional decline and needs pertaining to the comorbid conditions of the patient. 

The health plan, in its determination of medical necessity, has not acted reasonably, with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.

The requested health service/treatment of Daily Social Day Care (SDC) Services: Total of 3 Days per Week is medically necessary for the patient.  The services being provided are clinically appropriate to address ongoing symptoms of depressive disorder with persistent symptoms of depression and cognitive impairment (neurocognitive disorder) in a patient with multiple mental health issues and functional impairments. The continued use of a Day Program with behavioral health programming and the Day Care services provides for maintenance treatment for the patient's mental health needs and facilitates better functioning and cognition.

The patients functional decline in the context of the comorbid conditions could not be effectively addressed with only Home Attendant Services. The requested benefit of the Day Care Services is reasonable, in the patient's best interest, and reflects sound medical judgement. Thus, the proposed treatment and services with Social Day Care Services at a frequency of three days per week, is consistent with New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews and is consistent with the prevailing standards of care and with the scientific literature referenced below.

summary:

The insurer denied: Substance Abuse Inpatient Rehabilitation Admission
The denial is upheld.

The patient is an adult female, self-referred following a recent detoxification treatment episode for inpatient rehabilitation (rehab) substance use disorder treatment in order to address use of alcohol, cannabis, and stimulant (cocaine) class substances. Her history of substance use included use of up to two pints of vodka per day, $50 worth of crack cocaine up to three times per week or less, and intermittent use of marijuana. The patient was self-referred and indicated that she needed rehab. The patient has a history of psychiatric disorder and treatment for schizoaffective disorder bipolar type treated with Abilify and Paxil. The patient has a history of psychiatric hospitalizations, and multiple detoxification and substance use disorder treatment episodes including the recent detoxification treatment.

Drug screen was positive and consistent with history. The patient is tobacco dependent. Upon admission to inpatient level services, the patient received comprehensive evaluation and treatment. Psychiatric evaluation was provided, and the patient was prescribed the Abilify and Paxil with as needed (PRN) use of Vistaril for insomnia/sleep. The patient engaged in substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment. The patient had requested medication assisted treatment with Vivitrol and was started on naltrexone with a subsequent injection of Vivitrol 380 milligrams with plans for continued treatment. The patient continued to receive intensive rehabilitation services, monitoring, and structure including 24-hour monitoring and was discharged 17 days later with disposition to outpatient level care, and psychiatric follow up for the co-occurring disorder. 
During the time interval under review, the patient remained stable and had no significant withdrawal or post-acute withdrawal symptoms, no safety concerns, and no biomedical complications. 

The denial was on the basis of medical necessity and New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria indicating that the patient could have been treated with lower-level care suggesting residential treatment as being appropriate. The appeal was on the basis of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria indicating that the patient was at high risk for relapse together with general medical and psychiatric comorbidity that warranted inpatient level care.

The proposed treatment was not medically necessary.

The patient presented with substance use disorders, diagnosed with alcohol, cannabis, and stimulant/cocaine use disorders. She received inpatient level rehabilitation treatment and readily engaged in treatment and had no significant biomedical (withdrawal symptoms or signs) or psychiatric treatment issues. 

She continued treatment for the co-occurring psychiatric disorder, as well as started medication assisted treatment. During the time interval under review, the patient was noted to be in no distress with reasonable functioning and active participation in treatment. The application of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 
Criteria, as well as the Level of Care Utilization System (LOCUS) and the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria did indicate that the patient was clinically appropriate for treatment with lower-level care in a less restrictive treatment setting. Thus, medical necessity for the admission and continued rehabilitation substance use disorder services is not met in this case scenario.

Treatment: Intensive Outpatient Mental Health Services
The insurer denied Intensive Outpatient Mental Health Services. 
The health plan's determination is overturned.

The patient self-referred with the encouragement of family and his treating clinician in the context of severe psychosocial stress within the family constellation and ongoing psychosocial stressors related to his gambling with consequences, as well as worsening symptoms of depression. Medications and outpatient sessions with telemedicine had been ineffective prompting the step up to IOP level services.

Intensive Outpatient Mental Health Services was medically necessary for this patient.
The requested benefit of IOP Level Treatment is clinically appropriate and medically necessary in this case scenario. Moreover, the patient had severe symptoms of gambling addiction, mood and attentional disorders and severe psychosocial stressors with poor impulse control that did warrant the IOP level of care during the time interval under review. The IOP services were medically necessary with the continued psychiatric management of the symptoms of the gambling disorder and associated symptoms of comorbid conditions and psychosocial stressors within the primary support and other psychosocial domains. summary:
Diagnosis: Depression, suicidal ideation, and an inability to function
Treatment: Continued Mental Health Inpatient Admission 
The health plan denied the requested continued mental health inpatient admission as not medically necessary.
The health plan's determination is overturned.

The case involves a young adult female admitted for acute inpatient psychiatric care. The patient presented with worsening symptoms of depression, suicidal ideation with plan to overdose, and an inability to function. She had comorbidity that included an anxiety disorder, an eating disorder associated with restrictive intake and poor appetite, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and borderline personality traits with severe psychosocial stressors that including childhood physical abuse, as well as sexual assault and childhood molestation. At the time of presentation, the patient was anxious and dysphoric with hopelessness, worthlessness, and prominent suicidal thoughts. She had diminished sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, and volition. However, the patient did endorse having nightmares and sleep paralysis, and was noted to have poor control of impulses and urges to self-harm with cutting, as she had a history of self-injury with cutting.

The patient remained depressed with thoughts of suicide and urges to self-harm, and bouts of affective instability. The patient's medications were adjusted with the discontinuation of Cymbalta and the addition of Effexor XR (extended release), together with Lamictal and Buspar with as needed (prn) use of Vistaril and Clonidine and Quetiapine, as well as the supplemental use of Xanax. She was receiving therapeutic interventions to address coping and relationship functioning with identification of triggers regarding self-harming behavior. She had improved mood and functioning with diminished anxiety noted on the day of discharge. The patient's thought processing and content had improved with a more hopeful outlook and improved insight, and the treatment team was discharge planning in keeping with a safety plan, disposition with roommate and family support, and with appropriate aftercare including arrangements for medication management and therapy to continue in an outpatient setting.

The health plan's determination of medical necessity is overturned, in whole.

Yes, the requested health service/treatment of continued mental health inpatient admission was medically necessary for this patient.

The patient's continued inpatient stay and treatment was reasonable and in the best interest of the patient; she had severe symptoms of depression complicated by PTSD, disordered eating and personality disorder with ongoing suicidal ideation and urges to self-harm in the context of affective instability. She had deteriorated to the point that she was unable to function with worsening symptoms of depression that persisted during the time interval under review. The patient also continued to pose a safety risk during the time interval under review as noted in the appeal and contrary to the denial determination. 

The patient's severity of symptoms, functional decline, and risk of relapse necessitated the continued acute inpatient care. The presenting and continuing symptoms of depressive disorder were not amenable to treatment at an alternate level of care during the time interval under review, in view of the worsening depression while in outpatient treatment with ongoing suicidal risk, disordered eating and maladaptive coping in association with borderline personality disorder. The patient's progress notes clearly indicate that the patient displayed continued symptoms that required inpatient level structure and monitoring for the duration of inpatient treatment. Specifically, she remained anxious with persistent symptoms of depression requiring medication adjustments or monitoring and intensive psychotherapy and counseling.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Continued PHP (partial hospitalization program) Substance Use Treatment (0912)
The insurer denied the continued PHP substance use treatment (0912).
The denial is upheld.

The patient is an adult male. Under consideration is treatment at PHP (partial hospitalization program) level of care for five sessions. The original admission had been due to alcohol and cocaine use. The final adverse determination indicates that as 
of the time in question, ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) Criteria were not met for continued PHP. Medical records indicate the patient to have been admitted with 32 days of sobriety from cocaine and alcohol. At the time of intake, mental status exam was normal with PHQ (patient health questionnaire)-9 score of 3. Medical evaluation was also normal, with all vital signs within acceptable parameters. Prior to the time in question, the patient's mood was euthymic with normal mental status findings. Some thoughts and cravings have been present as well as fluctuating but minimal anxiety. Insight and motivation remain superficial and external with some struggles in asking for help. On the initial date in question, the patient participated actively and in an engaged manner in groups. No impairment in interaction with peers or staff was documented. A UDT (urine drug test) was negative. A note revealed some low mood with a great deal of thought about a friend with similar difficulties. Progress is noted to have been inadequate, but the patient is noted to have committed to changing his behaviors. Some anxiety and withdrawal are present.

The continued PHP substance use treatment (0912) was not medically necessary.

The patient was first admitted to PHP the month prior to the dates in question. Under consideration was continuation of PHP. The patient did not continue to demonstrate interpersonal and/or personal skills deficits through interactions with others, he was not demonstrating difficulty managing triggers or urges, he was connected to a social network supportive of recovery goals, he had established a therapeutic alliance with at least one professional helper. Under LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral), he did not meet medical necessity criteria for continued stay at outpatient day rehabilitation (the equivalent of ASAM Level 2.5 PHP).

The patient was noted to have intermittent episodes of irritability and some persistent anxiety and mood symptoms, which were noted to be his baseline and did not represent a significant change.

He was not reported to have any symptoms suggestive of psychosis including hallucinations, delusions, or paranoia. He was not reported to have any significant symptoms suggestive of mania or hypomania. He was not reported to have exhibited any significant and persistent agitation or aggressive behaviors. The patient was not reported to have engaged in any self-injurious behaviors recently and was not reported to have any significant urge. The patient was not reported to have any significant ongoing medical conditions that required interventions or monitoring. He was not reported to have any significant adverse effects from any prescribed psychotropic medications. The patient was not reported to have any significant functional impairments including age-appropriate activities of daily living or self-care that represented a change from his baseline. There was no indication that the patient had any significant barriers to treatment in the community including severe ongoing psychosocial stressors, unsafe living environment or lack of social support. There was no indication that the patient had any significant exacerbation or emergence of new symptoms for the rest of his stay at the residential treatment level of care. There was no indication that the patient continued to exhibit improvements in behavior with ongoing treatment at the residential treatment level of care. The clinical information reviewed indicates that the patient may have been treated safely and effectively in a less restrictive setting and lower level of care.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse.
Treatment: Inpatient Rehabilitation Treatment.
The insurer denied: Inpatient Rehabilitation Treatment.
The denial is upheld.

The patient is an adult male who received detoxification treatment earlier this year and was transferred for inpatient rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment in order to address use of alcohol and stimulant (cocaine) class substances. The patient has no reported history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens though there was a history of severe withdrawal symptoms in the past during detoxification treatment. The substance use included use of up to one pint of alcohol per day, $100 worth of crack cocaine daily and one to three grams of cocaine with inhalation. The patient was also tobacco dependent and had a history of opioid use disorder.

The patient has a history of psychiatric disorder and treatment for bipolar disorder and presented with severe symptoms of depression and anxiety. The patient has a history of psychiatric hospitalizations, and multiple detoxification and substance use disorder treatment episodes with no sustained sobriety or abstinence. The patient was noted to be engaged in the therapeutic activities, social with peers and participating in recovery groups, and adherent with medications. From date of admission to discharge, the patient continued to receive intensive rehabilitation services, monitoring, and structure including 24-hour nursing monitoring and was discharged with clinically appropriate care of his substance use disorders with referral for outpatient level care, and psychiatric follow up for the co-occurring mood disorder. The patient had no significant withdrawal or post-acute withdrawal symptoms other than cravings, no safety concerns, and no biomedical complications. 

The denial was on the basis of Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria indicating that there were no mental health or biomedical issues requiring 24-hour nursing care or inpatient structure and monitoring. The denial determination indicated that residential level care was appropriate in this case. 

The appeal was on the basis of Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria referencing the treatment history and presence of comorbidity requiring active psychiatric management. The issue under review is inpatient rehabilitation substance use disorder services.

The proposed treatment was not medically necessary for this patient. 

In this case, the patient could have been reasonably managed with lower-level care in a less restrictive treatment setting. During the time interval under review, based on the documentation submitted for review, the patient was noted to be in no distress with reasonable functioning and active participation in treatment including positive interactions with staff and peers. Throughout his inpatient stay, there were no complicating treatment issues or biomedical or co-occurring psychiatric issues or safety concerns that would have warranted inpatient level of care, structure or 24-hour nursing monitoring for the time interval under review. The application of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria, as well as Level of Care Utilization System (LOCUS) and the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria referenced below, did indicate that the patient was clinically appropriate for treatment with lower-level care in a less restrictive treatment setting, as the health plan asserts. Thus, medical necessity for the admission and continued rehabilitation substance use disorder services was not met in this case scenario, also consistent with the scientific literature referenced below, as well as prevailing standards of medical practice.

The case involves an adult male who was self-referred with admission to inpatient rehabilitation and substance use disorder treatment to address substance use disorders with alcohol and cocaine. The patient had no history of blackouts or withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens. He had been using up to 1 pints of liquor daily with daily use of cocaine with intranasal administration. He had multiple past treatments with the most recent detoxification immediately prior to his admission. He presented with no significant withdrawal symptoms. He reported craving and urges to use and had drug dreams during his first week of treatment. The patient was a non-smoker.

The patient was described as cooperative with fluent speech and organized thought processing. He displayed euthymic mood with no severe symptoms such as mania, formal thought disorder, psychosis, perceptual disturbance or severe cognitive impairment. He did not report suicidal ideation or aggressive impulses. There were no significant or severe withdrawal symptoms or post-acute withdrawal symptoms, though he had cravings and urges to use. He reported insomnia.

The health plan's determination of medical necessity is upheld, in whole.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance abuse
Treatment: Inpatient Detoxification Treatment
The insurer denied the inpatient detoxification treatment.
The health plan's determination is overturned.

The patient is a male who was self-referred and admitted to acute inpatient level services for detoxification and withdrawal management of Opioid (heroin), stimulant (crack cocaine) and alcohol use disorders. He was drinking two 40 ounce beers daily, using up to five bags of Heroin with intranasal administration and $100 dollars' worth of crack cocaine daily. The patient had experienced severe drug and alcohol withdrawal symptoms in the past and he had a history of blackouts and inadvertent overdoses including two weeks prior to admission. He had received detoxification in the past with relapse and has "no clean time."

The patient has no history of a co-occurring psychiatric disorder and denied psychiatric hospitalization or suicidal and self-harming behaviors.
The patient's physical examination and laboratory assessment were normal or unremarkable except for a positive drug screen consistent with his history. The patient's vital signs remained normal throughout the inpatient stay. His blood alcohol level was zero. The patient was tobacco dependent at one-half pack per day use.
The patient presented with anxiety, insomnia and tremors. He had no severe psychiatric symptoms such as mood disturbance, psychosis, perceptual disorder or cognitive impairment. His Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) scale score was 6 and his Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) scale score was 7 reflecting mild withdrawal symptoms.

The patient was admitted to an acute inpatient level care and placed on a detoxification regimen with a Methadone taper together with vitamin replacement therapy and medical monitoring. He was treated with comfort medications including Benadryl for insomnia.

Following his first day of treatment, the patient began to participate in counseling and educational sessions, as he was feeling better. His mental status examination included persistent symptoms of anxiety with associated symptoms of insomnia. During his inpatient stay, the patient demonstrated no severe symptoms such as mania, psychosis, perceptual disturbance or severe cognitive impairment. The patient completed the detoxification treatment without complications. The patient was discharged with a referral for clinically appropriate aftercare including plans for rehabilitation treatment and a follow up with primary care.

The patient also has severe psychosocial stressors with limited support and functional impairments.

The inpatient services, detoxification treatment and withdrawal management for severe poly-substance use disorder and other services noted in the clinical summary could not have been safely and effectively provided at a lower level of care. Twenty-four-hour monitoring was necessary in view of the severity of the substance use disorders with multiple substances of abuse and the associated psychosocial stressors and impairment of functioning. His withdrawal risk was managed with tapering dosages of Methadone, monitoring and as needed (prn) medications, as well as the availability of comfort medications and vitamin replacement therapy to prevent the onset of encephalopathy. Seizure and fall precautions were provided. Counseling and educational sessions with motivational techniques together with case management services were appropriately provided to motivate the patient's transition for appropriate rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment. Thus, the patient did require a safe and effective detoxification with inpatient level services and withdrawal management during the time frame under review, as it was reasonable that the patient would have been unable to abstain from the substances of abuse or remain in treatment if detoxification and treatment were attempted at a lower level of care.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Substance Abuse Inpatient Rehabilitation Admission
The insurer denied the substance abuse inpatient rehabilitation admission.
The denial is upheld.

The patient is an adult male. He was admitted to inpatient level services for treatment of substance use disorder with cannabis and phencyclidine (PCP) class substances. The patient was referred in the context of legal issues and recent release from 65 days of incarceration for charges of assault. After his release, the patient had begun using PCP, putting himself at risk for re-incarceration, and putting others at risk in view of his history of violence and impulsive aggression. The patient was externally motivated to enter substance abuse rehabilitation treatment with a court date pending. There are co-occurring psychiatric disorders diagnosed in this case including anxiety-depression with poor impulse control associated with bouts of anger. The patient has trauma history with physical and emotional abuse, and complicated grief related to the death of his brother. The patient has prominent history of legal issues including the recent incarceration with court date pending.

The patient's Mental Status Examination revealed no severe symptoms, and the patient was cooperative. He exhibited normal speech, thought processing and functioning. He lacked coping skills and demonstrated limited insight and impaired judgment due to the substance use disorder and his maladaptive coping skills. He reported sleep disturbance with nightmares. He was noted to be at high-risk for impulsive aggression, but denied suicidal ideation, homicidal ideation or aggressive impulses.

Comfort medications were available as needed, and he was prescribed an albuterol inhaler on a prn (as needed) basis together with Claritin and Allegra.

The patient engaged in substance use disorder treatment with active involvement in group and educational sessions, as well as other therapeutic interventions to support healthy living and the development of sober supports. In this regard, the patient worked on coping skills and a relapse prevention plan with the identification of triggers including the negative influence of the social environment and peers. Additionally, there was focus on anger management. The patient did complete the program, and he was discharged with referral for residential treatment.

The health plan's denial of coverage was on the basis of medical necessity and LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) Criteria, indicating that the patient did not warrant inpatient level services and had no general medical, psychiatric, or safety issues that would require inpatient level monitoring. The denial determination indicated that the patient was motivated and had no serious withdrawal symptoms.

The appeal was on the basis of LOCADTR Criteria, with reference to the clinical features, prior treatment episodes with relapses, and the mental status findings including high-risk for impulse aggression.

The substance abuse inpatient rehabilitation admission was not medically necessary.

The inpatient substance abuse rehabilitation treatment in this case scenario was amenable to treatment at a lower level of care. The patient was externally motivated and able to effectively engage in rehabilitation services, and the patient did not need the structure or monitoring of an inpatient setting in order to safely and effectively participate in rehabilitation substance abuse treatment. There were no biomedical or psychiatric complications, or severe psychiatric symptoms/disorders in this case that would have required inpatient level services and treatment. Moreover, the patient was motivated to participate in rehabilitation treatment, as noted in the clinical summary. Thus, the requested inpatient admission was not medically necessary for this patient.

summary:
Diagnosis: Unspecified Depressive Disorder

Treatment: Inpatient Behavioral Health Level of Care, Adult

The insurer denied coverage for Inpatient Behavioral Health Level of Care, Adult

The denial is overturned.

This adult female was admitted to inpatient hospital treatment due to severe depressive symptoms including a recent suicide attempt a few days prior to admission, depressed mood, suicidal thoughts, mood swings, and multiple substance use including alcohol. She reportedly was drinking 6-8 beers per day, using Xanax, Adderall, cocaine, hallucinogens, ketamine, and cannabis. She reportedly had diagnoses of Unspecified Depressive Disorder, Alcohol Use Disorder, Stimulant and Cannabis Use Disorder. She reportedly was in treatment with an outpatient psychiatrist for months. She was taking Desvenlafaxine, Lamotrogine, Trazodone, and Quetiapine. She attended group and individual psychotherapy and was in relational mentalization based therapy. 
  
The medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that the patient required inpatient level of care. The Milliman Care Guidelines (MCG) Behavioral Health Inpatient Level of Care Adult criteria reports that a patient needs to present as an imminent danger to self, imminent danger to others, with severe psychiatric or behavioral symptoms, have a severely dysfunctional living including inability to care for self, unwillingness to participate voluntarily, or a less restrictive level of care is not feasible meet criteria for inpatient behavioral health level of care. InterQual Behavioral Health-Adult Psychiatry-Inpatient medical necessity criteria reports that if one has assaultive behavior within 24 hours, catatonia, command hallucinations to harm self or others, destruction of property with poor impulse control within 24 hours, disorganized behavior, unstable eating disorder, fire setting, homicidal or suicidal attempt within 24 hours, suicidal or  homicidal ideation with high risk for an attempt, mania, risk of harm to self or others, non-suicidal self-injury and continued danger to self, positive psychotic symptoms with risk of harm to self or others, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) with risk of harm to self or others , psychomotor agitation and potential for violence, severe social withdrawal and refusing treatment, unavailable support or inability to provide needed care and supervision and there is acute deterioration, then one still meets criteria for hospital treatment.

In this case the patient was considered at high-risk for suicide due to the recent suicide attempt in the context of severe depression, increased alcohol use and multiple serious substances of use including using Xanax, Adderall, cocaine, hallucinogens, ketamine, and cannabis, as well as stressors including the overdose of a friend and strained family relations. She reportedly made the suicide attempt while under the influence. It was reported that she had limited insight and poor judgment and needed improvement in her coping skills and problems solving skills. 

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Suicidal Behaviors reports also that patients may require more time in the hospital to better assess suicide because they sometimes do not tell the truth regarding their suicidal thoughts in order to leave the hospital and that observation in the hospital is appropriate to better ensure their safety. This patient was considered a high-risk patient with a recent suicide attempt prompting this admission and had reports of severe depression, poor judgment, multiple stressors, and significant alcohol and substance use which put her at even higher risk of harm to self. 

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment in the best interest of the patient.

The insurer's denial of coverage for the Inpatient Behavioral Health Level of Care, Adult, is overturned. Medical Necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Opioid Withdrawal.

Treatment: Inpatient Hospital Admission.

The insurer denied coverage for Inpatient Hospital Admission.

The denial is overturned.

This is a patient admitted to the hospital for treatment of opioid withdrawal. The patient had opioid withdrawal symptoms including nausea and vomiting as much as 20 to 30 times, cold sweats, tachycardia, diarrhea, abdominal pain, poor oral intake, and had a Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Score (COWS) as high as 19. The patient had been drinking codeine a few times per day, taking 2 Percocet pills per day, and smoking cannabis 10 times per day. The patient also has a history of alcohol use. Patient had electrolyte abnormalities including a low potassium of 3.2, CO2 of 19, and bilirubin of 1.6. The patient received detoxification medication for opioid withdrawal including intravenous (IV) Methadone, IV antiemetics, IV Toradol, IV fluids, and Clonidine. Patient continued to have opioid withdrawal until the date of discharge.
  
The medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that the patient required this level of care. The American Psychological Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance, puts patients at high risk for complicated withdrawal. These patients are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. There was a recommendation from the medical team for inpatient substance treatment, but the patient declined. The patient was hemodynamically stable and not considered in further withdrawal at day of discharge. The medical records support that patient was at risk for more severe opioid withdrawal due to the large amount of daily opiate use and was at risk for overdose. Chart reports of inpatient medical issues included severe abdominal pain and electrolyte abnormalities and the patient required and received treatment for detoxification. 

The health plan did not act reasonably, with sound medical judgment or in the best interest of the patient. The insurer's denial of coverage for the inpatient admission is overturned. Medical necessity is substantiated.
