The denial is upheld.

The patient is an adult male with diagnoses of cannabis dependence, cocaine dependence, and alcohol dependence in early full remission. He was admitted to the inpatient rehabilitation level of care. History and physical reports that the patient was seeking admission for rehab for cocaine use. He had been using $100 worth on a daily basis and had last used the day before admission. He also admitted to daily marijuana use. He reported a history of drinking 1 pint of alcohol less than 3 times per week. He denied any withdrawal symptoms from alcohol.

The patient's urine drug screen was positive for cocaine and THC (tetrahydrocannabinol). Behavioral health progress note indicates that the patient stated that he was going to rehab. He declined to state if he had recently detoxed. His vital signs were stable. Counseling note indicates that the patient had no health concerns, was unemployed, and received SSI (supplemental security income) benefits. He reported a diagnosis of bipolar disorder but reported that he was not currently taking any medications. He denied any legal issues.

Behavioral Health consult note the day after admission reports that the patient declined to speak with the physician. It notes that the patient is known for having multiple admissions to the facility. There were no acute medical problems noted. Discharge summary indicates that the patient was discharged against medical advice. Outpatient follow up was arranged.

Coverage was denied by the health plan stating that medical necessity for inpatient substance abuse rehabilitation was not met using LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) guidelines, because the patient was able to participate in treatment outside of a 24-hour structured setting, did not have social, emotional, or developmental barriers to participation in treatment outside the inpatient level of care, did not have a co-occurring medical or psychiatric condition requiring inpatient care, was not at risk for complications from withdrawal, was not suicidal, homicidal, or psychotic, had some motivation to be in treatment, and did not require the 24-hour monitoring of the inpatient rehabilitation level of care. The denial decision was appealed by the treating facility who state that the admission was medically necessary because the patient's long-standing history of substance abuse, his disability, and his current social situation put him at high risk for relapse. The health plan upheld the denial decision using the same rationale as previously.

The Inpatient Rehabilitation Admission was not medically necessary.

Per LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) criteria, the patient does not meet criteria for inpatient rehabilitation services. There is no documentation of lack of a safe environment that can support outpatient treatment. There is no documentation of serious medical symptoms that need to be managed in an inpatient rehab setting in order for substance use disorder treatment to be effective. There is no document in of use in hazardous situations or frequencies likely to imminently cause severe physical or emotional harm to self or others. There is no documentation of interpersonal or personal skills deficits requiring the support of a residential setting. There is no documentation of strong cravings or urges to use that are unmanageable or behavioral or emotional instability. There is no documentation of lack of stable access to food and shelter. As such, the patient does not meet criteria for inpatient rehabilitation level of care per LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) criteria. Since medical necessity typically includes that a treatment or service must be appropriate in terms of setting, inpatient rehab level of care is not medically necessary for the patient.

summary:
Diagnosis: Trauma-Related Symptoms
Treatment: Inpatient Mental Health Services
The insurer denied Inpatient Mental Health Services
The determination is overturned.

The patient presented for partial hospital program treatment to address generalized anxiety disorder, major depressive disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, social anxiety disorder, body dysmorphic disorder and specific phobia. The patient also presented with co-occurring substance use disorder with misuse of benzodiazepines and intermittent use of cannabis. The presentation included worsening symptoms of depression and anxiety with suicidal ideation, a decline in functioning and social isolation, in part due to the pandemic. The patient had no history of psychiatric hospitalization or suicidal behavior; they had an extensive history of outpatient treatment with medication management and psychotherapy. The trauma was related to a sexual assault in high school, as well as witnessing friends who were sexually assaulted.

The patient had severe symptoms of depression, anxiety and anhedonia together with trauma related symptoms evidenced by flashbacks, hypervigilance, nightmares, and dissociation. The patient's mood was dysphoric with low self-worth, decreased energy, appetite sleep disturbance and volition, lower back pain related to scoliosis, and fair motivation for treatment.

The patient was provided treatment with intensive services, sober supports, monitoring, and structure provided within the Partial Hospitalization Program treatment program. The patient received five days per week of services that worked on trauma recovery and substance use disorder counseling. The patient was assessed with quantitative electroencephalography and was provided neurofeedback sessions, family focused sessions, and medication management with use of Wellbutrin, gabapentin and vitamin supplements including methyl folate.

During the Partial Hospitalization Program level treatment, the patient was noted to be making steady progress, however continued to struggle with anxiety. The patient continued to struggle with feelings of sadness, loneliness, resentfulness, and social isolation. There was intermittent use of cannabis during the stay prompting the substance use disorder counseling. Treatments were continued to address the co-occurring psychiatric disturbances and efforts to facilitate family support. 

By the last weeks of Partial Hospitalization Program treatment, the patient's mental status examination showed persistently improved mood and improved insight that was judged to be fair. The patient reported feeling better and was judged to be better motivated to remain in treatment. The patient was discharged to home with their parents and recommended to continue outpatient treatment and participate in sober living. At issue is the medical necessity of Partial Hospital Program Treatment.

The requested treatment of Inpatient Mental Health Services was medically necessary for this patient. The submitted documentation reflects that the services were medically necessary and clinically appropriate regarding the structure, intensity, and duration of treatment. The patient presented with worsening symptoms of their comorbid conditions, a decline in functioning, severe trauma related symptoms and substance abuse. The patient was considered high risk for relapse due to limited coping skills per the clinical summary, deficient recovery environment as well as a history of treatment failure with lower-level services.

Moreover, the patient's psychosocial stressors complicated this case, and the Partial Hospitalization Program level care was medically necessary to provide evidence-based psychosocial therapies and treatment interventions. Sessions also served to address the patient's social environment, recovery environment and family focused sessions with the development of a safe and clinically appropriate disposition and discharge plan.

summary:
Diagnosis: Alcohol withdrawal 
Treatment: Inpatient hospital admission
The insurer denied coverage for inpatient hospital admission
The denial is overturned

This adult male patient was admitted to this inpatient hospital due to alcohol withdrawal symptoms including elevated heart rate of 108, tremors, diaphoresis, anxiety, agitation, and headache, and hyponatremia with a low sodium of 125, increased lactate and anion gap, elevated D-dimer, and chest pain. He reportedly was given Valium 10 mg (milligrams) intravenously (IV) for acute withdrawal in the emergency department (ED) and an additional IV Diazepam for alcohol withdrawal. He reportedly had a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) score of 14 on admission and also a CIWA of 11. He reportedly was drinking up to 6 drinks per day.  His creatine kinase (CK) was very high at 3,347 which was consistent with rhabdomyolysis. He reportedly improved when his CIWA was 0 and sodium was 136. 
  
The medical records provided specific evidence to support that he required this level of care. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. It also reports that patients using large amounts of alcohol or benzodiazepines are at a higher risk of having delirium tremens 3-4 days after cessation of use. It also states that patients with comorbid medical conditions complicating that management of withdrawal are candidates for inpatient hospital treatment. 

In this case, this patient had active alcohol withdrawal symptoms including elevated heart rate of 108, tremors, diaphoresis, anxiety, agitation, and headache and on admission had a CIWA of 14 and had IV Diazepam 10 mg in the ED for detoxification treatment for alcohol withdrawal. He also reportedly had significant comorbid medical conditions including hyponatremia with a low sodium of 125, increased lactate and anion gap, elevated D-dimer, and chest pain and had a cardiac work up and continuous cardiac rhythm monitoring with telemetry as well as nephrology consultation who recommended fluid restrictions. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be overturned. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. The medical necessity for inpatient hospital admission services is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Inpatient Detoxification Treatment
The insurer denied: Inpatient Detoxification Treatment
The denial is overturned.

The patient is an adult male who presented for detoxification and withdrawal management. The patient has a history of severe substance use disorders with daily use of alcohol and stimulants (cocaine) class substances. At the time of presentation, the patient was feeling unwell and requesting detoxification. The patient provided no past history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens but did report severe alcohol withdrawal symptoms and frequent blackouts. He was medically screened and admitted for inpatient level detoxification for a five-day detoxification treatment with Librium and supportive measures. Withdrawal symptoms were moderate with a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) scale score of eight and persistent withdrawal symptoms throughout the stay together with elevated blood pressure and Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) scale score that increased to ten on day two of the inpatient stay. Medical screening drug screen was positive and consistent with history. The patient displayed limited insight and impaired judgment due to the addictions. He demonstrated symptoms of anxiety with generalized symptoms including insomnia, and anxious affect together with symptoms related to the alcohol and cocaine withdrawal, as noted. He was cooperative with normal speech and linear thought processing. Withdrawal symptoms included the anxiety and restlessness, as well as headache and tremor. The patient was admitted for inpatient treatment with detoxification protocol. He received tapering dosages of Librium and replacement of vitamins, as well as nicotine replacement for tobacco dependence with the availability of counseling and comfort medications and as needed (PRN) medications prescribed for pain, anxiety, and insomnia. Vital signs remained abnormal with blood pressure variability, and the patient reported mild anxiety, restlessness and insomnia with persistently mild symptoms of withdrawal that diminished. He was participating in counseling and educational sessions with introduction of 12-step self-help meetings. He was discharged with referral for rehabilitation substance-related treatment. The health plan denied coverage for the requested services on the basis of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria indicating that the patient could have been provided services with lower-level care. The treatment facility indicated that the requested services were medically necessary in keeping with New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Guidelines for the treatment of substance use disorders. 

The requested health service is medically necessary for this patient. 

The patient in this case was using large quantities of alcohol on a daily continuous basis together with cocaine that did warrant the admission and the continued inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring. The patient was at risk for withdrawal seizures and other complications that did necessitate the 24-hour monitoring and withdrawal management. The patient would not have been able to maintain abstinence if treatment were attempted with lower-level services. Medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published guidelines, the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and the scientific literature, and New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews including the appropriate application of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0. summary:
Diagnosis: Substance and alcohol abuse
Treatment: Inpatient substance use rehabilitation treatment
The health plan denied the requested inpatient substance use rehabilitation treatment as not medically necessary.
The health plan's determination is upheld.

This adult male patient was admitted for inpatient substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment to address alcohol, opioid, and stimulant (crack cocaine) class substances of abuse. The patient had no history of withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens, or other episodes of severe withdrawal symptoms. He had a history of substance use disorder with multiple prior detoxification treatments and participation in a methadone maintenance treatment program with continued use of substances. He reported having a daily use of alcohol, heroin and crack cocaine while receiving 55 milligrams (mg) of methadone through the methadone clinic.

The patient has a history of a psychiatric disorder and treatment for bipolar disorder with depression, including history of psychiatric hospitalization. Additionally, the patient reported multiple accidental overdoses.

There were no acute general medical issues in this case; the patient had been medically screened at the time of his admission for substance-related treatments, and generally had normal vital signs and no severe withdrawal or post-acute withdrawal symptoms, though he reported craving and urges to use substances. He was an every-day smoker at one pack per day with 30 pack-years.

Throughout the inpatient stay, the patient was engaged in treatment with intensive services, sober housing, monitoring, and structure provided within the residential treatment program. The patient was social with peers and participating actively in treatment with continued risk for relapse; the patient had no severe withdrawal symptoms or post-acute withdrawal symptoms and he had no complications with respect to biomedical, general medical, emotional or other treatment domains. Progress notes reflected stable mood with sleep, appetite, and energy that were okay. He was prescribed Lisinopril, Zyrtec, Lexapro, and low-dose Quetiapine at clinically appropriate dosages with tolerability and positive effect. The patient was discharged against medical advice due to issues with his social security check, but with plans to immediately return to outpatient level treatment with the methadone program and with a recommendation for continued involvement in recovery groups.

The requested health service/treatment of inpatient substance use rehabilitation treatment was not medically necessary for this patient. The patient in this case scenario was not clinically appropriate for the inpatient rehabilitation level of care during the time interval under review. The patient did not need the intensity or duration or 24-hour nursing staff monitoring of an inpatient level of care. The patient was motivated and engaged with treatment and involved with peer supported recovery groups while continuing medication assisted treatment with methadone. Thus, the health plan's determination was reasonable in this scenario. He readily engaged in treatment with continued use of methadone and comfort medications and medications to treat the mood disorder and associated symptoms of anxiety and insomnia. During the time interval under review, the patient was noted to be in no apparent distress with active participation in treatment including positive interactions with staff and peers. There were no treatment issues or biomedical or co-occurring psychiatric disturbances that would have warranted the admission or the continued inpatient level of care.

summary:
Diagnosis: Depressive Disorder.
Treatment: Inpatient hospital admission.
The insurer denied coverage for inpatient hospital admission.
The denial is overturned.

This patient was admitted to this hospital due to worsened depressive symptoms including suicidal thoughts as she wrote a suicide note which was found by the school staff. She reportedly was brought by EMS (emergency medical services) to the hospital. She reportedly had trauma issues and victimization issues including reports that she was sexually molested at an early age by a family friend and reported being sexually molested by her sister's boyfriend. She also reported that an ex-boyfriend tried to rape her. She reported nightmares regarding the trauma. She reported feeling hopeless, depressed in mood, tearful, guarded, and was impulsive. She reportedly had 3 past suicide attempts including 2 by overdose and one by cutting. She reportedly had 2 past hospitalizations including a 6 week stay for a serious suicide attempt by overdose. She reportedly had a cutting suicide attempt a few months prior to admission. She reportedly had a history of eloping. She reportedly had a diagnosis of Depressive Disorder. She reportedly continued to express suicidal thoughts with plan that she would not reveal and had a few self-injurious behavior episodes by cutting even on the unit. She reportedly took Prozac for depression and anxiety. She reportedly was on 1:1 observation for suicidality. She eventually improved enough for discharge.

The Interqual  Child and Adolescent Psychiatry guidelines report that  if symptoms were present it included at least one of the following: assaultive behavior, catatonia, command auditory hallucinations, destruction of property, disorganized behavior, unstable eating disorder symptoms, endangering behavior, fire setting, suicidal or homicidal attempt, homicidal ideation with a high risk of an attempt, mania, non-suicidal self-injury with continued danger to self, positive psychotic symptoms with risk of harm to self or others, mania and associated symptoms, psychomotor agitation or retardation, suicidal ideation with high risk of attempt, or support unavailable or unable to provide needed care or supervision. Also, if symptoms improved but the patient was not clinically stable for discharge or was a high risk for rehospitalization or a high risk of harm to self or others then criteria would have still been met. In this case this patient had severe psychiatric symptoms including suicidal ideation with plans which she would not reveal, self-injurious behavior while in the hospital and on 1:1 observation for suicidality, continued to have depressive symptoms, and was considered a high risk for suicide due to past suicide attempts including a serious one and attempts at self-injurious behavior even while in this hospital.  

The health plan did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment in the best interest of the patient.

The insurer's denial of coverage for the inpatient hospital admission is overturned. Medical Necessity is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Cannabis dependence, substance abuse, alcohol abuse, schizophrenia
Treatment: Substance Abuse Inpatient Rehabilitation Level of Care
The insurer denied the substance abuse inpatient rehabilitation level of care.
The health plan's determination is upheld.

The patient is a male who was admitted to inpatient rehabilitation for the substance use disorder treatment of stimulant (cocaine), alcohol, hallucinogen (phencyclidine [PCP]), and cannabis (marijuana). Despite participating in a court ordered treatment program, the patient was using cocaine intermittently with intranasal administration with daily use of marijuana (one blunt) and PCP and intermittent use of alcohol with four nips up to six times per week. The patient was also tobacco dependent with light use. His referral was prompted by repeated "dirty urines" with a mandate for rehabilitation treatment. He had a history of multiple past substance use disorder treatment episodes with the more recent rehabilitation treatment seven months prior to admission and ongoing outpatient treatment with supervised monitoring with court oversight.

The patient has no acute general medical issues that were a focus of treatment. He did report chronic pain due to dental problems and joint pain. The patient was medically cleared at the time of admission and his laboratory assessment was normal or unremarkable with a positive drug screen for tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and PCP and cocaine consistent with his history.

There was a co-occurring psychiatric disorder with a diagnosis of schizophrenia. The patient denied suicidal behavior but had a history of at least one psychiatric hospitalization. He was not taking his prescribed Risperidone due to side effects and intolerance.

The mental status examination revealed a cooperative male with clear speech and linear thought processing that was goal directed. The patient's mood was anxious with congruent affect. The patient's thought content included no morbid thoughts. The patient had auditory hallucinations and his insight was limited with impaired judgment due to his addictions. The patient also had sleep disturbance with insomnia.

The inpatient level substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment included the opportunity to participate in groups, individual counseling, educational sessions and recovery groups with peer support. He actively participated in individual, group and educational sessions. He was prescribed Olanzapine titrated to 20 milligrams (mg) together with Trazodone and vitamins with the availability of nicotine replacement therapy throughout his stay. He was also prescribed Bactrim and analgesics and muscle relaxants to address his general medical conditions.

The health plan, in its determination of medical necessity, did act reasonably, with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient. As the health plan asserts, the patient's alcohol, stimulant (cocaine), hallucinogen (PCP), and cannabis use disorders and co-occurring psychiatric disorder were amenable to treatment at a lower level of care in this case scenario.  

The requested health service/treatment of substance abuse inpatient rehabilitation level of care was not medically necessary for the patient. The structure and intensity of services necessary for the rehabilitation/substance use disorder treatment could have been effectively provided at a lower level of care in a less restrictive treatment setting with sober supports. 

The patient was motivated and was capable of effectively receiving substance use disorder treatment in a less restrictive treatment setting with sober supports and/or housing. The patient did not need the structure of an inpatient setting in order to effectively participate in rehabilitation substance abuse treatment, or to receive effective treatment for the co-occurring disorder (schizophrenia).

The patient had manic symptoms and past suicidal thoughts and a recent suicide attempt which prompted a psychiatric hospitalization but as of later date, there was no specific documented evidence to support that only acute psychiatric hospital treatment was required. Notes reported that the patient did not have suicidal thoughts or plans and was free from suicidal thoughts or plan. Notes reported that the patient was doing well and discussing feelings. It also reported that the patient was not suicidal and had overall improvement, no delusions, or hallucinations, had full range affect, normal speech, no psychomotor dysfunction, denied suicidal or homicidal ideation, plan, or intent, and had cooperative and calm behavior. He had no past history of withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens, or severe withdrawal symptoms, but did report frequent blackouts in the context of alcohol use. He had longstanding co-occurring mood and anxiety disorders best characterized as an unspecified depressive disorder and anxiety disorder treated with Wellbutrin and Lexapro. As noted, he had a decline in functioning related to the alcohol use. There was no history of suicidal behavior or psychiatric hospitalization. 

The evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination that was free of severe psychiatric symptoms such as psychosis, severe cognitive impairment, or perceptual disturbance. He was anxious and cooperative and superficially motivated for treatment in the contemplative stage of change. He displayed mood disturbance with affective lability, as well as hopelessness, shame and guilt. He had fluent speech and circumstantial and tangential thought processing that was goal directed. He had no aggressive impulses. He reported sleep disturbance. He had support from his family. His insight and judgment were characterized as limited and impaired with poor control of impulses. 

The patient had no acute general medical conditions. He was medically screened and had elevated blood pressure, elevated liver functions and mild withdrawal symptoms per the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA). 

The patient is married and college educated and employed and is living with his wife. Stressors included primary support and social environment domains, as well as other psychosocial stressors associated with the alcohol use disorder and health concerns. 

The patient received residential rehabilitation treatment that included focus on coping skills, relapse prevention techniques with identification of triggers, education about the disease model of addiction, and involvement with recovery groups as well as sessions with motivational techniques. The patient engaged in treatment with intensive services, sober housing, monitoring, and structure provided within the residential treatment program. During the residential stay, the patient had a brief period of detoxification treatment with Librium. The patient was considered at high risk for relapse and lacking coping skills; the risk diminished near the time of discharge though he continued to need work on identification of triggers and treatment of the co-occurring anxiety and depression. 

The need for a disposition with sober supports and family-focused therapy to address the issues within the family constellation are other factors that support the necessity for continued residential level services and the requested benefit through discharge.

summary:
Diagnosis: Polysubstance Use
Treatment: Inpatient Rehabilitation Treatment
The insurer denied: Inpatient Rehabilitation Treatment
The denial is Upheld.

The patient is an adult male with history of polysubstance abuse who was admitted to the inpatient rehabilitation level of care. The comprehensive evaluation note states the patient admitted to drinking 1-2 pints of rum daily and smoking $100 to $200 worth of crack cocaine daily. He also admitted to marijuana use 3 to 6 times per week. He had been admitted for detox multiple times previously and had most recently left rehab against medical advice 5 months ago. He reported a history of depression and post-traumatic stress disorder, which were diagnosed 4 years ago but stated that he only took medications while in rehab. He denied suicidal ideation, homicidal ideation, and hallucinations. He denied depressed mood and anxiety symptoms, and the psychiatric evaluation note states that no psychiatric intervention was warranted. The patient denied current withdrawal symptoms. He denied any comorbid medical conditions. He noted that he was homeless at the time of admission. The against medical advice nursing note indicates the patient requested discharge and stated he planned to travel to Florida. At issue is the inpatient rehabilitation level of care. Coverage was denied by the health plan as not medically necessary because the patient did not have any medical or mental health concerns that required 24 hour per day nursing support, nor did the patient meet Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral 3.0 (LOCADTR 
3) for substance use inpatient rehabilitation treatment. It notes the patient's care could be safely addressed in a less restrictive level of care such as stabilization services in a residential 
setting. The decision was appealed by the treating facility, who state that the patient met criteria for the inpatient rehab level of care. 

The proposed treatment was not medically necessary.

Per New York State Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0, the patient does not meet criteria for the inpatient rehabilitation level of care. There is no 
documentation of serious psychiatric or medical symptoms that need to be managed in an inpatient rehab setting for substance use disorder treatment to be effective. There is no documentation that the patient abuses substances in hazardous situations, in amounts or frequencies likely to imminently cause severe physical or emotional harm to self or others. There is no documentation of strong cravings or urges to use that are unmanageable or behavioral or emotional instability. As such, criteria for the inpatient rehabilitation level of care are not met. The definition of medical necessity generally includes that a treatment must be considered effective for the patient's condition and not primarily for the convenience of the patient or provider. Since the inpatient rehabilitation level of care does not fit this definition in this case, it is not medically necessary for the patient.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder
Treatment: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS)
The insurer denied the request for Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation. 
The health plan's determination is overturned.

The patient is a female with a history of major depression. She has had numerous trials of antidepressant medications. She has a several year history of failed cognitive behavioral therapy in addition to numerous trials of medications many at maximum doses. 
At issue is the medical necessity for the requested health service/treatment of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS).

The health plan in its determination of medical necessity did not act reasonably with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.

The TMS (Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation) treatment is medically necessary for this patient. The patient has evidence of significant treatment resistant depression which did not respond to 7 (seven) antidepressant regimens. Five of these antidepressants were used at maximum doses and combination strategies were used to improve outcomes. The claimant has also failed a prolonged course of cognitive behavioral therapy.
The patient also shows evidence of current symptoms that are impairing based on their depression. Given the above, transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is a medically necessary treatment which would be in the best interest of the patient. The TMS is Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved and a proven effective treatment for treatment-resistant depression. There is copious evidence that TMS is effective for the treatment of depression, particularly in treatment resistant cases and there is wide consensus in the psychiatric community that use of TMS provides significant results and improvement for patients (Irarte and George, 2018,. Perera et al., 2016, and Burke et al., 2019).

The health plan's determination of medical necessity is overturned in whole.

summary:

The patient has a history of withdrawal seizures and frequent blackouts, but no history of delirium tremens. He had an extensive history of detoxification treatments and rehabilitation treatment with relapses; the more recent substance related treatment was 7 months ago when he had left treatment against medical advice (AMA). During his longstanding use of alcohol, he reported only four months of abstinence. Upon admission to inpatient level services, the patient received comprehensive evaluation and treatment that included focus on coping skills, relapse prevention techniques with identification of 
triggers, education about the disease model of addiction, and involvement with groups, as well as peer-supported recovery meetings. He agreed to medication-assisted treatment with naltrexone/Vivitrol. He received intensive rehabilitation services, monitoring, and structure including 24-hour nursing monitoring and was discharged after completion of 21 days of inpatient rehabilitation treatment with referral for clinically appropriate care as an outpatient with MAT (medication-assisted treatment) and plan to work on developing sober supports, as well as arrangements for general medical care.

During the time interval under review, the patient had no significant withdrawal or post-acute withdrawal symptoms, no safety concerns, and no psychiatric or biomedical complications. summary:
Diagnosis: Polysubstance Abuse (Cocaine, Cannabis, Alcohol, Nicotine). 
Treatment: Substance Abuse Inpatient Rehabilitation Admission. 

The insurer denied the substance abuse inpatient rehabilitation admission. 
The health plan's determination is upheld. 

The patient is a male who was admitted to inpatient rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment of stimulant (cocaine), alcohol, and cannabis (marijuana) use disorders. The patient was using cocaine with intranasal administration together with daily use of marijuana (2 to 3 blunts) and use of alcohol with one nip and two beers. The patient was also tobacco dependent at one pack per day. His referral was prompted by his desire to stop using substances of abuse after longstanding use for half of his life. He had a history of multiple past substance use disorder treatment episodes with the more recent rehabilitation treatment with up to 14 months of sobriety. 

The patient has poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and he presented with an elevated glucose, as well as an elevated blood pressure with no history of hypertension. There were no other acute general medical issues that were a focus of treatment. The patient was medically cleared at the time of admission and his laboratory assessment was normal or unremarkable other than elevated blood glucose determinations and a positive drug screen consistent with history. There was no co-occurring psychiatric disorder or history of psychiatric hospitalization or suicidal behavior. 

The mental status examination revealed a cooperative male with clear speech and linear thought processing that was goal directed. His mood was anxious with congruent affect. The patient's thought content included no morbid thoughts. He had no evidence of cognitive impairment, perceptual disturbance, mood disturbance or psychosis. His insight was limited with impaired judgment due to the addictions. He had sleep disturbance with insomnia. 

The inpatient level substance-related rehabilitation treatment included the opportunity to participate in groups, individual counseling, educational sessions, and recovery groups with peer support. The patient easily transitioned to rehabilitation treatment. He actively participated in individual, group, and educational sessions. He was prescribed Gabapentin, Melatonin, Trazodone and vitamins with the availability of nicotine replacement therapy throughout his stay. 

Discharge planning occurred that included a recommendation for continued aftercare upon completion of the program. The patient was cooperative and engaged throughout his inpatient stay with reasonable motivation and participation in therapeutic activities. He indicated that he was going to remain sober. There were no psychiatric or biomedical complications during his stay with discharge. 

The structure and intensity of services necessary for the rehabilitation/substance use disorder treatment could have been effectively provided at a lower level of care in a less restrictive treatment setting with sober supports. There is no evidence that the inpatient level structure and 24-hour nursing monitoring is medically necessary for a successful outcome in this case. There were no biomedical, psychiatric, or general medical issues that warranted the requested inpatient level services. The diabetes and elevated blood pressures were amenable to management with lower-level services. 

The patient was motivated and was capable of effectively receiving substance use disorder treatment in a less restrictive treatment setting with sober supports and/or housing. The patient did not need the structure of an inpatient setting in order to effectively participate in rehabilitation substance abuse treatment, or to receive effective treatment for a co-occurring disorder (schizophrenia).

The patient is an adult male. He was admitted to inpatient level substance use disorder rehabilitation services. His presentation for substance-related treatment was prompted by a decline in functioning and in the context of escalating use cocaine together with co-occurring psychiatric disorders, depression and anxiety.
The patient had no acute medical issues. However, 2 years ago the patient had a stroke related to the heavy cocaine use with residual hemiplegia. The patient's mental status examination included a disheveled and cooperative male with clear speech and thoughts that were organized, and goal directed. There were concentration difficulties. He reported low energy and sleep disturbance. Insight was limited and judgment impaired, and he had poor control of impulses. The treatment provided structure, monitoring, and the intensity of inpatient level services, which included intensive rehabilitation services with sober supports and monitoring for abstinence. Treatment included group, individual, and educational services with emphasis on coping skills, and 
with the goal of the development of a relapse prevention plan. The patient received psychotropic medications included mirtazapine and prn (as needed) use of Vistaril, as well as nicotine replacement. There was the opportunity to participate in 12-step recovery groups with assignments, and he worked with peers to address relapse issues and identification of triggers to use cocaine. The patient struggled with PAWS (post-acute-withdrawal syndrome) that diminished with persistent craving, and sleep disturbance, as noted, with prn (as needed) medications. During his brief inpatient stay, the patient continued to display co-occurring symptoms of the mood disorder and the lack of coping skills. Thus, the patient focused on the development of better coping skills, and participated in mindfulness training, and continued working on a relapse prevention plan. By the day of discharge, arrangements were completed with discharge and step down to lower-level care in the community with continued substance use disorder and psychiatric services, and encouragement to participate in recovery groups with the obtainment of a sponsor.

The Inpatient Rehabilitation Admission was medically necessary.

The inpatient rehabilitation services were medically necessary in order to address issues related to relapse with focus on a relapse prevention plan and additional work on developing coping skills in a case that poses high risk for relapse; in order to address co-morbid psychiatric disorders with medication adjustments; in order to address the patient's lack of awareness of the seriousness of his illness with psycho-education and evidence-based psychosocial interventions; in order to address the social environment including development of a safe and clinically appropriate discharge plan and disposition; and in order to work on coping skills that will be necessary in building an effective sober support system and continued recovery efforts with community providers while maintaining his abstinence with peer supported recovery groups. None of this therapeutic work could have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in view of the multiple, complicating factors in this case, the high risk for relapse, the treatment history with relapses and continued use of substances despite access to treatment, and the lack of a reasonable recovery environment that includes high risk behaviors, and the patient's initial ambivalence towards treatment or lack of commitment to a recovery process.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major depressive disorder 
Treatment: Mental Health Residential Treatment Center
The insurer denied coverage for Mental Health Residential Treatment Center
The denial is overturned
 

This young adult was admitted to this inpatient mental health residential treatment due to mood instability, poor coping skills, emotional dysregulation, suicidal thoughts, anxiety symptoms, interpersonal struggles, and a history of self-harm behaviors. She reportedly had past suicide attempts by overdose within the past year prior to admission with resulting psychiatric hospitalizations. She had multiple psychotherapists and past medication trials including Lexapro, Prozac, Effexor, Trazodone, Wellbutrin, Lamictal, Abilify, Latuda, Seroquel, Risperidone, Ativan, Buspirone, Klonopin, and ketamine treatments, and she also had electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) treatments without efficacy reported. She had diagnoses of Borderline Personality Disorder, Bipolar Depression, and Generalized Anxiety Disorder. She was attending several Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) groups and individual treatment per day including DBT skills acquisition group, DBT skills struggle group, DBT skills activity group, and resident led DBT activity group. 
  
The reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient mental health residential treatment as this was a high-risk patient in need of a 24-hour inpatient therapeutic inpatient mental health residential treatment. The Milliman Care Guidelines (MCG) Residential-Behavioral Health Level of Care- guidelines report that one needs to have continued danger to self or others, moderately or severe psychiatric or behavioral symptoms requiring 24-hour daily treatment, or serious dysfunction in daily living. In this case this patient had moderate psychiatric symptoms and did not have the coping skills to deal with her multiple psychiatric issues and was a high risk for another suicide attempt without this structured treatment setting. She was a complex patient with multiple psychiatric diagnoses including Borderline Personality Disorder, Bipolar Depression, and Generalized Anxiety Disorder. She had multiple psychiatric diagnoses and symptoms and required more time in a 24-hour inpatient therapeutic residential treatment to learn sustained improved coping skills to decrease dangerous and maladaptive behaviors and use health coping skills and better regulate emotions to not use maladaptive behaviors such as self-harm and suicidal behaviors. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be overturned. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. 

The medical necessity for Mental Health Residential Treatment Center is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Polysubstance Abuse
Treatment: Inpatient Detoxification Admission
The insurer denied: Inpatient Detoxification Admission
The denial is overturned

This patient is an adult male who presented for detoxification treatment and was medically screened and admitted to acute inpatient level care in order to address substance use disorder with opioid, alcohol, and sedative-hypnotic-anxiolytic class substance use disorders. The patient had been using one-half pint of liquor together with ten bags of heroin with IV (intravenous) administration and with 2-4 (two to four) mg (milligrams) of Xanax, as well as intermittent use of cocaine with $ (dollars) 20 worth 1-2 (one to two) times per week. He had a history of prior detoxification and substance use disorder treatments with relapses. There was also a history of overdoses and suicidal ideation when using. His self-referral for treatment was prompted by multiple stressors and general health concerns. The patient presented without acute co-morbid general medical issues. He was tobacco dependent. Laboratory assessments were unremarkable or normal with a positive drug screen consistent with history. He did not report trauma or abuse history or legal issues. He had good social supports from family. Evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination that was free of severe psychiatric symptoms. The patient denied suicidal or homicidal ideation and did not have perceptual disturbances. Insight was limited with impaired judgment and poor control of impulses. His onset of mild withdrawal symptoms included anxiety, motor agitation, sweats, body aches, and tremor, scoring a 9 (nine) on the CIWA (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol) scale and 10 (ten) on the COWS (Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale) scale. The patient was admitted to detoxification treatment with a comprehensive detoxification protocol with tapering dosages of Ativan and Methadone and as needed medications for comfort, as well as vitamin replacement therapy. The program provided for case management with referral and access to rehabilitation treatment that included comprehensive evidence-based treatments. During detoxification the patient engaged in counseling sessions focusing on education about the disease model of addiction, and involvement with unit activities including peer support and educational sessions to motivate the patient to proceed to rehabilitation treatment. The patient completed the detoxification treatment and was discharged on Day #7 with referrals for clinically appropriate aftercare.

The proposed treatment of an Inpatient Detoxification Admission is "medically necessary" for this patient. 

The requested inpatient admission and continued treatment could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. The patient in this case was using heroin, together with alcohol and Xanax on a daily continuous basis with intermittent use of cocaine that did warrant inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring for the duration of the protocol; detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments pertinent to the detoxification treatment episode could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment that was provided at the time of admission. Moreover, the patient had a positive drug screen that included opioids and Benzodiazepines, as well as Methadone and cocaine. He had mild and persistent withdrawal symptoms, and the patient's social environment was not conducive to detoxification in the context of limited insight, impaired judgment and poor control of impulses. 
Therefore, medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published practice guidelines, ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) Criteria, and the scientific literature, referenced below, and New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews including the appropriate application of the NY State OASAS (Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (Level of Care Determination) Tool that requires the patient in this scenario to be defaulted to the higher level of care.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder
Treatment: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) Therapy Session(s)
The health plan denied the requested Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) Therapy Session(s) as not medically necessary.
The health plan's determination is overturned.

Clinical Summary: The patient is an adult female with a longstanding history of major depressive disorder, recurrent and severe without psychotic features. The patient has a documented history of multiple medication treatments for depression including treatment with more than two disparate classes of medication and at least four or more six-week or longer trials with antidepressant medications (Wellbutrin, Lexapro, Luvox, Effexor). Additionally, the patient has received augmentation with second generation antipsychotic medications (Vraylar and Seroquel) and Lamotrigine without a sustained clinical response or remission and/or with adverse effect. She has been treated with an evidence-based psychotherapy. She has not received electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) or vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) therapy. At the time of evaluation for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) therapy, the patient health questionnaire (PHQ-9) score was 25, in the severe range for symptoms of depression associated with severe impairment of functioning.

The patient has reportedly not had psychiatric hospitalization or suicide attempts or suicidal behavior. There is no report of other co-morbid psychiatric disorders or co-occurring substance use disorders in this case. The patient has no significant or acute general medical issues.

Mental status examination reveals depressed mood, sad affect with anxiety, and anhedonia together with hopelessness. She has loss of interest and low energy and other neuro-vegetative disturbances related to depression. Again, PHQ-9 score was at 25 at the time of evaluation for TMS therapy.

The health plan's determination of medical necessity is overturned, in whole.

The requested health service/treatment of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) is medically necessary for this patient.

The services proposed are in keeping with prevailing standards of medical practice for the condition under treatment in this case with an evidence-based augmentation treatment for depressive disorder with TMS therapy; and the requested service/treatment in this case is clinically appropriate, and is backed by credible scientific evidence known to benefit patients with the condition and clinical features in this case scenario.

In this case, at least four alternative therapeutic trials with augmentation together with other therapeutic measures have been provided, and the proposed treatment with TMS therapy is considered clinically appropriate and medically necessary. Additionally, the use of TMS therapy is reasonable, and in the best interest of the patient. The decision to proceed with TMS therapy reflects sound medical judgment based upon the current scientific literature and American Psychiatric Association practice guidelines concerning the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorder. The patient in this case has demonstrated that her depressive disorder is treatment refractory or resistant, and the proposed treatment of recurrent major depressive disorder using TMS therapy with a clinically appropriate number of sessions is warranted in this case scenario, and is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice.

summary:
Diagnosis: Oppositional defiant disorder (ODD)

Treatment: Inpatient care

The insurer denied coverage for Inpatient care

The denial is modified.

 
This teenager was admitted to inpatient mental health treatment due to mood and behavioral symptoms including mood swings, emotional dysregulation, oppositional defiant behavior, agitation, property destruction, self-injurious behavior including hitting self, lying, stealing, using profanities, talking about drugs, disrespectful behavior towards others, physical altercations, risky behaviors, impulsive behaviors, and difficulty following rules. He had a diagnosis of Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). He took Risperidone and Lamictal and attended group, individual, and family therapy. 

The Milliman Care Guidelines (MCG) Residential-Behavioral Health Level of Care- Psychiatry Child/Adolescent guidelines report that one needs to have continued danger to self or others, moderately or severe psychiatric or behavioral symptoms requiring 24-hour daily treatment, or serious dysfunction in daily living. The InterQual Behavioral Health Child/Adolescent Psychiatry Inpatient Level of Care residential treatment guidelines reports that one still has psychiatric or behavioral symptoms that put the patient at high risk for hospitalization if not in this 24-hour treatment, that they still have psychiatric or behavioral symptoms that are improving or expected to improve but they are not clinically stable yet. It also states that one could still have symptoms including disorganized behavior, command auditory hallucinations decreasing in frequency, delinquent behavior, still have a major depressive episode with certain symptoms including hopelessness, have high risk sexual behavior, eating disorder symptoms requiring 24-hour treatment, hypomanic symptoms associated with poor impulse control, or psychomotor agitation. 

In this case this patient did have continued reported psychiatric symptoms that were improving or expected to improve but were not clinically stable yet. He was considered at risk for worsened behavioral and mood symptoms if not in this inpatient therapeutic supervised and structured residential treatment due to his limited coping skills and problems solving skills, limited ability to regulate his emotions, and risky and impulsive behavior putting himself and others at risk including agitation, property destruction, self-injurious behavior including hitting self, stealing, physical altercations, risky behaviors, impulsive behaviors, and difficulty following rules. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be modified. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. 

The medical necessity for residential mental health treatment is partially substantiated but the insurer's denial is upheld in part.

summary:
Diagnosis:  Substance abuse.
Treatment:  Inpatient substance abuse admission.

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient substance abuse admission.  The denial is overturned.

This adult patient was admitted to inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment. He reportedly was using $100 per day of crack/cocaine, drinking a 6 pack of beer daily, and using $10 per day of cannabis. He reportedly requested inpatient substance rehabilitation in order to learn better coping skills to achieve sobriety and needed a structured environment to assist in this. He reportedly had diagnoses of Cocaine Use Disorder, Cannabis Use Disorder, and Alcohol Use Disorder. He reportedly was unemployed. He had a positive toxicology for cocaine and tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). He had past inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatments and still was unable to maintain sustained abstinence. He attended group therapy including mindfulness to try to learn better coping skills for abstinence. 

The medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that he required this inpatient level of care. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that inpatient treatment is indicated primarily for individuals whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. 

In this case this patient was considered in need of 24-hour substance rehabilitation treatment as he reportedly was using large amounts of serious substances daily including $100 per day of crack/cocaine and a six pack of beer daily as well as $10 worth of cannabis daily. This put him at risk of medical consequences to cocaine use and also at risk for overdose and for alcohol withdrawal. He reportedly lacked the coping skills and ability to identify relapse triggers to stop use. According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) he met criteria for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment as he continued to use large amounts of cocaine, cannabis, and alcohol use despite multiple past inpatient substance treatments and a past inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment, and still relapsed and could not maintain abstinence. He reportedly had a substance using social network which contributed to his relapse and continued use. He reportedly lacked enough sober support to maintain abstinence outside of this 24-hour supervised and structured inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment as he was considered a high risk to continue use. He reportedly lacked coping skills, needed to better identify relapse triggers, and needed to learn relapse prevention skills. He was unable to stop substance use without being in a sober and supervised therapeutic inpatient substance rehabilitation setting then. Without this structured and supervised therapeutic rehabilitation treatment he likely would have relapsed quickly again. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be overturned. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. The medical necessity for the inpatient substance abuse admission is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse/Addiction
Treatment: Substance Abuse: Inpatient
The insurer denied Substance Abuse: Inpatient
The determination is upheld.

This patient received inpatient level of care for substance use disorders. Diagnoses included alcohol use disorder, cocaine use disorder, and cannabis use disorder. The patient had a history of substance use problems dating back to age 16. The patient had been smoking crack cocaine 4 to 5 days weekly prior to admission and drinking alcohol and smoking cannabis. The patient had a history of overdose on fentanyl laced crack cocaine about one month prior to treatment. 

The patient reported that their family was supportive of them seeking substance use disorder treatment. They have a daughter and two granddaughters. The patient is married. The patient was reported as being motivated for recovery and participatory in various groups and other therapeutic offerings. At issue is the medical necessity of the requested health service/treatment of inpatient admission at the rehabilitation level of care.

The requested health service/treatment of inpatient admission was not medically necessary for this patient.
The patient did not have a life-threatening medical condition or severe psychiatric crisis. The patient clearly met criteria for multiple substance use disorders. The patient was not in full remission from a substance use disorder. The patient did not have serious medical symptoms that needed to be managed in an inpatient rehabilitation setting. The patient did not have serious psychiatric symptoms that needed to be managed in an inpatient rehabilitation setting. The patient had used in hazardous situations including using fentanyl laced cocaine. The patient did not need an inpatient rehabilitation setting to safely address cognitive or behavioral impairment leading to substance use. Based on documentation, the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Level of Care is: Stabilization Services in a Residential Setting.

summary:
Diagnosis: opioid withdrawal symptoms

Treatment is medically supervised inpatient detoxification

The insurer denied coverage for medically supervised inpatient detoxification

The denial is overturned

This adult male was admitted to the inpatient substance detoxification treatment for opioid detoxification treatment. He reportedly had opioid withdrawal symptoms including abdominal cramps, gastrointestinal upset, chills, tremors, fatigue, nausea, irritable mood, anxiety, joint pain, loose stools, body aches, restlessness, yawning, gooseflesh, and change in pupil size. It was reported that his COWS score (The Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale) was 13, and then 11, 10, and 9 so he still had withdrawal symptoms reported even while taking Methadone. He reportedly had a past inpatient substance detoxification treatment but did not complete it. He reportedly was discharged with an admission date to another facility for further substance rehabilitation treatment.
   
This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient substance detoxification treatment as the medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that he required this level of care. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. In this case this patient used multiple substances daily in large amounts, so he was at risk for severe withdrawal and overdose and required inpatient medical hospital detoxification treatment. 

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), he did require 24-hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive setting as he continued to use serious substances despite past recent inpatient substance treatment a few weeks prior to this admission, and he needed detoxification medication, Methadone, to modify withdrawal from opioids. He reportedly was taking Methadone and still had reported withdrawal during some of the detoxification treatment so he was at risk of severe withdrawal if not in this setting. He reportedly lacked sober support which resulted in his relapse so he likely could not stop use and get detoxification treatment if not in this 24-hour inpatient detoxification treatment setting. He also likely would have relapsed again as evidenced by relapsing after a recent past inpatient substance detoxification treatment in which he did not complete.

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be overturned. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. The medical necessity for medically supervised inpatient detoxification services is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Polysubstance Abuse 
Treatment: Inpatient Hospital Stay 
The insurer denied the inpatient hospital stay. 
The health plan's determination is overturned. 

The patient is a male who was self-referred and admitted to acute inpatient level services for detoxification and withdrawal management of opioid (Percocet) use disorder. He was using up to 90 milligrams (mg) of Percocet daily for the past 2-3 years with escalating use since. The patient had experienced severe drug and alcohol withdrawal symptoms in the past and he denied inadvertent illness. He had received detoxification and rehabilitation treatment in the past with a history of eight years of sobriety actively participating in Narcotics Anonymous (NA). The patient was tobacco dependent and was using cannabis with one joint per day for relaxation. The patient has no history of a co-occurring psychiatric disorder, and denied psychiatric hospitalization, or suicidal or self-harming behaviors. 
The physical examination and laboratory assessment were normal or unremarkable except for a positive drug screen consistent with history and normal vital signs that remained normal throughout the inpatient stay. His blood alcohol level was zero. The patient presented with diaphoresis, body aches, chills, fatigue, restlessness, and anxiety. He had no severe psychiatric symptoms such as mood disturbance, psychosis, perceptual disorder, or cognitive impairment. 
Following his first day of treatment, the patient began to participate in counseling and educational sessions, as he was feeling better. His mental status examination included persistent symptoms of anxiety with associated symptoms of insomnia. During his inpatient stay, the patient demonstrated no severe symptoms such as mania, psychosis, perceptual disturbance, or severe cognitive impairment. The patient completed the detoxification treatment without complications. The patient was discharged with referral for clinically appropriate aftercare including plans for rehabilitation treatment and resumption of involvement with 12-step recovery groups. 

The presenting clinical features and history and risk for withdrawal complications did warrant the admission and continued inpatient level services with a safe detoxification protocol and medical monitoring. 

The requested health service/treatment of inpatient hospital stay was medically necessary for this patient. The inpatient services and detoxification treatment and withdrawal management for severe poly-substance use disorder and other services noted in the clinical summary could not have been safely and effectively provided at a lower level of care, as noted in the answer to question 1 above. The adult inpatient treatment of this patient's substance-related disorders did warrant the admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level setting and 24-hour monitoring in view of the severity of the substance use disorders and the associated psychosocial stressors and impairment of functioning. 
Withdrawal risk was managed with tapering dosages of methadone and monitoring and as needed (prn) medications, as well as the availability of comfort medications and vitamin and nicotine replacement therapy. Seizure and fall precautions were provided. Counseling and educational sessions with motivational techniques together with case management services were appropriately provided to motivate the patient's transition for appropriate rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment. Thus, the patient did require a safe and effective detoxification with inpatient level services and withdrawal management during the time frame under review, as it was reasonable that the patient would have been unable to abstain from the substances of abuse or remain in treatment if detoxification and treatment were attempted at a lower level of care.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance abuse.
Treatment: Medically Supervised Inpatient Detoxification.
The insurer denied: Medically Supervised Inpatient Detoxification.
The denial is upheld.

The patient is an adult male who presented for detoxification and withdrawal management for opioid (heroin), crack cocaine, alcohol and cannabis class substances of abuse. He presented with a blood alcohol level of zero and mild symptoms of withdrawal with tremors, anxiety and intense cravings. He had received past substance use disorder treatments including the recent detoxification 4 months ago. The patient provided no history of withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens or severe alcohol or drug withdrawal symptoms. The patient had a history of psychiatric disorders and past treatment for anxiety and depression. He had no acute general medical problems; he was tobacco dependent at one-fourth pack per day. His substance use included up to five to six bags of heroin and two pints of alcohol (cognac) per day and intermittent use of crack cocaine and cannabis. The patient was medically screened and admitted for inpatient level detoxification with use of Suboxone, vitamin replacement therapy and comfort medications. His drug screen was positive for cocaine, tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), benzodiazepines and opiates. Mental Status Examination: There were no severe symptoms on mental status examination. He presented with anxiety/irritability and complaints of insomnia. He had fair control of his impulses. He reported tremors but no other somatic complaints. The patient's hospital course progressed without incident. Vital signs were consistently normal, and the patient was in no apparent distress. The patient slept with the use of mirtazapine and gabapentin. He was discharged against medical advice 2 days later with referral back to his outpatient clinic and recommendations to resume his involvement with 12-step recovery groups and continued use of Suboxone.

The denial was based on New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria. The denial determination indicated that the patient could have been treated with lower-level services such as residential care. 

The appeal was on the basis of Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria indicating that the patient had deficient coping skills and warranted inpatient level services.

The proposed treatment, inpatient substance abuse treatment was not medically necessary for this patient. The proposed inpatient stay and detoxification treatment and other medical services noted in the clinical summary could have been safely and effectively provided at a lower level of care. The acute inpatient treatment of this patient's substance use disorder did not warrant the structure of an inpatient setting or 24-hour monitoring. The patient displayed no serious disturbance of mental status despite having a history of ongoing substance use disorder. There was no co-occurring psychiatric disorder or psychiatric symptoms that would have warranted inpatient level treatment. Moreover, the patient did not show evidence for suicidal or aggressive behavior or risk, or severe cognitive impairment or psychosis, or perceptual disturbance, or other emotional disturbances that would have warranted an inpatient level admission and treatment. There were no severe symptoms of withdrawal or biomedical issues in this case, and the patient had received detoxification treatment and rehabilitation substance use treatment recently. The patient had fair insight and control of impulses, and a working knowledge of substance use disorder treatment with a past history of treatment. Thus, an inpatient admission for detoxification treatment was not medically necessary in this case scenario.

summary:
Diagnosis: Depression
Treatment: Transcranial magnetic stimulation
The health plan denied Transcranial magnetic stimulation. The denial is overturned.

The patient is an adult female with a diagnosis of major depressive disorder and treatment resistant depression with associated symptoms of anxiety. The patient's treatment plan includes the use of TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy. The patient has a longstanding history of depressive disorder. The patient has a documented history of multiple medication treatments for depression, including treatment with two antidepressants with disparate mechanism of action and at least four or more trials with antidepressant medications including SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) (Zoloft and Prozac), SNRIs (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors) (Cymbalta and Effexor), and amitriptyline resulting in lack of effectiveness or intolerance due to adverse effects.

The patient has received augmentation therapy with Tramadol and with cyclobenzaprine with associated antidepressant qualities, as well as supplemental use of hydroxyzine. Additionally, the patient has had extensive treatment with at least five years of weekly psychotherapy sessions combined with antidepressant medications. There is no mention of comorbid psychiatric conditions other than anxiety or co-occurring substance use disorder or comorbid general medical conditions that are a focus of treatment or represent a contraindication for TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy.

In this case scenario, Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Services are clinically appropriate and considered medically necessary as an adjunct and augmentation of the patient's antidepressant regimen in order to achieve a remission of symptoms related to severe depressive disorder in the context of treatment refractory/resistant depression and failed trials with at least four antidepressants including antidepressant medications with disparate mechanisms of action. Moreover, the coverage of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Services for a patient who meets criteria for treatment refractory depression and who is a reasonable candidate for the requested benefit of TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) should be approved in this case scenario; the requested TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy proposed is in the best interest of the patient, and reflects sound medical judgment with respect to the use of the requested treatment. Indeed, TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy for the treatment of major depressive disorder is a well-established treatment that is proposed for this patient in keeping with prevailing standards of medical practice for the condition under treatment in this case. Additionally, the patient had past trials that included combined medication treatments with weekly psychotherapy.

This answer is consistent with the scientific literature and published guidelines, referenced below.

The patient is an adult male. He self-referred for inpatient rehabilitation and substance use disorder treatment beginning three months ago. The patient has longstanding substance use disorders with cannabis and stimulant (crack cocaine) and opioid (heroin)-class substances with prior treatment with a chronic relapsing course. The patient has no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens. His substance use included $60 worth of crack cocaine and 3 to 4 bags of heroin with intranasal administration on a daily continuous basis, and daily use of marijuana with one to two joints. The patient has an extensive history of substance use disorder treatments with detoxifications and rehabilitation treatment but no sustained sobriety or abstinence despite receiving methadone maintenance assisted treatment. He had no significant withdrawal symptoms but did report mild symptoms. Evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination that reflected motivation for rehabilitation treatment, but limited insight, impaired judgment, and poor control of impulses. Throughout his inpatient rehabilitation stay, the patient remained stable with mental status and remained engaged with the treatment regimen. He received intensive rehabilitation services, monitoring, and structure provided within the inpatient treatment program including 24-hour monitoring. The patient became belligerent and was discharged administratively with plans for clinically appropriate aftercare of his substance use disorders and referral back to the methadone clinic. The health plan denied coverage of the requested dates of service based on New York State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) 3 Criteria indicating that there were no acute psychiatric or general medical problems that would have required inpatient level services and indicating that the patient's admission was not medically necessary, as treatment could have been provided with lower-level of care in a less restrictive treatment setting.

The treatment facility appealed based on New York State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) 3 Criteria and submitted records, indicating that inpatient level treatment was the appropriate level of care.

The Inpatient Rehabilitation Admission was not medically necessary for this patient.

The patient presented with substance use disorders, diagnosed with cannabis and stimulant/cocaine and opioid and tobacco use disorders. He self-referred and received inpatient level rehabilitation treatment with continued use of methadone. The application of NY (New York) State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) 3.0 Criteria (referenced below) did indicate that the patient was clinically appropriate for treatment with lower-level care in a less restrictive treatment setting, also as the health plan asserts. The patient in this case scenario is not clinically appropriate for an inpatient level of care during the time interval under review. The patient had presented with a level of medical stability and had no co-occurring psychiatric disorders or safety issues that would have warranted inpatient level care.
