summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Substance Abuse Inpatient Rehabilitation
The insurer denied the substance abuse inpatient rehabilitation.
The health plan's determination is upheld.

The patient is a male who was admitted to inpatient level services for the treatment of hallucinogens (phencyclidine [PCP]), cocaine and alcohol use disorders. The patient had been using PCP up to six times per week and crack cocaine daily together with the intermittent use of up to one pint of alcohol. The patient is self-referred for substance-related treatment in the context of severe psychosocial stressors. The patient has no acute general medical issues. The medical screening was negative and unremarkable except for a positive drug screen consistent with his history. He was tobacco/nicotine dependent with light use.

There are co-occurring psychiatric disorders in this case including post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and unspecified anxiety and depressive disorders with no current symptoms or treatment for these conditions. The patient is unemployed and homeless and he is not living in a shelter. There is a report of an unspecified trauma history in this case, including childhood abuse and domestic violence as an adult. There are no legal issues in this case.

The patient engaged in substance use disorder treatment with active involvement in group and educational sessions, as well as other therapeutic interventions to support healthy living and the development of sober supports. The patient was noted to adjust easily to the treatment program. In this regard, the patient worked on coping skills and a relapse prevention plan with the identification of triggers including peer support to address the negative influence of the social environment. The patient remained engaged during the brief inpatient stay with satisfactory progress. However, the patient was discharged against medical advice with the recommendation for clinically appropriate aftercare.

The structure and intensity of services necessary for a successful rehabilitation/substance use disorder treatment can be/could have been effectively provided at a lower level of care in a less restrictive treatment setting with sober supports. There is no evidence that inpatient level structure and 24-hour nursing monitoring is medically necessary for a successful outcome.

The requested health service/treatment of inpatient rehabilitation was not medically necessary for the patient. The Mental Status Examination revealed no severe symptoms and the patient was cooperative and dysphoric with normal speech, linear thought processing, and no disturbance of thought content such as paranoid thoughts or delusions. He lacked coping skills and demonstrated only fair insight. He reported urges to use PCP and cocaine and had post-acute withdrawal symptoms of restlessness, anxiety, and depression. He had been unable to cut down on his own. He was noted to have deficient coping skills and needed to identify triggers for his substance use.

The inpatient level substance disorder rehabilitation treatment included the opportunity to participate in groups, individual counseling, education and attendance at self-help recovery groups with peer support. Comfort medications were available as needed, and he was prescribed vitamins and he had the availability of a nicotine replacement. 

The inpatient substance abuse rehabilitation treatment, in this case scenario, was amenable to treatment at a lower level of care. The patient was able to effectively engage in rehabilitation services, and the patient did not need the structure or 24-hour nursing monitoring of an inpatient setting in order to safely and effectively participate in rehabilitation substance abuse treatment. There were no biomedical or psychiatric complications, or severe psychiatric symptoms/disorders in this case that would have warranted inpatient level services and treatment.

The patient is an adult male who was referred for inpatient rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment in order to address use of alcohol and stimulant (cocaine) class substances. The patient has no reported history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens though there was a history of severe withdrawal symptoms in the past during detoxification. The history of substance use included use of up to one-half pints of liquor and four 40-ounce beers per day and $ (dollar) 100 worth of crack cocaine per day. The patient was self-referred and indicated that he was tired of feeling unwell. He had an extensive history of detoxification treatments and rehabilitation treatment with relapses; the more recent substance-related treatment was 6 months ago. The patient has a history of psychiatric disorder and treatment for bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) treated with Lexapro and Seroquel and he presented without severe symptoms of depression. The patient has no history of psychiatric hospitalization. The patient is married and unemployed with public assistance and domiciled in a shelter or group home. He has 12 children. There were no reported legal issues, but there is trauma history. Evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination that reflected motivation for rehabilitation treatment, but limited insight, impaired judgment, and poor control of impulses. He did not report suicidal ideation or aggressive impulses. Upon admission to inpatient level services, the patient received comprehensive evaluation and treatment and involvement with groups, as well as peer supported recovery meetings, and other therapeutic activities within the treatment milieu. Psychiatric evaluation was provided, and he was prescribed Lexapro and Seroquel with as needed (PRN) use of trazodone for insomnia/sleep, and other comfort drugs. The patient continued to receive intensive rehabilitation services, monitoring, and structure including 24-hour nursing monitoring and was discharged against medical advice after ten days with referral for clinically appropriate care of the mental health and substance use disorders. In this case, the patient could have been reasonably managed with lower-level care in a less restrictive treatment setting, as the health plan asserted. During the time interval under review, the patient was noted to be in no apparent distress with reasonable functioning and active participation in treatment including positive interactions with staff and peers. This is a male patient who was referred for residential substance use disorder treatment to address substance use disorder with a stimulant class substance of abuse (methamphetamine) and co-occurring psychiatric disorders in the context of impairment of functioning and severe psychosocial stressors. The patient had one prior treatment episode with relapse and no significant period of abstinence or sobriety. He had used other substances of abuse recreationally including ketamine, gamma hydroxybutyrate (GHB), and alcohol, and he was tobacco dependent.
Evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination that was free of severe psychiatric symptoms such as mania, thought disorder, perceptual disturbance, or severe cognitive impairment. He was not clearly motivated for treatment in the pre-contemplative stage of change with a lack of insight and denial that the substance abuse was a problem. He was not clearly ready to engage in a recovery process, and had limited support due to family conflict and social isolation. The patient was described as having limited insight due to the addiction together with questionable judgment and extremely poor control of impulses. He denied active suicidal ideation or aggressive impulse. His energy and volition were impaired with poor appetite and concentration problems. Also, he had experienced and reported symptoms of anxiety and insomnia, as well as hopelessness and dysphoria with anergia and fatigue. The patient had no significant general medical conditions.
The patient underwent comprehensive psychiatric evaluation with admission to residential level services. Substance-related treatment included focus on coping skills, relapse prevention with identification of triggers, education about the disease model of addiction, and, involvement with peer-support recovery groups, as well as plans for family-focused sessions when clinically appropriate. Mental health treatment included groups, individual therapy including behavioral therapy, and access to psychiatric management. He was prescribed vitamin supplements and melatonin, as well as the availability of nicotine replacement.
From the date of admission forward, the patient had variably engaged in treatment with intensive services, sober housing, monitoring, and structure provided within the residential treatment program and therapeutic milieu. He was not well motivated due to maladaptive coping and comorbid disorders, and a lack of insight and motivation to change. He was cooperative, but continued to display a lack of insight and immaturity regarding impulse control and his stage of change. Nonetheless, he did participate in the rehabilitation treatment with plans to continue with residential level services with clinically appropriate step down. The patient continued participating in the treatment with a focus on coping skills and continued involvement with behavioral interventions including evidence-based psychosocial interventions, and involvement in recovery groups with peers and medication management. He struggled, had to be directed to complete assignments, and was developing a relapse prevention plan. 
At issue is the medical necessity of chemical dependency residential treatment. 
The requested health service/treatment of chemical dependency (CD) residential treatment (RTC) was medically necessary for this patient.
The patient did meet ASAM Criteria and continued to warrant the structure, monitoring, and intensity of level 3.5 residential treatment for the duration of the residential stay under review. The patient's lack of awareness or limitations of insight together with the seriousness of the comorbid psychiatric disorders and co-occurring substance use disorders is illustrated by his continued risk for problematic behavior and continued risk of relapse with use of a high-risk substance of abuse including the functional decline that had occurred despite having access to treatment in the community, and in the context of maladaptive coping skills and substantial psychosocial consequences.
The patient's lack of awareness or limitations of insight together with the seriousness of his psychiatric disorders and co-occurring substance use disorders is illustrated by his continued risk of relapse with use of a high-risk substance of abuse including the functional decline that had occurred despite having access to treatment in the community, and in the context of maladaptive coping skills.
The requested benefit of the continued residential treatment was medically necessary in order to address the immediate needs for rehabilitation of severe substance use disorder and to work toward relapse prevention; and in order to address the patient's lack of awareness and impulse control; and, in order to address issues within the social environment; and, in order to work on coping skills that will be necessary in building a sober support system and planning for continued recovery efforts with community providers and engagement with age-appropriate recovery groups, and, services to address the anxiety and trauma-related symptoms.
The development of a relapse prevention plan is critical in this case together with gains with insight and acquisition of better coping skills that are important components of the treatment being provided with clinically appropriate residential structure, intensity of services, and monitoring. It is therefore medically necessary that the patient have continued 24-hour monitoring and high intensity residential level services for the duration of the proposed treatment in order to prepare the patient for a safe and clinically appropriate disposition and discharge to the community. None of this therapeutic work could have been or can be safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in view of the multiple, complicating factors in this case for the time interval under review.
This answer is consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice and ASAM Patient Placement Criteria and the published guidelines and scientific literature, referenced below, and is consistent with New York State OASAS LOCADTR Criteria.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder

Treatment: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) Treatments (initial, including cortical mapping, motor threshold determination, delivery) 
The insurer denied: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) Treatments (initial, including cortical mapping, motor threshold determination, delivery) 

The denial is: Overturned.

The patient is a male diagnosed with major depressive disorder, recurrent and severe without psychotic features and treatment refractory/resistant depression. The patient has a documented history of multiple medication treatments for depression including treatment with more than two disparate classes of medication and at least three or more trials with antidepressant medications (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor [SSRIs] and Wellbutrin). He has had augmentation with Abilify and lithium, as well as ongoing treatment with Vyvanse for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Due to adverse effects and lack of efficacy, the patient continued to experience severe symptoms of depression which did respond robustly to a course of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) therapy. Subsequently, the patient experienced a return of depressive symptoms following a life-threatening illness with a bowel perforation complicated by sepsis requiring intensive medical treatment. The patient's clinician has recommended treatment with a repeat course of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) therapy sessions. The recommendation is in the context of the ongoing episode of depression that is treatment-resistant/refractory with a history of intolerance to antidepressant medications. 
The subject under review is the medical necessity for Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) Therapy for recurrent and severe Major Depressive Disorder without psychotic features and treatment refractory/resistant depression.

The requested health service/treatment of TMS Treatments (initial, including cortical mapping, motor threshold determination, delivery) is medically necessary for this patient.
The requested benefit of Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) is reasonable, clinically appropriate, and medically necessary in this case. The requested TMS service is backed by credible scientific study and is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice for the condition under treatment in this case, recurrent major depressive disorder and treatment refractory/resistant depressive disorder.
The proposed treatment can reasonably be expected to provide the patient with greater net health benefit than any other standard therapy in this case scenario. Repetitive TMS therapy as a primary or adjunctive therapy for treatment of depression has generally been evaluated in patients who have had treatment resistant or treatment refractory depression, as defined by one or more, treatment failures with or without augmentation. TMS therapy for depression is established as a safe treatment by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and the data as reflected in peer reviewed medical literature supports this assertion. Specifically, when treatments with antidepressant medication with or without augmentation, or electroconvulsive therapy, and/or psychotherapy (especially cognitive behavioral therapy) have failed, then TMS is clinically appropriate. This assertion is also noted in the American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorder, referenced below.
The patient in this case has demonstrated that his depressive disorder is treatment refractory with multiple failed trials of antidepressant medications of disparate mechanisms of action, as noted in the clinical summary. Thus, the proposed treatment of recurrent and severe major depressive disorder using rTMS therapy is considered medically necessary in this case.

summary:
Diagnosis: Problems with Mood, Anxiety and Coping Skills; PTSD (posttraumatic stress disorder).
Treatment: Inpatient Mental Health Services.
The insurer denied the inpatient mental health services.
The health plans determination is overturned.

The patient is a male who was referred to residential treatment by his outpatient clinician. The patient had severe symptoms of treatment refractory mood and trauma related disorder, comorbid attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)-inattentive type, and co-occurring substance use disorders. The patient had become increasingly anxious and depressed precipitated by a previous cycling crash with injury and a recrudescence of symptoms related to childhood traumas resulting in deterioration in functioning despite several treatment episodes and medication trials. He had received ongoing psychotherapy which had failed to produce a response or remission. He was diagnosed with bipolar mood disorder with intermittent psychotic features, posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) with dissociation, ADHD, and co-occurring substance use disorder with alcohol and cannabis class substances, as well as a history of recreational use of hallucinogens and stimulants. The patient presented with a clinical course that included worsening symptoms of comorbid psychiatric conditions and severe substance use disorder with unemployment, social isolation, and the inability to care for self. Thus, he was referred for residential treatment to provide for more intensive treatment in order to address the mood disturbance, anxiety and trauma-related problems together with deficient coping skills and co-occurring substance use.

During his continued stay, the patient became increasingly cooperative and receptive with treatment and social with peers with continued mood disturbance, affective instability and sleep disturbance. He received motivational interviewing and enhancement with regard to the substance use disorder, and dynamic and behavioral therapy with focus on mindfulness and distress tolerance, as well as emotional regulation, and trauma recovery. He denied active suicidal ideation, plan or intent during this time interval, and had no evidence for passive suicidal ideation or risk. The patient's insight, judgment and impulse control remained fair.

The patient required the admission and the continued inpatient residential level care in order to remain safe and for the administration of treatment for his psychiatric disturbances while conducting an evaluation, and while observing his functioning with the resumption/adjustment of clinically appropriate medications to address the mood disturbance and stabilize mood while implementing evidence-based treatments to address the comorbid conditions, PTSD and the co-occurring substance use disorder. The clinical course is complicated by his past history of complex medical trauma with a brain injury. Additionally, the treatment team was planning for a step down with intensive treatment targeting mood with trauma recovery in order to achieve a safe and clinically appropriate disposition and discharge plan that would also allow for co-occurring substance use disorders.
 
The continued structure and monitoring and intensity of services with residential level treatment is warranted for the patient in order to effectively address the patient's risk of relapse, allow the patient to begin learning adequate coping skills, and to continue treatment for the co-occurring mood and trauma-related disorders, as well as the work needed to develop a solid plan for step down with sober supports.

The continued stay is medically necessary in order to monitor the response to medications, to assure that the patient will have a sustained response to treatment, and to continue to address the risk of related to severe symptoms of bipolar mood disorder and PTSD.

summary:
Diagnosis:  Substance Abuse.
Treatment:  Medically Supervised Inpatient Detoxification.

The insurer denied the medically supervised inpatient detoxification.  The denial is overturned.

The patient is an adult male requesting detoxification and substance use disorder treatment, who was screened and admitted to acute inpatient level care in order to address substance use disorders with alcohol and stimulant (cocaine) class substances. The patient had a three-year history of substance use with progression of the disease. This patient had a history of one prior detoxification and no rehabilitation treatment episodes. The patient has a history of psychiatric disorder, schizophrenia, and no recent psychiatric hospitalizations. He was currently in treatment for his mental disorder with use of risperidone and quetiapine with questionable compliance with treatment. His withdrawal symptoms included anxiety, sweats, tremor, and restlessness with a CIWA (clinical institute withdrawal assessment) scale score of 10 (mild) and normal vital signs.
During the brief detoxification the patient did engage in counseling sessions focusing on education about the disease model of addiction, and, involvement with milieu activities including peer support and sessions to motivate the patient to proceed to rehabilitation treatment. His stage of change reflected a pre-contemplative stage and he tended to isolate but was social with peers and cooperative with staff. Withdrawal symptoms diminished, and he tolerated the Librium taper. The patient completed the detoxification protocol and was discharged on day #5 with immediate step down for rehabilitation treatment and with plans for medication assisted treatment and recommendations for involvement with self-help recovery groups, and consideration of appropriate treatment for his co-occurring mental disorder. At the time of his discharge, he remained with poor insight with high risk for relapse.

The Medically Supervised Inpatient Detoxification was medically necessary.

The patient in this case was using large quantity of alcohol on a daily continuous basis; and use of cocaine that did warrant inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring. Detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments pertinent to the detoxification treatment episode could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment that was provided at the time of admission and during the time interval under review. Moreover, the patient's social environment was not conducive to detoxification, and the patient struggled with symptoms of anxiety in the context of limited insight, impaired judgment and poor control of impulses. The patient's history of substance use (frequency and quantity) and functional impairments related to a severe and persistent mental disorder (schizophrenia) reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder and the need for a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management, as the patient was at high risk for treatment failure if the detoxification and withdrawal management were to be attempted at a lower level of care. Therefore, medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published practice guidelines, ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) Criteria and LOCUS (Level of Care Utilization System) Guidelines, and the scientific literature, referenced below, and, New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews including the appropriate application of the NY (New York) State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) Tool that requires the patient in this scenario default to the higher level of care.

summary:

Treatment: Substance abuse inpatient rehabilitation admission
The health plan denied substance abuse inpatient rehabilitation admission.
The determination is upheld.

This is a male patient with a history of substance use disorders including cocaine, marijuana, and alcohol. The patient received substance abuse inpatient rehabilitation level of care. The patient denied any history of seizures, blackouts, or overdose.

The patient denied any suicidal or homicidal ideation or history of suicide attempts. He denied any recent hospitalizations. There was no prior psychiatric history and the patient denied any past medical problems. A urine drug screen was positive for cannabis and cocaine but the blood alcohol content was zero upon admission. The clinical note describes the patient as participating in motivational interviewing. The patient reported no increase in symptoms of withdrawal or uncomfortable feelings. There was no evidence of a severe mood or anxiety problems during the session and there was no suicidal or homicidal ideation, intent, or plan. The mental status exam on admission was within normal limits. At issue is the medical necessity of substance abuse inpatient rehabilitation admission.

In reviewing the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) admission tool, the patient had no immediate need for hospitalization for a life-threatening medical condition or severe psychiatric crisis. Alcohol was the substance with the greatest potential for harm to self or others. The patient met criteria for alcohol use disorder and was not in remission. The patient was no longer at risk for withdrawal given the length of time that had passed since the prior last drink. The patient did not have serious medical or psychiatric symptoms that required inpatient rehabilitation. Clinical documentation does not establish that the patient had recently been using substances and hazardous situations or in amounts or frequencies likely to imminently cause harm to self or others. The patient did have interpersonal deficits including problems maintaining stable relationships and employment. The patient did not exhibit predatory behaviors. There was no evidence of strong cravings or behavioral or emotional instability. Based on responses, the LOCADTR Level of Care is rehabilitative services in a residential setting.

The health plan's determination is upheld.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance abuse
Treatment: Inpatient rehabilitation
The insurer denied coverage for inpatient rehabilitation
The denial is overturned

This adult was admitted to this inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment as he reportedly was using large amounts of serious substances of use.  He reportedly had 6 past treatment episodes and was unable to maintain abstinence. He had a positive toxicology for cocaine, heroin, fentanyl, THC(tetrahydrocannabinol), and methadone. He reportedly was in substance intensive outpatient program and Methadone maintenance (MAT) and still could not maintain abstinence. He lived alone and was socializing with active users. He attended group and individual therapy.

The medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that he required this level of care. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that inpatient treatment is indicated primarily for individuals whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. 

In this case this patient was considered in need of 24-hour substance rehabilitation treatment as he was discharged. He reportedly lacked the coping skills and ability to identify relapse triggers to stop use. 

According to the Level of Care Determination (LOCADTR) he met criteria for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment as he continued to use large amounts of serious substances of use and cannabis daily and was unable to stop use without a 24-hour substance free therapeutic treatment setting despite multiple past treatment episodes. He reportedly lacked coping skills for abstinence, the ability to identify triggers to use,  insight into use,  and needed to learn better coping skills, improve insight into use, and better identify relapse triggers. He was at risk for medical complications from his serious substances of use and also overdose as well as severe withdrawal symptoms. He was unable to stop substance use without being in a sober and supervised therapeutic inpatient substance rehabilitation setting. He required 24-hour inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment in this therapeutic, supervised, and structured treatment setting.  He required the entire time in this therapeutic structured and supervised inpatient rehabilitation treatment. Without this structured and supervised therapeutic rehabilitation treatment he likely would have relapsed and likely would not have been able to maintain abstinence and would have been at risk medically for overdose and severe withdrawal. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be reversed. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. 

The medical necessity for the admission at the substance abuse inpatient rehabilitation level of care is substantiated.

Progress notes indicate a PHQ-9 (Patient Health Questionnaire) scale score of 23 in the severe range for depression. The history includes failed treatment with Prozac 60 milligrams (mg) daily, Luvox 300 mg daily, and Lexapro 20 mg together with Concerta 36 mg. The patient has received psychotherapy with cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). There are no comorbid psychiatric disorders in this case or co-occurring substance use disorders, and the patient does not have an acute or chronic general medical condition that is a focus of treatment. 

Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) and Cranial Electrical Stimulation (CES) is not medically necessary for this patient.
In this case, the patient is diagnosed with major depressive disorder with severe symptoms as indicated with the scoring on the PHQ-9. However, the patient has only received treatment with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) class antidepressants and has not received augmentation with an FDA (Food and Drug Administration) approved augmentation agent. 
Per the prevailing standards of care, clinically appropriate approaches are available for treatment of depressive disorder in this case, including other antidepressants with a disparate mechanism of action or combination therapy, or an alternative established augmentation therapy, as well as specific forms of psychotherapy that would establish that the patient is treatment refractory. Thus, standard therapeutic treatments that are known to be effective in the treatment of Major Depressive Disorder should be used first prior to treatment with Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) and Cranial Electrical Stimulation (CES).

summary:
Diagnosis: Depression
Treatment: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) 
The insurer denied Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) 
The determination is upheld.

This is a male patient with a diagnosis of severe major depressive disorder without psychotic features. The patient has a history of depressive disorder with worsening and persistent symptoms of depression. He has received outpatient treatment with one antidepressant medication citalopram, as well as augmentation therapy with Seroquel and Abilify together with clonazepam and ongoing psychotherapy with cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). The patient's history of depression includes symptoms of depressed mood, hopelessness, guilt, shame, anxiety and disturbed sleep with low motivation and impaired functioning. The patient has reported suicidal ideation without a plan or intent. An assessment with a Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ) -9 scale scored 18 in the severe range.
The patient is diagnosed with comorbid post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and the patient has recent losses including the death of his father and a friend and a break up with his fiancé after three years. A recent progress note indicated that the patient's therapist left the practice and the patient was seeking another therapist/counselor. Also, the patient was started on sertraline with continued use of Seroquel and clonazepam.
There is no current substance use disorder or other comorbid psychiatric disorder in this case. There are no severe symptoms such as psychosis, mania, perceptual disturbance, or cognitive impairment. There is no report of psychiatric hospitalization or suicide attempt/behavior and the patient has not had a history of self-harm.
The health plan denied transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) therapy indicating that the requested treatment is not medically necessary because the patient has not had enough trials with antidepressant medications. The patient has received treatment with only one antidepressant medication with augmentation-as noted, and has not received treatment with at least one other antidepressant medication with a disparate mechanism of action as required under the plan's InterQual Criteria pertaining to TMS therapy.
The appeal argues that the patient meets the plan criteria with failed trials with the indicated medications and high risk for complications including hospitalization.
A case summary/case notes, health plan documents and peer advisor case notes, and correspondence from the health plan and treating clinician were reviewed, as well as appeal documents, and the plan's InterQual Medical Necessity Criteria pertaining to transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) therapy for major depressive disorder.
At issue is the medical necessity of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS).
The requested health service/treatment of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is not medically necessary for this patient.
The patient has only one treatment failure with one antidepressant medication with augmentation as noted in the clinical summary. Published guidelines and scientific literature would support that the patient has not had enough antidepressant medication trials prior to considering the use of TMS therapy. In this case, the patient does not meet the standard of care for the use of TMS therapy, as the patient has not demonstrated that they have treatment resistant depression. Standard therapeutic options known to be effective in the treatment of major depressive disorder are available to this patient to address the persistence or recrudescence of depressive symptoms. The requested TMS therapy is not medically necessary consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice and the published societal guidelines and scientific literature, referenced below.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse/Addiction
Treatment: Substance abuse inpatient rehabilitation admission
The health plan denied: Substance abuse inpatient rehabilitation admission
The determination is: Upheld

The patient is a male who was admitted to inpatient rehabilitation for substance use disorder as treatment of stimulant (cocaine), alcohol, and cannabis (marijuana) use disorders. The patient was using up to $100 worth of crack cocaine together with $50 worth of marijuana with daily use, and use of alcohol with one and one-half pints of rum and two beers daily. The patient was also tobacco dependent. His referral was prompted by his desire to stop using substances of abuse after longstanding use since adolescence. He had a history of multiple past substance use disorder treatment episodes with at least ten or more detoxification treatment episodes with the last occurring for five days.
There was a history of co-occurring psychiatric disorder best characterized as schizophrenia with depression or bipolar disorder with a history of psychiatric hospitalization due to suicidal risk. The patient is single, homeless and housed, and unemployed with an 8th grade education and public assistance. Peers were using substances of abuse, and he had limited social support. He denied legal issues.
Mental status examination revealed a cooperative male with clear speech and linear thought processing that was goal directed. His mood was anxious with congruent affect. The patient's thought content included no morbid thoughts. He had no evidence for cognitive impairment, perceptual disturbance, mood disturbance, or psychosis. His insight was limited with impaired judgment due to the addictions. He had sleep disturbance with insomnia.

The inpatient level substance-related rehabilitation treatment included the opportunity to participate in groups, individual counseling, educational sessions, and 12-step recovery groups with peer support. The patient easily transitioned to rehabilitation treatment. He actively participated in individual, group, and educational sessions. He was prescribed comfort medications and vitamins with the availability of nicotine replacement therapy and as needed (prn) medications to address anxiety and insomnia.

Discharge planning occurred that included recommendation for continued aftercare upon completion of the program. However, the patient left treatment against medical advice indicating that he was uncomfortable because his sister had been admitted to the treatment facility.

At issue is the medical necessity of substance abuse inpatient rehabilitation admission.
The health plan's determination of medical necessity is upheld. The requested health service/treatment of Substance Abuse Inpatient Rehabilitation Level of Care was not medically necessary for this patient.

The Inpatient substance use disorder rehabilitation services in this case scenario were amenable to treatment at an alternate level of care. The patient was motivated and was capable of effectively receiving substance use disorder treatment in a less restrictive treatment setting with sober support and/or housing. The patient did not need the structure of an inpatient setting in order to effectively participate in rehabilitation substance abuse treatment, or to receive effective treatment for the co-occurring disorder (schizophrenia or bipolar disorder with depression).

There were no biomedical or psychiatric complications, or severe psychiatric symptoms/disorders in this case that would have warranted the admission and the continued inpatient level services and treatment. Thus, the requested benefit of inpatient substance use disorder rehabilitation services was not medically necessary in keeping with NY (New York) State Guidelines.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse (withdrawal). 
Treatment: Inpatient Hospital Admission. 

The insurer denied: Inpatient Hospital Admission. 
The denial is overturned. 

The patient in this case is an adult male. He presented to the emergency department with severe chest pain and request for detoxification in the context of a four-week binge with consumption of up to three bottles of vodka per day. At the time of presentation to the emergency department, the patient was evaluated with laboratory assessments, EKG (electrocardiogram) and Chest X-Ray, which revealed multiple abnormalities. He had low calcium, elevated glucose, and normocytic anemia with elevated liver functions. His Chest X-Ray showed vascular congestion later diagnosed as a recurrent pulmonary embolus after ruling out myocardial infarction. EKG (electrocardiogram) revealed normal sinus rhythm. The patient received Ativan and Librium in the emergency department and was admitted to inpatient level care where he received monitoring, fluid replacement, and supportive measures to address alcohol withdrawal. He presented with a blood alcohol level of 260 mg/dl (milligrams per deciliter) and a CIWA (clinical institute withdrawal 
assessment) scale score of 15. He was maintained on a CIWA (clinical institute withdrawal assessment) protocol. The patient has a history of pulmonary embolus from last year but was not taking his medications for prophylaxis or for hypertension-apixaban and amlodipine. The patient's clinical course progressed without incident. He quickly stabilized and declined additional services but with plans to proceed to rehabilitation treatment after the holidays- arranged by social work. Discharge diagnoses included pulmonary embolus, and alcohol use disorder and alcohol withdrawal, and hypertension. The health plan denied coverage for the requested services based on medical necessity and MCG (Milliman Care Guidelines) Guidelines indicating that the inpatient admission was not medically necessary. The treatment facility indicated that the requested services were medically necessary in keeping with the clinical features of the case and risk for complications of the pulmonary embolus and alcohol withdrawal, as well as effort to rule out myocardial infarction.

The Inpatient Hospital Admission was medically necessary. 

The hospital admission providing ongoing monitoring together with detoxification treatment and withdrawal management and other medical services could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. The patient in this case was using large quantities of alcohol with a binge pattern of use with up to four weeks of heavy use of alcohol on a daily continuous basis, together with chest pain and history of recent pulmonary embolus that did warrant the admission and the continued inpatient level treatment. Detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments pertinent to the hospital stay could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment that was provided in the emergency department and at the time of admission. The patient's history of substance abuse (frequency and quantity) together with the general medical comorbidities do reflect the seriousness of the presenting clinical features and the need for further evaluation and monitoring while receiving a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management as the patient was at high risk for treatment failure or general medical complications such as seizures or encephalopathy if detoxification and withdrawal management were to have been attempted at a lower level of care. Therefore, medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published societal guidelines, ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) Criteria, and the scientific literature, referenced below.

The patient was using heroin together with crack cocaine on a continuous daily basis, as well as intermittent use of cannabis. There were no co-morbid general medical problems or co-occurring psychiatric disorders that would have warranted admission for inpatient level services. The withdrawal symptoms were not reported to be severe, and the patient's clinical symptoms were not serious enough to necessitate inpatient level detoxification treatment or monitoring. The presentation included worsening symptoms of depression and anxiety with suicidal ideation, a decline in functioning and social isolation in the context of problematic behaviors including bouts of anger with verbal violence and irritability, sneaking out of his home, and substance use including daily use of cannabis together with intermittent use of hallucinogens (lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) and Mushrooms) and alcohol with a binge pattern of use. 
He had an extensive history of outpatient treatment with medication management and psychotherapy, as well as the brief treatment episode with residential and intensive outpatient levels of care without sustained benefit.
At the time of admission for PHP level care, the mental status examination did reveal severe symptoms of depression with anxiety and anhedonia, hopelessness, and low self-worth. There was no evidence for psychosis, mood cycling, thought disorder, perceptual disturbance, severe cognitive impairment other than concentration and attention problems, or active suicidal ideation. His mood was dysphoric with low self-worth, and decreased energy, appetite, sleep disturbance and volition, as well as limited insight. He reported episodes of dissociation reflecting his psychedelic drug use with numbing and a sense of false reality.

The patient was provided treatment with intensive services, sober supports, safety monitoring, and structure provided within the PHP treatment program with five day per week services and sober living with structure and supervision and work on a recovery together with substance use counseling and 12-step recovery groups. He received group, family, individual and activity therapies including dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) and Motivational Enhancement Therapy (MET) and family focused sessions. He received ongoing psychiatric evaluations with medication management with use of Zoloft, Wellbutrin, Remeron, and melatonin with adjustments and titration as clinically appropriate last year with a regimen of Zoloft 75 milligrams (mg) twice daily, Wellbutrin extended release (XL) 150 mg, Remeron titrated to 15 mg and supplemental use of melatonin and vitamin D. 

The admission and continued PHP level intensity of services, structure, and monitoring were reasonable, in the best interest of the patient, and consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice. Specifically, the patient presented with worsening symptoms of the comorbid conditions with a decline in functioning, and related symptoms associated with substance use disorder with the cannabis class substance of abuse, as well as residual effects from the use of hallucinogens with dissociation. The patient was at high risk for relapse and had limited coping skills/insight-as noted in the clinical summary, and a treatment and recovery environment that was deficient in the context of parent-child relational problems, as well as treatment failure with lower-level services. These factors and treatment dimensions did warrant the admission and the continued PHP level services with sober supported housing, and intensive treatment with evidence-based therapy including DBT.  

The health plan's determination of medical necessity is overturned in whole.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Inpatient Rehabilitation Admission
The insurer denied: Inpatient Rehabilitation Admission
The denial is overturned.

The patient is an adult male. He presented for detoxification and withdrawal management. The patient has a history of severe substance use disorders beginning in early adolescence escalating to daily use of alcohol and cannabis (marijuana) class substances of abuse and intermittent use of cocaine. He has a 33-year history of substance use with five prior treatment episodes with relapse and no significant sobriety. He was using up to two pints of liquor on a continuous daily basis together with one marijuana joint and $20 worth of cocaine twice weekly with intranasal administration. The patient was single and homeless and unemployed with limited family support; he reported severe psychosocial stressors within the primary support, social environment, occupational, and housing domains. The patient reported functional decline as the substance abuse/disease had progressed, which prompted his self-referral for treatment of the comorbid substance use disorders. The patient has a history of psychiatric disorder and past treatment including one hospitalization for schizoaffective disorder, and no history of suicidal or self-harming behaviors. His Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) scale score was eight in the mild range. The patient was admitted for inpatient treatment with detoxification protocol. He received tapering dosages of Librium and replacement of vitamins, as well as the availability of nicotine replacement for tobacco dependence and with the availability of counseling and comfort medications and prn (as needed) medications prescribed for pain, anxiety, and insomnia. He was discharged on Day #6 after completion of the detoxification protocol with direct transfer for rehabilitation services. The health plan denied coverage for the requested services based on New York State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) Criteria indicating that the patient could have been provided services with lower-level care such as residential treatment. The treatment facility indicated that the requested services were medically necessary in keeping with 
New York State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) 3 Guidelines for the treatment of substance use disorders. The appeal referenced the lack of a reasonable recovery environment or supports, high risk for relapse and high risk for medical complications of withdrawal in the context of the quantity and frequency and duration of substance use and no recent exposure to treatment, as well as a lack of insight and knowledge about a recovery process requiring motivational enhancement and efforts to address deficient coping skills.

The Inpatient Rehabilitation Admission was medically necessary.

The requested benefit of inpatient detoxification and substance-related treatment could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. The patient in this case was using large quantities of alcohol on a daily continuous basis together with cocaine and cannabis that did warrant the admission and the continued inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring in an inpatient setting. Moreover, the patient's social environment was not conducive to an effective detoxification, and the patient had struggled with withdrawal symptoms that were being effectively addressed with a Librium protocol and supportive measures. Thus, the inpatient stay and detoxification treatment of this patient's substance use disorders did warrant the hospital admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level setting. Medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published guidelines, American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, the scientific literature, and New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews including the appropriate application of NY (New York) OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) 3.0 Criteria.

summary:
Diagnosis: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)
Treatment: Mental Health Services
The insurer denied the Mental Health Services.
The health plan's determination is overturned. 

The patient is an adult female admitted for residential mental health treatment in order to address severe complex posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) with comorbid major depressive disorder and skin picking disorder, as well as borderline personality traits with history of self-harming behavior (cutting and punching the wall) and suicidal behavior with at least two suicide attempts and other threats of suicide. The patient has co-occurring substance use with use of cannabis, and history of substance-induced mania and aggressive behavior directed towards her sister. She had posted videos outlining suicide plans by carbon monoxide poisoning and threats to jump from a building, as well as threats to overdose with at least two inpatient psychiatric hospitalizations. The patient was admitted for low-intensity residential treatment following a three-month high intensity residential stay which had followed the last inpatient psychiatric hospitalization. The residential program focused on trauma recovery and addressing suicidal and self-harming behaviors, as well as services to address the substance use disorder and impulsivity.
Despite treatment with therapy and antidepressant medications, the patient's mood and comorbid disorders had worsened with persistent suicidal ideation in the context of apathy and dysregulated emotions including suicidal ideation and aggressive impulses towards self with cutting/self-harming behavior and others when under the influence, including psychotic features and impulsive aggression. There was no evidence for mania other than substance induced mania, thought disorder or perceptual disturbance except a report of visual hallucinations while prescribed Prozac. The patient does dysregulate when experiencing trauma-related symptoms and reports nightmares. Insight and judgment were limited and marginal due to the multiple psychiatric conditions and substance use together with safety concerns.
At issue is the medical necessity of Mental Health Services.

The requested health service/treatment of Mental Health Services was medically necessary for this patient.
The admission and continued residential services were clinically appropriate and the services provided were not amenable to treatment at a lower level of care. The patient was working to learn improved coping skills and life skills together with the development of improved insight and motivation, as well as psychosocial and psychotherapeutic treatment to address the complex PTSD and mood disorder and substance use disorder and other evidence-based interventions to address the continued urges to self-harm in the context of borderline personality traits, critical in this case scenario. The admission was appropriate, and the patient did warrant the continued structure and monitoring of a residential setting in order to safely continue mental health treatment and services while maintaining safety with high risk for suicide or acting on aggressive impulses towards self or others. There were severe psychiatric symptoms including complications related to trauma history. Thus, the requested services are clinically appropriate and consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice and consistent with published guidelines (best practice).
The patient's Mental Health Services were in the patient's best interest, reasonable, clinically appropriate, and therefore, medically necessary.

summary:
Diagnosis: Alcohol withdrawal. 
Treatment: Inpatient Hospital Admission. 

The insurer denied: Inpatient Hospital Admission. 
The denial is overturned. 

The patient is an adult male with a past medical history of alcohol abuse, alcohol withdrawal, and withdrawal seizures. He was a patient in the detoxification unit. The patient had a witnessed seizure on that date. When the patient woke up, he was disoriented. He had bitten his tongue. The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit of the hospital. He was found to have lactic acidosis. Treatment consisted of intravenous fluids and intravenous Ativan. The following day, the patient had resolution of his acidosis. He was moved to a general medical unit. On day #3, the patient was found to be orthostatic. He was given additional intravenous fluids. Ongoing withdrawal symptoms were managed with oral medication. The patient was cleared to return to his detoxification program on day #6. The patient's health plan has denied coverage for this inpatient admission on the grounds that Milliman criteria for inpatient care have not been met. The hospital has appealed this denial. 

The proposed treatment of inpatient admission was medically necessary. 

Milliman Clinical Guideline ORG:M-595 (Substance Related Disorders) states that appropriate reasons to admit a patient with alcohol withdrawal to the hospital under inpatient status include: 
"Severe alcohol withdrawal not manageable at a lower level of care as indicated by 1) marked signs of withdrawal including heart rate greater than 120 beats per minute, and 2) signs of withdrawal that require inpatient care." 

This patient had multiple signs of severe alcohol withdrawal on admission including tachycardia with a heart rate of 126 beats per minute. Other signs of severe withdrawal requiring inpatient care include withdrawal seizure, altered mental status, and lactic acidosis. For these reasons, Milliman criteria for inpatient care have been met. The proposed treatment is medically necessary.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance abuse

Treatment: Residential Substance Use Treatment

The insurer denied coverage for Residential Substance Use Treatment

The denial is upheld
 

This adult male was admitted to this inpatient substance residential treatment due to his excessive substance use. He reportedly was using 5-8 bags of heroin per day, $(dollar) 20 of crack 1-2 times per week, and smoking 1-2 joints of cannabis per week. He reportedly had cravings, poor insight and judgment, was homeless, unemployed, and lacked sober supports. He reportedly had psychiatric conditions as well including a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder and post traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). He had an extensive treatment history. He attended group and individual therapy and was taking Lithium.
 
The insurer denied coverage for continued inpatient substance residential treatment stating that it was not medically necessary treatment. They stated that he did not meet Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment (LOCADTR) criteria anymore for this residential treatment level of care. They stated that he no longer had cravings or withdrawal, medical or psychiatric concerns requiring 24-hour treatment, and they recommended a less restrictive level of care with supportive housing.
There was no specific evidence in the medical records provided for review supporting that he required inpatient substance residential treatment level of care. He had been in this intensive inpatient residential treatment for 4 months. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders states that residential treatment is indicated primarily for individuals who do not meet clinical criteria for hospitalization but whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. In this case it was reported that this patient required this inpatient substance residential treatment and received this care since admission but there was no reported specific evidence in the records for review to support that he still required only 24-hour residential treatment still. There were no reports of life threatening or severe withdrawal symptoms or acute medical instability that would have required 24-hour treatment and no reports of dangerous behavior or harm to self or others. There were no reports of severe psychiatric or behavioral symptoms requiring 24-hour treatment and no reports of suicidal or homicidal thoughts or behavior, psychotic symptoms, self-injurious or aggressive behavior, or inability to adequately care for her basic needs. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be upheld. The health care plan did act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. 

The medical necessity for Residential Substance Use Treatment, revenue code 1002, is not substantiated.

They recommended a less restrictive level of care then such as outpatient substance abuse treatment.

The patient was discharged with plans/referral to start a rehabilitation treatment and with recommendations for involvement in 12-step recovery meetings, as well as continued mental health services. The adult inpatient treatment of this patient's substance disorders did require admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level setting and 24-hour monitoring given the severity of the alcohol use disorder, and the presentation with continued use of substances despite recent substance-related treatment. Withdrawal symptoms were managed with tapering dosages of benzodiazepine/Librium requiring monitoring, as well as comfort medications and vitamin and nicotine replacement therapy, and the co-occurring psychiatric disorders were managed with psychiatric consultation. Treatment: 10 hours per week of applied behavioral analysis (ABA) therapy, and 1 hour per week of supervision.

The patient reportedly had been in a 12:1:1 restrictive classroom with speech therapy and occupational therapy services, and behavioral consultant. The patient reportedly lives with their mother and siblings.

It was reported that the patient had developmental delays in social communication and social interaction still, needed verbal reminders and additional prompting to complete self-help skills on top of visual aids in place, needed monitoring for appropriate bites when eating, and that the patient was still scripting during activities of daily living (ADL's) such as showering which interfered with their ability to complete these tasks without prompting. The patient reportedly had verbal protests and negative statements in response to demands and nonpreferred tasks and it was at higher rates. summary:
Diagnosis: Cocaine and Alcohol Use Disorder
Treatment: Inpatient substance rehabilitation
The insurer denied coverage for: Inpatient substance rehabilitation
The denial is: Reversed
This patient was admitted to inpatient substance rehabilitation for alcohol/substance rehabilitation. The patient  was snorting 1 gram (gm) of cocaine 3-4 times per week and drinking 1 bottle of wine and up to 10 shots of tequila daily. The patient had diagnoses of Cocaine and Alcohol Use Disorder and was taking Adderall for Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) and Xanax for anxiety with reports of depression. The toxicology was positive for cocaine, tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), amphetamine, and benzodiazepines. The patient had hypertension and had elevated heart rate up to 98. There were past inpatient detoxification and rehabilitation treatments. The patient attended group and individual therapy. The patient was discharged against medical advice (AMA).

The reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment as the medical records provided support that the patient required this level of care. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that inpatient treatment is indicated primarily for individuals whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. In this case this patient was considered in need of 24 hour inpatient substance/alcohol rehabilitation treatment as the patient lacked sufficient coping skills and relapse prevention skills, ability to identify triggers, and enough sober supports to remain abstinent in a less restrictive setting. The patient was at risk for severe withdrawal due to the large amount of daily alcohol and cocaine use and also was at risk for overdose or medical complications from cocaine and alcohol use. According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) the patient met criteria for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment because drug/alcohol use put the patient at risk for more severe withdrawal, complicated or life threatening withdrawal such as delirium tremens. Also, the patient had comorbid psychiatric conditions including ADHD, anxiety, and depression as well as comorbid medical issues including hypertension (HTN). It was reported the patient could not maintain abstinence even after past inpatient substance/alcohol treatment and the patient tried to stop but couldn't without this 24 hour therapeutic treatment setting. The patient needed to develop healthy coping skills and relapse prevention skills, and the boyfriend used cocaine and drugs and was a bad influence, and also that the patient used with friends. The patient witnessed domestic violence. The patient continued to use cocaine and alcohol despite negative consequences at work and with family. Substance and alcohol use resulted in an inability to fulfill life's obligations, and that there were daily urges to use. It was reported that the patient required this intensive treatment for motivating strategies, activities, and processing that was only available in this 24 hour rehabilitation treatment setting. The patient left against medical advice (AMA). Without this structured and supervised therapeutic inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment, the patient likely would have relapsed as evidenced by the inability to stop use, relapse after a past inpatient substance treatment, and due to the lack of coping skills and sober supports. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be reversed. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. The medical necessity for inpatient admission is substantiated.

The insurer denied coverage for residential mental health treatment.

The denial is upheld.

This patient reportedly was admitted to this inpatient residential treatment due to mood and behavioral symptoms and anxiety symptoms. The patient reportedly had passive suicidal ideation and thoughts of self-harm, depressed and irritable mood, emotional instability, crying spells, flashbacks, dissociative symptoms, concentration problems, decreased activities of daily living (ADL's), isolation, and feelings of shame and guilt. The patient reportedly had 7 past psychiatric hospitalizations. The patient reportedly was attending group therapy and taking Sertraline for mood and anxiety symptoms. The patient had reported diagnoses of Borderline Personality Disorder, Generalized Anxiety Disorder, and Major Depressive Disorder. The plan was to step down to a partial hospital program with boarding.

The insurer denied coverage for continued inpatient behavioral health residential treatment not medically necessary treatment then. They stated that the patient did not require further 24 hour inpatient treatment, and they recommended a less restrictive level of care such as partial hospital program (PHP) treatment then. 

The Milliman Care Guidelines Residential-Behavioral Health Level of Care guidelines for adults report that one needs to have continued danger to self or others, moderately or severe psychiatric or behavioral symptoms requiring 24 hour daily treatment, or serious dysfunction in daily living. Also, the Interqual Behavioral Health Adult Inpatient Level of Care residential treatment guidelines reports that one still has to have psychiatric or behavioral symptoms that put the patient at high risk for hospitalization if not in this 24 hour treatment or that they still have psychiatric or behavioral symptoms that are improving or expected to improve but they are not clinically stable yet to step down to a less restrictive level of care. In this case it was reported that this patient had mood and behavioral symptoms and anxiety symptoms on admission and also reportedly had passive suicidal ideation and thoughts of self-harm, depressed and irritable mood, emotional instability, crying spells, flashbacks, dissociative symptoms, concentration problems, decreased ADL's, isolation, feelings of shame and guilt. However, there were no medical records for review reporting moderate to severe behavioral or psychiatric symptoms that required only 24 hour inpatient mental health treatment then or reports of specific evidence that the patient could not be treated in a less restrictive level of care then. 

There were no medical records for review that provided enough specific evidence to support that the patient only required 24 hour inpatient residential treatment or that the patient could not be treated in a less restrictive level of care then. There were no medical records reporting suicidal or homicidal ideation, plan, or intent, psychotic symptoms, self-injurious, aggressive, threatening, or severely agitated behavior, manic episodes, significant behavioral or mood symptoms requiring 24 hour treatment, or inability to care for the patient's basic needs. There were no reports of specific reported identifiable and quantifiable treatment goals that could only be achieved in a 24 hour residential treatment setting or that could not be achieved in a less restrictive setting or specific evidence that he was considered a danger to self or others. As a result, the recommendation is to uphold the previous decision and deny coverage for continued inpatient mental health residential treatment.

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be upheld. The health care plan did act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.

The medical necessity for residential mental health treatment is not substantiated.

summary:
Mental Health

Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder
treatment: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS)
The insurer denied Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS). The health plan's determination is overturned.

The patient is an adult female with history of a mood disorder best characterized as bipolar II disorder with most recent episode, major depressive disorder, severe and recurrent without psychotic features. The patient has a documented history of multiple medication treatments including treatment with Prozac, Celexa, Lexapro, and Cymbalta prescribed over the past ten years. She has received augmentation with Seroquel. Due to adverse effects or lack of efficacy or sustained benefit, the patient has continued to experience severe symptoms of depression and functional impairments scoring 22 on the PHQ-9 (Patient Health Questionnaire) in the severe range of depression. 

Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) is medically necessary for this patient.
TMS therapy as a primary or adjunctive therapy for treatment of depression has generally been evaluated in patients who have treatment refractory/resistant depression, as defined by one or more, antidepressant medication treatment failures with or without augmentation. TMS therapy for depressive disorder has been established by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as a safe treatment; and the data, as reflected in peer reviewed medical literature, supports this assertion. Specifically, when treatments with antidepressant medication with or without augmentation, or with electroconvulsive therapy, and/or psychotherapy, especially cognitive behavioral therapy, have failed to produce a response or remission, then TMS is an appropriate consideration. This assertion is noted in the American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorder, referenced below. Moreover, scientific literature indicates that a course of treatment with TMS therapy is reasonable in cases of treatment resistant depression as defined in the scientific literature.
In this case, at least four alternative therapeutic trials with augmentation together with other therapeutic measures have been provided, and the proposed treatment with TMS therapy is considered clinically appropriate and medically necessary. Additionally, the use of TMS therapy is reasonable, and in the best interest of the patient. The decision to proceed with TMS therapy reflects sound medical judgment based upon the current scientific literature and American Psychiatric Association practice guidelines concerning the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorder. The patient in this case has demonstrated that her depressive disorder is treatment refractory or resistant, and the proposed treatment of recurrent major depressive disorder using TMS therapy with a clinically appropriate number of sessions is warranted in this case scenario and is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice.

summary:
Diagnosis: Obsessive Compulsive Disorder. 
Treatment: Continued Residential Mental Health Treatment. 

The insurer denied Continued Residential Mental Health Treatment. 
The determination is overturned. 

This is a female patient who was diagnosed with severe obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD); skin picking disorder with excoriation; social anxiety disorder (social phobia); illness anxiety (hypochondriasis); and an unspecified depressive disorder.
She was referred and admitted for residential psychiatric treatment. Despite treatments in the community, the patient continued to have severe symptoms of anxiety, compulsive rituals, and intrusive thoughts and, she had a significant decline in functioning such in that he was unable to function socially or occupationally, or at times had been unable to do basic self-care. 
The patient was making progress with achievement of 75 percent (%) of her goals and participating in intensive treatment. She continued to struggle with symptoms related to anxiety and OCD with prominent compulsive rituals, skin picking in the bathroom, and a continued lack of skills and insight. At times, the patient was resistant to participating due to the severity of her symptoms and persistently impaired functioning; she required ongoing monitoring and coaching with regard the therapy (DBT, CBT, ERP, Life Skills), as well efforts to address social phobia, agoraphobia, and illness anxiety. 

The requested health service/treatment of psychiatric residential treatment was medically necessary for this patient. 

The patient's admission and continued residential level treatment is reasonable and warranted. She continued to display severe symptoms of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and associated symptoms of anxiety together with distress problems, interpersonal functioning problems and decline or impairment of functioning that had deteriorated to the point that she was unable to benefit from treatment at lower levels of care. She continued to display coping deficits and a lack of insight that did warrant the structure, monitoring, and intensity of treatment for the duration of the residential stay. The patient could not be effectively managed at a lower level of care in a less restrictive treatment setting during the time interval under review.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder.
Treatment: Social Day Care Increase to 3 Day(s) per Week.
The insurer denied Social Day Care Increase to 3 Day(s) per Week.
The determination is upheld.


This is a female patient with a medical history notable for major depressive disorder. The patient is approved for 19 hours per week of personal care service and two (2) days per week of social day care (SDC). The patient and her care team requested an increase to three (3) days per week of social day care, and this request was denied by the health plan.
The patient's psychiatrist provided a letter of support for this appeal. The letter states that the patient has depression and anxiety. The letter reports that she also has medical conditions which impact her functioning. The physician requests an increase in home health aide personal care hours. There was a request for Social Day Care in the letter.
The patient's nurse practitioner provided a letter of support for this appeal. The letter states that the patient has valvular heart disease, hypertension, and depression. She lives alone. The letter states that "per my professional opinion, the patient would greatly benefit from SDC, Social Day Care, three times a week." No further details were provided.
A Uniform Assessment System (UAS) was completed was available for review. The patient lives alone. She was alert and oriented with procedural memory intact. Her recall was 0/3 at five minutes. For her Instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs), she requires extensive or maximal assistance for all. A task tool associated with the UAS recommended 17.5 hours per week to address her personal care needs. At issue is the medical necessity of Social Day Care SDC - Center-Based Day Care Services; per diem Increase to 3 Day(s) per Week.

The requested health service of Social Day Care SDC - Center-Based Day Care Services; per diem Increase to 3 Day(s) per Week has not been demonstrated to be medically necessary for this patient.
The patient is receiving personal care hours which should be sufficient as recommended by the UAS task tool. Her psychiatrist's letter recommends additional home health hours, but this is not the question under review. The letter does not state which personal care needs, if any, are not being met with her current allotment of hours. The letter from the patient's primary nurse practitioner recommends the requested increase in Social Day Care as something that would "greatly benefit" the patient but does not provide any detail as to what benefit that would provide and if the increase is medically necessary. Therefore, there is insufficient evidence that the requested increase is medically necessary for this patient.
