summary:
Diagnosis Substance Use Disorders

Treatment Inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatment

The insurer denied coverage for Inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatment

The denial is Overturned

 
This adult male reportedly was admitted to this inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment as he reportedly was drinking 3-4 bottles of liquor per day with a 35-year history of use, snorting 1 bundle of cocaine daily, and also smoking cannabis. He reportedly had a past hospitalization 9 months prior to admission due to substance use. He reportedly could not stop substance and alcohol use without being in a 24-hour inpatient setting as it was reported that in the homeless shelter that there was substance and alcohol use. He reportedly lacked coping skills and a supportive sober system for abstinence. His urine toxicology were reportedly positive when tested in the shelter. He reportedly had a positive toxicology for cocaine and THC. He reportedly left against medical advice (AMA) despite recommendations to remain and complete his treatment.

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatment as not medically necessary treatment. They stated that he was not at risk of life-threatening withdrawal, did not have acute physical or psychiatric comorbid conditions requiring 24-hour inpatient rehabilitation or detoxication treatment, did not have suicidal or homicidal thoughts or psychotic symptoms, and was able to care for his basic needs. They recommended a less restrictive level of care.

The reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatment as the medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that he required inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatment. The American Psychological Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the treatment of patients with substance use disorders (SUD) reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. It also states that patients with past complicated or life-threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens are in need of inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal and reports that patients with comorbid medical condition that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification. The patient was at risk for serious medical problems, overdose, and severe, complicated or life-threatening withdrawal so he required inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatment. According to the Level of Care Determination (LOCADTR) he did require 24-hour treatment as he could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification or rehabilitation in a less restrictive setting as he continued to use very large amounts of alcohol daily and cocaine despite past inpatient substance treatment. The risk of delirium tremens can occur 3 - 4 days after heavy alcohol use so he was considered at risk for this and in need of 24-hour inpatient detoxification and rehabilitation treatment. The patient was considered a high risk for relapse without 24-hour therapeutic inpatient substance/alcohol rehabilitation treatment also. As a result, the recommendation is to reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatment.
Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be overturned. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. The medical necessity for the admission at a substance abuse inpatient detoxification level of care is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder.
Treatment: Mental health residential level of care.

The insurer denied the mental health residential level of care.  The health plan's determination is overturned.

The patient is a female, who was referred for residential mental health treatment in an outdoor wilderness-based program in order to address behavioral disturbances in the context of mood, anxiety, attentional, and neurodevelopmental disorders associated with impaired functioning and problematic behavior. The patient was diagnosed with major depressive disorder, social anxiety disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder-inattentive type, and an unspecified developmental disorder. The patient's presenting issues included low self-esteem, lack of confidence, and relationship problems together with stressors within the primary support, educational and social environment domains. The patient had been in past treatment settings but failed to engage with treatment with continued symptoms of depression and anxiety together with a history of social withdrawal, school failure/refusal, and mood instability associated with substance use with cannabis-vaping alone with social isolation and refusal to communicate with parents or leave her bedroom. The patient was referred to the residential treatment in an outdoor/wilderness setting in order to address the core symptoms of depression and relationship problems including parent-child relational problems and a lack of motivation.
The patient has a history of outpatient treatments without sustained benefit. There has not been a suicide attempt, or violent or aggressive behavior or impulse control problems. However, the patient has conflict with her parents that did include lack of motivation and problematic behavioral disruptions that included the school refusal, problems with peers, family conflict, uncooperative behavior, social isolation and refusal to communicate.

The program focused on organizational skills; self-care; peer relationships; and other life skills, as well as behavioral and emotional regulation with milieu, individual, group, family, and outdoor therapies/sport, as well as other interventions aimed at improving life skills. The patient actively participated in the treatment plan and worked on therapeutic, social, and emotional functions in the context of a therapeutic milieu with a residential level of structure and monitoring in a behavioral health program and setting that included educational assignments and psychiatric services with availability of ongoing medication management. 

The patient's admission and continued residential level treatment through discharge is reasonable and in the best interest of the patient; she continued to display clinical features and symptoms that necessitated the admission and the continued residential level services, as she struggled to engage in treatment and had intermittent bouts of affective instability that did require residential level structure and monitoring with active treatment. She had a history of treatment failure with lower-level services and had recently displayed significant problematic behaviors with maladaptive coping, emotional regulation problems, distress problems, interpersonal functioning problems and day-to-day functioning problems that included school refusal in the context of severe mood and anxiety disorders complicated by attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)-inattentive type and a neurodevelopmental disorder, as well as vaping cannabis class substances in isolation. The treatment provided was evidence-based and medically necessary and appropriate and could not have been effectively provided in a less restrictive treatment environment through discharge. 

The health plan's determination of medical necessity is overturned.

This adult male patient with a history of heroin use and withdrawal presented complaining of withdrawal symptoms that include headache, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. The patient was requesting detox. His vital signs were stable. His heart rate was 56 and respiratory rate was 16. The patient's exam was unremarkable. Pertinent labs include a white blood cell count of 21.41. The patient's electrocardiogram showed no ST changes. His chest x-ray; kidney, ureter, and bladder (KUB); and abdominal/pelvic computed tomography (CT) revealed no acute disease. The patient was admitted. Opioid withdrawal was resolved. The patient was to consider methadone taper. On day #2, the patient's vital signs were stable. Nausea and vomiting had resolved. The patient was to start Suboxone. On day #4, nausea was improving. Maximal temperature was 100.9. Clinical opiate withdrawal scale (COWS) score was eight. The diet was advanced to regular. The patient was continued on a methadone taper. The patient continued the methadone taper. On day #5, the patient complained of nausea and diarrhea. Clinical opiate withdrawal scale score was three. The patient was to continue methadone. There were no rehab beds available. The patient was discharged to rehab on day #7.

The proposed treatment was not medically necessary.

This patient was admitted for opiate withdrawal. His history was not remarkable for elevated risk due to historical or comorbid factors. The patient was hemodynamically stable with asymptomatic bradycardia. He did not have arrhythmia. He had nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. The patient's labs were unremarkable. He did not have electrolyte abnormalities or dehydration. The patient was admitted with a plan for medication assisted treatment and clinical opiate withdrawal scale (COWS) protocol. Treatment included methadone/Suboxone. The patient was awaiting transfer to rehab. He remained hemodynamically stable during the hospital stay and did not have symptoms of severe withdrawal. He did not have symptoms that required an acute inpatient level of care. He had not failed management in a lesser level of care. The requested inpatient hospital admission was not medically necessary.

The insurer denied: Inpatient Detoxification Admission
The denial is overturned.

The patient is an adult male who was admitted following medical screening to acute inpatient level services for detoxification and withdrawal management of severe alcohol, stimulant (cocaine), cannabis (marijuana), hallucinogen (phencyclidine [PCP]),
and sedative-hypnotic-anxiolytic (benzodiazepine) use disorders. The patient denied use of benzodiazepines despite a positive drug screen. His substance use began as a tween at age eleven with escalating use and progression of the disease with a chronic relapsing course despite at least two or more treatment episodes in the past. The patient presented with mild alcohol withdrawal. Withdrawal symptoms included tremor, insomnia, lightheadedness, and abdominal cramps with a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) scale score of 8. The patient has a history of psychiatric disorder related to a stabbing incident in 1990 with diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). He had a history of substance-related treatment episodes including at least two detoxification and rehabilitation treatment episodes with relapses. The patient was admitted to acute inpatient level care and placed on a detoxification regimen. Following his first day of treatment, the patient began to participate in counseling and educational sessions. His demeanor improved as he underwent detoxification treatment, and he was social with peers and moderately motivated for participation. He participated in educational sessions and counseling while in treatment with motivational interviewing with the goal of proceeding to rehabilitation treatment and considering medication assisted treatment. The patient was discharged on day #6 after completion of the detoxification protocol with plans/referral to start a rehabilitation treatment and with
recommendations for involvement in 12-step recovery meetings and medication assisted treatment with Vivitrol. The denial determination was based on Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Guidelines indicating that treatment could be safely provided with lower-level care, and that the patient was motivated with no severe withdrawal symptoms or history of complicated alcohol withdrawal. The appeal was based on New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria and the presenting clinical features including use of multiple substances of abuse, withdrawal symptoms, and a lack of coping skills, as well as history of a chronic relapsing course of the illnesses. The proposed health service/treatment was medically necessary for this patient. The proposed inpatient services and detoxification treatment and withdrawal management for severe alcohol and other substance use disorders, and other services noted in the clinical summary, could not have been safely and effectively provided at a lower level of care. The adult inpatient treatment of this patient's substance disorders did require the admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level setting and 24-hour monitoring in view of the severity of the alcohol use disorder, and the presentation with continued use of substances while receiving outpatient level substance-related services. The patient did require a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management and inpatient level monitoring during the time frame under review, as it was reasonable that the patient would have been unable to abstain from the substances of abuse if detoxification and treatment were to be attempted at a lower level of care. Medical necessity for the admission and the continued inpatient services, is met in this case, and is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice, published guidelines, and the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, referenced below.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance use disorder. 
Treatment: Substance Abuse Inpatient Rehabilitation. 
The insurer denied: Substance Abuse Inpatient Rehabilitation. 
The denial is upheld. 

The patient is an adult male. He was referred from residential treatment and admitted for inpatient rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment in order to address severe alcohol use disorder. The history of substance use included use of six 24-ounce beers twice weekly. He was failing his urine toxicology assessments while in the residential program. The patient has a history of psychiatric disorder best characterized as bipolar disorder with depression and anxiety but denied psychiatric hospitalization or suicidal behavior. He had no other substance use disorders but was tobacco dependent. There were no acute general medical issues; he was medically screened at the time of admission. Vital signs were normal and laboratory assessments were normal or unremarkable including a negative drug screen. 
The patient's evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination that reflected motivation for rehabilitation treatment, but limited insight, impaired judgment, and poor control of impulses. 
The patient readily engaged in substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment. The patient was noted to be engaged in the therapeutic activities, social with peers, and participating in recovery groups and most other group sessions. He was adherent with medication that included the vitamin supplements and comfort medications, as noted. He continued to receive intensive rehabilitation services, monitoring, and structure including 24-hour nursing monitoring, and was discharged after completion of inpatient rehabilitation treatment with referral back to his residential program. During the time interval under review, the patient had no significant withdrawal or post-acute withdrawal symptoms, no safety concerns, and no psychiatric or biomedical complications. The health plan's denial of coverage is based on New York State Office of Addiction Services and Supports Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (OASAS LOCADTR) 3 Criteria and medical necessity. 

The Substance Abuse Inpatient Rehabilitation was not medically necessary. 

The health plan's determination is clinically appropriate in keeping with prevailing standards of medical practice. In this case, the patient could have been reasonably managed with lower-level care in a less restrictive treatment setting, as the health plan asserted. The patient presented with substance use disorder, diagnosed with severe alcohol use disorder. He was medically screened and had no acute general medical issues. He received inpatient level rehabilitation treatment and readily engaged in treatment and had no significant biomedical (withdrawal symptoms or signs) or psychiatric treatment issues, as well as receiving motivational enhancement and consideration of the use of medication assisted treatment and ongoing vitamin replacement therapy. Throughout his stay, there were no complicating treatment issues or biomedical or co-occurring psychiatric issues or safety concerns that would have warranted inpatient level of care, structure, or 24-hour monitoring for the time interval under review. The application of New York State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) 3.0 Criteria, as well as Level of Care Utilization System (LOCUS) and American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria referenced below, did indicate that the patient was clinically appropriate for treatment with lower-level care in a less restrictive treatment setting, as the health plan asserts.

summary:
Diagnosis: depression
Treatment: transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)
The insurer denied transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS).
The health plan's determination is overturned. 

The patient is a young adult female with a history of major depressive disorder, recurrent and moderately severe without psychotic features and panic attacks. The patient has a documented history of multiple failed medication treatments for depression including treatment with more than two disparate classes of medication (Lexapro, Prozac, Luvox, Zoloft, Cymbalta, and Pristiq), as well as augmentation with Buspar. Additionally, the patient has received treatment with lorazepam and clonazepam targeting associated symptoms of anxiety and panic related to the mood disorder and comorbid generalized anxiety disorder. She has been treated with an evidence-based psychotherapy without a response or remission of depressive symptoms. She has not received electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) or VNS (vagus nerve stimulation) therapy. At the time of evaluation for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) therapy, the PHQ-9 (Patient Health Questionnaire) scale score was 15 in the moderately severe range for symptoms of depression associated with severe impairment of functioning.

Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) is medically necessary for this patient.

TMS therapy as a primary or adjunctive therapy for treatment of depression has generally been evaluated in patients who have treatment refractory/resistant depression, as defined by one or more, antidepressant medication treatment failures with or without augmentation. TMS therapy for depressive disorder has been established by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as a safe treatment; and, the data, as reflected in peer reviewed medical literature, supports this assertion. Specifically, when treatments with antidepressant medication with or without augmentation, or with electroconvulsive therapy, and/or psychotherapy, especially cognitive behavioral therapy, have failed to produce a response or remission, then TMS is an appropriate consideration. This assertion is noted in the American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorder, referenced below. Moreover, the scientific literature indicates that a course of treatment with TMS therapy is reasonable in cases of treatment resistant depression as defined in the scientific literature.

summary:
Diagnosis: Schizophrenia

Treatment: Inpatient Admission

The insurer denied coverage Inpatient Admission

The denial is Reversed

This adult patient reportedly was admitted to this inpatient hospital setting on for involuntary movements after taking extra Risperidone. It was reported that the patient had a fever, tachycardia, nausea, agitation, more paranoia, and had elevated creatinine kinase (CK) 0.95, low potassium (K) 3.0, magnesium (Mg) and Calcium (Ca) 8.6. The patient reportedly had a diagnosis of Schizophrenia and had past reported auditory hallucinations and also had past depression. The patient reportedly had Becker's Muscular Dystrophy. There was consideration of neuroleptic malignant syndrome in addition to dystonic reaction due to taking too much antipsychotic medication. There also was concern for sepsis. The patient was not cleared psychiatrically. The Risperidone was discontinued and Abilify started. The patient also reportedly had IV (intravenous) fluids, Benadryl, and electrolytes managed. 

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient hospital treatment as not medically necessary treatment. They stated that he did not require 24 hour hospital treatment, and they recommended a less restrictive level of care.

The reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient hospital treatment from as the medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that the patient required this level of care then. The Milliman Care Guidelines (MCG) Behavioral Health Inpatient Level of Care Adult criteria reports that a patient needs to present as an imminent danger to self, imminent danger to others, with severe psychiatric or behavioral symptoms, have a severely dysfunctional living including inability to care for self, unwillingness to participate voluntarily, or a less restrictive level of care is not feasible meet criteria for inpatient behavioral health level of care. Also, the American Psychological Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Schizophrenia reports that neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a rare but potentially life threatening side effect of antipsychotic medications and requires inpatient hospital treatment. In this case, it was reported that this patient took too many antipsychotic medications, Risperidone, and had dystonic reaction and rule out neuroleptic malignant syndrome so the patient required inpatient hospital treatment. The patient had medical symptoms including fever, tachycardia, nausea, agitation, more paranoia, and had elevated CK, low K, Mg, and Ca. Symptoms included staring at the walls on admission. The patient also had a history of psychotic and depressive symptoms and one had to rule out suicide attempt for taking too many pills or worsened psychotic symptoms as a cause as there was a past auditory hallucinations and reports of increased paranoia during the hospital stay. The patient had psychiatric consultation and these issues reportedly were being assessed and required inpatient hospital treatment due to the rule out for the potential life threatening neuroleptic malignant syndrome. The patient also needed to be assessed a few days in the hospital to assess if this were a suicide attempt or confusion and inability to care for self-such as taking too many medications resulting in risk to self. After the psychiatric consultant was done and the patient was medically cleared, the patient was discharged. As a result, the recommendation is to reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for continued inpatient hospital treatment.

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be reversed. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. The medical necessity for an inpatient admission is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder-severe-recurrent
Treatment: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation
The insurer denied coverage for: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation
The denial is: Upheld

This adolescent reportedly had depressive symptoms, attention problems, and behavioral issues including depressed mood, difficulty paying attention, tantrums, agitation, irritable and angry mood, and hyperactivity. The patient reportedly had difficulties in academic functioning. The patient had a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder-severe-recurrent and was taking Sertraline 150 milligram (mg) per day, Vraylar 4.5 mg per day, and Clonidine .1 mg per day. It was reported that the patient had transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy (TMS) reported improvement in symptoms and functioning. 

The reviewer agrees with the decision to deny coverage for transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy (TMS) for 21 sessions from as there is not sufficient evidence in the medical literature to support the efficacy and long-term safety of transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy (TMS) in patients under 18 years of age. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved Neurostar Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Therapy for the treatment of depression in October 2008 in patients 18 years old and older and transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy was cleared by the FDA in 10/2008 and indicated for the treatment of major depressive disorder in patients who failed or who did not have satisfactory improvement from 1 past antidepressant medication at or above minimal effective dose and duration in the current episode. However, there is not sufficient evidence in the medical literature to support the efficacy and long-term safety for patients 18 years old and younger. Also, according to the Journal of Child Adolescent Psychopharmacology 2016 26 (7) 5820589, "Magnetic Resonance Imaging Guided Open Label High Frequency Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation for Adolescents with Major Depressive Disorder by Croarkin PE, Marony-Smith MJ it states that transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy is feasible, tolerable, and effective in adolescents with treatment resistant major depressive disorder but larger blinded sham controlled trials are needed for definitive safety and efficacy. It states that further efforts to understand optimal delivery, dosing, and biomarker development for repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy treatment for adolescent depression is warranted. Transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy (TMS) is only FDA approved for treatment of patients 18 years and older with of major depressive disorder in patients who failed or who did not have satisfactory improvement from 1 past antidepressant medication at or above minimal effective dose and duration in the current episode. 

This patient was younger than 18 and there is not sufficient medical literature to support the safety and efficacy in patients treated with transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy (TMS) for that age. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be upheld. The health care plan did act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. The medical necessity for Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation is not substantiated.

The Inpatient Detoxification Services was medically necessary in

The patient had 3 past overdoses including a recent one 3 months prior to admission. The patient had multiple past treatment episodes including past inpatient substance detoxification treatment as recent as 3 months ago for 5 days. The patient reportedly was in a hospital last summer after an overdose. The patient was using 1 bag of heroin intra-nasally (IN) per day and reportedly used 4 bags the day most recent to this admission. The patient had a 14-year history of use. The patient was using Alprazolam 2 milligram (mg) a few times per week and had a history of Klonopin use and had a 14-year history of Benzodiazepine use. The patient was using Buprenorphine from the street. The patient smoked marijuana 3-6 times per week and had a 28-year history of use. The patient had a positive toxicology for Opiates, Benzodiazepines, Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), Buprenorphine, and Methadone. The patient was unemployed. The patient was put on a 5-day Methadone and Ativan protocol for detoxification treatment. The patient was discharged 5 days later to inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment level of care then for further treatment.
  
This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient substance detoxification treatment when the patient was transferred to inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment level of care then for further treatment and the medical records provided did provide enough specific evidence to support that the patient required this level of care. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. It also states that patients with past complicated or life-threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens need inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal and reports that patients with comorbid medical condition that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification. Also, the United States Department of Health and Human Services-Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) Center for Substance Abuse Treatment reports that inpatient treatment is necessary if the ability to attend outpatient treatment daily is a problem, one is unable to follow-up in outpatient treatment, if medical conditions complicate the treatment of withdrawal, if one has previous withdrawal seizures of delirium tremens, or if one does not have the capacity for informed consent. The patient was considered at risk for severe, complicated, and life-threatening withdrawal and another overdose so the patient required 24-hour inpatient substance detoxification treatment then. The risk of delirium tremens can occur 3-7 days after Benzodiazepine use. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be reversed. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. The medical necessity for inpatient substance abuse admission is substantiated.

The patient is an adult female with a history of a mood disorder best characterized as bipolar I disorder with the most recent episode, major depressive disorder, severe and recurrent without psychotic features. The patient has a documented history of multiple medication treatments, including Prozac, Zoloft, Celexa, Lexapro, Wellbutrin, Effexor extended release (XR), and Cymbalta, prescribed over the past several years without sustained benefit or remission. She has received augmentation with Seroquel, Vraylar, Abilify, Lithium, Tegretol, and supplemental treatment with clonazepam, gabapentin, and zolpidem targeting anxiety, as well as Ritalin and Vyvanse addressing attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Due to adverse effects, or lack of efficacy, or sustained benefit, the patient has continued to experience severe symptoms of depression and functional impairments, scoring as much as 26 on the PHQ-9 (personal health questionnaire) in the severe range of depression. Additionally, the patient has had treatment with evidence-based psychotherapy (cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)) combined with medication without sustained benefit or a remission of symptoms, along with an emotional support animal and other supports from family and her significant other.
The patient has no significant general medical issues that interfere with the treatment for depression and does not have a diagnosis of substance use disorder, eating disorder, or sleep disorder.
The patient's clinician has recommended transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). The recommendation is in the context of an episode of major depression that is treatment-resistant/refractory. The patient has severe depression with loss of interest, hypersomnia, low energy and appetite, concentration difficulties, and associated symptoms of anxiety and sleep disturbance. She has trauma history with childhood sexual abuse. The patient is functionally impaired and took a leave from college following a suicide attempt. She has been hospitalized for mania, depression, and suicidality, as well as having a history of self-harm with cutting and banging her head. The patient has borderline personality traits or disorder.

The requested health service/treatment of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) is medically necessary for this patient.
TMS therapy as a primary or adjunctive therapy for the treatment of depression has generally been evaluated in patients who have treatment-refractory/resistant depression, as defined by one or more antidepressant medication treatment failures with or without augmentation. TMS therapy for depressive disorder has been established by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as a safe treatment, and the data, as reflected in peer-reviewed medical literature, supports this assertion. Specifically, when treatments with antidepressant medication with or without augmentation, or with electroconvulsive therapy and psychotherapy, especially cognitive behavioral therapy, have failed to produce a response or remission, then TMS is an appropriate consideration. This assertion is noted in the American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorder, referenced below. Moreover, the scientific literature indicates that a course of treatment with TMS therapy is reasonable in cases of treatment resistant depression as defined in the scientific literature.
In this case, at least four or more alternative therapeutic trials with augmentation together with other therapeutic measures have been provided, and the proposed treatment with TMS therapy is considered clinically appropriate and medically necessary. Additionally, the use of repetitive TMS therapy is reasonable and in the best interest of the patient. The decision to proceed with TMS therapy reflects sound medical judgment based upon the current scientific literature and American Psychiatric Association practice guidelines concerning the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorder. The patient in this case has demonstrated that her depressive disorder is treatment refractory or resistant, and the proposed treatment of recurrent major depressive disorder using TMS therapy with a clinically appropriate number of sessions is warranted in this case scenario and is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice. Moreover, the scientific literature does support the use of TMS therapy in patients with both unipolar and bipolar depression consistent with the prevailing standards of medical practice for the condition diagnosed in this case, including treatment-resistant depression.

The patient is an adult male. He presented for detoxification and

The patient was medically screened and admitted for inpatient level detoxification with use of continued methadone, vitamin replacement therapy and comfort medications.

clear and thought production was linear and logical. There were no severe symptoms on mental 
status examination such as thought disorder, cognitive impairment, severe mood disturbance, 
psychosis or perceptual disturbance, or suicidal ideation.
The patient presented with anxiety and complaints of insomnia addressed with Vistaril prn (as 
needed). He had fair control of his impulses. The CIWA (clinical institute withdrawal 
assessment) and COWS (clinical opiate withdrawal scale) scale scores were both at a zero.
The patient was admitted for inpatient detoxification. The patient's hospital course progressed 
without incident until the day of discharge. Vital signs were consistently normal and the patient 
was in no apparent distress. The patient slept with the use of prn Vistaril. His monitoring 
occurred without incident, and he attended group sessions and received counseling with 
recommendation for clinically appropriate aftercare to include rehabilitation treatment. He was 
discharged against administratively with referral back to his outpatient clinic and 
recommendations to resume his involvement with 12-step recovery groups and continued use of methadone, as well as quarantine in a shelter. The health plan denied coverage of the admission based on New York State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) 3 Criteria indicating that the patient was not acutely ill, had no risk for severe withdrawal symptoms or general medical complications with no psychiatric symptoms warranting inpatient level services. summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Inpatient Detoxification Admission
The insurer denied: Inpatient Detoxification Admission
The denial is overturned.

The patient is a homeless and unemployed adult male. He was admitted following medical screening to acute inpatient level services for detoxification and withdrawal management of severe alcohol, stimulant (cocaine), and sedative-hypnotic-anxiolytic (benzodiazepine) use disorders. The patient was using up to two pints of liquor together with a six-pack of beer daily together with up to $300 worth of cocaine. He denied use of benzodiazepines despite a positive drug screen. His substance use began at age 15 with escalating use and progression of the disease with a chronic relapsing course despite at least two or more treatment episodes in the past. He reported that the longest period of sobriety was about two years. The patient presented with moderate alcohol withdrawal at the time of admission. Withdrawal symptoms included tremor, sweats, nausea, insomnia, lightheadedness, and agitation with a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) scale score of 15. He had a history of substance-related treatment episodes including at least two detoxification and rehabilitation treatment episodes with relapses. There were no acute medical issues or general medical concerns though he had a history of syphilis. The patient was admitted to acute inpatient level care and placed on a detoxification regimen. He participated in educational sessions and counseling while in treatment with motivational interviewing with the goal of proceeding to rehabilitation treatment and considering medication assisted treatment. The patient was discharged after completion of the detoxification protocol with plans/referral to start a rehabilitation treatment and with recommendations for involvement in 12-step recovery meetings. Denial determination was based on Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Guidelines indicating that treatment could be safely provided with lower-level care, and that the patient was motivated with no severe withdrawal symptoms or history of complicated alcohol withdrawal. The appeal was based on New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria and the presenting clinical features including use of multiple substances of abuse, moderately severe withdrawal symptoms with a Clinical Institute 
Withdrawal Assessment of 15, and a lack of coping skills, as well as history of a chronic relapsing course of the illnesses.

The requested health service was medically necessary for this patient.

The proposed inpatient services and detoxification treatment and withdrawal management for severe alcohol and other substance use disorders, and other services could not have been safely and effectively provided at a lower level of care. The adult inpatient treatment of this patient's substance disorders did require the admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level setting and 24-hour monitoring in view of the severity of the alcohol use disorder and the clinical features of the case. Withdrawal symptoms were managed with tapering dosages of benzodiazepine/Librium requiring monitoring. Thus, the patient did require a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management and inpatient level monitoring as it was reasonable that the patient would have been unable to abstain from the substances of abuse if detoxification and treatment were to be attempted at a lower level of care. Medical necessity for the admission and the continued inpatient services is met in this case and is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice, published practice guidelines, and American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria. This answer is also consistent with New York State instruction concerning medical necessity reviews including the required application of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria and Guidelines. Therefore, the requested health service is medically necessary for this patient.

summary:
Mental Health
Mental health inpatient 

Diagnosis: schizoaffective disorder
Treatment: inpatient mental health
The insurer denied Continued Stay for Inpatient Mental Health Level of Care

This case involves an adult male with a longstanding diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type versus schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. The patient presented with symptoms of psychosis and agitation after stopping his medication. He was kicked out of the shelter where he was staying due to aggressive behavior towards others. He was not sleeping and was pacing which prompted his presentation to the emergency department. He was evaluated, medically cleared, and admitted to acute inpatient level care. He had been discharged from another inpatient psychiatric facility recently after a two-week stay.

Continued Stay for Inpatient Mental Health Level of Care for an additional 54 days was medically necessary. However, after this time, the patient no longer required the inpatient mental health level of care. 

In this case scenario, the continued inpatient level services were necessary in view of the continued acuity and risk for aggressive behavior and need for continued inpatient level structure and monitoring. The patient had not reached a level of stability that he could have been safely or effectively managed with lower-level services. The patient continued to need the intensity of services, structure, and monitoring of an inpatient setting.
However, after the additional time, it was not medically necessary for this patient to have 24-hour monitoring in an acute care setting in view of his relative lack of impulsive behaviors, diminished symptoms of psychosis, and improvements in mood and sleep and daily functioning. There were no general medical issues or co-occurring substance use disorders complicating this case that would have required continued inpatient level services.

The patient is an adult male. He was referred from a general medical facility for inpatient rehabilitation and substance use disorder treatment. The patient has a history of longstanding substance use disorders with alcohol and stimulant (cocaine) class substances with no prior treatments. The patient has no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens. He was referred after presenting with chest pain in association with the 
substance use disorders due to difficulty with the social environment and coping problems mostly related to the substance use disorders in the context of family problems. His history of substance use included use of large quantities of alcohol and up to one gram of cocaine on a daily continuous basis. He identified psychosocial stressors and consequences as a major concern including problems with housing, occupational, primary support, and social environment domains. The patient has a history of psychiatric disorder with a diagnosis of an unspecified anxiety disorder and major depressive disorder, as well as trauma history with childhood sexual abuse and verbal abuse from his sister; he denied history of psychiatric hospitalization or suicidal behavior. The patient had been medically screened with detoxification prior to admission for rehabilitation treatment including laboratory assessment and physical examination which were grossly normal or unremarkable. The patient is employed and was living with his father and with limited family support. He denied legal issues, but has trauma history as noted, as well as ongoing abuse from his sister. There were no significant withdrawal symptoms or post-acute withdrawal symptoms though he displayed anxiety and motor agitation. He also reported insomnia. The patient was discharged on day # (number) 22 with plans for clinically appropriate aftercare. The denial was based on New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria indicating that there were no acute symptoms or serious withdrawal symptoms or general medical or psychiatric issues that would have required inpatient level services. The denial determination indicated that the patient was capable of participating in treatment with lower-level services. The treatment facility appealed based on New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria indicating that inpatient level treatment was the appropriate level of care. The appeal was based on the clinical features of the case with the negative influence of the social environment with severe psychosocial stressors and co-occurring psychiatric disorders.

The requested inpatient substance-related rehabilitation treatment was not medically necessary.

This patient presented with substance use disorders, diagnosed with alcohol and stimulant/cocaine use disorders. He received inpatient level rehabilitation treatment. During the time interval under review, the patient was noted to be in no apparent distress other than anxiety with reasonable functioning and active participation in treatment including positive interactions with staff and peers. Throughout the patient's inpatient stay, there were no complicating treatment issues or biomedical or co-occurring psychiatric issues that would have warranted inpatient level of care or structure or 24-hour nursing monitoring, as the health plan asserts. The application of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria (referenced below) did indicate that the patient was clinically appropriate for treatment with lower-level care in a less restrictive treatment setting. Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) criteria, the scientific literature and published guidelines, referenced below, and with the application of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 criteria.

Treatment: Inpatient Substance Abuse Admission

The denial is overturned.

The patient is an adult male who presented for detoxification treatment, was medically screened, and admitted to acute inpatient level care. The patient had been using three 24-ounce beers together with up to 10 bags of heroin with intravenous administration, 20 dollars' worth of cocaine with intravenous administration, 2 to 4 milligrams of Xanax, as well as 2 to 3 marijuana joints. He has no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens. The patient had a history of prior detoxification treatment episodes and substance use disorder treatments with relapses. His self-referral for treatment was prompted by multiple stressors and general health concerns including risk of losing his housing. The patient has no history of psychiatric disorder and no history of psychiatric hospitalization. The patient presented without acute co-morbid general medical issues. Laboratory assessments were unremarkable or normal with a positive drug screen consistent with history and history of hepatitis C positivity.
Insight was limited with impaired judgment and poor control of impulses. His onset of withdrawal symptoms included anxiety, motor agitation, sweats, body aches, abdominal pain, nausea and diarrhea, and irritability, scoring a 10 on the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) scale and 8 on the Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS). The patient was admitted to detoxification treatment with a comprehensive detoxification protocol with tapering dosages of Ativan and Methadone and as needed (PRN) medications for comfort, as well as vitamin replacement therapy. The program provided for case management with referral and access to rehabilitation treatment that included comprehensive evidence-based treatments. During detoxification the patient engaged in counseling sessions focusing on education about the disease model of addiction, and involvement with unit activities including peer support and educational sessions to motivate the patient to proceed to rehabilitation treatment. Vital signs remained normal during 
his inpatient stay. The patient completed four days of the detoxification treatment and was discharged against medical advice with referrals for clinically appropriate aftercare.
Denial Reason: The denial was based on medical necessity and New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria indicating that there was no serious withdrawal or general medical or psychiatric issues warranting inpatient level services.

The requested health services, inpatient substance-related services with withdrawal management and detoxification treatment, was medically necessary for this patient.

The requested inpatient admission and continued treatment could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. The patient in this case was using heroin, together with alcohol and Xanax and cocaine and cannabis (marijuana) on a daily continuous basis that did warrant inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and 
monitoring for the duration of the protocol; detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments pertinent to the detoxification treatment episode could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care. He had persistent withdrawal symptoms, and the patient's social environment was not conducive to detoxification in the context of limited insight, impaired judgment and poor control of impulses. Thus, the adult inpatient detoxification treatment and withdrawal management of this patient's substance use disorder did warrant the admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level detoxification setting with 24-hour monitoring and use of as needed (PRN) medications. Therefore, medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published practice guidelines, American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and the scientific literature, referenced below, and New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews including the appropriate application of the New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Tool that requires the patient in this scenario default to the higher level of care.

summary:
Diagnosis: Depression/social isolation
Treatment: Increasing the Social Day Care (SDC) from 2 to 3 days/week
The insurer denied coverage for: Increasing the SDC from 2 to 3 days/week
The denial is: Overturned
This is an adult with chronic medical problems including hypertension, diabetes and heart disease. The patient lives with their spouse, daughter and son-in-law. The daughter and son-in-law are paid and informal caregivers. The patient is currently receiving consumer directed personal assistance services (CDPAP) service 4 days/week, 5 hours/day (20 hours/week) and SDC services 2 days/week (combined total services of 28 hours/week).  

According to the Uniform Assessment System (UAS) report, the patient's cognition is described as modified independent. The patient requires extensive to maximal assistance for performing much of their Instrument Activities of Daily Living (IADL) tasks including meal preparation, ordinary housework and shopping. The patient requires limited assistance for bathing, lower body dressing, toilet transfer/use and ambulation. The patient is otherwise independent with personal hygiene, upper body dressing, bed mobility and eating. The patient reports being frequently incontinent of bladder and continent of bowel. There has been no change regarding the patient's ability to perform activities of daily living or self-sufficiency over the prior 90 days. The patient's cognitive and functional ability are much the same when compared to the UAS report.

The letter from the patient's treating physician describing their clinical condition and request for "social day care services" was reviewed.  The doctor does not provide the associated treatment notes to support his claim that the patient "Is socially isolated which led to depression and isolated feeling." There is no clinical evidence that the lack of social day care services is the etiology of the patient's reported depression. However, this physician would agree that an additional 4 hours of social day care would be beneficial for the patient (i.e., socialization, decreased isolation and participation in structured activities) particularly given that the patient's spouse also participates in SDC 3 days/week. This physician is also persuaded by the other appeal letter; who eloquently describes the emotional and practical benefits of the SDC program for the patient. Based on the documents reviewed, increasing the SDC from 2 to 3 days/week is medically necessary.  

From a physical medicine and rehabilitation perspective, increasing the SDC from 2 to 3 days/week is medically necessary.  

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be reversed. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. The medical necessity for Social Day Care (SDC) is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Suicide attempt
Treatment: Continued Inpatient Psychiatric Admission
The insurer denied: Continued Inpatient Psychiatric Admission
The denial is overturned.

This case involves an adult male who took an intentional overdose of heroin, street Xanax, and street Klonopin and was brought into the emergency department with subsequent admission for intensive care and general medical services. The patient was stabilized medically and transferred for psychiatric inpatient treatment to address severe symptoms of depression (major depressive disorder) and anxiety associated with the suicide attempt by overdose. He had become increasingly anxious and depressed with suicidal ideation and deterioration in functioning prior to his admission with three emergency department visits including the last when he had taken the 
overdose with 10 milligrams (mg) of Klonopin and 25 milligrams of Xanax together with the opioid-heroin or methadone. The patient had a history of severe opioid use disorder and was receiving methadone maintenance treatment with 50 milligrams daily. The patient exhibited depressed mood with recent suicidal ideation and the attempted suicide. The patient was admitted to inpatient psychiatric care with plans for close observation, safety monitoring, and antidepressant pharmacotherapy, as well as continued treatment with methadone and withdrawal management. The patient made steady and slow progress addressing the guilt associated with work stress and negative cognitions. He received group, individual, and milieu therapies, as well as counseling regarding the opioid use disorder. He became increasingly cooperative with treatment. He initially had nausea, vomiting, and withdrawal symptoms consistent with benzodiazepine withdrawal, as well as an intense craving prompting a Klonopin taper and seizure precautions. He continued to require as needed medications going forward while the psychotropic regimen was titrated as clinically appropriate. The patient continued to display depression, and he remained fragile with suicidal risk requiring continued safety monitoring and safety observations. Sertraline was increased to 100 milligrams daily together with 100 milligrams of trazodone and continued use of as-needed Vistaril. Case management was working with the patient on a safe and clinically appropriated discharge plan culminating in a discharge to home with outpatient mental health services, a safety plan, and continued involvement in the methadone maintenance treatment program.

The requested health service treatment with continued inpatient psychiatric services for co-occurring disorders is medically necessary.

The patient required the continued acute inpatient level care and the continued structure of an acute inpatient level setting to remain safe and to administer treatment for the psychiatric disturbance while conducting an evaluation, and while observing his functioning with the resumption/adjustment of clinically appropriate medications. The clinical course was complicated by co-occurring opioid use disorder and the overdose with street benzodiazepines, as well as safety observation warranted in a patient at high risk for suicide. Additionally, the treatment team was planning for a safe and clinically appropriate disposition with the need to reconnect the patient to substance-related treatment including methadone maintenance. The medical necessity for continued inpatient level structure and monitoring is reasonable, and in the patient's best interest in view of the patient's severe symptoms of mood disorder and continued risk for suicidal behavior and co-occurring substance use disorder in view of these clinical features and the complicated presentation with history of a serious suicide attempt and need for withdrawal management, continued active treatment with safety monitoring was warranted in the context of the patient's deteriorated functioning. The necessity for continued inpatient level services reflects sound medical judgment in keeping with prevailing standards of professional practice, and with the published societal guidelines (Level of Care Utilization System [LOCUS] Guidelines) and American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria. Additionally, New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria were met in this case scenario.

summary:
Diagnosis: Active alcohol withdrawal symptoms
Treatment: inpatient substance/alcohol detoxification treatment
The insurer denied coverage for: inpatient substance/alcohol detoxification treatment
The denial is: Overturned
This adult patient was admitted to this inpatient substance/alcohol detoxification treatment. The patient had alcohol withdrawal symptoms including sweats, tachycardia, palpitations, nausea, vomiting, tremors, anxiety, irritable mood, insomnia, headache, auditory and visual disturbance, and had a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) of 14. The patient reportedly also had a positive history for alcohol withdrawal seizures. The patient had a positive toxicology for benzodiazepines and ethyl glucuronide and a past positive toxicology for cocaine. The patient also had comorbid depression. The patient had a past inpatient detoxification treatment including a recent one. The patient was put on a Librium taper for detoxification treatment, was monitored with a pulse ox, and vital signs were monitored. The patient was discharged 5 days later.

The reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient hospital treatment as the medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that he required this level of care. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. It also states that patients with past complicated or life-threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens are in need of inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal and reports that patients with comorbid medical condition that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification. Also, the US Department of Health and Human Services-Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) Center for Substance Abuse Treatment reports that inpatient treatment is necessary if the ability to attend outpatient treatment daily is a problem, one is unable to follow-up in outpatient treatment, if medical conditions complicate the treatment of withdrawal, if one has previous withdrawal seizures of delirium tremens, or if one does not have the capacity for informed consent. The patient had a long history of alcohol use including a 42-year history and also had reports of past cocaine use. The patient had reported diagnoses of Alcohol and Cocaine Use Disorder and was at risk also for medical issues related to that and also overdose. The risk of life complicated withdrawal such as delirium tremens increases 3-4 days after alcohol use so the patient required inpatient detoxification treatment and was considered at high risk medically for severe, complicated, and life-threatening withdrawal. The patient had a past alcohol withdrawal seizure and the standard treatment is for inpatient hospital detoxification treatment when one has a history of alcohol withdrawal seizure.  

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be reversed. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. The medical necessity for the inpatient detoxification admission is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Autism Spectrum Disorder

Treatment: Applied Behavioral Analysis (ABA)

The insurer denied coverage for Applied Behavioral Analysis (ABA)

The denial is overturned
 

This young child reportedly has developmental delays in social communication and interaction and has a diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder. It was reported that his communication skills were not age appropriate, he was not able to use language to communicate socially or functionally, would use 1-2 word sentences with minimal detail, and often didn't acknowledge or greet others when engaging in conversation. He reportedly was struggling with one step directions, frequently required maximal prompting, had communication, social and behavioral deficits that prevented him from functioning at an age appropriate level in the environment, was not functionally communicating at an age appropriate level for his needs, was unable to interact socially with others and struggled to follow expectations, frequently had maladaptive behaviors including tantrums when unable to deal with change or given non preferred tasks. It was reported that he had significant regression across all domains in the short period of time he was without further applied behavioral analysis (ABA) therapy treatment. 

Multiple sources support that applied behavioral analysis is an appropriate and effective treatment behaviorally and educationally for autism spectrum disorder children and adolescents. In this case this patient had deficits still with social and communication domains, and deficits in adaptive functioning and behavioral control. He still required this intensity and frequency of services to progress further and also sustain previous gains and for generalization, and to not regress further when not having these services which was what was reported when he stopped this treatment. 

With applied behavioral analysis (ABA) therapy treatment he exhibited ability to maintain low levels of problem behaviors, was able to utilize some functional communication skills with prompting, and tolerate social interactions with family members. It was reported that he will continue to regress which impacts his ability to function in the environment without the same intensity and frequency of applied behavioral analysis (ABA) therapy treatment services. The long term goal was to be able to generalize skills without the need for a behavioral technician and have adequate stabilization of maladaptive behaviors. The requested intensity and frequency of applied behavioral analysis (ABA) services at 30 hours per week for now was considered medically necessary treatment. As a result, the recommendation is to reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for the previously denied requested intensity of applied behavioral analysis (ABA) services at 30 hours per week with tapering of services as outlined when certain objectives and goals were met. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be reversed. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.

The patient in this case was using opioid and alcohol class substances on a daily continuous basis with intermittent use of other substances of abuse that did warrant inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring for the duration of the protocol; detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments pertinent to the detoxification treatment episode could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment that was provided at the time of admission. Moreover, the patient had a positive drug screen that included opioids and benzodiazepines, as well as methadone and tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). He had mild and persistent withdrawal symptoms and the patient's social environment was not conducive to detoxification in the context of limited insight, impaired judgment, and poor control of impulses. There were general medical comorbidities that warranted inpatient treatments including intravenous antibiotics and supportive measures with ongoing evaluations including imaging studies.
Thus, the need for detoxification treatment and withdrawal management of this patient's substance use disorder did warrant the admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level detoxification setting with 24-hour monitoring and use of as needed (prn) medications and indicated treatment of the cellulitis and pain. The patient's history of substance abuse (frequency 
and quantity) together with the severe psychosocial stressors and functional impairments reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder and the need for a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management, as the patient was at high risk for treatment failure if the detoxification and withdrawal management were to be attempted at a lower level of care. Therefore, medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published practice guidelines, American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and the scientific literature, referenced below, and New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews including the appropriate application of the New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Tool that requires the patient in this scenario default to the higher level of care. Therefore, the requested health service was medically necessary for this patient.

summary:
Diagnosis: Intentional suicide attempt via overdose
Treatment: Inpatient admission
The insurer denied coverage for: Inpatient admission
The denial is: Overturned
The adult patient was admitted to this inpatient hospital after an intentional suicide attempt via overdose of 15 Seroquel pills while drinking wine. The patient got into an argument with significant other who wanted the patient to leave the house. It was reported that the patient was evasive, minimizing the situation, and was considered an imminent danger to self. The patient reportedly had a diagnosis of cocaine and alcohol abuse and had a Drugs of Abuse in Urine Scheme (DAU) positive for cocaine. The patient was seen by the Psychiatric consultant who did not clear the patient psychiatrically. The patient also had a blood alcohol level (BAL) of 117 and was put on a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) protocol including Ativan (prn) as needed. The patient reportedly had a poison control consult.  The patient also was on continuous telemetry, seizure precautions, had intravenous (IV) fluids, Thiamine, Lovenox, lab monitoring, and constant observation due to the suicide attempt. The patient was cleared by psychiatry and medically and was discharged with referral to outpatient mental health treatment.
 
This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient hospital treatment. The medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that the patient required this level of care. The Milliman Care Guidelines (MCG) Drug Ingestion or Overdose criteria reports that one meets criteria if one of the following are met: Hemodynamic instability, dangerous arrhythmia, respiratory abnormalities, hypertension requiring inpatient treatment, specific finding indicating severe and prolonged drug toxicity, or inpatient admission is required other than observation care. Also, the American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Suicidal Behaviors reports that patients with suicide attempts are at high risk of suicide. Suicide attempts are the single most reliable predictor of suicide. It also states that patients with substance use are at increased risk for suicide. This patient was considered an imminent danger to self-due to an intentional overdose. Also, the MCG General Admission Inpatient criteria reports that one meets criteria for inpatient admission if one is actively suicidal or if one presents as a danger to self. In this case this patient had reports of an intentional suicide attempt by overdose of 15 Seroquel pills while drinking wine after an argument with significant other, so there was active suicidality and was considered an imminent danger to self-requiring 24-hour inpatient hospital treatment. The patient had other risk factors including using cocaine and alcohol which put the patient at higher risk for suicide. The patient also had medical issues including being put on a CIWA protocol for potential alcohol withdrawal, had elevated ammonia of 62, and prolonged QT's interval of 430 on the electrocardiogram (EKG) which put the patient at risk for cardiac arrhythmias. The patient had a past medical history of depression and asthma. It was reported that the patient remained with suicidal ideation and that safety precautions needed to be resumed as a result, so psychiatry did not clear the patient as the patient was still considered a danger to self and needed 24-hour hospital treatment. It was reported that the patient was evasive, minimizing the situation, and was considered an imminent danger to self. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be reversed. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. The medical necessity for the inpatient admission is substantiated.

summary:

Treatment: Psychiatric residential treatment center care
The insurer denied: Psychiatric residential treatment center care
The denial is overturned.

The case involves an adult female diagnosed with severe obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and comorbid symptoms of anxiety and depression (social phobia and agoraphobia) with 
fear of contamination and extensive cleaning rituals with excessive time showering. The patient has not responded to prior treatments with inpatient, partial hospital program, and outpatient programs targeting obsessive compulsive disorder. Moreover, the patient has declined in functioning with daily activities and social and educational functions not having attended school for two years and not wanting to go outdoors. The patient was referred and admitted to a specialty residential psychiatric treatment facility 6 months ago with an administrative discharge last month due to the facility's COVID-19 protocol and a COVID-19 outbreak with return to the program earlier this month with resumption of 
residential treatment. Her admission had occurred despite treatments in the community such that the patient continued to have severe symptoms of anxiety, compulsive rituals, and intrusive thoughts; and, she had a significant decline in functioning-as noted, such in that she was unable to function socially, or at times had been unable to do basic self-care. The patient had been in outpatient mental health treatment that included therapy and medications, prior to her referral for more intensive and structured treatment that was recommended by community providers. Mental Status Examination included obsessive-compulsive related symptoms including rituals and obsessive anxiety together with agoraphobia, anxious and dysphoric mood with affective instability and elements of panic, and, social phobia, as well as illness anxiety due to fears of 
contamination. She had limited insight and judgment that was impaired due to her multiple conditions/symptoms together with maladaptive coping and dependency. The patient is single and lives with her parents. From earlier this month forward, the patient resumed treatment and prior to the administrative 
discharge, she was making progress with her goals and participating in intensive treatment, as indicated. However, she had regressed during the ten-day treatment hiatus, and she continued to struggle with symptoms related to anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorder with ongoing risk for prominent compulsive rituals, lengthy showering, and a continued lack of skills and insight. Going forward with her residential treatment, the patient had previously engaged more and more effectively in treatment with sustained improvement and setbacks during the treatment gap. Family focused feedback sessions were occurring with identification of family issues and triggers, as well as focus on coping skills. Thus, she was making progress in this regard with improvements with mood and interpersonal functioning and diminished levels of anxiety according to submitted information. 
The treatment plan included plans for step down with continued partial hospitalization program (PHP) level treatment of the obsessive-compulsive related disorder, as well as ongoing care to address her residual effects of the catastrophic illness she had incurred including the ongoing recovery from the symptoms of anxiety and depression.

The requested health service/treatment of psychiatric residential treatment was/is medically necessary for this patient.

The patient's re-admission and continued residential level treatment is reasonable and warranted as noted in the appeal; she continued to display severe symptoms of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and associated symptoms of anxiety and depression together with distress problems, interpersonal functioning problems and decline or impairment of functioning that had deteriorated to the point that she was unable to benefit from treatment at lower levels of care. She continued to display coping deficits and a lack of insight that did warrant the structure, 
monitoring, and intensity of treatment for the duration of the residential stay. The patient could not be effectively managed at a lower level of care in a less restrictive treatment setting during 
the time interval under review. Moreover, the patient had a reasonable likelihood of responding to the treatment and program of services provided by the residential treatment program, as described in the appeal. The requested benefit is therefore considered medically necessary.
