summary:
Diagnosis: post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)

Treatment: mental health residential treatment facility

The insurer denied coverage for mental health residential treatment facility

The denial is overturned
 

This is a teenage patient with a history of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), Major Depressive Disorder-Severe-recurrent, Generalized Anxiety Disorder, and Opioid Use Disorder. The patient was admitted to this inpatient mental health residential treatment due to mood, behavioral, anxiety, post traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms and substance use. The patient was reported to have mood dysregulation, aggressive and disruptive behavior, gang involvement, defiance, property destruction, poor impulse control, PTSD symptoms including intrusive thoughts, hypervigilance, and avoidance symptoms, irritable and sad mood, poor coping skills, and poor insight and judgment. The patient had a history of Percocet and benzodiazepine use, had cravings to use and reportedly glorified drug use. There was a history of multiple past treatment episodes including 2 past hospitalizations; one with a duration of 4-5 months. The patient attended individual and group therapy and was discharged.

The Milliman Care Guideline (MCG) Residential-Behavioral Health Level of Care - Child Adolescent Guidelines report that one needs to have continued danger to self or others, moderately or severe psychiatric or behavioral symptoms requiring 24 hour daily treatment, or serious dysfunction in daily living. For discharge, it states that there needs to be sufficient support at a lower level of care, absence of suicidal or homicidal thoughts or thoughts of harm to self or others. 

In this case, the patient continued to have moderate psychiatric symptoms and did not have the reported necessary coping skills to deal with their multiple psychiatric issues and substance use as of insurer's proposed discharge date. This was a complex patient with multiple psychiatric diagnoses including PTSD, Major Depressive Disorder-Severe-recurrent, Generalized Anxiety Disorder, and Opioid Use Disorder who reportedly had property destruction while in this setting and still had cravings and lacked coping skills and enough insight to stop substance use and did not have the reported impulse control to better control behaviors and emotions and to better deal with trauma. It was reported that the patient needed more improvement in their coping skills to better deal with their psychiatric symptoms and urges to use substances. It was reported that the patient lived in a neighborhood in which there was gang involvement and readily available drugs. The patient reportedly had been involved in illegal activities when not in this treatment setting including selling drugs in addition to using them, as well as physically aggressive, threatening, and disruptive behavior, and property destruction. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be overturned. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. The medical necessity for continued mental health residential treatment facility is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Withdrawal symptoms Opioid Addiction
Treatment: Medically Supervised Inpatient Detoxification
The insurer denied coverage for: Medically Supervised Inpatient Detoxification
The denial is: Overturned
This adult patient was admitted to this inpatient hospital for detoxification treatment. The patient had withdrawal symptoms including tremors, sweats, agitation, anxiety, irritable mood, diffuse discomfort, cravings, dilated pupils, nasal stuffiness, elevated heart rate, and had a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) of 9 and Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) of 11. The patient had a positive toxicology for opiates, cocaine, Methadone, and tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). The patient reportedly was drink a six pack of 24 ounce beer per day, using 1 bag of heroin IV per day, and using $20 of cocaine IV per day. The patient was in Methadone Maintenance Treatment Program and unable to have any abstinence from alcohol and substances.  The patient continued to use multiple serious substances of use and alcohol daily despite 2 past inpatient detoxification treatments in the past. The patient lacked coping skills for abstinence and lacked sober supports as the patient was homeless and unemployed. The patient had comorbid medical and psychiatric issues including a past overdose of pills 10 years prior to admission and had past depression and psychiatric hospitalization. Past medical history included hepatitis C and asthma. The patient was put on a 5 day Librium taper but left against medical advice (AMA) prior to completion of the detoxification treatment. The plan was to complete inpatient detoxification treatment and then be referred for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment.

The reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient hospital treatment as the medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that the patient required this level of care. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. It also states that patients with past complicated or life threatening withdrawal symptoms including withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens are in need of inpatient hospital treatment for the management of withdrawal and reports that patients with comorbid medical condition that complicate the management of withdrawal are also candidates for inpatient detoxification. Also, the United States (US) Department of Health and Human Services-Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) Center for Substance Abuse Treatment reports that inpatient treatment is necessary if the ability to attend outpatient treatment daily is a problem, one is unable to follow-up in outpatient treatment, if medical conditions complicate the treatment of withdrawal, if one has previous withdrawal seizures of delirium tremens, or if one does not have the capacity for informed consent. The risk of delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use so the patient was considered at risk for severe, complicated, and life threatening withdrawal and in need of 24 hour hospital treatment. According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral 
(LOCADTR) the patient did require 24 hour treatment as the patient could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive setting.
Based on above, the insurer's denial must be reversed. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. The medical necessity for Medically Supervised Inpatient Detoxification for dates of service is substantiated.

The patient was single, unemployed, and homeless and lives in a shelter that is drug infested with peers using. The patient has no family supports and indicated that he had significant stress and anger that triggered his substance use. The patient reported a personal emergency that resulted in his discharge against medical advice on day #12 with recommendations and referrals for continued and clinically appropriate aftercare of the substance use disorders to include long-term residential treatment. 

The denial was based on the New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 
Criteria/Guidelines indicating that the criteria for inpatient level treatment was not met. 
The treatment facility asserted that the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria were met based on the longstanding use of multiple substances, comorbidity, and the patient's need for monitoring and the structure of an inpatient rehabilitation setting. The appeal referenced the patient's adverse living situation, lack of support, and high risk for relapse. 

The proposed treatment and the requested benefit of inpatient substance abuse rehabilitation treatment was not medically necessary. 

The patient presented with substance use disorders, diagnosed with cannabis and stimulant/cocaine use disorders. During the time interval under review, the patient was noted to be in no apparent distress other than pain related to an earache, and he 
displayed reasonable functioning and active participation in treatment including positive interactions with staff and peers. Throughout the inpatient stay, there were no complicating treatment issues or biomedical or co-occurring psychiatric issues that would have warranted inpatient level of care, structure, or 24-hour nursing monitoring. The patient denied cannabis use for 1-2 months. The patient had received past partial hospital program (PHP) treatment for 3 months previously. The patient was reported to have had a past eating disorder residential treatment stay for 2 months previously and had received prior outpatient treatment. The patient was receiving services in the mental health residential treatment setting due to mood, anxiety, and behavioral symptoms. According to the psychiatric evaluation, the patient had depressive symptoms including sad and irritable mood, crying, isolation, loss of interest, low self-esteem, anxiety symptoms, fidgeting, and PTSD symptoms after witnessing violent acts in a past residential treatment center. The patient had past physical altercations with their mother in which police were called, impulsivity, school refusal, staying out past curfew, sneaking out of the house, stealing, oppositional behavior, past self-injurious behavior by scratching self, and past restricting and purging behaviors. It was reported that the patient had no current eating disorder symptoms. The patient had stopped Fluoxetine and Hydroxyzine, stating that they were ineffective. The patient was attending group therapy including dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT) skills which included core mindfulness, interpersonal effectiveness, distress tolerance, and emotional regulation.

The Milliman Care Guideline (MCG) Residential-Behavioral Health Level of Care guidelines report that one needs to have continued danger to self or others, moderately or severe psychiatric or behavioral symptoms requiring 24 hour daily treatment, or serious dysfunction in daily living. 

In this case, the patient had reported improvement in clinical symptoms from the psychiatric evaluation. Notes reported that the patient was not experiencing anxiety or depressive symptoms, had a stable emotional state, denied suicidal or homicidal ideation, or hallucinations, and there were no imminent safety concerns. The patient also reportedly was not taking psychotropic medication. Notes reported that the patient was mentally stable and hopeful and was doing outdoor activities to challenge development and enhance their self-concept and self-esteem.  Notes reported that the patient was anxious and cooperative, understood unhealthy behaviors and potential consequences. The patient's insight was improving. There were reports of euthymic mood, no hallucinations, suicidal or homicidal ideation, and good concentration. The patient denied cravings/urges. The patient had no reports of maladaptive eating behaviors. 

The medical records did not provide enough specific evidence that the patient could only be effectively treated in a 24 hour inpatient therapeutic mental health residential treatment or that the patient could not be treated in a less restrictive level of care. There were no reports of severe depressive symptoms, emotional dysregulation, aggressive or self-injurious behavior, suicidal ideation, plan, or intent or evidence of danger to self or others requiring 24 hour inpatient treatment, or reports of acute psychotic symptoms rendering them unable to care for basic needs. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be upheld. The health care plan did act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.

The insurer denied Applied Behavioral Analysis.  The denial is reversed.

This patient had significant deficits in language, communication, social interactions, and behaviors significantly impacting his ability to engage with others effectively. He reportedly had deficits in verbal and nonverbal communication, was inflexible, rigid, insisted on sameness, had an inability to have flexible thinking, had reduced sharing of interests and emotions, lacked social and emotional reciprocity, did not initiate social interactions, was not able to express wants and needs, could not communicate feelings in an age appropriate way, made statements helplessness, could not follow simple directions, was anxious, isolative, and withdrawn. He and could not remain in one place for long periods of time. He reportedly lacked attention and had maladaptive behaviors including defiant, disruptive, impulsive, and physically aggressive behavior, had absenteeism, and could not stay in one place for long periods of time. He reportedly touched others inappropriately and was intrusive. He had a diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder. The request was for 1368 units of applied behavioral analysis (ABA) services which was 22 hours per week.

The insurer denied the request for 1368 units of applied behavioral analysis (ABA) services and approved only 1160 units of applied behavioral analysis (ABA) services. They stated that the requested units of treatment for applied behavioral analysis (ABA)services was more than needed to address goals and symptoms reported in the records.

The American Academy of Pediatrics reports that the efficacy of applied behavioral analysis is well documented through 5 decades of work and has shown substantial sustained gains in adaptive, academic, language, social, and behavioral functioning, and better reported outcomes. 

The National Institute of Mental Health reports that applied behavioral analysis is widely accepted as an effective treatment. The National Academy of Sciences reports that 40 years of research testifies to the efficacy of time limited focused applied behavioral analysis methods in reducing or limiting specific problem behaviors and teaching new skills to children and adolescents with autism and other developmental disorder. 

According to Eikeseth, intensive applied behavioral analysis therapy for autism resulted in increases in an intelligence quotient (IQ) and adaptive functioning and had fewer aberrant behaviors and social problems. These multiple sources support that applied behavioral analysis is an appropriate and effective treatment behaviorally and educationally for autistic spectrum disorder children and adolescents. In this case this patient had significant developmental delays and had maladaptive behaviors interfering with his ability to function maximally and it impacted his quality of life. It was reported that the applied behavioral analysis (ABA) therapy had specific objectives and goals to decrease maladaptive behaviors, better engage him in appropriate social interactions, improve communication, decrease restricted and repetitive behaviors, improve flexibility in thinking, improve joint attention and boundaries, decrease impulsive behavior, and better regulate emotions and behaviors. It was reported that she required the intensity and frequency of applied behavioral analysis therapy (ABA) services requested at 22 hours per week for 1368 units and not just the approved 1160 units was needed to make more progress and attain more goals and to not regress further. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be reversed. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. The medical necessity for 1368 units of Applied Behavioral Analysis services is substantiated.

This patient reportedly had a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder (Recurrent, Severe without psychotic features) and had reported depressive symptoms including depressed mood, decreased energy, interest, self-care, libido, and appetite, hopelessness, and social withdrawal. The patient reportedly had a Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) scale depression score of 23 which indicated severe depression. The patient reportedly was suffering from depression for over a decade. The patient reportedly tried multiple medications without reported efficacy. The patient reportedly tried 3 selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRI) in Lexapro at 20 milligrams (mg) which is the maximum Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved dosage per day and reportedly took it for several years, Zoloft 50 mg for six years, Celexa at 40 mg per day for six years, and Prozac 60 mg per day for four years. The patient also reportedly took a serotonin norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) in Cymbalta at 60 mg per day, a dopamine norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor in Wellbutrin at 200 mg per day, Remeron, and Trazodone, as well as augmenting agent Seroquel for over 10 years with lack of efficacy. The patient also reportedly tried intravenous (IV) ketamine a few years ago without efficacy. The patient also reportedly had past trials of psychostimulants including Vyvanse, Dexedrine, Ritalin, and Adderall. The patient also had other diagnoses including Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD), post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). The request was for a trial of transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy (TMS).

This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy (TMS) as the medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy (TMS) was considered medically necessary treatment. The patient had a reported diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder-recurrent severe and had a PHQ-9 depression score of 23 which indicated severe depression and reportedly had multiple medication trials over the past decade without reported sustained efficacy. 

The medical records provided did provide enough evidence to support that transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy (TMS) was considered the best available treatment for the patient and they were considered a good candidate for it, and there is enough scientific evidence in the peer reviewed literature to support a result of improvement in health outcome, and the FDA approved it for their diagnosis of major depressive disorder (severe/recurrent). The medical records provided did support that transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy (TMS) was considered to be more beneficial than other standard treatments for this patient as they tried many standard antidepressant medications from several different classes and also ketamine. The medical records provided enough evidence to support that the patient had treatment resistant depression and supported the need for transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy (TMS) as requested. As a result, the recommendation is to reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy (TMS) for this patient.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Use Disorder.
Treatment: Inpatient Hospital Admission.
The insurer denied: Inpatient Hospital Admission.
The denial is overturned.

The patient is an adult male who presented to the emergency department requesting detoxification treatment. He was medically screened and admitted to acute inpatient level care to address substance use disorder with opioid, alcohol, cocaine, cannabis, and nicotine class substance use disorders. The patient had been using heroin with up to one bundle daily with snorting and one pint of liquor plus beers on a daily continuous basis, as well as use of $50 worth of cannabis/marijuana and $100 worth of crack cocaine daily with tobacco dependence. He has no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens but has a history of moderately severe withdrawal symptoms. He had a history of multiple prior detoxification and substance use disorder treatments with relapses and no sustained sobriety. The patient had a history of psychiatric disorder best characterized as bipolar depression and unspecified anxiety disorder and no history of psychiatric hospitalization or suicidal behavior and was not taking psychotropic medications. He was noted to have an untreated anxiety disorder pertinent to his substance use disorders. Laboratory assessments were unremarkable, but his vital signs included elevated blood pressure and pulse and his Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) scale and Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) scored in the mild range during treatment. He had nausea, tremor, sweats, leg cramps, and anxiety. Drug screen was positive for cocaine, cannabis, opiates, Fentanyl, and phencyclidine (PCP). The patient was admitted to detoxification treatment with a comprehensive detoxification protocol with Ativan, methadone, and as-needed (PRN) medications for comfort including vitamin and nicotine replacement therapy and use of Vistaril for anxiety and insomnia, as well as 
monitoring. The program provided for case management with referral and access to rehabilitation treatment that included comprehensive evidence-based treatments. During his inpatient stay, the patient continued to display mild symptoms of withdrawal despite as needed (PRN) use of methadone and Ativan. He received education and 
counseling with case management services. He received his final dose of methadone on day #5 with discharge the following day to substance-related rehabilitation services.

The proposed treatment, inpatient substance-related services was medically necessary.

The patient in this case was using opioid and alcohol class substances on a daily continuous basis, as well as daily use of other substances of abuse that did warrant inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management. 
Detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments pertinent to the detoxification treatment episode could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care. Moreover, there was an undiagnosed psychiatric comorbidity that warranted treatment as indicated in the appeal. Thus, the need for detoxification treatment and withdrawal management of this patient's substance use disorder did warrant the admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level detoxification setting with 24-hour monitoring and use of as needed (PRN) medications and indicated treatment with a methadone and Ativan protocol. The patient's history of substance abuse (frequency and quantity) together with functional impairments reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder and the need for a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management, as the patient was at high risk for treatment failure if the detoxification and withdrawal management were to be attempted at a lower level of care including observation level care. Therefore, medical necessity was met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published societal guidelines, the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, the scientific literature, and New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews including the appropriate application of the New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Tool that requires the patient in this scenario default to the higher level of care.

summary:
Diagnosis: complex posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
Treatment: Residential Mental Health Treatment
The insurer denied Residential Mental Health Treatment
The health plan's determination is overturned. 

The patient is a young adult female referred and admitted for residential mental health treatment in order to address severe complex posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) with comorbid recurrent and severe major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, other specified feeding and eating disorder, and premenstrual dysphoric disorder as well as cannabis use disorder and history of suicidal behavior with at least one suicide attempt by overdose and other threats of suicide resulting in a recent hospitalization. The residential program focused on trauma recovery and addressing suicidal and self-harming behaviors, as well as services to address the comorbid psychiatric disorders and substance use disorders.

Residential Mental Health Treatment is medically necessary for this patient. The patient has demonstrated coping deficits and behavior reflecting impaired functioning and safety risks that did require residential structure and monitoring with active treatment to address coping skills and symptoms related to the trauma/injury and the mood, anxiety, and eating disorders while maintaining abstinence from substances of abuse (cannabis). The patient's lack of awareness or limitations of insight and impulse control with regard to suicidal risk, together with the seriousness of her mental health disorders are pertinent treatment factors that warranted the admission and continued residential level services. The psychiatric symptoms of trauma, depression, anxiety, and stress within the social environment including a significant trauma history complicates this case, as the patient has symptoms that are triggering the risk for suicidal behaviors. These factors support the assertion that the patient could not have been effectively treated with a lower level of care for the time interval under review. These clinical factors needed to be effectively addressed prior to step down to a lower level of care in the community.

Treatment: Social Adult Daycare Days - 2 Days per Week

Social Adult Daycare Days for 2 days per week is medically necessary for this patient.

The services being provided are clinically appropriate to address ongoing symptoms and impairment from the chronic mental disorder, including cognitive impairment in a patient with multiple general health issues and functional impairments. The continued use of a day program, as requested, two days per week, with behavioral health programming and daycare services, provides maintenance treatment for the patient's mental health needs and facilitates better functioning and cognition. The patient receives active treatment, peer support, and psychosocial therapeutic interventions. Compliance with the services is supported, as well as the benefit of psychosocial interventions providing active treatment of the mental disorder and associated functional and cognitive impairment. The treatment provided could not be effectively provided through Home Attendant Services alone or with a lower frequency of participation.

summary:
Diagnosis: Alcohol use disorder
Treatment: Inpatient Hospital Admission
The insurer denied: Inpatient Hospital Admission
The denial is overturned.

This case involves an adult male who presented to an emergency department requesting detoxification treatment with plans to proceed to rehabilitation services to address severe alcohol use disorder. At the time of presentation to the emergency department, the patient gave a history of severe alcohol withdrawal symptoms in the past. He presented with tremors, tongue fasciculations, nausea, headache and itching, as well as restlessness, motor agitation, anxiety, and reports of auditory hallucinations and intermittent suicidal ideation associated with affective instability and hopelessness. The patient was treated in the emergency department with Librium and Ativan, supportive measures, and fluid and electrolyte and vitamin replacement with subsequent admission for inpatient level care with plans for withdrawal management and detoxification and stabilization with a Librium protocol with Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) monitoring and supportive measures. The medical screening had revealed evidence for elevated liver functions as well as elevated blood pressure and heart rate with tachycardia. The examination revealed abdominal tenderness with complaints of epigastric pain, as well as withdrawal symptoms including nausea, shaking, 
tremors, headache and restlessness with anxiety. The patient has a history of psychiatric disorder, bipolar mood disorder, with non-compliance with treatment and non-adherence with psychotropic medications. Mental Status Examination: There were severe symptoms on mental status examination and safety concerns about risk of harm to self with the suicidal ideation, affective instability, and hallucinations. The patient displayed limited insight, and impaired judgment. He demonstrated symptoms of anxiety with generalized symptoms including insomnia, and anxious affect together with symptoms related to the alcohol use and the withdrawal symptoms with a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) scale score of 10 despite presenting with a blood alcohol level (BAL) of 263. The patient was cooperative though agitated with normal speech and linear thought processing. The patient was admitted for inpatient treatment with detoxification protocol, supportive measures, and withdrawal management. The patient's hospital course progressed, but not without incident. The patient reported nausea, anxiety, restlessness, and insomnia with persistently mild to moderate symptoms of withdrawal and affective instability that diminished throughout his brief hospital course. He was discharged against medical advice on day #3 with recommendations for clinically appropriate aftercare.

The proposed treatment, inpatient hospital level care for detoxification treatment and withdrawal management and stabilization with monitoring and other medical services was medically necessary for this patient.

The requested benefit of inpatient admission for detoxification treatment and withdrawal management and monitoring and other medical services was warranted in this case scenario. The patient in this case was using large quantities of alcohol with a presentation and history that did warrant the admission and the continued inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring. Inpatient hospital level care with detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment that was provided in the emergency department and continued at the time of admission. The patient had associated clinical features that included lack of sober supports and functional impairments and general medical complications of the alcohol use disorder which did require the continued treatment on the dates of service under review. Medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published guidelines, the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) criteria, and the scientific literature, referenced below, as well as New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Continued Partial Hospital Substance Use Disorders Treatment.
The insurer denied Continued Partial Hospital Substance Use Disorders Treatment.
The determination is overturned.

The patient is an adult male who presented for partial hospital program (PHP) treatment in order to address severe substance use disorder with alcohol and co-occurring anxiety and depressive disorders best characterized as generalized anxiety disorder and moderately severe major depressive disorder. Additionally, the patient has a trauma history and symptoms of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in association with his job. 
The patient had been sober with a relapse five months prior to presentation using large quantities of alcohol with a binge pattern of use with up to 10 beers.  He was prescribed Xanax and Adderall with no report of misuse of these medications. 
He has been treated most recently with outpatient therapy and medication management.
The patient has a strong family history of alcoholism reflecting genetic predisposition.
At the time of admission for Partial Hospitalization Program (PHP) level care, the patient had intense craving, anxiety and depression rated at 5/10 and insomnia.
The treatment included focus on coping skills, development of relapse prevention techniques with identification of triggers, education about the disease model of addiction, and the opportunity for family-focused sessions to address sober supports and issues within the family constellation, as well as ongoing peer support and involvement with 12-step recovery groups. 
The patient was provided treatment with intensive services, sober supports, monitoring, and structure provided within the PHP treatment program.  
At issue is the medical necessity of Continued Partial Hospital Substance Use Disorders Treatment.

The requested health service/treatment of partial hospitalization mental health treatment was medically necessary for this patient.
The patient in this case was using alcohol with a binge pattern of use in the context of co-occurring psychiatric disorders and decline in functioning, as well as associated symptoms of anxiety, depression, and insomnia, and trauma related symptoms. The patient was at high risk for relapse and had limited coping skills, and a recovery environment that was deficient, as well as poor impulse control in view of continued use of alcohol despite severe consequences with regard to family and occupational domains. These factors and treatment dimensions did warrant the continued PHP level services with sober support housing, and intensive rehabilitation therapy.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse.
Treatment: 5 Days of inpatient substance use detoxification (detox).
The insurer denied 5 Days of inpatient substance use detoxification (detox).  The determination is overturned.

The patient is an adult male, who presented requesting substance-related detoxification and rehabilitation services and was admitted following medical screening for detoxification and withdrawal management of severe alcohol and stimulant (cocaine) use disorders, as well as intermittent and weekly use of Xanax with up to 4 milligrams (mg) and $10 worth of marijuana. The patient was using up to one pint of liquor together with two six-packs of beer and with $100 worth of crack cocaine daily.
The patient presented with alcohol withdrawal at the time of admission. Withdrawal symptoms included tremor, sweats, nausea, headache, insomnia, irritability, agitation, and anxiety with a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment (CIWA) scale score of 7. The patient has no history of psychiatric disorder. He denied psychiatric hospitalization, or suicidal or self-harming behavior. He had a history of substance-related treatment episodes with relapses including one rehabilitation treatment episode and multiple past detoxification treatment episodes. There were no acute medical issues or general medical concerns. 
At issue is the medical necessity of Inpatient admission and continued stay for a 5-day detoxification treatment with withdrawal management and stabilization.

The patient presented with a diagnosis of severe alcohol and stimulant use disorder with use of crack cocaine. The presenting clinical features and history and risk for withdrawal seizures and other psychosocial complications of alcohol and stimulant use disorders did warrant the admission and continued inpatient level services with medical monitoring in this case scenario. The patient's admission and continued inpatient stay with detoxification, withdrawal management, and other medical services through discharge could not have been effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario.
The adult inpatient treatment of this patient's substance disorders did require the admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level setting and 24-hour monitoring in view of the severity of the alcohol use disorder, and the presentation with a lack of insight, high risk for relapse and lack of a reasonable recovery environment. Withdrawal symptoms were appropriately managed with tapering dosages of benzodiazepine/Librium requiring monitoring, as well as comfort medications and vitamin and the availability of nicotine replacement therapy.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Inpatient Substance Use Rehabilitation
The insurer denied: Inpatient Substance Use Rehabilitation
The denial is upheld.

The case involves an adult male medically screened and admitted for inpatient rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment in order to address use of stimulant (crack cocaine), cannabis (marijuana) and phencyclidine (PCP) class substances with a history of opioid use disorder in full remission, as well as nicotine use disorder with one-half pack per day use. The patient has a history of five prior treatment episodes with relapse including a recent treatment episode earlier 3 months ago. His referral was made through the legal system with charges pending and a history of incarceration-prior legal problems. 
He had diagnoses of depressive disorder with associated treatment with fluoxetine and aripiprazole. He reported insomnia and had post-acute withdrawal syndrome (PAWS) that included anxiety and tremors. Upon admission to inpatient level services, the patient received comprehensive evaluation and treatment. The patient readily engaged in substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment. He actively received intensive rehabilitation services, monitoring, and structure provided within the inpatient treatment program including 24-hour monitoring and ongoing nursing assessments. He continued with active participation and engagement in substance-related programming. He was discharged against medical advice (AMA) on day #14 with recommendations and referrals for continued and clinically appropriate aftercare of the substance use disorders and co-occurring mental health disorders. The issue under review is inpatient substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment. The denial was based on the New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines indicating that the criteria for inpatient level treatment was not met. The treatment facility asserted that medical necessity was met based on the longstanding use of multiple substances and the patient's need for monitoring and the structure of an inpatient rehabilitation setting with reference to the severe psychosocial stressors including homelessness, unemployment, lack of sober supports, and legal issues. The appeal also referenced the lack of coping skills indicating that the patient was unstable.

The proposed treatment and the requested benefit of inpatient substance abuse rehabilitation treatment is not medically necessary.

The patient presented with substance use disorders, diagnosed with cannabis and stimulant/cocaine and phencyclidine use disorders. The patient was medically screened and had no acute general medical issues or general medical issues that warranted inpatient level care-as the health plan indicated in the denial. The patient readily engaged in treatment and had no biomedical (withdrawal symptoms or signs) or acute psychiatric treatment issues or instability of the co-occurring psychiatric disorder, i.e., he was stable with current treatment. During the time interval under review, the patient was noted to be in no apparent distress except for a bout of gastritis treated with Maalox. He was eating and sleeping okay, and he displayed reasonable functioning and active participation in treatment including positive interactions with staff and peers. Throughout the inpatient stay, there were no complicating treatment issues or biomedical or co-occurring psychiatric issues that would have warranted inpatient level of care, structure or monitoring. The application of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria did indicate that the patient was clinically appropriate for treatment with lower-level care in a less restrictive treatment setting, as the health plan asserted. Thus, medical 
necessity for the inpatient rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment is not met in this case. This answer is consistent with the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, the scientific literature, and published guidelines.

summary:
Diagnosis: Thoughts of Self Harm
Treatment: Continued Acute Psychiatric Inpatient Hospitalization
The insurer denied: Continued Acute Psychiatric Inpatient Hospitalization
The denial is upheld.

The patient is an adult female with MDD (major depressive disorder), GAD (generalized anxiety disorder), borderline personality disorder, and somatic symptom disorder. She presented voluntarily to the hospital for worsening suicidal ideation. Her suicidal ideation stemmed from medication side effects and recent changes made to medication. The patient was admitted to inpatient level of care. The last covered day was day #12. The health plan denied coverage of the inpatient days for days #13, #14, and #15. The denial is being appealed.
On day #15, the psychiatrist noted dizziness and symptoms related to dizziness, no SI (suicidal ideation). The orders were to eat bland diet, increase Topamax to 25 milligrams twice daily. The patient's mental status exam was normal unless otherwise noted. Her mood was subjectively anxious. Her thought processes were preoccupied, circumstantial. Her thought content included somatic delusions. Her Insight/Judgement was impaired. Unremarkable impression was noted. No SI suicidal ideation), HI (homicidal ideation), AH (auditory hallucination), VH (visual hallucination) was noted.
On day #14, per the psychiatrist note, the patient appeared tired due to her roommate keeping her up. Her dizziness improved, and she did not need a walker. She began Topamax and Lexapro. Her mental status exam was noted to be normal unless otherwise noted. Her mood was subjectively anxious. Her thought processes were preoccupied, circumstantial. Her thought 
content included somatic delusions. Her Insight/Judgement was noted to be impaired. Unremarkable impression was noted. No SI suicidal ideation), HI (homicidal ideation), AH (auditory hallucination), VH (visual hallucination) was noted.
On day #13, per the psychiatrist note, the patient slept well, and she went to groups. She was seen by medical due to tracking eye movement. Her mental status exam was noted to be normal unless otherwise noted. Her mood was subjectively anxious. Her thought processes were preoccupied, circumstantial. Her thought content included somatic delusions. Her Insight/Judgement was noted to be impaired/limited. Unremarkable impression was noted. No SI suicidal ideation), HI (homicidal ideation), AH (auditory hallucination), VH (visual hallucination) was noted. She had a neuro consult for dizziness. Orders included begin perphenazine 2 milligrams every three hours as needed.

The Continued Acute Psychiatric Inpatient Hospitalization was not medically necessary.

Based on InterQual Criteria MDD (major depressive disorder), Adult Inpatient 2023, the patient did not meet criteria for continued psychiatric inpatient hospitalization. The patient was not noted to be actively suicidal or homicidal. The patient was able to keep herself safe. Her behaviors were appropriate/adequate to maintain safety. Her symptoms continued to improve or were stable. She was not psychotic. There was no substance use concerns or withdrawal. She was able to care for her basic needs. She was participating in her care. She was not having medication side effects such required continued inpatient stay for monitoring. She was noted to be dizzy but had a workup by neurology with no indication that she needed continued hospital stay for this. She did not require 24/7 monitoring with nursing. The patient's symptoms were chronic and/or evaluated to an extent that they could have been addressed in a lesser restrictive setting. The patient could have been treated at a lower level of care for the dates of service in question.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance abuse.
Treatment: Inpatient Rehabilitation Admission.

The insurer denied: Inpatient Rehabilitation Admission.  The denial is upheld.

The patient is an adult male, who completed detoxification treatment with transfer for inpatient rehabilitation and substance use disorder treatment to address alcohol, cannabis (marijuana), and stimulant (crack cocaine) class substances of abuse. The patient has a history of one recent treatment episode with detoxification in the previous month with immediate relapse and was self-referred in the context of unemployment and with family support. He has chronic medical conditions including obesity and generalized seizure disorder treated with Keppra. The patient is married and unemployed. He lives with family. There were no reported legal issues and no trauma history in this case. Evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination that reflected motivation for rehabilitation treatment, but limited insight, impaired judgment, and poor control of impulses. The patient readily engaged in substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment. He was noted to be engaged in the therapeutic activities, social with peers and participating in recovery groups, and adherent with medication that included vitamin supplements and comfort medications with the availability of nicotine replacement for tobacco dependence. He received intensive rehabilitation services, monitoring, and structure provided within the inpatient treatment program including 24-hour nursing monitoring. The patient was discharged on day # (number) 24 against medical advice (AMA) with clinically appropriate recommendations for aftercare of his substance use disorders and plan to proceed to outpatient treatment. The patient declined medication assisted treatment with Vivitrol and smoking cessation. The denial of coverage was based on medical necessity and New York Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria/Guidelines indicating that the patient had no general medical or psychiatric issues warranting inpatient level care and 24-hour nursing support, had no severe or complicated withdrawal symptoms or history. The appeal was based on medical necessity and New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug (LOCADTR) Criteria/Guidelines indicating that the patient had limited supports and coping skills, as well as high risk for relapse warranting inpatient level rehabilitation services. The appeal referenced the need to monitor treatment for the seizure disorder with seizure precautions and continued treatment with Keppra.

The proposed treatment and the requested benefit of inpatient substance abuse rehabilitation treatment was not medically necessary.

The patient presented with substance use disorders, diagnosed with alcohol and stimulant/cocaine and cannabis use disorders. He tested positive for cocaine and cannabis, consistent with history. He was medically screened and had no acute general medical issues or laboratory abnormalities. He received inpatient level rehabilitation treatment. During the time interval under review, the patient was noted to be in no apparent distress with reasonable functioning and active participation in treatment including positive interactions with staff and peers. Throughout his inpatient stay, there were no complicating treatment issues or biomedical or co-occurring psychiatric issues that would have warranted inpatient level of care, structure or 24-hour nursing monitoring. The application of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug (LOCADTR) Criteria did indicate that the patient was clinically appropriate for treatment with lower-level care in a less restrictive treatment setting, as the health plan asserts. Thus, medical necessity for the inpatient substance abuse rehabilitation treatment is not met in this case scenario, also consistent with the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, the scientific literature, and published guidelines, referenced below.

summary:
Diagnosis: Polysubstance Use Disorder.
Treatment: Inpatient Psychiatry Admission.

The insurer denied an inpatient psychiatry admission. The determination is overturned.

This is a patient, who was admitted for inpatient rehabilitation treatment of severe polysubstance use disorder with opioid (Fentanyl), alcohol, stimulant (methamphetamine and 3-4 methylenedioxymethamphetamine [MDMA]), hallucinogen (ketamine), and cannabis use disorder (marijuana). The patient's substance use had started in adolescence and escalated with progression to daily use of one or more of the substances of abuse, as indicated. The patient reported a significant decline in functioning and severe psychosocial stressors within the housing, occupational, educational, primary support, and social environment domains, as well as a trauma history. 

At the time of presentation, the patient had received detoxification services and inpatient psychiatric treatment for the severe symptoms of depression and suicidality. There were no acute general medical issues in this case other than prominent post-acute withdrawal symptoms (PAWS). 

The patient received a comprehensive evaluation, including the New York Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) assessment and other structured assessments. He received rehabilitation treatment that included group, individual, and educational sessions, as well as the opportunity for peer support with 12-step recovery groups. Medications were prescribed to address anxiety, depression, and PAWS. Throughout the inpatient stay, the patient was noted to have PAWS with intense craving with titration of Suboxone and use of Baclofen, clonidine, and the addition of low-dose bupropion. His insight remained limited with impaired judgment and a high risk for relapse, but he did make gradual progress with advancement to a higher stage of change. 

Therapy included ongoing efforts to develop coping skills and a relapse prevention plan that included the identification of triggers. In the final week of treatment, stress within the social environment was addressed in the context of discharge planning. Throughout the stay, the patient was considered at high risk for relapse due to the lack of sober support. 

The issue under review is the medical necessity of inpatient psychiatry admission.

The requested health service/treatment of inpatient psychiatry admission was medically necessary for this patient.

Based on the diagnoses, mental status, and clinical course, the patient warranted admission and continued structure, monitoring, and intensity of services provided. The patient's lack of insight and coping skills, the need for sessions to develop sober supports and advance the stage of change, as well as treatment of associated symptoms of mood disturbance, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and anxiety, are other factors that supported the necessity for inpatient level services through discharge with safety monitoring and management of aggressive behavior.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse.
Treatment: Inpatient substance use detoxification.
The insurer denied inpatient substance use detoxification.
The determination is overturned.

The patient is an adult male who was admitted to acute inpatient level services for detoxification and withdrawal management of opioid (heroin and methadone), stimulant (crack cocaine), and alcohol use disorders.  The patient reported no history of severe withdrawal symptoms or accidental overdose. 
The patient has no history of a co-occurring psychiatric disorder, and denied psychiatric hospitalization, or suicidal or self-harming behaviors.
Physical Examination and laboratory assessment were normal or unremarkable except for a positive drug screen consistent with history and normal vital signs other than an initial elevated pulse that remained normal throughout the subsequent inpatient stay. The blood alcohol level was zero. 
Following his first day of treatment, the patient began to participate in counseling and educational sessions, as he was feeling better. His mental status examination included persistent symptoms of anxiety with associated symptoms of insomnia. During his inpatient stay, the patient demonstrated no severe symptoms, such as mania, psychosis, perceptual disturbance, or severe cognitive impairment. The patient completed the detoxification treatment without complications. 
At issue is the medical necessity of inpatient substance use detoxification.

The requested health service/treatment of inpatient substance use detoxification is medically necessary for this patient.
The patient presented with a diagnosis of severe alcohol, opioid, and stimulant use disorders with high risk for relapse or continued use. The patient also has severe psychosocial stressors with limited support and functional impairments.
The presenting clinical features and history and risk for withdrawal complications did warrant the admission and continued inpatient level services with a safe detoxification protocol and medical monitoring. The patient's admission and continued inpatient stay with detoxification, withdrawal management, and other medical services through discharge could not have been provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario.
 Withdrawal risk was managed with tapering dosages of methadone and monitoring and as needed (prn) medications, as well as the availability of comfort medications and vitamin replacement therapy to prevent the onset of encephalopathy. Seizure and fall precautions were provided. Counseling and educational sessions with motivational techniques together with case management services were appropriately provided to motivate the patient's transition for appropriate rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment. Thus, the patient did require a safe and effective detoxification with inpatient level services and withdrawal management during the time frame under review.

Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Inpatient Substance Use Detoxification, 5 days

The insurer denied inpatient substance use detoxification for five days. The determination is overturned.

The patient is an adult male who presented to the emergency department requesting detoxification and was admitted following the medical screening with acute inpatient-level services for detoxification and withdrawal management of severe alcohol and stimulant (crack cocaine) use disorders. The patient presented with alcohol withdrawal at the time of admission. Withdrawal symptoms included tremors, sweats, nausea, insomnia, irritability, and anxiety. The patient has no history of psychiatric disorders. 

The patient was admitted to the acute inpatient level care and placed on a detoxification regimen with a five-day Librium taper, vitamin replacement therapy, fluid replacement, and medical monitoring; the patient was offered smoking cessation treatment and nicotine replacement. Following his first day of treatment, the patient began participating in counseling and educational sessions. His demeanor improved as he underwent detoxification treatment, and he was social with peers, though he was agitated, restless, and had trouble sleeping. 

At issue is the medical necessity of inpatient substance use detoxification for five days.

The requested health service/treatment of continued medically supervised inpatient substance use detoxification, withdrawal management, and stabilization services is medically necessary for this patient.

The proposed inpatient services, detoxification treatment and withdrawal management for severe alcohol and cocaine use disorder, and other services noted in the clinical summary could not have been safely and effectively provided at a lower level of care. The adult inpatient treatment of this patient's substance disorders did require admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level setting, and 24-hour monitoring given the severity of the alcohol use disorder and the presentation with a lack of insight, high risk for relapse, and lack of a reasonable recovery environment. The patient's withdrawal symptoms were managed by tapering dosages of benzodiazepine/Librium, requiring monitoring. Comfort medications, vitamins, and nicotine replacement therapy were also made available. Thus, the patient did warrant a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management during the time frame under review, as it was reasonable that the patient would have been unable to abstain from the substances of abuse if detoxification and treatment were to be attempted at a lower level of care. Thus, medical necessity was met in keeping with New York State OASAS LOCADTR Criteria and Guidelines as required in this case.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major depressive disorder.
Treatment: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) - 35 Units.
The insurer denied: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) - 35 Units.
The denial is overturned.

The patient is a teenager with a history of major depressive disorder, recurrent and severe without psychotic features. The PHQ (patient health questionnaire)-9 scale score of 20-21 reflects severe symptoms of depression. The patient has a documented history of multiple medication treatments for depression, including treatment with two disparate classes of 
medication including sertraline and venlafaxine, as well as augmentation with lamotrigine, lithium, and aripiprazole. Due to adverse effects or lack of efficacy, the patient continued to experience severe symptoms of depression and functional impairments that impacted quality of 
life and day-to-day activities as a student. Additionally, the patient has had treatment with an evidence-based psychotherapy (CBT) combined with antidepressant medication together with supportive measures. The patient was referred and recommended for repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) therapy together with continued medication treatment and psychotherapy.
The patient has reportedly had psychiatric hospitalizations or suicide attempts or suicidal behavior, reflecting the severity of the depressive disorder. There are no co-morbid psychiatric disorders and no diagnosed co-occurring substance use disorder in this case. The patient has no acute general medical issues that would impact TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy.
The patient's mental status examination at the time of referral showed depressed mood, sad affect with anxiety, and anhedonia. She has loss of interest and low energy with fatigue and other neuro-vegetative disturbances related to depression, as scored with the PHQ (patient health questionnaire)-9.

The requested health service with TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy for the treatment of recurrent and severe major depressive disorder is medically necessary for this patient.

TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy as a primary or adjunctive therapy for treatment of depression has generally been evaluated in patients who have treatment refractory depression, as defined by one or more, antidepressant medication treatment failures with or without augmentation. TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy for depressive disorder has been established by the FDA (United States Food and Drug Administration) as a safe treatment. The data, as reflected in peer reviewed medical literature, supports this assertion, including more recent studies involving adolescents, reflected in the referenced scientific literature. Specifically, when treatments with two or more antidepressant medications with or without augmentation, or with electroconvulsive therapy, and/or psychotherapy, especially cognitive behavioral therapy, have failed to produce a response or remission, then TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) is an appropriate consideration. This assertion is noted in the American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorder, referenced below. 
In this case, at least two alternative therapeutic trials with augmentation together with other therapeutic measures have been provided including psychotherapy. Thus, in this case, the requested TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy is considered clinically appropriate and medically necessary. The patient in this case has demonstrated that her depressive disorder is treatment refractory or resistant, and the requested treatment of recurrent major depressive disorder using repetitive TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy with a clinically appropriate number of sessions is/was reasonable and warranted in this case scenario. This is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice.

TMS therapy for depressive disorder has been established by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as a safe treatment and the data supports this assertion.

In this case, at least two or more alternative therapeutic trials with augmentation together with other therapeutic measures have been provided, and the proposed treatment with TMS therapy is considered clinically appropriate and medically necessary. The decision to proceed with TMS therapy reflects sound medical judgment based upon the current scientific literature and American Psychiatric Association practice guidelines concerning the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorder. The patient in this case has demonstrated that her depressive disorder is treatment refractory or resistant, and the proposed treatment of recurrent major depressive disorder using TMS therapy with a clinically appropriate number of sessions is warranted in this case scenario, and is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major depressive disorder
Treatment: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) therapy.
The insurer denied TMS therapy.
The determination is overturned.

The patient is a female with a history of major depressive disorder, recurrent and moderately severe without psychotic features and comorbid generalized anxiety disorder. The patient has a documented history of multiple failed medication treatments for depression including treatment with more than two disparate classes of medication (Lexapro, Zoloft, and Wellbutrin), as well as augmentation with thyroid hormone (levothyroxine). Additionally, the patient has received treatment with hydroxyzine and clonazepam targeting associated symptoms of anxiety and insomnia related to the mood disorder and comorbid generalized anxiety disorder. She has been treated with an evidence-based psychotherapy [cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)] without a response or remission of depressive symptoms. Current treatment includes ongoing psychotherapy and continued use of Wellbutrin and thyroid hormone and Vitamin D3 and other supplements with only modest effect. The patient has no history of psychiatric hospitalization or suicide attempts or suicidal behavior.

At issue is the medical necessity of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) therapy.

The requested health service/treatment of TMS is medically necessary for this patient.
Repetitive TMS therapy as a primary or adjunctive therapy for treatment of major depression has generally been evaluated in patients who have treatment refractory or pharmaco-resistant depression, as defined by one or more antidepressant medication treatment failures with or without augmentation, and with or without psychotherapy, especially CBT. TMS therapy, as applied in major depression, is considered to be a safe treatment by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The data as reflected in peer reviewed medical literature supports this assertion. Specifically, when treatments with antidepressant medication with or without augmentation, electroconvulsive therapy, and/or psychotherapy (especially CBT) have failed, then TMS is an appropriate treatment for major depressive disorder. This assertion is noted in the American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorder, referenced below, and consistent with the scientific literature pertaining to TMS and its application to depressive disorder. The patient has also failed to achieve a remission of symptoms with combined treatment with psychotherapy (CBT) and medication regimens.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance use disorder.
Treatment: Inpatient Medically Supervised Detoxification.
The insurer denied: Inpatient Medically Supervised Detoxification.
The denial is overturned.

The patient is an adult male who presented for detoxification treatment and was medically screened and admitted to acute inpatient level care to address substance use disorder with opioid, alcohol, cannabis, and nicotine class substance use disorders. The patient had been using heroin with one to three bags daily and two 24-ounce beers on a daily continuous basis, as well as intermittent use of cannabis/marijuana with tobacco dependence. The patient has no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens but has a history of moderately severe withdrawal symptoms. He had a history of prior detoxification and substance use disorder treatments with relapses and associated legal problems with parole status. His referral for treatment was prompted by multiple stressors and mandated by his parole officer or the legal system. The patient had no history of psychiatric disorder and no history of psychiatric hospitalization or suicidal behavior and was not taking psychotropic medications. He was noted to have an untreated anxiety disorder pertinent to his substance use disorders. Laboratory assessments were unremarkable, but the patient's vital signs included elevated blood pressure and his Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) was scored in the mild range of 8 increasing to 11 during treatment. He had nausea/vomiting, tremor, sweats, altered sensorium, and anxiety. The patient is married with unemployment and living with family. He did not report trauma or abuse history but had prominent legal issues. He had limited social supports. The patient was admitted to detoxification treatment with a comprehensive detoxification protocol with tapering dosages of methadone, and as needed (PRN) medications for comfort, as well as monitoring. The program provided for case management with referral and access to rehabilitation treatment that included comprehensive evidence-based treatments. The patient was discharged on day # (number) 4. Denial of coverage was based on medical necessity and New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria indicating that there were no serious withdrawals or abnormal vital signs or history/risk of withdrawal complications. The denial determinations indicated that the patient had no significant general medical or psychiatric conditions with intensive outpatient program (IOP) or residential level care suggested as clinically appropriate. The appeal asserted that the admission and treatment was medically necessary and met New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria with abnormal vital signs-elevated blood pressure, untreated anxiety, and withdrawal risk. 

The proposed treatment, inpatient substance-related services with withdrawal management and detoxification treatment, is medically necessary.

The requested inpatient admission and continued treatment could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. The patient in this case was using opioid and alcohol class substances on a daily continuous basis with intermittent use of other substances of abuse that did warrant inpatient level detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring for the duration of the protocol; detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments pertinent to the detoxification treatment episode could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment that was provided at the time of admission. Moreover, the patient had mild and persistent withdrawal symptoms, and the patient's social environment was not conducive to detoxification in the context of limited insight, impaired judgment, and poor control of impulses, as well as prominent legal problems. There was an undiagnosed psychiatric comorbidity that warranted treatment as indicated in the appeal. Thus, the need for detoxification treatment and withdrawal management did warrant the admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level detoxification setting.

Treatment: Residential Mental Health Services
The insurer denied: Residential Mental Health Services

The case involves an adult male who was admitted to residential level services with severe symptoms of depression and anxiety and trauma-related symptoms associated with co-occurring substance use disorders, suicidal behavior, and inability to function. The patient's admission had been precipitated by an aborted suicide attempt with a gun, a clinical course with worsening symptoms of depression and anxiety in the context of suicidal ideation, and serious suicide attempts with persistent suicidal ideation in the context of use of moderately severe or severe opioid (Oxycontin), sedative-hypnotic-anxiolytic (Klonopin), and cannabis (marijuana) use disorders. Thus, the patient has a history of severe and recurrent major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, and complex PTSD (posttraumatic stress disorder) with severe co-occurring substance-related disorders and suicidality. The patient has a history of trauma related to his work as a medic during the World Trade Center attack. Mental Status Examination on admission: The patient was cooperative with anxious and depressive demeanor. He displayed a depressed mood with anxiety and slowed mentation that included reports of cognitive clouding. He had decreased concentration, energy, appetite, sleep, and volition including trauma related symptoms. The patient's insight and judgment were limited and impaired by his persistent suicidal ideation and the effects of multiple substances of abuse. He displayed hopelessness, helplessness, and self-reproach with guilt indicating that he was having frequent thoughts of suicide. He was cooperative with staff and was medication adherent though his medications were not effective, and he required active medication management. By day # (number) 9, the patient began to think more clearly and participate more actively in the Trauma-informed CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) and other evidence-based therapeutic interventions. The patient continued to display severe symptoms of anxiety and depression with continued safety-monitoring to address suicidal risk. From day #9 -day #29, progress notes reflect ongoing bouts of anger requiring prn (as needed) medications and staff interventions. His anxiety diminished and mood improved such that he was noted to be more stable and euthymic. A discharge plan was developed with family education and focused interventions allowing for discharge on day #45.

The requested health service of Residential Mental Health Services is considered medically necessary.

The patient could not have been safely or effectively managed within a less restrictive setting or with a lower level of care during the time interval under review. The patient's presentation and clinical features included a major depressive episode in the context of a recent potential suicide attempt, severe symptoms of anxiety and complex PTSD (Post Traumatic Stress Disorder) with high risk for suicide, a decline in functioning, and severe substance-related disorders including the misuse of prescription opiates and Klonopin. During the time interval under review, the patient remained acutely ill with residual symptoms of mood disturbance and anxiety symptoms, and continued risk for relapse or suicide with need for safety monitoring. The patient's severity of symptoms and need for safety monitoring while receiving active treatment did warrant the admission and the continued structure of a residential setting and 24-hour monitoring in a safe environment through discharge. 
Thus, it was medically necessary and clinically appropriate for this patient to remain in a residential setting with 24-hour monitoring in view of the presenting clinical features and residual symptoms of a severe and recurrent mood disorder and complex PTSD (Post Traumatic Stress Disorder) in the context of impaired functioning requiring safety monitoring and staff direction, structure, and supervision. The insurer denied coverage for continued intensive rehabilitation, physical and psychiatric.  The denial was reversed.

According to notes, this is a teenaged female admitted for comprehensive rehabilitation following injuries sustained after a suicide attempt by jumping in front of a train. 
A Progress Note indicates the patient's parents had secured an intake for an intensive dialectic behavioral therapy (DBP) program that will include therapy 3x weekly, DBT (dialectical behavior therapy) phone coaching, parent work, etc. They have also worked with the team to get a referral to a partial hospital program (PHP) program as a back-up in case the patient does not engage adequately in her therapies. The recommendation has been to discharge to an IOP (intensive outpatient) level of care. However, they prefer at this time to utilize the intensive program. This was considered a reasonable alternative to intensive outpatient therapy (IOP), and they can always escalate the level of care if needed through the child's outpatient psychiatrist/therapist and/or the emergency room if safety concerns arise. While fair and improving in general, the patient's limited insight into her affective and cognitive experience precipitating the suicide attempts reflects chronic underlying cognitive and psychological deficits. 

According to the Milliman Care Guidelines (MCG) general treatment course, transition of care must include that the individual's neurobehavioral and neurocognitive status are manageable at a lower level of care, patient is safe to go home if the mental status is stable. The patient's condition and functional status must be manageable at a lower level of care.

According to Dalton-Locke et al., Mental health rehabilitation services provide essential support to people with complex and longer-term mental health problems. They include inpatient services and community teams providing clinical input to people living in supported accommodation services. Access to inpatient rehabilitation services was associated with a reduction in acute inpatient service use post discharge. Fewer than one half of people moved on from higher to lower levels of supported accommodation within expected timeframes. Inpatient rehabilitation services may reduce the need for inpatient service use over the long term but more high-quality research of contemporary rehabilitation services with comparison groups is required.

Five months ago, she was already ambulating independently with a straight cane in her hospital room and throughout the hospital (300-500 feet) under distant observation. Furthermore, the patient was seen to complete a 15-minute static standing activity with intermittent upper extremity assistance and observation. However, the patient's limited insight into her affective and cognitive experience precipitating the suicide attempts reflects chronic underlying cognitive and psychological deficits (including in terms of awareness of affective and cognitive state, distress tolerance, affect regulation, problem-solving, interpersonal communication, and effectiveness) that are best addressed psychotherapeutically. As per MCG, transition of care must include that the individual's neurobehavioral and neurocognitive status are manageable at a lower level of care. According to peer reviewed literature, inpatient rehabilitation treatments were related with a decrease in acute inpatient care utilization following discharge. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be reversed. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient.
