summary:
Diagnosis: Mania
Treatment: Inpatient admission
The health plan denied inpatient admission. The denial is overturned.

The patient is an adult male. He was admitted for treatment of mania in the context of a diagnosis of bipolar I disorder and a recent psychosocial stressor with a difficult college roommate and non-adherence with his medication. He had stopped his Zyprexa with subsequent onset of mania associated with agitation and psychosis characterized by prominent irritability, aggression towards others, and dysphoric mood. The acute episode of mood disturbance was negatively impacting his ability to function at college prompting his presentation for emergency services with treatment and observation in the emergency department followed by hospital admission with psychiatric consultation and plans for an involuntary emergency admission for psychiatric care.

A comprehensive evaluation was conducted/completed with testing that had included laboratory assessments, Chest X-ray, drug screen, and physical examination. Results were normal or unremarkable as the evaluation was completed, and there was no evidence for illicit substance use or use of alcohol or marijuana. He had a history of asthma but no other general medical issues. His agitation required restraint and prn (as needed) medications, as well as starting risperidone, Depakote and Klonopin.

The patient was admitted from the emergency department to acute inpatient level services with one-to-one observation, safety monitoring, and psychiatric management regarding pharmacotherapy supplemented with prn medications to enhance sleep and to address anxiety and agitation. While conducting an evaluation for an underlying medical condition, his medications were adjusted with titrations of Depakote and risperidone and Klonopin.

For the dates of service under review, the patient was evidenced to be less preoccupied with his thought content and was improved with respect to thought processing, mood, and functioning. He continued to display disturbed mood and labile affect with intermittent episodes of agitation and an episode of attempting to elope from the hospital. Prior to transfer for inpatient psychiatric care, the patient was cooperative, with intense eye contact and fidgeting. Speech was clear and coherent. His insight was limited and poor, and judgment was impaired, and he indicated that he would be better off without medications. Case management worked with the patient's mother to achieve the transfer to a psychiatric treatment facility. He was tolerant of the prescribed medications.

Overall, the patient was more spontaneous with improved mood and diminished anxiety. He had consistently denied suicidal ideation. He was discharge with a transfer, and submitted documentation indicates that he remained hospitalized after the transfer.

The patient required the admission and the continued acute inpatient level care and the structure and monitoring of an acute inpatient level setting in order to remain safe and to administer treatment for his psychiatric disturbance, bipolar mood disorder. The admission was warranted in order to conduct evaluations and observe his functioning and mental status with the resumption and adjustment of clinically appropriate medications. The clinical course was complicated by the presence of impaired judgment and impulsive aggression/agitation with functional impairment being addressed during the time interval under review. Additionally, the treatment team was planning for a safe and clinically appropriate disposition with transfer for acute inpatient psychiatric treatment.

Peer-reviewed scientific literature and published guidelines support the continued inpatient care through discharge, as the patient remained at risk for erratic behavior and medication non-adherence, as well as safety concerns in view of the continued disturbance of mood and behavior.

summary:

The patient is a young adult male who completed residential level treatment and was referred for partial hospital program (PHP) treatment to address substance use disorder with alcohol and cannabis class substances of abuse. The patient has a history of using one joint of marijuana and daily use of alcohol with binge drinking up to twenty shots of tequila while working as a bartender. The substance abuse had started at an early age in adolescence with escalating use in the two years prior to treatment. He had no history of delirium tremens or withdrawal seizures, but did report frequent blackouts. His referral for PHP level care occurred after residential treatment with immediate referral for PHP level services.
Mental status examination on admission to PHP level services was free of severe psychiatric symptoms including mania, psychosis, perceptual disturbance, and cognitive impairment. He had no suicidal ideation and was generally motivated for treatment. Insight was limited and judgment impaired with poor coping skills.
The patient was single, employed with family support. 
At the time of admission for PHP level services, the patient had been participating actively in the rehabilitation treatment. He had no biomedical complications or severe withdrawal symptoms. The patient did not show for his treatment and was administratively discharged from the PHP program.
At issue is the medical necessity of Partial Hospitalization Services for Substance Use Disorders.
The requested health service/treatment of Partial Hospitalization Substance Use Treatment was not medically necessary for this patient.
The structure and intensity of services necessary for a successful rehabilitation/substance use disorder treatment could have been effectively provided at a lower level of care in a less restrictive treatment setting with sober supports. There is no evidence that PHP level structure or services is medically necessary for a successful outcome in this case. There were no biomedical, psychiatric, or general medical issues that warranted the PHP level of care.
The patient's substance use disorders were amenable to treatment at a lower level of care in this case scenario, and the health plan's determination of medical necessity was consistent with the application of NY State OASAS LOCADTR 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines.
The patient's continued substance abuse rehabilitation treatment, in this case scenario, was amenable to treatment at a lower level of care. The patient was generally motivated and capable of effectively engaging and continuing his substance use disorder treatment in a less restrictive treatment setting with sober supports and/or housing. 
Again, there were no biomedical or psychiatric complications, or severe psychiatric symptoms/disorders in this case that would have warranted PHP level services and treatment, as requested. Thus, the requested partial hospitalization services for substance use disorders were not medically necessary for this patient.

summary:
Diagnosis: Psychotic Disorder
Treatment: Inpatient Mental Health Services

The insurer denied inpatient mental health services. The denial is upheld.

The patient is an adult male with a diagnosis of psychotic disorder who was admitted to the inpatient level of care. The patient was initially admitted for worsening symptoms of psychosis in the context of medication noncompliance. The psychiatric progress notes from the date of admission and forward indicate the patient consistently denied suicidal ideation, homicidal ideation, hallucinations, and delusions, and it was noted that his psychotic symptoms had remitted, and the patient was at his baseline. His mood was noted to be euthymic. He was noted to be sleeping well, was compliant with medications, and denied medication side effects. He was noted to be awaiting placement and to be participating in discharge planning. The treatment plan update notes report the patient was intermittently interactive with social workers. He was noted to attend group therapy sessions sporadically. The medical progress notes report the patient was stable without any acute medical issues or concerns. At issue is the inpatient level of care. 

The health plan denied coverage because the patient was not accepting treatment for thought disorder symptoms and was felt to be at baseline, was not at risk of harm to self or others, was taking medications, had been seeing his psychiatrist, therapist, and social worker, was not engaged in treatment, did not have severe medical problems that require care 24 hours a day and did not require further psychiatric inpatient hospital care in a 24-hour setting. The health plan upheld the decision as not medically necessary due to documentation that the patient was doing better, was not having any unsafe thoughts, was thinking more clearly, was no longer depressed or paranoid, was calm and cooperative, and was taking better care of himself and was participating in treatment and was compliant with medications. The decision was appealed again by the treating facility, which stated that the patient's symptoms were still of severity and that inpatient care was necessary on the denied dates. It was also noted that securing a safe discharge plan for him was difficult.

The requested health service was not medically necessary.

For the dates of service in question, there is no documentation of imminent danger to self or others as indicated by the patient's denial of suicidal ideation, homicidal ideation, or command hallucinations. There is no documentation of severe symptoms of depression, anxiety, mania, or psychosis. There is no documentation of persistent behavioral problems, including agitation or aggression. There is no documentation of severe dysfunction in daily living compared to the patient's baseline. These are the symptoms and circumstances for which the inpatient level of care is warranted. A review of the medical literature concludes that treatment with antipsychotic medications and psychosocial interventions, including psychoeducation and psychotherapy, are effective in the treatment of patients with schizophrenia spectrum illnesses. These treatment options are available at lower levels of care than inpatient. The definition of medical necessity generally includes that services must be in accordance with generally accepted standards of medical practice. Since the inpatient level of care for dates of service under review does not fit this definition in this case, it is not medically necessary for the patient.

He reportedly had difficulty identifying social cues, was socially awkward, had rigid thinking and behavior, difficulty with social perception, struggled to recognize multiple perspectives, had difficulty managing emotional regulation, lacked insight, was the victim of bullying, and had difficulties dealing with his father's death. He reportedly had diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder, Generalized Anxiety Disorder, Persistent Depressive Disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) - Inattentive presentation, and Learning Disorder. He reportedly was in group, individual, and family therapy and pharmacotherapy. He reportedly lacked coping skills to regulate emotions and behaviors and required this structured treatment setting. 

The insurer denied coverage for mental health partial hospital program level of care for 6 hours per day and 5 days per week from last December forward stating that it was not considered medically necessary treatment then. They stated that his symptoms were improving, he had no thoughts to harm self or others, was taking medications, was active in treatment, and had a supportive mother. They recommended a less restrictive level of care then.

Notes from last October through February of this year still reported that he was in need of a high level of containment to manage behaviors and emotions while working on interpersonal skills, school, social and coping skills, behavioral and emotional control. Other goals included to decrease rigidity and flexibility in thinking and behaviors, gain understanding of developmental issues and learning struggles and how it impacts him and how he perceives the environment and interact with others, and to decrease avoidance behaviors. The patient reportedly needed more time at least this mental health partial hospital program (PHP) setting to sustain gains and make further gains to decrease maladaptive behaviors and improve functional skills and functioning including ability to care for basic needs. He reportedly had difficulty implementing therapeutic rules without this supervised and structured therapeutic treatment setting which required at least 6 hours per day and 5 days per week of treatment. He had multiple areas of deficits and required at least this level of care.

summary:

The patient is an adult male who was self-referred and admitted to acute inpatient level services for detoxification and withdrawal management of opioid (heroin) and cannabis and nicotine use disorder. He was using up to 7 bags of heroin daily with a chronic relapsing course since age 36 and using cannabis and tobacco since adolescence, using 8-9 marijuana blunts per day together with ½ (half) pack per day use of tobacco. The adult inpatient treatment of this patient's substance-related disorders did warrant the admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level setting and 24-hour monitoring in view of the severity of the substance use disorders. Counseling and educational sessions with motivational techniques together with case management services were appropriately provided to motivate the patient's transition for appropriate rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment. Thus, the patient did require a safe and effective detoxification with inpatient level services and withdrawal management during the time frame under review, as it was reasonable that the patient would have been unable to abstain from the substances of abuse or remain in treatment if detoxification and treatment were attempted at a lower level of care.

summary:
Diagnosis: Post-traumatic Stress Disorder. 
Treatment: Residential treatment center services. 
The insurer denied residential treatment center services. 
The determination is overturned. 

The patient is a female who was admitted to extended residential level treatment for severe mood, trauma-related, and eating disorders complicated by a history of self-destructive behavior and problematic behaviors with deterioration in functioning. Her symptoms of mood disturbance were associated with suicidal ideation and behaviors with previous suicide attempts (hanging, drowning) and bouts of self-harm with cutting and asphyxiation for which she had required inpatient level services at least twice and subsequent high-intensity residential treatment. 
The patient had received multiple medication trials and psychotherapy in the past without sustained benefit or a remission of symptoms. Moreover, she was noted to have impulsivity and aggressive behavior that complicated her ability to function socially, occupationally, and educationally, and within the family constellation and social settings and at school. 
These clinical features and treatment dimensions in this case prompted the referral to extended residential treatment to include structured intensive behavioral therapy and other treatments to address the psychosocial issues within the primary support/family and social environment domains. The high-risk behaviors including self-harm, elopement risk, suicidality, and verbal aggression as well as disordered and restrictive eating prompted the plan for extended residential treatment. Her referral for residential treatment was also prompted by her clinical providers' safety concerns and the dysregulated mood associated with her co-morbid mood and trauma-related disorders that were self-defeating. Thus, the patient was admitted to residential level care in the context of worsening longstanding mood disturbance with anxiety and depression and high risk for suicidal and self-destructive behavior associated with poor control of impulses together with maladaptive coping and prominent family and peer relationship problems, as well as the eating disorder. 
Evaluation revealed a mental status examination with severe psychiatric symptoms in the context of a primary diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and severe and recurrent major depressive disorder and co-morbid eating disorder. The patient was cooperative with evaluation. There was suicidal ideation, and she had reported urges to self-harm with self-destructive behavior with maladaptive coping. There was no evidence of frank psychosis, mania, thought disorder, or severe cognitive impairment though the patient had concentration and attention deficits in association with executive function deficits and high-risk for impulsive behavior. She reported sleep disturbance with nightmares, but no other trauma related symptoms. 
The patient is single; she was characterized as a good student. There are prominent family problems and relationship problems, and the trauma history and oppositional behaviors that included elopement and running away, as well as restrictive eating.
The patient was admitted to residential level treatment with a comprehensive evaluation to affirm her diagnoses that supported the diagnostic evaluations. The program provided for comprehensive treatment that includes focus on coping skills, education, and involvement with groups and individual therapy, as well as milieu and activity therapy with safety monitoring and the opportunity for family focused sessions. Medications, Prozac and Abilify were prescribed and adjusted to address the patient's mood-related symptoms and to address symptoms of anxiety. The patient received cognitive-behavioral techniques and intensive and modified dialectical behavioral therapy (CBT & DBT); family therapy, activity therapies to address coping skills, and, psychoeducation, as wells as family-focused sessions with family involvement. She was engaged in therapy, working on assignments, and participating in sessions to address strained relationships with family. Medication management was provided with use of lithium, venlafaxine, lurasidone, and trazodone, as well as metformin and Deplin; she had no adverse effects with medications that were adjusted with tolerability and adherence with evidence for a clinical response with improved mood and reduction of the suicidal ideation. The treatment team was planning for extended residential treatment and for subsequent referral to the community with clinical providers to provide continued therapy and medication management and with plans to return home with step down to a Partial Hospitalization Program (PHP) or an Intensive Outpatient Program (IOP) level services when clinically appropriated.
The denial was based on medical necessity indicating that the patient was making progress, medication adherent and participating and that 24-hour monitoring was not warranted as there were no remaining safety concerns or risk factors. The denial determination referenced InterQual Guidelines pertaining to residential level services for children and adolescents. 
The appeal was based on medical necessity and continued safety and risk concerns warranting structure and supervision in a residential setting. The appeals referenced the negative influence of peers and social environment, deficient coping skills, high risk for relapse and self-harming behavior, and the evidence for progress with treatment. 
The health plan documents and case notes, appeal documents, and correspondence from the health plan and treating clinicians, and the health rationale for the denial of certification for coverage of the requested treatment, were reviewed. This review is New York State mandated. At issue is the medical necessity of the requested residential treatment services. 
The requested health service/treatment of residential treatment center services is medically necessary for this patient. 
The residential services are clinically appropriate and the conditions in this case are not amenable to treatment at a lower level of care. The risk factors in this case for suicidal or self-harm; the clinical features that include treatment refractory mood and trauma-related disorders in the context of functional decline and behavioral problems that includes impulsive aggression towards self and others with verbal aggression, problematic relationships, and the treatment dimensions warrant the requested benefit of Mental Health Residential Level of Care with the structure necessary to maintain safety.
Specifically, the patient's complicated clinical issues did require a treatment setting to facilitate the development of improved coping skills and life skills together with the development of improved insight and motivation, as well as family intensive work. She did need the admission and continued structure and monitoring of a residential setting to safely continue mental health treatment and services. There are psychiatric complications related to the family functioning, and severe psychiatric symptoms including impulsive aggression towards self and others that required residential level services, structure and monitoring, as indicated in the appeals. The case is complicated by high-risk behaviors and safety concerns including suicidal risk. 
Thus, the requested services, Mental Health Residential Level of Care, is clinically appropriate, medically necessary, and consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice and consistent with the scientific literature, referenced below.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse.
Treatment: Residential Substance Use Treatment.

The insurer denied Residential Substance Use Treatment. The health plan's determination is overturned.

This case involves an adult female, who received inpatient psychiatric-level treatment and was referred and transferred to residential-level substance use disorder rehabilitation services. The presentation for substance-related treatment was prompted by continued complications associated with bipolar disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and co-occurring drug and alcohol use. The patient had a precipitous decline in functioning in the context of escalating use of alcohol, benzodiazepines, and cocaine, together with ongoing symptoms of co-occurring psychiatric disorders, bipolar I disorder, and PTSD. The submitted information noted that the patient presented with associated symptoms of anxiety related to her primary diagnoses and psychosocial stressors within the social environment with a stormy clinical course.

Residential Substance Use Treatment forward was medically necessary for this patient.

The continued residential services are medically necessary to address issues related to relapse with a focus on a relapse prevention plan and additional work on developing coping skills in a case that poses a high risk for relapse, to address co-morbid psychiatric disorders with clinically appropriate treatment of the co-occurring bipolar disorder and PTSD; to address the patient's lack of awareness of the seriousness of her illness with psycho-education and evidence-based psychosocial interventions; to address the social environment including use of multiple substances of use with severe psychosocial stressors; and, to work on coping skills that will be necessary for building an effective sober support system and continued recovery efforts while maintaining abstinence with peer-supported recovery groups. None of this therapeutic work could have been/can be safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in view of the multiple complicating factors in this case, such as the high risk for relapse, the treatment history with relapse, continued use of substances despite access to treatment, and the lack of a reasonable recovery environment that includes high-risk behaviors including use of dangerous combinations of substances (alcohol and benzodiazepines and cocaine), and, the patient's comorbid psychiatric conditions that serve to trigger her use of alcohol and drugs.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse.
Treatment: Inpatient Detoxification Admission.

The insurer denied: Inpatient Detoxification Admission.  The denial is upheld.

The patient is an adult male, who was admitted for detoxification services for alcohol use disorder. The patient was using alcohol on a continuous daily basis with up to five 24-ounce beers, and use of $20 worth of crack cocaine per month, as well as a few puffs of marijuana daily. He presented with minimal symptoms of withdrawal in the context of the alcohol use disorder with a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) scale score of 1/67. The patient has a history of multiple prior detoxification treatments with relapse. Onset of alcohol use was in early adulthood with escalation of use and progression of the disease, and subsequent use of cocaine. The patient had a remote history of co-occurring psychiatric disorder diagnosed as bipolar depression but no history of suicidal behavior and no recent hospitalization. The patient provided no history of withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens or severe alcohol or drug withdrawal symptoms. Mental Status Examination: There were no severe symptoms on mental status examination such as thought disorder, cognitive impairment, severe symptoms of a mood disturbance or mania, psychosis or perceptual disturbance, or suicidal ideation. The patient was motivated for substance use disorder treatment with fair insight indicating that his substance use was out of control and initially indicating his desire to proceed to rehabilitation treatment. The patient was admitted for inpatient detoxification. The patient's hospital course progressed without incident, and he had the opportunity to attend group sessions and receive counseling and education with planning for clinically appropriate aftercare. At the time of discharge, the patient declined transfer for rehabilitation services, indicating that he just wanted to go home and rest. He was discharged against medical advice. The issue under review is the inpatient admission with detoxification treatment and withdrawal management. The denial was based on New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria, indicating that inpatient level treatment was not medically necessary, as there were no biomedical or psychiatric concerns or complicated withdrawal in the case. The appeal was based on New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Guidelines, indicating that the detoxification was medically necessary.

The proposed treatment was not medically necessary for this patient.

The proposed inpatient stay and detoxification treatment and other medical services could have been safely and effectively provided at a lower level of care, as the denial determination asserts. The treatment of this patient's substance use disorder did not require the structure of an inpatient setting or 24-hour nursing monitoring. The patient displayed no serious disturbance of mental status despite having a history of bipolar depression and an ongoing substance use disorder with alcohol, cocaine, cannabis and tobacco. There were no severe/objective symptoms of withdrawal or biomedical issues in this case, and the patient had received detoxification and substance use disorder treatment in the past with knowledge of substance use disorder treatment protocols. Thus, the inpatient admission for detoxification treatment and the requested inpatient level services were not medically necessary.

summary:
Diagnosis: Alcohol abuse, bipolar disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder
Treatment: Residential level of care treatment to transition
The insurer denied coverage for residential level of care treatment to transition.
The denial is overturned.

This young adult female reportedly was admitted to this inpatient mental health residential treatment due to emotional dysregulation and dangerous behaviors, mood and behavioral symptoms, trauma related symptoms, attachment issues, and also had a history of alcohol use and vaping. She reportedly had impairments in functioning interpersonally and academically. This patient reportedly had diagnoses of bipolar disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)-complex, reactive attachment disorder, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). She reportedly also had low scores in cognition, academics, and emotional areas. She reportedly also had severe trauma including reportedly being drowned by her biological father. She reportedly was completely abandoned by her biological parents when she was a child. She reportedly was in group homes and eventually adopted by her current mother. It was reported that her adoptive parents divorced. The patient reportedly had multiple psychiatric hospitalizations and inpatient residential treatments and still had reports of emotional dysregulation, dangerous behavior including physical aggression, property destruction, severe agitation, poor impulse control, and eloping behaviors including eloping and aggression while in a 24-hour inpatient residential treatment setting. She reportedly was receiving group therapy, individual therapy, and family therapy, and had pharmacotherapy and was taking Sertraline, Buspirone, and Adderall. It was reported that she was stepped down from inpatient mental health residential treatment to a transitional inpatient setting which included supervised living.

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient mental health residential treatment as not medically necessary treatment. They stated that she was no longer at risk for serious harm needing 24-hour inpatient residential treatment. They recommended a less restrictive level of care.

The medical records provided did provide enough specific evidence to support that she required this level of care. This was a complex high-risk patient who had multiple psychiatric issues and diagnoses with a history of dangerous behavior including physical aggression, property destruction and throwing objects, violent tantrums, poor impulse control, suicidal thoughts, emotional dysregulation, poor behavioral control, eloping from home and even from inpatient mental health residential treatments. She also stole vaping pens to vape and did not want to stop alcohol or vaping use. She reportedly had attachment problems and severe trauma including being drowned by her father. She reportedly had mood swings and difficulty functioning. She had poor academic functioning. She reportedly had limitations in social functioning. She reportedly had poor coping skills and limited insight and impairments in functioning. She reportedly required long term inpatient 24-hour inpatient residential treatment to try to learn better coping skills, improve emotional regulation and behavioral control, improve communication skills and social skills, improve judgment and decision making, work on trauma issues, and improve interpersonal and academic functioning. 

She was not able to be safely treated at a less restrictive level of care. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be reversed. The health care plan did not act reasonably, with sound medical judgment, or in the best interest of the patient. The medical necessity for residential level of care treatment to transition is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse.
Treatment: Inpatient Admission.

The insurer denied coverage for an inpatient admission. The denial is overturned.

This patient was admitted to this inpatient hospital treatment for detoxification treatment. The patient reportedly had withdrawal symptoms, including tremors and anxiety/nervousness. The patient reportedly was drinking large amounts of alcohol, including 1-2 pints of liquor plus two 25-ounce cans of beer, using 10 bags of intranasal heroin, and taking up to 4 milligrams (mg) of Alprazolam per day. It was reported that the patient was unable to remain abstinent after multiple past inpatient detoxification treatments and inpatient rehabilitation treatments. The patient reportedly had a positive toxicology for opiates, fentanyl, methadone, and benzodiazepines. The patient reportedly was put on an Ativan detoxification protocol and given Ativan until the day of discharge. The plan was for the patient to go to an inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment after completing inpatient detoxification treatment, but the patient left against medical advice (AMA), stating that they had to take care of their daughter.

The insurer denied coverage for detoxification treatment in an inpatient hospital as not medically necessary treatment. They stated that he had no medical or mental health concerns that were unmanageable or unstable and required 24-hour per day nursing support. They recommended a less restrictive level then.

The reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for inpatient hospital treatment for detoxification treatment as the medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that he required this level of care. The patient did require 24-hour treatment as they could not safely and effectively be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive setting as they continued to use large amounts of alcohol, Alprazolam, and heroin daily and had a positive toxicology for opiates, fentanyl, methadone, and benzodiazepines despite multiple inpatient detoxification treatments and an inpatient rehabilitation treatment, and required and received detoxification medication including Ativan to prevent more severe, complicated, or life-threatening withdrawal symptoms. It was reported that the patient had Ativan 1.5 mg three times daily (TID) on the first two days of admission, Ativan 1 mg TID on day 3 of admission, and Ativan 1 mg on the day of discharge. The patient reportedly had past inpatient substance detoxification treatment on multiple occasions and had an inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment as well. Also, the risk of delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use, so the patient was considered at risk for severe, complicated, and life-threatening withdrawal, so they needed 24-hour hospital treatment. The patient also was at risk medically due to their use of multiple substances of use including heroin, Alprazolam, and alcohol. The patient did require 24-hour inpatient medical hospital treatment for alcohol detoxification, and it was considered unsafe for them to be treated for detoxification in a less restrictive level of care then. The patient was considered at high risk for relapse if not in this 24-hour inpatient hospital setting for detoxification treatment then and could not stop using on their own outside of a 24-hour inpatient hospital setting as they lacked coping skills, did not have community support and lacked structure and stability in life. The medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that the patient required inpatient hospital treatment for detoxification treatment. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be reversed. The health care plan did not act reasonably, with sound medical judgment, and in the patient's best interest. 

The medical necessity for 3 days of inpatient substance use detoxification is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, ovarian cancer, coronary heart disease, hypertension, and hyperlipemia

Treatment: social day care (SDC) services 2 days per week

The insurer denied coverage for social day care (SDC) services 2 days per week

The denial is overturned


This is an elderly female with diagnoses including depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, ovarian cancer, coronary heart disease, hypertension, and hyperlipemia. 

A Uniform Assessment (UAS-NY) was completed. It was reported that the patient participated in social activities of long-standing interest, visiting with long-standing social relations or family members, and other interaction which had occurred in the last 3 days. The patient was reported to have no decline in her level of participation in social, religious, occupational, or other preferred activities. She was noted alone for 1-2 hours during the day (morning and afternoon) and has no major life stressors in the last 90 days. 

A Person-Centered Service plan was completed. The documentation stated that the patient has informal support from her daughter and daughter-in-law. It was also stated that the patient received 52.50 hours per week of personal care assistance and 2 days per week of social day care. 

In an appeal letter the provider indicated that Social Day Care services provided an integral part of the patient's care plan before her cancer diagnosis. They reported that Social Day Care Services provided the patient with emotional support, companionship, and a sense of belonging. 

According to the New York State Department of Health (NYS DOH) Guidelines, Social Day Care (SDC) offers personal care, nutrition, recreational and social activities at a community-based center Social Day Care services cannot be substituted for personal care services the patient requires for physical needs. 

Per the cited references, social interactions with family, friends, peers, and community influences successful and healthy aging in the elderly population. 

It was reported that the patient has been receiving social day care services even before being diagnosed with cancer. It is essential for this patient to have social interaction especially with her peers. The services being provided by personal care assistance are limited to help or assistance with Activities of daily Living (ADLs) and Instrumental Activities of Daily Living (IADLs). The requested service can enhance the patient's physical and emotional welfare and improve her quality of life.

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be reversed. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. The medical necessity for social day care services is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major depressive disorder
Treatment: Additional 36 sessions of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) sessions beyond the completed 36 sessions
The insurer denied the additional 36 session of TMS sessions beyond the completed 36 sessions.
The denial is overturned.

The patient is an adult male with diagnosis of major depressive disorder. His provider is requesting an additional 36 sessions of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) sessions beyond the completed 36 sessions. The clinical documentation indicates the patient had experienced depression intermittently since his teen years but reported significant worsening of his symptoms over the past three to four years, which impacted his ability to maintain work, exercise, and socialize. The progress note dated 4 months ago reports the patient had completed 36 sessions of TMS the week prior and had found the treatment to be "a little helpful." He noted a slight improvement near the end of the course of treatment. He noted his mood had not greatly improved but attributed this to ongoing psychosocial stressors. He reported continued fatigue, hopelessness, and passive suicidal ideation, although he reported some improvement in this regard as well. Both pre-treatment and post-treatment HAM-D (Hamilton Depression Rating Scale) scores were recorded as 26. His current medications included bupropion XL (extended release) 300 mg (milligrams) daily, lamotrigine 50 mg daily, and venlafaxine ER (extended release) 225 mg daily. Previous medication trials included fluoxetine, mirtazapine, vortioxetine, lithium, Abilify, and Ritalin. He was noted to have completed treatment with IV (intravenous) ketamine, and IOP (intensive outpatient program) program, and was attending CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) on a weekly basis from 2021 to present. The plan was to continue treatment with TMS.

At issue is an additional 36 session of TMS sessions beyond the completed 36 sessions. Coverage was denied by the health plan due to lack of improvement in HAM-D score after 36 TMS treatments, noting that criteria for continuation of treatment requires documentation of a 50% (percent) improvement in symptoms, and as such there is no evidence to suggest that further TMS would be of significant benefit. The decision is being appealed by the treating provider, who states the patient meets the medical necessity requirements for extension of treatment with TMS due to his partial response as indicated by the improvement in his Beck Depressive Inventory score of 33 pre-treatment to 22 post-treatment. The provider states the positive response indicates that more treatments are clinically required for the patient to receive full benefit.

The requested additional 36 session of TMS sessions beyond the completed 36 sessions are medically necessary.

Review of the medical literature indicates that there is evidence to support the continuation of TMS in patients who have exhibited either a partial or late response to the treatment with regards to benefit from treatment and reduction of depressive symptoms. This includes the extension of treatment from 36 to 72 sessions. The literature also supports a strong correlation between clinical improvement and number of treatments with TMS. The definition of medical necessity generally includes that services must be in accordance with generally accepted standards of medical practice. Since continuation of treatment with TMS in this patient with a partial/late response to treatment fits this definition, it is medically necessary in this case.

summary:
Diagnosis: Autism
Treatment: 10 Hours of Direct 1:1 Applied Behavioral Analysis (ABA) Treatment 
The insurer denied 10 Hours of Direct 1:1 Applied Behavioral Analysis (ABA) Treatment 
The health plan's determination is upheld. 

The patient is a young boy who was diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder. He has been receiving applied behavioral analysis (ABA). An undated letter by his behavior analyst describes that the patient has poor articulation and inappropriate vocal volume. He has limited naming skills. He lacks social skills. He is noted not to have any maladaptive behaviors that warrant a behavioral intervention plan in his ABA therapy.

10 Hours of Direct 1:1 Applied Behavioral Analysis (ABA) Treatment are not medically necessary for this patient. It is unlikely that the additional hours requested would improve the patient's outcome. He is not noted to have any maladaptive behaviors that indicate a need for a behavioral intervention plan. There are conflicting opinions in the medical literature regarding whether the intensity (number of hours per week) of ABA therapy is related to long-term outcome. Smith et al. [1] compared young children with pervasive developmental disorder who were randomly assigned to intensive treatment or parent training. The authors found that the intensive treatment group outperformed the parent training group on measures of intelligence, visual-spatial skills, language, and academics, though not adaptive functioning or behavior problems. Reed et al. [2] evaluated "the effectiveness of home-based early behavioral interventions for children (2:6-4:0 years old) with autistic spectrum disorders was studied over 9-10 months. Measures of autistic severity, intellectual, educational, and adaptive behavioral functioning were taken. The authors found that "high-intensity behavioral approaches (mean 30 hours/week) produced greater gains than low-intensity programs (mean 12 h/week)", but also noted that "within the high-intensity groups, increased temporal input on the program was not associated with increased gains in the children." Linstead et al [3] investigated the relationship between treatment intensity and treatment outcomes. The authors followed 726 children, ages 1.5 to 12 years old, receiving community-based behavioral intervention services. They found that results indicated a strong relationship between treatment intensity and mastery of learning objectives, where higher treatment intensity predicted greater progress.

The patient is an adult homeless and unemployed male. He was admitted to acute inpatient level services for detoxification and withdrawal management of severe alcohol and stimulant (crack cocaine) use disorders. The patient was using up to one and one-half pints of liquor together with $100 worth of crack cocaine daily. He denied the use of benzodiazepines despite a positive drug screen. He was tobacco dependent at one-and-one-half pack per day for 30+ years. His substance use began at age 14 with escalating use and progression of the disease with a chronic relapsing course despite multiple detoxification treatment episodes and at least two limited rehabilitation treatment episodes in the recent past with immediate relapse. The patient presented with moderate alcohol withdrawal at the time of admission. Withdrawal symptoms included tremors, sweats, nausea, insomnia, anxiety, headache, and agitation with a CIWA (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment) scale score of 8. He denied psychiatric hospitalization or suicidal or self-harming behavior. He had a history of substance-related treatment episodes as noted. There were no acute medical issues or general medical concerns. The patient was admitted to acute inpatient-level care and placed on a detoxification regimen with a Librium taper, vitamin replacement therapy, fluid replacement, and medical monitoring. Following his first day of treatment, the patient began to participate in counseling and educational sessions. He was maintained on fall and seizure 
precautions but had no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens (complicated withdrawal). His demeanor improved as he underwent detoxification treatment, and he was social with peers and moderately motivated to participate. The patient was discharged on day #5 after completion of the detoxification protocol with plans/referral to start rehabilitation treatment. The health plan denied coverage of the stay based on LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) Guidelines indicating that treatment could be safely provided with lower-level care. The appeal was based on New York State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) 3.0 Criteria and 
the presenting clinical features, including use of multiple substances of abuse, withdrawal symptoms with a CIWA (clinical institute withdrawal assessment) of 8, and a lack of coping skills, as well as history of a chronic relapsing course of the substance-related illnesses.

The Inpatient Detoxification Admission was medically necessary.

The inpatient services detoxification treatment and withdrawal management for severe alcohol and other substance use disorders, and other services noted in the clinical summary, could not have been safely and effectively provided at a lower level of care. Withdrawal symptoms were managed

substances of abuse if detoxification and treatment were to have been attempted at a lower level of care.

The patient is an adult female who was admitted for detoxification services for alcohol and stimulant (crack cocaine) use disorders. The patient was using alcohol three to six times per week with up to one pint of liquor and one 40-ounce beer, and use of $10 worth of crack cocaine three to six times per week. She presented with mild symptoms of withdrawal in the context of the alcohol use disorder with a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) scale score of 2/67 with tremor and anxiety. The patient has a history of multiple prior detoxification treatments with relapse. Onset of alcohol use was at age 12 years with escalation of use and progression of the disease, and subsequent use of cocaine in her twenties. The patient had a history of a co-occurring psychiatric disorder diagnosed with bipolar disorder, but no history of suicidal behavior or psychiatric hospitalization. The patient was admitted for inpatient detoxification with a 5 day Librium protocol and vitamin replacement therapy. The patient's hospital course progressed without incident, and she had the opportunity to attend group sessions and receive counseling and education with planning for clinically appropriate aftercare. She did not complete the detoxification treatment and was discharged against medical advice on day #4. She engaged in treatment and tolerated the Librium taper. She was noted to be sleeping and eating okay with no biomedical complications during her stay. At the time of discharge, the patient declined referral for rehabilitation services. The denial of services was based on the New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria indicating that inpatient level treatment was not medically necessary as there were no biomedical or psychiatric concerns or complicated withdrawal in the case warranting 24-hour nursing support. Residential level care was suggested as clinically appropriate. The appeal was based on New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Guidelines and Criteria indicating that the detoxification was medically necessary and that the patient had a lack of coping skills and needed stability and structured treatment setting.

Inpatient Admission for Detoxification Services was not medically necessary. 

The proposed inpatient stay and detoxification treatment and other medical services could have been safely and effectively provided at a lower level of care. The treatment of this patient's substance use disorder did not require the structure of an inpatient setting or 24-hour monitoring. The patient displayed no serious disturbance of mental status despite having a history of bipolar disorder together with ongoing substance use disorder with alcohol, cocaine, and tobacco. Moreover, the patient did not show evidence for suicidal or aggressive behavior or risk, or severe cognitive impairment, or psychosis, or perceptual disturbance that would have warranted an inpatient level admission and treatment. There were no severe/objective symptoms of withdrawal or biomedical issues in this case, and the patient had received detoxification and substance use disorder treatment in the past with knowledge of substance use disorder treatment protocols. The patient had fair insight and reasonable motivation and was in no apparent distress throughout the inpatient stay. Thus, the inpatient admission for detoxification treatment and the requested inpatient level services were not medically necessary in this case scenario. summary:
Diagnosis:	Head injury	
Treatment: 	Psychological testing
The insurer denied psychological testing
The denial is upheld 

This patient had a concussion last year while rock climbing and was in treatment with this provider since. It was reported that he had headache, vestibular dysfunction, oculomotor dysfunction, emotional distress, severe anxiety, moderate depression, and sleeping problems. The provider requested neuropsychological testing due to his concussive symptoms and head injury. It was reported he had complex recovery after a previous head injury as well. He also reportedly had a clinically significant change in symptoms including dizziness.
 
The insurer denied coverage for neuropsychological testing for codes 96132, 96138, and 9616 stating that the required testing covered was not considered medically necessary treatment. They stated that the required test is covered for the evaluation of mild traumatic brain injury, concussion, or post concussive syndrome in which there is significant functional impairment that has not improved after 3-6 months of standard care. 
  
The American Academy of Clinical Neuropsychology (AACN) Practice Guidelines for Neuropsychological Assessment and Consultation reports that neuropsychological evaluations vary in content depending on their purpose, but they typically assess multiple neurocognitive and emotional functions. Primary cognitive domains tested include intellectual functions; academic skills, receptive and expressive language skills, simple and complex attention; learning and memory, visuospatial abilities, executive functions, problem solving and reasoning abilities, and sensorimotor skills. 

Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) can contribute to cognitive and psychiatric symptoms, and neuropsychological testing can assist in determining if current symptoms are more a result of TBI versus other psychiatric disorders. In this case there was not specific documentation supporting why neuropsychological testing was considered medically necessary as the patient had reported improvement after 5 weeks post injury and no longer had acute or significant neurological or medical or cognitive symptoms significantly impairing his functioning for 3-6 months after injury. He had reported improvement in symptoms and functioning 5 weeks post injury and required no further follow up.  It was reported that the doctor saw the patient several times. The insurer's criteria require that one must have significant impairment in functioning that has not improved after 3-6 months of standard care. The notes reported that 5 weeks post injury his symptoms were resolving and were near resolution. It also was reported that according to the neurocognitive data and symptoms reported from the VOMS (Vestibular Ocular Motor Services) that the results were entirely within normal limits. It was reported that he was able to engage in physical activities including dancing, running, and weight training without any provocation of symptoms. It was also reported that he returned to normal physical activity and work, as well as normal life activities with no reported difficulties. It was reported that the patient was discharged from care at this time and not required to follow up now unless needed. 
This presentation did not support the medical necessity for neuropsychological. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be upheld. The health care plan did act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. The medical necessity for neuropsychological testing (codes 96132, 96138, and 96116) rendered is not substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse

Treatment: Medically Supervised Inpatient Detoxification

The insurer denied coverage for Medically Supervised Inpatient Detoxification

The denial is overturned

This patient reportedly was admitted to this inpatient hospital for alcohol detoxification treatment. The patient reportedly had alcohol withdrawal symptoms including nausea, tremors, sweats, anxiety, irritable mood, sleeping problems, and had a Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) score of 10. The patient reportedly was drinking 2 pints of liquor per day and started use when a teenager with last use the day of admission. The patient also reportedly was smoking 3 grams of cocaine daily with first use at a young age and last use one day prior to admission. The patient had a positive toxicology for cocaine. The patient reportedly was abstinent for 8 years until the death of their mother several years ago. The patient reportedly had 3 past inpatient rehabilitation/long term facility treatments. The patient reportedly was started on a Librium protocol for detoxification treatment. The patient reportedly took Librium 15 milligrams (mg) 3 times per day, then 15 mg twice per day, then 10 mg twice per day, and then 10 mg once per day. The patient reportedly was discharged to inpatient substance/alcohol rehabilitation level of care. 

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient substance detoxification treatment for medically supervised inpatient detoxification as not medically necessary treatment then. They stated that he did not require inpatient hospital treatment then, and they recommended a less restrictive level of care then.

The patient reportedly could not maintain abstinence as the patient reportedly was drinking large amounts of alcohol daily and was at increased the patient's risk of more severe withdrawal symptoms and medical issues as the patient also reportedly was using cocaine daily with alcohol. The patient also likely would not have been able to maintain abstinence without being in a 24 hour inpatient hospital setting as evidenced by the patient's lack of sustained abstinence despite 3 past inpatient substance rehabilitation treatments. The risk of delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use so the patient was considered at risk for this. The patient reportedly lacked coping skills and stability and structure in their life to maintain abstinence without treatment in a 24 hour treatment setting. It was reported that the patient had sought rehabilitation treatment for alcohol but required detoxification treatment first. This patient was at risk medically for worsened withdrawal, complicated, or life threatening withdrawal and required inpatient alcohol detoxification treatment. As a result, the recommendation is to reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for inpatient hospital treatment. It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably, with sound clinical judgment, or in the best interests of the patient then.

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be reversed. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. 

The medical necessity for Medically Supervised Inpatient Detoxification is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Autism
treatment: Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) with Additional Provider
The insurer denied Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) with Additional Provider
The health plan's determination is upheld.

The patient is a young boy who was diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder. He was noted to have deficits in social - emotional reciprocity, social communication and cognitive skills, together with restrictive, repetitive patterns of behavior and sensory processing deficits.

Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) with Additional Provider is not medically necessary for this patient.
The patient is already receiving ABA therapy from another provider. Additional ABA therapy is duplicative and not medically necessary.

In the most recent American Academy of Paediatrics Guidelines on the Identification, Evaluation, and Management of Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), Hyman et al [1] describe that:
"Most evidence-based treatment models are based on principles of ABA. ABA has been defined as "the process of systematically applying interventions based upon the principles of learning theory to improve socially significant behaviors to a meaningful degree, and to demonstrate that the interventions employed are responsible for the improvement in behavior." The use of ABA methods to treat symptoms of ASD suggests that behaviors exhibited can be altered by programmatically reinforcing skills related to communication and other skill acquisition. Thus, ABA treatments may target development of new skills (eg, social engagement) and/or minimize behaviors (eg, aggression) that may interfere with a child's progress."
An extensive body of scientific literature has accrued over the past forty years demonstrating the success of ABA- based interventions to decrease problem behavior and increase skills in adults and children with intellectual disabilities and autism. Several meta-analyses indicate that comprehensive ABA intervention leads to medium to large effects in terms of intellectual functioning, acquisition of daily living skills, social functioning and language development in children with autism [2,3].

The reviewer was unable to find peer-reviewed literature reporting outcomes of children receiving simultaneous ABA therapy from two providers using different therapeutic approaches.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Inpatient Substance Use Detoxification 
Admission
The insurer denied: Inpatient Substance Use Detoxification 
Admission
The denial is overturned.

The patient is an adult male who presented requesting detoxification treatment. He was medically screened and admitted to an acute inpatient level of care to address substance use disorder with opioid, alcohol, cocaine, and nicotine class substance use disorders. The patient had been using heroin with up to two bags daily with snorting and one six pack of 12-ounce beers on a daily continuous basis, as well as the use of $100 worth of crack cocaine daily with tobacco dependence at one pack per day for 30 years. He started using alcohol at an early age, and subsequently used opioid and cocaine class substances in early adulthood. He has no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens but has a history of moderately severe withdrawal symptoms and at least four prior accidental overdoses. He had a history of multiple prior detoxification and substance use disorder treatments with relapses and no sustained sobriety. Additionally, he was participating in a methadone program at 37mg (milligrams) per day. The patient had a history of psychiatric disorder best characterized as bipolar depression and unspecified anxiety disorder, and a remote history of psychiatric hospitalization. However, there 
was no history of suicidal behavior for the patient, and he was not taking psychotropic medications other than low-dose Seroquel. Laboratory assessments were unremarkable. A drug screen was positive for cocaine, opiates, fentanyl, and methadone, which were consistent with the patient's history. The patient was admitted to detoxification treatment with a comprehensive detoxification protocol, which included treatment with Librium, and the continued use of Methadone. The program provided for case management with 
referral and access to rehabilitation treatment. 

The requested health service of Inpatient Substance Use Detoxification Admission is considered medically necessary.

The patient in this case was using opioid, cocaine, and alcohol class substances on a daily continuous basis that did warrant an inpatient level of detoxification and withdrawal management, and monitoring for the duration of the protocol. Detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments pertinent to the detoxification treatment episode could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care. Moreover, there was psychiatric comorbidity and history of accidental overdoses and continued use of heroin in the context of Methadone treatment that warranted inpatient level treatment as indicated in the appeal. Thus, the need for detoxification treatment and withdrawal management of this patient's substance use disorder did warrant the requested admission, and the continued structure of an inpatient level detoxification setting with 24-hour monitoring and the use of prn (as needed) medications, indicated treatment with Methadone, and an alcohol withdrawal protocol with Librium and vitamin replacement therapy. The patient's history of substance abuse (frequency 
and quantity) together with functional impairments reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder and the need for a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management, as the patient was at high risk for treatment failure. Therefore, medical necessity is met in this case, as it is consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published societal guidelines, ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) Criteria, the scientific literature, and New York State instruction for medical necessity reviews including the appropriate application of the NY State OASAS (Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) Tool that requires the patient in this scenario to default to the higher level of care.

Treatment: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS).
The insurer denied: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS).
The denial is overturned.

The patient is a teenage adolescent male. He has a history of major depressive disorder, recurrent and severe without psychotic features. The PHQ-9 (patient health questionnaire) scale score up to 20-21 reflects severe symptoms of depression. The patient has a documented history of multiple medication treatments for depression, including treatment with two disparate classes of medication including SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) (Zoloft, Prozac, Lexapro), SNRIs (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors) (Cymbalta, Pristiq), Remeron, and Wellbutrin, as well as augmentation with Abilify, Vraylar, Buspirone, and supplemental use of propranolol and vitamin D. Due to adverse effects or lack of efficacy, the patient continued to experience severe symptoms of depression and functional impairments that impacted quality of life and day-to-day activities, including a hospitalization following a suicide attempt by overdose 3 years ago. Additionally, the patient has had treatment with an evidence-based psychotherapy 
(cognitive behavioral therapy) combined with antidepressant medication together with supportive measures. The patient was referred and recommended for repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) therapy, together with continued medication treatment and psychotherapy with current use of Seroquel XR (extended release) and Lamictal. The patient has reportedly had psychiatric hospitalizations and suicide attempts or suicidal behavior reflecting the severity of the depressive disorder. There is co-morbid generalized 
anxiety disorder with a GAD (generalized anxiety disorder) 7 scale score of 17, and no other psychiatric disorders and no diagnosed co-occurring substance use disorder in this case. The patient has no acute general medical issues that would impact TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy. The patient's mental status examination at the time of referral showed depressed mood, sad affect with anxiety, and anhedonia. He has loss of interest and low energy with fatigue and other neuro-vegetative disturbances related to depression as scored with the PHQ-9 (patient health questionnaire) and evidence for mood instability and poor control of impulses together with anxiety, nervousness, tension, irritability and excessive worry. The patient's clinician recommended treatment with a course of repetitive transcranial magnetic 
stimulation (rTMS) therapy with up to 39 treatment episodes. The recommendation is in the context of the treatment refractory depression without sustained benefit from treatment as usual and without a remission.

The requested TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy is medically necessary for this patient.

In this case, at least two alternative therapeutic trials with augmentation together with other therapeutic measures have been provided, including psychotherapy with CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy). Thus, in this case, the proposed TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) 
therapy is considered clinically appropriate and medically necessary in keeping with prevailing standards of medical practice. Additionally, the proposed TMS (repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy is reasonable, and in the best interest of the patient. The patient in this case has demonstrated that his depressive disorder is treatment refractory or resistant. This answer is consistent with the scientific literature pertaining to TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy for major depressive disorder, referenced below, and with the growing 
literature on the effective use of TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy for depression in adolescent patients.

The patient is an adult male admitted  for acute inpatient psychiatric treatment with a diagnosis of bipolar mood disorder, manic phase. The patient was brought to the emergency department with shortness of breath and an exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). He was seen by psychiatry who determined that he was manic in the context of stopping all psychotropic medications with worsening symptoms of the mood disorder. Additionally, he was not sleeping and had become out of control losing his job and housing. He had a history of psychiatric hospitalization and suicidal behavior.

There was substance use disorders with psychedelic mushrooms and psilocybin as drugs of choice with intermittent use of methamphetamine, alcohol, and marijuana. His drug screen was positive for tetrahydrocannabinol (THC).

The patient was medically screened prior to admission for acute inpatient mental health treatment. He was restarted on Symbicort with an albuterol rescue inhaler.
The patient was admitted to inpatient level services with close observation, a structured milieu with programming, and pharmacotherapy with antipsychotic and mood stabilizing medications that initially included risperidone with a change to Seroquel together with Depakote, titrated as clinically appropriate. He remained expansive with labile affect, grandiose, and intrusive requiring ongoing redirection while medications were adjusted. Sleep remained disturbed with apprehension, anxiety, nervousness, and tension. His mental status examination remained essentially unchanged, but improved with medication adherence and cooperation with staff direction.

During the latter part of this time frame, the patient began to show sustained improvement with diminished levels of anxiety and lower risk for impulsivity and mood swings; however, he continued to display poor self-control with safety concerns due to residual mania and he required frequent re-direction. Tthe patient stabilized to the point that he could return to the home of a friend. At issue is the medical necessity of Acute Inpatient Mental Health Level of Care.

The requested health service/treatment of Inpatient Mental Health Treatment was medically necessary for this patient.

The patient's treatment could not have been safely or effectively provided with lower-level care during the time interval under review. The patient's severity of symptoms and need for safety monitoring, while receiving active treatment, did warrant the continued structure of an acute inpatient setting and 24-hour monitoring in a safe environment through discharge. The discharge planning with the development of a safety plan and plans for continued treatment in the community, as well as additional management of the severe mood disorder, were warranted.

The continued inpatient services served to provide intensive treatment in a patient with high risk for relapse/recidivism, and severe symptoms of bipolar disorder including persistent features of mania with poor insight and control of impulses, and risk for medication non-adherence. Thus, the continued acute inpatient level care was necessary to continue a safe and clinically appropriate treatment with the appropriate structure and monitoring of an inpatient setting and further efforts to address remaining psychosocial stressors including housing and appropriate aftercare that could result in medication non-adherence and relapse. Only by the date of discharge did the patient exhibit calm demeanor without evidence for symptoms that were out of control or with clear thinking that would support a discharge to the community with a clear discharge plan.

The patient is an adult male with a history of a mood disorder best characterized as bipolar disorder with the most recent episode, major depressive disorder, severe and recurrent without psychotic features. The patient has a documented history of multiple antidepressant medication treatments including treatment with Zoloft, Prozac, Paxil, and Wellbutrin prescribed together with Lithium and risperidone without sustained benefit or remission. Due to adverse effects, or lack of efficacy or sustained benefit, the patient has continued to experience severe symptoms of depression and functional impairments scoring as much as 24 on the Personal Health Questionnaire (PHQ)-9 in the severe range of depression. Additionally, the patient has had treatment with an evidence-based psychotherapy (CBT) combined with medication without sustained benefit or a remission of symptoms.
The patient's clinician has recommended transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to address the major depressive disorder. The recommendation is in the context of the episode of major depression that is treatment-resistant/refractory.
At issue is the medical necessity of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS).
 

The requested health service/treatment of Therapeutic Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) is medically necessary for this patient.
TMS therapy as a primary or adjunctive therapy for treatment of depression has generally been evaluated in patients who have treatment refractory/resistant depression, as defined by one or more, antidepressant medication treatment failures with or without augmentation. TMS therapy for depressive disorder has been established by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as a safe treatment; and, the data, as reflected in peer reviewed medical literature, supports this assertion. Specifically, when treatments with antidepressant medication with or without augmentation, or with electroconvulsive therapy, and/or psychotherapy, especially cognitive behavioral therapy, have failed to produce a response or remission, then TMS is an appropriate consideration. This assertion is noted in the American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorder, referenced below. The scientific literature indicates that a course of treatment with TMS therapy is reasonable in cases of treatment resistant depression as defined in the scientific literature.
In this case, at least two or more alternative therapeutic trials with augmentation together with other therapeutic measures have been provided, and the proposed treatment with TMS therapy is considered clinically appropriate and medically necessary. Additionally, the use of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) therapy is reasonable, and in the best interest of the patient. The decision to proceed with TMS therapy reflects sound medical judgment based upon the current scientific literature and American Psychiatric Association practice guidelines concerning the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorder. The patient in this case has demonstrated that his depressive disorder is treatment refractory or resistant, and the proposed treatment of severe major depressive disorder using TMS therapy with a clinically appropriate number of sessions is warranted in this case scenario, and is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice. The scientific literature does support the use of TMS therapy in patient with both unipolar and bipolar depression consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice for the condition diagnosed in this case including treatment resistant depression.

Diagnosis: 	anxiety, depression, obsessive compulsive disorder
Treatment: partial hospitalization program
