This patient was admitted due to obsessive compulsive symptoms, depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, and behavioral symptoms. He reportedly had depressed, irritable, and anxious mood, behavioral symptoms including hitting others and throwing items, intrusive sexual thoughts and compulsive repetitive behaviors, oppositional behavior, fire setting, agitation, yelling and screaming, and suicidal thoughts. He reportedly had multiple past inpatient hospitalizations for eating disorder symptoms and suicidal thoughts and depression. He reportedly had diagnoses of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder, Major Depressive Disorder, Generalized Anxiety Disorder, attention deficit disorder (ADHD), and a history of a diagnosis of Anorexia Nervosa. He reportedly had past intensive outpatient program (IOP), partial hospital program (PHP), and residential treatment in addition to past hospitalizations. He reportedly was taking Sertraline, Clonidine, and Memantine. He reportedly was attending group, individual, and family therapy. He reportedly was also utilizing exposure response prevention cognitive behavior therapy (CBT). 
 
The insurer denied coverage for behavioral health partial hospital program treatment as not medically necessary treatment. They stated that he was making progress, no longer had thoughts to harm self, had not recently demonstrated actions that could not be managed in a less restrictive level of care, and that he was able to meet functional needs. They recommended a less restrictive level of care.
 
The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Obsessive Compulsive Disorders (OCD) reports that the least restrictive level of treatment for safe and effective treatment is appropriate and that longer durations of treatment are often necessary to treat obsessive compulsive disorder as this is a difficult disorder to treat. This was the case with this patient. In this case this patient required at least this level of care as the patient had continued reports of psychiatric symptoms interfering with his functioning. The InterQual Behavioral Health Psychiatry Partial Hospitalization medical necessity criteria reports that patients with functional impairment and significant psychiatric symptoms including behavioral, mood, psychotic symptoms, eating disorder symptoms, or if treatment is not expected to be safe in a less restrictive level of care, then one meets criteria for partial hospital program level of care. It also states that criteria are met if symptoms are improving and expected to improve but the patient is not clinically stable yet for a less restrictive level of care, or if symptoms are worsening then, one meets criteria and also if there is substantial evidence that the patient is a potential danger to self or others. 

In this case it was reported that he was oppositional and ignoring staff prompts, threw a hanger at a peer, threw and spilled food, called another student autistic and used explicit language, had intrusive thoughts, walked off the trail, was stuck in an OCD ritual and stopped multiple times in the trail, was suicidal, was disruptive and refused to do homework, reported that he was curled in a ball on the floor and had difficulty rejoining the group, was stuck in a ritual, screamed, and expressed frustration, he refused to come out of his room to take medications, he had intrusive thoughts, and his OCD symptoms were worse and significantly interfering with functioning. It was reported that his parents felt hopeless in helping him and the patient struggled to engage. He struggled with blurting, twitching, fidgeting, was quite disorganized, and made inappropriate remarks, caused himself to vomit after eating, he was unable to complete daily responsibilities due to being stuck in his room, and he used explicit language and was disrespectful, he was screaming and using inappropriate language despite staff prompts and redirection, and he was hitting other students, and struggling with rituals and repetitive behavior, he was throwing food,  continued to struggle and had suicidal thoughts, aggression, self-induced vomiting, intrusive thoughts and compulsive rituals and behavior, and continued to struggle during the denial period. He continued with intrusive sexual thoughts and compulsive behavior and although he was making some progress, he required more time in this treatment setting to improve further in order to decrease symptoms and improve functioning. He reportedly had multiple past hospitalizations.

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be reversed. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. The medical necessity for a partial hospital behavioral health level of care is substantiated.

The insurer denied Outpatient Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) 
the health plan's determination is overturned in part. 

The patient is a boy who was diagnosed as having mild autism spectrum disorder when he was younger. A more recent report by his applied behavioral analysis (ABA) analyst states that he is in the Severe range of autism spectrum disorder for communication, socialization and maladaptive behaviors. An evaluation by hiss pediatrician indicated that the patient had a Full Scale intelligence quotient (IQ) of 91 on the Wechsler Preschool & Primary Scale of Intelligence Fourth Edition (WPPSI-4). On the Vineland 3, his Adaptive Behavior Composite was on the 4th percentile. He scored on the 3rd percentile on the Communication domain, the 8th percentile on Daily Living Skills, and 5th percentile on the Socialization domain.

The requested 20 hours per week of direct 1:1 Outpatient Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) Therapy Care is not medically necessary for this patient. However, the patient should continue to receive 8 hours per week of direct 1:1 ABA therapy, together with 1 hour of assessment, 1 hour of supervision and 1 hour of parent training per week for the next 6 months, with re-evaluation at the end of that time. This is medically necessary as the abrupt cessation of ABA therapy is contrary to recommended good clinical practice, as explained by the Council of Autism Service Providers [1] which states:
"Discharge and transition planning from all treatment programs should generally involve a gradual step down in services. Discharge from a Comprehensive ABA treatment program often requires six months or longer. For example, a client in a Comprehensive treatment program might step down to a Focused treatment model to address a few remaining goals prior to transitioning out of treatment."

The requested 20 hours per week of direct 1:1 ABA therapy appears excessive and probably counterproductive, given that the patient attends school for 5 hours per day, with a commute of at least 1 hour per day. There is a discrepancy between the assessment of his level of autism spectrum disorder. The provider reported that the patient was in the Severe range for Communication, Socialization and Maladaptive Behaviors, while a formal assessment by the psychologist performed when the patient was 2 years 9 months old diagnosed him as having mild autism spectrum disorder. He has been making somewhat slow but steady progress with ABA therapy, which he has been receiving since 2021. He continues to have maladaptive behaviors which need to be addressed. These include hitting, kicking, elopement, ripping paper and screaming when he has sensory overload, or when he is asked to do non-desired activities.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder.

Treatment: Inpatient admission.

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient admission.

The denial is overturned.
 

This patient reportedly was admitted to this inpatient hospital due to worsened depressive and anxiety symptoms including depressed mood, suicidal thoughts with plans to commit suicide by jumping into a river or cutting his artery with a knife. He had 2 recent suicide attempts by hanging with a rope, and he had feelings of worthlessness, hopelessness, low energy, sleeping problems, concentration problems, and feelings of being a failure. He also reportedly had homicidal ideation towards his daughter who reportedly had homicidal thoughts towards him and his wife. It also was reported that there was significant stress with his daughter and that she also threatened suicide and 911 had been called as well. He reportedly had severe anxiety and panic attacks as well.

He reportedly had diagnoses of Major Depressive Disorder, Generalized Anxiety Disorder, and Panic Disorder. He also reportedly had a past hospitalization and had past medication trials of Sertraline and Fluoxetine. He reportedly had Mirtazapine and Olanzapine discontinued and was started on Escitalopram 5 mg per day which was titrated eventually to 20 mg per day. He reportedly had side effects including headache, chest pain, excessive sweating, and severe anxiety which eventually subsided. He reportedly had poor functioning as he reportedly could not work and struggled with activities of daily living including driving, grocery shopping, and meal preparation. He reportedly was applying for disability due to his inability to work due to severe anxiety and suicidal ideation when under severe stress. He reportedly was discharged.

The reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for continued inpatient hospital treatment. The medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that he required this level of care, as he was considered a high-risk patient with difficulty functioning. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Suicidal Behaviors reports that patients with suicide attempts are at high risk of suicide and also that hopelessness increases the risk of suicide. The Milliman Care Guidelines (MCG) Behavioral Health Inpatient Level of Care Adult criteria reports that a patient needs to present as an imminent danger to self, imminent danger to others, with severe psychiatric or behavioral symptoms, have a severely dysfunctional living including inability to care for self, unwillingness to participate voluntarily, or a less restrictive level of care is not feasible meet criteria for inpatient behavioral health level of care. 

This patient reportedly was not considered ready yet for discharge. As a result, the recommendation is to reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for continued inpatient psychiatric hospital treatment. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be reversed. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. 

The medical necessity for the continued inpatient mental health stay is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance abuse
Treatment: Inpatient substance use rehabilitation
The insurer denied the inpatient substance use rehabilitation.
The determination is upheld.

The patient is an adult male who was admitted to inpatient rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment of stimulant (cocaine), alcohol, and nicotine use disorders. There was no history of withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens, or blackouts. 

There was a report of co-occurring psychiatric disorders in this case including unspecified trauma and stressor related disorder and depression/anxiety with reports of psychiatric hospitalizations.

The mental status examination revealed a cooperative male with clear speech and linear thought processing that was goal directed. His mood was anxious with congruent affect. 
The inpatient level substance-related rehabilitation treatment included the opportunity to participate in groups, individual counseling, educational sessions, and recovery groups with peer support. From the time of admission forward, the patient easily engaged in rehabilitation treatment. He actively participated in individual, group, and educational sessions. He was prescribed vitamins with the availability of nicotine replacement therapy throughout his stay, as well as comfort medications and consideration of medication assisted treatment. He was prescribed Benadryl for insomnia.

Discharge planning occurred that included a recommendation for continued aftercare with consideration of transition to sober living upon completion of the program. 

At issue is the medical necessity of inpatient substance-related disorder rehabilitation services.

The requested health service/treatment of substance abuse inpatient rehabilitation level of care was not medically necessary for this patient.

The inpatient substance use disorder rehabilitation services in this case scenario were amenable to treatment at a lower level of care, as noted above. The patient was motivated and was capable of effectively receiving substance use disorder treatment in a less restrictive treatment setting with clinically appropriate structure, monitoring, and sober supports. The patient did not need the structure of an inpatient setting to effectively participate in rehabilitation substance abuse treatment.

There were no biomedical or psychiatric complications, or severe psychiatric symptoms/disorders in this case that would have warranted the admission and the continued inpatient level services and treatment. Thus, the requested inpatient substance use disorder rehabilitation services was not medically necessary for this patient.

This answer is consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and the published guidelines and the scientific literature, referenced below, with the application of New York (NY) State OASAS LOCADTR 3.0 Criteria, referenced below.

summary:
Diagnosis: Autism Spectrum Disorder.

Treatment: Residential treatment center level of care.

The insurer denied coverage for residential treatment center level of care.

The denial is overturned.
This teenager reportedly was admitted to this mental health residential treatment due to behavioral symptoms including physical aggression, property destruction, poor impulse control, inability to control anger, refusing to attend school, emotional dysregulation, isolating self, anxiety, and social delays including difficulty understanding social skills which made it difficult to make friends, and had hyperfixation. He reportedly had diagnoses of Major Depressive Disorder, Generalized Anxiety Disorder, Unspecified Disruptive, Impulse Control, and Conduct Disorder, and autism spectrum disorder (ASD). He reportedly had numerous trials of psychotropic medications and was in outpatient mental health treatment and his parent could not maintain his safety or control him from harming others in the house, so he was admitted to this inpatient residential treatment. He reportedly had aggressive behavior and self-injurious behavior in this treatment setting. 

The insurer denied coverage for continued inpatient mental health residential treatment as not medically necessary treatment then. They stated that after initial treatment the patient was no longer considered a risk of harm to self or others then. They recommended a less restrictive level of care then.

This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for continued inpatient mental health residential treatment as the medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that he required this level of care then. The Milliman Care Guidelines (MCG) Residential - Behavioral Health Level of Care - Child adolescent guidelines report that one needs to have danger to self or others, moderately or severe psychiatric or behavioral symptoms requiring 24-hour daily treatment, or serious dysfunction in daily living. In this case this patient continued to have moderate psychiatric symptoms and did not have the reported support system or ability to live in his parent's house as it was reported that they could not keep him or others safe due to his behaviors and their lack of structure. This patient had reports of physical aggression prior to admission and even had reports of physical aggression and self-injurious behavior while in this supervised and structured residential treatment. It was reported that he had self-injurious behavior by using a tree branch and also had property destruction. The patient had functional impairment, and his parents had an inability to create a safe environment for effective treatment at home then. He required 24-hour inpatient therapeutic structured and supervised residential treatment level of care during the denial period.  If not in a 24-hour inpatient supervised and structured therapeutic 24-hour inpatient residential setting during the denial period, the patient likely would not be able to learn the necessary skills to improve coping skills, decision making, emotional control, decrease impulsivity, decrease maladaptive aggressive and self-injurious behavior, and better regulate emotions. He likely would have had worsened symptoms and functioning and had increased risk of harm to self and others. As a result, the recommendation is to reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for continued mental health residential treatment. It did not appear that the insurer acted with good clinical judgment, reasonably, or in the best interests of the patient then.

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be reversed. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. 

The medical necessity for residential treatment center level of care is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse.
Treatment: Inpatient Substance Use Detoxification Admission.
The Insurer denied: Inpatient Substance Use Detoxification Admission.
The Denial is: Upheld.

The patient is an adult female. She was admitted for detoxification services for alcohol and stimulant (crack cocaine) use disorders. The patient was using alcohol 
three to six times per week with up to one pint of liquor and one 40-ounce beer and using $ (dollar) 50 worth of crack cocaine three to six times per week. She presented with mild symptoms of withdrawal in the context of the alcohol use disorder with a CIWA (clinical institute withdrawal assessment) scale score of 2/67, with tremor and anxiety. The patient has a history of multiple prior detoxification treatments with relapses. Her onset of alcohol use was at an adolescence, with escalation of use and progression of the disease, and subsequent use of cocaine in her twenties.

The patient had a history of a co-occurring psychiatric disorder diagnosed with bipolar disorder, but no history of suicidal behavior or psychiatric hospitalization. Her chronic medical conditions included GERD (gastroesophageal reflux disease) and COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) with asthma in the context of tobacco dependence with the use of a rescue inhaler. The patient provided no history of withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens or severe alcohol or drug withdrawal symptoms.

On mental status examination, there were no severe symptoms, such as thought disorder, cognitive impairment, severe symptoms of a mood disturbance or mania, psychosis or perceptual disturbance, or suicidal ideation. The patient was motivated for substance use disorder treatment with fair insight, indicating that her substance use was out of control and initially indicating a desire to proceed to rehabilitation treatment. The patient was admitted for inpatient detoxification with a five-day Librium protocol. The patient's hospital course progressed without incident. She did not complete the detoxification treatment and was discharged against medical advice on day # (number) 3. At the time of discharge, the patient declined referral for rehabilitation services.

The Inpatient Substance Use Detoxification Admission was not medically necessary.

The inpatient stay and detoxification treatment and other medical services could have been safely and effectively provided at a lower level of care, as the denial determination asserts. The treatment of this patient's substance use disorder did not require the structure of an inpatient setting or 24-hour monitoring. The patient displayed no serious disturbance of mental status despite having a history of bipolar disorder together with ongoing substance use disorder with alcohol, cocaine, and tobacco.

Moreover, the patient did not show evidence for suicidal or aggressive behavior or risk, or severe cognitive impairment, or psychosis, or perceptual disturbance that would have warranted an inpatient level admission and treatment. There were no severe/objective symptoms of withdrawal or biomedical issues in this case, and the patient had received detoxification and substance use disorder treatment in the past with knowledge of substance use disorder treatment protocols, as noted in the clinical summary. The patient had fair insight and reasonable motivation and was in no apparent distress throughout the inpatient stay. Thus, the inpatient admission for detoxification treatment and 24-hour monitoring, and the requested inpatient level services were not medically necessary in this case scenario.  This answer is consistent with New York State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) 3.0 Criteria/Guidelines and with published guidelines, the scientific literature, and ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) Criteria.

Substance Abuse: Inpatient

Diagnosis: Polysubstance Abuse (Suboxone, Cannabis, Crack Cocaine); Bipolar Disorder, Depression, Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder
Treatment: Inpatient Rehabilitation
The insurer denied Inpatient Rehabilitation.
The health plan's determination was overturned. 

This patient is an adult male with an admission for inpatient rehabilitation treatment of opioid use disorder (street Suboxone at 24 milligrams (mg) daily); stimulant use disorder (crack cocaine at ½ gram daily); and cannabis use disorder (marijuana/hashish at 2 grams daily). The patient's substance use had started in adolescence and escalated following release from prison with progression of the disease. He had experienced serious general medical complications, including lower back pain with sciatica and malnourishment, in the context of co-occurring post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and antisocial personality disorder. He reported past treatment episodes with relapses. He was tobacco dependent at ½ pack per day use.

The requested Inpatient Rehabilitation is medically necessary for this patient.

The necessity for admission and the continuation of inpatient level services in this particular case could not have been effectively fulfilled through a lower level of care due to the patient's numerous comorbidities and a history of unsuccessful treatment with lower levels of care. The patient under discussion was utilizing multiple substances of abuse amidst severe psychosocial stressors that spanned various domains, accompanied by a decline in functioning and general medical complications. 

These general medical complications, which are associated with high-risk behaviors and an absence of sober support systems, represent a typical set of complications that necessitated the patient's admission to an inpatient level structure with continuous monitoring. The patient exhibits high-risk substance abuse that poses a significant threat to their own safety. Furthermore, the patient's ongoing substance use is facilitated by peers who also engage in substance use and a detrimental social environment. 

Consequently, the patient's recovery environment was insufficient to maintain abstinence during treatment. The patient's clinical features necessitated round-the-clock nursing supervision to ensure abstinence while receiving treatment for substance use disorder and addressing his general medical conditions. In addition, the patient's lack of insight and coping skills necessitated the structure, monitoring, and intensity of services provided at the inpatient level.

summary:
Diagnosis: substance abuse.
Treatment: Substance-Related Intensive Outpatient Treatment.
The insurer denied Substance-Related Intensive Outpatient Treatment.
The health plan's determination was overturned.

The patient is a young adult female who was admitted for intensive outpatient program (IOP) level treatment. The treatment was initiated to address severe symptoms of co-occurring substance use disorder with cannabis, alcohol, and hallucinogens as drugs of choice. Additionally, the patient experienced recurrent and moderately severe major depressive disorder associated with trauma spectrum and familial issues. These symptoms have served to trigger ongoing substance use coupled with a history of suicidal and self-harming behavior. Thus, the patient was referred to a treatment facility that offered a structured dual diagnosis IOP services with at least nine hours or more of programming at a frequency of three days per week with appropriate monitoring for abstinence.

Substance-Related Intensive Outpatient Treatment was medically necessary for this patient.
The requested substance use treatment could not have been effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. The patient in this case presented with a co-occurring mood disturbance, including suicidal risk and maladaptive coping; the use of large quantities drugs and alcohol; and severe psychosocial stressors and functional impairments that warranted the admission and the continued Intensive Outpatient Program (IOP) level structure, monitoring, and services. The patient's social environment was not conducive to lower-level treatment as the patient was not sufficiently motivated to maintain abstinence without the continued IOP structure and a sober living environment. Additionally, the patient struggled with symptoms of mood disturbance, anxiety, insomnia, and cravings. She displayed limited insight, impaired judgment, and poor impulse control.
Therefore, the clinical features and treatment dimensions in this case did warrant the admission and continued structure of an IOP level setting, including intensive treatment, structure, supports, and safety monitoring. The patient's history of substance use, both frequency and quantity, together with the severe psychosocial stressors and co-occurring psychiatric disorders, create a complicated clinical picture. This supports the need for a safe and effective treatment environment, in light of the patient's history of high-risk behaviors and the potential for continued high-risk behaviors while under the influence of alcohol and drugs. The documentation clearly indicated that the patient was at high risk for treatment failure if treatment were to be attempted at a lower level of care or without sober supports and appropriate monitoring. Therefore, medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published practice guidelines, American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and the scientific literature, referenced below, as well as New York State instruction and application of the Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance use disorder
Treatment: Inpatient substance use rehabilitation 
The insurer denied the inpatient substance use rehabilitation.
The determination is upheld. 

The case involves an adult male who was admitted for inpatient rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment to address substance use disorder with alcohol, opioid, cannabis, and nicotine class substances of abuse. The patient had no history of withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens or other episodes of severe withdrawal symptoms but he did admit to multiple overdoses with the more recent occurring two years prior to presentation. He had a history of substance use disorder with alcohol and subsequent use of other substances in adolescence and history of prior treatments and up to three years of sobriety relapsing when his mother died. He reported daily use of alcohol with up to one pint of liquor plus beer; and, up to six bags of heroin per day with snorting as well as cannabis and nicotine use. The patient has a history of psychiatric disorder and treatment for bipolar disorder with anxiety.

Evaluation on admission for inpatient level services revealed a mental status examination that was free of severe psychiatric symptoms. He was generally motivated for rehabilitation treatment. The patient was described as cooperative with fluent speech and dysphoric mood with associated symptoms of anxiety, and with fair insight regarding the substance use disorder. He had no evidence of acute mania, thought disorder, psychosis, perceptual disturbance, or severe cognitive impairment. He did not report suicidal or homicidal ideation. He reported insomnia, but no other prominent somatic concerns.

The patient was admitted to inpatient rehabilitation treatment with replacement of vitamins and comfort medications. The patient was engaged in treatment with intensive services, sober housing, monitoring, and structure provided within the residential treatment program. The patient was social with peers and participating actively in treatment with continued risk for relapse; the patient had no severe withdrawal symptoms or post-acute withdrawal symptoms, and he had no complications with respect to biomedical, general medical, emotional, or other treatment domains. The patient was discharged upon completion of the rehabilitation program with plans to immediately proceed to outpatient level treatment with recommendation for continued involvement in recovery groups.

At issue is the medical necessity of the inpatient substance use rehabilitation.

The requested health service/treatment of inpatient substance use rehabilitation was not medically necessary for this patient.

The patient presented with substance use disorders with use of alcohol, opioid, cannabis, and nicotine class substances. He was admitted to inpatient level rehabilitation treatment. He readily engaged in treatment with nicotine and vitamin replacement therapy, as well as medication assisted treatment with gabapentin and use of trazodone and melatonin for sleep/insomnia. During the time interval under review for the entire stay, the patient was noted to be in no apparent distress with active participation in treatment including positive interactions with staff and peers. There were no treatment issues or biomedical or co-occurring psychiatric disturbances that would have warranted the admission or the continued inpatient level of care. The health plan's determination is reasonable in this case scenario.

Medical necessity is not met in this case scenario consistent with American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, the scientific literature, and published guidelines, as well as New York (NY) State instruction for this binding review and the application of NY State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Criteria.

summary:
Diagnosis: Agitation, aggressive behavior, homicidal ideation, auditory and visual hallucinations, schizophrenia, intellectual disability
Treatment: Inpatient mental health services
The insurer denied the inpatient mental health services.
The health plan's determination was overturned. 

The case involves a young adult female presenting to the emergency department (ED) with agitation, impulsive aggression towards others, and acute psychosis in the context of hallucinations, preoccupation with death, homicidal ideation directed towards her mother, and stalking. She was acutely agitated and psychotic with aggressive impulses, initially requiring as needed (prn) medications of Haldol and Ativan. The patient has been diagnosed with schizophrenia, accompanied by a comorbid intellectual disability. Additionally, she has been diagnosed with "Deletion Syndrome" and Velo-Cardio-Facial Syndrome. Medical screening in the ED included computed tomography (CT) scan of the head, electrocardiogram (EKG), and laboratory assessments that were unremarkable except for an elevated thyroglobulin and evidence for anemia. The patient was admitted to inpatient psychiatric level care for continued treatment, monitoring with safety measures, supportive measures with laboratory monitoring, and consultations with endocrinology.

The requested health service/treatment of inpatient mental health services was medically necessary for this patient.

The patient's symptoms, including acute psychosis and exacerbation of schizophrenia, together with continued risk of harm, warranted inpatient level structure and monitoring. The case is complicated by an endocrine disorder and intellectual disability. The lingering symptoms of psychosis, the potential for aggressive behavior, and the necessity to arrange a safe and clinically appropriate discharge plan all warranted the continuation of services at an acute inpatient level of care. This included safety monitoring, ongoing medication management, and other therapeutic interventions. The continued inpatient stay until discharge was therefore clinically appropriate and medical necessary. This treatment provided the continued inpatient level structure, intensity of treatment with medication adjustments and monitoring, endocrine consultation, and 24-hour monitoring through the day of discharge. At this point, the patient had reached a level of stability that she could return to the community with clinically appropriate follow-up and aftercare.

summary:
Diagnosis: substance abuse.

Treatment: inpatient substance use detoxification.

The insurer denied coverage for inpatient substance use detoxification.

The denial is overturned.

This patient was admitted to inpatient hospital treatment for alcohol/substance detoxification treatment. 

The patient reportedly could not maintain abstinence as they were drinking large amounts of alcohol daily and were at increased risk of more severe withdrawal symptoms and medical issues, as the patient was also using crack cocaine daily with alcohol. The patient also likely would not have been able to maintain abstinence without being in a 24-hour inpatient hospital setting, as evidenced by their lack of abstinence despite multiple past inpatient substance detoxification and rehabilitation treatments. It was reported that the patient left past inpatient rehabilitation treatments against medical advice (AMA) on at least 2 occasions and had multiple past inpatient substance detoxification treatments and still could not stop alcohol use.

The risk of delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after alcohol use, so the patient was considered at risk for this. The patient reportedly lacked coping skills, stability, and structure in the patient's life to maintain abstinence without treatment in a 24-hour treatment setting. The patient reportedly lacked support and structure as they were homeless and unemployed. It was reported that the plan was for inpatient alcohol/substance rehabilitation treatment, but the patient required inpatient hospital detoxification treatment first. This patient was at risk medically for worsened withdrawal, complicated or life-threatening withdrawal, and required inpatient alcohol detoxification treatment.

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be overturned. The health care plan did not act reasonably, with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient. The medical necessity for inpatient substance use detoxification, 3 days, is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Alcohol and stimulant use disorders.
Treatment: Inpatient Substance Use Detoxification Admission.
The Insurer denied: Inpatient Substance Use Detoxification Admission.
The Denial is: Overturned.

The patient is an adult male who was admitted to acute inpatient level services for detoxification and withdrawal management of severe alcohol and stimulant (freebase 
cocaine and crack cocaine) use disorders. The patient was using up to four pints of liquor together with $60 worth of crack cocaine and four grams of freebase cocaine with intranasal administration daily. He denied use of benzodiazepines despite a positive drug screen. His substance use began as an adult for at least 30 years with crack cocaine with escalating use and the addition of alcohol with daily use and progression of the disease in the past four years with a chronic relapsing course despite multiple detoxification treatment episodes and at least three limited rehabilitation treatment episodes in the recent past that had resulted in immediate relapses. The patient presented with mild alcohol withdrawal at the time of admission. Withdrawal symptoms included tremor, insomnia, and anxiety. He denied psychiatric hospitalization, or suicidal or self-harming behavior. He had been treated in the past for an anxiety disorder but was not receiving treatment at the time of presentation. He had a history of substance-related treatment episodes as noted. There were no acute medical issues or general medical concerns though he had a history of asthma with use of a rescue inhaler and low back pain. The patient was admitted to acute inpatient level care and placed on a detoxification regimen with a Librium taper, vitamin replacement therapy, fluid replacement, and medical monitoring. The patient was discharged on day #6 after completion of the detoxification protocol with step down to rehabilitation treatment. The denial determination was based on Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) Guidelines indicating that treatment could be safely provided with lower-level care, and that the patient was motivated with no severe withdrawal symptoms or history of complicated alcohol withdrawal. The appeal was based on medical necessity and New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria and the presenting clinical features as well as history of a chronic relapsing course of the substance-related illnesses.

The requested health was medically necessary.

The proposed inpatient services and detoxification treatment and withdrawal management for severe alcohol and other substance use disorders could not have been safely and effectively provided at a lower level of care. The adult inpatient treatment of this patient's substance disorders did require the admission and the continued structure of an inpatient level setting and 24-hour monitoring in view of the severity of the alcohol and stimulant (cocaine) use disorders, and the clinical features of the case. The patient did require a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management and inpatient level monitoring during the time frame under review, as it was reasonable that the patient would have been unable to abstain from the substances of abuse if detoxification and treatment were to be attempted at a lower level of care. Medical necessity for the admission and the continued inpatient services, is met in this case, and 
is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice, published practice guidelines, and the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, referenced below. This answer is also consistent with New York State instruction concerning medical necessity reviews including the required application of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria and Guidelines.

summary:
Diagnosis: Depression.
Treatment: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS).
The insurer denied Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS).
The determination is overturned. 

The patient is an adult female with a history of major depressive disorder, recurrent and severe without psychotic features. The patient has a documented history of multiple failed medication treatments for depression including treatment with more than two disparate classes of medication (Effexor, Zoloft, Trazodone), as well as augmentation with buspirone and topiramate. Additionally, the patient has received combination antidepressant treatment with Effexor and Trazodone currently prescribed together with buspirone. She is on a waiting list for evidence-based psychotherapy. She has not received electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) or vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) therapy. At the time of evaluation for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) therapy, the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ)-9 scale score was 20 in the severe range for symptoms of depression associated with severe impairments of functioning. The patient has no significant or acute general medical issues.
At issue is the medical necessity of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS).

The requested health service/treatment of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) is medically necessary for this patient.
The services proposed are in keeping with prevailing standards of medical practice for the condition under treatment in this case with an evidence-based augmentation treatment for depressive disorder with TMS therapy; and the requested service/treatment in this case is clinically appropriate and is backed by credible scientific evidence known to benefit patients with the condition and clinical features in this case scenario.
TMS therapy as a primary or adjunctive therapy for treatment of depression has generally been evaluated in patients who have treatment refractory/resistant depression, as defined by one or more, antidepressant medication treatment failures with or without augmentation. Specifically, when treatments with antidepressant medication with or without augmentation, or with electroconvulsive therapy, and/or psychotherapy, especially cognitive behavioral therapy, have failed to produce a response or remission, then TMS is an appropriate consideration. This assertion is noted in the American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorder. Moreover, scientific literature indicates that a course of treatment with TMS therapy is reasonable in cases of treatment resistant depression as defined in the scientific literature.
In this case, at least two or more alternative therapeutic trials with one augmentation treatment have been provided along with placement on a wait list for psychotherapy, and the proposed treatment with TMS therapy is considered clinically appropriate and medically necessary. Additionally, the use of TMS therapy is reasonable, and in the best interest of the patient. The decision to proceed with TMS therapy reflects sound medical judgment based upon the current scientific literature and American Psychiatric Association practice guidelines concerning the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorder. The patient in this case has clearly demonstrated that her depressive disorder is treatment refractory or resistant, and the proposed treatment of recurrent major depressive disorder using TMS therapy is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice.

Treatment: Initial Applied Behavioral Assessment (ABA)
The insurer denied Initial Applied Behavioral Assessment (ABA)
The health plan's determination is overturned. 

The patient is a young boy who has been diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder and developmental speech and language disorder (expressive and receptive language) by his pediatrician. An evaluation when he was 31 months old describes that he was referred for evaluation because he was exhibiting behaviors of concern. He was toe-walking, spinning his body, tensing his arms and hands, clenching and grinding his teeth, and bouncing and jumping repetitively. He made poor eye contact and responded poorly to his name. His attention span was poor. He did not play with other children, and did not respond to verbal prompts or commands. He had delayed speech, and did not use words. He made some repetitive sounds, such as 'da-da-da' and 'go-go-go', but his family members had to interpret his wants and needs.
The patient did not like crowds or loud noises. He was fixated on screens and turned light switches on and off repetitively.

Initial Applied Behavioral Assessment (ABA) is medically necessary for this patient.
The patient has been diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder, Level 3, requiring very substantial support. The Standard of care in the United States involves evaluation for, and provision of Applied Behavioral Assessment (ABA).
An extensive body of scientific literature has accrued over the past forty years demonstrating the success of ABA based interventions to decrease problem behavior and increase skills in adults and children with intellectual disabilities and autism.
The most recent American Academy of Pediatrics Guidelines on the Identification, Evaluation, and Management of Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) authored by Hyman et al [1] recommend applied behavioral analysis (ABA therapy) as a primary intervention. The authors state: 'Most evidence-based treatment models are based on principles of ABA. ABA has been defined as "the process of systematically applying interventions based upon the principles of learning theory to improve socially significant behaviors to a meaningful degree, and to demonstrate that the interventions employed are responsible for the improvement in behavior." The use of ABA methods to treat symptoms of ASD suggests that behaviors exhibited can be altered by programmatically reinforcing skills related to communication and other skill acquisition. Thus, ABA treatments may target development of new skills (eg, social engagement) and/or minimize behaviors (eg, aggression) that may interfere with a child's progress.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder.
Treatment: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS).
The insurer denied: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS).
The determination is: overturned.

The patient is an adolescent female with a history of major depressive disorder, recurrent and severe without psychotic features with severe symptoms of depression including suicidal ideation. The patient has a documented history of medication treatments for depression including treatment with two or more Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved medications for adolescents including Prozac, Zoloft, and Cymbalta. Due to adverse effects and lack of efficacy, the patient continued to experience symptoms of depression and functional impairments. Additionally, the patient has had treatment with an evidence-based psychotherapy completing a course of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and augmentation therapy with buspirone and hydroxyzine. The patient was referred to and recommended for repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) therapy together with continued medication treatment and psychotherapy as indicated.
At issue is the medical necessity of TMS therapy.
The health plan's determination of medical necessity is overturned in whole.
In this case scenario, the proposed treatment, Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) with treatment sessions, is medically necessary per protocol and in keeping with the current scientific literature and standards of care. 
TMS therapy as a primary or adjunctive therapy for treatment of depression has generally been evaluated in patients who have treatment refractory depression, as defined by one or more antidepressant medication treatment failures with or without augmentation. TMS therapy for depressive disorder has been established by the FDA as a safe treatment including approval for adolescents; and, the data, as reflected in peer reviewed medical literature, supports this assertion including more recent studies involving adolescents, reflected in the referenced scientific literature.
Specifically, when treatments with two or more antidepressant medications with or without augmentation, or with electroconvulsive therapy, and/or psychotherapy, especially cognitive behavioral therapy, have failed to produce a response or remission, then TMS is an appropriate consideration. This assertion is noted in the American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorder, referenced below. Moreover, the scientific literature has increasingly supported the use of TMS therapy in adolescents, as well as adults, with treatment refractory depression, as in this case.
In this case, at least two alternative therapeutic trials with augmentation together with other therapeutic measures have been provided including psychotherapy with a completed course of CBT and psychotherapy which is planned to continue. Thus, in this case, the proposed TMS therapy is considered clinically appropriate and medically necessary in keeping with prevailing standards of medical practice. Additionally, the proposed TMS therapy per protocol is reasonable, and in the best interest of the patient. The decision to proceed with TMS therapy reflects sound medical judgment based upon the current scientific literature concerning the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorders in patients with treatment resistant depression- such as the one in this case. The patient in this case has demonstrated that her depressive disorder is treatment refractory or resistant, and the proposed treatment of recurrent major depressive disorder using repetitive TMS therapy with a clinically appropriate number of sessions is/was reasonable and warranted in this case scenario, and again, is consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice including evidence in the peer reviewed scientific literature for application of TMS in adolescents.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance abuse. 

Treatment: substance abuse residential treatment services. 

The insurer denied coverage for substance abuse residential treatment services. 

The denial is overturned. 
 
This adult male was admitted to this inpatient substance residential rehabilitation treatment as he could not maintain sobriety and was drinking alcohol, using cannabis and cocaine. He reportedly had strong urges to use and lacked insight regarding warning signs for his alcohol and substance use. He reportedly had difficulty identifying relapse triggers and had poor judgment and poor impulse control. This was his first reported treatment episode, and he reportedly was making some progress but needed more time in this setting to learn more coping skills to avoid triggers and relapse when outside of this 24-hour setting. He also had comorbid psychiatric diagnoses including Major Depressive Disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). He was attending group and individual psychotherapy.  

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that inpatient treatment is indicated primarily for individuals whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. In this case this patient was considered in need of continued 24-hour substance residential rehabilitation treatment and reports still stated that he still needed to learn more coping skills to avoid triggers and relapse. It was reported that he needed more time in this therapeutic supervised and structured setting to get to the root of his substance use disorder, needed to work on codependency in his relationship and needed to practice consequential thinking to take responsibility for his life. It was reported that he still had difficulty regulating emotions, lacked enough sober supports outside of his family, needed more time to learn, develop, and implement more coping skills as he was in denial at times about his substance and alcohol use. Initially, he reportedly did not view his recent relapse as a problem. He reportedly still had limited insight regarding the warning signs and maladaptive behavior that led to substance and alcohol use and had exaggerated confidence about recovery. He reportedly was making progress but needed more time as this was his first treatment episode. He reportedly lacked the coping skills and ability to identify relapse triggers to stop use. 

According to the Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) he met criteria for inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment as he continued to use alcohol, cannabis, and lacked sober supports outside of his family to maintain abstinence outside of this 24-hour supervised and structured inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment. He also had comorbid depression, PTSD, and ADHD.  He reportedly lacked coping skills, needed to better identify relapse triggers, and needed to learn relapse prevention skills, and improve his sober support. Without this structured and supervised therapeutic rehabilitation treatment he likely would have relapsed and been at medical risk due to his use of alcohol and cocaine in addition to cannabis. 

As a result, the recommendation is to reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for continued inpatient substance residential rehabilitation treatment. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be reversed. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. 

The medical necessity for inpatient substance abusers' residential treatment services is substantiated.

The case involves an adolescent female who was admitted to residential level treatment for severe mood and anxiety disorders complicated with co-occurring cannabis and nicotine use disorders and a history of oppositional and problematic behaviors with deterioration in functioning. Her symptoms of mood disturbance in the context of deregulated mood and emotions are compounded by use of cannabis and nicotine primarily with vaping. The patient had received outpatient level mental health services in the past without sustained benefit or a remission of symptoms. Moreover, she was noted to have impulsive behavior in the context of the substance use that complicated her ability to function socially and within the family constellation with parents with whom she lived. These clinical features and treatment dimensions in this case prompted the referral to residential treatment to include intensive behavioral therapy with modified dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) and other treatments to address the psychosocial issues within the primary support/family and social environment domains. Her referral for residential treatment was also prompted by her clinical providers' safety concerns and the dysregulated mood associated with her co-morbid mood and anxiety disorders and personality traits with maladaptive coping that was self-defeating. Thus, the patient was admitted to residential level care in the context of worsening symptoms of mood disturbance with anxiety including elements of social anxiety and high risk for continued self-destructive behavior associated with poor control of impulses together with maladaptive coping and prominent family and peer relationship problems, as well as the severe substance use disorders with cannabis and nicotine. Evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination with severe psychiatric symptoms in the context of a primary diagnosis of severe and recurrent major depressive disorder and co-morbid generalized anxiety disorder and history of oppositional defiant disorder (ODD), and co-occurring cannabis and nicotine use disorder. Throughout the residential stay, the patient continued to be at high risk for harm in view of her ongoing problematic emotional control and persistent symptoms of anxiety. 

The requested health service is medically necessary in this case.

The patient's continued treatment in this case was not amenable to treatment at a lower level of care, and is not excluded from coverage, as medical necessity is met per New York State instruction. The patient continued to display active symptoms of mood, anxiety, and oppositional features that did require the continued structure and intensity of services of a residential setting including safety precautions while participating in intensive, evidence-based treatment for her psychiatric disorders and while assessing the response to medication and ongoing family therapy and other therapeutic interventions to address residual problematic symptoms and risk for relapse prior to discharge. There are/were severe psychiatric symptoms with functional impairment and safety issues that had failed to respond to lower-level treatments, and that had resulted in safety concerns with problematic behaviors with continued high risk for problematic behaviors and use of substances (nicotine and cannabis). The patient required the continued residential level services and intensive treatment and monitoring, as requested, and medical necessity was met for the requested Continued Residential Mental Health Treatment. This answer is consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published societal guidelines including the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and the scientific literature.

summary:
Diagnosis: Alcohol Dependence, Cocaine Abuse.
Treatment: Inpatient Substance Use Rehabilitation.
The insurer denied the Inpatient Substance Use Rehabilitation.
The health plan's determination is overturned. 

This is an adult male patient who was admitted for inpatient treatment due to concurrent substance use disorders involving cannabis, cocaine, and alcohol-based substances of abuse. Additionally, he has been diagnosed with a mood and anxiety disorder, which is best described as an unspecified depressive disorder accompanied by symptoms of anxiety. 

The patient's history reveals an escalating pattern of substance use, with the progression of substance use disorders and increasing symptoms related to the co-existing psychiatric condition that was triggering the substance use. The onset of the patient's mental health and substance-related disturbances can be traced back to his adolescence, during which the severity of symptoms and behavioral disturbances escalated. These disturbances included high-risk behaviors associated with substance use. 

The patient demonstrated limited insight and impaired judgment in relation to his addictions. His past attempts at treatment have been unsuccessful, including at least one detoxification treatment followed by a rehabilitation treatment earlier this year. The patient's substance use encompassed the consumption of up to one pint of liquor and varying quantities of cocaine, with the intake of up to three grams through snorting and smoking up to 200 dollars' worth of crack cocaine three to six days per week. His substance use also included daily consumption of tobacco and marijuana, with the latter amounting to a quarter of an ounce per day.


The mental status examination of the patient revealed symptoms indicative of anxiety and depression, coupled with a low sense of self-worth and disturbances in sleep and concentration. The patient demonstrated a lack of insight, impaired judgment, and poor impulse control. However, there was no evidence of severe symptoms such as mania, mood cycling, thought disorder, psychotic features, or perceptual disturbances. The patient was well-groomed, cooperative, and exhibited clear speech. His thought processing was linear, logical, and goal-oriented.

In terms of general medical conditions, there were no acute issues present in this case. However, it is noteworthy that the patient has a history of hypothyroidism and is currently undergoing replacement therapy. The patient has completed high school education but is currently unemployed. There are no ongoing legal issues associated with the patient. He reported no problems related to trauma and had limited support in maintaining sobriety.

The patient presented for residential treatment and underwent comprehensive evaluations that confirmed his diagnoses of severe substance use disorders involving alcohol, cocaine, nicotine, and cannabis class substances. Additionally, he was diagnosed with depression and anxiety. There was no history of suicidal behavior or psychiatric hospitalization. The patient actively participated in various therapies, including group, individual, and educational sessions, with a focus on developing coping skills and maintaining abstinence from substances of abuse. Life skills and recovery groups were provided, along with other age-appropriate therapeutic interventions as permitted by the program. The patient was placed on a waiting list for transfer to a residential treatment facility when one becomes available.


During his residential stay, the patient actively engaged in the structured programming of services, which was closely monitored within the confines of an inpatient setting. Despite being identified as highly susceptible to relapse, he demonstrated limited insight but a reasonable level of motivation to persist with treatment, aided by the application of motivational interviewing techniques. His recovery environment was deemed unsupportive, thus discussions were underway regarding the potential transition to a sober living environment. His prescribed medication regimen included Lexapro, Trazodone, and vitamin replacement therapy, supplemented by the availability of comfort medications.

The devised treatment plan encompassed educational sessions and peer support meetings, psychosocial programming, and a variety of activity/milieu therapies. These were specifically designed to address the patient's lack of self-confidence and to enhance his coping skills. Psychiatric evaluations were conducted regularly, accompanied by medication management and monitoring. Safety monitoring was ensured within the structure of the residential program, with clinically appropriate programming that included the necessary intensity, duration, and monitoring for the levels of care being provided. This included sober supports, involvement in recovery groups, and the development of a relapse prevention plan. Upon completion of the program, the patient was discharged with a safe and clinically appropriate disposition. He was subsequently transferred to a residential substance-related rehabilitation treatment facility.

The Inpatient Substance Use Rehabilitation admission was medically necessary.

In this particular instance, the patient was admitted to an inpatient level of care, which was the least restrictive treatment setting available. The patient suffers from multiple concurrent disorders and is at a high risk of relapse. It is not reasonable to anticipate that the patient could have been safely or effectively managed with lower-level services in a less restrictive care setting. Furthermore, the patient persistently exhibited a lack of insight, a propensity for impulsivity and relapse, and a need for motivational techniques while undergoing treatment for the concurrent psychiatric disorder.

The appropriate application of the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Patient Placement Criteria in this case was to default to the inpatient level of care due to the high risk of relapse, the absence of a reasonable recovery environment, and the patient's lack of skills and readiness to change, all in the context of a relevant concurrent psychiatric disorder. This care was suitable for this case scenario and included work on coping and life skills, a relapse prevention plan, and a discharge or step-down plan that incorporated sober supports or living arrangements and continued intensive treatment in a residential setting.

The counseling and psychosocial interventions, medications to address the concurrent mood disorder, and the initial work for the development of a relapse prevention plan and motivational techniques were critical in this case. These, along with the additional gains in insight and acquisition of better coping skills, were all important components of the treatment. These were provided with a clinically appropriate structure, intensity of services, and monitoring for the duration of the treatment under review. It was clinically appropriate and medically necessary for the patient to have continued 24-hour monitoring and inpatient level services for the duration of the proposed treatment in order to prepare the patient for a safe and clinically appropriate disposition and transfer to residential care. None of this therapeutic work could have been safely or effectively provided for the time interval under review at a lower level of care, given the multiple complicating factors in this case.

summary:

Treatment: Inpatient mental health treatment.

This adult female reportedly was admitted to inpatient mental health treatment in the hospital due to worsened depressive symptoms including suicidal ideation and plan to overdose with pills, depressed mood, psychomotor retardation, decreased energy and appetite, sleeping problems, hopelessness, worthlessness, and feelings of being useless. She reportedly had 2 past suicide attempts and multiple past psychiatric hospitalizations due to depression and suicidal thoughts. She reportedly was in outpatient treatment and receiving Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) treatments. She reportedly had past Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) treatments. She reportedly had multiple past psychotropic medication trials. She reportedly had multiple medications changed in the hospital including starting and stopping Wellbutrin, Zoloft, Zyprexa, Lamictal, Klonopin, and Pamelor. She reportedly received some ECT treatments and had some efficacy with depression but had confusion and memory loss so ECT was stopped. She reportedly took Abilify, Buspirone, and Cymbalta. 

In this case she was considered a high-risk patient for suicide due to her two past suicide attempts and multiple psychiatric hospitalizations and worsened depressive symptoms and continued confusion and inability to adequately function on her own until discharged. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Suicidal Behaviors reports that patients with past suicide attempts are at high risk for suicide and this patient had two past reported suicide attempts and had suicidal plan to overdose with pills on admission. She had multiple past medication trials for depression, ECT treatment, and TMS treatment. She was not considered safe for discharge due to her continued confusion and inability to function on her own and multiple medication adjustments ongoing. 

Also, the APA Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Suicidal Behaviors reports also that patients may require more time in the hospital to better assess suicide because they sometimes do not tell the truth regarding their suicidal thoughts in order to leave the hospital and that observation in the hospital is appropriate to better ensure their safety. This patient had a long history of severe depression and had past suicide attempts and worsened depression on admission including suicidal plan to overdose and had multiple past psychiatric hospitalization and psychotropic medication trials, so she was considered at risk for suicide if not at baseline and if still confused and also not able to function on her own if still confused. During the denial period she had multiple medication adjustments as well. The medical records provided supported the medical necessity for continued hospital treatment until discharged. As a result, the recommendation is to reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for continued inpatient psychiatric hospital treatment. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be reversed. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. The medical necessity for inpatient mental health treatment is substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis:	Unspecified eating disorder	

Treatment: 	Psychological testing

The insurer denied psychological testing

The denial is upheld

This patient had 2 hours of psychological testing. She reportedly had a diagnosis of Unspecified eating Disorder and also had a history of anxiety symptoms, sad mood, and feelings of guilt. She reportedly had a history of preoccupation with food, body image and weight, and had excessive exercising. She reportedly had feelings of guilt after eating disorder behaviors. There was no reported history of alcohol or substance abuse. Her medical history was significant for Raynaud's and removal of gallbladder. It was reported that provider PsyD requested psychological testing.

The insurer denied coverage for psychological testing for 2 hours of testing with codes 96130 and 96131 stating that it was not considered medically necessary treatment then. They stated that there was no documentation that psychological testing was needed to rule in or rule out a presented mental illness. They stated that this was based on Medical Policy for Psychological Testing.

In this case there was no documentation that the provider needed more assistance for diagnostic clarification after utilizing other standard methods and treatments including having a psychiatric evaluation.  It is not considered standard practice to have psychological testing for evaluation of eating disorders. Psychological testing is indicated when there is a need for intellectual functioning testing, adaptive functioning testing, or cognitive functioning testing. In this case there were no indications that the patient needed these assessed. 

Eating Disorder diagnoses are typically made from clinical assessments by mental health or medical professionals and not by psychological testing. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with eating Disorders reports that the least restrictive level of care for safe and effective treatment is appropriate and there is no mention that it is considered standard care for psychological testing to be done to assist in diagnostic concerns. The standard assessment for eating disorders by medical and mental health assessment by a pediatrician or medical provider, or by a psychiatric or psychological evaluation, or by a nutritional consultant. Also, anxiety and depressive disorders are assessed by mental health professionals by clinical assessment and there was no reported psychiatric evaluation, and psychological testing is not considered standard treatment for anxiety and depressive disorder diagnoses.  In the standard diagnostic work up there is a psychiatric evaluation and assessment including mental status, history of present illness, a past psychiatric history, a medical work up to rule out possible medical causes of mood or anxiety symptoms, family assessment, and the recommended treatments are pharmacotherapy to target mood or anxiety symptoms as well as psychosocial interventions, cognitive behavioral therapy, interpersonal therapy, or psychotherapy. Psychological testing also is not considered standard for the diagnosis or treatment of anxiety or depressive disorders but rather clinical diagnostic assessment by a psychiatrist or psychologist or mental health provider are considered standard. If a provider needs additional information to assist in assessing intellectual or cognitive functioning or to assess for possible neurological deficits, neuropsychological tests can be performed by a psychologist, but this was not reported in the notes to be reviewed. Also, psychological testing is not generally considered medically necessary treatment for diagnosis or diagnostic clarification of common mental disorders in the absence of severe symptoms, psychosis, or complicating factors that may confuse a clinical picture. A comprehensive psychiatric or psychological assessment is expected prior to a referral for psychological testing. Psychological testing is only indicated if there is a strong indication that useful information from testing would impact the patient's care and treatment or make a diagnosis that a provider is unable to make by other methods such as a psychiatric evaluation. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be upheld. The health care plan did act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. The medical necessity for psychological testing is not substantiated.

He reportedly had medication adjustments as Seroquel and Abilify were held due to prolonged QTc (heart rate corrected QT interval) of 505 and Gabapentin was given. The insurer denied coverage for inpatient hospital treatment as not medically necessary treatment. They stated that he did not require 24-hour hospital treatment, and they recommended a less restrictive level of care.

He had comorbid psychiatric issues including having several past suicide attempts including driving into a pole, walking into traffic with his eyes closed, and overdose and had multiple past hospitalizations including a recent one, so he was at increased risk for suicide as well.

The patient had been using Fentanyl and heroin with intravenous administration together with daily use of Xanax and/or Valium. He also reported use of "olly," resulting in a 
prolonged period of psychosis. He has a history of withdrawal seizures and hallucinations or delirium tremens. He had a history of prior detoxification and substance use disorder treatments with relapses. His self-referral for treatment was prompted by multiple stressors and general health concerns. His presentation included early withdrawal symptoms and signs, visual hallucinations, and general medical complications related to intravenous drug use.
The patient presented with acute comorbid general medical issues including a malnourished state and cellulitis with an abdominal abscess requiring irrigation and debridement and antibiotics. He was tobacco dependent. Laboratory assessments were unremarkable or normal with a positive drug screen consistent with history. He had a chest X-ray and multiple electrocardiograms due to ongoing concern with cardiac ischemia. The patient is homeless and unemployed, living under a bridge. The patient was admitted to detoxification treatment with a comprehensive detoxification protocol with tapering dosages of Valium and Suboxone and as-needed medications for comfort, as well as antibiotics. He was discharged one day early against medical advice with referrals for clinically appropriate aftercare and plans to pursue medication assisted treatment for the opioid use disorder and long-term rehabilitation services. The health plan's denial of coverage was based on medical necessity and MCG (Milliman Care Guidelines) Criteria pertaining the substance-related disorders indicating that there was no risk for complicated withdrawal or abnormal vital signs. The appeal was based on the clinical features of the case including history of complicated withdrawal and presentation with acute medical issues and visual hallucinations. The appeal asserted that the patient could not have been safely managed with lower-level care in a less restrictive treatment setting.

The inpatient admission was medically necessary.

The requested Inpatient admission and continued treatment could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in this case scenario. The patient in this case was using heroin and Fentanyl with intravenous administration together with Xanax and/or Valium on a daily continuous basis with recent use of "olly," complicating the clinical presentation. This did warrant inpatient level hospital care with detoxification and withdrawal management and monitoring for the duration of the protocol. Detoxification, as necessary, and other treatments pertinent to the detoxification treatment episode could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care following the comprehensive assessment that was provided at the time of admission. Moreover, the patient had acute medical issues requiring monitoring and evaluation and treatment as indicated in the clinical summary. The patient's history of substance abuse (frequency and quantity) together with the severe psychosocial stressors and functional impairments reflect the seriousness of the substance use disorder and the need for a safe and effective detoxification with withdrawal management, as the 
patient was at high risk for treatment failure if the continued detoxification and withdrawal management were to be attempted at a lower level of care. Therefore, medical necessity is met in this case, consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, published societal guidelines, American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and the scientific literature, referenced below. Therefore, the inpatient admission was medically necessary.
