summary:
Diagnosis: Opioid Use Disorder, Severe; Tobacco Use Disorder, Severe
Treatment: Inpatient Substance Abuse Rehabilitation Treatment
The insurer denied the Inpatient Substance Abuse Rehabilitation Treatment.
The health plan's determination was overturned.

This is a male patient with admission for inpatient rehabilitation treatment of opioid use disorder (heroin) in the context of participation in a methadone maintenance treatment program (MMTP) with a dose of 270 milligrams (mg) daily. The patient's opioid use disorder was characterized as a chronic relapsing course and had escalated in the context of homelessness. He was tobacco dependent and had a history of anxiety and depression with associated treatments, as well as a remote history of alcohol use disorder.

At the time of presentation, the patient exhibited craving with wish to achieve sobriety or better control of his substance abuse and engage in treatment and a recovery process. He had significant decline in functioning with primary support, social environment, occupational and housing stressors as he was homeless and unemployed and living on the street or in shelters with minimal supports.

Evaluation on admission revealed a mental status examination that included symptoms of anxiety and intense craving. He was motivated for rehabilitation treatment in the contemplative stage of change and had limited supports. There was no evidence for thought disorder, severe cognitive impairment, mania, psychosis, or violent intent. He denied suicidal ideation.

The patient underwent a comprehensive evaluation, which encompassed psychiatric, psychosocial, and general medical assessments. The rehabilitation treatment he received incorporated group, individual, and educational sessions, in addition to the opportunity for peer support through 12-step recovery groups. Medications were prescribed to manage his cravings, in conjunction with the continued use of methadone at a dosage of 270 milligrams daily and nicotine replacement, with the provision of comfort medications.

Furthermore, motivational techniques and activity therapies were administered. The patient demonstrated consistent progress, albeit with ongoing struggles with persistent cravings. Consequently, therapy incorporated continuous efforts to cultivate coping skills and devise a relapse prevention plan. This plan, which included the identification of triggers, was addressed in the final week of treatment within the framework of discharge planning. This process was delayed by two days due to an outbreak of COVID-19 at the receiving step-down facility.

Throughout his stay, the patient was deemed to be at a high risk of relapse due to the absence of sober supports and his history of a chronic relapsing course. Upon discharge, the treatment plan entailed continued participation in rehabilitation treatment and recovery. It was recommended that he maintain involvement in peer-supported groups, with ongoing treatment with methadone and his psychotropic regimen. This regimen included the use of Zoloft, Cymbalta, Buspirone, and Remeron. Additionally, a referral for extended residential treatment was made.

The Inpatient Substance Abuse Rehabilitation Treatment was medically necessary.

The patient's psychiatric comorbidities, severe psychosocial stressors, and history of treatment failure with a chronic relapsing course necessitated this level of care. 

The patient in question was consistently using heroin in the context of severe psychosocial stressors that spanned multiple domains. This was coupled with a decline in functioning, despite the patient's participation in a methadone program. The absence of sober supports, homelessness, and a history of relapses represent a quintessential set of complications that necessitated the patient's admission to an inpatient level structure with ongoing monitoring and structure. 

The patient's high-risk substance abuse posed a significant risk to their own safety. Furthermore, the patient's ongoing substance use was enabled by an adverse social environment. Consequently, the patient's recovery environment was not adequate to sustain abstinence while in treatment. The patient's clinical features warranted 24-hour monitoring to ensure abstinence while receiving substance use disorder treatment and other treatments to address their comorbid conditions. 

Moreover, the patient's lack of insight and coping skills necessitated the inpatient level structure, monitoring, and intensity of services. These services were requested to ensure the patient's safety and to facilitate their recovery.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance abuse

Treatment: Intensive outpatient substance use treatment for 3 days a week, and 3 hours a day

The insurer denied coverage for intensive outpatient substance use treatment for 3 days a week, and 3 hours a day

The denial is overturned

This patient reportedly had cocaine use disorder and had a history of snorting 1 ½ grams of cocaine daily. He reportedly first used cocaine at age 16 but had regular use for 4 years prior to inpatient substance rehabilitation treatment. It was reported that he relapsed 30 days after this inpatient substance treatment. He reported that he also drank 3-4 tequila or wines 3 times per week. He reported that his substance use interfered with his functioning including having arguments with friends and family. He reportedly that his past partner also drank alcohol and used cocaine. He reportedly was in sober living. He reportedly had impulsive decision making and was irritational at times when using cocaine. 

The insurer denied coverage for substance related intensive outpatient program treatment (IOP) for 3 hours per day 3 days per week stating that it was not medically necessary treatment then. They stated that he had a sober environment and supportive family and was motivated for treatment. They stated that he did not have withdrawal symptoms. They recommended a less restrictive level of care then.
 
This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for substance related intensive outpatient program treatment (IOP) for 3 hours per day 3 days per week as the medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that he required at least this level of care then. According to the American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders intensive outpatient programs are programs that provide an intensive, structured treatment experience for individuals with substance use disorders who require more services than those generally available in traditional outpatient settings. Alternatively, these programs are sometimes used as "step-down" programs for individuals leaving hospital or residential settings who are at a high risk of relapsing because of problems with motivation, the presence of frequent cravings or urges to use a substance, poor social supports, immediate environmental cues for relapse and/or availability of substances, and co-occurring medical and/or psychiatric disorders. The goal of such a "step-down" approach is to stabilize patients by retaining them in treatment and providing more extended intensive outpatient monitoring of relapse potential and co-occurring disorders. Intensive outpatient programs use individual therapy, group therapy, family therapy, and urine toxicology but vary in the amount of other therapeutic components used. As a result of the above, the recommendation is to reverse the previous decision and approve substance related intensive outpatient program treatment and for another 2 months if still in that program, then going forward. It did not appear that the health care plan acted reasonably, with sound medical judgment, or in the best interests of the patient then.

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be reversed. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. 

The medical necessity for intensive outpatient substance use treatment for 3 days a week, and 3 hours a day is substantiated.

The patient is an adult male. He was admitted for residential level substance use disorder rehabilitation services. His presentation for substance disorder treatment was prompted by a precipitous decline in functioning in the context of escalating and ongoing use of alcohol together with unspecified co-occurring psychiatric disorders treated with lithium and trazodone. The patient presented with associated symptoms of anxiety and depression related to psychosocial stressors within the primary support, social environment, housing, financial, and occupational domains. He denied history of delirium tremens or withdrawal seizures, and he had received treatments in the past with relapse triggered by psychosocial stressors, including several tragic events and his mother's injury, which required emergency medical services. The patient had no acute medical issues.

The health plan denied coverage of the admission for the dates of service in questions based on medical necessity and LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) Guidelines. The denial determination indicated that the patient was participating in treatment and motivated, making progress, and had no remaining safety issues or withdrawal symptoms. The denial asserted that the patient had no health problems or behaviors that required continued 24-hour supervision and that the patient was medication adherent and had a supportive environment. The appeal was based on the clinical features and treatment dimensions including the severe psychosocial stressors and comorbid conditions. The appeal asserted that the patient was at high risk for relapse without a reasonable recovery environment, persistent anxiety and PAWS (post-acute-withdrawal syndrome), and the stage of change reflecting the need to remain in a structured setting with develop a solid discharge plan and disposition.

The Inpatient Residential Treatment was medically necessary for this patient.

The continued residential rehabilitation treatment was medically necessary in order to address issues related to risk of relapse with focus on a relapse prevention plan and additional work on developing coping skills in a case that poses high risk for relapse in the context of an inadequate recovery environment and homelessness and lack of sober supports; in order to address co-morbid psychiatric disorders with medication and therapy including CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy); in order to address the patient's lack of awareness of the seriousness of his illness with psycho-education and evidence-based psychosocial interventions including involvement in 12-step groups and motivational techniques; in order to address the social environment including use of substances of abuse with job and family stress and prolonged grief; and in order to work on coping skills that will be necessary in building an effective sober support system and continued recovery efforts with community providers while maintaining his abstinence and continuing treatment for the co-occurring disorders with symptoms that were triggering substance use. None of this therapeutic work could have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in view of the multiple, complicating factors in this case, the high risk for relapse, the treatment history with relapses and continued use of substances despite access to treatment in the community, and the lack of a reasonable recovery environment with work in a setting where alcohol is prevalent and readily available. This answer is consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice and ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) Criteria and scientific literature and published guidelines referenced below, as well as New York State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) Guidelines and Criteria.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Partial Hospitalization Substance Use Disorder Services
The Insurer denied: Partial Hospitalization Substance Use Disorder Services
The Denial is: Overturned.

The patient is an adult male. He was admitted to partial hospital program (PHP) level-of-care with boarding for treatment of severe cannabis (marijuana/ tetrahydrocannabinol), hallucinogen (ketamine) and nicotine (vaping) use disorders with severe comorbid psychiatric disorders, including PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder), generalized anxiety disorder, obsessive-compulsive related disorder, and major depressive disorder. He presented for readmission for substance-related disorders and co-occurring psychiatric disorders in the context of deterioration of functioning occupationally, socially, and with daily functioning. His case was complicated by a chronic relapsing course with frequent blackouts and high risk for overdose, as well as complex trauma history in an Orthodox Jewish patient needing treatment in a culturally sensitive treatment setting-as was the case with the admitting treatment facility. 
The patient has a history of substance use disorder beginning in young adulthood with poly-substance use disorder with progression of use of substances as noted and resulting in job jeopardy, social and relationship deterioration and decline in functioning. The patient is diagnosed with co-occurring disorders. He also presented with associated symptoms of anxiety and depression, as well as trauma-related symptoms previously diagnosed as posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) related to a history of physical abuse. He had no history of psychiatric hospitalization but did report suicidal behavior. 
The health plan's denial of coverage was based on medical necessity and ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) Criteria, indicating that treatment could be effectively provided with lower-level services with a lower frequency of treatment interventions. The appeal was based on medical necessity referencing the high risk for relapse, lack of coping skills and impulse control and safety issues.

The Partial Hospitalization Substance Use Disorder Services was medically necessary.

The PHP (partial hospitalization program) intensity of services, structure, and monitoring were reasonable, in the best interest of the patient, and consistent with prevailing standards of medical practice. The patient could not have been safely or effectively treated in a less restrictive setting during the time interval under review. The patient needed the requested time with PHP (partial hospitalization program) level services to work toward a clinically appropriate discharge plan together with consideration of sober living and the need for sober supports, as well as active treatment to work on a reasonable relapse prevention plan and more effective coping skills with 
motivational techniques in a culturally sensitive treatment environment. The patient had essentially demonstrated that he was unable to effectively participate in lower-level rehabilitation treatment with the lack of coping skills and control over impulses to use ketamine, nicotine, and marijuana, and other issues related to readiness to change, and lack of a reasonable recovery environment including problems within the social environment. Thus, the plan should cover the requested services of Partial Hospital Substance Use Disorder Treatment with a single case agreement-as requested to the extent that the requested PHP (partial hospitalization program) level care is indicated, appropriate and medically necessary under the plan in order to provide intensive and culturally sensitive rehabilitation services combined with evidence-base treatment while maintaining abstinence from substances of abuse with monitoring and motivational techniques. The requested benefit of Partial Hospital Substance Use Disorder Treatment was clinically appropriate, and medically necessary.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse.

Treatment: Residential rehabilitation services.

The insurer denied coverage for residential rehabilitation services.

The denial is upheld.

This patient reportedly was admitted to this substance residential rehabilitation, due to cocaine and cannabis use. He reportedly was inhaling 3-4 grams of cocaine and had used since age 15 and last use the previous month. He also reportedly was smoking marijuana or hashish 12 blunts, which was up to 2 grams, and started at age 9 with last use the previous month. He also reportedly was using synthetic cannabis. He reportedly had numerous attempts at recovery. He reportedly had a diagnosis of bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) also. It was reported that he was incarcerated for 22 years and was released in the recent past. He reportedly took Mirtazapine, Lithium, Depakote, and Ziprasidone. He reportedly attended group therapy. It was reported that on admission he had difficulty identifying relapse triggers, needed to learn better coping skills, better regulate emotions, improve insight into substance use, and better understand consequences to substance use. He reportedly got employment and was working on discharge plans. He reportedly was discharged following that.
 
The insurer denied coverage for continued inpatient substance residential rehabilitation treatment stating that the medical records provided did not support that it was still medically necessary treatment then. They stated that the medical records provided did not show that he was still unable to manage triggers. They recommended a less restrictive level of care then.

This reviewer agrees with the decision to deny coverage for continued inpatient substance residential rehabilitation treatment as the medical records provided did not provide enough specific evidence to support that he still required only 24-hour residential rehabilitation treatment then or that he could not safely and effectively be treated in a less restrictive level of care then. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders states that residential treatment is indicated primarily for individuals who do not meet clinical criteria for hospitalization but whose lives and social interactions have come to focus exclusively on substance use and who currently lack sufficient motivation and/or substance-free social supports to remain abstinent in an ambulatory setting. In this case substance residential rehabilitation was reportedly approved from admission on but there was no reported specific evidence in the records for review to support that he still required only 24-hour residential treatment from the date in question until discharge. There were no reports of life threatening or severe withdrawal symptoms or acute medical instability that would have required 24-hour treatment and no reports of dangerous behavior or harm to self or others. There were no reports of severe psychiatric or behavioral symptoms requiring 24-hour treatment and no reports of suicidal or homicidal thoughts or behavior, psychotic symptoms, self-injurious or aggressive behavior, or inability to adequately care for his basic needs then. 

According to Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR), people are appropriate for residential treatment if they have co-occurring psychiatric or medical conditions or are using substances in a way that put them in harm. In this case there was no specific evidence in the medical records stating that his psychiatric conditions or substance use issues were still severe enough to warrant that he could not be stepped down to a less restrictive level of care then or only required inpatient substance residential treatment then. Although it states that a patient is more of a candidate for inpatient treatment if unable to remain abstinent in an outpatient setting, this patient was not stepped down to a less restrictive structured and supervised multimodal partial hospital program treatment as of the date in question. If he were to relapse again after that, then he would meet criteria for a more extensive inpatient substance residential treatment stay then. It was reported that he obtained employment and was also attending 3 groups per week during the denial period. The medical records reported that he made progress, and there was not enough specific evidence to support that he still only required 24-hour residential treatment still. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be upheld. The health care plan did act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. 

The medical necessity for residential rehabilitation services is not substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Depression.

Treatment: repetitive TMS-Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation.

The health plan denied repetitive TMS-Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation.

The health plan determination is Overturned. 

The patient has a history of major depressive disorder, recurrent and severe without psychotic features. The Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) scale score up to 18 reflects severe symptoms of depression including suicidal ideation. The patient has a documented history of multiple medication treatments for depression including treatment with medication including Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs) (Zoloft, Lexapro), Serotonin and Norepinephrine Reuptake Inhibitors (SNRIs) (Effexor), and Norepinephrine and Dopamine Reuptake Inhibitor (NDRI) (Wellbutrin), as well as augmentation with Abilify, Vraylar, and supplemental use of Deplin and vitamin D. Due to adverse effects or lack of efficacy, the patient continued to experience severe symptoms of depression and functional impairments in the context of comorbid anxiety disorder with generalized symptoms, panic attacks, and social anxiety. Additionally, the patient has had treatment with an evidence-based psychotherapy currently combined with antidepressant medication with Lamictal, Lithium, propranolol, and Seroquel together with supportive measures. The patient was referred and recommended for repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) therapy, together with continued medication treatment and psychotherapy as indicated, and is the subject of this review.

In this case scenario, the health plan should cover the proposed treatment, Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) with treatment sessions per protocol and in keeping with the current scientific literature and standards of care. The requested treatment with Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) is reasonable, in the best interest of the patient, and is recommended and to be provided with sound medical judgment in keeping with the scientific literature and standard of care for the conditions under treatment in this case.

TMS therapy as a primary or adjunctive therapy for treatment of depression has generally been evaluated in patients who have treatment refractory depression, as defined by one or more, antidepressant medication treatment failures with or without augmentation. TMS therapy for depressive disorder has been established by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as a safe treatment; and, the data, as reflected in peer reviewed medical literature, supports this assertion including more recent studies involving adolescents, reflected in the referenced scientific literature.

Specifically, when treatments with two or more antidepressant medications with or without augmentation, or with electroconvulsive therapy, and/or psychotherapy, especially cognitive behavioral therapy, have failed to produce a response or remission, then TMS is an appropriate consideration. This assertion is noted in the American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorder, referenced below. Moreover, the scientific literature has increasingly supported the use of TMS therapy in adolescents, as well as adults, with treatment refractory depression, as in this case.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Inpatient Rehabilitation Admission with 24 Hours a Day Nursing Support
The Insurer denied: Inpatient Rehabilitation Admission with 24 Hours a Day Nursing Support
The Denial is: Upheld

The case involves an adult male who self-referred, presenting to the emergency department and was admitted for inpatient rehabilitation and substance use disorder treatment. The patient has longstanding substance use disorders with alcohol, stimulant (cocaine), hallucinogen (PCP), and nicotine class substances with prior treatments that failed to result in sustained abstinence or a successful recovery process. He self-referred due to difficulty with his social environment and coping problems mostly related to the substance use disorders in the context of a history of schizoaffective disorder with no current treatment and severe psychosocial stressors with homelessness and unemployment. The patient has a history of psychiatric disorder with a diagnosis of schizophrenia and depression (schizoaffective disorder); he has no history of psychiatric hospitalization and denied suicidal behavior. The patient's assessments revealed a positive drug screen consistent with history. He had chronic conditions including obesity and osteoarthritis. There were no significant withdrawal symptoms or post-acute withdrawal symptoms though he displayed anxiety and insomnia. He was noted to be malnourished and obese. Psychiatric evaluation was provided and affirmed that the patient had no acute symptoms of co-occurring mood or psychotic disorder. The patient engaged in substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment. He was noted to be engaged in the therapeutic activities, social with peers, and participating in recovery groups. Throughout the patient's inpatient stay, the patient remained stable with mental status and had engaged with the treatment regimen, as noted. He received intensive rehabilitation services, monitoring, and structure provided within the inpatient treatment program including 24-hour nursing monitoring. The patient was discharged with plans for clinically appropriate aftercare of his substance use disorders with referral for continued treatment. He had declined medication assisted treatment. 

The requested inpatient substance-related rehabilitation treatment was not medically necessary for this patient.

The patient presented with substance use disorders, diagnosed with alcohol, phencyclidine, nicotine, and stimulant/cocaine use disorders. He received inpatient level rehabilitation treatment. He readily engaged in treatment and had no biomedical or psychiatric treatment issues that warranted inpatient level care. During the time interval under review, the patient was noted to be in no apparent distress other than anxiety and insomnia with reasonable functioning and active participation in treatment including positive interactions with staff and peers. Throughout the patient's inpatient stay, there were no complicating treatment issues or biomedical or co-occurring psychiatric issues that would have warranted inpatient level of care or structure or 24-hour nursing monitoring, as the health plan asserts. The application of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 criteria did indicate that the patient was clinically appropriate for treatment with lower-level care in a less restrictive treatment setting as asserted in the denial determination. Thus, medical necessity is not met in this case scenario, consistent with the American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) criteria, the scientific literature and published guidelines, and with the required application of New York State Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 criteria.

summary:
Diagnosis: Depression

Treatment: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS)

The insurer denied coverage for Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS)

The denial is overturned

This adult female reportedly had severe depressive symptoms including depressed mood, suicidal ideation, anhedonia, lack of motivation, decreased energy, feelings of hopelessness, concentration problems, and had significant distress and impairment in functioning. She also reportedly was the victim of physical abuse. She reported stressors including problems with infertility and marital difficulties. She reportedly had a Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) of 18 which is moderate severe depression and also a Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7 (GAD-7) score of 18 which is considered severe anxiety. She reportedly was unemployed and her husband was working 2 jobs which also added more stress maritally. She reportedly had multiple antidepressant trials with multiple different classes. She also reportedly had individual and marital therapy. The request by her provider was for transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy (TMS).

The medical records provided for review did provide enough specific evidence to support that transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy (TMS) was considered medically necessary treatment for her current severe major depressive episode and that she did have treatment resistant depression. She met the plan criteria of taking at least 2 antidepressant medications from at least 2 different classes and also had evidenced based treatment in the form of psychotherapy as well. She reportedly had weekly individual and marital therapy. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved Neurostar Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Therapy for the treatment of depression in October 2008 in patients 18 years old and older and transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy was cleared by the FDA in 10/08 and indicated for the treatment of major depressive disorder in patients who failed or who did not have satisfactory improvement from 1 past antidepressant medication at or above minimal effective dose and duration in the current episode. 

Transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy (TMS) is considered to be more beneficial than other standard treatments for this patient. The medical records provided enough evidence to support the need and medical necessity for transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy (TMS). As a result, the recommendation is to reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy (TMS) for this patient.

Diagnosis: Substance Abuse.
Treatment: Inpatient admission.
The Insurer denied: Inpatient admission.
The Denial is: Overturned.

The patient is an adult male. He was admitted to inpatient level substance use disorder rehabilitation services with admission 4 months ago. His presentation for substance-related treatment was prompted by a decline in functioning and in the context of escalating use of cocaine together with discovery of active syphilis upon medical screening. His presentation was complicated by prolonged and complicated grief due to the recent death of both parents with cancer, and with severe psychosocial stressors including homelessness and unemployment. The patient had no history of prior substance-related treatment. There was no history co-occurring psychiatric disorder or suicidal behavior. The patient had no acute medical issues other than the infection with syphilis. Laboratory assessments were normal or unremarkable other than a positive rapid plasma reagin (RPR) titer and with a positive drug screen consistent with history. 

The inpatient admission was medically necessary in this case. 

The inpatient rehabilitation services were medically necessary in order to address issues related to the complication of an acute infection with syphilis requiring treatment and monitoring, as well as the high-risk use of cocaine with risk for relapse in a treatment-naïve patient with severe psychosocial stressors including homelessness and prolonged and complicated grief. The medically necessary treatment was provided with focus on a relapse prevention plan and additional work on developing coping skills in a case that poses high risk for relapse; in order to address the comorbid psychiatric disorders with psychosocial interventions; in order to address the patient's lack of awareness of the seriousness of his illness with psycho-education and evidence-based psychosocial interventions; in order to address the social environment including development of a safe and clinically appropriate discharge plan and disposition to residential care; and in order to work on coping skills that will be necessary in building an effective sober support system and continued recovery efforts with community providers while maintaining his abstinence with peer-supported recovery groups, and while providing appropriate treatment for syphilis with monitoring and appropriate public health provisions. None of this therapeutic work could have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care in view of the multiple complicating factors in this case, the high risk for relapse, the treatment history with high-risk use of cocaine despite access to treatment, and the lack of a reasonable recovery environment 
that includes high risk behaviors including use of large quantities of cocaine, and the patient's 
initial ambivalence toward treatment or lack of commitment to a recovery process. This answer is consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice and American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria and scientific literature and published practice guidelines.

summary:
Diagnosis: Substance Abuse
Treatment: Inpatient Rehabilitation Admission
The Insurer denied: Inpatient Rehabilitation Admission
The Denial is: Upheld

The patient is an adult male. He self-referred for inpatient rehabilitation and substance use disorder treatment. The patient has longstanding substance use disorders with alcohol and stimulant (cocaine) class substances with prior treatments which failed to result in sustained abstinence or a successful recovery process. The patient has no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens. He self-referred due to difficulty with the social environment and coping problems mostly related to the substance use disorders in the context of a mood disorder and severe psychosocial stressors with homelessness and unemployment. His history of substance use included use of large quantities of alcohol with up to 10 beers per day and 1-2 grams of cocaine on a daily continuous basis with intranasal administration. He identified psychosocial stressors and consequences of the substance use as a major concern including problems related to homelessness. The patient has a history of psychiatric disorder with a diagnosis of an unspecified mood disorder and past diagnoses of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. He has history of psychiatric hospitalization but denied suicidal behavior. The patient was medically screened with admission for rehabilitation treatment including laboratory assessment and physical examination. The patient engaged in substance use disorder rehabilitation treatment. He was noted to be engaged in therapeutic activities, social with peers, and participating in recovery groups. Throughout his brief inpatient stay, the patient remained stable with mental status and had engaged with the treatment regimen, as noted. He received intensive rehabilitation services, monitoring, and structure provided within the inpatient treatment program including 24-hour nursing monitoring. The patient was discharged with plans for clinically appropriate aftercare of his substance use disorders with referral and transfer to residential level treatment and recommendation for involvement in 12-step recovery groups with obtainment of a sponsor. He declined medication assisted treatment.

The requested Inpatient Rehabilitation Admission was not medically necessary for this patient.

The patient presented with substance use disorders, diagnosed with alcohol and stimulant/cocaine use disorders. He received inpatient level rehabilitation treatment. He readily engaged in treatment and had no biomedical or psychiatric treatment issues that warranted inpatient level care. During the time interval under review, the patient was noted to be in no apparent distress other than anxiety and insomnia with reasonable functioning and active participation in treatment including positive interactions with staff and peers. Throughout his inpatient stay, there were no complicating treatment issues or biomedical or co-occurring psychiatric issues that would have warranted inpatient level of care or structure or 24-hour nursing monitoring, as the health plan asserts. The application of NY State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) 3.0 Criteria (referenced below) did indicate that the patient was clinically appropriate for treatment with lower-level care in a less restrictive treatment setting. Thus, medical necessity for the inpatient substance use rehabilitation treatment is not met in this case scenario, consistent with ASAM (American Society of Addiction Medicine) Criteria, the scientific literature and published guidelines, referenced below, and with the required application of New York State OASAS (New York Office of Addiction Services and Supports) LOCADTR (Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral) 3.0 Criteria.

summary:
Diagnosis: depression.
Treatment: Mental Health Residential Stay.
The insurer denied Mental Health Residential Stay.
The health plan's determination is overturned.

The case involves an adult male who was admitted to residential level services with moderately severe symptoms of depression and generalized and social anxiety disorders with history of gambling addiction, childhood obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and maladaptive coping skills associated with a personality disorder including obsessive-compulsive, paranoid, narcissistic, and dependent traits. He presented with an inability to function and severe psychosocial stressors, as well as self-harm, self-destructive behavior including abuse of cannabis and alcohol, and bouts of dysregulated mood.

The Mental Health Residential Stay was medically necessary for this patient.

The patient's presentation and clinical features included major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders in the context of personality with narcissistic and paranoid and grandiose features and high risk for suicide or continued self-destructive behaviors, a decline in functioning and social isolation with impaired functioning. The patient exhibited severe symptoms of anxiety and depression with deterioration in functioning and suicidal risk, and other symptoms related to impaired relationship and social functioning and dysregulated emotions
During the time interval under review, the patient remained acutely ill with residual symptoms of mood disturbance and anxiety symptoms, and continued risk for relapse or suicide or self-harming behavior. The patient's severity of symptoms and need for safety monitoring while receiving active treatment did warrant the continued structure of a residential setting with monitoring in a safe environment.
Thus, it was medically necessary and clinically appropriate for this patient to remain in a residential setting with monitoring in view of the presenting clinical features and residual symptoms of a severe and recurrent mood disorder with maladaptive personality traits, and continued disturbance of mood, affect and volition in the context of impaired functioning requiring safety monitoring and staff direction, structure, and supervision. Additionally, the residential stay during the time interval under review was medically necessary and clinically appropriate in terms of the intensity of services, duration of treatment and level of structure required in this case scenario with ongoing treatment planning to determine a clinically appropriate disposition and discharge plan in concert with the patient and the patient's family with whom he lived.

summary:
Diagnosis: Suicidal Ideation
Treatment: Inpatient Mental Health Treatment with 24 Hours a Day Nursing Support
The insurer denied inpatient mental health treatment with 24 Hours a day nursing support.
The denial is overturned.

The case involves an adult female referred for inpatient level treatment with major depressive disorder and a suicide attempt, borderline personality disorder, and co-occurring cannabis use disorder. She presented with worsening symptoms of depression with suicidal ideation after a suicide attempt. The patient was noted to have history of the mood disorder best characterized as major depressive disorder in the context of borderline personality disorder and substance use disorder-as noted. Mental status examination on admission included casual dress and poor eye contact and cooperative but guarded stance. Mood was depressed with a full range of affect with anxiety with sleep disturbance and low energy. Thought processing was linear with no evidence of psychosis, mania, thought disorder, or severe cognitive impairment. The patient had suicidal ideation with limits of insight and judgment and poor impulse control related to the addiction and the borderline traits. She displayed hopelessness, low interest, concentration difficulties, and low self-worth. The patient was assessed with a comprehensive psychiatric and psychosocial evaluation. Medications were continued with adjustments to include Trintellix, switch from Trileptal to Lamictal with titration, mirtazapine, melatonin, and trazodone. The patient had the opportunity to participate in group, individual, educational and milieu activities including educational sessions aimed at assisting the patient with improved coping skills, as well as the opportunity for family focused sessions to address family dynamics and work toward an appropriate step down. The patient had the availability of comfort medication and was prescribed supplements including N-acetylcysteine (NAC) and vitamins, as well as nicotine replacement therapy to address nicotine dependence. Psychotherapeutic interventions including use of dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT) and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) techniques, as well as dynamic therapy focusing on borderline personality traits. The patient gained insight modestly with continued suicidal ideation and persistent symptoms of depression. Sleep improved and the patient was participating in groups and other milieu activities. The treatment team and case manager were pursuing an appropriate step down with partial hospital program (PHP) level services. On the last day before discharge, the patient denied suicidal ideation and was noted to be more social with brighter affect. A safety plan was developed with plans for return home with family and participation in an intensive outpatient program (IOP) until a partial hospital program (PHP) bed was available. Thus, she was discharged with clinically appropriate aftercare including referral to her community providers of services for medication management and continued therapy, as well as recommendations to address the co-occurring substance-related problems with cannabis and a safety plan.

The requested health service was medically necessary.

The patient's severity of symptoms and risk of suicidal behavior necessitated the continued acute inpatient care to develop a safety plan and assess the recent titration of antidepressant medications. The presenting and continuing symptoms of depressive disorder and comorbid borderline personality disorder and substance related disorder were not amenable to treatment at a lower level of care during the time interval under review, in view of the persistent and ongoing suicidal risk and maladaptive coping in association with borderline personality traits. The patient's progress notes clearly indicate that the patient displayed continued risk that required inpatient level structure and safety monitoring for the duration of inpatient treatment.

The patient is an adult male who was admitted to inpatient rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment of stimulant (methamphetamine) and cannabis (marijuana) use disorders. The patient had longstanding daily use of marijuana (five blunts), and a more recent history of past use of methamphetamine use with up to 2 grams daily, as well as tobacco dependence. He had a limited history of substance use disorder treatment episodes with lack of follow up treatment and no sustained abstinence or sobriety. The patient was medically cleared at the time of admission and his laboratory assessment was normal or unremarkable with a positive drug screen consistent with history. There was history of co-occurring psychiatric conditions described as schizophrenia or bipolar disorder and PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder). The patient denied suicidal behavior or psychiatric hospitalization. He was receiving mental health services with medication management with low-dose Seroquel and Celexa. The patient was homeless and unemployed with unspecified trauma history and no history of legal issues. Mental status examination revealed a cooperative male with clear speech and linear thought processing that was goal directed. There were no severe symptoms such as psychosis, perceptual disturbance, depression or mania, or cognitive impairment. He had sleep disturbance with insomnia. The inpatient level substance-related rehabilitation treatment included the opportunity to participate in groups, individual counseling, educational sessions, and recovery groups with peer support. From admission forward the patient easily engaged with rehabilitation treatment. He actively participated in individual, group, and educational sessions. He was prescribed vitamins with the availability of nicotine replacement therapy throughout his stay. He was also prescribed comfort medications and his usual medications as noted. summary:
Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder

Treatment: 36 units of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS)

The insurer denied coverage for 36 units of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS).

The denial is overturned.

This patient reportedly had a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder (recurrent, severe) without psychotic features, as well as Generalized Anxiety Disorder, and Obsessive Compulsive Disorder. It was reported that the patient had severe depression including depressed mood, passive suicidal ideation, feelings of emptiness and exhaustion, little interest and pleasure. The patient reportedly had a Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ)-9 score of 17 which is moderate to severe depression. The patient also reportedly had Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD)-7 score of 17 which is severe and a Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Score (YBOCS) of 25 which also is severe. The patient reportedly also had intrusive thoughts and fears of having schizophrenia, social anxiety, excessive worrying, and physical symptoms of anxiety. The patient reportedly had past victimization issues. The patient reportedly had a past trial of transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy (TMS) which ended. The patient reportedly was taking Luvox 150 milligrams (mg) per day, Abilify 5 mg per day, Adderall 40 mg per day, and Ativan 0.5 mg per day. It was reported that the patient took Fluoxetine 60 mg per day and Wellbutrin 300 mg per day. The patient reportedly also had outpatient psychotherapy. 
 
The insurer denied coverage for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) for 36 sessions (units). They stated that the patient had past transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) for 36 sessions which was completed and stated that according to the InterQual Behavioral health Services 2024 Release for TMS treatment it requires 6 months elapsed between treatments for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). 
  
This reviewer disagrees with the decision to deny coverage for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) for 36 sessions (units) as the medical records provided enough evidence to support that this treatment was considered medically necessary treatment. This patient had reports of severe depressive symptoms including depressed mood, passive suicidal ideation, feelings of emptiness and exhaustion, little interest and pleasure, and he reportedly had a PHQ-9 score of 17 which is considered moderate to severe depression. 

This patient appeared to be a good candidate for the additional TMS sessions, as they had reports of severe depression 5 months after a previous trial of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) treatment. The InterQual Behavioral Health Services 2024 Release for TMS treatment states that one needs a 6-month period to elapse prior to treatment again for 36 sessions.  However, this patient had severe depression with suicidal ideation and needed this treatment or they would be at higher risk for worsened symptoms and possible hospitalization. The time between treatments was less than 4 weeks prior to the insurer's 6 month cut off, but because there is some medical literature supporting the treatment of additional TMS treatment even up to 72 sessions and also since the patient had severe depression including suicidal ideation, this TMS treatment was considered medically necessary and appropriate. 

As a result, the recommendation is to reverse the previous decision and approve coverage for another trial of transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy (TMS) services for 36 sessions. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be reversed. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. 

The medical necessity for 36 units of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) is substantiated.

The patient is a teenage female with a diagnosis of disordered eating behaviors. The issue under review is the inpatient mental health treatment. The patient presented to the emergency department due to food refusal, with a 20-pound weight loss, and decreased oral intake. The patient was told to come to the emergency department for further evaluation from her psychiatrist. Her pertinent past medical history (PMH) and/or past surgical history (PSH) includes anorexia and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). Pertinent medications include Prozac and Olanzapine. Upon arrival, the patient had vital signs measured, pertinent labs, urine studies collected, and serial electrocardiograms (EKGs). The patient was now 53.84 kilograms. The parents of the patient reported that patient had been nonadherent with her Prozac and Olanzapine, as she tries to hide pills in her braces and refuses them. Per the chart note, the patient was not eating properly because she felt that her face and stomach were bloated. The patient was admitted to the Telemetry Unit with a diagnosis of anorexia and protein calorie malnutrition. The inpatient plan of care included vital signs, pertinent labs, daily weights, respiratory viral panel, Registered Dietitian Consult, Social Work Consult, Case Management Consult, and Behavioral Health/ Pediatric Adolescent Consult. Treatment included Prozac/ Zyprexa/ Phos-Nak/ and intravenous (IV) Dextrose 5% (percent) Sodium Chloride 0.9% at 60 milliliters per hour. summary:

Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) is medically necessary for this patient.
Applied Behavioral Analysis (ABA) therapy is a form of behavioral therapy that uses principles of learning and behavior to increase positive behaviors and reduce negative or unwanted behaviors. ABA therapy has been scientifically demonstrated to improve the behaviors and learning abilities of people with autism. ABA therapy is commonly prescribed for children with autism. This patient has autism. Therefore, it is reasonable to assume that she may benefit from ABA therapy, and indeed she has shown improvement since starting the therapy.

In this case, the treatment plan does include specific and clearly-defined goals regarding communication, social engagement, and behavior regulation that are quantifiable and in alignment with ABA principles.
The patient's goals are aimed at improving deficits in social communication and repetitive and restricted behaviors, all of which are core deficits of autism. The treatment plan targets behaviors at home, in school, and in community settings. The patient displays problems with communication, social interaction, and behavioral control that are constantly present and challenging. The treatment plan provides for behavioral services to be provided by technicians under the direct supervision of a BCBA (Board Certified Behavioral Analyst). These trained individuals can provide ABA therapy in ways and to an extent that untrained people cannot.

summary:
Diagnosis: Major depressive disorder
Treatment: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS)  Units
The Insurer denied: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS)  Units
The Denial is: Overturned

The patient is an adult male with a diagnosis of recurrent and moderately severe major depressive disorder without psychotic features and comorbid ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder)-inattentive type and generalized anxiety disorder. The patient has a history of depressive disorder with persistent symptoms of depression despite past treatments with SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors), Lexapro-current and Prozac, Cymbalta (duloxetine), and Wellbutrin, as well as augmentation with buspirone and treatment with Vyvanse targeting symptoms of ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder). Submitted case notes indicate that the patient has a history of prior treatment with rTMS (repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation) and a positive response. Mood is anxious and depressed with a PHQ (patient health questionnaire)-9 scale score of 12 and a GAD (general anxiety disorder) 7 scale score of 16 in the moderately severe and severe range, respectively. 

The requested health service with TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy is medically necessary in this case.

Clinically appropriate approaches have been tried and failed for treatment of depressive disorder in this case, including trials and failure using antidepressants with a disparate mechanism of action or combination therapy, as well as augmentation with buspirone and a stimulant, as well as psychotherapy that have established that the patient is treatment refractory. Thus, alternative, standard therapeutic options and treatment as usual would not be likely to be as effective as augmentation with TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) Therapy in the treatment of the patient's Major Depressive Disorder. Thus, in this case, the proposed repetitive TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy is likely to be more beneficial for the enrollee than other available standard therapy, and the requested TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy is considered medically necessary in keeping with the New York State instruction for this review. Of note, repetitive TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy as a primary or adjunctive therapy for treatment of depression has generally been evaluated in patients who have treatment refractory depression, as defined by one or more, antidepressant medication treatment failures with or without augmentation. TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy for depressive disorder has been established by the FDA (United States Food and Drug Administration) as a safe treatment, and the data, as reflected in peer reviewed medical literature, supports this assertion. Specifically, when treatments with antidepressant medication with or without augmentation, electroconvulsive therapy, and/or psychotherapy, especially cognitive behavioral therapy, have failed, then TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) may be an appropriate consideration. This assertion is also noted in the American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the assessment and treatment of major depressive disorder, referenced below. The documentation in this case does meet those guidelines regarding the use of TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) for augmentation therapy in this case scenario. Specifically, the patient has had a trial and treatment failure with antidepressants with a disparate mechanism of action or combination treatment with two or more antidepressants, as indicated in the clinical summary. The scientific literature notes that individual differences with response to various antidepressant medications is to be expected and supports the assertion that the patient's depressive disorder is treatment resistant, supporting the use of TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) therapy.

summary:

This case involves a female for review of denial of coverage for a continued stay at a psychiatric residential treatment center (RTC). The Medical Necessity Letter indicated that the patient receives individual therapy 2x (times)/week, family therapy weekly and 5 hours of group therapy with licensed clinicians since enrollment. When not in therapy, her treatment is augmented by weekly therapeutic assignments and interventions. She also participates in 24/7 therapeutic milieu. The following are her diagnoses: F34.1 (persistent depressive disorder), F41.1 (generalized anxiety disorder), F12.20 (cannabis use disorder), F89 (unspecified neurodevelopmental disorder), and Z62.820 (parent-child relational problem). Her medications since 01/26/2025 are Zoloft 150 milligrams (mg) once daily, Lamictal 100mg twice daily, and Strattera 40mg once daily. She had outpatient treatment and wilderness treatment program trials with some success but demonstrated the need for long term therapeutic support. She was enrolled to psychiatric RTC due to a significant history of ongoing debilitation depression, anxiety and mood dysregulation, including significant substance use, disordered eating patterns, and harmful peer relationships. Upon presentation, she was superficially cooperative but resistant to treatment. The patient has become increasingly engaged, accountable, and receptive to the therapeutic process in recent weeks. She is avoidant of therapy assignments but attempts to apply learned lessons with mixed success. She has had several successful weekend visits by her parents and will have her first home visit scheduled in the coming weeks. Despite progress, she remains highly susceptible to significant regression outside of a structured residential setting. She personally expressed acknowledgement of the lack of internalization/application of these new skills and commented several times that if she were to return home at this point "I would definitely be using drugs again and end up right back here." She also is not ready to address in depth the reported sexual assaults that were identified superficially. The patient will likely continue making progress but a return to home setting would be highly contraindicated as it will most certainly result in a regression to her previous level of functioning. 

The medical records submitted for review do not support the continued psychiatric RTC since there were no documented serious emotional disturbances after the patient's home visit. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be upheld. The health care plan did act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. The medical necessity for a continued stay at a psychiatric residential treatment center to discharge is not substantiated.

summary:
Diagnosis: Bipolar I Disorder, Cannabis use Disorder, Moderate.
Treatment: Inpatient Psychiatric Facility (IPF).
The insurer denied the Inpatient Psychiatric Facility (IPF).
The health plan's determination is overturned. 

This is a female patient who was admitted for inpatient psychiatric treatment due to severe symptoms of bipolar mood disorder, characterized by a manic phase with mixed features. Her clinical history includes self-harm and intermittent suicidal ideation, occurring in the context of mood cycling.

The patient presented with substance use concerns, including daily use of marijuana and alcohol consumption characterized by a binge pattern. Additionally, the patient reported intermittent use of other substances of abuse, including hallucinogens (such as mushrooms) and Xanax. The patient was also nicotine-dependent, with vaping as the primary method of use. Prior to admission for acute inpatient mental health treatment, the patient underwent a medical screening. As part of the treatment plan, vitamin supplementation and nicotine replacement therapy were provided, along with withdrawal management interventions.

The Inpatient Psychiatric Facility (IPF) medically necessary.

In this case scenario, the patient's treatment could not have been safely or effectively provided at a lower level of care. The severity of the patient's symptoms and the need for safety monitoring while receiving active treatment justified the continued structure of an acute inpatient setting with 24-hour monitoring in a secure environment until discharge. Furthermore, discharge planning, which included psychoeducation, the development of a safety plan, and arrangements for continued Intensive Outpatient Program (IOP) level treatment in the community, represented critical treatment components that necessitated the continuation of inpatient care.

The admission and subsequent inpatient services were provided to deliver intensive treatment for a patient at high risk of relapse or recidivism, exhibiting severe symptoms of bipolar disorder characterized by active mood cycling, including mixed features associated with poor insight and impaired impulse control. The patient was actively using substances of abuse, including cannabis, alcohol, and other substances, which posed significant safety concerns in the context of suicidal risk and a history of self-harm. Consequently, inpatient-level care was deemed necessary to ensure safe and clinically appropriate treatment, including close monitoring, while addressing multiple severe psychosocial stressors and other factors that could lead to medication non-adherence or a relapse into substance abuse.

Additionally, the patient demonstrated safety concerns due to erratic behavior, placing herself at risk of harm, and remained at high risk for relapse during the period under review. This warranted intensive evidence-based interventions, motivational and family therapy sessions, and continuous safety monitoring. Therefore, the Inpatient Psychiatric Facility (IPF) medically necessary.

The patient is an adult female. She was brought by emergency services with screening and psychiatric consultation. She was admitted for inpatient level treatment with mood, anxiety, and trauma-related problems and co-occurring substance-related disorders, as well as attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). She presented with worsening symptoms of depression and anxiety with suicidal risk and impaired functioning compounded by a breakup with her boyfriend, who kicked her out of his apartment and called emergency medical 
services. Her mood had recently worsened with increased anxiety, depression, and sleep disturbance together with a presentation that included positive drug screen for benzodiazepines and tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). From day #3 to day #9, the patient remained dysphoric and depressed with anxious distress and suicidal risk with flat affect, hopelessness, and impaired judgment and functioning with activities of daily living. From day #7 to day #10, the patient was improving with continued hopelessness and safety concerns, as well as concern for an appropriate discharge plan to address homelessness and lack of supports and resources. From day #10 forward she was noted to be calm and cooperative with improving mood and diminished anxiety and better sleep. Insight was improved. Case management was working to develop a safe and appropriate discharge plan and disposition. She was discharged on day #12 with clinically appropriate aftercare including referral to community providers of 
services for medication management, outpatient program treatment, and a sober living environment for women with supports and assistance from social services.

The requested health service was medically necessary in this case.

The continued inpatient services served to provide intensive treatment in a patient with high-risk for suicide noted in the clinical summary and due to co-occurring disorders and with severe symptoms of anxiety and depression including severe psychosocial stressors, poor impulse control, and trauma and stressor related disorders. Thus, the continued acute inpatient level care was necessary to provide a safe and clinically appropriate treatment setting and to address the severe psychosocial stressors that had precipitated the patient's worsening symptoms of the co-occurring psychiatric disorders. The patient's treatment could not have been safely or effectively provided with lower-level care during the time interval under review in this case scenario. The patient's presentation and clinical features included a recurrent major depressive episode in the context of severe symptoms of anxiety and trauma/stressor related symptoms. During the time interval under review, the patient remained acutely ill with residual symptoms of mood disturbance and anxiety symptoms, and continued risk for relapse due to a lack of insight and/or poor impulse control. The patient's severity of symptoms and need for safety monitoring while receiving active treatment did warrant the admission and the continued structure of an acute inpatient setting and 24-hour monitoring in a safe environment through discharge, at which time the patient was noted to display improved mood, diminished anxiety, and a more hopeful outlook despite continued symptoms, as noted in the clinical summary. A discharge planning meeting had occurred with the development of a safety plan and plans for continued treatment with step down to appropriate care in the community, as well as additional management of the severe psychosocial stressors and a safety plan. Therefore, the requested health service was medically necessary in this case.

Moreover, the scientific literature indicates that a course of treatment with TMS therapy is reasonable in cases of treatment resistant depression as defined in the scientific literature.

summary:
Diagnosis: Alcohol detoxification.
Treatment: Inpatient substance use detoxification, 5 days. 
The insurer denied coverage for inpatient substance use detoxification, 5 days. 
The denial is upheld.

This case involves a patient with a subject of review for the medical necessity of the inpatient substance use detoxification, 5 days.

The patient with a past medical history including alcohol use disorder (AUD), cannabis and nicotine dependence, hyperlipidemia (HLD), and insomnia presented for care following a relapse involving alcohol consumption. Prior to admission, they underwent detoxification, during which they were treated with Librium for alcohol withdrawal. They reported consuming two nips and two 24-ounce beers to the point of blacking out, along with smoking one joint of marijuana. Laboratory results were positive for tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and benzodiazepines, with a blood alcohol level (BAL) of 0.039. Their Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA-Ar) score was 4. The Fagerström Test for Nicotine Dependence scored 5 (medium dependence).

The patient denied any suicidal or homicidal thoughts, mental health concerns, legal issues, or domestic violence. They noted that they had previously attended detox three times and that it was the only form of treatment they had. They were admitted for alcohol detoxification followed by rehabilitation. Their treatment included Librium 10 milligrams (mg) and amoxicillin 500 mg for a dental abscess. Both were well tolerated. During their stay, they completed the Librium tapering protocol and remained medically stable with no signs of withdrawal. They were observed to be socializing positively with peers. The patient successfully completed detox and expressed an intent to return for rehabilitation. Although Narcan training and a kit were offered, they declined, stating they had already completed the training. They were discharged with instructions to follow up with their primary care provider (PCP).

In this case, the patient with a past medical history including alcohol use disorder (AUD), cannabis and nicotine dependence, hyperlipidemia (HLD), and insomnia presented for care following a relapse involving alcohol consumption. 

After reviewing all the medical information presented, a denial overturn cannot be supported, since the patient was overall medically stable and did not demonstrate imminent risk factors, so they did not meet the requirements for treatment at an inpatient substance use detoxification facility. There was a strong motivation to recover and attain alcohol abstinence with strict adherence to their medications. The clinical records received did not show attempts to harm themselves or others, and there were no apparent serious mental status abnormalities. They can understand follow-up treatment plans. Furthermore, there were no additional medical needs or severe withdrawal symptoms requiring 24-hour care. A less intensive level of care could have been used to deliver the denied service.

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be upheld. The health care plan acted reasonably, with sound medical judgment, and in the best interest of the patient. The medical necessity for inpatient substance use detoxification, 5 days is not substantiated.

The patient engaged in substance-related rehabilitation treatment. He was noted to be engaged in therapeutic activities, social with peers, and participating in recovery groups. Throughout his inpatient stay, the patient remained stable with mental status and had engaged with the treatment regimen, as noted. He received intensive rehabilitation services, monitoring, and structure provided within the inpatient treatment program including 24-hour nursing monitoring. Diagnosis: Substance Use Disorder.
Treatment: Inpatient Substance Use Rehabilitation (28 days).
The insurer denied Inpatient Substance Use Rehabilitation (28 days).
The determination is upheld.

The patient is an adult male, who received detoxification treatment and was admitted to inpatient rehabilitation substance use disorder treatment of stimulant (cocaine), alcohol, and nicotine use disorders. The patient was using 4 grams of cocaine with intranasal administration and 1 gram of crack cocaine together with approximately four pints of liquor with daily use. The patient was also tobacco dependent. He had a longstanding history of substance use disorder beginning with use of crack cocaine with more recent use of alcohol and cocaine as indicated. He has received multiple past substance use disorder treatment episodes including four or more rehabilitation treatment episodes, as well as chronic conditions including obesity with dyslipidemia, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with asthma, and lower back pain with associated treatments. There was no history of withdrawal seizures, delirium tremens, or blackouts.
Mental status examination revealed a cooperative male with clear speech and linear thought processing that was goal directed. Mood was anxious with congruent affect. The patient's thought content included no morbid thoughts. Insight was limited with impaired judgment due to the addictions. He had sleep disturbance with insomnia.
The inpatient level substance-related rehabilitation treatment included the opportunity to participate in groups, individual counseling, educational sessions, and recovery groups with peer support. From the time of admission forward the patient easily engaged in rehabilitation treatment. He actively participated in individual, group, and educational sessions. He was prescribed vitamins with the availability of nicotine replacement therapy throughout his stay, as well as comfort medications. He was prescribed trazodone for insomnia along with mirtazapine, and home medications including gemfibrozil, Symbicort, and albuterol inhaler.
Discharge planning occurred that included recommendation for continued aftercare with consideration of transition to extended residential and sober living upon completion of the program. The patient was cooperative and engaged throughout his inpatient stay with reasonable motivation and participation in therapeutic activities. There were no psychiatric or biomedical complications during his stay with discharge and step down. Inpatient substance Use Rehabilitation (28 days) is under review.
The requested health service/treatment of Inpatient substance Use Rehabilitation (28 days) was not medically necessary for this patient.
The inpatient substance use disorder rehabilitation services in this case scenario were amenable to treatment at a lower level of care, as noted above. The patient was motivated and was capable of effectively receiving substance use disorder treatment in a less restrictive treatment setting with clinically appropriate structure, monitoring, and sober support. The patient did not need the structure or 24-hour nursing monitoring of an inpatient setting to effectively participate in rehabilitation substance abuse treatment.
There were no biomedical or psychiatric complications, or severe psychiatric symptoms/disorders in this case that would have warranted the admission and the continued inpatient level services and treatment. Thus, the requested benefit of inpatient substance use disorder rehabilitation services was not medically necessary for this patient.
This answer is consistent with prevailing standards of professional practice, American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) Criteria, and the published guidelines and the scientific literature, referenced below, as well as the application of Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services (OASAS) Level of Care for Alcohol and Drug Treatment Referral (LOCADTR) 3.0 Criteria, referenced below.

summary:
Diagnosis: Alcohol withdrawal symptoms.
Treatment: Inpatient admission.
The insurer denied coverage for inpatient admission.
The denial is overturned.

This is an adult male admitted due to alcohol withdrawal symptoms. He reportedly had tremors, sweats, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, tingling, headache, anxiety, depressed mood, elevated blood pressure of 165/119,  elevated heart rate of 122, and Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA) score of 9. He also reportedly had alcohol hepatitis, elevated liver functions tests (LFT's) and bilirubin. He reportedly was drinking 25 drinks per day with a mixture of liquor and beer. He reportedly had 10-year history of alcohol use. He reportedly was drinking 40 straight days. He reportedly had a medical history significant for hypertension. He reportedly was given detoxification medication as he was on a CIWA protocol and given Librium and also received additional Ativan doses for detoxification. He reportedly was given intravenous (IV) fluids, folic acid and thiamine, and was on continuous cardiac monitoring. He was interested in alcohol rehabilitation treatment. 
 
The medical records provided enough specific evidence to support that he required this level of care then. The American Psychiatric Association (APA) Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Patients with Substance Use Disorders reports that failure to achieve abstinence or patients who relapse frequently, or failure to be cooperative with or benefit from outpatient detoxification, current abuse of other substances, very heavy use or tolerance putting one at high risk for complicated withdrawal are candidates for inpatient detoxification treatment. 

Also, the US Department of Health and Human Services-Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) Center for Substance Abuse Treatment reports that inpatient treatment is necessary if the ability to attend outpatient treatment daily is a problem, one is unable to follow up in outpatient treatment, if medical conditions complicate the treatment of withdrawal, if one has previous withdrawal seizures of delirium tremens, or if one does not have the capacity for informed consent. 

The Milliman Care Guidelines (MCG) Substance Related Disorder Psychoactive Substance Withdrawal, Common Complications, and Conditions criteria report that one meets criteria if one was withdrawal signs with high risk indicators. 

This patient had active alcohol withdrawal symptoms including tremors, sweats, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, tingling, headache, anxiety, depressed mood, elevated blood pressure of 165/119, elevated heart rate of 122, and CIWA of 9. His CIWA was elevated, and he required additional detoxification medication with Ativan in addition to Librium treatment for detoxification. He reportedly had medical issues as well related to alcohol use including alcohol hepatitis and elevated LFT's. He was at risk for even worsened alcohol withdrawal symptoms including severe withdrawal, complicated or life-threatening withdrawal such as delirium tremens due to his heavy alcohol use with active withdrawal symptoms. The risk of delirium tremens can occur 3-4 days after cessation of alcohol use so he required the entire time in this inpatient hospital setting for detoxification treatment. 

Based on the above, the insurer's denial must be reversed. The health care plan did not act reasonably and with sound medical judgment and in the best interest of the patient. The medical necessity for Hospital Admission is substantiated.
